Of the 700 recruited, 617 were included based on completeness of imaging and TBI data, and absence of incidental magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) findings (eFigure 1 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
Imaging markers of SVD were assessed on 3T MRI (Siemens; acquisition parameters in eAppendix of Supplement 1 [this file] ) according to the Standards for Reporting Vascular Changes on Neuroimaging (STRIVE) guidelines. Further details on SVD quantification and interrater reliability evaluation can be found in the eAppendix in Supplement 1 [this file] and previous publications. 
Composite scores for each cognitive domain were computed by averaging the -scores of relevant tasks in each domain as previously defined (eAppendix in Supplement 1 [this file] ). For the CES-D and PSQI, higher scores indicate greater depressive symptoms and sleep disturbances, respectively (eAppendix in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
Participants with TBI were defined as those experiencing at least 1 blow to the head resulting in LOC, with mild TBI (mTBI) defined where LOC was less than 30 minutes (eAppendix in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
Standard statistical techniques were used for descriptive analyses ( Table 1 [rid=zoi240828t1] ; eAppendix in Supplement 1 [this file] ). To compare the relative contribution of TBI and vascular risk factors to clinical deficits in the subset of participants with prior TBI, dominance analysis and relative weights analysis were conducted (eAppendix in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
All analyses were conducted in the full sample and repeated in a subgroup of individuals to compare mild TBI and non-TBI controls (eAppendix in Supplement 1 [this file] ), where applicable. 
Specifically, higher CVD risk was associated with greater WMH volume, lacunes, and PVS (in BG, but not CSO) (eTable 2 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
In adjusted analysis, CMB numbers were greater in individuals with prior TBI than in those without TBI, with a dose-response association observed with increasing number of TBI events (95% CI, 0.01-0.09) (eTable 3 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). Results were unchanged in sensitivity analyses adjusting for the additional covariate(s) of smoking alone (model 2), or smoking, APOE4, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, diabetes, alcohol, and CVD risk score (model 3) (eTable 3 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
In adjusted regression models, greater numbers of TBI events were associated with poorer sleep, gait disturbances, greater depression symptoms, and memory but not attentional deficits (eTable 4 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). Results were unchanged in sensitivity analysis adjusting for different sets of covariates (eTable 4 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
For CMB detection, future studies with greater CMB burden could benefit from automated methods (eAppendix in Supplement 1 [this file] ).

The complete list of codes utilized in this study can be found in Supplementary Table S1 [this file] . The distribution of time‐to‐event was illustrated in Supplementary Fig. S2 [this file] . 
The codes of covariates utilized in our study can be found in Supplementary Table S2 [this file] . 
The risk of incident dementia was significantly associated with decreased M10 and RA, increased L5 and advanced L5 onset time (Fig. 1 [rid=pcn13671-fig-0001] ; Supplementary Table S3 [this file] ). The results remained robust after additionally adjusting for sleep duration, sleep efficiency and moderate to vigorous physical activity (Supplementary Table S3 [this file] ) and in a series of sensitivity analysis by conducting COX regression analysis in complete data restricted to participants without any missing covariate data Supplementary Table S4 [this file] and S5 [this file], or by excluding events that occurred within the first year of follow‐up (Supplementary Table S6 [this file] ) or by censoring up to December 31, 2019 Supplementary Table S7 [this file]or by using competing risk regression Supplementary Table S8 [this file]. 
In the subsequent interaction analysis, CRAR parameters were reclassified into two groups according to their associations with incident dementia (Fig. 1 [rid=pcn13671-fig-0001] ; Supplementary Table S3 [this file] ): L5 (quartiles 1–3, quartile 4), M10 (<50 g/min, ≥50 g/min), RA (quartiles 2–4, quartile 1), and L5 onset time (intermediate to delayed, advanced), to facilitate the interpretation of interaction effects. Subgroup analyses revealed that the detrimental effect of lower M10 on incident dementia was more pronounced at younger ages, while the effect of advanced L5 onset time on incident dementia was higher in females (Supplementary Fig. S3 [this file] ). Through joint analysis and additive interaction analyses, the detrimental effects of higher L5, lower M10 and RA on incident dementia were exacerbated by ε4 carrier status (Table 2 [rid=pcn13671-tbl-0002] ; Supplementary Table S9 [this file] ). 
Furthermore, decreased IS and increased IV were associated with better performance in all cognitive domains (Supplementary Table S10 [this file] ). 
Both higher M10 and RA were significantly associated with larger volumes of cerebral white matter and greater global surface areas in both the left and right hemispheres (Fig. 3 [rid=pcn13671-fig-0003] , Supplementary Table S11 [this file] ). Furthermore. higher M10 was associated with a larger volume of cerebrospinal fluid (Supplementary Table S11 [this file] ). 
Among CRAR parameters, M10 and RA showed the primary significant relationships with regional brain structure (Fig. 4 [rid=pcn13671-fig-0004] , Supplementary Table S12 [this file] ). Higher RA was predominantly associated with higher FA and lower MD in the posterior and anterior thalamic radiation, superior and inferior longitudinal fasciculus, inferior fronto‐occipital fasciculus and cingulate gyrus (Fig. 3 [rid=pcn13671-fig-0003] , Supplementary Table S13 [this file] ). 
Regarding the regional brain structure, only subcortical structures and white matter microstructures exhibited mediating effects Fig. 4 [rid=pcn13671-fig-0004] , Supplementary Table S14 [this file].

A detailed flow chart with the exact number of participants included or excluded at each step is presented in Figure S 1 [this file] . 
Excluded participants were more likely to be male, have higher levels of education, be unpartnered, consume alcohol, have fewer documented medical conditions, and exhibit obesity during the age range of 50–65 years (Table S 1 [this file] ). 
BMI trend, BMI variations and average BMIs at 50–65 years of age were correlated with each other (Figure S 2 [this file] ). Additionally, the baseline characteristics of BMI indicators, categorized based on cognitive status after the age of 65 were shown in Table S 2 [this file] . 
According to the logistic regression model with restricted cubic spline analysis, we found a nonlinear association between the BMI trend in late-middle age and dementia in older age ( for no-linear test = 0.038, Fig. S 3 [this file] A) while for the BMI variation in late-middle age, this association was linear ( for no-linear test = 0.589, Fig. S 3 [this file] B). Conversely, a declining BMI trend continues to exhibit a significant association (RR = 1.2, 95% CI = 1–1.44, = 0.048, Table S 3 [this file] ), suggesting that while the risk of dementia may be influenced by complex non-linear patterns in BMI during late-middle age, a consistent decline in BMI remains consistently linked to an elevated risk of dementia in older age. 
Detailed participant characteristics are provided in Table S 4 [this file] . High PGS scores for general cognitive function were significantly associated with a reduced risk of dementia in older age (RR = 0.37, 95% CI = 0.25–0.53, < 0.001, Table S 5 [this file] ), indicating the PGS for general cognitive function's predictive value for subsequent dementia risk in older individuals. Adjusted for PGS and PC1-5, a decline in BMI with high variation was significantly linked to an increased dementia risk in older age (ARR = 2.02, 95% CI = 1.44–2.85, < 0.001, Figure S 4 [this file] ), implying an independent association, not influenced by participants' genetic predisposition to general cognitive function. 
Modified effects on education level was found in the association between BMI trajectories and dementia in older age ( for interaction < 0.001, Figure S 5 [this file] ). The results of sensitivity analyses were consistent with the main analyses (Table S 6 [this file] ).

To single out the impact of -ε4 and polygenic load separately, we excluded , Lactase Gene, human leukocyte antigen, and 2 inversion regions located on 8p23.1 and 17q21.31 ( 40 [rid=CIT0040] ) ( Supplementary Material [this file] ). Furthermore, samples were removed based on call rate (<0.99), heterozygosity, and relatedness and if the recorded sex phenotype was inconsistent with genetic sex ( Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). 
To decide which for PGS to take forward for further analyses, using information on sample size ( ), total number of independent markers ( ), and lower and upper -values, we estimated the power encompassed in each ( Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ) ( 45 [rid=CIT0045] ). 
There were no significant differences in sociodemographic characteristics between participants with and without -ε4 ( Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ). 
To ensure our analyses were well-powered, we calculated a minimal impact size that could be detected in our sample with the power of 0.80 and type I error of 0.05 using powerSurvEpi R package ( Supplementary Material [this file] and Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ) ( 48 [rid=CIT0048] ). 
Before we ran the Cox PH model, we checked that all assumptions for this model were met using the Schoenfeld residuals test ( 52 [rid=CIT0052] ), which they were ( Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ). 
The baseline sample characteristics of ELSA participants stratified by age are shown in Supplementary Table 8 [this file] . Of the whole sample, = 194 (2.7%) adults were diagnosed with dementia by the end of the mean 10-year follow-up period ( Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). The diagnosis of dementia mediates the effect of -ε4 status on other causes of mortality in women with the percent mediated being 34%; though the value was .061 ( Supplementary Table 15 [this file] ). As deaths caused by dementia had been part of “other” mortality events, it was expected that the dementia diagnosis would be strongly associated with “other” causes of mortality; this was indeed the case ( Supplementary Table 16 [this file] ).

For transparency, Supplementary Fig. 14 [this file] includes the main results of the study, shown both covariate-adjusted and unadjusted results for reference. PC abundance was lower in the SAD group relative to the controls ( = 0.035) and AAD group ( = 0.054), and a marginally greater reduction was observed for phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) in SAD group, resulting in a slightly lower ratio of PC to PE in controls (Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] ). Overall, the phospholipid classes were at similar levels in control and AAD groups, but trended lower in SAD (Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] ). By dissecting lipid classes into subclasses by desaturation status and acyl chain length, the lowest mean abundances of phospholipids including PC, PE, PG, PS, PI, LPC, and LPE at either the level of desaturation or that of acyl chain length were mostly observed in the SAD group (Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] , 4a [this file] and 5a [this file] ). The TAG species with 2 to 7 double bonds and acyl chain lengths between 50 and 58 carbons were generally higher in the SAD group than controls, with most species showing increased levels (Supplementary Figs. 3 [this file] , 4b [this file] , 5b [this file] ). In comparison to controls, phospholipids with acyl chain lengths of 22, 34, 35, 40, 44 net carbons (Supplementary Fig. 4a [this file] ) and TAG with 52, 56, and 58 net carbons were significantly lower in AAD, while TAG with 47, 48, 51, 53 carbons was slightly higher in AAD (Supplementary Fig. 4b [this file] ). Concerning desaturation status, AAD showed levels similar to SAD for TAG containing 0-4 double bonds, except those with 2 double bonds, while AAD had the lowest values compared to the other groups considering TAG containing 5–11 double bonds, except TAG containing 7 double bonds (Supplementary Fig. 5b [this file] ). 
To highlight the most statistically significant differences between groups, the 50 lipids with the lowest values were selected for visualization (Fig. 3a [rid=Fig3] , abundance of all lipid species is shown in Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] ). Fragmentation in the mass spectrometer at the sn-2 position of lyso-phospholipids with a PUFA, such as docosahexaenoic fatty acid (DHA; 22:6) is shown in Supplementary Fig. 7d, e [this file] . When DHA is at the sn-1 position of lyso-phospholipids (Supplementary Fig. 7f-g [this file] ), a peak at m/z 196 is also present . A peak at m/z 196 is also present in commercially available internal standard sn-1 18:1D7 LPE (Supplementary Fig. 7b, c [this file] ). This trend is appreciated in Supplementary Fig. 7d–g [this file] ; here the predominant species is LPE 22:6 [sn-1]. 
The ranking sPLSDA analysis revealed that LPE 22:6 has the highest eigenvalue of Component 1 and mainly contributes to the discrimination of controls from other groups (Supplementary Fig. 8a [this file] ). The lipids with top 30 VIP scores were further used for ROC analysis using binominal regression model demonstrating the ability to distinguish between SAD vs. controls, AAD vs. controls, and SAD vs. AAD with AUC values of 0.784 (95%CI [0.725, 0.842]), 0.712 (95%CI [0.632, 0.792]), and 0.767 (95%CI [0.677,0.819]), respectively (Supplementary Fig. 8b [this file] ). The sPLS-DA algorithm model yielded a substantially higher AUC than any individual annotated lipid, such as LPE 22:6 which had the highest individual species AUC value (AUC for SAD versus Control cases of 0.653, (95%CI [0.582, 0.725]), P = 3.0E-05) (Supplementary Fig. 8c [this file] ). 
Using DIABLO’s model, although the averaged components (referred to X-variates) from proteomic, lipidomic, and clinical datasets did not show clear discrimination among the three groups, control samples were evident as a separate cluster and could already be discriminated from most SAD samples (Supplementary Fig. 9d [this file] ). DIABLO analysis identified 5 lipid modules, 30 protein modules, and 5 clinical AD traits that distinguished SAD from the control group (Supplementary Fig. 9e-g [this file] ). It also had significantly correlations (|cor | >0.5) with ~300 proteins, that were also broadly associated with multiple other lipid species (Supplementary Fig. 10 [this file] ). We found that LPE 22:6 [sn-1] is significantly associated with Echinoderm microtubule-associated protein-like 4 (EML4), which is essential for the stabilization of microtubules (cor = -0.605, = 0.0008; Supplementary Fig. 13a [this file] ). LPE 22:6 [sn-1] is also significant correlated to Protein phosphatase 1 and regulatory subunit 1 A (PPP1R1A), which is positively correlated with amyloid aggregates (cor = -0.592, = 0.001; Supplementary Fig. 13b [this file] ). 
Additionally, significantly lower ether-linked PC (PC_e) was observed in SAD vs. controls ( = 0.021) (Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] ). This resulted in a slightly lower PC/PE ratio in controls relative to the SAD group, in line with decreased BACE1 and APP (Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] and 12 [this file] ). Targeted lipidomics showed a decreased ratio of PC/PE was also observed in controls compared to SAD and AAD (Supplementary Fig. 11d [this file] ). In general, controls tended to have slightly higher levels than other groups of phospholipids incorporating omega-3 and omega-6 PUFA, including DHA (omega-3), DPA (omega-3), AA (omega-6), and LA (omega-6) (Supplementary Fig. 11b, c [this file] ). 
While most calcium signaling-related proteins were not significantly different among the three AD phenotypes in our proteomic dataset, proteins related to N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDAR) activation and post-synaptic signaling were significantly up-regulated in controls vs SAD (Supplementary Fig. 12c [this file] ). and double knockin mouse models demonstrate that a decrease of Glutamate ionotropic receptor AMPA type subunit (AMPAR) efficacy is relevant to synaptic downscaling, an early onset phenomenon in AD, and AMPAR is crucial for long-term potentiation, critical for memory encoding as well as memory flexibility . 
We found that LPE 22:6 is highly associated with Echinoderm microtubule-associated protein-like 4 (EML4), which is essential for the stabilization of microtubules (Supplementary Fig. 13a [this file] ). Our correlation analysis showed that LPE 22:6 has a negative correlation to PPP1R1A and a positive correlation to PPP1CA (cor = 0.26, = 0.19), suggesting a possible role of LPE 22:6 in AD development (Supplementary Fig. 13a-c [this file] ). Consistent with our multi-omics integration results, our correlation analysis (Supplementary Fig. 13d [this file] ) showed that LPE 22:6 and LPE 20:4, which belong to the M2 module, demonstrated a negative correlation with PPP1R1A, and CHGA, which is associated with the synapse pathway. 
To focus our analysis and ensure data quality, we filtered the dataset to contain only lipids with a signal to noise ratio of greater than 3, a peak quality of greater than 0.6, and high MS/MS confidence identification (levels A, B and C in LipidSearch version 4.2), resulting in 343 high confidence lipids (excluding internal standards) for further statistical analysis (Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] ). 
The results with covariate adjustment are provided in the Supplementary Fig. 14 [this file] , while the main manuscript presents the results without covariate adjustment to maintain clarity and simplicity, as the conclusion remains unchanged.

During follow-up time until June 2023 (mean follow-up years = 12.4), 3344 participants developed dementia, including 1,582 diagnosed with AD and 878 with vascular dementia (VAD). 85 of the 172 metabolites were significantly associated with all-cause dementia (FDR < 0.05) adjusting for ethnicity, age, sex, fasting time, BMI, smoking status, alcohol intake, education, 27 medications for various chronic conditions, assessment centre, fasting time and spectrometer used for the NMR measurements, (Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). These included 65 that were significantly associated with dementia and an additional 12 mainly consisting of increased levels of low-density lipoprotein (LDL) subfractions (Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] ). VAD showed a slightly different metabolomic signature associating with only 36/172 metabolites, of which 16 overlapped with dementia and AD (Supplementary Table 1 [this file] , Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] ). Sensitivity analysis (performed for AD) by additionally removing all prevalent and incident cases of CVD, diabetes, and kidney and liver diseases did not influence the results (Supplementary Table 2 [this file] , Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] ). 
Also consistent with the findings for dementia, high levels of BHBA were significantly associated with lower fluid intelligence (Beta = −0.06, FDR = 1.6*10 , Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ) and increased reaction time (Beta = 1.26, FDR = 2.4*10 ). 
Results of MR for AD suggest that changes in metabolite levels of BHBA and BCAAs (valine, leucine and isoleucine) (Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ) are downstream of the disease process. The sensitivity analysis shows that the results for BHBA are only driven by the locus (rs429358/rs7412) (Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] ), which is the key instrumental variable for both AD and BHBA. However, the test for horizontal pleiotropy was not significant (Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ) and the Steiger test for directionality suggests that high plasma concentration of BHBA is a consequence of the disease process (Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). 
However, BHBA levels in the ε44 and ε24/ε34 carriers were significantly higher compared to the non-carriers across all age groups (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] , Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ). However, a sensitivity analysis excluding all incident and prevalent cases of non-communicable diseases showed the same pattern for BHBA (Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] ) and the differences in BHBA concentration across the genotypes remain significant. 
For BCAAs (valine, leucine and isoleucine), their levels increase until age 58 and do not significantly differ across the age groups between the carriers and non-carriers of the allele (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] , Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ). 
There were 257/2923 proteins significantly associated (FDR < 0.05) with ε4, of which 180 were downregulated and 77 were upregulated (Supplementary Table 9 [this file] ). The downregulated proteins were enriched in pathways involved in the regulation of insulin-like growth factor (IGF) transport and uptake (Reactome; FDR < 4.9*10 ), immune system (Reactome; FDR < 1.5*10 ), and lysosome (KEGG; FDR = 2.9*10 ) among several others that were less significant (Supplementary Table 10 [this file] ). Of these, IGF transport/uptake and the immune system were also involved in the upregulation of plasma BHBA and downregulation of BCAAs (Supplementary Tables 11 [this file] and 12 [this file] , Supplementary Figs. 5 [this file] and 6 [this file] ), with immune system (FDR = 5.2*10 ), more specifically involving neutrophil degranulation (6.6*10 ) being much more significant in the upregulation of the plasma levels of BHBA. Further, upregulated BHBA associated proteins in plasma were also significantly enriched in the lysosome pathway (KEGG; FDR = 1.4*10 ) (Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] ). Looking into the cellular localization, the ε4-downregulated proteins were enriched in extracellular region (FDR = 2.1*10 ), lysosome (FDR = 7.9*10 ) and azurophil granules (FDR = 4.8*10 ) (Supplementary Fig. 7 [this file] ). 
Proteins that were upregulated in ε4 carriers in plasma were not enriched in any specific pathway (Supplementary Table 13 [this file] ). Proteins that were downregulated with increased plasma BHBA concentration were involved in glycosaminoglycan binding, heparin binding, vitamin digestion and absorption, nitrogen metabolism and neurogenesis among several other pathways (Supplementary Table 14 [this file] ). Proteins that were upregulated with high levels of BCAAs (valine) were enriched in pathways involved in the immune system, platelet activation, apopotosis and lysosome among several others (Supplementary Table 15 [this file] ). 
The two known proteomic markers of AD, i.e., neurofilament light (NEFL) and glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) were significantly associated with BHBA (NEFL; beta = 0.05, FDR = 6.1*10 , GFAP; beta = 0.086, FDR = 2.5*10 ), valine (NEFL; beta = −0.04, FDR = 7.2*10 , GFAP; beta = −0.04, FDR = 1.0*10 ), leucine (NEFL; beta = −0.05, FDR = 2.8*10 , GFAP; beta = −0.05, FDR = 1.2*10 ) and isoleucine (NEFL; beta = −0.04, FDR = 7.3*10 , GFAP; beta = −0.07, FDR = 1.5*10 ) (Supplementary Table 9 [this file] ). 
Low levels of BHBA were significantly associated with Braak stage (beta = −0.05, p = 7.3*10 ) but not with amyloid pathology (Supplementary Table 16 [this file] ). 
Using the proteomic signatures, we then identified molecular pathways involved in up-/downregulation of these metabolites in the brain and compared those with the pathways differentially regulated in ε4 carriers (Supplementary Table 17 [this file] ). Proteins that were downregulated in the ε4 carriers in the brain tissue were enriched in pathways including neurexins & neuroligins (Reactome: FDR = 2.4*10 ), TCA cycle (Reactome; FDR < 3.6*10 ) and clathrin-mediated endocytosis (Reactome; FDR = 2.3*10 ) (Supplementary Table 18 [this file] ). 
Proteins that were upregulated with high levels of BHBA in the brain were significantly enriched in the mitochondrial translation pathways (Reactome; FDR < 7.81*10 ; Supplementary Table 19 [this file] ), while those involved in downregulation were enriched in cholesterol metabolism (Reactome; FDR = 2.9*10 ) and immune system (Reactome; FDR = 2.1*10 ; Supplementary Table 20 [this file] ). Control and AD training groups were determined for each region using a combination of CERAD scores, Braak stages and study-specific diagnostic criteria ( Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). Patient cohort demographics were also assessed between control and AD groups to evaluate potential confounding differences ( Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ). Statistically significant DEGs were identified using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure to control for false positives, with a p adjusted ( -adj) ≤ 0.05, and region-specific log2 fold change (LFC) thresholds to optimize the downstream predictive performance ( Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ). 
This required region-specific control and AD training groups using stricter criteria than in DGE analysis ( Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). 
TCX and hippocampus FPKM datasets from the Aging, Dementia, and TBI study ( GSE104687 (GSE104687) ) was filtered to retain genes common across all signature development datasets, excluding samples with RIN < 5 or reported traumatic brain injury (TBI), and including only those diagnosed with “Alzheimer’s Disease Type” or “No Dementia,” followed by log2-normalization ( Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). Control and AD training sets for each region were defined using CERAD scores, Braak stages, and DSM-IV clinical diagnosis ( Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ). 
To better understand the mechanisms driving AD pathology, this analysis captured gene expression changes across brain regions affected at different stages of the disease using PMB tissue ( Supplementary Tables 7A–F [this file] ). 
Predictions of AD were validated against the known AD status of established neuropathological, clinical, and cognitive assessments ( Table 1 [rid=tab1] ; Supplementary Figure 1 [this file] ). 
Signature predictions, along with genetic and sociodemographic factors, were evaluated for their influence on AD status ( Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ). 
Next, McFadden’s pseudo-R was calculated to assess model fit for predicting AD status ( Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ). 
To further understand molecular changes underlying dysregulation across regions, this analysis examined overlapping signature genes revealing notable commonalities, as shown in Figure 3A [rid=fig3] ( Supplementary Figure 2 [this file] ; Supplementary Table 9 [this file] ). Next, fourteen other genes were found across four of the six brain regions with upregulation of and downregulation of and ( Figure 3 [rid=fig3] ; Supplementary Table 10 [this file] ). Notably, , , , and showed overlap with hub genes identified across regions further supporting their importance in dysregulation ( Supplementary Table 10 [this file] ). 
Pathway enrichment analysis also identified significant variability across regions ( Supplementary Tables 11A–F [this file] ). 
Similarly, network analysis identified functional modules revealing early-to-mid affected regions (PHG, TCX, STG) showing greater network dysregulation than mid-to-late affected regions (IFG, DLPFC, CER; Supplementary Table 12 [this file] ). This may suggest a possible protective mechanism ( Supplementary Tables 13A–F [this file] ).

Finally, the CER showed heightened immune and inflammatory responses, including Toll-like receptor 4 upregulation, potentially driving increased chemotaxis and angiogenesis regulation ( Supplementary Figure 4 [this file] ; Supplementary Table 13F [this file] ).

We implemented MOFA integrating 7 different omics datasets (hereafter referred to as ) sourced from a partially overlapping set of brain samples, totaling 1,358 ROS/MAP participants ( Supplementary Figure S1 [this file] ). MOFA was set to decompose the data into 50 largely orthogonal latent factors ( Supplementary Figure S2 [this file] ) representing the underlying sources of variation across samples. In addition, different contribution patterns where observed from each view, for example Factors 3, 5, and 6 were mostly driven by transcriptomics from DLPFC, AC, and PCG respectively, while others views had their variance explained by at least 2 or more omics views, indicating possible more complex interplay between different molecular levels or tissues ( Figure 1c [rid=F1] , Supplementary Figure S3 [this file] ). 
From the 50 decomposed factors, we selected nine that were associated ( < 0.05) either with pathological diagnosis of AD (NIA-Reagan score) or clinical diagnosis of Alzheimer’s dementia for downstream analysis ( Supplementary Figure S4 [this file] ). These factors accounted for a range of total variance, from 20.5% (Factor 1) to 1.7% (Factor 42) ( Supplementary Figure S5 [this file] ). Most of these persisted after adjusting for ε4 ( Supplementary Figure S6 [this file] ). 
To assess the robustness of the MOFA model, we compared feature weight correlations across different subsampling strategies ( Supplementary Figure S7 [this file] ). We then performed regression analyses on all phenotypes to evaluate how the presence or absence of proteomics measurements influences the results ( Supplementary Figure S8 [this file] ). 
Here we highlight results from Factor 8, but a detailed description of other factors can be found in the Supplementary Material [this file] - Supplementary Notes [this file] and Supplementary Figures S9 [this file] – S16 [this file] . 
Both factors were strongly enriched for processes involving immune response and displayed overlapping functional terms across their , with the key difference that these enrichments were mostly in opposite directions ( Supplementary Figures S10a [this file] and S11a [this file] ). Among the top feature contributors to Factors 2 and 3, we identified several genes related to neuroinflammatory processes and β-amyloid metabolism, such as and ( Supplementary Figures S10b [this file] and S11b [this file] ). 
Factor 1 ( Supplementary Figure S9 [this file] ), which explains the largest proportion of total data variation, was negatively enriched in mitochondrial and ribosome-related terms, and positively enriched with MAPK and sugar metabolism, RNA splicing, and ubiquitination terms. Factor 14 ( Supplementary Figure S14 [this file] ) demonstrated the second strongest association with AD pathology after Factor 8, uniquely correlating with both PD pathology ( = 4.87 × 10 ) and major depressive disorder ( = 2.78 × 10 ). Factor 42 ( Supplementary Figure S16 [this file] ), despite explaining only 1.7% of total variance, captured some aspects of vascular biology relevant to AD pathogenesis. 
Factor 26 ( Supplementary Figure S15 [this file] ) exhibited the strongest protective effect, with enrichment for RNA processing mechanisms, vascular-related pathways, and cytoskeletal organization that may preserve cognitive function despite pathological burden. Factor 4 ( Supplementary Figure S12 [this file] ) emerged as the second strongest protective factor, negatively associated with AD dementia ( = 2.34 × 10 ) and NIA-Reagan score ( = 5.78 × 10 ), while positively correlating with global cognitive function ( = 1.74 × 10 ). Finally, Factor 12 ( Supplementary Figure S13 [this file] ) showed protective effects through increased cell activation, cell signaling, and extracellular matrix organization, strongly driven by H3K9ac epigenetic markers. 
More detailed descriptions are provided in the Supplementary Material [this file] - Supplementary Notes [this file] .

Using levels of Aβ plaques and neurofibrillary tangles and the presence or absence of cognitive impairment [ 62 [rid=CR62] ], we classified ROSMAP participants into mutually exclusive groups: healthy controls, resilient, and AD (Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] A and Figure S1 [this file] ). To functionally characterize differentially regulated pathways in resilience and AD, we applied pathway-activity analysis ( Extended results [this file] ). 
By comparing bulk RNAseq profiles between each group, we found a higher number of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in AD compared to resilient individuals than in resilience compared to healthy controls (Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] B, Tables S1 [rid=MOESM2] - S3 [rid=MOESM2] ), reflecting more substantial transcriptomic changes in AD (see also Extended Results [this file] ). Concordantly, single-cell expression of in the DLPFC was significantly upregulated in resilience ( Extended Results [this file] ). 
Of the 54 genes significantly associated with cognitive impairment (54 genes with adj- < 0.1; 46 genes with adj- < 0.05, adjusted for pathology burden, Table S5 [this file] ), 20.4% (11 out of 43 DEGs with adj- < 0.1; 4 out of 8 with adj- < 0.05) were also differentially expressed in AD compared to resilience (Figure S2 [rid=MOESM2] A and Table S5 [rid=MOESM2] ). 
In the resilient group, the AD-PRS, which evaluates risk prediction for AD considering AD-associated single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), was positioned between AD and controls (Figure S4 [this file] ). 
As with the bulk RNAseq, we classified individuals into AD, resilient, and control groups, and carried out clustering and differential gene expression analyses ( , Figures S5 [this file] - S7 [this file] , Tables S11 [rid=MOESM2] - S13 [rid=MOESM2] ). 
Individual cell types in the DLPFC, EC, and HC showed a consistently higher number of DEGs in AD compared to resilience than controls (Figure S8 [this file] A, Table S12 [rid=MOESM2] , ADvsRES compared to ADvsCTRL). Astrocytes, particularly in the DLPFC, exhibited more pronounced upregulation and downregulation of genes in AD (Figure S8 [this file] B, Table S12 [rid=MOESM2] ). Excitatory neurons from all brain regions, as well as inhibitory neurons from the DLPFC and EC, also showed more pronounced gene expression changes in AD (Figure S8 [this file] B, Table S12 [rid=MOESM2] , ADvsRES compared to ADvsCTRL). Alongside the broad transcriptomic shifts detailed below, we observed changes in gene expression of established AD loci, including , , and ( Extended Results [this file] ). 
Gene ontology (GO) enrichment analysis of upregulated and downregulated DEGs in major cell types from each comparison (ADvsRES, ADvsCTRL, and RESvsCTRL) identified multiple terms related to protein folding in resilience (Figure S10 [this file] , “‘de novo’ protein folding” downregulated in AD compared to resilient, and “protein refolding” upregulated in resilient compared to controls). 
Inhibitory neurons from the DLPFC and EC (Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] ) were significantly enriched for the expression of ‘protective’ genes associated with rare variants (Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] C, Figure S11 [this file] C), independently of group classification. This was also true for those in HC (Figure S11 [this file] C). The expression of ‘risk’ genes associated with rare variants was also significantly enriched in inhibitory neurons as well as oligodendrocyte progenitor cells (OPCs) in all brain regions tested (Figure S11 [this file] A-C), which we confirmed and validated in an independent DLPFC snRNAseq dataset [ 72 [rid=CR72] ] (Figure S11 [this file] D). Risk genes associated with common variants [ 11 [rid=CR11] ] showed a strong expression bias in microglia and immune cells in all brain regions (Figure S11 [this file] E), consistent with recent studies [ 73 [rid=CR73] ]. 
Consistent results showing enrichment of protective genes in inhibitory neurons were replicated across several SST+ subtypes in an independent dataset [ 72 [rid=CR72] ] (Figure S11 [this file] G). In the EC, SST+ EC:Inh3 interneurons also showed significant enrichment for protective variant-associated genes (Figure S11 [this file] F). 
Cell proportions for SST+ (RBFOX1+ KIF26B+) DLPFC:Inh1 and SST+ MEF2C DLPFC:Inh7, which were enriched for protective (Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] D) and risk (Figure S11 [this file] B) genes, respectively, showed a decrease in AD (Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] E-F). and , identified as protective genes harboring rare genetic variants, emerged as potential markers of protection-associated SST+ DLPFC:Inh1 interneurons. Indeed, we confirmed the co-expression of RBFOX1 and KIF26B in cortical neurons using multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF) applied to DLPFC sections from an independent cohort ( Extended Results [this file] ). The proportion of PVALB+ DLPFC:Inh10 cells decreased in resilient individuals compared to controls (Figure S11 [this file] H, adj- = 0.02). 
Resilient brains showed a greater number of significant L-R pairs across major cell classes and subpopulations in both DLPFC and EC compared to AD and control (Figure S15 [this file] A–B), consistent with a compensatory or preserved communication response. The SST signaling pathway was downregulated in AD across all brain regions but upregulated in resilient individuals (Figure S16 [this file] ). In the EC, in contrast with resilience and controls, there was a complete loss of communication originating from the SST+ EC:Inh9 subtype in AD (Figure S17 [this file] A), which could be explained at least in part by reduced expression of in this subpopulation (Figure S17 [this file] B). The SST receptor SSTR2 was predicted to interact with SST in all diagnostic groups, whereas SSTR1 was involved in interactions between subclasses of inhibitory and excitatory neurons from the EC solely in resilient individuals (Figure S17 [this file] B and Table S19 [rid=MOESM2] ). Both classes of SST+ inhibitory neurons were predicted to interact with multiple classes of excitatory neurons, including EC:Exc2, EC:Exc3, and EC:Exc5 (Figure S17 [this file] A). 
Analysis of differential gene expression from bulk DLPFC (Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] B) in the snRNAseq ROSMAP dataset revealed that genes downregulated in AD compared to resilient individuals were disproportionately enriched in excitatory neurons (Figure S3 [this file] A-B). Genes whose expression was associated with cognitive decline exhibited downregulation in excitatory neurons, particularly excitatory neurons from cortical layers L2-4 (DLPFC:Exc0 and DLPFC:Exc1) (Figure S3 [this file] C-D). 
In addition, we observed AD-associated depletion of two subtypes of excitatory neurons, one expressing (EC:Exc0) and the other and (EC:Exc4), which did not exhibit significant changes in composition in resilience (Figure S14 [this file] B).

To further explore excitatory neuronal subpopulations with a potential role in cognitive resilience, we mapped MEF2C, ATB8B1, and RELN proteins in EC sections from our independent cohort ( = 16 subjects; and Extended Results [this file] ) by staining for MEF2C, ATP8B1, RELN, NeuN, and Aβ (Fig. 4 [rid=Fig4] F). We followed the same procedure as in the DLPFC ( Extended Results [this file] ) to preprocess the resulting mIF data and identify and validate the presence of EC:Exc2, EC:Exc3, and EC:Ex5 (Figure S12 [this file] C-F). As a quality control, we also reproduced the increase in Aβ+ cells in AD and resilient brains (Figure S14 [this file] G). 
To our surprise, we found two distinct cell clusters expressing MEF2C, ATP8B1, and RELN proteins, based on the mIF analysis, both equivalent to the EC:Exc2 from the snRNAseq ROSMAP dataset: (1) pExc2, expressing similar levels of MEF2C in all cellular compartments, and (2) pExc2-N, which expressed MEF2C in the nucleus (Figure S14 [this file] H). Moreover, the levels of nuclear MEF2C were significantly higher in resilient than in control brains among pExc-N cells (Figure S14 [this file] I). 
Additional signaling pathways showing changes in resilience (Figure S16 [this file] and S18 [this file] ) with EC:Exc5 as source included ncWnt (non-canonical wingless-related integration site, targets: oligodendrocytes), periostin (target: EC:Inh1), BMP (bone morphogenetic protein, targets: subtypes from all major cell types), and TGF-β (transforming growth factor beta, target: ECFib). Also, we observed a loss of TULP (tubby-like proteins) signaling between all three resilient excitatory neuronal subtypes (EC:Exc2, EC:Exc3, and EC:Exc5) and subtypes from multiple major cell types (Figure S18 [this file] C). Signaling pathways observed to be lost in AD, with EC:Exc2, EC:Exc3, or EC:Exc5 as sources, are shown in Figure S19 [this file] , and included, for example, KIT (or c-Kit) and EGF/EGFR signaling. Intriguingly, we noticed a shift of the EGF signaling pathway from EC:Exc2 as the source in controls to EC:Exc3 in resilience (Figure S19 [this file] C, ligand: BTC; receptors: EGFR and ERBB4), which may represent a compensatory response in resilient brains. 
Our results contribute to the growing body of evidence suggesting critical involvement of SST+ interneurons in the pathogenesis of AD, with and (previously identified as candidate AD-protective genes from rare genetic variants [ 57 [rid=CR57] , 71 [rid=CR71] ]) appearing as markers of protected SST+ interneurons (Figure S20 [this file] and Tables S21 [rid=MOESM2] and S22 [rid=MOESM2] ). 
Protective rare variants are associated with and its interaction partner, . , a negative regulator of BDNF-NTRK2 (Figure S21 [this file] ), was upregulated in AD across cell types but not in resilient brains.

Table  S5  :  Genes  associated  with  loss  of  cognition  from  bulk  RNAseq  data.  The  association  of  gene  expression  profiles  with  loss  of  cognition  was  analyzed  using  a  proportional  odds  model  (POM)  for  ordinal  categorical  data  analysis  applied  to  ROSMAP  bulk  RNAseq  data.  Gene  expression  levels  were  adjusted  for  confounding  covariates  prior  to  performing  POM.  The  POM  analysis  was  applied  to  the  subjects  with  either  no  cognitive  impairment,  mild  cognitive  impairment,  or  AD  dementia.  The  POM  analyzed  cognitive  impairment  as  a  function  of  gene  expression  and  pathology  status  (plaque  and  tangle  stages).  P  -values,  adjusted  for  multiple  hypothesis  comparison  using  the  Bonferroni  correction  method  (column  “adj.P.Val”),  represent  the  significance  of  the  association  of  each  gene  with  cognitive  status.  The  column  “Direction”  denotes  whether  the  expression  of  a  gene  positively  or  negatively  correlates  with  loss  of  cognition.  The  column  “ADvsRES”  denotes  genes  that  were  also  differentially  expressed  between  AD  and  resilient  subjects,  “ADvsRES  dir”  reports  the  direction  in  AD  compared  to  the  resilient  group  (related  with  Table  S1),  and  “Change  consistency”  reports  the  consistency  between  the  two  analyses.  Table  S6  :  Dysregulated  pathways  in  AD  compared  to  cognitive  resilience  in  bulk  DLPFC.  Differential  pathway  activity  analysis  was  performed  between  AD  and  resilient  subjects  based  on  ROSMAP  bulk  RNAseq  data.  Significant  pathway  dysregulation  was  determined  using  Storey-adjusted  p  -value  (q-value)  <  0.1.  P  -values  were  determined  using  a  linear  regression  model  that  accounts  for  confounding  covariates  such  as  sequencing  batch,  RNA  integrity  number,  and  postmortem  interval. By comparing bulk RNAseq profiles between each group, we found a higher number of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in AD compared to resilient individuals than in resilience compared to healthy controls (Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] B, Tables S1 [this file] - S3 [this file] ), reflecting more substantial transcriptomic changes in AD (see also Extended Results [rid=MOESM1] ). Notably, the expression of only two genes, (KLF transcription factor 4; RESvsCTRL Log2FC = -0.56, adj- = 0.04) and (encoding for glial fibrillary acidic protein; RESvsCTRL Log2FC = 0.40, adj- = 0.07), was downregulated and upregulated, respectively, in resilient subjects compared to controls (Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] B and Table S3 [this file] ). was also a top upregulated DEG in AD (Table S2 [this file] , ADvsCTRL log2FC = 0.43, adj- = 4.0 × 10 ). 
Of the 54 genes significantly associated with cognitive impairment (54 genes with adj- < 0.1; 46 genes with adj- < 0.05, adjusted for pathology burden, Table S5 [rid=MOESM1] ), 20.4% (11 out of 43 DEGs with adj- < 0.1; 4 out of 8 with adj- < 0.05) were also differentially expressed in AD compared to resilience (Figure S2 [this file] A and Table S5 [this file] ). 
As with the bulk RNAseq, we classified individuals into AD, resilient, and control groups, and carried out clustering and differential gene expression analyses ( , Figures S5 [rid=MOESM1] - S7 [rid=MOESM1] , Tables S11 [this file] - S13 [this file] ). 
Individual cell types in the DLPFC, EC, and HC showed a consistently higher number of DEGs in AD compared to resilience than controls (Figure S8 [rid=MOESM1] A, Table S12 [this file] , ADvsRES compared to ADvsCTRL). Astrocytes, particularly in the DLPFC, exhibited more pronounced upregulation and downregulation of genes in AD (Figure S8 [rid=MOESM1] B, Table S12 [this file] ). Excitatory neurons from all brain regions, as well as inhibitory neurons from the DLPFC and EC, also showed more pronounced gene expression changes in AD (Figure S8 [rid=MOESM1] B, Table S12 [this file] , ADvsRES compared to ADvsCTRL). 
, a negative regulator of BDNF-NTRK2-mediated neurotrophic signaling [ 65 [rid=CR65] , 66 [rid=CR66] ] that has been implicated in axonal and synaptic loss [ 67 [rid=CR67] ], was consistently upregulated in AD but downregulated in resilience (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] B, Table S13 [this file] ). Relative to controls, expression was ubiquitously decreased across cell types in DLPFC and EC tissue of resilient individuals (Table S13 [this file] ). Conversely, resilient HC astrocytes, microglia, and oligodendrocytes showed higher levels (Table S13 [this file] ), indicating that the resilience-associated downregulation of expression is largely cortex-specific.

Both transcripts were broadly higher in AD than resilience, with levels of rising in most classes of neuronal and glial cells across the DLPFC, EC, and HC, and increasing mainly in AD excitatory neurons and oligodendrocytes (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] C and Table S13 [this file] ). 
Protein-protein interaction (PPI) network analysis generated a single cluster from the list of upregulated genes in resilient DLPFC excitatory neurons compared to AD (ADvsRES, Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] D, Table S15 [this file] ). Concurrently, PPI analysis of upregulated genes in resilient excitatory neurons relative to controls (RESvsCTRL) produced one cluster enriched for “protein folding” ontology terms (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] E, Table S16 [this file] ), which included the same members and Hsp families. In sum, in contrast with AD, although Hsp90 isoforms were downregulated in all regions and cell types in resilience, genes encoding other chaperones – Hsp40, Hsp70, and Hsp110 – were consistently upregulated in resilient neurons (Table S13 [this file] ), Taken together, these findings indicate complex transcriptomic dynamics in inhibitory and excitatory neurons that are distinct in resilience compared with AD and healthy controls.

Cell subtypes were identified from brain region-, cell type-specific subclusters, and annotated using two independent brain references (Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] B and Table S14 [this file] ). 
To identify which inhibitory neuron classes are associated with resilience, we investigated changes in the composition of cell subtypes in each brain region according to group classification in the snRNAseq ROSMAP dataset (Dirichlet test, Table S17 [this file] ). We observed lower levels of gene expression in EC inhibitory neurons in AD (Table S13 [this file] , ADvsRES: 4th DEG ranked by -value, log2FC = -0.52, adj- = 3.54 × 10 , ADvsCTRL: log2FC = -0.41, adj- = 1.79 × 10 ). 
The SST receptor SSTR2 was predicted to interact with SST in all diagnostic groups, whereas SSTR1 was involved in interactions between subclasses of inhibitory and excitatory neurons from the EC solely in resilient individuals (Figure S17 [rid=MOESM1] B and Table S19 [this file] ). 
We explored the subpopulations of excitatory neurons in the ROSMAP snRNAseq dataset, which were identified from brain region- and cell type-specific subclusters and annotated using two independent brain references (Fig. 4 [rid=Fig4] B and Table S14 [this file] ). Consistently, two inhibitory neuron subclasses with as a marker gene – the largest EC subcluster (EC:Inh0, Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] I) and the DLPFC subtype DLPFCInh7 (Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] F) – were over-represented in resilience, underscoring that -expressing neurons are preferentially preserved during AD pathogenesis when cognition is maintained. expression was significantly upregulated in EC excitatory neurons of resilient subjects compared to controls (RESvsCTRL, Table S13 [this file] ). expression showed no significant changes in the EC in major cell types but was significantly upregulated in AD and downregulated in resilience in multiple EC neuronal subtypes (Table S20 [this file] ). was also significantly upregulated in AD and downregulated in resilience in hippocampal neurons in major cell types (Table S13 [this file] ) and subtypes (Table S20 [this file] ).

Our results contribute to the growing body of evidence suggesting critical involvement of SST+ interneurons in the pathogenesis of AD, with and (previously identified as candidate AD-protective genes from rare genetic variants [ 57 [rid=CR57] , 71 [rid=CR71] ]) appearing as markers of protected SST+ interneurons (Figure S20 [rid=MOESM1] and Tables S21 [this file] and S22 [this file] ).

This study focused on offspring cohort (Generation 2) participants who had genome-wide genotyping and serum MCP-1 measurement data from Exam 7 (baseline) and who were followed up on AD/dementia outcomes up to 2019 (Figure S1 [this file] ). 
After filtering out self-reported non-European ancestry subjects and those without MCP-1 and genotype information, 398 ADNI-1 participants were included in the analysis (Figure S1 [this file] ). 
ROSMAP data were further used to investigate whether -regulatory variants affect DNA methylation and gene expression in the brain and their relationships with AD (Figure S1 [this file] ). 
A total of 78 participants with the above four neuropathology variables and blood MCP-1 measurements were included in the analysis (Figure S1 [this file] ). 
To increase the number of AD cases, we included both prevalent and incident AD cases in a logistic regression model to identify novel genetic variants that interact with blood MCP-1 levels in AD patients by conducting a G×E GWAS with an interaction term between MCP-1 and SNPs as a predictor and AD as an outcome adjusting for age at baseline, sex, years of education, and PCs (Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] and Figure S2 [this file] ). Notably, one locus on chromosome 12 reached genome-wide significant interactions with MCP-1 for AD association (p < 5.0 × 10 ) (Table S1 [this file] ), including 19 SNPs in the intronic region of the gene Among the SNPs that exhibited genome-wide significance (p < 5.0 × 10 ), rs696468 (minor allele=T, MAF = 0.14) in was selected as a sentinel SNP for further analyses (Fig. 1B [rid=Fig1] ). 
Although the results did not reach genome-wide significance (p < 5 × 10 ) in FHS cohort, we still included it for further characterization because of the following reasons: (1) Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] and Table S1 [this file] are results from the discovery FHS cohort, where the two SNPs reach a near genome-wide significance (p = 8.3 × 10 , Table S1 [this file] ). Notably, these SNPs have a lower minor allele frequency (MAF = 0.06) compared to those at (MAF = 0.14, Table S1 [this file] ), which may explain the fewer tightly linked variants observed. 
However, the interactive effects of the two SNPs and MCP-1 levels on AD risk were significant: rs696468 (p = 1.64 × 10 ) and rs72659964 (p = 8.36 × 10 ) (Table S1 [this file] ). 
We found that the relationships between blood MCP-1 levels and AD were significantly different between the two genotype groups of and , respectively (Table S2 [this file] . 
Similar associations were observed if the variants were stratified by three genotypes (Tables S3 [this file] ). 
Of note, adjusting for ε4 in the models does not change our conclusion (Figure S3 [this file] ). 
The interaction of rs696468 with blood MCP-1 concentration significantly influenced the Braak stage (p = 0.02), CERAD score (neocortical neuritic plaque) (p = 0.03), and CERAD semiquantitative score (diffuse plaques) (p = 0.03). rs72659964 significantly interacted with blood MCP-1 to influence the CERAD semiquantitative score (p < 0.001) (Table S4 [this file] ). 
The interaction effects between the SNPs and MCP-1 on AD risk did not reach statistical significance according to the ADNI, probably due to the small sample size (n = 398) (Table S5 [this file] ).

The methods are summarized here, and a full description can be found in the Supplementary material [this file] , ‘Methods’ section. 
Participant characteristics are described in Table 1 [rid=awaf161-T1] , and the overlap of participants in each dataset is shown in Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] . 
As described more fully in the Supplementary material [this file] , ‘Methods’ section, to identify marker genes characteristic of human brain pericyte subtypes, we reanalysed published snRNAseq data from two sources. 
First, we confirmed the correspondence of the pericyte clusters in the Yang dataset with those in the Green dataset—M-pericytes (Cluster 9) with Peri.1 and T-pericytes (Cluster 1) with Peri.2 respectively—by examining the expression of M-pericyte ( , , ) and T-pericyte ( , , and ) marker genes across empirically derived pericyte clusters in both snRNAseq datasets ( Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] ). 
Next, as described in more detail in the Supplementary material [this file] , ‘Methods’ section, in each snRNA seq dataset, we identified candidate M-pericyte marker genes by comparing gene expression in nuclei labelled M-pericytes to all other cell type nuclei in a differential expression analysis, selecting genes that were expressed in at least 10% of nuclei and meeting an adjusted -value threshold of 0.05 (Wilcoxon rank sum test). 
We did this for both M-type and T-type pericytes ( Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). 
As described more fully in the Supplementary material [this file] , ‘Methods’ section, all ROS and MAP participants underwent structured annual cognitive evaluations with a battery of 19 cognitive tests assessing episodic memory, semantic memory, visuospatial ability, perceptual speed and working memory. 
Assessments of the percentage of amyloid beta coverage in the cortex, neurofibrillary tangle pathology, diagnosis of Alzheimer’s disease, presence of Lewy bodies and cerebrovascular pathologies, including presence of gross and microinfarcts, cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA), cerebral atherosclerosis or arteriolosclerosis, are described in the Supplementary material [this file] , ‘Methods’ section. 
Detailed sequencing and pre-processing methods are described in the Supplementary material [this file] , ‘Methods’ section. 
Frozen lateral orbitofrontal cortex tissue samples from MAP participants were manually dissected and homogenized for sequencing, detailed methods of which are described in the Supplementary material [this file] , ‘Methods’ section. We preprocessed, normalized and batch corrected these gene expression count data using the same pipeline used for the DLPFC bulk RNAseq with minor variations described in the Supplementary material [this file] , ‘Methods’ section. 
The second dataset, referred to as the ‘Green’ dataset, sequenced 1 511 615 individual nuclei from the DLPFC of 424 older adults from the ROS and MAP cohorts, confirming clusters of pericytes expressing the M-pericyte and T-pericyte markers identified in the Yang dataset ( Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] ). Moreover, when we generated a combined dataset consisting of vascular niche nuclei from both the Yang and Green datasets, T-pericytes from Yang and Green overlapped substantially and did not overlap with M-pericytes from Yang and Green, which themselves overlapped substantially ( Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] ). Moreover, pericytes from both datasets were clearly distinct from other vascular cell types ( Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] ). 
After excluding genes where total abundance-weighted non-pericyte expression was expected to exceed pericyte expression, and excluding genes whose bulk expression was not associated with the proportion of M- or T-pericyte nuclei in the = 421 DLPFC samples with both snRNAseq and bulk RNAseq, data ( Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ), four M-pericyte marker genes ( , , and ) and three T-pericyte marker genes ( , and ) remained. 
As expected, , , and were much more highly expressed by M-pericytes and , and by T-pericytes ( Supplementary Fig. 5 [this file] ). 
Despite the reduced sample size, our putative marker genes remain strongly predictive of M- and T-pericyte proportions ( Supplementary Fig. 7 [this file] ). 
When we extended this to other cell types, we found that composite expression of M- and T-pericyte gene sets much more strongly predicted the respective proportion of M- and T-pericytes than any other cell type ( Supplementary Fig. 8 [this file] ). 
Composite expression of marker genes for pericytes in general was lower in the presence of amyloid pathology, similar to M- and T-pericytes as noted earlier ( Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ). 
In a linear regression model adjusted for age at death, sex, years of education, post-mortem interval, amyloid-β and arteriolosclerosis, greater average sleep fragmentation (log-adjusted kRA) was associated with higher composite expression of M-pericyte (estimate = +0.37, SE = 0.16, = 0.024, FDR q = 0.048; Fig. 2A [rid=awaf161-F2] and Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ) but not T-pericyte marker genes (estimate = +0.12, SE = 0.16, = 0.47, FDR q = 0.63; Fig. 2B [rid=awaf161-F2] and Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). 
Pericytes accounted for <0.5% of all nuclei in the Green dataset and with ∼3000–4000 nuclei per sample, many samples had only 0–5 pericyte nuclei ( Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] ). In secondary analyses of the small number of participants with snRNAseq data, at least one pericyte nucleus, and measurement of ante-mortem sleep fragmentation ( = 56), there was a positive trend between sleep fragmentation and the proportion of M-pericyte nuclei that was nevertheless concordant in direction with the results seen in our bulk RNAseq data (estimate = +5.32 × 10 , SE=+4.12 × 10 , = 0.2; Supplementary Fig. 9A [this file] ). 
However, the association between sleep fragmentation and the composite expression of M-pericyte marker genes remained significant in both the DLPFC and LOFC in models controlling for amyloid-β burden (% of cortex covered), neurofibrillary tangles (cortical area mm ), Lewy body pathology, large vessel atherosclerosis, arteriolosclerosis, CAA, microscopic cortical infarcts and macroscopic cortical infarcts ( Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). 
We observed that greater expression of M-pericyte genes was associated with more rapid decline (estimate = −8.3 × 10 , SE = 3.4 × 10 , = 0.014, FDR q = 0.048; Fig. 3A [rid=awaf161-F3] and Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). In contrast, expression of T-pericyte marker genes was not associated with cognitive outcomes (estimate = +6.5 × 10 , SE = 3.5 × 10 , = 0.99, FDR q = 0.94; Fig. 3B [rid=awaf161-F3] and Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). 
In this subset of participants, there was a trend towards decreased proportions of M-pericyte nuclei in the DLPFC and more rapid cognitive decline that was concordant in direction with the results seen in our bulk RNAseq data (estimate = −1.15 × 10 , SE = +7.48 × 10 , = 0.12; Supplementary Fig. 9B [this file] ).

Our analysis identified 42 plasma proteins associated with cognitive progression, 30 with motor progression, and 39 with composite progression (see Table S4 [this file] and Figure 2A–C [rid=cns70294-fig-0002] ). Notably, APOE exhibited the most significant association with cognitive progression ( = 3.12e‐14), while NSF was most significantly associated with both motor ( = 3.90e‐21) and composite ( = 5.42e‐10) progressions (Table S4 [this file] ). 
Applying stringent criteria—SMR (FDR‐corrected) < 0.05 and HEIDI > 0.05—we identified 12 plasma proteins causally associated with cognitive progression, 5 with motor progression, and 6 with composite progression (Table S5 [this file] , Figure 3 [rid=cns70294-fig-0003] ). A subsequent colocalization analysis (PP > 0.8) confirmed that, of the 12 proteins linked to cognitive progression, 10 (ALKBH3, GLO1, IDO1, SERPINA3, SORD, TPST1, GM2A, MICB, SH3BGRL3, and TGFBI) shared causal variants with PD cognitive progression loci (Table S6 [this file] , Figure 3 [rid=cns70294-fig-0003] ). Finally, reverse MR analyses revealed no significant bidirectional associations ( < 0.05/114) between these proteins and the three PD progression phenotypes (Table S7 [this file] ). 
Notably, 54 proteins reached significance in both datasets, with NSF exhibiting the most robust association (= 2.06e‐56,= 1.87e‐224) (Table S4 [this file] , Figure 4A [rid=cns70294-fig-0004] ). 
Overall, 22 plasma proteins demonstrated significant causal evidence for PD onset (< 0.05 and> 0.01) (Table S5 [this file] ). Colocalization analysis confirmed that nine of these proteins (ARSA, EHBP1, FCGR2A, GGH, GPNMB, HDHD2, DNAJB4, HAVCR2, and PDCD1LG2) shared a common causal variant with PD onset (PP > 0.8; Table S6 [this file] , Figure 4B [rid=cns70294-fig-0004] ). To examine potential bidirectional causal relationships, we also performed reverse MR analyses with no significant association detected, reinforcing the robustness of the observed causal links between the identified proteins and PD onset (Table S7 [this file] ). 
Consequently, no brain proteins were identified as candidate targets for further sensitivity analyses (Figures S1–S3 [this file] and Table S8 [this file] ).

In the PVALB+ DLPFC:Inh10 subtype, the top significant change in cellular distributions, we observed a decrease in the number of these interneurons in the resilient group compared to controls ( Figure S10H [this file] , adj-P = 0.02), suggesting that PVALB+ inhibitory neurons may be important for a distinct process of protection against AD, such as resistance to AD pathology. The SST+ DLPFC:Inh1 and SST+ DLPFC:Inh7 subpopulations, which showed enrichment for genes from ‘protective’ and ‘risk’ genetic variants, respectively ( Figure 3D [rid=F3] and S9B [this file] ), also showed a change in cell proportions in AD ( Figure 3E [rid=F3] – F [rid=F3] ).

In addition, we observed a depletion of two populations of excitatory neurons expressing CDH9+ (EC:Exc0) and RBFOX1 (EC:Exc4), respectively ( Figure S12 B [this file] ).

We observed oligodendrocyte and CD44-high astrocyte enrichment in the white matter adjacent to cortical gray matter ( Fig. 1I [rid=F1] ), and also confirmed that our cortical glutamatergic neuron subsets ( Table S2 [this file] ) localized to grey matter layers predicted by Azimuth human motor cortex reference ( Fig 1J [rid=F1] and 1K [rid=F1] ). 
In donors with primary or secondary demyelination, however, we found only the GABA_6_CCK_LAMP5 subtype lower in the DLPFC in donors with primary demyelination and secondary demyelination ( Fig. 2A [rid=F2] , 2B [rid=F2]Table S3 [this file] ). 
From a global perspective, we identified genes such as Myelin basic protein ( ) and Alpha-crystallin B ( ) differentially expressed in oligodendrocytes between control and demyelination groups ( Fig 2E [rid=F2] , Table S4 [this file] ). We then clustered oligodendrocytes into subgroups ( Fig 2F [rid=F2] , 2G [rid=F2] , Table S5 [this file] ) and examined compositional differences across brain regions and demyelination states ( Table S6 [this file] ). Genes distinguishing this Oligo_0_MOBP compared to other oligodendrocyte subgroups showed enrichment of expression programs related to cellular morphogenesis and axonogenesis ( Fig S1A [rid=SD2] , Table S7 [this file] ), suggesting a myelinating phenotype for this subgroup. 
Analysis of these two subgroups showed enrichment of marker genes associated with distress or dysregulation by means of active protein folding, response to temperature stimulus and response to unfolded protein ( Fig S1B [rid=SD2] , S1C [rid=SD2] , Table S8 [this file] and S9 [this file] ). 
We next performed the same analysis on oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs), where we identified subgroups and genes differentially abundant between control and demyelination groups ( Fig 2M [rid=F2] , 2N [rid=F2] , 2O [rid=F2] , Table S10 [this file] , S11 [this file] ). In our MS donors, we observed higher proportions of subgroup OPC_2_TPST1_ARHGEF3 in NAWM; this subgroup showed enrichment of expression programs related to cell projection organization ( Fig 2P [rid=F2] , S1J [rid=SD2] , Table S12 [this file] ). 
Taking all microglia together, we identified genes - including and - differentially expressed between control and both demyelination groups ( Fig 3A [rid=F3] , Table S13 [this file] ), which also distinguish subgroups of microglia identified by clustering analysis ( Fig 3B [rid=F3] , 3C [rid=F3] , Table S14 [this file] ). 
GO analysis of genes distinguishing these two clusters pointed to processes such as immune cell differentiation, proliferation, migration and reactive inflammatory response pathways respectively ( Fig S2A [rid=SD3] , S2B [rid=SD3] and Table S15 [this file] , S16 [this file] ). This suggests the existence of a microglial signature - enriched for genes associated with inflammatory activation ( Fig S2C [rid=SD3] , Table S17 [this file] ) - that is present in non-lesional tissue specifically in MS-associated demyelination. By contrast, we observed a fourth microglial cluster, Micro_2_SOCS6_MYO1E, which showed enrichment only in the secondary demyelination group, again in all 3 brain regions ( Fig 3G [rid=F3] , Fig S2D [rid=SD3] , Table S18 [this file] ), suggesting that this signature may be a unique hallmark of demyelination accompanying diseases such as AD.

The same criteria as with ADNI data were applied (three visits with AV-1451 tau PET, structural MRI scan and a measure of amyloid), with the exception of the amyloid cut-off: since the composite reference region is not available in these datasets, we used the available regions from the cortical summary region (that is made up of frontal, anterior/posterior cingulate, lateral parietal, lateral temporal regions: full list in Supplementary file Results.xlsx [this file] , tab ‘amyloid.target’) and ‘inferior cerebellum grey matter’ as the reference. Then, we fit a 2-component Gaussian mixture model (see Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] ) and derived the cut-off of 1.53 for the ¹¹C-Pittsburgh Compound B PET, to determine amyloid positivity. 
The complete list of brain regions made available to our model is provided in the Supplementary File Results.xlsx [this file] (‘regions.available’ tab).

The top 5 biomarkers found, as well as the effect of different random initializations are shown in Supplementary File [this file] Results.xlsx, ‘Random.seeds_top.n’ tab. 
Using a 12th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-12700H, with 2.70 GHz and 20 cores, we ran the search algorithm for <3 mins per experiment ( Supplementary File Results.xlsx [this file] , tab Random.seeds_top.n, shows different random initializations of BioDisCVR). 
Table 2 [rid=fcae438-T2] highlights selected biomarkers for Experiment 1 (all results are included in Supplementary material [this file] File Results.xlsx as a spreadsheet). 
To aid with visualization, we show a representation of the brain, with the regions in the numerator in blue, and the ones in the denominator in red, in Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] . 
Table 3 [rid=fcae438-T3] highlights selected biomarkers for Experiment 2 (all results are included in Supplementary material [this file] File Results.xlsx as a spreadsheet). 
Supplementary Table 1 [this file] shows BioDisCVR results when fixing either the numerator (meta-temporal) or the denominator (inferior cerebellum grey matter). Full information on regions selected is given in Supplementary File Results.xlsx [this file] . Regional ablation analysis is shown in Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] , where we re-evaluate a biomarker after removing one region, shows remarkably consistent performance suggesting that no single region dominates the CVR biomarkers, with the exception of the biomarker tested in Experiment 3—validation set, where removing the inferior temporal gyrus reduces the performance considerably (from 362 to 854 SSE). 
We advise caution in drawing conclusions comparing the few CVR biomarkers among each other, though, since multiple configurations show similar performance (see ablation analysis in Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] ). 
Braak stage SUVR biomarkers (using the composite reference region) produced results comparable to the best biomarkers from the literature, but still worse than CVR (see Supplementary File [this file] Results.xlsx, tab Exp1_and_2). As observed in the regional ablation analysis ( Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] ), where different biomarkers exhibited similar performances, at the final computed generation of the genetic algorithm, the top 5 biomarkers exhibited comparable performance metrics, with a fitness coefficient of variation below 10% for Experiment 1 (preclinical) and below 5% for Experiment 2 (clinical), ( Supplementary File [this file] Results.xlsx). 
Furthermore, both the 95% confidence intervals and the ablation study on influential regions ( Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] ) suggest a robust fit in the available data, free of questionable influential regions. 
Third, future work could consider deriving a theoretical guarantee that a given search algorithm will find the global optimum biomarker, but in practice we found that multiple runs with random seeds produced very similar results (see ablation analysis in Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] and top-n biomarkers in Supplementary File Results.xlsx [this file] ).

PTau-217 was associated with clinical impairment (mean log hazard ratio: 1.62 (SD: 0.13), p-value range: 3.39e-33 – 8.34e-9 across scenarios; Table S2 [this file] , Table S1 [this file] ) but did not significantly increase predictive performance beyond demographics, APOE, and Lancet factors. The range of increases in mean AUROC when adding pTau-217 was 0.045–0.084 compared to Demographics+APOE+Lancet (0.616 (CI: 0.51–0.723) vs. 0.701 (CI: 0.609–0.793); Figure 2B [rid=F2] ). 6/25 p-values were statistically significant ( Figure S1 [this file] ), occurring at Years 4 (2/5 folds), 5(1), and 7(3). Years 3 and 6 had no significant p-values, and neither did Folds 1 and 5, pointing to a lack of robustness ( Table S3 [this file] ). 3/6 significant p-values were all at 7 years, which had less stable estimates due to lower sample sizes (i.e., by 7 years, more patients had been censored or experienced the event). All AUROC statistics are in Table S6 [this file] . 
Amyloid-PET was significantly associated with clinical impairment (mean log hazard ratio: 1.01 (SD: 0.0035), p-value range: 3.16e-32 – 0.0017; Table S2 [this file] ). The largest difference in mean AUROC between PET+Demographics+Lancet and Demographics+Lancet was 0.108 at 5 years compared to Demographics+APOE+Lancet (0.615 (CI: 0.533–0.696) vs. 0.722 (CI: 0.655–0.789)), indicating increased predictive performance. 15/25 p-values were statistically significant ( Figure S2 [this file] ), occurring at Years 3 (1/5 folds), 4 (2), 5 (5), 6 (3), 7 (4) ( Table S4 [this file] ). 
These results were consistent when only including patients who were amyloid-positive at enrollment time ( Figure S4 [this file] ). 
Using the PACC score as a continuous outcome, Demographics+APOE+Lancet had a similar (mean: 0.125, SD: 0.026) to pTau-217 alone (mean: 0.137, SD: 0.033), but inferior to pTau-217+Demo+Lancet (mean: 0.199, SD: 0.029) ( Figure S5 [this file] ). 
Again, pTau-217 was statistically associated with AD (mean hazard ratio: 2.37 (SD: 0.4), p-value range: 4.12e-11 – 1.13e-3, Figure S6A [this file] ; Table S8 [this file] ) but did not increase predictive performance when added to a model consisting of demographics, APOE genotype, and Lancet factors. 
The range of differences in mean AUROC was 0.021–0.04, with 0.04 at 7 years compared to Demographics+APOE+Lancet (0.927 (CI: 0.885–0.97) vs. 0.967 (CI: 0.943–991); Figure S6B [this file] ). 9/30 p-values were statistically significant, occurring at Years 2 (3/5 folds), 3 (1), 4 (2), 5 (1), 6 (1), and 7(1) ( Table S9 [this file] ). 
These results remained largely unchanged when using all-cause dementia as the outcome ( Figure S7 [this file] ). 
Amyloid-PET was associated with AD diagnosis (mean log hazard ratio: 1.013 (SD: 0.0015), p-value range: 1.05e-36 – 4.79e-14 ( Table S10 [this file] , S12 [this file] ), but its predictive performance in combination with demographics and APOE genotype was comparable to demographics and APOE alone across nine yearly time points ( Figure 3 [rid=F3] ). The range of differences in mean AUROC was 0.055–0.074, with 0.074 at 5 years compared to Demographics (0.561 (CI: 0.468–0.653) vs. 0.635 (CI: 0.537–0.733); Figure 3B [rid=F3] ; Table S14 [this file] ). 15/45 p-values were statistically significant ( Figure S8 [this file] ) at Years 4 (1), 5 (3), 6 (2), 7 (1), 8 (2), 9 (3), 10 (3) (Years 2 and 3 had none; Table S3 [this file] ), pointing to a lack of robust differences. 
These results remained largely unchanged when using all-cause dementia as the outcome ( Figure S9 [this file] ). 
Next, we predicted AD in NACC using CSF Abeta42, pTau-181, total tau, and pTau-181/Abeta42 ratio, along with demographics, APOE, and Lancet factors ( Table S15 [this file] ). 
The range of mean AUROC differences between Demo+APOE+Lancet and CSF+Demo+APOE+Lancet was 0.072–0.127, with 0.127 at 2 years (0.627 (CI: 0.438–0.816) vs. 0.754 (CI: 0.577–0.931); Figure 4B [rid=F4] ; Table S17 [this file] ). 20/45 p-values were statistically significant ( Figure S10 [this file] ) at Years 2 (2/5 folds), 3 (2), 4 (2), 5 (2), 6 (3), 7 (3), 8 (2), 9 (2), 10 (2) ( Table S16 [this file] ), showing a lack of robustness. 
These results remained largely unchanged when using all-cause dementia as the outcome ( Figure S11 [this file] ). 
Using auto-machine learning, we trained LightGBM classifiers models on the UK Biobank plasma proteomics sample (N=10669; 496 cases) ( Figure S12 [this file] ), using combinations of proteomics (Note: this dataset does not include pTau-217 or any other form of pTau), demographics, APOE genotype, and Lancet factors. 
These results were largely similar when either removing the age filter ( Figure S12 [this file] ), when the outcome was all-cause dementia ( Figures S15 [this file] , S16 [this file] ), and when using logistic regression models instead of LightGBM ( Figures S13 [this file] , S14 [this file] , S17 [this file] , S18 [this file] ). 
The top 20 features for the Demo+APOE+IDPs+Lancet model showed mostly IDPs, with the top five being volume of the subiculum-body, APOEe4 heterozygosity, mean isotropic volume fraction in the corticospinal tract, a rfMRI correlation amplitude, volume of left presubiculumhead, and another rfMRI correlation magnitude ( Figure S19D [this file] ). These results were largely similar when removing the age filter ( Figure S19 [this file] ), when the outcome was all-cause dementia ( Figures S22 [this file] , S23 [this file] ), and when using logistic regression models instead of LightGBM ( Figures S20 [this file] , S21 [this file] , S24 [this file] , S25 [this file] ). 
Examining the top 20 features for the maximal Demo+APOE+Cognitive Tests+Lancet model showed a blend of cognitive tests (symbol-digit matches, fluid intelligence score, nervous mood over the last week), demographics (Age, APOE genotype), and Lancet factors (head injury, distance to nearest major road, depression, air pollution, smoking, LDL) ( Figure S26D [this file] ). These results were largely similar when removing the age filter ( Figure S26 [this file] ), when the outcome was all-cause dementia ( Figures S29 [this file] , S30 [this file] ), and when using logistic regression models instead of LightGBM ( Figures S27 [this file] , S28 [this file] , S31 [this file] , S32 [this file] ). 
The criteria and methodology for AD diagnosis in each cohort is described in the Supplemental Methods [this file] .
