Although oligomers of a variety of sizes have been implicated in Aβ-mediated synaptotoxicity, [xref] [rid=bib6] we chose to focus on the effects of a well-characterized, pathologically relevant synthetic preparation of small oligomers of Aβ ( Figure S1 [this file] A), which have consistently been identified as the most synaptotoxic Aβ species and are present in AD-affected brains. [xref] [rid=bib7] [xref] [rid=bib8] Although there is a risk that synthetic oligomers might not replicate the posttranslational modifications of those isolated from native mouse or human brain, multiple studies have demonstrated that, in practice, their properties at both the structural and the pathological level align extremely well with those of their brain-derived counterparts. [xref] [rid=bib6] 
A 2 h incubation with 200 nM Aβ induced an increase in overall excitatory glutamatergic synaptic activity, while inhibitory activity was unchanged ( Figures S1 [this file] B–S1D). However, we found that none of these parameters were altered by Aβ treatment ( Figures S1 [this file] E–S1I), although we note that these recordings were made at the soma, and it remains formally possible that the voltage waveform at the presynaptic terminal, which is not feasible to record directly, could be different. Incubation with Aβ s produced a >40% potentiation of exocytosis in response to a 10 Hz stimulus train ( Figures 1 [rid=fig1] B–1D), an effect that was similar across a wide range of Aβ concentrations ( Figures S2 [this file] A and S2B). To confirm that this effect does not reflect changes at inhibitory terminals, we expressed a pHluorin fused to the vesicular GABA transporter (vGAT-pHluorin) under the control of the GAD67 promoter, which restricts expression to GABAergic synapses. [xref] [rid=bib10] This showed no change in exocytosis following Aβ incubation ( Figures S2 [this file] C–S2E). 
We found that a brief incubation in a set concentration of cell-permeative EGTA-AM (200 μm for 90 s) depressed exocytosis in response to a single stimulus to a lesser extent following Aβ incubation ( Figures S2 [this file] F and S2G), indicating tighter physical coupling of VGCCs to the release machinery. 
We then directly linked Ca 2.3 to the effects of Aβ s on synaptic vesicle exocytosis by using SypHy-expressing neurons to show that SNX-482 abolishes potentiation of the response to a 10 Hz stimulus train ( Figure S2 [this file] H). We therefore tested the potential involvement of this mechanism, finding that mGluR5 blockade with the specific antagonist SIB-1757 did not prevent the increase in exocytosis seen following Aβ exposure ( Figure S2 [this file] H). 
We found that Aβ treatment increased PKC activity in the synaptosomes ( Figure 2 [rid=fig2] F), and this effect was blocked by the inclusion of SNX-482 ( Figure S2 [this file] I), corroborating an essential upstream role of Ca 2.3 in Aβ -linked PKC activation. 
As before, we found that Aβ treatment increased the proportion of phospho-GSK-3β within presynaptic terminals, but that this effect was prevented in the presence of any of the inhibitors ( Figure S3 [this file] A), confirming that GSK-3β lies mechanistically downstream of each of them. We found that tautomycin alone resulted in a small but significant reduction in exocytosis in SypHy-expressing neurons, while Aβ s and tautomycin together restored exocytosis to approximately control levels ( Figure S3 [this file] B). 
We showed that axons and boutons of neurons lacking surface α7-nAChR bound significantly fewer Aβ s conjugated with the fluorophore tetramethyl rhodamine (TAMRA) ( Figures 3 [rid=fig3] E and 3F), a tag that has previously been shown to have no effect on the proportions of different Aβ assembly states present in Aβ preparations made according to our protocol. [xref] [rid=bib38] Knockout of α7-nAChR did not significantly alter the postsynaptic/dendritic binding of Aβ s ( Figure S3 [this file] C), suggesting that their predominant postsynaptic binding partners are likely to be proteins other than α7-nAChR. We then used immunofluorescence to show that α-bungarotoxin treatment of Aβ -incubated neurons prevents the insertion of ENaCs into the presynaptic cell membrane ( Figure S3 [this file] D), confirming that Aβ -mediated activation of α7-nAChR lies mechanistically upstream of ENaC recruitment. 
We used 10 nM Aβ for these experiments, which has an essentially identical effect to the higher concentration used in culture work ( Figures S2 [this file] A and S2B). The paired-pulse ratio (PPR), which is the ratio of response amplitudes to each of a pair of closely spaced stimuli, is an electrophysiological index of the probability of release. [xref] [rid=bib39] We first assessed PPR at CA3-CA1 (Schaffer collateral) synapses and found no apparent effect of Aβ incubation ( Figure S4 [this file] A). 
We found that, under these conditions, exposure to Aβ s did result in a significant reduction in PPR, indicating an enhanced release probability ( Figure S4 [this file] B). 
To gain insight into the mechanism underlying enhanced release in hAPP transgenic mouse slices, we crossed the J20 line with transgenic mice bearing a heterozygous deletion of the gene encoding the pore-forming α1 subunit of Ca 2.1 VGCC ( ). [xref] [rid=bib46] While homozygous ablation results in severe ataxia, seizures, and premature mortality, [xref] [rid=bib46] mice carrying a heterozygous deletion lack any readily apparent phenotype. [xref] [rid=bib47] However, synaptic transmission in slices shows a reduced dependence on Ca 2.1 ( Figure S4 [this file] C), and we therefore hypothesized that if enhanced Ca 2.1 activity mediates the effects of Aβ s on neurotransmitter release, these effects would be ameliorated by the genotype. To support the relevance of these experiments to the earlier acute slice work, we also confirmed that the genotype conferred resistance to the effects of Aβ incubation on presynaptic function as measured using PPR ( Figure S4 [this file] D). 
Because it is not possible to assess this directly in postmortem material, we instead took advantage of an indirect index of Ca 2.1 activation, namely the tighter physical coupling of Ca 2.1 to the neurotransmitter release machinery that is part of the upregulation of Ca 2.1 function by Aβ s ( Figures S2 [this file] F and S2G) and of Ca 2.1 regulation by GSK-3β more generally. [xref] [rid=bib32] The strength of Ca 2.1 binding to syntaxin 1, a SNARE protein that mediates vesicular neurotransmitter release, provides a measure of this coupling that can be assessed by co-immunoprecipitation. Accordingly, Ca 2.1 was immunoprecipitated from cortical synaptosomal membrane samples prepared from a cohort of AD patients and non-demented control subjects ( Table S1 [this file] ). We corroborated this observation in aged hAPP mice, supporting their relevance to human disease ( Figures S5 [this file] A and S5B).

Given that 50–80% of LBDs have concomitant AD pathology ( Robinson et al., 2018 [rid=R42] ), where possible we minimized the number of individuals with advanced Braak NFT stage in our cohorts based on inclusion criteria for a neuropathological primary diagnosis of LBD ( Figure 1 [rid=F1] , Supplementary Table 1 [this file] , Methods [rid=S10] ). We identified three differentially methylated positions (DMP’s) associated with LB pathology stage at a genome-wide significance association threshold of p < 9 × 10 ( Figure 2A [rid=F2] & B [rid=F2] ), whilst a further 27 DMPs were identified at a more lenient false FDR corrected p-value threshold (q-value < 0.05) ( Figure 2A [rid=F2] , Supplementary Table 2 [this file] , Supplementary Figure 2 [rid=SD1] ). 
As expected from this reduced sample size, we observed a reduced number of significant DMPs, with only one site passing both thresholds for significance (cg13847853) ( Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). 
Next to determine potential biological function underpinning the methylation signature identified in our primary full cohort LB pathology meta-analysis, we employed gene ontology (GO) analysis on genes identified in the primary meta-analysis, identifying a set of nine FDR-significant enriched terms ( Figure 3A [rid=F3] , Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ). The method employed for the ontological analyses, which aggregates methylation around gene annotations to provide a set of genes to be tested for over representation analysis using robust rank aggregation (RRA), identified 245 genes as significant based on the fixed-effect p-value from our primary full cohort LB pathology meta-analysis ( Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ). 
Although this analysis did not highlight the region as a formal DMR, we did identify three significant DMRs ( Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ) overlapping the genes ( Figure 3B [rid=F3] , Chr3:46506206–46506519, Šidák corrected p-value = 2.69 × 10 ), the ( Figure 3C [rid=F3] , Chr16:58535416–58535556, Šidák corrected p-value = 9.76 × 10 ) and ( Figure 3D [rid=F3] , Chr 13:109741030–109741117, Šidák corrected p-value = 9.18 × 10 ). 
Taking the effect sizes for the Braak-LB associated DMPs from our primary full cohort LB pathology meta-analysis at a suggestive significance threshold (p < 1 × 10 , n = 72 loci), we found a significant overlap with the direction of effect to Braak NFT associated changes for the 21 CpGs that overlapped between the studies (i.e. present across both array platforms) ( Figure 4A [rid=F4] & B [rid=F4] , Supplementary Table 7A [this file] , binomial test probability = 0.81, q = 0.011), with 17 of the common 21 CpGs showing the same direction of effect. Similarly, we also observed a significant overlap in the direction of effect for the 72 Braak-LB associated DMPs with HD-associated changes at these CpG sites in the entorhinal cortex ( Figure 4A [rid=F4] & C [rid=F4] , Supplementary Table 7A [this file] , binomial test probability = 0.74, q = 2.3 × 10 ), with 53 of the 72 CpGs assessed across both studies showing the same direction of effect. When we took the Bonferroni significant Braak NFT associated DMPs from the Smith et al study (p < 1.24 × 10 , n = 208 loci present on the EPIC array), we found a significant overlap in the direction of effects to Braak-LB associated changes at these CpG sites ( Figure 4A [rid=F4] & D [rid=F4] , Supplementary Table 7B [this file] , binomial test probability = 0.89, q = 9.24 × 10 ), with 186 of these 208 sites showing the same direction of effect. However, we did not observe a significant overlap in the direction of effect for these NFT-associated sites with HD-associated changes in the entorhinal cortex ( Supplementary Table 7B [this file] ). Notably, neither the Braak-LB DMPs, nor the Braak NFT DMPs showed any significant overlap in the direction of effect with the midbrain HD-associated effects in the striatum ( Supplementary Table 7A [this file] & B [this file] ), indicating effects are cortex specific. Outside of this overlapping locus, no other sites even showed suggestive significance (p < 1 × 10 ) in either the Braak NFT or HD EWASs ( Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ) and similarly, none of the Bonferroni DMPs from the Braak-NFT meta-analysis (aside from cg13847853) showed suggestive significance (p < 1 × 10 ) in the primary full cohort LB pathology meta-analysis, nor in the HD EWASs ( Supplementary Table 9 [this file] ). 
Following training, the elasticnet model retained 40 sites for optimum prediction of LB pathology ( Supplementary Table 10 [this file] ) and achieved a moderate accuracy in the training cohort (Area under Receiver operator curve (AUC) = 0.86, Mathews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) = 0.54, Balanced Accuracy = 0.75). 
Both models were tested in the BDR cohort as this was not used for training ( Supplementary Table 11 [this file] ). When assessing binary cortical LB status as the outcome, better prediction performance was observed for the model trained for LB cortical pathology (AUC = 0.68, MCC = 0.31, Balanced Accuracy = 0.66) than the model trained on NFT cortical pathology (AUC = 0.66, MCC = 0.09, Balanced Accuracy = 0.53) ( Figure 4E [rid=F4] & F [rid=F4] , Supplementary Table 12 [this file] ). Similarly, when assessing binary cortical NFT status as the outcome, better prediction performance was observed for the model trained for NFT cortical pathology (AUC = 0.70, MCC = 0.29, Balanced accuracy = 0.64), than one trained for LB pathology (AUC = 0.61, MCC = 0.16, Balanced Accuracy = 0.58) ( Figure 4E [rid=F4] & F [rid=F4] , Supplementary Table 12 [this file] ). 
We identified 176 cis-mQTLs annotated to six methylation loci: cg05523624 ( ), cg09966204 ( ), cg07837822( ), cg21912448 ( ), cg15054019 and cg22516725 ( ) ( Supplementary Table 13 [this file] , Supplementary Figure 4 [rid=SD1] ), and four trans-mQTLs annotated to four methylation loci: cg05523624 ( ), cg10604836 ( ), cg06441533 ( ) and cg16262110 ( ) ( Supplementary Table 14 [this file] , Supplementary Figure 5 [rid=SD1] ). 
Finally, to test if genomic regions prioritized by GWAS of AD ( Kunkle et al., 2019 [rid=R24] ), PD ( Kim et al., 2024 [rid=R22] ) and DLB ( Chia et al., 2021 [rid=R10] ) show enrichment for LB pathology associated methylation, we employed Brown’s method to combine p-values across the disease-associated linkage disequilibrium (LD) regions ( Supplementary Table 15 [this file] ). 
Models were trained for binarized prediction of cortical LB pathology (total n = 625, Braak LB 0: n = 246, Braak LB 5–6: n = 379) across 10-fold cross validated folds and with the alpha value set to 0.5 ( Supplementary Table 8 [this file] & 9 [this file] ).

Microglia were the only cell type where the majority of interactions were driven by AD cases (Supplementary Fig. 8 [this file] ), highlighting the impact of Alzheimer’s pathology on microglial gene regulation . 
There was a strong correlation between the number of colocalizations for a particular phenotype and the number of genome-wide significant GWAS loci for that phenotype (Pearson correlation = 0.93, = 2.52 × 10 ; Supplementary Fig. 9 [this file] ).

That is, in those with multimorbidity, clinical dementia was less likely to be associated with Alzheimer’s pathology, compared to those without multimorbidity (see Supplementary Figure S1 [this file] ). 
In contrast to the physical multimorbidity measures, multimorbidity of brain LTCs was clearly associated with substantially increased risks of dementia (see Supplementary Figure S2 [this file] ). This effect seemed to be driven primarily by Parkinson’s disease, depression and mental disorders: presence of any of these was associated with greater odds of dementia (OR=1.8, 1.2-3.0), which increased further as more predictors were observed (see Supplementary Figure S1A [this file] ). 
Examining the association with neuropathological changes, the individual and combined presence of Parkinson’s disease, depression, and non-depressive mental disorders were associated with increasing risks of Lewy body pathology specifically as more of these conditions were observed (see Supplementary Figure S1B [this file] ), and adjusting for presence of Lewy body pathology largely attenuated the association between these conditions and clinical dementia (OR=1.49, 0.85–2.58). 
The association between mental health conditions and clinical dementia remained (OR=1.74, 1.03–2.99 for presence of one; 3.03, 1.06–8.94 for multimorbid depressive and non-depressive mental disorders; see Supplementary Figure S1C [this file] ). The association with Lewy body pathology however was not supported in the absence of Parkinson’s disease (OR=1.58, 0.86–2.76 for presence of one; OR=2.48, 0.73–7.61 for psychiatric multimorbidity; see Supplementary Figure S1D [this file] ), and there remained no clear relationship between these and Alzheimer’s disease pathology, nor cerebrovascular pathology. 
We also assessed the impact of missing pathological data (see Supplementary Table S1 [this file] ) or APOE status with imputed datasets, which similarly did not change any findings.

In this study, we doubled the sample size ( = 212) by including not just more healthy controls, but also brains from patients with Parkinson’s disease (PD) and Alzheimer’s disease (AD), the two most common neurodegenerative disorders (Supplementary Fig. 1a [this file] ). After stringent quality control (Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] ), 197 samples were available for downstream analysis (Fig. 1a, b [rid=Fig1] ). 
With this cutoff, we discovered an initial set of 111,419 circular RNAs expressed in neurons in overall 190 brain samples (Fig. 1a [rid=Fig1] ). circRNAs identified here were highly reproducible in replicate samples (Pearson’s = 0.63; Supplementary Fig. 1e [this file] ). 
Paired RNase R-treated and -untreated RNAseq experiments were performed in six independent samples (see Method and Supplementary Fig. 2a [this file] ). We rigorously required at least 20 unique reads per circular RNA in RNase R treated samples with at least two-fold enrichment compared to untreated samples in at least one pair (Supplementary Fig. 2a [this file] ). These circRNAs were conservatively used for downstream analyses (Fig. 1a [rid=Fig1] , validated circular RNAs in brain neurons). 98.2% of the validated circular RNAs were exon-derived circRNAs, suggesting that our filtering strategy effectively removed false-positive or lowly expressed circular RNAs (e.g., intron lariats from splicing ; Supplementary Fig. 2b, c [this file] ). 
For example, the AD-associated gene produces 25 distinct circular RNA isoforms (Supplementary Fig. 2d [this file] ). The number of circular RNAs per gene was linearly correlated with the number of exons of the host gene (Supplementary Fig. 2e [this file] ). Circularized exons were significantly longer than the average exons in the human genome (Supplementary Fig. 2e [this file] ), and had significantly less overlapping RNA binding protein (RBP) binding activity (using ENCODE eCLIP data ) than non-circularized exons (Fig. 1d [rid=Fig1] ). Similarly, the introns flanking circRNAs were longer; harbored significantly more repetitive elements; and had less overlapping RBP binding activity compared to the introns flanking non-circularized exons (Fig. 1e, f [rid=Fig1] , Supplementary Fig. 2e [this file] , see Methods). 
Cell type-preferential expression of five dopamine neuron-specific, five pyramidal neuron-specific, and one non-neuronal cells-specific circRNA was confirmed in an independent set of substantia nigra and temporal cortex samples (e.g., the source regions for laser-captured dopamine and pyramidal neurons, respectively) using RNase R treatment and qPCR (Supplementary Fig. 3a [this file] ). 
We observed the same trend even only considering the host gene with single circRNA (Supplementary Fig. 3c [this file] ). The abundance of total linear reads (i.e., spliced + unspliced reads) surrounding the back-splicing site only weakly correlated with the abundance of their associated circular reads (Spearman’s rho = 0.10, see Supplementary Fig. 2f [this file] for detail). RNA Binding Protein activity superimposed from the ENCODE eCLIP track highlighted subsets of RBPs statistically associated with these types of cell type-specific circRNAs (Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] ). 
We observed prominent expression of circRNAs from loci linked to neurodegenerative diseases (Fig. 4a [rid=Fig4] ). 80.2% of GWAS-derived AD candidate genes implicated by ref. (174 of 217) produced one or more filtered circRNAs including , , , and (see Supplementary Fig. 5 [this file] ). 12.4% of AD GWAS genes (27 of 217) produced at least one rigorously validated circRNAs. These included pleomorphic genes linked to both Mendelian and sporadic forms of PD, e.g., , and (see Supplementary Fig. 5 [this file] ). 
Unbiased enrichment analysis using the gene-disease annotations defined in DisGeNET (updated for PD and AD GWAS-implicated susceptibility genes from refs. ) showed that 20 neuropsychiatric diseases were statistically significantly enriched in circRNA loci compared to only three non-CNS diseases (Fig. 4c [rid=Fig4] , Supplementary Fig. 2g [this file] , Supplementary Data 6 [rid=MOESM4] ) out of a total of 4638 human diseases and traits. Ten addiction traits related to drug and substance abuse were enriched in circRNAs active in dopamine neurons (see an example of circRNAs from addiction-related genes and in Fig. 4e [rid=Fig4] and Supplementary Fig. 5 [this file] ). 
We confirmed and evaluated circRNA expression from two of the implicated familial disease loci— and —using a second method, qPCR with RNase R treatment. circ is one of several circRNAs back-spliced from 4 exons of the familial AD gene (Supplementary Figs. 3 [this file] , 5 [this file] ). It was highly expressed in brain neurons with over 100 unique back-splice junction reads. qPCR confirmed that circ is >20-fold enriched in both temporal cortex and substantia nigra after RNase R treatment (Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] ). 
Consistent with this, qPCR and RNase R treatment confirmed high expression in the substantia nigra, moderate expression in the temporal cortex, and minimal expression in the non-neuronal cells (Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] ). 
Furthermore, 51 circRNAs expressed in AD-vulnerable pyramidal neurons had suggestive associations with neurofibrillary tangle Braak stages with nominal values ≤ 0.05 (Supplementary Fig. 6c [this file] ). 
The mechanisms controlling the biogenesis of cell type-specific circRNAs could involve subsets of RNA binding proteins (e.g. refs. and Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] ). 
Samples with distances clearly different from the rest samples were marked as outliers (Supplementary Fig. 1c [this file] ). We also calculated pair-wise Spearman correlations of gene expression quantification across samples and measured the outlier via hierarchical clustering (Supplementary Fig. 1b [this file] ). Moreover, we tested for concordance between reported clinical sex and sex indicated by the expression of the female-specific gene and male-specific Y-chromosome gene (Supplementary Fig. 1d [this file] ). In addition to these samples used for cell type-specific transcriptome analyses, various additional control samples were analyzed (e.g., amplification controls, tissue homogenate), and technical replicates (Supplementary Fig. 1e [this file] ). In the end, 197 out of 221 samples passed QC and are used for downstream analysis (Supplementary Fig. 1a [this file] ). 
To confirm the expression of lcRNAseq-derived circRNAs in dopamine neurons and pyramidal neurons, relative abundances of target circRNAs were evaluated by qPCR in human substantia nigra or temporal cortex samples, as well as in human fibroblast and PBMC samples (shown in Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] ).

In this paper, across six cohorts, we meta-analyzed the PD burden of rare variants using the optimized sequence kernel association test (SKAT-O) per-domain in 8,888 PD cases and 69,412 controls (detailed in Supplementary Data 1 [this file] ). 
The average coverage across the four cohorts sequenced locally at McGill exceeded 652X, with over 99% of nucleotides achieving coverage greater than 30× (Supplementary Data 2 [this file] ). The complete list of these variants is provided in Supplementary Data 3 [this file] and 4 [this file] for the local and external cohorts, respectively. 
The per-domain burden analysis showed a post-False Discovery Rate (FDR) significance in the Kinase domain regions in the SKAT-O results across five of the six cohorts (Supplementary Data 5 [this file] ) and the MetaSKAT results of the meta-analysis (See Table 1 [rid=Tab1] and, for more detail, Supplementary Data 6 [this file] ). 
In our variant-level OR calculations, we did not observe any p-value significance except for p.G2019S (See Supplementary Data 3 [this file] and 4 [this file] ). 
The exclusion of p.R793M from the burden analysis resulted in the loss of the nominal significance in the ANK domain (See Supplementary Data 5 [this file] and 6 [this file] ), showing that the p.R793M was driving the nominal regional association of its domain in McGill cohort and the meta-analysis. 
In addition, the exclusion of p.Q1353K from the burden analysis did not nullify any nominal association, which limits the evidence for its protective role in PD to being solely observational (See Supplementary Data 5 [this file] and 6 [this file] ). 
While other associations in other domains did not survive the FDR corrections, nominal associations were observed (See Supplementary Data 5 [this file] and 6 [this file] ), with the ANK and Roc-COR domain region rare variants showing domain-level nominal significance in the meta-analysis. 
In this study, we include six large cohorts with a total of 8888 PD patients and 69,412 controls (further detailed in Supplementary Data 1 [this file] ), post-quality control. Additionally, two external patient cohorts from UKBB and AMP-PD, which mainly consist of European samples, were accessed and analyzed (See Supplementary Data 1 [this file] ). 
The probes used to target can be found in Supplementary Data 7 [this file] along with the full protocol at https://github.com/gan-orlab/MIP_protocol (https://github.com/gan-orlab/MIP_protocol) . 
The widest range was taken based on the aggregation of domain annotation data, and the genomic intervals were established for the following six domain regions: ARM, ANK, LRR, Roc-COR, Kinase, and WD40 (See Supplementary Data 8 [this file] ).

NERINE incorporates information on network vertices (genes) and edges (interactions) into a parametric model and is robust to the presence of uninformative genes in the network (see Table S1 [this file] for comparison with existing methods). 
The asymptotic distribution of LLR arises from a weighted mixture of a point mass at zero and a chi-squared distribution with one degree of freedom, [xref] [rid=bib30] [xref] [rid=bib31] which we confirm through null simulations ( = 0) using canonical pathways ( Figures S1 [this file] and S2 [this file] ) and artificial topologies ( Figure S3 [this file] ). 
We benchmarked NERINE’s performance against existing gene- and pathway-based rare variant tests (CMC-Fisher, Fisher minimum value, Fisher combined test, SKAT-O, and RVTT) in simulations under the alternative hypothesis ( > 0) ( Figures 2 [rid=fig2] , S4 [this file] , and S5 [this file] , STAR Methods [rid=sec8] ). NERINE consistently showed higher empirical power compared to other tests, especially in noisy networks ( Figures 2 [rid=fig2] , S4 [this file] , and S5 [this file] ). Positive control experiments on LDL and HDL cholesterol (LDL-C and HDL-C) phenotypes in UKBB whole-exome sequencing (WES) data confirmed NERINE’s ability to detect significant burden in key lipid-related pathways in European ancestry-specific ( Figures S6–S8 [this file] ; STAR Methods [rid=sec8] ) as well as pan-ancestry ( Figure S9 [this file] ; Table S2 [rid=mmc2] ; STAR Methods [rid=sec8] ) analyses. Compared with SKAT-O, NERINE yielded lower values, demonstrating its ability to leverage network connectivity to improve power ( Figure S6 [this file] C). NERINE’s estimated gene-level effect sizes and directions recapitulated known biology [xref] [rid=bib32] : rare loss-of-function (LoF) variants in and were associated with low LDL-C levels, and those in were linked to high LDL-C levels ( Figure S6 [this file] D). Similarly, for the HDL-C phenotype, it linked rare LoF variants in , , and to low HDL-C levels and those in , , , and to high HDL-C levels. ( Figure S6 [this file] E). 
In simulations with canonical pathways (NOTCH, WNT, protein export, and EGFR signaling) for an artificial binary phenotype, NERINE yielded greater power with ground-truth topologies than with randomized ones ( Figure S10 [this file] ; STAR Methods [rid=sec8] ). Additionally, it achieved higher LLRs and lower values with real topologies than with random ones in simulations focusing on significant lipid-related pathways for binarized LDL-C and HDL-C phenotypes in the UKBB ( Figure S11 [this file] ; STAR Methods [rid=sec8] ). 
For example, liver co-expression best captured core HDL-related genes (Bonferroni [Bonf.] = 1.34 × 10 ), physical/genetic interactions best described the VLDLR pathway (Bonf. = 2.50 × 10 ), and liver co-essentiality best represented lipid metabolism (Bonf. = 1.58 × 10 ) ( Figures 3 [rid=fig3] A and S12 [this file] ; Table S3 [rid=mmc3] ).

Additionally, we conducted performance benchmarking for NERINE on different simulated network architectures for 25 genes ( Figure S5 [this file] ). 
Furthermore, we evaluated NERINE’s performance with true versus randomized network architectures in simulations with the same four well-studied pathways ( Figure S10 [this file] ). 
Even without and , the module of core LDL-related genes, along with the LDL clearance and chylomicron clearance pathways remained significant for the LDL phenotype after Bonferroni correction ( Figure S22 [this file] ). 
We downsampled the high LDL vs. low LDL cohort at different case-control ratios (1/3, 1/10, and 1/60) and competitively applied NERINE across the pathway database, demonstrating NERINE’s effectiveness even in a cohort with as few as 500 cases and 500 controls ( Figure S23 [this file] ). 
Since rare variants are more susceptible to subtle effects of population stratification than common variants, we performed stratified analysis of the LDL-C phenotype in all five major ancestry groups (i.e., European, American, African American, South Asian, and East Asian) and meta-analyzed the results using Fisher’s combined test ( Figure S9 [this file] ; Table S2 [rid=mmc2] ). 
We further evaluated NERINE on real versus randomized network topologies for binarized LDL-C and HDL-C phenotypes ( Figure S11 [this file] ).

For PD GWAS genes, we identified six such modules ( Table S12 [this file] ) and for DA neuron essentiality genes, we identified 10 such modules ( Table S15 [this file] ).

Computationally, MariNET was markedly faster than mlVAR and comparable to EBICGlasso, highlighting its efficiency on larger datasets (Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). In the small dataset, the structure remained consistent, proven by the Jaccard Index (> 0.8 in all pairwise comparisons) although mlVAR exhibited higher edge weights, EBICGlasso produced more uniform and reduced connections, while MariNET provided intermediate and more consistent estimates (Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). These patterns were amplified in the medium dataset, where edge weight correlations between methods decreased: mlVAR continued to produce stronger, sometimes extreme connections, EBICGlasso remained conservative, and MariNET maintained stable, interpretable edge magnitudes (Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ). The results showed that the three methods produce stable networks with mostly similar topological characteristics (Supplementary Tables 3, 6, 9 [this file] ). 
The analysis revealed a strong positive relationship between (time spent on coronavirus-related activities, such as watching news, thinking about the pandemic, or discussing it with friends) and (concerns about the pandemic) (Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] A and Supplementary Table 11 [this file] ). 
We also analyzed the data with the two-step mlVAR [ 14 [rid=CR14] ], which is the method used in the data source study, as well as EBICGlasso [ 15 [rid=CR15] ] (Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] B, Supplementary Table 12 [this file] and Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] C, Supplementary Table 13 [this file] , respectively). The three methods find similar relationships among the variables, as shown on Supplementary Tables 14, 15 [this file] , were similar topological measurements and small differences between methods output are measured. 
Continuous variables were represented as nodes in the network, capturing their pairwise interactions over time (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] A and Supplementary Table 16 [this file] ). 
Nevertheless, the algorithm captures general interactions due to the inverse distribution of variables such as UPSIT, MOCA, and Schwad ADL (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] B and Supplementary Table 17 [this file] ). 
We found that the greatest difference between the MariNET and EBICGlasso networks comes from the ADL39 and Mob39 relationships, which is positive when both methods are used but higher in the case of MariNET (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] C and Supplementary Table 18 [this file] ). 
Upon deeper analysis, this positive interaction was observed only in patients who exhibit a Hoen and Yahr scale of 2 or lower, indicating that this positive relationship is induced only during the early stages of PD, becoming close to 0 or negative in higher stages of the disease (Supplementary Table 21 [this file] ). 
In the first case, MariNET successfully corrected the artificially imposed negative interaction between UPSIT and UPDRS3 (Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] A and Supplementary Table 22 [this file] ). However, skipping this covariate adjustment resulted in a spurious significant interaction (Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] B and Supplementary Table 23 [this file] ). In this study, the details of X chromosome genotyping data quality control and imputation were shown in Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] . 
The complete QC pipeline was described in Supplementary Methods [this file] . After QC, a total of 4,467 PD patients (3,996 MEGA and 471 WGS), including 2,822 males and 1,645 females across 15 cohorts ( Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ), encompassing 33,406 clinical follow-up visits, with 213,758 X chromosome SNPs were retained for downstream analysis. 
Only CoxPH models with more than 10 events (defined as occurrences of GCI or HY3) were reported ( Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). 
These SNPs were then compared to those showing significant linkage disequilibrium (r > 0.6) with susceptibility SNPs for AD, PD, or LBD (total 485 SNPs showed LD with 11 susceptibility SNPs in Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ), ensuring a focused examination of potential unique genetic signatures and overlaps. 
Detailed methods, including statistical parameters and tools used for colocalization, are provided in the Supplementary Methods [this file] . 
The quantile–quantile (QQ) plot of the XWSS analysis revealed inflation (genomic inflation factor (λ ) = 1.055–1.135) ( Supplementary Fig. 2A [this file] – C [this file] ), yet the LDSC intercept estimates (0.977–1.003) demonstrated that this inflation primarily reflected polygenic architecture rather than confounded by population stratification. 
The LD patterns analysis revealed that rs138116640 was in linkage disequilibrium with 31 SNPs in the combined analysis ( Supplementary Fig. 3A [this file] ). Compared to non-carriers, rs138116640 carriers exhibited a significantly higher risk, with a HR of 3.23 (95% CI = 1.94 – 5.37, -value = 6.36×10 ) for progression to GCI ( Supplementary Fig. 4A [this file] ). Additionally, rs193287960 was in linkage with 34 SNPs in the male-only analysis ( Supplementary Fig. 3B [this file] ). rs193287960 carriers exhibited a higher risk with a HR of 4.02 (95% CI = 2.26 – 7.14) and -value = 2.18×10 ( Supplementary Fig. 4B [this file] ). Carriers of these independent SNPs also showed a significantly higher risk for GCI compared to non-carriers ( Supplementary Fig. 4C [this file] – M [this file] ). 
In the PPMI cohort, rs144112368 was associated with GCI in both combined and male-only analyses, while rs185903733 was associated in male-only analysis ( -value < 0.05) ( Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). 
Based on 11 previously reported independent SNPs associated with the risk of developing PD (three SNPs) , AD (seven SNPs) , or LBD (one SNP) on the X chromosome ( Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ), we identified a total of 485 SNPs (134 SNPs in PD; 350 SNPs in AD; one SNP in LBD) in high linkage disequilibrium (LD) (r > 0.6) with these 11 SNPs. 
To address the moderate genomic inflation (λ = 1.106–1.17) identified in the XWSS HY3 analysis ( Supplementary Fig. 5A [this file] , C [this file] , E [this file] ), where the LDSC intercept (1.089–1.111) indicated potential confounding biases, we corrected the test statistics based on the LDSC intercept. This adjustment successfully reduced genomic inflation, with post-correction λ values ranging from 1.009 to 1.075 ( Supplementary Fig. 5B [this file] , D [this file] , F [this file] ). 
The LD patterns analysis showed rs111708875 was only in linkage with four SNPs in female-only analysis ( Supplementary Fig. 6A [this file] ), and the rs111708875 carriers exhibited a higher risk with an HR of 4.14 (95% CI = 2.55 – 6.67) and -value = 5.20×10 ( Fig. 3 [rid=F3] ). rs3128076 showed linkage disequilibrium with 33 SNPs, and many of these SNPs also exhibited X-chromosome-wide associations with motor impairment in combined analysis ( Supplementary Fig. 6B [this file] ). It should be noted that the rs3128076 carriers showed a reduced risk of motor impairment (HR = 0.72, 95% CI = 0.62–0.84, -value = 3.19×10 ) ( Supplementary Fig. 7 [this file] ). 
We observed that rs3128076 was associated with HY3 in the combined analysis in the HBS cohort, while rs111708875 was associated with HY3 in female-only analysis in the PPMI cohort ( -value < 0.05) ( Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). 
Of the 40 identified variants (34 from GCI and six from HY3), one was significantly associated with gene expression in GTEx (FDR < 0.05, Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ). Colocalization analysis revealed that no posterior probabilities of > 0.70 were identified, indicating a lack of evidence supporting the hypothesis that the identified variants in the eQTL and XWSS datasets were associated with a shared causal variant ( Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ).

Through visual inspection of the 40 components, we retained 11 ICA components that showed clear grey matter binding excluding remaining components capturing non-relevant signal (e.g. white matter, ventricles, skull, etc.) ( Supplementary Figure 1 [this file] ). When partitioning the sample again (i.e. k=4) one of the Aβ positive groups was almost entirely preserved ( Supplementary Figure 2 [this file] ). Visualising the centroid locations for each of the three clusters we observed low binding across the cortex in the Aβ negative cluster (IDEAS: n=4729, mean CL=2), and within the Aβ positive clusters: the Aβ+ (IDEAS: n=3148, mean CL=86) had loading in components capturing the canonical regions used for Aβ-PET quantification (i.e. CL like) whereas the Aβ+ (IDEAS: n=2484, mean CL=76) cluster had binding across the cortex with predominant binding in occipital components ( Supplementary Figure 3 [this file] ). Calculating these mean difference maps for each tracer independently produced the same gradient, indicating this was not a feature of Aβ-PET tracer ( Supplementary Figure 4 [this file] ). 
In general, there was a higher proportion of Aβ+ participants assigned to the Aβ+ cluster compared to the Aβ+ cluster, except for the LEADS cohort where proportions were similar (% Aβ+ vs. Aβ+ : IDEAS 24% vs. 30%; ADNI 20% vs. 28%; UCSF 20% vs. 25%; LEADS 38% vs. 38%) ( Supplementary Figures 5a [this file] ). Contrasting CL values for each Aβ positive cluster showed no consistent differences in overall Aβ load as defined within standard regions for quantification ( Supplementary Figure 5b [this file] ). 
We observed that cluster assignment over time was consistent ( Supplementary Figure 6 [this file] ), with both cohorts showing similar within cluster stability ranging from 85–95%. Finally, we observed in participants assigned to the Aβ negative cluster at one observation there are similar proportions moving to either the Aβ+ (4% ADNI; 6.1% LEADS) or the Aβ+ (3.5% ADNI; 9.1% LEADS) cluster indicating divergent pathways from Aβ negative to either Aβ positive group ( Supplementary Figure 6 [this file] ). 
We next compared sex, age, and MMSE for each Aβ cluster ( Supplementary Figure 7 [this file] ). We observed no consistent age differences between the Aβ+ vs. Aβ+ groups ( Supplementary Figure 7b [this file] ). However, there were reproducible sex differences between the two Aβ+ groups, with the Aβ+ cluster having a significantly (p<0.05) higher frequency of females in three out of four cohorts (%female Aβ+ Aβ+ IDEAS: 55% vs. 50%; LEADS: 59% vs. 48%; ADNI: 41% vs. 43% (not significant); UCSF: 62% vs. 47%) ( Supplementary Figure 7a [this file] ). 
There were marginal and weak group differences in MMSE, with the Aβ+ cluster having significantly lower MMSE score in all cohorts except the UCSF sample (mean MMSE Aβ+ vs. Aβ+ : IDEAS 23.3 vs. 23.6, Cohen’s d =−0.069; LEADS 20.2 vs. 22.4, Cohen’s d =−0.404; ADNI 24.8 vs. 25.8 Cohen’s d =−0.31; UCSF 21.0 vs. 21.5, Cohen’s d =−0.068 (not significant)) ( Supplementary Figure 7c [this file] ). 
To exclude the possibility that Aβ positive PET differences were an artifact due to head size we compared total intracranial volume observing no differences ( Supplementary Figure 8a [this file] .). Finally, we assessed if there were differences in bilateral hippocampal volume between the two Aβ positive clusters with only LEADS showing significant differences indicating the Aβ+ cluster has greater bilateral hippocampal volume (Aβ+ vs. Aβ+ LEADS t(368)=2.664, p=0.008) ( Supplementary Figure 8b [this file] .). 
Finally, postmortem assessment was available in a subset of the UCSF and ADNI participants (n=215 total; Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). We observed participants with an Aβ+ pattern of Aβ-PET binding presented with more severe CAA pathology at autopsy (t(114)=2.45 β=0.14, p=0.015) ( Figure 6 [rid=F6] ), with consistent relationships within each cohort ( Supplementary Figure 9 [this file] ). In general, Aβ+ patients tended to be at a more advanced Braak stage than Aβ+ patients (t(114)=1.93; β=0.08, p=0.056) ( Figure 6 [rid=F6] ), with consistent relationships within each cohort ( Supplementary Figure 9 a [this file] , b [this file] .). Finally, we did not observe any clear differences in Aβ histopathological stage, with most participants having Thal stage 4/5 pathology ( Supplementary Figure 10 a [this file] , b [this file] .). Similarly, there did not appear to be clear differences in the presence or distribution of Lewy body pathology ( Supplementary Figure 10 e [this file] , f [this file] .). 
Furthermore, is not uniformly expressed across the cortex, with gene expression showing an anterior to posterior gradient ( Supplementary Figure 11 [this file] ). 
All code and learnt matrices to project new Aβ-PET data into the ICA and PCA basis set, as well as perform cluster assignment is provided in the supplementary information [this file] of this publication.

Among 10 136 participants (median age 64, representing 50 209 090 community-dwelling adults) in the main analytic sample, 14.4% experienced loneliness at baseline (unweighted in Table 2 [rid=TB2] , applying sampling weights in Table S4 [this file] , after applying multiple imputation in Table S5 [this file] ). 
Among 8184 participants with loneliness assessed at all six waves (80.7% of the analytic sample), 169 (2.1%) experienced persistent loneliness (lonely at all waves), 5122 (62.6%) experienced persistent non-loneliness (never lonely), and 2893 (35.3%) experienced transient loneliness (variability in loneliness across waves) ( Figure 2 [rid=f2] and Table S6 [this file] ). 
In analyses stratified by baseline age, sex/gender, and social isolation at baseline, we did not find evidence of an association between either the baseline or sustained loneliness intervention and memory function in any subgroup ( Tables S7 [this file] - S9 [this file] ). 
The direction and magnitude of the estimated effects were consistent with those from the main analyses in sensitivity analyses using the 3-item scale of the Revised UCLA Loneliness Scale ( Table S10 [this file] ), applying inverse probability of censoring weighting ( Table S11 [this file] ), without using sampling weights ( Table S12 [this file] ), including only one participant within a household ( Table S13 [this file] ), and using 10 imputed datasets ( Table S14 [this file] ). As a second linear regression analysis (model 2; Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ) we included an interaction term of protein level × diagnostic group, to study whether the associations were dependent on diagnostic group as well as to study the stage specific associations. 
In ADC, we found a total of 704 proteins (23% of 3097 total proteins; Fig. 3A [rid=fcag257-F3] ) that were associated with lower small-worldness coefficients ( Supplementary Tables 1 [this file] and 4 [this file] ). Lower levels of 19 out of 37 proteins tested were related to lower small world index values, and these also included NPTX2, NPTXR, VGF and APP ( Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). These proteins were related to neuroplasticity processes ( Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). 
( ) Heatmap of CSF proteins levels ( = 3097) associated with SW values across the AD clinical spectrum in ADC as tested with linear regression. ( ) Gene Ontology (GO) biological pathways associated with lower SW using PANTHER (see Supplementary Table 2 [this file] for all pathways). 
In the ADC, we observed that a total of 74 proteins were associated with lower small world values in CU A+ of which 48 proteins were specific to this preclinical stage ( Fig. 5 [rid=fcag257-F5] ; Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). In the prodromal stage, 527 proteins were associated with small world properties of which approximately half ( = 274, 52%) were specific to this stage ( Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). These 129 proteins were mainly related to immune responses such as complement activation (GO:0006956; p = 2.15E−05; Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ) and immunoglobulin mediated immune response (GO:0016064; p = 1.29E−04). All associated GO terms can be found in Supplementary Tables 2 [this file] and 3 [this file] . 
These stage-dependent effects were most pronounced in contrasts involving MCI A+ and dementia, where protein levels frequently displayed stronger relationships with small world properties compared with earlier stages (i.e. controls versus MCI A+, controls versus dementia, CU A+ versus MCI A+ and CU A+ versus dementia; Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). 
Some of these proteins overlapped with proteins found in other stages (3 proteins in CU A+, 11 proteins in MCI A+ and 19 proteins in dementia; Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ).

We first examined sex differences in BBMs levels ( Supplemental Figure 2 a [this file] - f [this file] ). 
We first performed standard linear regression analyses to examine the associations between baseline GFAP levels and baseline BBMs ( Supplemental Figure 3a [this file] - b [this file] ). In the whole cohort ( Supplemental Table 2 [this file] ), baseline GFAP was positively associated with Aβ40 (p < 0.001), Aβ42 (p = 0.002), p-Tau231 (p < 0.001), and NfL (p < 0.001), and negatively associated with the Aβ42/40 ratio (p<0.001). When analyses were stratified by sex, all significant associations were maintained, except that in males the association with Aβ42/40 was no longer significant ( Supplemental Table 3 [this file] ). In females, significant associations remained, including the negative association with the Aβ42/40 ratio, but interestingly, Aβ42 was no longer significant ( Supplemental Table 4 [this file] ). 
We first performed standard linear regression analyses to examine the associations between baseline GFAP levels and baseline BBMs. In the whole cohort ( Supplemental Table 5 [this file] ) and females only ( Supplemental Table 6 [this file] ), baseline GFAP was positively associated with Aβ40 (Whole cohort: p = 0.008; Females: p = 0.029), p-Tau (p < 0.001), and NfL (p < 0.001). When analyses were stratified by sex, all significant associations were maintained, except that in males the association with Aβ40 was no longer significant ( Supplemental Table 7 [this file] ). 
Finally, there were no significant sex × GFAP interactions on any BBMs ( Supplemental Table 8 [this file] ). 
In the whole cohort ( Supplemental Table 9a [this file] ), which included both females and males, baseline GFAP levels were significantly associated with longitudinal increases in Aβ40 (p = 0.045), p-Tau (p < 0.001), and NfL (p < 0.001). When analyses were stratified by sex, both the association with p-Tau and NfL remained significant in males ( Supplemental Table 9b [this file] ). Whereas in females all significant associations between baseline GFAP levels and longitudinal BBMs were maintained ( Supplemental Table 9c [this file] ) and Aβ was significantly, negatively associated with GFAP (p = 0.025). Finally, there were no significant sex × GFAP interactions on any BBMs ( Supplemental Table 10 [this file] ). 
We first performed standard linear regression analyses to examine the associations between baseline GFAP levels and baseline cognitive performance ( Supplemental Figure 3a [this file] - b [this file] ). In the whole cohort ( Supplemental Table 2 [this file] ), baseline GFAP was negatively associated with global cognition (p < 0.001) and several domain-specific tests, including AVLT Total Learning (p = 0.002), AVLT Delayed Recall (p < 0.001), verbal fluency (letters) (p = 0.046) and verbal fluency (category) (p < 0.001). In males ( Supplemental Table 3 [this file] ), only MMSE (p = 0.049) and AVLT Total Learning (p = 0.026) were significantly and negatively associated with GFAP, indicating that higher GFAP levels were linked to lower MMSE scores and poorer Total Learning performance on the AVLT. In females ( Supplemental Table 4 [this file] ), baseline GFAP was negatively associated with global cognition (p < 0.001), AVLT Total Learning (p = 0.001), AVLT Delayed Recall (p < 0.001), and verbal fluency (category) (p<0.001). 
There were no significant associations between baseline GFAP and global cognition or domain-specific assessments in the whole cohort ( Supplemental Table 5 [this file] ) or stratified by males and females ( Supplemental Table 6 [this file] and 7 [this file] ). 
Finally, the sex × GFAP interaction term was significant for AVLT Delayed Recall (p = 0.017), suggesting baseline GFAP was associated with steeper declines in episodic memory in females compared to males ( Supplemental Table 11 [this file] ). 
In the full cohort, baseline GFAP was associated with poorer semantic memory performance ( Supplemental Table 12a [this file] ), reflected by longitudinal decreases in verbal fluency (category) test (p = 0.002) and poorer executive function, reflected by increased time to complete Trail Making B (p = 0.007). When analyses were stratified by sex, in males ( Supplemental Table 12b [this file] ) the same associations were found with semantic memory (p = 0.007) and additional a decrement in language was found (verbal fluency letter test p = 0.043). In females ( Supplemental Table 12c [this file] ), the same associations with executive function were observed (p = 0.002), and baseline GFAP was marginally associated with poorer performance on a semantic memory measure, the verbal fluency (category) test (p = 0.073). Finally, there were no significant between sex × GFAP interactions on either global or domain-specific cognition ( Supplemental Table 13 [this file] ). 
First, we performed linear mixed-effects regressions to examine the associations between longitudinal GFAP levels and longitudinal BBMs. In the whole cohort, increases in GFAP were significantly associated with increases in Aβ40, Aβ42, p-Tau231, and NfL (p < 0.001; Supplemental Table 14a [this file] ). Increases in GFAP were also associated with decreases in the Aβ42/40 ratio (p = 0.001); however, this association remained significant only in females ( Supplemental Table 14c [this file] ). In both the whole cohort and in males only, increases in GFAP were associated with declines in MMSE performance ( Supplemental Table 15 [this file] ). In the whole cohort, increases in GFAP were associated with declines in episodic memory performance ( Supplemental Table 16a [this file] ), reflected by longitudinal decreases in AVLT Total Learning (p < 0.001) and AVLT Delayed Recall (p = 0.003). We developed the regional vulnerability index for AD (RVI-AD) by first calculating regional effect sizes for amyloid-positive (Aβ+) AD individuals and healthy amyloid-negative (Aβ-) stable controls from two datasets: the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) (132 Aβ+ dementia cases and 223 Aβ- healthy controls) and the Open Access Series of Imaging Studies (OASIS) (36 Aβ+ dementia cases and 180 healthy Aβ- controls) (Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] , Table S1 [this file] ). The white matter effect sizes were previously published [ 45 [rid=CR45] ], now included in Table S4 [this file] . 
Cortical, subcortical (top and middle rows) effect sizes (Cohen’s d) for N = 571 subjects that included N = 168 amyloid positive AD cases and N = 403 amyloid negative controls; white matter effect sizes (third row) were reported in Table 4S [this file] [ 45 [rid=CR45] ]. 
In total, we extracted 64 regions from the whole brain, including 33 regional cortical thickness measures, 7 subcortical gray matter volumes and 24 regional white matter integrity measurements where data from left and right hemispheres were averaged (Table S1 [this file] ). 
All datasets provided APOE genotypes for all individuals and the genotyping methodology is provided in the Supplement [this file] . 
Accordingly, we computed the modified RVI as a normalized dot product of two vectors: the vector of individual regional deviations (coded as z-score deviations from the mean of the group) and the vector of AD effect sizes (Table S1 [this file] ). 
Overall, whole-brain RVI-based models demonstrated the highest robustness and consistency in capturing the APOE and FCVRS risks (see Table S2 [this file] ). 
Including the APOE genotype only slightly improved the AUC to 75% (Table S3 [this file] ,supplement [this file] ). 
To estimate RVI-AD’s long-term predictive value as part of a hypothetical regular screening program, we simulated annual, triennial, and quinquennial structural MRI assessments (Methods in Supplementary Information [this file] ). The simulations suggest that once MCI is diagnosed, RVI-AD calculated based on annual MRI had the strongest performance (AUC = 0.80), and even triannual follow-up still had clinically relevant AUC (AUC = 0.75) for a ten-year prediction of conversion to dementia (Figure S1 [this file] ).

An initial list of 69 SNPs was compiled ( Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). 
Finally, three SNP subsets were formed for analysis as follows: Group 1 consisting of 9 previously signalized subtype-SNPs, Group 2 based on 18 GWAS risk-SNPs, and Group 3 composed of combined 24 SNPs ( Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). 
Despite several SNPs appearing to be tri- or even tetra-allelic ( Supplementary Tables 1 [this file] , 2 [this file] ), no evidence was found in the current set of samples and therefore, the same numeric system (0, 1, and 2) was applied to all markers. 
For DBSCAN, various epsilon (eps, distance threshold) and minimum samples (core points threshold) were systematically tested ( Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). 
Comprehensive validation metrics for all algorithms, runs, sample sets, and k values are provided in Supplementary Table 3 [this file] . SNPs with RFI ≥ 0.1 are highlighted as high-impact drivers in Table 2 [rid=T2] ; full values for all SNPs across all groups are in Supplementary Table 4 [this file] . 
Full internal clustering validation metrics across runs, settings and algorithms that produced at least two clusters can be consulted in the Supplementary Table 3 [this file] . 
Group 1 analysis of 9 subtyping-associated SNPs ( Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ) revealed a robust two-cluster structure in biomarker-confirmed sAD cases ( Table 2 [rid=T2] and Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ), with optimal performance from agglomerative clustering at k = 2 (silhouette = 0.309, CH = 178.9, DB = 1.37) and concordant results from K-means, GMM, and DBSCAN. Alternative-allele frequency plots for Group 1 ( Figure 1A [rid=F1] ) show a marked bimodality at rs7245858, with one cluster exhibiting high alternative-allele frequency and the other low-to-absent, consistent with its overwhelming random-forest importance (RFI = 0.9455, MI = 0.2516; Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ), whereas the remaining SNPs display only modest contributions. When APOE2 (rs7412) is added (Group 1 APOE2; Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ), the same two-cluster topology is preserved (silhouette = 0.261), with rs7245858 and APOE2 emerging as the main drivers (RFI = 0.4949 and 0.4042, respectively; Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ), indicating that APOE refines but does not redefine the underlying structure. 
Peak silhouette scores varied across subsets ( Table 2 [rid=T2] ), but agglomerative clustering consistently ranked among the top performers and showed high stability across iterations, matching patterns observed for Group 1 + 2 ( Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ) Gaussian Mixture Models peaked for full Group 2 (k = 2; silhouette = 0.245), though iteration variability was notable. Noteworthy, excluding Miss_SNP (rs10456232) nearly doubled sample size, markedly improved cluster compactness (CH: 61.5→95.0, +54.6%), and enhanced solution reproducibility ( Table 2 [rid=T2] and Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ), despite its negligible contribution to clustering (RFI = 0.000; Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ). Only rs2421847 demonstrated consistent importance across all Group 2 conditions while rs10456232 (Miss_SNP) exclusion was required to unmask the full polygenic structure ( Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ). 
Indeed, rs2421847 was the most consistent Group 2 driver, exceeding RFI > 0.1 across all four subsets ( Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ), with statistically differential allele frequencies between clusters ( Figure 2 [rid=F2] ). Its importance peaked at RFI = 0.743 in the MissSNP-excluded + 2 analysis, ranging 0.149–0.743 regardless of data quality (+/− Miss_SNP) or 2 inclusion, outperforming all other markers ( Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ). 
Such sensitivity underscores the necessity of multi-step validation (MissSNP exclusion, stratification) to distinguish genuine ancestry markers from methodological illusions, positioning this thorough approach as essential for robust SNP selection in Alzheimer’s genomic studies ( Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ). Indeed, group-stratified analyses revealed distinct SNP hierarchies also for rs7245858 that dominated Group 1 clustering but showed limited influence in Group 2 (RFI = 0.0060 in raw data; 0.2226 when – Miss_SNP, and 0.0033 when + 2), exemplifying panel-optimized, population-specific ancestry signals ( Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ). This hierarchical resolution: Miss_SNP exclusion then stratification distinguishes true ancestry drivers from methodological artifacts, validating the multi-step approach essential for robust sAD genomic subtyping ( Figure 2 [rid=F2] and Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ). 
Full clustering trial results can be observed in Supplementary Table 3 [this file] and the best scoring results are depicted in Table 2 [rid=T2] . 
Average and median values considering all clustering tests are markedly lower for other k values, showing consistency for all methods ( Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). 
These results validate Miss_SNP exclusion (improved metrics throughout) while showing that smaller, panel-optimized datasets with appropriate algorithm choice yield superior sAD subtyping compared with redundant 24-SNP combinations ( Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). 
Clustering comprehensiveness is evidenced by Supplementary Table 3 [this file] reporting all metrics (silhouette, CH, DB), runs, and settings across five algorithms (k = 2–5, 3 stochastic replicates). 
While the moderate sample sizes reflect the stringent ADNI filtering prioritizing diagnostic quality over quantity - a strategy aligning with international guidelines ( McKhann et al., 2011 [rid=B30] ; Jack et al., 2024 [rid=B23] ) and whose violation has drawn critiques ( Escott-Price and Hardy, 2022 [rid=B17] ; Xavier and Pinto, 2025 [rid=B55] ), they enable robust internal replication across panels and algorithms, as evidenced by consistent k = 2 preference and Supplementary Table 3 [this file] metrics.

The leakage diagnostic supported this interpretation, as mean leakage was near zero for MULTIRF across the 16 InterSIM scenarios, whereas methods that reached high ARI but did not return a separate specific partition showed substantial cross-leakage (mean leakage 0.115 for SNF, 0.135 for RGCCA, 0.112 for mixKernel), indicating that their fused output absorbed shared-cluster structure into what should have been a modality-specific assignment ( Figure 2c [rid=F2] ; Supplementary Table 3 [this file] and full results in Supplementary Note 4 [this file] ). 
Under this setting , all factor-based methods performed well, with MOFA2, RGCCA, O2PLS, and multiRF all achieving mean ARI near 0.87 ( Figure 2a [rid=F2] ; per-method per-scenario breakdown in Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] ). The same qualitative pattern held in the heterogeneous NL-JIVE setting, where the view-specific signals differed in strength across views: multiRF retained high shared recovery (mean ), high specific recovery (mean ), and near-zero cross-evaluation leakage, whereas several baselines either lost specific recovery or showed higher leakage (full results in Supplementary Table 3 [this file] and Supplementary Note 4 [this file] ). 
On the larger NL-JIVE setting with = 1,000 and up to 500 features per view, multiRF was about twice as fast as MOFA2 ( Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). 
We selected four clusters using the shared similarity matrix on 517 HNSCC tumors derived from MULTIRF, and unsupervised assignment aligned with the four canonical Walter/TCGA subtypes without seeing any subtype label ( Figure 3a [rid=F3] , Table 2 [rid=T2] , per-pair tests and agreement statistics in Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ). Cluster-level marker and phenotype profiling then showed that this shared partition corresponds to the known HNSCC disease axis rather than to an arbitrary clustering of mixed features ( Figure 3b [rid=F3] , per-cluster tests and full marker heatmap in Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] and Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ). The same partition was concordant with the Keck five-subtype classification and, for the three mostly HPV-negative clusters, with CPTAC-like axes ( Table 2 [rid=T2] , signature scores and per-cluster axis profiles in Supplementary Fig. 5 [this file] and Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). 
Bootstrap resampling and random-seed reinitialization further showed that the shared partition was highly reproducible ( Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] ). Benchmarking against four alternative integrative methods on the identical feature panel ( Table 3 [rid=T3] ) showed that MULTIRF had the best overall balance across subtype agreement, survival separation, and survival discrimination, with full method-by-method comparisons deferred to the Supplementary Results [this file] . 
Once the shared subtype axis had been removed, the leading gene-specific axis tracked immune infiltration more strongly than any shared-component dimension ( Figure 4a [rid=F4] , b [rid=F4] , full statistics in Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ). 
These associations held after spectral re-clustering of the gene-specific similarity matrix and in sensitivity analyses restricted to HPV-negative tumors or adjusted for stage, subsite, and purity ( Supplementary Fig. 7 [this file] ). However, in the full clinical sensitivity models this association was attenuated after adding tumor purity, ESTIMATE immune score, or ESTIMATE stromal score (HR = 0.85–0.89, all 0.28; Supplementary Table 14 [this file] ), indicating that the gene-specific survival signal is largely tied to microenvironmental composition. 
The leading eigenvector loaded negatively on the EMT/stromal program and positively on keratinization, with only a weak interferon- association ( Supplementary Fig. 9 [this file] ). More than half of the top-weighted contributors mapped to the chromosome 14q32 DLK1–DIO3 imprinted cluster, with additional loading on the primate-specific C19MC trophoblast cluster, while HPV-responsive and miR-200 reference sets showed no enrichment ( Figure 4c [rid=F4] , full hypergeometric statistics and target-program assignments in Supplementary Table 8 [this file] , Supplementary Fig. 9 [this file] , and Supplementary Tables 9 [this file] and 10 [this file] ). 
Spectral re-clustering on the miRNA-specific similarity separated EMT-high from keratinization-high tumors more sharply than the shared partition did ( Supplementary Fig. 9 [this file] ), and adding the miRNA-specific cluster assignment to a Cox model already containing shared cluster, age, sex, HPV status, stage, subsite, and smoking improved the C-index from = 0.624 to = 0.652 (likelihood-ratio = 4.9×10 ) ( Supplementary Table 11 [this file] ). When the three leading modality-specific eigenvectors were modeled together with shared cluster and the same full clinical covariates, the C-index increased from = 0.624 for the clinical baseline to = 0.663 ( = 272 complete cases; Table 4 [rid=T4] , Supplementary Fig. 10 [this file] , and Supplementary Table 13 [this file] ; PFI estimates in Supplementary Table 15 [this file] ). Unlike gene EV1, the miRNA EV1 association was stable after adding tumor purity, ESTIMATE immune score, or ESTIMATE stromal score to the full clinical model (HR = 0.71–0.72, all 5×10 ; Supplementary Table 14 [this file] ). 
Full per-cluster canonical-marker tables, the Keck five-subtype crosswalk, the gene-specific axis with sensitivity-stratified Cox estimates, miRNA-specific program-overlap and putative-target analyses, the methylation-specific component, the multi-method clustering benchmark with parallel progression-free interval analyses, the nested Cox model decomposition, and bootstrap stability of the shared partition are reported in Supplementary Note 5 [this file] (HNSC Supplementary Results [this file] ). 
Additional direct-coordinate Cox benchmarks, which add each learned representation directly to the clinical Cox model rather than first reducing it to scalar age acceleration, are reported in Supplementary Results [this file] and Supplementary Table 18 [this file] . The CpG-panel ablation in Supplementary Results [this file] showed that the shared age-conversion signal was directionally consistent when the DNAm feature space was restricted to either component of the biologically motivated union panel ( Supplementary Table 19 [this file] ), supporting the use of the union panel as the primary AD- and brain-informed feature space for this preclinical analysis. 
Additional ADNI analyses, including direct Cox benchmarks, CpG-panel ablation, all-DNAm sensitivity, modality-specific quadrant analysis, per-eigenvector annotations, discrete subtype Cox modeling, and embedding-dimension robustness, are reported in Supplementary Note 6 [this file] . 
Repeating DNAm PCA and established DNAm aging measures in all available baseline CN participants with DNAm data (213 subjects, 64 conversion events) again yielded no significant adjusted associations, which eases the concern that the matched-subject restriction alone explains the DNAm-only baseline results ( Supplementary Results [this file] ).

Some of these junctions generate isoforms with a PTC within 50 nucleotides of an annotated stop codon, and are not expected to induce NMD as correctly assessed by GENCODE ( Supplementary Fig. 3a [this file] ). Other junctions classified as NMD by LeafCutter2 correspond to transcripts that lack a defined open reading frame (ORF), but are nonetheless annotated as protein-coding by Gencode ( Supplementary Fig. 3b [this file] ). 
LeafCutter2’s approach performs similarly compared to using the “nonsense_mediated_decay” transcript annotation from GENCODE ( Fig. 1f [rid=F1] ), but increases the number of annotated unproductive splicing junctions by an order of magnitude (12.1-fold, Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] ). 
To evaluate LeafCutter2’s ability to detect unproductive splicing events in a large-scale RNA-seq dataset, we applied it to 17,329 GTEx samples spanning 49 tissue types ( Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). Some of this variation may be due to technical factors, such as differences in RNA integrity ( Supplementary Fig. 5 [this file] ). Remarkably, we found a highly significant positive correlation ( ) between the expression level of and unproductive splicing levels across tissue types ( Fig. 2a [rid=F2] ) and across samples within tissue-types ( Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] ). Correlations withand expression levels across tissues were also significant ( Supplementary Fig. 7 [this file] ). 
We found a slight bias toward larger PSI for unproductive (but not productive) junctions in testis and cerebellum, consistent with reduced NMD activity in these tissues ( Supplementary Fig. 8a [this file] , b [this file] ). However, we also observed many unproductive junctions with substantially lower usage in testis or cerebellum compared to other tissues, indicating that at least some of the variation in unproductive splicing usage arise from regulated splicing rather than variation in NMD activity ( Supplementary Fig. 8a [this file] , b [this file] ). This approach allowed us to adjust for the effect of NMD efficiency by using the percentage of unproductive splice junctions out of all splice junctions as a covariate ( Supplementary Fig. 8c [this file] , d [this file] ). Indeed, we found that the correlations between delta PSI of unproductive junctions and differential gene expression Z-scores were overwhelmingly negative (635/765 pairwise comparisons with >50 differentially spliced unproductive clusters had a significant Spearman correlation between splicing and expression; 99.7% were negative) ( Fig. 2b [rid=F2] , Supplementary Fig. 9 [this file] ). 
Additional examples are shown in Supplementary Fig. 10 [this file] . 
The most significant enrichments include genes involved in RNA splicing (OR = 2.15, adjusted p = 5.1×10 in gene group III, IV and V), response to DNA damage (OR = 2.14, adjusted p = 3.1 ×10 in gene group VI), and ncRNA metabolic processes (OR = 1.90, adjusted p = 3.8 ×10 in groups I and II), all of which are enriched in tissue-regulated unproductive splicing events relative to genes with at least one unproductive splicing junction but no tissue-specificity ( Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). 
When considering the fraction of splice junction that are unproductive in each sample, similar to our analysis of GTEx samples ( Fig. 2a [rid=F2] ), we find that most samples contain 0.5–2% unproductive junction reads, with some variability between species, tissues, and developmental stages ( Supplementary Fig. 11 [this file] ). These measures of the total fraction of unproductive splice junction reads are similar whether using annotations from various sources (e.g., RefSeq, Ensembl) which sometimes differ in comprehensiveness even within species ( Supplementary Fig. 12 [this file] ). This elevation in unproductive splicing coincides developmentally with sexual maturation of the testis ( Fig. 3c [rid=F3] ), as well as an increase in the expression of relative to expression in most species ( Supplementary Fig. 13 [this file] ). 
While differences in sample sizes impaired our power to assess the correlation between unproductive splicing and gene expression in some tissues and developmental stages, the same negative correlation was generally recapitulated in well-powered comparisons across all species ( Supplementary Fig. 14 [this file] ). 
Notably, the negative correlation between unproductive splicing changes and host gene expression is observed when comparing juvenile to adult (spermatogenic) testis ( Supplementary Fig. 14 [this file] ). 
We identified thousands of conserved splicing events using progressively stringent filters for evidence of conservation ( , Supplementary Fig. 15a [this file] ). Many of these poison exons are highly conserved at the nucleotide level while lacking signatures of strong amino acid coding constraint ( Supplementary Fig. 15d [this file] - e [this file] ), consistent with selection targeting the regulatory potential of the alternative splicing event.

We then assessed the association of these PGSs with the 11 NPEs in the Adult Changes in Thought (ACT) cohort ( = 677, including 12.9% with dementia) and in the Alzheimer’s Disease Centers/National Alzheimer’s Coordinating Center (ADC/NACC) dataset ( = 5,808, including 82.7% with dementia; Supplementary Table 16 [this file] ) . The main score was significantly associated ( ≤ 2.27 × 10 ) with the three AD-related NPEs and with LATE-NC in the ADC/NACC dataset, and the signals were in the same direction in the smaller ACT study (Fig. 2a [rid=Fig2] , Supplementary Table 17 [this file] and Supplementary Supplementary Note [rid=MOESM1] ). None of the scores was significantly associated with cerebrovascular NPEs, hippocampal sclerosis or Lewy bodies (Fig. 2a [rid=Fig2] and Supplementary Table 17 [this file] ), while the genetic correlation between ADRD and Lewy body dementia was significant after the exclusion of . Results were similar across the main, no-proxy and no-biobank PGS (Supplementary Table 17 [this file] ). Regarding AF, we observed outstanding performance in imputing SVs with higher AF ( Figure 3 [rid=fig3] ; Table S6 [this file] ). Further investigation revealed that the performance of imputing SVs is poorly correlated with SV lengths ( Figure S3 [this file] ). 
The imputation accuracy was assessed by calculating the squared Pearson correlation between obtained genotypes of SNVs/indels from imputations and WGS, revealing nearly identical imputation accuracies ( Figure S4 [this file] ). 
Upon comparing the results of single-variant association tests on pooled sample imputations generated using the ADSP-Short-Var and ADSP-All-Var panels (N = 14,811 and N = 19,565), we identified 6 consensus genome-wide significant loci across 35 genes ( Table S7 [this file] ) in both association tests ( Figure 4 [rid=fig4] ). 
Our subsequent single-variant association test on the imputed SVs revealed one genome-wide significant SV ( < 5 × 10 ) and three suggestively significant ( < 1 × 10 ) SVs ( Figure S5 [this file] ). 
Further experimental validation by PCR confirmed this insertion ( Figure S6 [this file] ). 
With this larger sample set, 85.71% (48 out of 56) SVs exhibited an increase in AC, and 33.33% (16 out of 48) showed enhanced statistical significance ( Table S8 [this file] ). All the well-imputed SVs had highly similar AFs ( = 0.9939) to SVs discovered from ADSP ( Figure S7 [this file] ). 
In association analyses, ADSP-Short-Var imputation yielded more genome-wide significant signals (43) compared to TOPMed (30 signals; Table S9 [this file] ). 
Of note, 10 out of 55 indels were absent in TOPMed-r2 imputation ( Table S10 [this file] ), which are in , , , , , (polynucleotide kinase-phosphatase), , and . 
To evaluate the accuracy of imputed genotypes for those disease susceptibility indels, PCR validation was conducted on 6 indels, which are located in , , , , , and , using 17 available DNA samples from the ADGC cohorts ( Table S11 [this file] ). 
For those well-imputed SNVs and indels, 53.13% (34 out of 64) showed an increase in ACs as sample size expanded, and 52.94% (18 out of 34) increased statistical significance ( Table S12 [this file] ). Our analysis on pooled samples across ethnicities revealed 6 genome-wide significant loci, including 594 genome-wide significant variants across 31 genes, that were concordant in all 3 association tests ( Table S13 [this file] ). Regarding discordant signals, we found 31, 10, and 32 genome-wide significant variants uniquely identified in the ADSP-Short-Var, TOPMed-r2, and meta-imputation tests, respectively ( Figures 5 [rid=fig5] and S9 [this file] A).

Testing and training datasets come from totally independent databases (see Tables S1 [this file] and S2 [this file] for details). 
For this purpose, we used brain MRI from 461 patients with AD, 155 with bvFTD, 39 with semantic dementia, 41 with PNFA, 91 with PSP, and 126 with DLB for the construction of the branches of a , as well as 5346 healthy young subjects to build the trunk of the tree and 31,181 cognitively normal subjects older than 44 years to build the cognitively normal (CN) branch (see Tables 1 [rid=hbm70336-tbl-0001] and S1 [this file] for details). 
For testing, we used an independent dataset consisting of 528 CN, 488 , 90 bvFTD, 44 semantic dementia, 40 PNFA, 67 PSP, and 47 DLB subjects from entirely independent external databases (see Tables 1 [rid=hbm70336-tbl-0001] and S2 [this file] for details). 
In this experiment, the of brain anatomy obtained significantly better Top‐1 BACC ( value < 0.0001) with 55% (randomness being 14%) while the SVM‐based method achieved 46% Top‐1 BACC, indicating a lack of sensitivity for some classes, such as DLB, and an over‐detection of the CN class (see Table 2 [rid=hbm70336-tbl-0002] and confusion matrices in Figure S1 [this file] ). 
As a result, some AD patients (44% Top‐1 sensitivity) were misclassified as CN, some CN subjects were identified as DLB patients, and many DLB patients (with only 32% Top‐1 sensitivity) were incorrectly assigned to the AD and CN classes (see Table 2 [rid=hbm70336-tbl-0002] and confusion matrices in Figure S1 [this file] ). 
While on average this population is distinct from others (i.e., in terms of distance between branches), the classification of test subjects exhibits high variability (see confusion matrices in Figure S1 [this file] ). 
However, both methods, especially SVM, encountered difficulties in distinguishing MSA patients from PD patients (see confusion matrices in Figure S2 [this file] ), resulting in low Top‐1 sensitivity for MSA (ranging from 27% for the SVM‐based method to 42% for the of brain anatomy) although our lifespan tree produced higher sensitivity for this population. 
So far, the large majority of AI‐enhanced MRI analysis has been proposed for binary classification tasks between a specific pathology and healthy conditions (see Tables S6 [this file] and S7 [this file] for validation of the on binary tasks) and mainly on AD diagnosis and prognosis (see Tables S3–S5 [this file] and Figure S3 [this file] for validation of our method on AD tasks). 
For instance, when using MRI alone, Harper et al. ( 2016 [rid=hbm70336-bib-0025] ) reported that human experts using the best available visual rating scales achieved a BACC of 77% [69%–83%] for distinguishing AD from CN on post‐mortem confirmed cases, whereas our method achieved a BACC of 80% [77%–82%] for the same comparison (see Table S6 [this file] ). 
Binary classification tasks, such as distinguishing patients from controls, yield higher performance measures due to their relatively simpler nature (see the results of binary classification achieved with our framework in Tables S3–S7 [this file] ). Moreover, patterns of atrophy that easily differentiate AD from healthy subjects (see Table S4 [this file] ) become less informative when considering differential diagnoses (see Table 1 [rid=hbm70336-tbl-0001] ).
