This study focuses on 6 cognitive tests developed by Datacubed Health comprising an adaptive associative memory task (Humi’s Bistro) and gamified versions of classic executive functioning paradigms: flanker (Ducks in a Pond), Stroop (Color Clash), 2-back (Animal Parade), go/no-go (Go Sushi Go!), and card sort (Card Shuffle) ( Figure 1 [rid=zoi240187f1] and eMethods in Supplement 1 [this file] ). The app test results were summarized as a composite score (eMethods in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
Participants completed the UDS Neuropsychological Battery, version 3.0 (eMethods in Supplement 1 [this file] ), which includes traditional neuropsychological measures and the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), a global cognitive screen. 
Details of image acquisition, harmonization, preprocessing, and processing are provided in eMethods in Supplement 1 [this file] and prior publications. Voxel-based morphometry was used to test unbiased voxel-wise associations of volume with smartphone tests (eMethods in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
Internal consistency, which measures reliability within a task, was estimated for participants’ first exposure to each test using Cronbach α (details in eMethods in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
To complement ROI-based neuroimaging analysis based on a priori hypotheses, we conducted voxel-based morphometry (eMethods in Supplement 1 [this file] ) to uncover other potential neural correlates of test performance. 
Of 1163 eligible participants, 360 were enrolled, 439 were excluded, and 364 refused to participate (additional details are provided in the eResults in Supplement 1 [this file] ). The discovery and validation cohorts did not significantly differ in terms of demographic characteristics, disease severity, or cognition (eTable 1 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
Except for go/no-go, internal consistency estimates ranged from good to excellent (Cronbach α range, 0.84 [95% CI, 0.81-0.87] to 0.99 [95% CI, 0.99-0.99]), and test-retest reliabilities were moderate to excellent (interclass correlation coefficient [ICC] range, 0.77 [95% CI, 0.69-0.83] to 0.95 [95% CI, 0.93-0.96]), with slightly higher estimates in participants with prodromal or symptomatic FTLD ( Table 2 [rid=zoi240187t2] , Figure 2 [rid=zoi240187f2] , and eFigure 1 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). Reliability estimates showed overlapping 95% CIs regardless of distractions (eFigure 2 in Supplement 1 [this file] ) or operating systems (eFigure 3 in Supplement 1 [this file] ), with a pattern of slightly lower reliability estimates when distractions were endorsed for all comparisons except Stroop (Cronbach α). 
Cognitive tests administered using the app showed evidence of convergent and divergent validity (eFigure 4 in Supplement 1 [this file] ), with very similar findings in discovery ( Figure 3 [rid=zoi240187f3] A) and validation cohorts ( Figure 3 [rid=zoi240187f3] B). 
Worse performance on all app measures was associated with greater disease severity on CDR plus NACC-FTLD ( range, 0.38-0.59) ( Table 1 [rid=zoi240187t1] , Figure 3 [rid=zoi240187f3] , and eFigure 4 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
Compared with the MoCA (AUC, 0.68 [95% CI, 0.59-0.78), app composite performance (AUC, 0.82 [95% CI, 0.76-0.88]) more accurately differentiated participants without symptoms and with prodromal FTLD ( of comparison, −2.49 [95% CI, −0.19 to −0.02]; = .01), with similar accuracy to the UDS3-EF (AUC, 0.81 [95% CI, 0.73-0.88]); highly similar results (eTable 2 in Supplement 1 [this file] ) were observed in the discovery ( Figure 3 [rid=zoi240187f3] C) and validation ( Figure 3 [rid=zoi240187f3] D) cohorts. 
Voxel-based morphometry (eFigure 5 in Supplement 1 [this file] ) suggested worse app performance was associated with widespread atrophy, particularly in frontotemporal cortices. 
Only for card sort were distractions (eTables 3 and 4 in Supplement 1 [this file] ) associated with task performance; those experiencing distractions unexpectedly performed better (β = 0.16 [95% CI, 0.05-0.28]; = .005).

Supplementary Table 1 [this file] reports the demographic and clinical characteristics for the 116 autosomal dominant FTLD mutation carriers and 39 familial controls, representing cognitively normal non-mutation carriers from families with a known , or mutation. 
Protein module membership assignments are provided in Supplementary Table 2 [this file] . On the basis of Gene Ontology (GO) and cell type enrichment analyses (Supplementary Table 3 [this file] and Supplementary Fig. 1 [rid=MOESM1] ), 28 out of the 31 modules had a clear primary ontology that was used for annotation, while 3 modules did not evidence clear ontology (labeled ‘ambiguous’). 
The exact values are reported in Supplementary Table 4 [this file] . , Module eigenprotein levels by case status for six of the most strongly FTLD-associated modules. 
Seven of 31 modules showed significant differences between symptomatic carriers and controls (Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ). 
We also examined correlations with CDR + NACC-FTLD sum of boxes, CSF NfL and frontotemporal volumes (Fig. 2b [rid=Fig2] and Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ). 
To complement network analyses, we examined differential abundance of all 4,138 proteins to identify individual CSF proteins driving module-level differences in gene-stratified comparisons of symptomatic carriers, presymptomatic carriers and controls (Supplementary Table 5 [this file] and Extended Data Fig. 1 [rid=Fig6] ). M26 spliceosome had the highest proportion of individual differentially abundant proteins in symptomatic and carriers (Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ), including the nuclear proteins TRA2B, TMPO and HNRNPAB. 
Supplementary Table 7 [this file] reports AUC values with 95% confidence intervals and sensitivity/specificity thresholds for all differentially abundant proteins across group comparisons. 
Module correlations with global cognitive trajectories in the full sample are provided in Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Table 7 [this file] . 
Information on the association between all network module eigenproteins and cognitive trajectory in the full sample, within each gene and within presymptomatic mutation carriers is provided in Supplementary Table 8 [this file] . Color-filled triangles represent individual proteins that survived FDR correction in two-tailed proteome-wide differential correlational analyses ( = 646 total proteins; full list in Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ). 
To determine whether cognitive findings were driven by specific gene groups, post hoc analyses examined gene-stratified correlations between modules and cognitive trajectories (Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ). 
On differential correlational analyses, 646 proteins were significantly correlated with global cognitive trajectories in the full sample (FDR < 0.05; Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ). 
We applied the same WGCNA methods to CSF SomaScan data from an independent cohort of individuals with sporadic PSP-Richardson syndrome (RS) to determine whether protein co-expression patterns identified in genetic FTLD could be reproduced in sporadic FTLD, specifically a sporadic FTLD tauopathy (Supplementary Table 9a [this file] ). Of the 31 synthetic eigenproteins derived from the genetic FTLD protein module assignments, five were significantly altered in sporadic PSP-RS versus controls after FDR correction (decreased in PSP-RS: M28 synapse assembly/axon, M2 presynapse, M3 postsynapse/glycosylation and M19 neuron migration; increased in PSP-RS: M29 ECM; Fig. 4b [rid=Fig4] and Supplementary Table 9b [this file] ). 
The exact values are reported in Supplementary Tables 9 [this file] and 10 [this file] . , , Synthetic eigenprotein box plots for key modules from 4RTNI (35 CTL and 30 PSP-RS) ( ) and BioFINDER 2 (248 CTL, 58 AD and 29 FTLD) ( ) analyses. 
To assess whether proteomic signatures from the FTLD network were specific to FTLD or more broadly reflective of neurodegeneration, irrespective of molecular etiology, we constructed synthetic eigenproteins in a second replication cohort (BioFINDER 2; Supplementary Table 10a [this file] ) comprising 29 patients with frontotemporal dementia clinical syndromes, 87 AD patients matched on demographics and disease severity, and 248 AD biomarker-negative controls. Thirteen synthetic eigenproteins differed between FTLD and controls, six differed between FTLD and AD and only two differed between AD and controls (all FDR < 0.05; Supplementary Table 10b [this file] ). 
The stronger concordance between FTLD and PD was driven by shared decreases in neuronal markers of neurodegeneration from M2 presynapse (for example, NPTX2, LRFN2 and NRXN1) and M22 autophagy (for example, SEMA4D), whereas these modules were enriched for proteins with increased abundance in AD (Extended Data Fig. 3g [rid=Fig8] and Supplementary Table 11 [this file] ). 
These AD networks were built using multiplatform (SomaScan + tandem mass tag-based mass spectrometry (TMT-MS); Dammer et al. ) and TMT-MS (Modeste et al. ) proteomic approaches, which also allowed us to probe the influence of platform on FTLD and AD network overlap (Fig. 5 [rid=Fig5] and Supplementary Table 12 [this file] ). 
The exact values are reported in Supplementary Table 12 [this file] . 
Clinical and demographic characteristics across the three gene groups and controls are provided in Supplementary Table 1 [this file] . 
The exact p-values are reported in Supplementary Table 11 [this file] .

For DTI-based FA analyses as well as for GM volumetry analyses, no significant differences between SCD and healthy controls could be detected (Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] , Supplementary Tables 8 [this file] and 9 [this file] ). 
For the longitudinal WBSS analysis of voxel-wise FA values, an increase in the size of all the clusters could be observed in 10 patients with nfPPA vs 39 controls (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] , Supplementary Tables 1 [this file] and 2 [this file] ): longitudinal white matter degeneration could be observed along the corpus callosum and frontal lobes, with a prominent additional involvement of the left frontal lobe white matter. The gini importance of the left temporal lobe was in every cross-validated fold the most important feature, while the other features differed in between every fold in their hierarchical order (Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ). 
The increase of the differences from controls in both extent of the clusters (Supplementary Tables 1 [this file] – 4 [this file] ) and significance for the involved TOIs (Figs. 2 [rid=Fig2] and 3 [rid=Fig3] ) supports the hypothesis of trans-axonal spreading of FTLD pathology [ 44 [rid=CR44] ].

Furthermore, IF was conducted on two NDCs and a subset of four to five cases per group (FTLD‐GRN, FTLD‐C9orf72, sFTLD‐TDP, FTLD‐MAPT, sFTLD‐Tau, AD) in affected regions (FC, TC) to study the colocalization of WDR49‐positive cells with pathological inclusions (TDP‐43 for FTLD‐TDP subtypes, tau for FTLD‐Tau subtypes and AD, amyloid‐beta for AD; Table S1 [this file] ). WDR49 was visualized using antirabbit Cy3, and pathology markers were visualized (anti‐TDP‐43, antiphospho‐Tau, anti‐β‐amyloid) using antimouse Alexa 488 (Table S1 [this file] ).

Plasma samples were obtained from the Bio-Hermes study , the Emory Goizueta Alzheimer’s Disease Research Center (GADRC), the Religious Orders Study and Rush Memory and Aging Project (ROSMAP) as well as a collection of clinical research studies at Emory University (Emory Other) (Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] and Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). Using linear models, we associated each plasma protein measurement with the Aβ PET standardized uptake value ratio (SUVR) in Bio-Hermes, plasma pTau217 in Emory GADRC, CSF total Tau (tTau)/Aβ42 in Emory Other and a composite measure of neuritic and diffuse plaque load in ROSMAP, adjusting for age, sex and race as needed in each cohort based on exploratory analyses (Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). 
After adjustment for false discovery, 214 proteins were observed to be significantly associated with β-amyloidosis in the meta-analysis, with 131 proteins positively associated and 83 proteins negatively associated (Fig. 2a [rid=Fig2] and Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). Most of the proteins identified as significantly associated with Aβ plaque using a quantitative linear modeling approach were also observed as significant in a logistic meta-analysis model in which β-amyloidosis was defined using a binary cutoff in each cohort (Extended Data Fig. 1b [rid=Fig8] and Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). Because genotype is strongly positively associated with β-amyloidosis, we assessed which amyloid-associated proteins were dependent upon (Supplementary Tables 2 [this file] and 3 [this file] ). Therefore, approximately 75% of proteins were no longer significantly associated with amyloid after adjustment, including SPC25 (Fig. 2c [rid=Fig2] and Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). 
Seventeen proteins out of 425 plaque-enriched or plaque-depleted proteins in brain identified by laser capture microdissection mass spectrometry-based proteomics of Aβ plaques were found in common with plasma proteins associated with Aβ plaque (Fig. 2f [rid=Fig2] and Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ). We identified 150 plasma proteins positively associated and 87 plasma proteins negatively associated at a nominal statistical threshold with levels in brain (Extended Data Fig. 1h [rid=Fig8] and Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ). 
The best one-protein, two-protein, three-protein and four-protein ratios ( = 2, 4, 6 and 8 total proteins) are provided in Supplementary Table 6 [this file] . Discrimination accuracy did not improve using proteins less influenced by ε4 in non-ε4 individuals (Extended Data Fig. 2d [rid=Fig9] and Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). 
One protein, the neuronal pentraxin receptor (NPTXR), was nominally significantly positively associated with cognitive function across all cohorts (Extended Data Fig. 3a [rid=Fig10] and Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ). After meta-analysis, synaptic vesicle membrane protein VAT-1 homolog (VAT1) and amyloid-β precursor-like protein 1 (APLP1) were most strongly positively associated with cognitive function (higher levels associated with better cognitive function), whereas ACHE and SPC25 were most strongly negatively associated with cognitive function (higher levels associated with worse cognitive function) (Fig. 3a [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ). Out of a total of 283 proteins associated with cognitive function, 42 were also significantly associated with cerebral β-amyloidosis (Fig. 3b [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ). After adjusting for Aβ, VAT1 and APLP1 remained significantly positively associated, and ACHE remained significantly negatively associated with cognitive function (Fig. 3a [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ). When comparing proteins associated with cognitive function from the meta-analysis with brain-linked proteins from ROSMAP, we identified 11 proteins that overlapped, including apolipoprotein A-IV (APOA4) and Ras-related protein Rab-1A (RAB1A) that were positively associated with cognitive function and ACHE that was negatively associated with cognitive function (Fig. 3e [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ). 
The list of overlapping proteins is provided in Supplementary Table 7 [this file] . , Proteins associated with cognitive function most dependent upon . Proteins associated with each neuropathology are provided in Supplementary Table 8 [this file] , with BPs for each neuropathology association provided in Supplementary Fig. 1 [rid=MOESM1] . , Overlap of proteins associated with cognitive function and proteins associated with levels in brain (top) and overlap of proteins associated with cognitive function and no other neuropathology with proteins associated with levels in brain (bottom). 
We used the rich neuropathological data from ROSMAP to identify plasma protein associations with multiple different neuropathologies commonly observed in AD cases at autopsy, including Lewy bodies, TDP43, cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA) and different types of vascular disease (Fig. 3f [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ), adjusting for age, sex and race as needed but without adjustment for other pathologies. We found that approximately half of the proteins associated with cognitive function in ROSMAP (255 out of 496) were also associated with at least one neuropathology (Fig. 3f [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ). A large majority of plasma proteins associated with each neuropathology were not significantly correlated with brain levels (Extended Data Fig. 4 [rid=Fig11] and Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ). 
A total of 211 proteins were associated with CI.other after meta-analysis (Extended Data Fig. 5a [rid=Fig12] and Supplementary Table 9 [this file] ). We observed minimal overlap between proteins associated with CI.other and proteins associated with different neuropathologies in ROSMAP (Extended Data Fig. 5c [rid=Fig12] and Supplementary Table 9 [this file] ), consistent with the findings observed within the ROSMAP-only analysis.

A convenience sample of 6514 participants pooled from 21 different cohorts was included ( eMethods 1.1 [this file] and eTable 1 [this file] ). Participants were either cognitively unimpaired (defined as not MCI, dementia or any other major neurological disorder; see eMethods 1.1 [this file] ) or met established clinical criteria for a syndromic diagnosis of MCI, AD dementia (including posterior and logopenic variants), dementia with Lewy Bodies, behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia, semantic or nonfluent variant primary progressive aphasia, Parkinson disease with cognitive impairment, progressive supranuclear palsy, or corticobasal syndrome. 
Additional details can be found in eMethods 1.2 [this file] . 
To visually assess the large number of tau-PET scans in our sample, we gathered a team of 18 readers, including nuclear medicine physicians and neuroimaging researchers, who were trained using materials provided by Avid Radiopharmaceuticals to interpret [ F]flortaucipir PET scans ( eMethods 1.3 [this file] – 1.4 [this file] ). The robustness of our visual interpretation procedure was validated in inter-rater agreement analyses (Cohen’s κ across readers, mean: 0.89, range 0.78–0.97, eResults 2.1 [this file] and eFigure 2 [this file] ). 
Additional details can be found in eMethods 1.5 [this file] . 
Generalized additive mixed models were used to estimate average temporal trajectories of the CDR-SB score ( eMethods 1.6 [this file] ). 95% confidence intervals were calculated using the Wald approximation. 
This approach combines the “naïve” hazard functions for clinical progression and mortality to account for the competing risk of death during follow-up precluding clinical progression, allowing for the estimation of unbiased probabilities of progression ( eMethods 1.7 [this file] ). These estimates were further adjusted to account for the increased mortality risk associated with MCI or dementia (see eMethods 1.7 [this file] ). 95% confidence intervals of the estimated absolute risks were computed using bootstrap (n=1000 repetitions). 
Analyses of the clinical outcomes of the Aβ-PET-negative/tau-PET-positive groups were regarded as exploratory due to reduced sample size and reported in the Online Supplement [this file] . 
Analyses of between-cohort variability in the frequency of positivity and risk estimates were performed by estimating the additional explained variation that can be attributed to cohort membership ( eMethods 1.8 [this file] ). 
Baseline and follow-up characteristics of the included participants are reported in Table 1 [rid=T1] , eTables 2 [this file] – 9 [this file] , and eFigure 1 [this file] . 
Quantitative neuroimaging analyses revealed significantly elevated tau-PET signal in temporo-parietal and frontal regions ( eResults 2.2 [this file] and eFigure 3 [this file] ). The estimated frequency of tau-PET positivity in cognitively unimpaired aged under 50 years was below 1%, and increased from 3% [95% CI, 3%–4%] at 60 years to 19% [95% CI, 15%–24%] at 90 years ( Figure 1A [rid=F1] , eTable 10 [this file] ). The estimated frequency of Braak stages V-VI in cognitively unimpaired participants from the Neuropathology cohort paralleled that of tau-PET positivity until ~60 years of age but was consistently lower for older ages ( Figure 1A [rid=F1] , eTable 10 [this file] ). 
In patients with MCI, the estimated frequency at 40 years was 26% [95% CI, 20%–33%] and increased with age (from 35% [95% CI, 31%–39%] at 60 years to 51% [95% CI, 46%–57%] at 90 years, Figure 1B [rid=F1] , eTable 10 [this file] ). Among participants with clinically diagnosed AD dementia, tau-PET positivity was estimated to be >85% under 65 years of age; however, its estimated frequency decreased with advancing age (from 88% [95% CI, 86%–91%] at 60 years to 65% [95% CI, 58%–72%] at 90 years, Figure 1C [rid=F1] , eTable 10 [this file] ). This decreasing trend was also observed for the frequency estimates of Braak stages V-VI in the Neuropathology cohort, which closely matched the frequency curve of tau-PET positivity ( Figure 1C [rid=F1] , eTable 10 [this file] ). 
The estimated frequency of positivity was relatively high in frontotemporal dementia patients, particularly in those with semantic variant primary progressive aphasia (20/29, 69% [95% CI, 49%–85%]), the majority of whom were Aβ-PET negative ( eFigure 4D [this file] ). 
Among cognitively unimpaired participants and those with a clinical diagnosis of MCI and AD dementia, tau-PET positivity was more frequently observed in Aβ-PET-positive than in Aβ-PET-negative individuals (Aβ-PET-positive vs Aβ-PET-negative, cognitively unimpaired: 268/1074, 25% [95% CI, 22%–28%] vs 46/2071, 2% [95% CI, 2%–3%]; MCI: 511/695, 74% [95% CI, 70%–77%] vs 43/505, 9% [95% CI, 6%–11%]; AD dementia: 976/1050, 93% [95% CI, 91%–94%] vs 33/107, 31% [95% CI, 22%–40%], eFigure 4A [this file] – C [this file] ). Older age was associated with higher frequency estimates of tau-PET positivity among Aβ-PET-positive cognitively unimpaired individuals, but with lower frequencies among those Aβ-PET-positive participants with MCI or AD dementia ( Figure 2A [rid=F2] , eTable 11 [this file] ). In Aβ-PET-negative participants, the estimated frequency of positivity increased with age in the cognitively unimpaired and MCI groups, while remained approximately constant or decreased slightly for those Aβ-PET-negative participants with AD dementia ( Figure 2B [rid=F2] , eTable 11 [this file] ). Higher Aβ levels (Centiloids) were associated with increased probability of a positive tau-PET scan in a dose-dependent manner ( eFigure 5 [this file] ). 
Frequency estimates of tau-PET positivity according to age, Aβ-PET status, sex, and APOE ε4 carriership can be seen in eFigures 6 [this file] – 7 [this file] and eTables 12 [this file] – 15 [this file] . The estimated frequency of tau-PET positivity was higher in Aβ-PET-positive cognitively impaired women than in men (75-year-old MCI, 74% for women vs 62% for men, difference 12% [95% CI, 6%–19%]; 75-year-old AD dementia, 91% for women vs 85% for men, difference 6% [95% CI, 3%–9%], eFigure 6 [this file] ), but this association was not statistically significant in cognitively unimpaired individuals ( eFigure 6C [this file] – D [this file] , eTables 12 [this file] – 14 [this file] ). APOE ε4 carriership was associated with increased probability of tau-PET positivity in both Aβ-PET-negative and Aβ-PET-positive cognitively unimpaired (75-year-old Aβ-PET-negative: 4% for carriers vs 2% for non-carriers, difference 2% [95% CI, 0%–3%]; 75-year-old Aβ-PET-positive: 32% for carriers vs 21% for non-carriers, difference 11% [95% CI, 7%–17%]) and Aβ-PET-positive impaired individuals (75-year-old MCI, 71% for carriers vs 59% for non-carriers, difference 12% [95% CI, 5%–19%]; 75-year-old AD dementia, 90% for carriers vs 85% for non-carriers, difference 5% [95% CI, 2%–10%]) ( eFigure 6A [this file] – B [this file] , eTables 12 [this file] – 14 [this file] ). These associations were largely attenuated in Aβ-PET-negative cognitively impaired individuals ( eFigure 7 [this file] , eTable 15 [this file] ). 
Visual inspection of study-specific estimates also confirmed low variability ( eFigure 8 [this file] ). 
The Aβ-PET-positive/tau-PET-positive profile was associated with a significantly increased estimated risk of experiencing all the evaluated clinical outcomes compared to both the Aβ-PET-negative/tau-PET-negative and Aβ-PET-positive/tau-PET-negative profiles ( Figure 3 [rid=F3] , Table 2 [rid=T2] , eTables 16 [this file] – 17 [this file] ). 
The Aβ-PET-positive/tau-PET-positive profile was associated with a high absolute risk of progression to MCI or dementia among initially cognitively unimpaired individuals (5-year absolute risk: 57.4% [95% CI, 45.4%–70.8], Figure 3A [rid=F3] and eTable 18 [this file] ) as well as to progression to dementia among participants with MCI (5-year absolute risk: 69.9% [95% CI, 59.3%–81.2%], Figure 3B [rid=F3] and eTable 19 [this file] ). Similarly, Aβ-PET-positive/tau-PET-positive individuals were at high risk of progression on all the CDR-G outcomes ( Figure 3C [rid=F3] – D [rid=F3] , Table 2 [rid=T2] , eTables 17 [this file] , 20 [this file] – 22 [this file] ). Additional estimates of the absolute risks of clinical progression, conditional on age and sex, are provided in eTables 18 [this file] – 22 [this file] . 
The outcomes of the Aβ-PET-positive/tau-PET-negative groups were more similar to those of the corresponding Aβ-PET-negative/tau-PET-negative groups, particularly among symptomatic (MCI or AD dementia) participants ( Figure 3 [rid=F3] and eTable 23 [this file] ). Analyses of the Aβ-PET-negative/tau-PET-positive groups revealed numerically higher rates of clinical decline compared with their Aβ-PET-negative/tau-PET-negative counterparts ( eFigure 9 [this file] ). 
Explainable variation in risk of clinical progression attributable to cohort membership ranged from 8.8% to 33.3% ( eTable 24 [this file] ). Percent deviance on CDR-SB trajectories attributable to cohort membership was low (0.2% for cognitively unimpaired and 0.3% for symptomatic participants), and visual inspection of cohort-specific trajectories confirmed limited variability ( eFigure 10 [this file] ). 
Moreover, the fact that most of the tau-PET-positive cognitively unimpaired individuals were also Aβ-positive (85%), exhibited elevated tau-PET signal in regions consistent with Braak V-VI stages ( eFigure 3 [this file] ), and were at high risk of clinical progression ( Figure 3 [rid=F3] ) suggest that the FDA/EMA-approved method for defining tau-PET positivity is indeed reflecting neurofibrillary tangle pathology in these individuals. 
Between 10% to 30% of the participants with a clinical diagnosis of dementia with Lewy bodies, behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia, semantic or nonfluent variant primary progressive aphasia, or corticobasal syndrome exhibited an Aβ-positive/tau-PET-positive profile ( eFigure 4 [this file] ). 
However, complementary analyses showed limited cohort-related variability, with relatively small between-cohort differences ( eFigures 8 [this file] , 10 [this file] , and eTable 24 [this file] ). However, comparisons with estimates derived solely from the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging—a population-based cohort—revealed only minimal differences ( eFigure 11 [this file] ), suggesting that any potential bias is likely limited. 
See Supplement 2 [this file] . 
Exploratory analyses of the Aβ-PET-negative/tau-PET-positive group are reported in the Online Supplement [this file] ( eFigure 9 [this file] ).

Importantly, these islands were driven primarily by etiology, and not by contributing site ( Fig. S1 [this file] ). 
To investigate these trends, we clustered cases with the same diagnosis based on embedding coordinates ( Fig. S2 [this file] ). To discover new robust Aβ-independent and tau-independent correlates of CI in AD, we performed large-scale proteomics (SomaScan, mass spectrometry (MS)) on the CSF of 3,397 individuals across six deeply phenotyped case–control cohorts with AD spanning both sporadic and autosomal dominant AD (ADAD): Stanford (includes the Stanford Alzheimer’s Disease Research Center (ADRC), Stanford Aging and Memory Study (SAMS) and Poston cohort); Knight-ADRC; Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI); Dominantly Inherited Alzheimer’s Network (DIAN); BioFINDER2; and Kuopio University Hospital (Fig. 1a [rid=Fig1] and Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). 
We identified 675 significantly (Benjamini–Hochberg < 0.05) upregulated and 721 significantly downregulated proteins with CI (Fig. 1b [rid=Fig1] and Supplementary Tables 2 [this file] and 3 [this file] ). 
We validated the association of YWHAG:NPTX2 with CI across all cohorts with SomaScan data (ADNI = 0.54; Knight-ADRC = 0.55; Stanford = 0.62; DIAN = 0.66; total = 2,067) including both sporadic AD and ADAD (Fig. 1e [rid=Fig1] and Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ). 
We found that while pTau :Aβ had better performance in distinguishing individuals with MCI versus cognitively normal individuals, YWHAG:NPTX2 had better performance in the later stages (Fig. 1g [rid=Fig1] , Extended Data Fig. 1f [rid=Fig7] and Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ). 
YWHAG:NPTX2 significantly predicted future cognitive decline across all cohorts; in a meta-analysis, an s.d. deviation increase in YWHAG:NPTX2 conferred a 124% increased risk of cognitive decline (meta hazard ratio (HR) = 2.24, meta = 8.16 × 10 ; Fig. 4f [rid=Fig4] and Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). 
Interestingly, we found that relative to ‘correctly’ classified individuals with MCI (group 1), those classified into the ‘cognitively normal’ group (group 0) had a 73% reduced risk of cognitive decline (meta HR = 0.27, meta = 7.35 × 10 ), while those classified into the ‘mild dementia’ group (group 2) had a 2.3-time increased risk of cognitive decline (meta HR = 2.30, meta = 2.74 × 10 ), adjusted for pTau :Aβ , CSF NfL, CSF Ng, age, sex and (Fig. 5b [rid=Fig5] , Extended Data Fig. 5a [rid=Fig11] and Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ). Specifically, only 17 of 77 (22%) individuals in group 0 experienced cognitive decline, while 93 of 133 (70%) in group 2 declined over 15 years (Fig. 5b [rid=Fig5] and Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ). 
Next, among cognitively normal A+T + individuals ( = 168), those in the ‘MCI’ group (group 1) had a 2.7-time increased risk of cognitive decline (meta HR = 2.72, meta = 7.16 × 10 ), and those in the ‘mild dementia’ group (group 2) had a 4.9-time increased risk of cognitive decline (meta HR = 4.92, meta = 2.39 × 10 ) compared to ‘correctly’ classified cognitively normal individuals (group 0), adjusted for pTau :Aβ , CSF NfL, CSF Ng, age, sex and (Fig. 5c [rid=Fig5] , Extended Data Fig. 5b [rid=Fig11] and Supplementary Table 9 [this file] ). 
We performed SomaScan plasma proteomics on 4,245 samples from the Knight-ADRC, Stanford and ROSMAP cohorts (Supplementary Table 10 [this file] ); 3,899 samples had complete CI diagnosis and 519 samples from the Knight-ADRC and Stanford cohorts were collected within 6 months of CSF samples from the same individuals, enabling direct plasma–CSF comparisons. 
The plasma signature (Supplementary Table 11 [this file] ) correlated with CI across all training and test cohorts (Knight-ADRC = 0.66; ROSMAP = 0.62; Stanford = 0.51; GNPC-L = 0.54; GNPC-E = 0.47; GNPC-P = 0.23; GNPC-I = 0.68; GNPC-N = 0.54; total = 6,301; Fig. 6a [rid=Fig6] and Supplementary Table 12 [this file] ). Proteins with strong weights included CPLX2, PTPRD, PI3, MAG and PTGDS (increased with CI), and NPTXR, SEZ6L, CD93, TPPP3 and PIANP (decreased with CI) (Supplementary Table 11 [this file] ). 
The plasma signature significantly predicted future cognitive decline across all cohorts; in a meta-analysis, an s.d. increase in the plasma signature conferred a 56% increased risk of cognitive decline (meta HR = 1.56, meta = 3.16 × 10 ; Fig. 6g [rid=Fig6] and Supplementary Table 13 [this file] ). 
We then examined conversion from cognitively normal to dementia (total = 4,753) and found that an s.d. increase in the plasma signature conferred an 86% increased risk, adjusting for age, sex and dose (meta HR = 1.86, meta = 9.97 × 10 ; Fig. 6h [rid=Fig6] and Supplementary Table 14 [this file] ). 
Model weights and intercept are provided in Supplementary Table 7 [this file] and details on testing the signature in independent cohorts are provided in the ‘Code availability’ section of the article. 
The plasma signature of CI can be derived from independent plasma SomaScan data (assay v.4 and later) by following a tutorial on the synapsesignature GitHub repository ( https://github.com/hamiltonoh/synapsesignature (https://github.com/hamiltonoh/synapsesignature) ), which uses the protein weights provided in Supplementary Table 7 [this file] .

The final dataset comprised 35,120 cross‐sectional diffusion MRI scans aggregated from 50 independent, population‐based cohorts (Figure 1A [rid=hbm70519-fig-0001] ; see Table S1 [this file] for a detailed description of each cohort). Acquisition parameters varied across studies (see Table S2 [this file] for detailed description of voxel sizes and b‐values), necessitating downstream harmonization—including both standardized preprocessing (see Section 2.2 [rid=hbm70519-sec-0004] ), uniform tract segmentation (see Section 2.3.1 [rid=hbm70519-sec-0006] ), and statistical modeling within the lifespan (see Section 2.4.2 [rid=hbm70519-sec-0010] ). In studies with handedness available, self‐report or a questionnaire (typically the Edinburgh Handedness Inventory) was used to determine handedness (handedness experiments are given as Supporting Information [this file] ). 
Analysis of asymmetry in these same pathways and features according to handedness was also performed (Figure S1 [this file] ). 
Full charts for all tracts and features are provided in Figure S2 [this file] . 
All individual lifespan charts for all 30 tracts and 6 features are provided in Figure S2 [this file] . 
Compared with prior reports studying asymmetry—typically smaller, age‐restricted, and focused on a few tracts or metrics (Table 2 [rid=hbm70519-tbl-0002] , for a review of sample size and age range see Table S3 [this file] )—our lifespan curves generally corroborate well‐established findings, such as the leftward FA and volumetric asymmetry of the arcuate fasciculus in adulthood, validating our large‐scale harmonization. 
Across exemplar tracts and features, handedness‐related differences in the modeled median LI were consistently small (Cohen's [calculated at every integer age 1–80 and averaged across the lifespan] typically < 0.08 and often < 0.02; Figure S1 [this file] ), indicating that handedness explains little additional variance in tract‐level asymmetry in these data.

This component exhibited higher and more broadly distributed loadings across the aging population compared to the loadings of other components (Supplementary Fig. 7 [this file] ), consistent with the hypothesis that it may reflect general aging effects rather than a specific pathological process. 
The CCL-NMF components align with, yet extend beyond, the five atrophy dimensions reported by Yang et al. , who applied a different methodology (Surreal-GAN, Supplementary Method 6 [this file] ) to the same dataset (Supplementary Fig. 8 [this file] ).

Using generalized additive models for location, scale and shape (GAMLSS; Stasinopoulos and Rigby (2008) [rid=R66] and Borghi et al. (2006) [rid=R10] ), we derived hemisphere-specific trajectories of regional brain development with age, stratified by sex ( SI Fig. 3 [this file] , 4 [this file] ), for cortical grey matter volume (GM), thickness (CT), surface area (SA), and subcortical volume ( SI Fig. 5 [this file] – 13 [this file] ). These trajectories were characterized in terms of milestones of development: (i) the peak rate-of-growth; (ii) the peak of the trajectory; and (iii) the peak rate-of decline ( SI Fig. 14 [this file] ; SI Table 1 [this file] ). In line with previous bilaterally-averaged results ( Bethlehem et al. 2022 [rid=R7] ), left and right regional tissue trajectories peaked largely in (early) childhood and adolescence ( Fig. 2A [rid=F2] ), with left-right age differences in hemispheric peaks of up to 6 years across phenotypes ( Fig. 2B [rid=F2] ; see SI Fig. 15 [this file] – 16 [this file] and SI Table 2 [this file] for further details). In contrast, the relationship for surface area was positive, such that regions that expand their surface early also decline earlier in later life ( SI Fig. 17 [this file] ). Lastly, the trajectories allow us to derive subject-specific centile scores, and contrast deviations from the norm in cases and controls (see SI Fig. 18 [this file] for details). 
We modeled lifespan development of asymmetry using GAMLSS; see Supplementary information [this file] for details). 
Asymmetries in surface area and grey-matter volume either emerge or consolidate during the first two years of life – with left-dominant association regions (e.g. inferior parietal and superior temporal cortices) gradually amplifying their lateralization – and then remain relatively stable through adulthood and into old age; cortical thickness asymmetries peak neonatally but decline steeply over the first few postnatal years and approach symmetry by adolescence, possibly suggesting an early ”fine-tuning” of cortical architecture ( Fig. 3A [rid=F3] ; see SI Fig. 19 [this file] – 21 [this file] for bootstrapped trajectories). 
To highlight overall trends in asymmetry, we estimated the ranked average area under the curve of the trajetories as an indicator of overall lifetime asymmetry ( SI Table 3 [this file] ; Fig. 3B [rid=F3] ; SI Fig. 22 [this file] ). To add temporal resolution to these analyses, we estimated the average asymmetry as the area under the curve of the trajectory in a given age bin ( SI Table 4 [this file] ). In addition, to evaluate patterns of asymmetry change across the lifespan, we estimated the pairwise spatial correlation of these maps of epoch-specific asymmetry and identified two clusters of asymmetry development (early vs late; ( SI Fig. 23 [this file] )): early asymmetry prominence, corresponding primarily to association cortical areas that exhibit relatively later peaks in bilateral growth, and late asymmetry prominence, corresponding primarily to sensory areas that reach their peak growth earlier ( SI Fig. 24 [this file] )). 
Cortical surface maps of these groupings highlighted spatially coherent clusters of asymmetric development ( SI Table 5 [this file] ). Regions with developmental reversals are notably distributed across both association and primary cortices ( Fig. 4A [rid=F4] , , SI Fig. 24 [this file] – 25 [this file] ). Interestingly, regions with greatest magnitude of changes in asymmetry over the lifespan showed an anatomical overlap with the two phylogenetically primitive areas (paleocortex and archicortex) of the dual origin theory of cortical evolution ( Pandya, Petrides, and Cipolloni 2015 [rid=R44] ; Abbie 1940 [rid=R1] ) ( SI Fig. 26 [this file] ). 
We then estimated case-control differences in asymmetry centile scores for individuals with autism spectrum disorder, schizophrenia, and Alzheimer’s disease ( Fig. 4B [rid=F4] ; Fig. 27 [this file] – 28 [this file] ; SI Table 6 [this file] ). The use of centile scores allows us to combine diverse and unmatched cohorts (see SI Table 2 [this file] ). Of note, case-control differences in mean group-level asymmetry centile scores were less widespread than for centile scores derived from each hemisphere separately, which may be more sensitive to global alterations in brain size (see SI Fig. 18A [this file] for left/right regional case-control maps). As expected, we observed far more extreme centile scores in cases compared to controls, most pronounced in temporal lobe regions in Alzheimer’s disease ( Fig. 28 [this file] ). More specifically, we observed far more extreme centile scores in cases compared to controls, quantified as a greater standard deviation in centile scores in individuals with neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disorders ( SI Fig. 30 [this file] ). 
Given that handedness has been associated with altered patterns of asymmetry and risk for neuropsychiatric disorders ( Webb et al. 2013 [rid=R77] ; Sha, Pepe, et al. 2021 [rid=R58] ), we estimated effects of handedness on asymmetry centile scores ( SI Fig. 31A [this file] , 32 [this file] ). We found that non-right-handers across the lifespan exhibited a trend of reduced cortical and subcortical grey matter volume asymmetries, compared to right-handers ( SI Fig. 31B [this file] ). 
Using UK Biobank data, we estimated the genetic correlation between left and right centile scores for all phenotypes, which quantifies the proportion of interregional covariance due to shared genetic factors ( SI Table 7 [this file] ). We found that regions with lower left-right genetic correlation tended to show greater asymmetry across the lifespan ( , Fig. 4C [rid=F4] , SI Table 8 [this file] ; see SI Fig. 33 [this file] for other phenotypes). 
Most regions showed modest, but significant , SNP-based heritability values between 2–6%, indicating that common genetic variants account for a small but non-negligible proportion of individual differences in asymmetry trajectories ( Fig. 4D [rid=F4] ; see SI Fig. 34 [this file] for all phenotypes). In contrast, a number of language regions, including the superior temporal gyrus, transversetemporal, and supramarginal cortices, as well as multiple regions in the association cortex stand out as having higher SNP-based heritability (Correlation with sensorimotor-association: ; see SI Fig. 35 [this file] ). 
We demonstrate the adaptability and translational potential of centile modeling to varying image resolutions and scanner environments using ultra-low-field MRI systems deployable outside of traditional neuroimaging research and clinical settings ( Váša, Bennallick, et al. 2024 [rid=R73] ) (see SI Fig. 36 [this file] ).

Further evidence for the overall high quality of these data is shown by additional metrics ( Extended Data Fig. 1 [this file] ), particularly the high alignment rates across all samples, with a median of 99.96% of reads successfully aligned to GRCh38 ( Extended Data Fig. 1g [this file] ; Supplementary Tables 2 [rid=SD4] - 3 [rid=SD5] ). 
To generate a comprehensive and high-quality catalog of SVs for our cohort, we established and applied an evidence-driven ensemble variant calling and multi-stage processing pipeline ( Fig. 1a [rid=F1] and Extended Data Fig. 2a [this file] , b [this file] ). For each of the 100 individuals, we generated initial SV calls using three distinct tools: Cue2 (a new release of Cue optimized for long reads), PBSV , and Sniffles2 ( Methods [rid=S14] ; Extended Data Fig. 2a [this file] ). 
The initial callset of 84,525 SVs was subsequently refined by removing 6,768 (8%) SVs located within challenging genomic regions known to be prone to false-positive calls , namely segmental duplications (repeats > 1kb), assembly gaps, and centromeres ( Methods [rid=S14] ; Extended Data Fig. 2b [this file] ). After further removing 3,205 low quality SVs based on read-based metrics ( Methods [rid=S14] ; Supplementary Table 4 [this file3] ), the final callset contained 74,552 high-confidence SVs. 
We first looked at the genome locations where SVs are most often found ( Extended Data Fig. 3a [this file] ). Next, to identify SVs with potential functional impact, we compared the positions of our SVs with known regulatory regions in functional genomics databases using AnnotSV ( Methods [rid=S14] and Supplementary Table 5 [this file4] ). This identified 6,225 (8.35% with 9.64% expected overlap with random SV genomic intervals; Methods [rid=S14] ) SVs overlapping regulatory elements and 1,036 (1.39%) SVs overlapping brain-active promoters and enhancers ( Extended Data Fig. 3b [this file] , c [this file] ). We extended the overlap analysis to other functionally relevant regions annotated for GRCh38, including repeat regions from RepeatMasker (62.7%; 61.5% expected at random), transcription factor binding sites (36.9%; 36.2% expected at random), histone methylation (63.4%; 77.4% expected at random), and acetylation (70.3%; 86.0% expected at random), CpG islands (5.0%; 1.7% expected at random), DNase hypersensitivity (20.1%; 27.5% expected at random), and evolutionary conserved regions (91.9%; 98.7% expected at random) ( Methods [rid=S14] , Extended Data Fig. 3c [this file] ). 
This discrepancy could be explained by the lack of uniformity in how SV types are classified and reported across the various reference databases ( Extended Data Fig. 3d [this file] ), complicating the process of matching SVs regardless of comparison parameters. 
Our analysis identified 173 unique SVs (286 SV-gene pairs) with significant -regulatory effects on gene expression in MTG and midbrain across all cell types assessed, many of which appear specific to a single cell type ( Fig. 4 [rid=F4] , Extended Data Fig. 4a [this file] , 5 [this file] , Supplementary Table 8 [rid=SD8] ). Among these SV-gene pairs, 43.0% (123 pairs) showed significant effects in both brain regions, and 67 and 96 pairs were uniquely significant in MTG and midbrain, respectively ( Extended Data Fig. 5a [this file] , b [this file] ). Our results show that the same highly significant SVs, including insertions (e.g., chr17_46252361_INS_828), deletions (e.g., chr17_46237501_DEL_−724), and the 45,106 bp inversion (chr17_46231903_INV_45106), are associated with expression of these genes in both brain regions ( Fig. 5a [rid=F5] , Extended Data Figs. 6a [this file] , b [this file] and 7a [this file] , b [this file] ). Second, the Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA) region on chromosome 6 has the most -eQTLs (87 and 77 significant SV-gene pairs across 48 and 51 unique SVs in MTG and midbrain, respectively) ( Extended Data Fig. 4a [this file] ). Third, the and locus on chromosome 4 has multiple SVs associated with expression of these genes (e.g., chr4_1372768_INS_323 and chr4_1324644_DEL_−94) in both brain regions ( Fig. 4 [rid=F4] , Extended Data Figs. 6c [this file] , and 7c [this file] , d [this file] ). The observed down-regulation was specific to in midbrain ( Extended Data Figs. 6d [this file] and 7c [this file] - e [this file] ). 
In the midbrain analysis, SV eQTLs absent or less prominent in the MTG results ( Extended Data Fig. 5a [this file] ) included genes such as (associated with chr4_76150170_DEL_−109). While was expressed in both regions ( Supplementary Fig. 2a [rid=SD2] , b [rid=SD2] ), its association with the SV was only significant in the midbrain ( Extended Data Figs. 6e [this file] and 7f [this file] ). By contrast, several SV-eQTLs were found to be significant only in the MTG ( Extended Data Fig. 5b [this file] ), such as (associated with chr14_55489789_DEL_−65) ( Extended Data Figs. 6f [this file] and 7g [this file] ). 
While both SVs were significant eQTLs in the MTG, the deletion was associated with increased expression and the insertion with decreased expression in all cell types significantly affected ( Extended Data Fig. 7h [this file] , i [this file] ). This insertion is an LTR5Hs element of the HERV-K endogenous retrovirus ( Methods [rid=S14] ; Dfam bit score = 1215.9 with E-value = 0) and it was inserted into a AluSx1 repeat element present ~20 kb upstream of ( Extended Data Fig. 10a [this file] ). This deletion removes a simple repetitive DNA sequence found in the 3' end of long interspersed nuclear element-1 (LINE-1) ( Extended Data Fig. 10a [this file] ). 
The ASE results identified mostly the same SV-gene pairs outside of the HLA locus compared to the eQTL results, recapitulating the strong effects on gene expression in multiple cell types at 17q21.31 and multiple SVs significantly associated with and genes on chromosome 4 ( Fig. 4 [rid=F4] , Extended Data Fig. 7a [this file] - e [this file] , Supplementary Table 9a [rid=SD9] , b [rid=SD9] ). By contrast, in the HLA locus, especially in the MTG, the two methods largely disagreed ( Extended Data Fig. 4a [this file] ), which could be due to difficulties in phasing the HLA region, lower expression levels for these genes in some cell types decreasing power for ASE analysis ( Extended Data Fig. 4b [this file] , c [this file] ), or other unidentified issues. 
While several SVs in 17q21.31 (e.g., chr17_45778945_INS_55 and chr17_45969567_DEL_−103) down-regulated expression in multiple cell types including both glial and neuronal types in the MTG, their effects were only identified to be significant with ASE ( Extended Data Figs. 6g [this file] , h [this file] and 7 [this file] ). Similarly, in the midbrain, while the ASE method identified significant down-regulation of in oligodendrocytes, OPCs and astrocytes, the eQTL method only detected a significant effect in oligodendrocytes ( Extended Data Fig. 6i [this file] , j [this file] ). 
To overcome potential snRNA-seq sequencing depth limitations contributing to such discordance, we generated a targeted MTG and midbrain snRNA-seq dataset using hybrid selection ( Methods [rid=S14] ) to specifically enrich for reads mapping to a subset of our prioritized PD risk loci and performed ASE analysis ( Extended Data Fig. 8a [this file] , b [this file] ). Hybrid selection targeted an overlapping, but not identical set of genes for each brain region ( Supplementary Table 10 [this file0] ). This targeted ASE approach revealed mostly consistent effect sizes compared to ASE using non-selected snRNA data (Pearson correlation r = 0.958 and 0.933 in midbrain and MTG among SV-gene pairs that are significant in at least one of the two methods, respectively; Extended Data Fig. 9a [this file] , b [this file] ). For targeted genes in MTG and midbrain, we observed more significant SV-gene pairs with hybrid selection than without hybrid selection (291 vs. 113 and 180 vs. 154, respectively ( Supplementary Table 9 [rid=SD9] and Extended Data Fig. 9c [this file] )). 
To illustrate the diverse regulatory patterns identified in this study, we highlight several examples ( Fig. 5a [rid=F5] , c [rid=F5] - e [rid=F5] , Extended Data Figs. 6 [this file] , 7 [this file] ) in the context of existing genome annotations. In proximity to this deletion, there is a larger (45,106 bp) inversion (chr17_46231903_INV_45106), significantly affecting the same genes in multiple cell types ( Fig. 4 [rid=F4] , Extended Data Figs. 6a [this file] , k [this file] and 7a [this file] , b [this file] ). 
Furthermore, SV type-specific correlation analysis ( Extended Data Fig. 9d [this file] ) revealed distinct characteristics. For insertions, SV length showed weaker correlation with eQTL effect size compared to that of MAF across all cell types except for dopaminergic neurons (mean magnitude of Pearson r = 0.19 and 0.03 for MAF and SV length, respectively; Extended Data Fig. 9d [this file] ). A consistent positive correlation was observed between SV length and eQTL effect size in 8 out of 9 cell types in MTG (Pearson r ranges from 0.036 to 0.32), and 10 out of 11 cell types in midbrain (Pearson r ranges from 0.16 to 0.446) ( Extended Data Fig. 9d [this file] ). By contrast, MAF showed mostly positive correlation except in those two MTG cell types ( Extended Data Fig. 9d [this file] ). 
To distinguish among these possibilities, we categorized specific effects based on gene expression and cell count thresholds ( Methods [rid=S14] ; Extended Data Fig. 9e [this file] , f [this file] ). Examples of such candidates include a 60 bp insertion on chromosome 10 (chr10_15531400_INS_60) that was linked to a significant increase in expression only in OPCs (eQTL FDR = 2.39e-07, ASE FDR = 8.68e-19, Fig. 5c [rid=F5] , e [rid=F5] , Extended Data Fig. 7k [this file] ), and a 330 bp insertion on chromosome 8 (chr8_22625880_INS_330) that was associated with up-regulation of ( Extended Data Fig. 7l [this file] ). The coordinates and size of this SV are virtually identical to the SV that we identified as a significant eQTL specific to glutamatergic neurons (eQTL padj = 1.22e-02, ASE with selection padj = 9.74e-03) in MTG ( Extended Data Figs. 5b [this file] , 7l [this file] and 8b [this file] ). This insertion overlaps a chromatin accessibility peak identified in glutamatergic neurons that was not found in other cell types ( Extended Data Fig. 10b [this file] ). 
Although neuronal populations in the MTG, particularly glutamatergic neurons, have more significant SV-gene pairs (81 SVs), while glial cell types showed fewer associations (12-25 SVs, Fig. 5g [rid=F5] ), this may be due, in part, to gene expression level and cell number differences among cell types ( Supplementary Fig. 2a [rid=SD2] - d [rid=SD2] , Extended Data Fig. 9e [this file] , f [this file] ), or the genes selected for analysis (since they are based on PD GWAS loci). The eQTL analysis of midbrain endothelial cells highlights them as a potentially abundant source of significant SV-gene pairs with cell type specificity ( Extended Data Fig. 9f [this file] ). Interestingly, we provided cell-type resolution for an SV near , a known PD locus, finding that the ~330 bp insertion acts as a significant eQTL with ASE specifically in glutamatergic neurons ( Extended Data Figs. 5b [this file] , 7l [this file] , and 8b [this file] ), thereby complementing a previous bulk tissue study that characterized it as a mQTL. 
We then performed read-level quality control to exclude low-confidence SVs ( Extended Data Fig. 1g [this file] ).

Interestingly, we observed a neuropathology-associated inversion of the association between rs679515 major allele dosage and these hematological traits (Supplementary Fig. 2B [this file] , Supplementary Dataset 5 [rid=MOESM8] ), whereby major allele dosage was positively associated with hematocrit/RBC/Hb (and inversely associated with the presence of anemia) in subjects with low NFT burden (Braak stage: 0–II), and inversely associated with hematocrit/RBC/Hb (and positively associated with the presence of anemia) in subjects with high NFT burden (Braak stage: V–VI). 
Conversely, we observed upregulation of many of DAM signatures genes, such as , , , , and (Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] ). We also noted the overlap between DA9 differential expression and several dystrophic and other microglia signatures reported in the scientific literature (Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] ). 
Banner CD83(+) microglia DEG overlapped significantly with both Fujita-ROSMAP CD83(+) microglia DEG ( -value: 4.04e−120, Odds ratio: 28.2, Fisher’s Exact Test, Supplementary Dataset 8 [rid=MOESM11] , Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] ) and Mathys-ROSMAP CD83(+) microglia DEG ( -value: 1.69e−74, Odds ratio: 18.3, Fisher’s Exact Test, Supplementary Dataset 8 [rid=MOESM11] , Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] ).

Among the five regulatory regions associated with , we identified the presence of bound motif in the microglia-specific open chromatin region located 22 kb upstream of (Supplementary Fig. 6B [this file] ). Detailed characteristics of these 14 European ancestry cohorts are shown in Table S1 [this file] and previous studies [ 5 [rid=CR5] ]. 
Primary MR analysis of brain pQTLs and SA GWAS revealed 94 proteins with genetically determined effects that showed suggestive evidence ( < 0.05; Tables S2 [this file] and S3 [this file] ). Similar findings were found when applying robust MR approaches, including maximum likelihood, weighted median and penalized weighted median methods (Table S4 [this file] ). The Steiger filtering analysis confirmed the correct causal direction from the protein level to SA for all MR-identified proteins (Table S5 [this file] ). However, Bayesian colocalization analysis revealed strong evidence of genetic colocalization with SA for only three out of the ten proteins, namely GLRX5, GMPPB, and FUCA2 (Table S6 [this file] ). 
Primary MR analysis of blood pQTLs and SA GWAS identified 109 proteins that showed suggestive evidence of genetically determined effects ( < 0.05; Tables S7 [this file] and S8 [this file] ), but only one protein survived after multiple testing correction (FDR < 0.05; Table 1 [rid=Tab1] and Fig. 2B [rid=Fig2] ). The results from maximum likelihood MR analysis for PEAR1 plasma protein were consistent with those from the IVW method, and no heterogeneity was detected (Table S4 [this file] ). The Steiger filtering analysis supported that the correct causal direction from protein level to the development of SA for PEAR1 plasma protein (Table S5 [this file] ). 
When we relaxed the significance threshold to < 0.001, the three additional proteins (NDE1, EVA1C, and B4GALT2) identified by the MR analysis did not provide strong evidence for a causal association with SA in the colocalization analysis (Table S6 [this file] ), taking into account that the higher number of proteins analyzed in the blood affected the number of proteins that survived multiple corrections. 
Firstly, the causal associations of these three proteins with SA remained significant when considering strict independent IVs ( < 0.001) for SA from the discovery protein dataset and SA-EUR GWAS (Table S9 [this file] ). Secondly, we replicated the MR analysis of the multiple corrected surviving proteins in the discovery dataset, and found that the direction of effect of the available proteins was consistent with the findings in the discovery dataset (Table S10 [this file] ). Thirdly, the significant causal associations of the three candidate brain proteins with SA were confirmed after external validation using mtCOJO adjustment for MDD as a secondary outcome (Table S11 [this file] ). 
In addition, through confirmatory PWAS, we found that all three candidate brain proteins showed significant associations with SA risk (GLRX5: -score = −3.49, = 4.83E−04; GMPPB: -score = 3.67, = 2.39E−04; FUCA2: -score = −3.53, = 4.22E−04) (Table S12 [this file] ). At the perspective of transcription level, two of the three candidate genes had suitable IVs, and MR analysis showed consistent results between the transcription level and the protein level (GLRX5; OR: 0.7; 95% CI: 0.58–0.85; GMPPB; OR: 1.15; 95% CI: 1.09–1.22) (Table S13 [this file] ). 
We utilized human single-cell RNA-seq data to investigate the specific enrichment and expression patterns of the three candidate brain proteins in different brain cell types (Table S14 [this file] ). 
GO and KEGG enrichment analysis revealed that the three significant brain-based proteins were associated with various biological pathways, including metabolic pathways, lysosomes, neuronal cell bodies, and glutathione oxidoreductase activity (Table S15 [this file] ). 
Lastly, we performed a comprehensive phenotypic GWAS scan of the candidate proteins identified in the MR analysis (Table S16 [this file] ), which showed that the IVs for these candidate proteins were not strongly correlated with other risks that may affect SA risk, suggesting that the candidate proteins are unlikely to exhibit widespread horizontal pleiotropy.

In a sensitivity analyses accounting for the false discovery rate, we adjusted the values using the two-stage linear step-up procedure described by Benjamini et al. [ 2 [rid=CR2] , 14 [rid=CR14] ]. (Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S4). 
In the present study, IHC and MP-ISH/IHC revealed that regional, laminar, cellular and subcellular (dendritic) distributions of ApoER2 and expression parallel well-established selective vulnerability to develop NFT pathology—with strong expression in ErC L2 neurons, the ProS-CA1 border region, a subset of L5 and L3 neocortical pyramids, and pontine LC and raphe nuclei neurons—and lower or absent expression in neuron populations that are spared from NFT pathology (Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] , Additional file 1 [this file] : Ext Fig S3.1). The cohort comprised of 12 cases stratified by APOE genotype and AD status into four groups: APOE4/4 individuals with AD (E4-AD; n = 5, median age = 84.2 years), APOE4/4 cognitively normal individuals (E4-CN; n = 2, median age = 75.5 years), APOE3/3 individuals with AD (E3-AD; n = 3, median age = 78 years), and APOE3/3 cognitively normal individuals (E3-CN; n = 2, median age = 83 years) ( Figure 1A [rid=F1] – B [rid=F1] ; Table S1 [this file] ). 
Our 40-plex antibody panel was designed to capture metabolic, immune, and structural features across major central nervous system cell types ( Figure 1D [rid=F1] ; Table S2 [this file] ). Cytoplasmic localization of metabolic enzymes ( Figure 1G [rid=F1] ) and nuclear restriction of histone modifications further confirmed marker specificity and subcellular fidelity ( Figure S1A [this file] – B [this file] ). Optimal thresholds minimized marker variability and preserved biologically meaningful cell morphologies ( Figure S1C [this file] ). Nucleated cells were identified by area-normalized Histone H3 signal intensity ( Figure S1D [this file] ). 
Unsurprisingly, PHF-tau was diagnosis-driven across all three cell types ( Figure 2A [rid=F2] ), with no significant G×D interaction, confirming the model’s sensitivity to established AD pathology ( Figure S2A [this file] – B [this file] ). While several regulatory histone modifications (macroH2A1.2, γH2A.X, H3K9ac, H3K27me3) displayed significant G×D interactions in neurons ( Figure 2A [rid=F2] ; S2A [this file] – B [this file] ), inspection of single-cell distributions revealed that these effects largely reflected broader dispersion in E3-CN neurons negative for these markers rather than uniform genotype-dependent shifts ( Figure 2B [rid=F2] ). Senescent 1 was significantly enriched in AD, with no difference in abundance between E3-AD and E4-AD groups ( Figure S2C [this file] ). Relative to the two other clusters, Senescent 1 neurons showed markedly elevated γH2A.X (magenta) and increased phosphorylated ribosomal S6 (pS6) (cyan) ( Figure 2D [rid=F2] – E [rid=F2] ; S2D [this file] ), consistent with persistent DNA damage and a stress-associated phenotype . 
In contrast, an APOE genotype-driven effect was observed in microglia: TMEM119 expression was significantly reduced in APOE4 compared with APOE3 individuals (β = −0.717, 95% CI = [−1.15, −0.289]; FDR = 0.028), independent of diagnosis and without a G×D interaction ( Figure 2A [rid=F2] ; S2A [this file] – B [this file] ). 
TMEM119 and P2RY12 defined the homeostatic axis, with TMEM119 P2RY12 cells representing the non-activated population ( Figure S3A [this file] , ). Of the non-homeostatic fraction, cells that were CD68 L-Ferritin were considered dystrophic , while cells that were CD68 L-Ferritin were considered reactive ( Figure S3A [this file] , ). 
Within the combined homeostatic population, APOE3 Homeostatic cells were preferentially enriched in APOE3/3 individuals, whereas APOE4 Homeostatic cells were enriched in APOE4/4 individuals ( Figure S3B [this file] ), indicating genotype-dependent redistribution within the homeostatic compartment. 
The Transitional cluster was preferentially enriched in the E4-AD group ( Figure 3D [rid=F3] ; S3C [this file] ), despite its lack of strong condition-specific likelihood estimates ( Figure 3G [rid=F3] ). 
Relative to the APOE3 Homeostatic population, Reactive 1 microglia showed increased expression of microglial activation features TREM2 and CD11c, consistent with an early reactive, actively surveillant phenotype ( Figure 3C [rid=F3] ; S3D [this file] ). Notably, neither Reactive 1 nor Reactive 2 differed in abundance between the APOE-diagnosis groups ( Figure S3C [this file] ). 
Conversely, the Activation-Limited cluster – hereafter referred to as Activation-Limited Microglia (ALMs) – was differentially enriched in E4-AD relative to E3-AD ( Figure 3D [rid=F3] ; 3G [rid=F3] ; S3C [this file] ). ALMs exhibited elevated expression of several activation markers, including TREM2, L-Ferritin, CD68, HLA-DR, CD44 and GPNMB, relative to APOE3 Homeostatic and Reactive 1 ( Figure 3H [rid=F3] , , S3E [this file] ) microglia. 
Homeostatic microglia exhibited minimal associations with pathologic spatial features and the lowest median neighborhood Shannon entropy, aligning with their expected residence in relatively undisturbed tissue with low local diversity, rather than pathology-enriched microenvironments ( Figure 4A [rid=F4] – B [rid=F4] ; S4A [this file] ). Consistent with their DAM-like activation profile, Reactive 2 microglia were most strongly enriched for Aβ plaque association (purple), followed by ALMs ( Figure 4A [rid=F4] – C [rid=F4] ; S4B [this file] ). Comparison of plaque-associated cells between these two states revealed that ALMs resided at significantly greater distances from plaques compared to Reactive 2 microglia ( Figure S4C [this file] ), suggesting ALMs are less directly responsive to proximal Aβ and reside in the broader plaque-adjacent environment. Instead, ALMs were more frequently localized to GFAP CD44 gliosis zones (green), and regions containing γH2A.X (blue) and PHF-tau (red) neighbors ( Figure 4A [rid=F4] – C [rid=F4] ; S4A [this file] ; S4D [this file] ), indicating a distinct inflammatory niche composed of non-Aβ stressors. Overall, microglia in E3-AD were more spatially concentrated around plaques than in E4-AD ( Figure S4E [this file] ), further reinforcing the fact that APOE4 alters not just cell-intrinsic microglial states, but their spatial targeting of pathology. 
To better understand how pathological features organize across the hippocampal landscape, we examined their global pairwise co-occurrence relationships ( Figure S4F [this file] ). In contrast, ALMs displayed co-occurrence patterns not seen in DAM-like microglial niches, such as (gliosis, senescence) and (myelinated axons, senescence), suggesting a unique convergence of multiple pathological stressors in their local environment ( Figure S4G [this file] ). 
Pixel-level metabolic features emerged as the strongest predictors of cluster identity ( Figure S4H [this file] ). 
Analysis of donor-level cluster frequencies demonstrated a marked depletion of APOE3 Homeostatic microglia and significant enrichment of Transitional, Early Dystrophic, and Dystrophic population in E4-AD relative to E3-AD, indicating a genotype-dependent shift in microglial state composition ( Figure S3C [this file] ). Distribution of condition-associated likelihoods across E3-AD and E4-AD similarly revealed a continuous gradient across these states ( Figure S5A [this file] ). 
While ALMs, Early Dystrophic, and Dystrophic cell states emerged predominantly at late pseudotime, the early and mid-pseudotime regions were largely defined by the Homeostatic population and ensuing emergence of Transitional microglia ( Figure S5B [this file] ). 
To comprehensively characterize lineage-specific programs underlying these transitions, we predicted feature expression along aligned pseudotime using generalized additive modeling ( Figure S5C [this file] ) and quantified inter-lineage divergence by cosine dissimilarly between aligned expression profiles ( Figure S5D [this file] ). This revealed a shared early state program across all three lineages, with all three lineages subsequently adopting distinct terminal profiles ( Figure S5E [this file] ). Overlaying MELD-derived likelihoods onto the trajectory structure further showed that E4-AD association increased toward late pseudotime across all lineages, with the strongest enrichment in Lineage 1 (ALM) terminal states ( Figure S5F [this file] ). 
Lineage 1 (ALM) retained inflammatory and iron-handling markers (HLA-DR, GPNMB, L-ferritin, CD68, ApoE), in contrast to Lineage 2 (Dystrophic), which saw rapid downregulation of these features beyond mid-pseudotime ( Figure 5E [rid=F5] ,S5G [this file] ). 
To independently validate the APOE-associated microglial continuum observed in our spatial proteomic and trajectory analyses, we analyzed an orthogonal single-nuclear multiome dataset consisting of matched snRNA-seq and snATAC-seq profiles from hippocampal microglia isolated from eight AD donors (n = 4 APOE3/3; n = 4 APOE4/4) ( Table S3 [this file] ). Integration effectively removed donor-driven variation while preserving genotype-associated structure in the joint RNA-ATAC latent space ( Figure S6A [this file] ). Clusters corresponding to highly proliferative cells and T cells ( Figure S6B [this file] ) were excluded to restrict downstream analyses to resident microglia. 
While MELD-high cells were enriched for APOE4/4 individuals and MELD-low cells for APOE3/3 individuals, all cases were represented across multiple bins ( Figure S6C [this file] ). 
Donor-aware pseudobulk differential expression analysis comparing MELD-high and MELD-low populations identified a coordinated APOE4-associated transcriptional signature ( Figure 6B [rid=F6] ; S6D [this file] ). 
To determine how these programs varied continuously along the full APOE-associated manifold, and to identify broader pathway-level regulation, we modeled gene expression as a continuous function of MELD while controlling for donor identity ( Figure 6B [rid=F6] ; S6E [this file] ). A prominent APOE4-enriched module captured the integrated stress response (ISR) and translational control, including GCN2-mediated amino acid starvation signaling, SRP-dependent co-translational protein targeting to the endoplasmic reticulum, and cellular responses to nutrient deprivation ( Figure 6C [rid=F6] ; S6F [this file] ). 
Although differential accessibility between MELD-high and MELD-low microglia was modest and involved a relatively small fraction of peaks ( Figure S6G [this file] ), genome-wide chromatin accessibility patterns across transcription factor (TF) motifs revealed coordinated regulatory changes along the APOE continuum. Motif activity analysis using chromVAR identified enrichment of several TF families in APOE4-associated microglia ( Figure 6D [rid=F6] ; S6H [this file] ), including CREB/ATF (CREB5, CREB1, ATF1, ATF7), NFAT (NFATC4), and Ikaros zinc-finger family TFs (IKZF1, IKZF4). 
Overlaps between our APOE4-associated transcriptional signature and published microglial gene signatures were greater than expected by chance, based on one-sided Fisher’s exact tests performed over the set of 36313 genes tested in the continuous MELD analysis ( Figure S6I [this file] ). Notably, the strongest APOE4-associated signals were preferentially shared with ferroptosis- and senescence-related programs rather than the DAM signature alone, including and ( Figure S6J [this file] ). 
To isolate APOE genotype effects in a controlled human system, we use human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived microglia from APOE4/4 parental clones that were CRIPSR/Cas9-corrected to APOE3/3, generating genetically matched APOE3/3-APOE4/4 isogenic clone pairs, differing only at the APOE locus ( Figure 7A [rid=F7] ; S7A [this file] – C [this file] ), and differentiated into microglia over 42 days. Functional assessment using the pHrodo assay demonstrated that both APOE3 and APOE4 microglia are proficient in phagocytosis, with each genotype demonstrating the ability to effectively initiate and carry out phagocytic activity. ( Figure 7C [rid=F7] ; S7E [this file] ). 
Cells were profiled by single-cell mass cytometry, as previously described in Bendall et al., 2012 ( Figure 7D [rid=F7] ), with a panel spanning activation, phagocytic lipid handling, metabolism, and regulatory signaling activity ( Table S4 [this file] ). Notably, APOE4 microglia exhibited reduced CD44, TREM2, and GLS expression together with elevated mTOR signaling (pS6 and p4EBP1) and Iba1 expression, indicative of activation and structural remodeling ( Figure 7D [rid=F7] ; S7F [this file] ). We next assessed early stimulus-induced responses following acute perturbation with either Aβ/PFF or CpG/LPS ( Figure 7E [rid=F7] ; S7G [this file] ). 
Donor details are listed in Table S1 [this file] . 
Object composite channels were created using combined lineage phenotyping marker expression ( Table S5 [this file] ). 
To determine whether the frequency of feature-associated microglia differed across clusters, we annotated each microglial cell as ‘feature-associated’ or ‘non-feature-associated’ based on expansionzone expression of relevant markers ( Table S6 [this file] ).

We calculated feature contributions to RP prediction using Shapley Additive Explanation (SHAP) [ 30 [rid=pdig.0000479.ref030] ] values ( Fig 4 [rid=pdig.0000479.g004] , S1 Appendix [this file] ) and grouped features into seven modalities: demographics, comorbidities and medications, plasma levels of Aβ, brain regional volumes, cognitive tests (ADAS-Cog14, CDR, MMSE), quality of life (ADCS-ADL, EQ-5D, QoL-AD), and neuropsychiatric symptoms (NPI). In total, the days since consent was imputed for 43 (2.8%) of the tau PET scans ( Figure S2 [this file] ). 
A total of 9 of the 2211 MRI scans had a visit number of 42, 48, 72, or 84 with missing information for days since consent, and for these scans, the expected study schedule interval was added to the last known days since consent value ( Table S2B [this file] ). 
Within the A+ groups, A+T + were older than both A+T and A+T + ( Figure S3 [this file] ). There was a stepwise increase in baseline amyloid levels from A-T to A+T to A+T + to A+T + and there were significant differences between groups in baseline global tau with the highest levels in A+T + ( Figure S3 [this file] ). 
All three A+ groups showed significant tau accumulation across all ROIs except for the frontal lobes in A+T ( Figure 2A [rid=F2] ; Figure S4 [this file] ; Table S3 [this file] ). 
In all cortical regions, A+T + accumulated tau at significantly faster rates than all other groups with the biggest differences in lateral temporal, medial parietal, and lateral parietal regions ( Figure 2A [rid=F2] ; Table S4 [this file] ). Results were consistent even after accounting for baseline global levels of tau in all participants ( Table S5 [this file] ) and both global levels of tau and amyloid burden in A+ only ( Table S6 [this file] ), indicating that results were not driven by globally elevated pathological burden in the A+T + group. Faster tau accumulation was observed in A+T + in nearly all cortical regions when compared to A-T and A+T and in MTL when compared to A-T ( Table S4 [this file] – S6 [this file] ). 
Given that the A+T + group consisted of asymmetrical left and right subgroups at baseline, we then examined change in hemispheric asymmetry within A+T + subtypes and A+T +, A+T , and A-T groups ( Figure 2B [rid=F2] ; Figure S5 [this file] ; Table S7 [this file] ). 
By definition, A+T + did not show significant hemispheric asymmetry at baseline, but this group developed left hemisphere dominance (i.e., more negative asymmetry indices) in lateral temporal and frontal regions ( Table S7 [this file] ), with some participants reaching asymmetry levels similar to what was observed in A+T + participants ( Figure 2B [rid=F2] ; Figure S5 [this file] ). 
To assess rate of neurodegeneration, we examined change in hippocampal volume and cortical thickness ( Figure S6 [this file] ). All biomarker groups showed significant neurodegeneration across the brain over time ( Table S8 [this file] ). Comparisons between groups revealed significantly greater loss in hippocampal volume and MTL cortical thickness in A+T + compared to all other groups ( Table S9 [this file] ). 
Both A+T + and A+T + showed significant functional and cognitive decline over time ( Figure 6 [rid=F6] ; Figure S6 [this file] ; Table S8 [this file] ). 
Finally, we examined differences in rate of clinical decline between groups ( Table S9 [this file] ). Function, cognition, and computerized cognition results were similar when accounting for baseline global levels of tau in all participants ( Table S10 [this file] ) and baseline global tau and amyloid burden in A+ only ( Table S11 [this file] ), indicating that results were not driven by globally elevated pathological burden in the A+T + group. 
In the A+T group that represented 61% of preclinical AD participants, tau accumulation (around 0.001 SUVRs across MTL and cortical regions; Table S3 [this file] ), functional change (e.g., increase of 0.101 points on the CDR-SOB per year; Table S10 [this file] ), and cognitive decline (e.g., decrease of 0.05 points on the MMSE per year; Table S10 [this file] ) were minimal. Changes in tau burden (around 0.010 SUVRs across MTL and cortical regions; Table S3 [this file] ), functional status (e.g., increase of 0.182 points on the CDR-SOB per year; Table S10 [this file] ), and cognition (e.g., decrease of 0.189 points on the MMSE per year; Table S10 [this file] ) were significant albeit relatively small (in comparison to the A+T + group) in the A+T + group that represented 30% of preclinical AD participants. 
Furthermore, given that change in neurodegeneration was greatest in the A+T + group ( Figure S6 [this file] ; Table S9 [this file] ), partial volume correction would inflate the tau effect sizes since greater atrophy would translate to higher tau SUVRs after partial volume correction.
