We pretrained BrainIAC using contrastive SSL on 32,015 multiparametric MRIs curated from 16 datasets across ten medical conditions (Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] and Supplementary Tables 1 [this file] – 4 [this file] ). The seven tasks are MRI sequence classification, brain age prediction, detection of isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) mutation, survival prediction for brain tumors, early dementia prediction through mild cognitive impairment (MCI) versus healthy control, time-to-stroke prediction, and adult glioma segmentation (Supplementary Methods A.2.1–A.2.7 [this file] ). We evaluated performance in few-shot scenarios with one data sample per class ( = 1) and five data samples per class ( = 5) (Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Methods A.3 [this file] ) by fine-tuning the entire model end-to-end. Finally, we analyzed resiliency of BrainIAC and benchmark models to image-related artifacts (Fig. 5 [rid=Fig5] and Supplementary Methods A.4 [this file] ). 
We used 5,004 scans for fine-tuning, with a reserved holdout set of 876 scans encompassing the four primary sequences used in brain tumor assessment (T1, T2, T1CE or FLAIR) from the BraTS 2023 dataset (Supplementary Methods A.2.1 [this file] and Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ). At lower data availability, BrainIAC outperformed MedicalNet, BrainSegFounder and Scratch (Fig. 2c [rid=Fig2] and Supplementary Table 24 [this file] ). For 100% data BrainIAC demonstrated better clustering performance with Davies–Bouldin index of 0.68 compared to 0.72 of Scratch, 0.82 of MedicalNet and 0.70 of BrainSegFounder (Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). 
To evaluate BrainIAC as a foundation for improved brain age prediction, we aggregated a dataset of 6,249 T1-weighted scans, allocating 3,882 for training or validation and 1,295 as an in-distribution, internal test set and an out-of-distribution test set of 1,072 scans (Supplementary Tables 7 [this file] and 8 [this file] and Supplementary Methods A.2.2 [this file] ). 
BrainIAC demonstrated increased accuracy at all age predictions compared with MedicalNet, BrainSegFounder and Scratch models (Supplementary Tables 9 [this file] and 10 [this file] ). 
For IDH classification, we used 396 scans for training and validation; 99 were reserved as a test set from the UCSF-PDGM dataset (Supplementary Table 12 [this file] and Supplementary Methods A.2.3 [this file] ). At 100% data availability ( = 396), BrainIAC yielded AUC 0.79 (95% CI: 0.64–0.89), compared to 0.68 (95% CI: 0.54–0.81, = 0.052) for MedicalNet, 0.59 (95% CI: 0.45–0.72, = 0.031) for BrainSegFounder and 0.61 (95% CI: 0.48–0.73, = 0.038) for Scratch (Supplementary Tables 13 [this file] and 15 [this file] ). 
Of 671 patients in total, 668 patients with complete survival information were included (Supplementary Table 16 [this file] ). AUC was reported for patients at risk up to the 1-year mark (that is, not censored and no event); five patients in our external test data met this criterion and were excluded from AUC calculation (Supplementary Methods A.2.4 [this file] ). 
The concordance index with 95% CI is reported in Supplementary Tables 17 [this file] and 18 [this file] . 
The DeLong test was used for checking statistical significance and calculating values (Supplementary Table 20 [this file] ). 
For MCI classification, we used 195 scans (106 healthy control, 89 MCI) for training and validation, with 40 (29 healthy control, 11 MCI) reserved as a test set from the OASIS-1 dataset (Supplementary Methods A.2.5 [this file] ). 
For time-to-stroke prediction we allocated 170 scans for training and validation and reserved 40 scans as a holdout test set (Supplementary Methods A.2.6 [this file] ). 
Increasing training data availability to 100% ( = 170), BrainIAC yielded MAE of 38.87, compared to 62.24 for MedicalNet, 63.73 for BrainSegFounder and 50.63 for Scratch (Fig. 2g [rid=Fig2] and Supplementary Table 22 [this file] ). 
To assess the transferability of BrainIAC for segmentation, we fine-tuned each backbone on the BraTS23 adult glioma dataset, reformulated as a single-channel binary segmentation task using FLAIR sequences (Supplementary Methods A.2.7 [this file] ). Performance was quantified by mean Dice coefficient (DSC) across varying data fractions (Fig. 2e [rid=Fig2] and Supplementary Table 26 [this file] ). 
This performance advantage expanded in the = 5 setting, with BrainIAC achieving BA of 0.73 versus 0.49 (MedicalNet), 0.40 (BrainSegFounder) and 0.43 (Scratch) (Fig. 3b [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Table 25 [this file] ). 
The performance improvement persisted in the = 5 setting, with MAEs of 7.24, 15.03, 10.24 and 14.28 years, respectively (Fig. 3c [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Table 11 [this file] ). 
Similar performance was observed in the = 5 setting with AUC: 0.64 (95% CI: 0.52–0.76) (BrainIAC), AUC: 0.44 (95% CI: 0.30–0.58) (MedicalNet), AUC: 0.62 (95% CI: 0.50–0.74) (BrainSegFounder) and AUC: 0.55 (95% CI: 0.41–0.68) (Scratch), respectively (Fig. 3d [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Table 14 [this file] ). 
The = 5 setting yielded AUCs of 0.60 (95% CI: 0.51–0.70], 0.55 (95% CI: 0.44–0.65), 0.58 (95% CI: 0.47–0.67) and 0.48 (95% CI: 0.39–0.58), respectively (Fig. 3a [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Table 19 [this file] ). 
The = 5 setting showed similar relative performance, with AUCs of 0.79 (95% CI: 0.64–0.92), 0.63 (95% CI: 0.45–0.79), 0.53 (95% CI: 0.33–0.71) and 0.51 (95% CI: 0.29–0.72), respectively (Fig. 3e [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Table 21 [this file] ). 
BrainIAC demonstrated superior performance in both few-shot settings, achieving MAE of 66.10 days versus 83.97 (Scratch), 75.98 (BrainSegFounder) and 85.97 (MedicalNet) for = 1 and 69.46 days versus 65.63 (Scratch), 65.15 (BrainSegFounder) and 85.15 (MedicalNet) for = 5 (Fig. 3f [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Table 23 [this file] ). 
For the tumor segmentation task, BrainIAC demonstrated robust adaptation under few-shot constraints (Fig. 3g [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Table 27 [this file] ). 
To benchmark the representational quality of learned pretrained embeddings, we performed linear probing across seven downstream tasks using the full training datasets (Fig. 3h [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Tables 28 [this file] – 34 [this file] ). 
BrainIAC maintained more stable performance than MedicalNet, BrainSegFounder and Scratch, especially in low-data tasks such as mutation prediction, time-to-stroke and survival prediction where other models noticeably degraded (Fig. 5 [rid=Fig5] and Supplementary Methods A.4 [this file] ). 
The data pool was aggregated from the following datasets: ABCD , ADNI, DFCI/BCH LGG, OASIS-3 , MCSA , SOOP , ABIDE (https://fcon_1000.projects.nitrc.org/indi/abide/databases.html), CBTN LGG , MIRIAD , PPMI ( https://www.ppmi-info.org (https://www.ppmi-info.org) ), DLBS , RadArt , OASIS-2 , DFCI/BCH HGG, QIN-GBM , RIDER , UPENN-GBM , BraTS 2023 , UCSF-PDGM , HCP S1200 , LONG579 , BABY , AOMIC ID1000 ( https://openneuro.org/datasets/ds003097 (https://openneuro.org/datasets/ds003097) ), Calgary Preschool MRI ( https://osf.io/axz5r/overview (https://osf.io/axz5r/overview) ), HaN , NIMH , ICBM, IXI ( https://brain-development.org/ixi-dataset/ (https://brain-development.org/ixi-dataset/) ), PING , Pixar , SALD , PETfrog OASIS-1 , ATLAS further details and acknowledgements are in Supplementary Methods A.1 [this file] . 
Both pretrainings was conducted over 200 epochs with a batch size of 32 on an NVIDIA A6000 graphics processing unit, requiring approximately 72 h for completion (Supplementary Table 26 [this file] ). 
This study used publicly available, controlled-access and institutional neuroimaging datasets as detailed in Supplementary Table 2 [this file] and Supplementary Methods A.1 [this file] . Publicly available datasets include OASIS-1/2/3 ( https://sites.wustl.edu/oasisbrains/ (https://sites.wustl.edu/oasisbrains/) ), IXI ( https://brain-development.org/ixi-dataset/ (https://brain-development.org/ixi-dataset/) ), BRATS23 ( https://www.synapse.org/Synapse:syn51156910/ (https://www.synapse.org/Synapse:syn51156910/) ) and others as listed in Supplementary Table 2 [this file] . Controlled-access datasets require registration and data use agreements: ABCD ( https://nda.nih.gov/abcd (https://nda.nih.gov/abcd) ), ADNI ( https://adni.loni.usc.edu/ (https://adni.loni.usc.edu/) ), CBTN ( https://cbtn.org/ (https://cbtn.org/) ) and others as specified in Supplementary Table 2 [this file] . Full access procedures are detailed in Supplementary Methods A.1 [this file] .

We compared demographic factors and clinical characteristics between the cohorts and did not observe statistically significant ( value < 0.05 from Chi-square test) differences between each of the five groups in education level or race (Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). We did note statistically significant differences in the sex ratios of the groups, driven by the higher proportion of males (90%) in the LBD cohort and AD/ALB cohort (84.2%) as compared to the AD, AD/LBD, and control groups (Supplementary Table 1 [this file] , Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ); however, LBD is shown in the literature to be more common in men . Statistical comparison of differences using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) in mean age of symptom onset, mean age at time of sample collection, and mean age at death yielded no significant value < 0.05 differences between the five groups (Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). Principal component analyses (PCAs) were performed to further interrogate age and sex as confounders for miRNA expression data from all five cohorts for GluR2+ (Supplementary Fig. 2A [this file] ) or GLAST+ (Supplementary Fig. 2B [this file] ) EVs, isolated using the mTENPO platform as described below. 
For SEM, we identified particles with consistent size and morphology as EVs within pores of our mTENPO devices (Fig. 1D [rid=Fig1] , E [rid=Fig1] , Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] ). We also identified eluted EVs on SEM, HIM, and cryo-TEM bound to MNPs approximately 50 nm in size (Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] , Supplementary Fig. 5 [this file] ). To compare the GluR2 and GLAST pulldowns, we performed nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA) on eluted EVs from mTENPO and found no differences in EV concentration or size distribution for either pulldown (Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] ). 
Full-length images of the blots presented in Fig. 1F [rid=Fig1] are pictured in Supplementary Fig. 7A–C [this file] . GluR2 mTENPO EV lysates showed a substantial increase in GluR2 western blot signal relative to GLAST (Supplementary Fig. 7D [this file] ); likewise, GLAST mTENPO EV lysates showed increased GLAST signal relative to GluR2 (Supplementary Fig. 7E [this file] ). Both pulldowns showed positivity for extracellular vesicle marker TSG101 (Supplementary Fig. 7C [this file] ). 
We confirmed the specificity of the GluR2+ EV and GLAST + EV-derived miRNA signals by finding ΔC values > 0 in the expression of multiple brain-relevant miRNAs, when comparing EVs isolated from plasma using GluR2 or GLAST versus isotype controls (Supplementary Fig. 8 [this file] ). 
NTA was performed on EVs eluted off-chip, showing additional EV-sized particles isolated using GluR2 mTENPO from mixed neuron media that were not present when performing GLAST mTENPO on the same sample (Supplementary Fig. 9A [this file] ). Similarly, for astrocyte-only media, NTA showed additional EV-sized particles for GLAST mTENPO that were not present for GluR2 mTENPO (Supplementary Fig. 9B [this file] ). Furthermore, NTA for GLAST mTENPO on mixed neuron media and GluR2 mTENPO on astrocyte-only media showed similar size distributions to bead-only NTA measurements (Supplementary Fig. 9C [this file] ), suggesting that the particles detected for these two conditions may be primarily from beads that passed into the eluate, with a rightward shift of the NTA peak for the former, presumably due to the presence of astrocytes within the mixed cultures. 
The miRNA and protein profiles revealed complex patterns of expression, with outliers and heterogeneity within disease cohorts, even for strongly predictive markers (Supplementary Fig. 10 [this file] ). Some downregulated GluR2 markers (miR-490-3p, miR-34a-5p, miR-1299, miR-9-3p) appeared to be influenced by outlier expression profiles in a few patients, resulting in correspondingly low AUCs (AUCs of 0.58, 0.55, 0.54 and 0.53, respectively) (Fig. 2D [rid=Fig2] , Supplementary Fig. 10A [this file] ). ROC curves for the Delong’s-significant differentially expressed markers are shown in Supplementary Fig. 11A-C [this file] . We also performed a comparison of the AUCs for the top 30 miRNA markers between the GluR2 and GLAST pulldowns to assess their degree of correlation, identifying that the pulldowns did not yield significant correlation for these miRNAs (Supplementary Fig. 11D [this file] ). 
As performed previously for LBD versus AD, we generated hierarchically clustered heatmaps of the z-score of log (expression) between patients for all three comparisons (Supplementary Fig. 12 [this file] ). 
Of these biomarkers, three GLAST + EV miRNAs and one protein were upregulated in the combined dementia cohort, while the remaining biomarkers were upregulated in the control cohort (Supplementary Fig. 13A–D [this file] ). By performing an ROC analysis on each biomarker with a statistically significant fold-change (Supplementary Fig. 13E, F [this file] ), we identified one GLAST + EV miRNA (miR-204-5p, AUC = 0.67, Delong’s value = 0.062) and two protein biomarkers (Aβ42/Aβ40, AUC = 0.67, Delong’s value = 0.051; Aβ42, AUC = 0.66, Delong’s value = 0.045) with a significant AUC as compared to a non-predictive (AUC = 0.5) marker using Delong’s test, for which Aβ42/Aβ40 featured the highest classifying AUC (Supplementary Fig. 13G [this file] ). miR-204-5p has been previously identified as a dementia biomarker in CSF; however, it was downregulated in AD patients versus controls , whereas it is upregulated in the combined LBD and AD cohort in this study. 
Within these biomarkers, eight miRNAs (seven from GluR2, one from GLAST), Aβ42/Aβ40, and p-Tau181 were upregulated in the AD cohort; the remaining biomarkers were upregulated in the control cohort (Supplementary Fig. 14A–D [this file] ). ROC analysis of these biomarkers yielded four biomarkers (GluR2+ EV miR-132-3p alongside proteins p-Tau181, Aβ42, and Aβ42/Aβ40) with statistically significant AUCs per Delong’s test (Delong’s value = 0.0039, 0.027, 0.017, and 0.018, respectively), with miR-132-3p having the highest AUC of the group at 0.76 (Supplementary Fig. 14E–G [this file] ). 
Our comparison of LBD versus control yielded only two differentially expressed biomarkers (p-Tau231 and GLAST + EV miR-200b-3p) (Supplementary Fig. 15A–C [this file] ), and only p-Tau231 had a statistically significant AUC at 0.69 (Delong’s value = 0.020) (Supplementary Fig. 15D, E [this file] ). 
Additional significantly enriched (FDR value < 0.05) GO BP terms associated with brain-related processes and neuroinflammation are shown in Supplementary Table 4 [this file] and significantly enriched (FDR value < 0.05) KEGG pathways associated with the nervous system, neuron development, and brain-specific diseases are shown in Supplementary Table 5 [this file] . 
The top 10 enriched KEGG pathways showed the greatest interaction between differentially expressed GluR2+ EV miRNAs with target genes (inhibition of which is linked to Aβ accumulation and tau phosphorylation) , (inhibition of which causes memory deficits in mice) , and (which influences a wide network of genes affected in LBD and AD) (Supplementary Fig. 16A [this file] ). For differentially expressed GLAST + EV miRNAs, KEGG pathways showed the greatest interaction with apoptosis regulators and , along with , which controls tau-induced neurotoxicity (Supplementary Fig. 16B [this file] ). 
In sweeping the number of selected biomarkers from two to 20, we generated a composite list of biomarkers including 14 GluR2+ EV miRNAs, four GLAST + EV miRNAs, p-Tau231, and p-Tau181 (Table 2 [rid=Tab2] ), with many of the LASSO-selected markers having been identified by previous literature concerning neurological conditions (Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). 
The ROC curve for the combined 15-marker panel shows that the panel greatly outperformed each individual LASSO-selected biomarker (Supplementary Fig. 17 [this file] ), showing an improvement in AUC of 0.21 over the best performing individual LASSO biomarker, and non-overlapping 95% confidence intervals between the 15-marker panel and any of the individual LASSO biomarkers (Fig. 4E [rid=Fig4] ). 
To confirm whether we had included a sufficient number of patients necessary to train our model, we then generated a learning curve by evaluating the model’s performance using different sizes of training data with 100 bootstraps per size (Supplementary Fig. 18 [this file] ). 
Features within the 15-marker panel were assessed for contributions to model discrimination using (1) permutation feature importance (Supplementary Fig. 19 [this file] ), which quantifies how perturbing each of the features independently degrades model AUC and accuracy ; and (2) Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analyses (Supplementary Fig. 20 [this file] ), which measures the contribution of each feature to model predictions . We found good agreement between permutation feature importance and SHAP value rankings; the highest ranked markers were GluR2+ EV miR-4748, GLAST + EV miR-148b-5p, and p-Tau231 in all three feature importance rankings: permutation feature importance by change in AUC (Supplementary Fig. 19A [this file] ) and accuracy (Supplementary Fig. 19B [this file] ), as well as SHAP value (Supplementary Fig. 20A [this file] ). 
Only one feature showed a negative decrease in AUC when perturbed (GluR2+ EV miR-200c-3p, decrease in AUC = –0.0006) (Supplementary Fig. 19A [this file] ) although the magnitude of this change was small and indicative of only a marginal improvement in performance. 
Feature stability was then examined by generating a Spearman’s rank correlation matrix of SHAP-based feature rankings (Supplementary Fig. 20B [this file] ). 
We then examined the relative expression levels of LASSO-selected biomarkers in mixed-pathology patients with histopathologic diagnoses of AD/LBD ( = 30) or AD/ALB ( = 19) as compared to LBD and AD patients (Supplementary Fig. 21 [this file] ). 
Assuming a more modest model performance within the validation cohort of AUC = 0.9 and an event prevalence of 0.5, we determined that at least an additional = 158 subjects within our independent validation set would be necessary to achieve a 95% confidence interval width of ≤0.1 (Supplementary Fig. 22 [this file] ). 
The mTENPO platform is being commercialized, and through a startup company, a fluid handling system was built to automate mTENPO isolation and minimize user variability (Supplementary Fig. 23 [this file] ). 
Comparison of the libraries run on different batch days showed average Kendall correlation > 0.9 for the sequencing reads from the same patient sample run on two different batch days (Supplementary Fig. 24 [this file] ), as well as close rank-order matching of individual patient samples between sequencing runs (Supplementary Fig. 25 [this file] ).

Bootstrap validation (500 iterations) yielded a median AUC of 0.859 (95% CI: 0.753–0.944) for Random Forest ( Supplementary Figure 25 [this file] and Supplementary Table 25 [rid=TS1] ). 
In the extended analysis (see Supplementary Figure 4 [this file] ), a consistent pattern of minimized bias across folds was observed, further validating the stability of our model selection process. 
Further evaluation metrics, including precision-recall (PR) parameters ( Supplementary Tables 9 [rid=TS1] , 10 [rid=TS1] and Supplementary Figure 5 [this file] ), Brier score ( Supplementary Tables 11 [rid=TS1] , 12 [rid=TS1] ), and metrics based on the confusion matrix such as sensitivity, specificity, predictive value, accuracy, recall, and F1 score, further validated the superior stability of Random Forest compared to other algorithms. A direct comparison of the AUC distributions across models ( Supplementary Table 13 [rid=TS1] and Supplementary Figure 6 [this file] ) further supported these findings. Specifically, the Random Forest model achieved a calibration slope of 1.007 and intercept of −0.002, indicating good agreement between predicted probabilities and observed event rates ( Supplementary Figure 7 [this file] and Supplementary Table 14 [rid=TS1] ). DCA demonstrated that Random Forest provided the greatest net clinical benefit across the clinically meaningful threshold range of 10–40% ( Supplementary Figure 8 [this file] ). At the default threshold of 0.50, sensitivity was 62.1% and specificity 86.5%; a lower threshold of 0.25 yielded sensitivity of 86.2% with specificity of 69.2%, which may be more appropriate for screening purposes ( Supplementary Figure 9 [this file] and Supplementary Table 15 [rid=TS1] ). 
As shown in Supplementary Table 16 [rid=TS1] and Supplementary Figure 10 [this file] , Random Forest achieved a mean AUC of 0.885 ± 0.029 (five-fold CV) and 0.877 ± 0.029 (10-fold CV), consistently demonstrating competitive performance across all strategies. The multi-strategy comparison heatmap ( Supplementary Figure 11 [this file] ) confirms that Random Forest maintained stable AUC values (range: 0.845–0.885) regardless of the data-splitting approach. Learning curve analysis ( Supplementary Figure 12 [this file] ) further demonstrated convergence of training and validation performance with increasing sample size. 
Similar results were obtained in the validation set, with an accuracy of 77.8%, sensitivity of 62.1%, specificity of 86.5%, precision of 72%, recall of 62.1%, and an F1 score of 66.7% ( Supplementary Figure 13 [this file] ). Subgroup analysis confirmed consistent model performance across age and sex subgroups ( Supplementary Figure 14 [this file] ). Predictor correlation analysis confirmed absence of severe multicollinearity among the eight selected features (|r| < 0.7 for all pairs; Supplementary Figure 15 [this file] ). 
To further enhance clinical interpretability, we also provide SHAP dependence plots for key predictive variables ( Supplementary Figure 16 [this file] ). The SHAP summary plot ( Supplementary Figure 17A [this file] ) shows the feature importance, highlighting the most influential variables, with smoking having the highest contribution. The mean SHAP value plot ( Supplementary Figure 17B [this file] ) shows that features such as smoking and MCA have the highest average SHAP values. The SHAP heatmap ( Supplementary Figure 17C [this file] ) visualizes the individual-level contribution patterns of the final selected predictive factors in the best-performing Random Forest model. The SHAP effects and interaction network graph ( Supplementary Figure 17D [this file] ) illustrates the interactions between features and their collective impact on the model output, with features like smoking and MCA showing strong interactions. 
After considering their individual impact on the model’s output, we also examined how they interact to collectively influence the predicted outcome ( Supplementary Figure 18 [this file] and Supplementary Table 18 [rid=TS1] ). 
Demographic factors were pre-existing, imaging features were measured during the acute phase, and treatment adequacy reflects ongoing management ( Supplementary Figure 19 [this file] ). 
The inclusion of treatment adequacy variables (APT Standard and LDL-C Control) is appropriate within the follow-up monitoring framework, as these represent modifiable risk factors reflecting the quality of secondary prevention ( Supplementary Table 23 [rid=TS1] and Supplementary Figure 26 [this file] ). 
To contextualize our findings, we compared our model’s performance with prior ML-based prediction studies targeting stroke-related endpoints ( Supplementary Table 20 [rid=TS1] and Supplementary Figure 20 [this file] ).

Participants with a history of stroke or dementia at baseline (criteria provided in eTable 1 in Supplement 1 [this file] ) were excluded from the analyses. Table 1 [rid=zoi241083t1] and eTable 1 in Supplement 1 [this file] summarize each study. 
Stroke was self-reported in all studies except 2, where the information came from an inpatient register or via examination (eTable 2 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). Year and month of stroke was recorded or approximated by the midpoint between 2 assessments (eTable 2 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). Demographic and medical history data were harmonized as per previous COSMIC projects (see eTable 3 and eTable 4 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). Table 2 [rid=zoi241083t2] lists the categories for each harmonized variable; eTable 3 and eTable 5 in Supplement 1 [this file] provide the criteria and levels of missing data. 
Refer to eTable 5 in Supplement 1 [this file] for the number of missing values for each variable. 
See eTable 6 in Supplement 1 [this file] for the tests used in each domain from each study. 
Missing covariates in the pooled sample were imputed using multiple imputation with chain equations (eMethods in Supplement 1 [this file] ). See eTable 7 in Supplement 1 [this file] for detailed interpretation of the model coefficients. 
Follow-up durations ranged from 3 to 17 years ( Table 1 [rid=zoi241083t1] ; eFigure 1 in Supplement 1 [this file] ), with a mean (SD) duration of 7.51 (4.2) years. Participant characteristics in each study are detailed in eTable 8 and eTable 9 in Supplement 1 [this file] . Participants who dropped out compared with those assessed until study end were significantly older, had fewer years of education, and had higher proportions with vascular risk factors at baseline (eTable 10 in Supplement 1 [this file] ), though Cohen and values suggest that apart from age, these differences were small. 
Baseline factors associated with global cognition in the basic model were ethnic and racial groups, study entry period, diabetes, hypertension, CVD, high cholesterol, systolic blood pressure, APOE4, depression, physical activity, and alcohol use (eTable 11 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). The percentage of missing data was less than 6% for most covariates, except for between 9% and 38% for systolic blood pressure, high cholesterol, APOE4, and physical activity (eTable 12 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
Results from the unadjusted and adjusted models were similar, differing by less than 8% in effect sizes (eTable 13 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). Figure 1 [rid=zoi241083f1] A illustrates the results based on projected values and mean covariate values (eTable 14 in Supplement 1 [this file] ) for an incident stroke occurring 4.6 years (mean time to incident stroke) into the study. 
Common values were based on subsample with global cognition data (see eTable 12 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). Plots of projected values with 95% CIs are shown in eFigure 4 in Supplement 1 [this file] . 
By including a stroke group interaction term in the model using the full sample, we showed that the slopes and baseline levels were not significantly different between the stroke and no-stroke groups (eTable 15 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
Unadjusted results are shown in eTable 13 in Supplement 1 [this file] . 
The analysis using complete data (75% of full sample) showed slightly larger effect sizes (by 21%-24%), while excluding assessments less than 1 year after stroke resulted in no change (eTable 16 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). Excluding 3 studies with more than 50% loss to follow-up resulted in 66% greater poststroke difference in slope (eTable 16 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
The acute outcome of stroke on cognitive function was significant across all domains, with effect sizes ranging from −0.17 to −0.22 SD, as well as for the MMSE (−0.36 SD) (eTable 17 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
There was no significant difference in cognitive level or slope between the stroke group before stroke and the no-stroke group in all cognitive outcomes (eTable 15 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). As subgroup analyses results were consistent with the full sample analysis (eTable 18 in Supplement 1 [this file] ), we plotted cognitive trajectories using the latter ( Figure 2 [rid=zoi241083f2] ). 
Common values were based on subsample with global cognition data (see eTable 14 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). Plots of predicted values with 95% CIs are shown in eFigure 5 in Supplement 1 [this file] . 
None of the interaction terms were significant, except for age and acute outcome (0.013 SD; 95% CI, 0.002 to 0.023 SD) (eTable 19 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). To facilitate interpretation, we conducted a stratified analysis after dichotomizing age using the median value (<72 or ≥72) (eTable 20 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). We found that older stroke survivors experienced less acute decline, but exhibited lower cognitive levels at baseline and significantly faster decline without stroke (−0.063 SD per year vs −0.034 SD per year). eFigure 2 in Supplement 1 [this file] shows no crossing of the trajectory lines. 
Subgroup analyses suggested that individuals with diabetes exhibited lower cognition scores at baseline and faster, although they did not have a statistically significant decline poststroke (eTable 19 and eTable 21 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). Cognitive performance remained worse for those with diabetes throughout the follow-up (eFigure 3 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
This means individuals without a previous stroke who had diabetes, hypertension, CVD, high cholesterol, smoked, or carried APOE4 exhibited faster cognitive decline (eTable 19 in Supplement 1 [this file] ).

Immunocytochemistry staining revealed a significant expression of the key microglial markers CX3 CR1, IBA1, P2RY12, PU.1, TMEM119, and TREM2 in the MDMi, whereas these markers were not abundantly detected in the monocytes and no unspecific staining was observed in negative controls (Additional file 1 [this file] , Fig. S4). 
Biallelic deletion had a more robust effect on the gene and protein expression in all conditions when compared to individuals homozygous for the common variant (Additional file 1 [this file] Fig. S5 A-E, Additional file 6 [rid=MOESM6] ) or monoallelic deletion carriers (Additional file 1 [this file] Fig. S6 A-E, Additional file 7). As expected, was not detected in the NHD MDMi at either the transcript or protein level, whereas a well-established NHD microglial marker CD163 was significantly upregulated at both transcript and protein levels in NHD MDMi when compared to individuals homozygous for common variant in all comparisons, except in the DEG analysis of untreated cells (Additional file 1 [this file] Fig S5). 
Multiple inflammation related gene sets were upregulated in the NHD compared to common variant or monoallelic deletion MDMi, including interferon gamma response, TNFα signaling via NFKB, IL2-STAT5 signaling, and IL6-JAK-STAT3 signaling (Additional file 1 [this file] Fig S5 F, S6 F), which were also significantly upregulated in the NHD brain microglia according to a recent single nucleus RNA-sequencing (sn-RNAseq) analysis [ 47 [rid=CR47] ]. 
To assess how deletion affects downstream signaling, we generated KO BV2 microglial cell lines by lentiviral CRISPR-Cas9 editing (Additional file 1 [this file] Fig. S7 A-B). In addition, we used siRNA-mediated silencing to mimic cells with monoallelic deletion (Additional file 1 [this file] Fig. S7 A-B). M-CSF induced a robust increase in the phosphorylation of Syk in control and siRNA-treated cells, but not in KO cells (Additional file 1 [this file] Fig. S7 C). Total Syk levels remained unaltered between control and siRNA-treated cells, while approximately 20% reduction in total Syk levels was observed in the KO cells (Additional file 1 [this file] Fig. S7D).

Histopathological examination of the biopsies identified 19 with Aβ plaques (Aβ+), eight with both Aβ plaques and phosphorylated tau pathology (Aβ+Tau+), and 25 that were free of histopathology ( Table S1 [this file1] ). From the stereotactic position of the catheter insertion site recorded by post-surgical CT or MRI, we determined that the anatomical location of sampling did not correlate with AD histopathological burden ( Figure S1A [this file] ). We further divided the Aβ+ biopsies into three groups by their level of plaque burden ( Figures S1B [this file] and S1C [this file] ). 
Human studies included postmortem samples from individuals with AD, Parkinson’s disease (PD), multiple sclerosis (MS), and autism spectrum disorder (ASD) ( Table S1 [this file1] ). Mouse datasets included models of AD and ALS, as well as de/re-myelination, aging, prenatal, and food deprivation conditions among others ( Table S1 [this file1] ). Comparison across human datasets demonstrated our biopsy cohort had among the highest number of cells sampled per cell type and minimal expression of artifactual genes often associated with sample quality ( Figure S1 [this file] ). Together, our results, in combination with the expression patterns of artifact associated genes ( Figure S1E [this file] ), indicate loss of transcriptional complexity in both inhibitory and excitatory neurons, as well as an increase in artifact-related genes in microglial cells in response to peri- and post-mortem events. 
Distributions of the quality metrics are included in Figures 1C [rid=F1] and S1E [this file] .

Markers of microglia states correlated strongly across different human brain regions, which is consistent with previous reports ( Figures S5A [this file] – S5D [this file] ). 
Differential expression analysis across all microglia in our cohort identified a pattern that was highly similar in each of the 13 states ( Figure S5E [this file] ), suggesting that all microglia states respond similarly to Aβ accumulation. This transcriptional pattern was also highly consistent across postmortem cohorts and increased in magnitude with further clinical progression of AD ( Figures S5F [this file] – S5H [this file] ). 
Supporting this notion, we found a strong positive correlation between the expression of in astrocytes and the expansion of GPNMB-EYA2 and LPL-CD83 microglia states in our cohort ( Figure S5I [this file] ). 
In contrast to the human datasets, only the GPNMB-NACA state was consistently expanded in AD mouse models ( Figure S5J [this file] ). This state was also increased in several other mouse datasets, including a model of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, in both juvenile and aged mice, and in response to demyelinating injury ( Figure S5J [this file] ). Corroborating this finding, we observed that the cis-regulatory regions of marker genes for GPNMB-EYA2 and LPL-CD83 populations are significantly enriched in human accelerated regions (HARs) , fast-evolving regions of the human genome that modulate human-specific transcriptional regulatory programs ( Figure S5K [this file] ).

Applying this analysis to the Aβ+ biopsy samples identified a specific and significant (FDR-adjusted p-value < 0.01) correlation between NDNF-PROX1 depletion and upregulated ExN DE genes in the LINC00507-COL5A2 excitatory neurons ( Figures 3A [rid=F3] and S3A [this file] ), which themselves are vulnerable to loss in early AD pathology ( Figure 2A [rid=F2] ). Alternative analysis methods confirmed the strength of association between the ExN DE signature in LINC00507-COL5A2 with the loss of + expressing cells in Aβ+ individuals ( Figures S3B [this file] – S3E [this file] ). Moreover, this association was also significant (FDR-adjusted p-value < 0.05) within the control biopsy samples ( Figures S3F [this file] and S3G [this file] ), reinforcing that this pair of neuronal changes–loss of NDNF-PROX1 and induction of a specific transcriptional state in LINC00507-COL5A2–occurs early in disease. 
In our integrative analysis of astrocytes, we identified one + type with low expression of and high expression of , , and genes, which encode for critical components of glutamate/glutathione cycling ( Figures S3I [this file] and S3J [this file] ). 
First, to assess the robustness of the results, we tested the sensitivity of the results to the presence of technical variation in cell gene counts by, iterating 30 times, adding Poisson noise to the transcriptome data of each individual cell before calculation of the meta-gene expressions ( Figure S3B [this file] ). In addition, iterating 30 times we randomly down sampled the cell types to examine the association of the cell type sizes on the results ( Figure S3C [this file] ). 
Second, as an alternative analysis method to support our findings ( Figure S3D [this file] ), we constructed meta-genes through principal component analysis of the normalized and scaled expression of the top 300 upregulated protein-coding genes (sorted based on jack-knifed p-values).

We further confirmed that the observed changes in neuronal populations do not correlate with possible confounding factors ( Figure S2E [this file] ). 
In subjects with high histopathological burden, the proportional losses of the NDNF-PROX1 and LINC00507-COL5A2 neuronal populations were no longer significant ( Figures 2A [rid=F2] and 2B [rid=F2] ), likely due to additional loss of other cortical neurons, since the overall proportions of excitatory and inhibitory neurons were both lower in these subjects ( Figure S2F [this file] ). 
Meta-analysis p-values (and Z-scores) were generated using Stouffer’s method, taking into account the directionality of the abundance change ( Figure S2F [this file] ). 
We used cell-class level DE genes to construct meta-genes since: 1) cell class level DE genes were highly conserved within cell types ( Figure S2G [this file] ); 2) DE genes were not driven by the variation in the cell counts of the cell types.

To establish regulatory pathways of neurogenesis in the adult human brain, we first examined sequencing profiles of 85,977 nuclei from 8 cognitively intact adults aged 20–40 years (YA cohort; Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). Of these, 80 pathways were associated with dendritic, axonal, postsynaptic density and neurotransmission pathways (Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). 
Examination of the other subcluster compared with astrocytes revealed 766 DEGs (671 upregulated and 95 downregulated) compared with the rest of the astrocytes (Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). Pathway analysis revealed that 25 out of the 65 pathways were related to neuronal development, including axonal development, node of Ranvier, initial segment, growth cone, axonal guidance, dendritic spine and postsynaptic density (Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). A comparison of our neurogenesis signature with previous studies that observed neurogenesis in the human dentate gyrus revealed a high level of concordance (Extended Data Figs. 2 [rid=Fig7] – 4 [rid=Fig9] and Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ). 
The top DEGs and differentially accessible regions (DARs) in NSCs were downregulated in neuroblasts and further downregulated in immature neurons (Fig. 1a,b [rid=Fig1] , Extended Data Fig. 5 [rid=Fig10] and Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ). Pathways enriched in immature neurons were related to synaptic function and plasticity (Fig. 1c [rid=Fig1] and Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). As there is no universally accepted criterion standard measure of anticholinergics, we used strong anticholinergics from the American Geriatrics Society (AGS) Beers Criteria to focus on medications most likely associated with physical decline (eTable 1 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
Subsequently, we calculated the sum or mean of SDDs for all prescriptions each participant had in each exposure window of pre-specified length to obtain the total SDD (TSDD) and mean SDD (mSDD) (eMethods in Supplement 1 [this file] ). We evaluated a secondary exposure that combined anticholinergics and sedatives or hypnotics (eTable 1 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
Race and ethnicity data were collected to describe the study sample. eTable 2 in Supplement 1 [this file] illustrates how comorbidities were defined, including coronary heart disease (CHD), anxiety, Parkinson disease, insomnia, depression, and stroke. 
We also examined 5 WCE models that summarized the cumulative exposure in the prior 2, 4, 6, 8, and 10 years (eMethods in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
The prevalence of each medication class is provided in eTable 3 in Supplement 1 [this file] . 
The estimated weight function from the 4-year WCE model demonstrated that the most proximal anticholinergic exposure had the strongest associations with the change rate (eFigure 2 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
The estimated weight function under the 6-year WCE model is shown in eFigure 3 in Supplement 1 [this file] . 
The long-term consistent use pattern was associated with an MD of −0.0034 (95% CI, −0.0048 to −0.0019) m/s of decline per year in gait speed, greater than 2-fold faster than what a model with unweighted mSDD would infer. eTable 4 in Supplement 1 [this file] illustrates the differences in 6-year weighted mSDD and the corresponding differential change rate for grip strength for the 3 use patterns. 
These results illustrate use patterns associated with this threshold of decline in 1 year (eFigure 4 in Supplement 1 [this file] ) and in 5 years (eFigure 5 in Supplement 1 [this file] ).

All post-mortem neuropathological assessments, clinical evaluations, and pathological grouping are detailed in Supplementary Table 1 [this file] [ 46 [rid=b46-ad-16-3-1598] ]. 
The table of p-values and log fold changes for all genes across all brain regions and cell types is provided in Supplementary Tables 2-4 [this file] [ 46 [rid=b46-ad-16-3-1598] ]. 
Certain pathways were renamed to optimize clarity and standard nomenclature, with specific modifications enumerated in Supplementary Table 5 [this file] [ 46 [rid=b46-ad-16-3-1598] ]. Estimates of β coefficients, along with additional statistics as outlined in Fig. 1 [rid=F1-ad-16-3-1598] , are comprehensively documented in Supplementary Tables 6-8 [this file] [ 46 [rid=b46-ad-16-3-1598] ], including both nominal p-values and FDR-corrected p-values. 
The selected soft power thresholds, demonstrating a fit to the scale-free topology model, are reported in Supplementary Fig. 3-5 [this file] . Module dendrograms were visualized using the PlotDendrogram function ( Supplementary Fig. 6-8 [this file] ). 
Supplementary Tables 9-11 [this file] [ 46 [rid=b46-ad-16-3-1598] ] contains additional statistics for each cell type across tested brain regions. 
Preliminary analysis of the principal components of the aggregated expression data revealed that other covariates, such as age at death and post-mortem interval, are not correlated with biological or technical variation ( Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] ), and as a result were excluded from the design matrix, ensuring that the data modeling focused solely on the biologically relevant factors [ 56 [rid=b56-ad-16-3-1598] ]. Pathology groups were defined based on the ADNC levels ( Supplementary Table 1 [this file] [ 46 [rid=b46-ad-16-3-1598] ], ), with individuals categorized as early-pathology (low or intermediate ADNC) or late-pathology (high ADNC). 
Remarkably, the affected pathways displayed substantial similarity across brain regions, with some showing consistent directional changes across cell types, while others exhibited complex patterns of distinct alterations in each cell type ( Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] ; see Supplementary Table 12 [this file] for full list of overlapping pathways [ 46 [rid=b46-ad-16-3-1598] ]). 
To identify consistently perturbed processes across the three brain regions, we assessed the overlap of differentially perturbed pathways in a cell-type-specific manner ( Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] ; see Supplementary Table 12 [this file] for full list of overlapping pathways [ 46 [rid=b46-ad-16-3-1598] ]). Interestingly, excitatory and inhibitory neurons showed the most pronounced concordance in disrupted processes ( Supplementary Fig. 2A [this file] ), with 31 pathways in excitatory neurons and 84 pathways in inhibitory neurons showing consistent dysregulations across the three regions. 
Excitatory neurons, on the other hand, consistently expressed disruptions in pathways related to mitochondrial autophagy and Ca -dependent exocytosis, underscoring the role of Ca signaling in AD-associated cellular perturbations ( Supplementary Fig. 2B [this file] ). Among the affected processes were intracellular pH regulation, mitochondrial autophagy, and neurotransmitter receptor transport ( Supplementary Fig. 2B [this file] ). 
see Supplementary Table 13 [this file] for full list of hub genes 
DME analysis of MTG derived neuronal modules revealed marked differences in the magnitude and direction of module expression from control to AD ( Fig. 5 [rid=F5-ad-16-3-1598] and 6J [rid=F6-ad-16-3-1598] ) (Wilcoxon rank-sum test Bonferroni-adjusted p <0.05; Supplementary Tables 9-11 [this file] [ 46 [rid=b46-ad-16-3-1598] ]). 
To further identify potential common drivers directing these pathway perturbations across regions, we examined recurrent hub genes within each cell type ( Supplementary Table 14 [this file] [ 46 [rid=b46-ad-16-3-1598] ]).

Preliminary analysis of the principal components of the aggregated expression data revealed that other covariates, such as age at death and post-mortem interval, are not correlated with biological or technical variation ( Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] ), and as a result were excluded from the design matrix, ensuring that the data modeling focused solely on the biologically relevant factors ( 56 [rid=R56] ). 
Remarkably, the affected pathways displayed substantial similarity across brain regions, with some showing consistent directional changes across cell types, while others exhibited complex patterns of distinct alterations in each cell type ( Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] ;Supplementary Table 12 [rid=SD12]). 
To identify consistently perturbed processes across the three brain regions, we assessed the overlap of differentially perturbed pathways in a cell-type-specific manner ( Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] ;Supplementary Table 12 [rid=SD12]). Interestingly, excitatory and inhibitory neurons showed the most pronounced concordance in disrupted processes ( Supplementary Fig. 2a [this file] ), with 31 pathways in excitatory neurons and 84 pathways in inhibitory neurons showing consistent dysregulations across the three regions. Excitatory neurons, on the other hand, consistently expressed disruptions in pathways related to mitochondrial autophagy and Ca -dependent exocytosis, underscoring the role of Ca signaling in AD-associated cellular perturbations ( Supplementary Fig. 2b [this file] ). Among the affected processes were intracellular pH regulation, mitochondrial autophagy, and neurotransmitter receptor transport ( Supplementary Fig. 2b [this file] ).

context_description:
ADNC, including amyloid plaques (APs; assessed by Thal phase or its derivative National Institute on Aging and Alzheimer’s Association [NIA-AA] A score), neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs; assessed by Braak stage or its derivative NIA-AA B score), neuritic plaques (NPs; assessed by Consortium to Establish a Registry for AD [CERAD] NP score or its derivative NIA-AA C score), and the combined NIA-AA ADNC ABC score [ 27 [rid=pgen.1012170.ref027] ] were strongly positively correlated with each other (r = 0.70 to 0.87) and had moderate correlations with ε4, cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA), and LBD (r = 0.14 to 0.51, S1 Fig [this file] ). 
TDP-43 proteinopathy and HS are correlated ( S1 Fig [this file] ) and are commonly observed in FTLD-TDP, LATE-NC, and ADNC. 
Given the phenotypic correlations ( S1 Fig [this file] ) and cooccurrence of neuropathological lesions, we assessed candidate variants from clinic-based AD and PD association studies for pleiotropic effects across the spectrum of neuropathological lesions. 
Phenotypic correlations ( S1 Fig [this file] ) motivated the assessment of genetic correlations among traits with significant heritability. 
The correlated nature of some of the neuropathological phenotypes ( S1 Fig [this file] ) may allow for improved efficiency and power with more complex multivariate modeling (e.g., MANCOVA), at least for some ensemble hypotheses; this will be the subject of future studies.

As expected, we found strong GWS associations in the locus for the dual proteinopathies of AD ( Fig 1 [rid=pgen.1012170.g001] , S2 Table [this file] ).

title: A priori and a posteriori power calculations for clinical-AD risk variants.
caption: Abbreviations: chr, chromosome; pos, position; min, minor allele; maj, major allele; MAF, minor allele frequency; OR, odd’s ratio. Yellow highlights denote moderate power (0.5-0.8) and green highlights denote strong power (0.8-1). A priori power denotes the power of observing an association with the designated variant, if the current study has the same additive effect size as those reported in the Bellenguez et al GWAS. Power (A) denotes the power if that effect size is observed with ‘A Score’ and its sample size and ordinal trait distribution, under the proportional odds assumption. Similarly, Power (B) is with B Score (e.g., AD Braak), and Power (C) is with CERAD. The a posteriori power section denotes power to observe association when the true effect sizes are those observed in our study. “A Score” uses the effect sizes we estimated for A Score, “B Score” with B score, etc. Power (Bonf.) denotes power when using a Bonferroni-correct alpha threshold (p < 0.05/78) and Power (Nom.) denotes power when using a nominal alpha threshold (p < 0.05). All calculations were performed using simulations. Briefly, a population of 10,000,000 was created for each SNP, with the appropriate effect size (under proportional odds), ordinal trait distribution, and minor allele frequency (assuming Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium). To calculate power, 1000 samples were drawn from this population, with sample size equivalent to the “N” for the A Score, B Score, and C Score phenotypes. Each iteration was then tested for association between variant and ordinal trait using ordinal logistic regression under the proportinal odds assumption. Power is then the portion of iterations with effect-size p-value less than the required alpha threshold (Bonferroni or nominal).

Performance was generally worsened when temporal adjustments were applied to business and rush hour designs (see Figure S8 [this file] for R comparisons and Figure S9 [this file] for site-specific prediction errors). Sensitivity and secondary analyses of 10–100 nm PNC, 20–1,000 nm PNC, and NO as well as showed similar patterns ( Figure S10 [this file] – S11 [this file] ). 
Exposure predictions for sampling campaigns varied across campaigns ( Figure S12 [this file] ). Predictions from the all-data exposure model were strongly correlated with those from most sampling campaigns (median Pearson correlations [R] > 0.85), indicating similar exposure surface although the business hour design consistently predicted exposures with lower correlations (R ~0.77–0.78; Figure S13 [this file] ). 
In the reduced health inference model, each 1,900 pt/cm increment in PNC was associated with an adjusted mean baseline CASI-IRT score that was 0.020 (95% CI: −0.036, −0.004) lower, equivalent to approximately 7.5 (95% CI: −13.6, −1.5) months of aging ( Table S2 [this file] ). Figures S14 [this file] provides additional details, including the point estimates and 95% CIs of selected designs. 
In the primary health inference model, each 1,900 pt/cm increment in PNC was associated with an adjusted mean baseline CASI-IRT score that was 0.002 (95% CI: −0.016, 0.020) higher, equivalent to approximately 0.7 (95% CI: −5.8, 7.3) fewer months of aging ( Table S2 [this file] ). Figure S15 [this file] shows point estimates for selected designs along with their 95% CIs. 
Table S2 [this file] presents these results along with those from alternative PNC measures, which yield similar findings. Consistent with the main analyses, business and rush hour designs led to health inferences that deviated from the reference estimates ( Figure S16 [this file] ). 
Sensitivity analyses restricted to participants enrolled since 2010 produced similar health inferences ( Table S3 [this file] ), with the mean baseline CASI-IRT score decreasing by 0.003 (95% CI: −0.034, 0.028) per 1,900 pt/cm increment in PNC and decreasing by 0.001 (95% CI: −0.044, 0.042) per 3 ppb increment in NO . 
When compared to the all-data monitoring campaign, campaigns with fewer visits (4–12) but no temporal restrictions, shorter durations (2–3 seasons), and a fixed number of visits across sites (12) produced only slightly worse exposure model performances ( Figure S7 [this file] ) ( Blanco, Doubleday, et al., 2022 [rid=R6] ; Blanco et al., 2023 [rid=R5] ; Sheppard & Blanco, Under Review); highly correlated (mostly >~0.85) participant exposures ( Figure S13 [this file] ); and health inferences with only a small degree of variability ( Figure 2 [rid=F2] ). 
Temporally adjusting business hours design data did not consistently improve health estimates ( Figure 2 [rid=F2] , Figure S8 [this file] , Figure S9 [this file] ). 
Interestingly, collecting less balanced visit data across sites generally resulted in worse and more variable exposure models, but this had a less pronounced impact on health inferences ( Figure S7 [this file] and Figure 2 [rid=F2] ). 
Despite this, this approach produced strong PNC predictions and captured much of the observed temporal variation in UFP concentrations ( Figure S2 [this file] – Figure S4 [this file] ).

A π value greater than zero also indicates that the rank ordering of DEGs reflects meaningful biological associations ( Figure S7B [this file] ).

Moreover, these lead BLNPs also exhibited high mRNA delivery efficiency in bEnd.3 cells ( Supplementary Fig. 2a [this file] – f [this file] ). Meanwhile, these BLNPs displayed minimal toxicity in both N2a and bEnd.3 at the tested dose (80% or higher cell viability in all the treated groups; Supplementary Fig. 3a [this file] , b [this file] ). Their apparent pKa ranged from 5.28 to 9.79 ( Supplementary Fig. 4a [this file] – f [this file] ). 
Both MK6 BLNPs and MC3 LNPs showed similar signal intensity in other major organs ( Fig. 2i [rid=F2] and Supplementary Fig. 5a [this file] ). MK6 BLNPs were around 139.8 ± 3.5 nm in diameter with a polydispersity index of <0.15 ( Supplementary Fig. 5b [this file] ). Approximately 83.1 ± 2.7% of mRNA was encapsulated in MK6 BLNPs, and they were slightly positively charged ( Supplementary Fig. 5c [this file] ). 
To further improve the brain delivery efficiency of BLNPs through systemic administration, we conducted several rounds of experiments to optimize MK6 BLNP formulations ( Supplementary Fig. 6a [this file] ). 
These MK BLNPs exhibited similar particle size, encapsulation efficiency and zeta potential ( Supplementary Fig. 6b [this file] , c [this file] ). They also presented similar apparent pKa values, with a narrow range from 6.70 to 6.99 ( Supplementary Fig. 6d [this file] ). Moreover, MK6, MK6E and MK16 displayed comparable distribution trends in other major organs ( Supplementary Fig. 7a [this file] , b [this file] ). Additionally, MK16 BLNPs showed 7.4-fold and 6.5-fold higher luminescence intensity than ALC-0315 and SM-102 LNPs in brains after intravenous administration, respectively ( Supplementary Fig. 8a [this file] , b [this file] ). The MK16 BLNPs exhibited a particle size of 137.0 ± 4.1 nm and an mRNA encapsulation efficiency of approximately 84.8 ± 1.5% ( Supplementary Fig. 9a [this file] , b [this file] ). The particles were positively charged and displayed spherical morphology in cryogenic transmission electron microscopy images ( Supplementary Fig. 9c [this file] ). Additionally, MK16 BLNPs showed potent mRNA delivery efficiency in both bEnd.3 cells and N2a cells with negligible cytotoxicity at the tested dose ( Supplementary Fig. 9d [this file] , e [this file] ). 
Substantial levels of fluorescent signals were observed in the brain at the time points of 1 h and 6 h, with no detectable signals at and after the 18 h time point ( Supplementary Fig. 10a [this file] ). Using this method, we observed nearly 56.6 ± 2.5% of the MK16 BLNPs in the liver, 6.5 ± 1.1% in the spleen, 7.4 ± 0.8% in the kidneys, 10.5 ± 1.0% in the lungs and 3.7 ± 1.4% in the heart ( Supplementary Fig. 10b [this file] ). 
Then, we quantified the cellular distribution through the flow cytometry analysis of brain tissues 12 h after administration ( Supplementary Fig. 11a [this file] ). MK16 BLNPs preferentially delivered GFP mRNA to neurons (4.64 ± 1.00% GFP ), astrocytes (6.63 ± 0.62% GFP ) and brain capillary endothelial cells (BCECs; 5.62 ± 0.78% GFP ) at an mRNA dose of 0.5 mg kg , the efficiency of which is particularly superior to those achieved by MC3 LNPs in the corresponding cell types ( Fig. 3f [rid=F3] , g [rid=F3] and Supplementary Fig. 11b [this file] ). Furthermore, increasing the dose of GFP mRNA to 1 mg kg led to enhanced GFP expression in neurons (7.36 ± 0.78%), astrocytes (9.71 ± 0.70%), BCECs (9.18 ± 0.80%) and microglia (2.85 ± 0.44%), suggesting the mRNA delivery efficiency of MK16 BLNPs to brain cells is dose dependent ( Fig. 3f [rid=F3] , g [rid=F3] and Supplementary Fig. 11b [this file] ). 
To explore the possible mechanisms of BBB transportation by MK16 BLNPs, we constructed a transwell assay consisting of bEnd.3 cells to mimic the BBB using the method reported before ( Supplementary Fig. 12a [this file] ) . In this model, MK16 BLNPs encapsulated with Alexa Fluor 647-labelled RNA exhibited dramatically higher fluorescence intensity in the lower compartment than the groups of phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) and MC3 LNPs, respectively ( Supplementary Fig. 12b [this file] ). When methyl-beta-cyclodextrin (MβCD; a caveolae-mediated endocytic inhibitor) was used to pretreat cells, a 43.3 ± 1.7% decrease in transcytosis efficiency was observed ( Supplementary Fig. 12c [this file] ). Furthermore, pretreatment with MK-0752, the small molecule incorporated as the BBB-crossing module in MK lipids, resulted in a 63.8 ± 3.1% decrease in the transcytosis efficiency of MK16 BLNPs, indicating that MK-0752 competitively inhibited the transcytosis of MK16 BLNPs ( Supplementary Fig. 12c [this file] ). Co-incubation with MβCD or NGST sharply diminished the luminescence intensity in both bEnd.3 cells in the upper compartment and N2a cells in the lower compartment, compared with the groups treated only by MK16 BLNPs ( Fig. 3h [rid=F3] , i [rid=F3] and Supplementary Fig. 12d [this file] ). 
In PBS-treated mice, tdTomato expression was undetectable 5 days after administration, but on MK16 BLNP delivery of Cre mRNA, a tdTomato signal was observed throughout most regions of the brain, with the strongest signal detected in brain margins ( Fig. 4b [rid=F4] and Supplementary Fig. 13a [this file] , b [this file] ). 
As shown in Supplementary Fig. 14a [this file] , mice treated with MK16 BLNPs displayed expression levels of most NOTCH genes that were similar to those in the PBS-treated group. The proinflammatory cytokine and chemokine profiles elicited by MK16 BLNPs were comparable with or milder than those induced by MC3 LNPs at the same mRNA dose ( Supplementary Fig. 14b [this file] ). The levels of most biomarkers in both groups reverted to the baseline, as established by the PBS control, at 24 and 48 h after injection ( Supplementary Fig. 14b [this file] , c [this file] ). The levels of aspartate aminotransferase, alanine aminotransferase and blood urea nitrogen remained within the normal range, suggesting that the hepatic and renal functions were not adversely affected by the administration of MK16 BLNPs ( Supplementary Fig. 14d [this file] ). Furthermore, thorough histopathological evaluations of harvested tissues including the brain, heart, liver, lungs, spleen and kidneys at various time intervals revealed no notable pathological alterations ( Supplementary Figs. 14e [this file] , 15 [this file] and 16 [this file] ). Finally, blood biochemical analysis and histopathological evaluations of major organs of the Ai14 mice revealed that multiple injections of MK16 BLNPs did not elicit obvious systemic toxicity ( Supplementary Fig. 17a [this file] – d [this file] ). 
Immunofluorescence staining of brain sections containing GBM demonstrated greater accumulation of MK16 BLNP- mRNA within the tumour region rather than adjacent normal tissue ( Supplementary Fig. 18a [this file] ). Histological analysis revealed that mice treated with MK16 BLNP- mRNA exhibited smaller residual tumours than both PBS group and MK16 BLNP-control mRNA group ( Supplementary Fig. 18b [this file] ). Additionally, mice treated with MK16 BLNP- mRNA showed significantly reduced tumour growth and enhanced survival rates compared with those receiving MC3 LNP- mRNA ( Supplementary Fig. 19a [this file] – c [this file] ).

caption: For both the RNA sequencing and LC-MS datasets, an iterative procedure was employed to identify technical, biological, and clinical variables (“covariates”) that explain the variance in molecular feature expression between samples that is not due to a variable of interest (in this case, LIV-PM status). The QC process begins by compiling covariates and correlating them to (1) the first five principal components of the molecular expression data, (2) LIV-PM status, and (3) each other. A bioinformatician trained in this QC process then performs a manual review of each covariate’s correlations and selects one covariate to add to the regression model. The molecular data is then transformed by regressing out the effects of the covariates in the updated model, covariate-PC correlations are recalculated using the transformed molecular data, the manual review is performed, and the next covariate is selected. This entire procedure is repeated until the bioinformatician determines that no additional covariates are having a meaningful effect on the variance in molecular expression. The key step of the manual review performed by the bioinformatician involves inspecting a figure such as the one shown here for the covariate “PCT_UTR_bases.” This covariate is calculated using the RnaSeqMetrics tool in the GATK package (indicated by the “RNASeqMetrics_” string in the label) and captures technical aspects of the library preparation step in RNA sequencing. In each plot, a point represents a sample, and the same samples are shown in each of the four plots. Points are colored from green (lower PCT_UTR_bases values) to red (higher PCT_UTR_bases values). Two of the top five principal components of the gene expression data are shown in each plot (one on the x-axis and one on the y-axis). The bioinformatician selected this covariate for inclusion in the regression model primarily due to its visually evident correlation with PC1 in the top left plot (i.e., points with x-axis values above zero are greener and points with x-axis values below zero are redder). The visual analysis of the top right plot also factored into the selection, as it suggested a meaningful correlation between the covariate and PC3.

While there were trends of reduced pumping rate in the mutant models with WT background ( Supplementary Fig. 1C [this file] ) (data from several points showed statistical differences), overexpression significantly improved pumping rates in WT, hTau[P301L] and Aβ at a late life stage (adult Day 10) ( Supplementary Fig. 1D [this file] ). It statistically increased larval and adulthood development in hTau[P301L] animals ( Supplementary Fig. 1E–G [this file] ). 
For P301S mice, while they displayed an inferior performance in comparison to WT, 2 months of REST overexpression did not significantly improve results in these memory tests (though a tendency) ( Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] ). 
For this experiment, 7-month-old 5xFAD mice were bilaterally injected with AAV-REST in one side and AAV-Empty vectors in the other side of the CA1 region of the HIP, followed by a 3-month waiting period to allow protein expression to develop ( Fig. 4C [rid=awaf261-F4] and Supplementary Fig. 3A [this file] and C [this file] ). When the two sides of the brain were compared for each mouse, the size ( Supplementary Fig. 3B [this file] ) and the total number ( Fig. 4D [rid=awaf261-F4] ) of Aβ plaques were dramatically reduced (around 29% and 71%, respectively) in the REST-overexpressed region. 
For this purpose, a set of long-term potentiation (LTP) experiments ( Supplementary Fig. 3D [this file] ) was conducted on the HIP of 6- to 7-month-old 5xFAD and WT control mice to evaluate changes of synaptic strength. However, while there was a trend towards reduced LTP in 5xFAD in comparison to WT mice, no significant differences were noted ( Supplementary Fig. 3E [this file] ). 
Transcriptomic profiles revealed that REST overexpression altered gene expression compared to vehicle in both WT and P301S mice ( Supplementary Fig. 3F [this file] ), particularly affecting genes in clusters 4, 6 and 7 ( Fig. 4E [rid=awaf261-F4] and F [rid=awaf261-F4] and Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). These clusters were mainly related to gene regulation ( Supplementary Fig. 4C [this file] ), developmental processes ( Supplementary Fig. 4E [this file] ) and synaptic plasticity ( Supplementary Fig. 4F [this file] ). These genes were enriched in clusters 1, 3 and 8 ( Fig. 4E [rid=awaf261-F4] and F [rid=awaf261-F4] and Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ) and were involved in Aβ clearance ( Supplementary Fig. 4A [this file] ) and chromatin remodelling ( Supplementary Fig. 4H [this file] ). Overall, pathway analysis shows that most of the pathways that exhibited changes in expression in the AD model and subsequently recovered after REST overexpression were mainly involved in cognition, memory and synaptic homeostasis ( Fig. 4G [rid=awaf261-F4] and Supplementary [this file]Figs 3G [rid=awaf261-F3] and 4A– [rid=awaf261-F4] H [this file] ). 
Since REST is a transcription factor, we further evaluated transcriptional profiles of REST-regulated genes, directly and indirectly ( Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ). Compared with WT, changes in expression of the REST-regulated genes in the P301S group were involved in immune response, neural differentiation and synaptic homeostasis ( Supplementary Fig. 3H [this file] ). Additionally, upregulation of REST in the HIP led to changes in mRNA expression of genes involved in pathways important for neuronal survival and function, such as endo-lysosomal pathway, oxidative stress and chromatin remodelling ( Fig. 4H [rid=awaf261-F4] and Supplementary Fig. 3H [this file] ).

Nevertheless, REST mutants treated with NR showed an extension in lifespan but not in health span ( Supplementary Fig. 5H [this file] ). 
For this purpose, we selected 69 well-characterized genes involved in REST-regulated molecular pathways related to autophagy/mitophagy and synaptic activity ( Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ). Some of these proteins were significantly increased after NR treatment in the 5xFAD mice, such as the autophagy proteins PKRN/Parkin and LC3B-II, as well as a trend of increase in the neurotrophin brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) ( Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] ).

In contrast, downregulation of REST did not affect the protein concentration of SIRT1 at the lowest concentration ( Supplementary Fig. 7B [this file] and C [this file] ).

Downregulation of SIRT1 decreased the transcriptional expression of the studied isoforms of ( Fig. 6F–H [rid=awaf261-F6] and Supplementary Fig. 7F [this file] and G [this file] ). Moreover, NR increased mRNA levels of specific REST target genes, such as , , and ( Supplementary Fig. 7H–K [this file] ).

For the other cognitive outcomes, impairment status was determined by a score of either 2 SD below or above the mean of the control group, depending on the direction of the score (Table S2 [this file] ). 
Specifically, 15 dementia risk factors were used for the calculation of the CAIDE and LIBRA scores based on the previously established weights[rid=alz14061-bib-0010] ,[rid=alz14061-bib-0011] (Tables S3 [this file] and S4 [this file] ). 
See Tables S3 and S4 [this file] for the exact risk factor weights. 
Subsequently, the LDAK tool (v5.2)[rid=alz14061-bib-0041] was applied to calculate the polygenic (risk) scores (PGSs) for 11 of the 14 dementia risk factors as well as AD status (including the APOE region) using the HapMap reference panel and the summary statistics of 12 genome‐wide association studies (GWASs) listed in Table S5 [this file] . 
Before constructing these models, we evaluated multiple supervised and unsupervised feature selection methods to investigate which method is suitable for reducing the large dimensionality of the DNA methylation data and found superior performance of the “correlation‐based feature selection method” (see Supplementary Information [this file] for a more detailed description of the applied methodology and results). 
Accordingly, we applied five‐repeated five‐fold cross‐validation to find the optimal hyperparameter values that yield the minimal MAE (the searched hyperparameter space is shown in Table S6 [this file] ). 
In the method, the 10,000 CpGs that have the highest absolute Spearman correlation coefficient with the target variable (i.e., predicted dementia risk factor) in the training set were selected for model training ( Text S1 [this file] ). 
In the method, the CpGs that reached genome‐wide significance in a previously performed epigenome‐wide association study (Table S7 [this file] ) for the corresponding risk factor were selected for model training. 
These include an ElasticNet model without prior feature selection, an ElasticNet and Random Forest model with correlation‐based feature selection, as well as an ElasticNet and random Forest model trained on the CpGs that reached genome‐wide significance in previously performed epigenome‐wide association studies (EWAS) (Table S6 [this file] ). 
Accordingly, for each of these five models, five‐repeated five‐fold cross‐validation was applied to find the optimal hyperparameter values that yield the maximal area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) (for discrete risk factors) or minimal MAE (for continuous risk factors) (the searched hyperparameter space is shown in Table S7 [this file] ). 
For this, the Kennard‐Stone algorithm[rid=alz14061-bib-0044] was first applied to the MPSs to split the data into a training ( = 436) and an independent test set ( = 187) (Table S8 [this file] ). Accordingly, an ElasticNet (EN), sparse partial least squares‐discriminant analysis (sPLS‐DA), and Random Forest model with recursive feature elimination (RF‐RFE) models were trained by five‐repeated five‐fold cross‐validation to find the optimal hyperparameter combination that yields the highest AUROC (the searched hyperparameter space is shown in Table S9 [this file] ). 
It should be noted that not all cognitive measures were available for each individual; hence, the number of samples per risk category was different per cognitive outcome (Table S2 [this file] ). 
To compare the performance of models based on MPSs, PGSs, and CSF biomarkers individually or in combination, we re‐trained the EMIF‐AD MBD data using the 14 MPSs along with 12 PGSs (Table S5 [this file] ) and/or three CSF biomarkers (i.e., Aβ1‐42, t‐tau, and p‐tau z‐scores) as additional variables. 
However, the prediction of the LIBRA score proved challenging, with a maximal cross‐validationof 0.04 (Table S10 [this file] ). 
Nevertheless, with an AUROC ≤ 0.61, both the epi‐CAIDE and epi‐LIBRA scores as predicted by the best‐performing random Forest models were shown to be poor estimators of both MCI and AD status in the independent test set of the EMIF‐AD MBD study (Figure 2 [rid=alz14061-fig-0002] and Table S11 [this file] ). 
Besides age (= 0.92) and sex (AUROC = 1), the best‐predicted dementia risk factors by blood‐derived DNA methylation data in the EXTEND cohorts included notable performance for smoking (AUROC = 0.91), type II diabetes (AUROC = 0.89), and heart disease status (AUROC ≈ 0.80) (Tables S12 [this file] and S13 [this file] ). Particularly, similar to the findings in the EXTEND cohort, age (= 0.87), sex (AUROC = 1), smoking (AUROC = 0.80), and heart disease status (AUROC = 0.67) were identified as the best‐predicted risk factors by the methylation data of the EMIF‐AD MBD study (Table S12 [this file] ). 
As shown in Figure 2 [rid=alz14061-fig-0002] and outlined in Table S11 [this file] , our MMRS‐AD models, incorporating the 14 MPSs as variables, did not show significant predictive capability for AD status in the independent EMIF‐AD MBD test set (AUROC ≤ 0.60 However, our MMRS‐MCI model (RF‐RFE) demonstrated a notable ability to predict MCI status, achieving an AUROC of 0.68 ( = 2.0 × 10 for a linear regression model adjusted for age and sex). 
Notably, at baseline, the risk score of our MMRS‐MCI (RF‐RFE) model demonstrated associations with all cognitive outcomes and CSF biomarkers in the anticipated direction (Table S14 [this file] ). 
This reached nominal statistical significance for RAVLT – learning (HR = 2.27, = 0.01) and RAVLT – percent forgetting (HR = 1.73, = 0.045) (Figure 3B [rid=alz14061-fig-0003] , Table S15 [this file] , and Figure S1 [this file] ). 
However, the MMRS score did not exhibit evidence for association with any of the other cognitive scores analyzed (Table S16 [this file] ). 
The distribution of the MPSs among the diagnostic groups is shown in Figure S2 [this file] . 
“AMPA glutamate receptor clustering (GO:0097113)” stands out as the most overrepresented GO term by the union of the CpGs used in these 10 risk factor models (7,571 CpGs, unadjusted = 4.2e‐4) (Table S17 [this file] ). Notably, the model's CpGs that are associated with this GO term reside within the untranslated region (UTR) or gene body of the APOE, DLG, NLGN1, SHANK3, SHISA6, SHISA7, SLC7A11, and SSH1 genes (Figure S3 [this file] ). Particularly, for PRS, less than 3% of the variance in DNA methylation data is explained by genetic variation (Figure S4 [this file] ). Finally, the colocalization analysis indicated that only 11 CpGs out of 7,571 CpGs, forming the 10 contributing MPSs to the best‐performing MMRS model, are likely to share a common genetic basis with AD risk loci, with a posterior probability larger than 0.99. (Table S18 [this file] ). 
Despite the significant associations observed between most PGSs and their corresponding dementia risk factors in the EXTEND and EMIF‐AD MBD cohorts, their predictive performance remains poor, characterized byvalues of 0.1 or lower (Table S18 [this file] ). Furthermore, we found low correlations, as indicated by Pearson correlation coefficients consistently below 0.1, between most PGSs and their corresponding MPSs (Figure S5 [this file] ). 
This was further confirmed with low correlation between corresponding PGSs and MPSs (Figure S6 [this file] ) and the outcomes of the JIVE analysis and colocalization analyses, which collectively underscored the limited impact of genetic variation on the predictive capacity of the model (Figure S4 [this file] and Table S18 [this file] ).

This performance increased to 90% when predicting the group that progressed to MCI or dementia due to AD (i.e. amyloid positive only, Supplementary Material: Figure 5 [this file] a), underpinning the relevance of the proteins´ panel and their mechanisms for progression to AD dementia. In line with those results, panel positivity at baseline was associated with increased risk of clinical dementia (Hazard ratio = 8.37; < 0.0001; Supplementary Material: Fig. 5 [this file] b). Linear mixed model analysis further showed that panel positivity was associated with a steeper cognitive decline over time as measured by mini mental score examination (MMSE, = 0.01, Supplementary Material: Fig. 6 [this file] ), supporting the clinical relevance of the panel. 
We next modelled biomarker levels along the AD pathology using CSF Aβ as the proxy of early pathological changes [ 6 [rid=CR6] ] (Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] f), and evaluated at what point of amyloid load the levels of these novel biomarkers start to change (structural break; Supplementary Material 1 [rid=MOESM1] , Supplementary Material: Fig. 7 [this file] ). Of note, all proteins except GLB1 and MCFD2 had a structural break before CSF Aβ positivity (i.e., CSF-Aβ < 813 pg/mL; Supplementary Material: Fig. 7 [this file] ).
