We implemented MOFA integrating seven different omics datasets (hereafter referred to as “views”) sourced from a partially overlapping set of brain samples, totaling 1,358 ROS/MAP participants ( Figure S1 [this file] ). To reduce the impact of technical confounders in the model, all input data were normalized and adjusted prior to running MOFA ( Figures S2A [this file] – S2H [this file] ). MOFA was set to decompose the data into 50 largely orthogonal latent factors ( Figure S3 [this file] ) representing the underlying sources of variation across samples. Importantly, technical and biological confounders, such as postmortem interval (PMI), RNA integrity number (RIN), omics-specific metrics, and genetic principal components, were not strongly correlated with the resulting factors ( Figure S2I [this file] ). We did not observe a clear bias toward low-abundance features in the driving factors ( Figures S4 [this file] and S5 [this file] ). In addition, different contribution patterns were observed from each view, for example, factors 3, 5, and 6 were mostly driven by transcriptomics from DLPFC, AC, and PCG, respectively, while other views had their variance explained by at least two or more omics, indicating possible more complex interplay between different molecular levels or tissues ( Figures 1E [rid=F1] and S6 [this file] ). 
From the 50 decomposed factors, we selected nine that were associated (false discovery rate [FDR] < 0.05) either with pathological diagnosis of AD (NIA-Reagan score) or with clinical diagnosis of Alzheimer’s dementia for downstream analysis ( Figures 1D [rid=F1] and S7 [this file] ). These factors accounted for a range of total variance, from 20.5% (factor 1) to 1.7% (factor 42) ( Figure S8 [this file] ). These analyses revealed multiple associations (FDR < 0.05) between factors and phenotypes, primarily with cognitive and AD pathological traits but also with motor function and disabilities, most of which persisted after adjusting for APOE ε4 ( Figure S9 [this file] ). For example, associations with motor phenotypes remained significant after adjustment for pathological AD but were no longer significant after adjustment for clinical diagnosis, suggesting that these associations are more closely linked to clinical AD diagnosis than to AD pathology alone ( Figure S10 [this file] ). 
To assess the robustness and the replication of the MOFA results, we compared feature weight correlations across different scenarios ( Figure 2 [rid=F2] ; Figures S11 [this file] – S13 [this file] ). 
We found that this had little effect on the results ( Figure S14 [this file] ). 
Here, we highlight results from factor 8; results for other factors can be found in Figures S15 [this file] – S22 [this file] . 
Both factors were strongly enriched for processes involving immune response and displayed overlapping functional terms across their views, with the key difference that these enrichments were mostly in opposite directions ( Figures S16A [this file] and S17A [this file] ). Among the top feature contributors to factors 2 and 3, we identified several genes related to neuroinflammatory processes and β-amyloid metabolism, such as and ( Figures S16B [this file] and S17B [this file] ). 
Factor 1 ( Figure S15 [this file] ), which explains the largest proportion of total data variation, was negatively enriched in mitochondrial and ribosome-related terms and positively enriched with MAPK and sugar metabolism, RNA splicing, and ubiquitination terms. Factor 14 ( Figure S20 [this file] ) demonstrated the second strongest association with AD pathology after factor 8, uniquely correlating with both PD pathology (FDR = 4.87 × 10 ) and major depressive disorder (FDR = 2.78 × 10 ). Factor 42 ( Figure S22 [this file] ), despite explaining only 1.7% of total variance and being less robust to changes in the input ( Figure 2 [rid=F2] ), captured some aspects of vascular biology relevant to AD pathogenesis. 
Factor 26 ( Figure S21 [this file] ) exhibited the strongest protective effect, with enrichment for RNA processing mechanisms, vascular-related pathways, and cytoskeletal organization that may preserve cognitive function despite pathological burden. Factor 4 ( Figure S18 [this file] ) emerged as the second strongest protective factor, negatively associated with AD dementia (FDR = 2.34 × 10 ) and NIA-Reagan score (FDR = 5.78 × 10 ), while positively correlating with global cognitive function (FDR = 1.74 × 10 ). Finally, factor 12 ( Figure S19 [this file] ) showed protective effects through increased cell activation, cell signaling, and extracellular matrix organization, strongly driven by H3K9ac epigenetic markers.

Consistent with what’s reported in the literature, the final model chosen was an MLP for each brain region because of its best classification performance, with the respective hyperparameters in each model and classification metrics reported in Supplementary Table 3 [this file] , and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves shown in Supplementary Fig. 1 [rid=MOESM1] . We also compared the results obtained from other DNN methods as well as traditional machine learning methods such as support vector machine (SVM) and random forest (RF) and confirmed that MLP outperforms them considerably in the cortical regions (Supplementary Table 3 [this file] and Supplementary Fig. 1 [rid=MOESM1] ). 
We indeed observed that SI correlated strongly with all AD-specific biomarkers excluding diffuse plaques ( < 2.2E–16, R > 0.31, Fig. 2C, D [rid=Fig2] , Supplementary Tables 4 [this file] , 5 [this file] ), with most correlations still highly significant even after excluding those samples used in the training process (i.e. only considering OTHER samples), or within the AD samples only. 
Our findings demonstrate that R and values to associate SI with phenotypical traits remain stable across different parameter combinations, with the embeddings consistently forming progressive trajectories (Supplementary Fig. 2E [rid=MOESM1] , Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). 
We also observed that the model trained on DLPFC data was the most predictive of biomarkers in the MAYO cohort, whereas the model based on HCN data showed the least predictive performance (Fig. 3C, D [rid=Fig3] , Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ). 
For the MSBB cohort, the models were applied to the gene expression profile of all four sampled regions [frontal pole (FP, Brodmann area BM10), superior temporal gyrus (STG, BM22), parahippocampal gyrus (PHG, BM36), and inferior frontal gyrus (IFG, BM44)] and all regions show similar albeit slightly different trajectories (Fig. 4A–D [rid=Fig4] , DLPFC model only), with the SI consistently significantly correlated with all the neuropathological and clinical biomarkers (Braak score, PlaqueMean, CDR scale and CERAD score, Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ), for the models from DLPFC and PCC. Still, the model from HCN does not predict some of the biomarkers well when applied to certain brain regions, such as Braak or CERAD score in FP (Fig. 4E, F [rid=Fig4] , Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ). 
Following this procedure, we selected 1317, 1594, and 1643 genes for the models from three brain regions, respectively (Supplementary Table 9A–C [this file] ). 
Functional annotations implicated them in different cellular processes from five major cell types (Fig. 5F [rid=Fig5] , Supplementary Table 9A [this file] ). In contrast, we obtained 14 and 18 modules ranging from 25 to 227 genes for PCC and HCN profiles respectively (Supplementary Table 9B, C [this file] ), some of which are subsets of the five modules from DLPFC. We still observe sizeable submodules in common between the networks of DLPFC and PCC, especially for the networks from neurons, astrocytes, and microglia (Fig. 5A, D, E [rid=Fig5] ), with at least two out of three submodules in microglia, two submodules in astrocytes and two submodules neurons overlapped respectively (Supplementary Table 10 [this file] ). 
We observed that the gene nodes are enriched for genetic risk loci from genome-wide association studies (GWAS) in the two glial modules (e.g. TREM2, MYO1E, PLCG2, CD33, HLA genes among others in microglia, = 7.45E-6, OR = 8.75; and CR1, ADAMTS1, C2, C4A/B, IQCK among others in astrocytes, = 2.87E-3, OR = 2.65, Supplementary Table 9A [this file] ). 
We assessed the transcriptional regulation of SVOP using the expression profile of the DLPFC neuron module and identified the candidate TFs that regulate SVOP expression (Supplementary Table 11 [this file] ). 
A simple linear regression shows that the expression of both genes is significantly correlated with SVOP expression, although ZFY at a much lesser degree (Fig. 7A [rid=Fig7] , Supplementary Table 12 [this file] ). Indeed, we observed that the cumulative expression of ZFX and ZFY completely explains the sex differences of SVOP expression by inverse correlation, with no residual sex effect, or additional diagnosis difference unaccounted for in the linear model (Fig. 7A [rid=Fig7] , Supplementary Table 12 [this file] ). 
We observed a significant inverse correlation between the expression of SVOP and the combined expression of ZFX and ZFY across all analyzed brain regions (Supplementary Figs. 5 [rid=MOESM1] – 7 [rid=MOESM1] , Supplementary Table 12 [this file] ). 
These findings were consistent across various evaluation metrics (Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ) and ROC plots (Supplementary Fig. 1 [rid=MOESM1] ), further validating the robustness of the MLP approach. 
Moreover, they distinguish nuanced variations in the data from the two cortical regions (DLPFC vs. PCC), evident in the observable differences in predictive accuracy when applied to data from other relevant regions in an external cohort (MSBB, Fig. 4 [rid=Fig4] , Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ).

The details of the variables can be found in Supplementary Table 2 [this file] with the characterizations summarized in ref. . 
Total number of samples used in the training for each model, their diagnosis classifications and split by training/test sets for a fivefold cross validation, and the model configurations are reported in Supplementary Table 3 [this file] . 
Other parameters are tuned to be specific for each brain region as reported in Supplementary Table 3 [this file] , together with the parameters we used for other deep/machine learning methods for the same task for comparison. 
Their detailed definitions can be found in Supplementary Table 2 [this file] and data collection is reported in Tasaki et al. . The target dependent variables (biomarkers) are the AD neuropathological and clinical measurements, also reported in Supplementary Table 2 [this file] .

Our initial attempts to apply VINE-seq to post-mortem human brain tissue yielded high-quality RNA data, but we could not recover high-quality ATAC-seq data from vascular nuclei ( Figure S1C [this file] – D [this file] ). After systematically exploring alternative tissue processing, we found that homogenizing brain tissue with loose-fit Douncers and extracting nuclei from microvessels using Collagenase III successfully disintegrated vascular basement membranes without harming nuclei, enabling separation and subsequent high-quality single-cell multi-omic RNA/ATAC-seq following washing and FACS ( Figure S1C [this file] – D [this file] ). 
To ensure representation across major brain cell types, we complemented vascular and perivascular cell capture by also sorting for microglia (Erg+ nuclei), given that ErgLo+ endothelial fractions show microglial transcript enrichment ( Figure S1C [this file] ) . Samples spanned no cognitive impairment (NCI), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and dementia, exhibiting a range of neurodegenerative and cerebrovascular pathologies, and were balanced for sex and APOE status ( Figure 1A [rid=F1] , Figure S1B [this file] , Table S1 [rid=SD2] ). 
After quality control, we retained 65,948 nuclei ( Figure 1B [rid=F1] , Figure S1A [this file] , S2A [this file] – B [this file] , Table S2 [rid=SD3] ). UMAP dimensionality reduction and Louvain clustering of the paired dataset identified 15 distinct cell types ( Figure 1B [rid=F1] , Figure S2A [this file] – B [this file] ; Leiden/Louvain comparison Figure S2C [this file] ). Batch effects were corrected using Harmony ( Figure S2E [this file] – G [this file] ) . Cell type proportions and marker protein localization are shown in Figure S2D [this file] – G [this file] and Figure 1D [rid=F1] , respectively . 
Comparison of distal regulatory elements from our ATAC-seq data revealed a one-to-many relationship between promoters and enhancers: while 65-82% of active promoters were shared between cell types ( Figure 2A [rid=F2] , Figure S3A [this file] ), only 0.24-0.50% of enhancers overlapped ( Figure 2B [rid=F2] , Figure S3B [this file] ). 
This analysis revealed the hierarchical relationship of specific TFs governing cell type specification ( Figure 2C [rid=F2] – D [rid=F2] , Figure S3C [this file] ). 
Proportions were calculated by dividing the SNP count per cell type by the total SNP count for each disease ( Figure 3B [rid=F3] , Figure S4A [this file] ). This approach showed 5,454 GWAS-nominated variants are found within chromatin-accessible regions specific to vascular and immune (microglia, T cells, perivascular macrophages) cell types, a significant enrichment over background (P < 0.01, permutation test ) ( Figure S4F [this file] ). Further analysis revealed that 25% of variants overlapped with peaks in either myeloid cell population ( Figure S4F [this file] ). Comparisons between disease stages revealed only a limited number of significant Differentially Accessible Regions (DARs), primarily restricted to vascular cell types ( Figure S5A [this file] – G [this file] , Table S9 [rid=SD9] ). Additionally, comparing APOE genotypes identified a small set of DARs in arterial BECs and pericytes ( Figure S8A [this file] – G [this file] ). 
Leveraging chromatin accessibility and gene expression data captured from the same cells, we identified peak-to-gene (p2g) links between these modalities, suggesting gene regulatory interactions ( Figure S4B [this file] – C [this file] ). We then examined the distribution of p2g links across vascular endothelial, mural, and stromal cell types for cerebrovascular diseases, such as intracranial aneurysms, stroke, small vessel disease, and white matter hyperintensities ( Figure 3C [rid=F3] , Figure S4D [this file] ). 
Thus, beyond microglia, many AD myeloid risk variants are active in or specific to PVMs. Neurodegenerative disease variants were also active in T cells and BECs across zonation, representing approximately 25% of neurodegenerative peak-to-gene links ( Figure 3B [rid=F3] , D [rid=F3] , S4E [this file] ). 
With our vascular multi-ome dataset, we mapped 2,605 previously unmapped variants across diseases in our catalog, 956 of which overlap with vascular and immune cell type-specific chromatin peaks ( Figure 3E [rid=F3] – F [rid=F3] , Figure S4H [this file] ). While most newly mapped variants are active in a single cell type, over 34 are shared between microglia and perivascular macrophages ( Figure S4H [this file] ), underscoring the potential functional overlap between these two myeloid cell populations in the context of disease. 
Our analysis revealed that shared genetic variants were largely confined to diseases within the same category, with minimal genetic overlap observed between the neurodegenerative and cerebrovascular disease groups ( Figure 3G [rid=F3] , Figure S4G [this file] ). 
Motif analysis suggests this variant increases the binding affinity for the SOX2 TF ( Figure 4C [rid=F4] – D [rid=F4] , Figure S6A [this file] ), and consistent with this, public eQTL data in cultured fibroblasts associate the variant with increased expression . 
This disease variant is predicted to modulate LBX2 factor binding site ( Figure 4G [rid=F4] – H [rid=F4] , Figure S6B [this file] ). eQTL data from the tibial artery suggests this variant is associated with an increase in expression of LAMC1, which our data suggests could be caused by enhanced LBX2 binding site affinity Laminins and Collagen IV are the two major functional components of the basement membrane of vessels that substantially contribute to cell anchoring, signal transduction, and BBB function . We identified similar examples in the (rs11838776) locus ( Figure S7A [this file] – C [this file] ).Thus, these data suggest that dysregulation of brain vascular ECM structure may be a key contributor to cerebrovascular disease risk. 
Motif analysis suggests that rs6014720 upstream of the gene’s promoter is predicted to enhance a FOXL1 factor binding site ( Figure 5J [rid=F5] , Figure S6C [this file] ). 
Motif analysis revealed that rs11585858, located upstream of the promoter, disrupts a RUNX2 binding site, potentially altering its regulatory influence ( Figure 5L [rid=F5] , Figure S6E [this file] ). 
Furthermore, motif analysis indicates rs56152541 strengthens SP1’s binding affinity at this location, potentially enhancing transcriptional regulation ( Figure 5K [rid=F5] , Figure S6D [this file] ). We identified similar examples in the (rs12792791 ) locus ( Figure S7D [this file] – F [this file] ).

There were 5, 6, and 5 suggestive causal traits identified for pan-glioma, GBM, and non-GBM, respectively (Supplementary Table 22 [this file] ). Reported pleiotropy mostly concerned potential causal phenotypes (Supplementary Table 23 [this file] ). 
We collected 87 drugs targeting 28 genes in more than one clinical trial: 57 (65.51%) for tumor therapy, 21 (24.13%) for brain diseases, and 18 (20.69%) for glioma therapy (Supplementary Table 24 [this file] ). 
GWAS data for causal inference included 209 phenotypes (Supplementary Tables 1 [this file] and 21 [this file] ). 
The largest brain-specific cis-eQTL datasets from whole brain ( = 3,154) [ 65 [rid=CR65] ] and five brain regions ( = 108 to 2,683) [ 66 [rid=CR66] ] were included (Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ).

Nevertheless, graph-based pipelines remain vulnerable to the redundancy of raw omics profiles: when pairwise similarities are uniformly high—as we observe across all cohorts studied here (mean cosine similarity 96%–99%; Table 1 [this file] , available as supplementary data [this file] at online)—heuristic graphs become dense and noisy, introducing spurious edges that obscure genuine biological heterogeneity. 
Cohort composition, modalities, and post-selection feature counts are summarized in Table 1 [rid=btag468-T1] and Table 1 [this file] , available as supplementary data [this file] at online. 
For each cohort, architectural depth and embedding dimension were tuned to balance expressivity and overfitting risk ( Table 2 [this file] , available as supplementary data [this file] at online). 
Training and inference cost on the cohorts was measured on a single NVIDIA RTX 4070ti (20 seeds, mixed precision; Table 3 [this file] , available as supplementary data [this file] at online). 
Baseline hyperparameters were tuned under the same evaluation protocol ( Table 4 [this file] , available as supplementary data [this file] at online). 
We report (i) Robust Gradient Drivers obtained by union aggregation after patch alignment across runs and (ii) the Minimum Essential Core obtained by strict intersection across aligned patches ( Tables 5–8 [this file] , available as supplementary data [this file] at online). 
Across all cohorts studied, raw omics features are highly redundant—mean cosine similarity consistently exceeds 96%–99% ( Table 1 [this file] , available as supplementary data [this file] at online)—a regime in which similarity-based graph construction yields topologically noisy, poorly discriminative structures ( Aggarwal[rid=btag468-B1] ). 
Sensitivity analyses revealed that moderate masking rates ( ) and an embedding subspace count of yield optimal performance ( Figs 1 and 2 [this file] , available as supplementary data [this file] at online), plausibly corresponding to the intrinsic dimensionality of the underlying biological manifolds. 
By distinguishing robust gradient drivers—identified through union aggregation across ensemble runs—from a minimum essential core identified through intersection aggregation, we prioritized high-confidence biomarkers for both diagnostic and prognostic tasks ( Tables 5–8 [this file] , available as supplementary data [this file] at online). 
In practice, omics profiles are both high-dimensional and strongly correlated ( Table 1 [this file] , available as supplementary data [this file] at online), and it is well established that distance and similarity metrics concentrate in high-dimensional spaces, rendering nearest-neighbour structures unstable and highly sensitive to preprocessing choices ( Aggarwal[rid=btag468-B1] ). 
This is consistent with both the observed performance margins over DeepKEGG and the biologically interpretable, non-canonical biomarker profiles recovered from Table 8 [this file] , available as supplementary data [this file] at online. 
Repeating training across 20 independent runs yields two complementary biomarker sets: a Minimum Essential Core (intersection across runs) that captures stable lineage and identity anchors, and Robust Gradient Drivers (union across runs) that capture continuous progression and state factors ( Tables 5–8 [this file] , available as supplementary data [this file] at online).

Focusing on the 25 multi-cell-type candidate drugs, we found usage records for 10 of these drugs, as only a subset of the drugs from CMap is FDA-approved and prescribed ( Table S3 [this file] ). Although three drugs (etoposide, trifluoperazine, and vorinostat) showed reduced risk, statistical significance was not achieved due to insufficient patient representations ( Table S3 [this file] ). 
Despite the female-skewed cohort (approximately 33 females per male), AD prevalence was comparable between sexes, with a relative risk score of 0.431 in females and 0.444 in males in the sex-stratified analysis ( Table S3 [this file] ). 
A two-way ANOVA test assessing variance contributions revealed that letrozole and irinotecan exert independent effects on multiple behavioral and neuropathological measures, with minimal evidence of interactive effect ( Table S4 [this file] ). 
In our matched control groups, the prevalence of AD was 2.18% for letrozole and 1.83% for irinotecan ( Table S3 [this file] ), both lower than the national average and consistent with rates observed among cancer patients in the UC-wide EMR. 
The matched controls were identified using a propensity score matching approach based on these covariates: age or age at death (if applicable), race, ethnicity, sex, original indications for the drugs (for example, breast cancer was used for letrozole and colorectal cancer was used for irinotecan, also listed in Table S3 [this file] under “drug indications”), AD comorbidity (such as hypertension), and UC center locations (including UC San Francisco, UC Davis, UC Los Angeles, UC Irvine, UC San Diego, and UC Riverside). 
In addition to considering Gene Ontology (GO) cellular components, biological processes, and molecular functions as supplementary data [this file] , we focused our analysis on the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) functional pathways.

As expected, sequencing bias reduced the accuracy of estimation when only read depth information was used, particularly at higher LOY fractions ( Fig. 2A [rid=F2] - B [rid=F2] ; Supplementary Fig. S2 [this file] ). BaySeq-Y using phased PAR1 data consistently achieved the best performance ( Fig. 2C [rid=F2] and Supplementary Fig. S3 [this file] ), and its accuracy remained stable under different levels of phasing quality. 
Under the WES setting, where only a limited number of informative variants ( variants) were available, the prediction accuracy of BaySeq-Y (Y-non-PAR + PAR) depended strongly on coverage, with substantial improvement from 10x to 30x ( Supplementary Fig. S4 [this file] ). 
With the fast grid-search implementation, the runtime is reduced to less than 1 minute per sample while maintaining performance comparable to the MCMC-based estimation approach ( Supplementary Fig. S5 [this file] ). 
We also applied BaySeq-Y using both PAR and Y non-PAR data and confirmed high consistency between the two approaches ( ) ( Supplementary Fig. S6 [this file] ), despite their use of different LOY-associated signals. 
LOY estimates remained low in males younger than 50 years and showed an age-related increase across the cohort after 50 ( , ) ( Supplementary Fig. S7 [this file] ), consistent with the known age-related accumulation of LOY. 
We further systematically evaluated the effects of LOY on gene expression across different LOY levels. 17 out of 21 blood-expressed genes in the PAR and Y-non-PAR regions showed significant susceptibility to LOY (FDR < 0.05) ( Supplementary Table S1 [this file] ), including five genes reported to be LOY-associated ( , , , , and ) . 
Across a wide range of simulated conditions, BaySeq-Y generally achieved high accuracy, with prediction errors typically below 5% ( Fig. 2 [rid=F2] and Supplementary Fig. S2 [this file] ). Notably, using LOY estimates from BaySeq-Y, we replicated associations for all five genes in the Y chromosome (PAR and Y-non-PAR) previously reported for MoChA-inferred LOY and further identified 12 additional genes ( Supplementary Table S1 [this file] and Fig. 6C [rid=F6] - D [rid=F6] ), despite differences between the datasets.

neurons, while NDF/ATOH was more specific to fetal excitatory neurons ( Figure 1B [rid=F1] , Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ). 
Shared variants
were closer to the nearest gene transcription start site (TSS), had larger
predicted effects, and were linked to functionally heterogeneous nearest genes,
whereas specific variants were more distal and were enriched near genes involved
in developmental programs ( <
10 ; Supplementary Figure 2C [this file] , Supplementary Notes 2 [this file] – 3 [this file] , Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). 
Although shared
variants tended to be more proximal and larger in effect, effect sizes increased
genome-wide with distance from the TSS, where variants were also more likely to
be cell-type-specific ( Figure 1D [rid=F1] , Supplementary Figure 3 [this file] ). Together, these results suggest that broad variant effects are
often driven by disruption of ubiquitous TF motifs, while distal elements tend
to accumulate cell-type-specific variants ( Figure
1F [rid=F1] , Supplementary
Table 5 [this file] , Supplementary Notes 4 [this file] – 6 [this file] ). 
Among adult brain
and artery/heart eQTLs overlapping accessible regions, we found that fine-mapped
variants (posterior inclusion probability, PIP > 0.9) had significantly
elevated ChromBPNet scores and exhibited more cell-type-shared regulatory
effects than non-fine-mapped variants (PIP < 0.01) (see Methods [rid=S16] , Figure
2A [rid=F2] , Supplementary
Figure 4 [this file] , Supplementary Notes 7 [this file] – 8 [this file] , Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). 
Fine-mapped bulk eQTLs also showed elevated ChromBPNet scores across
multiple related contexts ( Figure 2A [rid=F2] , Supplementary Figure 4 [this file] ),
consistent with shared regulatory architectures and overlapping cell types
across tissues. 
First, using stratified LD-score regression (S-LDSC), we discovered that
SNP-heritability was concentrated within a functionally-enriched subset of
accessible variants prioritized by ChromBPNet ( Supplementary Notes 9 [this file] – 11 [this file] , Supplementary Table 7 [this file] , Supplementary Figures 5 [this file] and 6A [this file] ). Models trained in disease-relevant contexts selectively
prioritized causal variants—brain models for BMI, neuroticism, and
Alzheimer’s disease (with strongest effects in adult microglia), and
heart models for atrial fibrillation and coronary artery disease—while
showing little signal in mismatched contexts ( Figure 2C [rid=F2] , Supplementary Notes 12 [this file] – 14 [this file] , Supplementary Figure
6B [this file] – C [this file] , Supplementary Table
8 [this file] ). 
In addition, an AlphaGenome sequence
model trained on CD14+ monocytes predicted a 9.1% reduction in expression for rs113706587 (ranking in the extreme 0.000032% percentile of all
common variants tested), whereas rs116347724 showed only a negligible effect
(0.6% reduction) ( Supplementary Figure 7A [this file] ). We observed a robust and significant knockdown of expression using both promoter- and
variant-targeting guide RNAs, as measured by RNA-seq, relative to a
non-targeting control guide RNA ( Supplementary Figure 7B [this file] ; see Methods [rid=S16] ). Additionally, in contrast to
the single candidate variant prioritized at the locus,
multiple regulatory variants were prioritized at a non-coding GWAS locus near , challenging the common assumption of a single
underlying causal variant ( Supplementary Note 15 [this file] , Supplementary Figure
8A [this file] ). 
Although many
enriched gene sets overlapped those identified by cell-type-agnostic GSEA that
ignored ChromBPNet ( Supplementary Figure 8 [this file] ), several showed microglia-specific
enrichment, including GTPase binding (FDR = 0.003, involving SNPs linked to and ) and regulation of the ERK1/2 cascade (FDR = 0.006,
involving and ) ( Figure 2E [rid=F2] , Supplementary Tables
9 [this file] – 10 [this file] ). Together, these analyses illustrate how
integrating (1) fine-mapping, (2) chromatin accessibility profiling, and (3)
deep learning-based variant effect prediction in a disease-relevant cell type
can dissect non-coding GWAS loci and illuminate disease mechanisms ( Supplementary Tables
9 [this file] – 10 [this file] ). 
By contrast, immune cells showed smaller differences between common and
ultra-rare variants ( = 1.0 × 10 ),
suggesting weaker constraint in immune contexts which may facilitate the
emergence of new mutations that enable adaptation ( Supplementary Figures
9 [this file] – 11 [this file] , Supplementary Notes
16 [this file] – 17 [this file] , Supplementary
Table 11 [this file] ). 
This trend was most pronounced in the fetal brain,
consistent with purifying selection of regulatory mutations affecting brain
development ( Figure 3C [rid=F3] , Supplementary Figure 11C [this file] ). 
In contrast, ultra-rare variants that were common in founder populations
did not follow this pattern, consistent with differences in selective constraint
across population histories ( Figure 3D [rid=F3] , Supplementary Note
18 [this file] ). Additional analysis suggested that the multi-cell-type impact of
ultra-rare variants partially reflected their localization near essential,
broadly active genes ( Supplementary Note 19 [this file] , Supplementary Tables
12 [this file] – 13 [this file] ). Finally, the same overall trends were supported by correlations
between ChromBPNet scores and sequence conservation (using PhyloP ), and were not simply an
artifact of differences in the predictive model performance ( Figure 3E [rid=F3] , Supplementary Figures
12 [this file] – 13 [this file] , Supplementary
Table 11 [this file] , Supplementary Note 20 [this file] ). 
As expected, fetal-specific
variants had significantly greater constraint on average ( Figure 3F [rid=F3] , Supplementary Note 21 [this file] ). 
To define the regulatory mechanisms underlying adult- and fetal-specific
variants, we used context-specific model interpretations from ChromBPNet ( Figure 3G [rid=F3] , Supplementary Table 13 [this file] ). Moreover, these same variants were rarely
predicted to disrupt EGR or AP-1 binding in fetal neurons, consistent with the
limited role of these motifs in fetal chromatin accessibility ( Figure 1B [rid=F1] , Figure
3H [rid=F3] , Supplementary
Figure 14 [this file] , Supplementary Note 22 [this file] ). In contrast, fetal-specific variants
disrupted a broader set of motifs, including the fetal-enriched NDF/ATOH motif
as well as SP/KLF, ZEB/SNAI, NRF1, and ATF, several of which are also active in
adult neurons ( Figure 3G [rid=F3] , Supplementary Figure 15 [this file] ). These
development-specific motif disruptions were further supported by position weight
matrix-based disruption scores and predicted allelic effects from models trained on
SNP-SELEX TF binding data ( Supplementary Note 23 [this file] , Supplementary Figure 16 [this file] , Supplementary Tables
14 [this file] – 15 [this file] ). 
This highlighted the importance of fetal
neuronal contexts and sequence-based predictions in explaining evolutionary
conservation ( Supplementary
Figure 17 [this file] , Supplementary Notes 24 [this file] – 26 [this file] ). 
We therefore analyzed mutations from ASD families, focusing on 1,855 non-coding variants near genes
implicated in syndromic autism ( Supplementary Note 27 [this file] ), and asked
whether high-scoring FLARE outlier variants were enriched in cases ( Figure 4B [rid=F4] ). 
FLARE models trained on fetal brain data (FLARE-fb) effectively
prioritized non-coding outlier mutations enriched in
ASD cases ( Supplementary Table
16 [this file] , Supplementary
Note 28 [this file] ). Across
all 1,855 mutations, FLARE-fb showed a significant difference in mean scores
between cases and controls ( -test =
6.8×10 ) but not in median scores (Mann-Whitney U
test > 0.05), indicating that the signal was
concentrated in a small subset of high-scoring outliers ( Supplementary Figure 18A [this file] ). These
results support the importance of using context-specific FLARE models for
prioritizing rare non-coding variants relevant to ASD risk ( Supplementary Note 29 [this file] ). 
NFI family TFs regulate neural progenitor differentiation during
fetal development , and haploinsufficiency is associated
with intellectual disability and brain malformations , supporting the nomination of the regulatory mutations near as candidate contributors to ASD cases in a subset of families ( Supplementary Note 30 [this file] ). 
Finally, after accounting for conservation-linked mutability, we
estimated the excess burden of high-impact regulatory mutations in probands relative to sibling-matched controls (see Methods [rid=S16] , Supplementary Figure 18B [this file] ). 
In contrast, ChromBPNet variant
effect scores from individual cell types did not effectively prioritize variants
near outlier genes ( Supplementary Figure 19A [this file] ). 
This signal was driven primarily by TSS-proximal variants (< 2 kb
from the TSS) ( Figure 5D [rid=F5] , Supplementary Figure 19B [this file] ). 
Schizophrenia showed broad enrichment across fetal brain cell types and has been
linked to cardiac outcomes ( Supplementary Figure
5E [this file] ). FLARE-fb
outperformed the strongest fetal brain peak annotation, indicating that FLARE
adds information beyond region-based annotations and can extend beyond rare
variant prioritization to provide a fine-resolution annotation framework for
common variants ( Figure 5F [rid=F5] , Supplementary Note 31 [this file] ). 
Chromosome-fold assignments and additional
details are provided in the Supplementary Methods 1 [this file] . 
Curation of variant annotations and variant exclusion
criteria are described in the Supplementary Methods 2 [this file] . 
We assessed statistical significance using empirical null distributions
constructed as described in Supplementary Methods 3 [this file] , with code available at https://github.com/kundajelab/variant-scorer (https://github.com/kundajelab/variant-scorer) . 
We identified the cell-type-specific motif instances that are predictive
of accessibility using the methods described in detail in Supplementary Methods 4 [this file] . We annotated the consensus motif of based on similarity to known
transcription factor motifs from JASPAR , CIS-BP , and HOCOMOCO , obtained from the curated set at https://resources.altius.org/~jvierstra/projects/motif-clustering-v2.1beta/ (https://resources.altius.org/~jvierstra/projects/motif-clustering-v2.1beta/) ( Supplementary Data
1 [this file] ). 
Methods regarding analysis
of large-effect cell-type-specific versus shared variants are detailed in Supplementary Methods
5 [this file] . 
We obtained publicly available cis-eQTL fine-mapping data from the
Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) Project (see Supplementary Methods 6 [this file] for further
processing details), and evaluated whether fine-mapped variants with PIP
> 0.9 had greater predicted impact on chromatin accessibility. 
Methods
regarding analysis of GTEx bulk eQTLs to genome-wide regulatory variants are
detailed in Supplementary
Methods 7 [this file] . 
Specific details are described in Supplemental Methods 8 [this file] and 9 [this file] . 
The methods to obtain fine-mapped GWAS variants are described in detail
within Supplementary Methods
10 [this file] and 11 [this file] . Given the smaller number of fine-mapped variants identified for certain GWAS
phenotypes compared to GTEx eQTL analyses, we applied PIP > 0.2 to retain
more putative causal variants for downstream analyses ( Supplementary Methods 12 [this file] ). 
The methods are described in detail within Supplementary Methods 13 [this file] and 14 [this file] . 
Methods for
additional (sensitivity) analyses are described in Supplementary Methods 15 [this file] . 
We evaluated the genomic context of common and ultra-rare variants using
methods detailed in Supplementary Methods 16 [this file] . We further analyzed rare variants from the
1000 Genomes Project (1KG) that exhibited higher minor allele frequencies (MAF
> 1%) in different gnomAD populations using methods detailed in Supplementary Methods
17 [this file] . 
We then
analyzed the evolutionary constraint, predicted motif disruptions, and predicted
TF binding disruptions of development-specific variants (detailed methods
provided in Supplementary
Methods 18 [this file] – 20 [this file] ). 
mutations from 1,902 children with Autism
Spectrum Disorder (ASD) and their unaffected siblings were obtained from the
Simons Simplex Collection, as previously described in An et al. 2018 , with further details
described in Supplementary
Methods 21 [this file] .

The total number of significant bulk TWAS-O risk genes shown in Supplementary Data 1 [this file] is less than the one reported in the previous publication (70 vs. 113), for using a more stringent genome-wide significance threshold -values < 2.5E-6 versus the FDR < 0.05 use in the previous work. Bulk PWAS-O was newly performed in this study ( = 716) as shown in Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] , with results provided in Supplementary Data 2 [this file] . 
For astrocytes, we identified 65 significant cell-type-aware TWAS-O risk genes (Fig. 2A [rid=Fig2] and Supplementary Data 3 [this file] ), including 20 that were previously linked to AD clinical or pathological traits in GWAS Catalog . 
For microglia, we identified 64 TWAS-O significant cell-type-aware risk genes (Fig. 2B [rid=Fig2] and Supplementary Data 4 [this file] ), including 23 that were previously reported to be associated with AD-related traits in the GWAS Catalog . 
In neurons, we identified 77 significant cell-type-aware TWAS-O risk genes in excitatory neurons (Supplementary Data 5 [this file] ) and 49 in inhibitory neurons (Supplementary Data 6 [this file] ), including 24 and 13 that were previously associated with AD-related traits in GWAS Catalog . 
In oligodendrocytes and OPCs, we identified 50 and 45 significant TWAS-O risk genes, respectively (Supplementary Data 7 [this file] and 8 [this file] ), including 18 and 14 that were previously associated with AD-related traits in GWAS Catalog. 
Significant PMR-Egger FDRs are presented in Supplementary Data 3 [this file] – 8 [this file] . 
We identified 21 PWAS-O significant risk genes of AD dementia, including 14 risk genes for AD-related traits previously listed in the GWAS Catalog , 14 overlapped with previous bulk TWAS-O findings , and 3 novel findings that were not associated with AD in GWAS Catalog, nor detected by our previous bulk TWAS-O analyses (Fig. 4 [rid=Fig4] and Supplementary Data 2 [this file] ). 
In addition, pathways significantly enriched with our PWAS-O and cell-type-aware TWAS-O findings are found by the pathDIP tool (Figs. 4B [rid=Fig4] and 6 [rid=Fig6] and Supplementary Data 9 [this file] ).

As secondary analyses, we applied a three-range positivity approach using two cohort-specific thresholds ( Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ), one maximizing sensitivity and one maximizing specificity, to classify P-tau217 status. 
Parallel post hoc analyses using P-tau217 positivity defined by cohort-specific thresholds were performed as secondary analyses and are reported in Supplement [this file] . 
Descriptive statistics at baseline are presented in Table 1 [rid=T1] , and those for the subset in the longitudinal analysis are presented in Supplementary Table 2 [this file] . 
In cohort-specific analyses, significant interactions were observed only in Wisconsin and ADNI, both of which were enriched for non-Hispanic White participants ( Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). Results from positivity-based analyses are presented in Supplementary Figure 1 [this file] . 
RMST analyses showed a similar overall pattern ( Supplementary Figure 2 [this file] ), supporting a delayed emergence of the association between higher P-tau217 and cognitive-impairment-free survival, particularly among -ε4 carriers. 
Consistent with these findings, pooled AFT models showed a significant -ε4 by P-tau217 interaction, indicating that the association between higher P-tau217 and earlier cognitive impairment was stronger among -ε4 carriers than among non-carriers ( Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ). Similar patterns were observed in the positivity analyses ( Supplementary Figures 1 [this file] – 2 [this file] , Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ), and results were broadly consistent across cohorts (Survival curve: Supplementary Figures 3 [this file] – 5 [this file] ; RMST: Supplementary Figures 6 [this file] – 8 [this file] ). 
Results from the positivity-based analyses are presented in Supplementary Figure 9 [this file] , and cohort-specific results are shown in Supplementary Figures 10 [this file] – 15 [this file] . Findings were also generally consistent when positivity was defined using a uniform cut-off derived from the Wisconsin cohort and applied across datasets ( Supplementary Figures 16 [this file] – 17 [this file] ). Time-dependent AUC values exceeded 0.75 at most time points, and the magnitude of performance improvement increased with longer follow-up time across cohorts ( Supplementary Figure 18 [this file] ). 
Study-specific analyses showed that -ε4 was significantly associated with P-tau217 levels in all cohorts, including among cognitively unimpaired individuals within each cohort ( Supplementary Figure 19A [this file] ). -ε4 was also associated with P-tau217 levels among biomarker negative individuals, regardless of whether negativity was defined using sensitivity- or specificity-based threshold. Similarly, -ε4 was associated with P-tau217 positivity under both threshold definitions ( Supplementary Figure 19B [this file] ). 
In contrast, the association between ε4 and clinically impaired but P-tau217-negative individuals was substantially weaker, with only minor variation by ancestry ( Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ).

description: 1  Data  S1-S25  .  Proteomics  quality  control,  intra-disease  analyses,  and  inter-disease  analyses,  related  to  Figures  1  –  6
context_description:
Rigorous quality control (QC) procedures were implemented, including normalization of batches, covariates, and cellular composition ( Data S1 [this file] – 10 [this file] ). 
We further identified 2,056 proteins with false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.05, with 340 differentially abundant proteins (DAPs) meeting the additional |log FC-z| > 2.5 threshold ( Figure 2C [rid=F2] , Data S11A [this file] ). Comparison with three recent AD brain proteomics studies revealed substantial concordance ( Data S11B [this file] – D [this file] ), and comparison with AD transcriptome and CSF proteomes showed weak but positive correlations ( Data S11E [this file] – G [this file] ). Functional analyses indicated enrichment in processes such as amyloid fibril formation, extracellular matrix organization, fatty acid transport, and long-term synaptic potential among DAPs ( Data S11H [this file] ). 
To identify molecular heterogeneity within AD, we performed clustering analyses in the Banner Sun cohort (discovery cohort) ( Data S11I [this file] – J [this file] ). These proteomic subtypes differed from established pathological and clinical classifications, although they showed some associations (ANOVA p < 0.05) with tangle and plaque burden, Braak stages, and cognitive scores ( Data S11K [this file] , Data S12 [this file] ). 
These insoluble proteins were primarily associated with protein complexes such as the spliceosome, SMN, and CDC5L complex ( Data S11L [this file] ). Phosphorylated and ubiquitinated proteome analyses ( Table S2 [rid=SD9] ) further identified site-specific PTM dysregulation in proteins such as MAPT, NEFH, NEFM, and SPP1, suggesting a role for PTMs in modulating neuronal cytoskeleton and vesicular transport ( Figure 2K [rid=F2] – L [rid=F2] ; Data S11M [this file] – N [this file] ). 
In LBD, we profiled whole proteome (14,442 proteins and 148 PTM peptides from 55 controls and 397 LBD cases), insoluble proteome (12,235 proteins and 102 PTM peptides from 16 controls and 89 LBD cases), and PTM-enriched fractions (5,141 Pho-peptides and 2,372 Ub-peptides shared in 14 controls and 84 LBD cases) ( Figure 3A [rid=F3] , Table S3 [this file0] ). Statistical analysis identified 2,400 proteins with FDR < 0.05, including 627 DAPs (|log FC-z| > 2.5, Figure 3C [rid=F3] , Data S13A [this file] ). The DAPs shared some similarities with AD ( Data S13B [this file] ) and were enriched in biological processes such as fatty acid beta-oxidation, mitochondrial gene expression, and supramolecular fiber organization ( Data S13C [this file] ). 
Consensus clustering of the proteome stratified LBD (discovery cohort) into four molecular subtypes (ST1-ST4) ( Figure 3D [rid=F3] , Data S13D [this file] ), with PCA confirming distinct clustering patterns ( Figure 3E [rid=F3] ). These subtypes differed from previously defined pathological and clinical groups, although they displayed weak associations with Lewy body pathology, Thal phase, and Aβ staging ( Data S13E [this file] , Data S14 [this file] ). 
Crucially, insoluble proteome analyses ( Table S3 [this file0] ) showed elevated levels of Aβ, pTau, SNCA and plaque-associated proteins such as MDK, PTN, ANKRD11, and GPNMB ( Figure 3I [rid=F3] – J [rid=F3] ), and enrichment of multiple protein complexes ( Data S13F [this file] ). Furthermore, PTM-enriched analyses ( Table S3 [this file0] ) revealed extensive dysregulation of phosphorylation and ubiquitination in proteins like SPP1, NUCKS1, NEFH, NEFM, and MAPT ( Figure 3K [rid=F3] – L [rid=F3] , Data S13G [this file] – H [this file] ). 
To resolve molecular heterogeneity within FTLD-TDP, we performed consensus clustering and identified four subtypes (ST1-ST4) with distinct proteomic signatures ( Figure 4D [rid=F4] , Data S15A [this file] – B [this file] ). These subtypes showed different levels of TDP-43 ( Data S15C [this file] ) and were distinct from previously defined pathological and clinical types, although they were associated with genetic groups ( Data S15D [this file] – F [this file] ). The four subtypes were also observed in the re-analysis of another previously published FTLD cohort (39 cases, Data S15G [this file] – I [this file] ). 
Among upregulated DAPs, we identified 211 proteins that were altered in at least two NDs and 11 proteins that were altered in at least four NDs ( Figure 5A [rid=F5] , Table S6 [this file3] ). For example, proteins such as SPOCK2 and PTN in AD, ATP5PO and CHMP2A in LBD, ZC3HAV1 and PSME2 in FTLD-TDP, S100A8 and NPTX1 in VAD, HOPX and L1CAM in PD, and SH3BGRL3 and HNRPQ in PSP, showed distinct dysregulation in a disease-specific manner ( Figure 5D [rid=F5] , Data S17E [this file] ). 
In total, 150 downregulated proteins were shared by at least two NDs, and 8 proteins were commonly downregulated in four or more diseases ( Figure 5E [rid=F5] , Table S6 [this file3] ). In contrast, disease-specific downregulated proteins reflect distinct molecular deficits across different NDs ( Figure 5H [rid=F5] , Data S17F [this file] ). 
Further ROC analysis indicated that these disease-specific alterations (e.g., top 25 proteins for each disease) can distinguish each disease from others with high confidence, achieving an average AUC of ~0.9 ( Data S16A [this file] – F [this file] , Table S6 [this file3] ). 
Similarly, analysis of the insoluble proteome revealed 143 insoluble proteins altered in at least two NDs and 9 proteins among four or more NDs ( Data S17A [this file] , Table S6 [this file3] ). For instance, ANKRD11, CTSH, APP, GPNMB, CEP250, GM2A, TPP1, CTSV, and CALHM1 were commonly enriched in the insoluble proteome from multiple NDs ( Data S17B [this file] ). Despite the overlap, a substantial number of proteins displayed disease-specific patterns, such as ADAMTS1 and SPOCK2 selectively enriched in AD, UGCG and RYBP in LBD, TARDBP and GRN in FTLD-TDP, NBR1 and RER1 in PSP, and SMPD1 and MMP9 in PD, indicating distinct molecular aggregation mechanisms ( Data S17C [this file] – D [this file] ). In addition, comparative analysis of enriched PTM proteomes between AD and LBD illustrated some common modifications, including phosphorylation of SPP1, NEFH, and NUCKS1, as well as ubiquitination of MAPT, SNCG, and RNF126, while the majority of PTM events were disease-specific ( Data S18 [this file] ). 
Our analysis revealed 263 DAPs in BD and 612 DAPs in SZ ( Data S19A [this file] – B [this file] , Table S5 [this file2] ). When comparing DAPs in psychiatric disorders with those in NDs, only 74 proteins were shared ( Data S19C [this file] ). 
Each module contained an average of 74 member proteins ( Data S20 [this file] , Table S7 [this file4] ). 
For AD, >80% of the top 30 modules were conserved in three independent cohorts ( Data S21A [this file] ), consistent with previous reports . Similarly, 97% of the top 30 modules were conserved between the two LBD cohorts ( Data S21B [this file] ). Next, we investigated the functional implications of the top 30 modules in each ND using Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis, which revealed largely disease-specific biological processes with minimal overlap between diseases ( Data S21C [this file] , Table S7 [this file4] ). 
To gain insight into cell-type specificity, we annotated the top modules using human brain cell-type signatures ( Data S21D [this file] – E [this file] , Table S7 [this file4] ). 
This revealed 197, 397, 296, 44, 178, and 391 GHPs for AD, LBD, FTLD-TDP, PSP, VAD, and PD, respectively ( Figure 6B [rid=F6] , Table S7 [this file4] ). Specifically, MDK emerged as a top-ranked GHP in the AD co-expression network ( Figure 6C [rid=F6] ), and the MDK subnetwork was activated, as many of its connected nodes are upregulated in both whole proteome and insoluble proteome ( Data S22A [this file] – B [this file] ). MDK accumulation in AD brains was further validated by western blot, and its localization within amyloid plaques was confirmed by immunostaining ( Data S22C [this file] – E [this file] ). 
To delineate disease progression trajectories, we employed pseudo-lineage trajectory analysis of NDs, controls, and mild cognitive impairment (MCI, a prodromal disease stage), identifying three distinct lineages ( Data S23A [this file] ). Early-stage samples (controls and MCI) clustered at the trajectory start, while AD, FTLD-TDP, VAD, and LBD samples were more dispersed, reflecting increasing molecular heterogeneity ( Data S23B [this file] ). 
AD and VAD each followed one trajectory ( Data S23C [this file] , S23F [this file] ), LBD had two ( Data S23D [this file] ), and FTLD-TDP had three ( Data S23E [this file] ). The pseudo-time trajectory results were consistent with the Braak stages observed in these diseases ( Data S23G [this file] ). 
Indeed, ROC analysis of these subtype-specific proteins demonstrated high classification performance (average AUC > 0.8, Data S24 [this file] ). 
GPNMB stands out as a notable candidate due to its alteration in multiple NDs ( Data S25 [this file] ). NPTX2 also emerges as a compelling candidate due to its consistent downregulation in multiple NDs ( Data S25 [this file] ).

Within our AD cohorts, we integrated multilayer proteomes: whole proteome (10,924 proteins and 71 PTM peptides from 187 controls and 510 AD cases), insoluble proteome (12,235 proteins and 102 PTM peptides from 16 controls and 21 AD cases), and PTM-enriched proteome (5,141 Pho-peptides and 2,372 Ub-peptides from 14 controls and 21 AD cases) ( Figure 2A [rid=F2] , Table S2 [this file] ). 
The insoluble proteome ( Table S2 [this file] ) provided a complementary view of AD pathogenesis by enriching aggregated and co-aggregated proteins . Phosphorylated and ubiquitinated proteome analyses ( Table S2 [this file] ) further identified site-specific PTM dysregulation in proteins such as MAPT, NEFH, NEFM, and SPP1, suggesting a role for PTMs in modulating neuronal cytoskeleton and vesicular transport ( Figure 2K [rid=F2] – L [rid=F2] ; Data S11M [rid=SD1] – N [rid=SD1] ). 
Integrative network analyses based on combined DAPs from multilayer proteomics showed aberrant RNA splicing, axon development, synaptic regulation, and transport function ( Figure 2M [rid=F2] – N [rid=F2] , Table S2 [this file] ). To prioritize individual DAPs, we performed integrative ranking based on multi-omics datasets (GWAS , transcriptome , whole proteome, insoluble proteome, PTM-enriched proteome, interactome), identifying MAPT, APP, APOE, MDK, NTN1, and NEFH as top candidates ( Figure 2O [rid=F2] , Table S2 [this file] ).

Crucially, insoluble proteome analyses ( Table S3 [this file] ) showed elevated levels of Aβ, pTau, SNCA and plaque-associated proteins such as MDK, PTN, ANKRD11, and GPNMB ( Figure 3I [rid=F3] – J [rid=F3] ), and enrichment of multiple protein complexes ( Data S13F [rid=SD1] ). Finally, integrative ranking consistently positioned MAPT, SNCA, and APP as top-ranked proteins, with additional emerging candidates such as GPNMB, SPP1, and HBA1 ( Figure 3O [rid=F3] , Table S3 [this file] ).

Further ROC analysis indicated that these disease-specific alterations (e.g., top 25 proteins for each disease) can distinguish each disease from others with high confidence, achieving an average AUC of ~0.9 ( Data S16A [rid=SD1] – F [rid=SD1] , Table S6 [this file] ). 
Similarly, analysis of the insoluble proteome revealed 143 insoluble proteins altered in at least two NDs and 9 proteins among four or more NDs ( Data S17A [rid=SD1] , Table S6 [this file] ). 
To investigate how known protein aggregates link to broader proteomic changes, we correlated Aβ, pTau, SNCA, TDP-43, and U1-70K (SNRNP70) with other proteins in both whole and insoluble proteomes ( Figure 7A [rid=F7] , Table S6 [this file] ).

Because of the large number of independent subjects in the dataset, we were able to develop a machine learning model to impute genotypes with a high degree of accuracy (94% after 100-fold cross validation on hold-out test data) for those individuals who did not have an genotype listed in the dataset ( Supplementary Tables 1 [this file] and 2 [this file] ). 
Cases with imputed genotypes represented a minority of each group (ε4/ε4 =50, 12.1%; ε3/ε3 =658, 23.8%) ( Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). 
We identified a total of =881 proteins that were different in ε4 homozygotes compared to ε3 homozygotes at any timepoint ( Figure 2 [rid=F2] , Extended Data 4 [rid=F10] , Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ). To gain insight into the biological pathways associated with the altered proteins in ε4 homozygotes, we generated a protein co-expression network on the entire GNPC dataset ( =22,392 samples) which yielded 12 protein co-expression modules associated with different biological pathways ( Extended Data 6A [rid=F12] , Supplementary Tables 5 [this file] and 6 [this file] , Supplementary Information), and mapped each protein to its cognate module ( Figure 2 [rid=F2] ). Considering the association of diabetes with dementia and previous links of HKDC1 to gestational and type II diabetes, we profiled HKDC1 expression in different organs in one of our mouse models and observed that it is highly expressed in the brain (Figure S1A,B [this file] ). Next, leveraging the mouse brain atlas, we further observed that it is most highly expressed in the cortex and hippocampus in mice (Figure S1C,D [this file] ). We also looked at publicly available datasets on AD to look at the expression of HKDC1 using the gene expression omnibus (GEO) profiling tool and observed a reduction in the expression of HKDC1 in AD; while it is expressed in all the major regions of the normal human brain (Figure S1E,F [this file] ). And finally, considering these relationships in human databases, we assessed if HKDC1 expression is impacted in mouse models of AD by evaluating its expression in 5X FAD mice, and we observed a drastic decrease in RNA and protein expression levels (Figure S2A,B [this file] ). 
To determine the physiological consequences of loss of HKDC1 in the brain, we generated a brain specific HKDC1 knock‐out mouse model (BKO) by crossing HKDC1 female mice with C57BL/6 Nestin‐cre male mice (Jackson Laboratories) (Figure S2C [this file] ). This model was validated for knockout of HKDC1, as seen in Figure S2D–F [this file] where we found that HKDC1 mRNA expression levels within the brain were significantly reduced ( < 0.0001) in the BKO mice compared to expression levels in the HKDC1 littermate control group, and the expression remained unchanged in other tissues (Figure S2D [this file] ), including at the protein level (Figure S2E [this file] ). We observed that 9‐month‐old male and female HKDC1 brain knockout mice had memory and learning deficits compared to the HKDC1 littermate control group (Figure 2D,E [rid=acel70419-fig-0002] ), which was not observed at 4 months (Figure S3 [this file] ). We observed that 9‐month‐old HKDC1 brain knockout male mice had significant anxiety compared to the HKDC1 littermate control group (Figure 2G [rid=acel70419-fig-0002] ), which was not observed at 4 months (Figure S3 [this file] ). To begin to understand the brain‐specific role of HKDC1, we explored the impact of chronic HKDC1 loss on the brain transcriptome via bulk RNA sequencing of the mouse brain (Figure S4 [this file] ). The RNA sequencing showed distinct transcriptomic profiles with transcripts significantly different between the groups (Figure S4A–D [this file] ). 
To investigate if changes in metabolic homeostasis due to the absence of HKDC1 in the brain occurred and impacted our outcomes, both male and female BKO and HKDC1 mice underwent a metabolic characterization on a standard chow diet from week 4 to week 44 (9 months) of age (Figure S5 [this file] ). No differences in either body weight or ad libitum glucose (Figure S5A–D [this file] ), percent lean and fat mass (Figure S5E,F [this file] ) were observed between the two groups throughout the study. We also compared the brain tissues of both groups following sacrifice at 9 months and observed that HKDC1 and BKO mice also did not differ in brain morphology, brain weight, or brain/body weight ratios (Figure S5G,H [this file] ). Furthermore, no differences in fasting glucose levels, glucose tolerance by intraperitoneal injection (Figure S5I,J [this file] ), or insulin tolerance (Figure S5K,L [this file] ) were observed. 
To understand if the absence of brain HKDC1 impacts other hexokinases that could potentially compensate for HKDC1 loss, we evaluated their expression in the brain of male and female BKO and HKDC1 mice at 4 and 9‐months of age and observed that HK1 RNA and protein expression remain consistent, regardless of age, sex and HKDC1 ablation (Figure S6A–E [this file] ), where HK1 is the other predominant HK in the brain. Consistent with previous reports, subcellular fractionation of HKDC1 and BKO mouse brains showed no difference in HK1 localization or total protein amount (Figure S6F,G [this file] ). As expected, HK2 and HK3 expression were not observed (Figure S6H [this file] ). 
By evaluating the expression of senescence markers (p21 and p53) and inflammation markers (TNFα, COX‐2, and IL‐1β), we observed that loss of HKDC1 results in an increase in the expression of markers of neuroinflammation (Figure 4A–C [rid=acel70419-fig-0004] , Figure S7A,B [this file] ) and senescence (Figure 4D,E [rid=acel70419-fig-0004] ). To gain further insights into the effect of HKDC1 loss on autophagy, we performed immunoblotting for LC3‐I and II and observed that LC3‐II expression, which is a marker of autophagosomes, was trending higher in HKDC1‐BKO animals without reaching significance (Figure S7C,D [this file] ), indicating that the absence of HKDC1 alone at 9 months is not sufficient to upregulate autophagy. 
For this, we reanalyzed single‐nuclei RNA sequencing data (data not shown) generated by the Rush Alzheimer's disease center (RADC) from the ROSMAP study (Bennett et al. 2018 [rid=acel70419-bib-0008] ) and observed that the expression of HKDC1 is highest in astrocytes in the human brain and is significantly reduced in patients with AD compared to individuals with no or mild cognitive impairment ( adj < 0.01) (Figure S8A–C [this file] ). To confirm that this was also the case in our mouse models, we performed immunofluorescence to examine HKDC1 expression in astrocytes and observed co‐localization between the astrocyte marker GFAP and HKDC1 (Figure S8D [this file] ). 
Additionally, we observed that the expression of TFEB does not change with age or absence of HKDC1 in the brain, indicating that aging up to 9 months specifically reduces recruitment of TFEB to the HKDC1 promoter without changing its overall level of expression (Figure 6D–F [rid=acel70419-fig-0006] , Figure S7E [this file] ). We also failed to observe a detectable amount of signal in the nucleus, indicating that TFEB‐controlled autophagy pathway genes are not upregulated as a result of loss of HKDC1 at 9‐months alone in the absence of an acute physiological insult (Figure S7F [this file] ). 
Additionally, our results show that genetic deletion of HKDC1 at 9 months leads to memory and learning deficits in both sexes and anxiety in male mice (Figure 2 [rid=acel70419-fig-0002] and Figure S3 [this file] ). 
Noteworthy, among the different cell types in single cell RNA Sequencing data that we analyzed from RUSH RADC database (data not shown), HKDC1 expression was found to be highest in astrocytes (Figure S8A–C [this file] ), whereby these are primarily glycolytic cells that supply metabolic substrates to neurons and other cells and play a well‐established role in the removal of neuronal debris (Sollvander et al. 2016 [rid=acel70419-bib-0054] ).

All the coexpression networks followed a scale-free topology where a few hub genes present a large number of connections, as expected in real-world biological data ( Supplementary Figure 4 [this file] ). 
We used two bulk RNASeq datasets: one previously published by Mostafavi et al. (2018) [rid=R42] , which included 478 samples, and our updated version with additional samples totaling 1,210 participants ( Supplementary Tables 11 [rid=SD2] – 13 [rid=SD2] and Supplementary Figures 5 [this file] – 8 [this file] ). Pairwise preservation metrics, the complete module preservation and normalized mutual information results are available on the Supplementary Tables 14 [rid=SD2] – 16 [rid=SD2] and Supplementary Figure 9 [this file] . 
The same trends were observed when comparing the preservation with bulk RNASeq alone ( Supplementary Figure 10 [this file] ). 
Overall, we found many modules with significant overlaps ( Supplementary Figures 11 [this file] – 13 [this file] and Supplementary Tables 25 [rid=SD3] – 29 [rid=SD3] ).

We found that the ast_M19 had its expression partially explained by the stress response Ast.10 (34%); the enhanced mitophagy Ast.3 (9%); the homeostatic-like Ast.1 (7%); and to a less extent by the Ast.7, Ast.8 and Ast.9 cells ( Supplementary Figure 15 [this file] ). 
Supplementary Figure 16 [this file] shows the acyclic graphic for the network built for the top 100 genes associated with AD traits within inh_M6. 
In addition, we showed that our modules not only can capture signatures of annotated cell populations (e.g., mic_M46 and the subpopulations annotated as Mic.12 and Mic.13) but also can discover new biological systems (e.g., ast_M19) not previously identified by the single-cell clustering ( Figures 3 [rid=F3] and Supplementary Figures 10 [this file] – 12 [this file] ).

Details for each cohort are in eTable 4 in Supplement 1 [this file] . 
Cohort-specific participant characteristics are detailed in eTable 5 in Supplement 1 [this file] . Aβ status was determined as positive if either CSF (using cohort-specific thresholds) or PET (Centiloids >25 or visual assessment; eFigure 1A-B in Supplement 1 [this file] ) [xref] [rid=noi250060r35] was positive. 
As expected, plasma p-tau217 levels were higher in participants assessed as Aβ positive (eFigure 2A in Supplement 1 [this file] ). Plasma p-tau217, together with age, predicted Aβ positivity in cognitively unimpaired individuals with an area under the curve of 83% (95% CI, 81-85) (eFigure 2B in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
When determining an optimal cutoff yielding 95% specificity in the training set, the accuracy of the model was 81% (95% CI, 80-82) with PET or CSF as the reference standard ( Figure 1 [rid=noi250060f1] A and B; eTable 6 in Supplement 1 [this file] ) and PPV was 79% (95% CI, 74-84). 
Other specificity thresholds are presented in eFigure 1C in Supplement 1 [this file] showing that only very high specificity thresholds (99.5%) could render PPVs higher than 90%. 
Of all CSF-positive participants (reference), only 49% (95% CI, 41-57) were detected using plasma p-tau217 alone, 61% (95% CI, 59-64) with PET alone, and 44% (95% CI, 37-50) with the 2-step approach (eTable 7 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
Plasma p-tau217 alone detected 60% (95% CI, 50-67) of all PET-positive participants (reference), CSF alone detected 93% (95% CI, 91-94), and the 2-step approach detected 59% (95% CI, 50-66) (eTable 7 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
Comparison of individuals’ characteristics selected by each approach is presented in eFigure 3 in Supplement 1 [this file] . 
We also explored how the different approaches would translate into costs of recruitment using different plasma:CSF:PET costs ratios (1:4:16, 1:5:10, 1:6:25, and 1:8:20) due to the large cost differences between centers (eFigure 4 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
Therefore, we performed a head-to-head comparison in all the participants with %p-tau217 measured mass spectrometry vs p-tau217 measured by immunoassay (n = 964, eTable 8 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). The difference between Aβ-positive vs Aβ-negative cases in 964 individuals was larger in mass spectrometry–based %p-tau217 than for immunoassay-based p-tau217 (Cohen , 1.47 vs Cohen , 1.29, respectively; < .001) (eFigure 2C-E in Supplement 1 [this file] ). The mass spectrometry method also had significantly higher overall accuracy (88% [95% CI, 86-90] vs 82% [95% CI, 79-84]; < .001) and true Aβ-positive detection rate (69% [95% CI, 64-75] vs 49% [95% CI, 43-55]; < .001), while PPVs were not significantly different (85% [95% CI, 81-90] vs 80% [95% CI, 74-86]; = .12) ( Figure 4 [rid=noi250060f4] ; eTable 9 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). Similar results were obtained when studying BioFINDER-2 only individuals, in which only 1 method was used for immunoassay and 1 for mass spectrometry (eTable 10 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
Additional analyses incorporating both age and ε4 carriership showed significantly improved accuracy (81% vs 83%) and detection rates for Aβ-positive cases (46% vs 51%) (eFigure 5 in Supplement 1 [this file] ), compared to using age alone. Findings using alternative Aβ PET positivity thresholds are presented in eFigure 6 in Supplement 1 [this file] . 
This strategy increased the proportion of positive cases (55%-81% for 85% specificity vs 44%-59% for 95% specificity threshold) while maintaining high PPVs (81%-97% vs 91%-99%) (eFigure 7 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). Similar to our previous analysis, using a more sensitive plasma p-tau217 threshold increased the number of CSF and PET tests performed (−57% for 75% specificity vs −75% for 97.5% specificity threshold, compared to using them with all individuals) and the final number of participants included in the trial (30% vs 6%) (eFigure 8 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). Also, less participants required plasma screening (17% for 75% specificity vs 131% for 97.5% specificity threshold), but lower percentage of plasma-positive cases were subsequently confirmed by CSF or PET tests (61% vs 87%) (eFigure 8 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
Sensitivity analyses restricted to plasma p-tau217 measurements from a single assay and site (Eli Lilly, measured in Lund University; n = 1670) showed improved accuracy (85% vs 81%) and detection rates (56% vs 46%), although PPVs remained similar (80% vs 79%) (eTable 11 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). PPVs also increased with age (<60 years: 38% to ≥80 years: 93%), while NPVs decreased with age (<60 years: 91% to ≥80 years: 66%), when using plasma p-tau217 levels as predictor of Aβ positivity (eTable 12 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
To better align PET classification with CSF detection in early-stage populations, [xref] [rid=noi250060r36] we applied a relatively sensitive quantitative Aβ-PET threshold (25 Centiloids) while being clinically relevant, consistent with prior studies [xref] [rid=noi250060r35] and supported by our own data (eFigure 1 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). For each participant (row), the standardized concentration of 2944 CSF proteins, sorted by increasing absolute association with the mean standardized CSF protein level (Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] ), is displayed. 
In a multiple linear regression model, significant associations with a higher mean standardized CSF protein level were found for higher age ( = 0.544, = 4e-31), male sex ( = −0.159, = 2e-4), and lower ventricular volume ( = −0.321, = 5e-11), see Supplementary Tab. 1 [this file] . 
The clustering was relatively well in line with the OLINK panel division (see Supplementary Fig. 5 [this file] ), where the area of interest was likely to not benefit a certain panel. 
Cluster 11 had high expression in mainly neuronal cells (Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] ) but showed no significant expression difference compared to the other 2725 OLINK proteins, which was assessed with a bootstrap enrichment test. Cluster 11 was enriched on cell surfaces and membranes (Supplementary Fig. 7 [this file] ). Additionally, we observed that the proteins of cluster 11 had higher brain expression than the other highly expressed OLINK proteins (Supplementary Tab. 2 [this file] ). 
See Supplementary Note 1 [this file] : Reference Protein Candidate Profiles for a biological description of the three proteins and BF2 data information further confirming the proteins’ potential as suitable references (e.g., high association with mean standardized CSF level, small concentration differences between diagnostic groups, high association with the main predictors, low model performance when used without a main predictor and high detectability in majority of subjects [missing frequency ≤ 0.0008]). 
See Supplementary Note 1 [this file] : Reference Protein Candidate Profiles for a biological description of the three proteins and BF2 data information further confirming the proteins’ potential as suitable references. 
Additionally, as the three candidates were highly correlated (Pearson correlation 0.85–0.91, see Supplementary Fig. 8a [this file] ), the first component of a singular value decomposition was also evaluated as a possible reference, created from the three candidates (SVD1). For all models using BF2 data, the P-tau181-specific reference protein candidates (CBLN4, PTPRN2 and PTPRS, Pearson correlation 0.79–0.89, see Supplementary Fig. 8b [this file] ) and their corresponding first component of a singular value decomposition (SVD2) were evaluated as well. 
The two models P-tau181→TauPET and Aβ42→AβPET were retrained on the full BF2 training dataset and evaluated on the BF2 test dataset (Fig. 5a–d [rid=Fig5] and Supplementary Tab. 3 [this file] ). 
Quantitative details, including exact values, can be found in Supplementary Table. 3 [this file] . 
To validate the generalizability of the reference candidates, Aβ42→AβPET was applied in BF1 and the new model P-tau181→ADDconv was applied in both BF2 and BF1 (Fig. 5e–g [rid=Fig5] and Supplementary Table. 3 [this file] ). 
Figure 7a [rid=Fig7] and Supplementary Figs. 9 [this file] – 11 [this file] show how concentrations of sTREM2, sAXL and sTyro3 turned out to be substantially less differentiable between AT(N) groups when adjusting for a reference protein during grouping. Further examples of this effect can be seen in Supplementary Tables 4 [this file] , 5 [this file] , where correlations between P-tau181 and sTREM2, sAXL, sTyro3 and α-synuclein were clearly attenuated when adjusting for a reference protein. 
Proteins were sorted according to decreasing association with mean standardized CSF level (see Supplementary Table 10 [this file] ). For details, see Supplementary Results: CSF pQTL Analysis and Supplementary Table 8 [this file] . 
In Fig. 7b [rid=Fig7] and Supplementary Fig. 12 [this file] , partial correlations between ten established biomarkers from the NeuroToolKit assay panel proteins with and without adjusting for a reference are given. This includes strengthened associations of apolipoprotein E (APOE) ε4 alleles with protein levels of ApoE4 and reduced/disappeared associations of trans-protein quantitative trait loci (pQTL) with genes from the GMNC-OSTN region (previously shown to be associated with variations in ventricular volume and suggested to be linked to both CSF P-tau and several other CSF proteins ), Fig. 7c [rid=Fig7] , Supplementary Tables 6 [this file] – 8 [this file] and Supplementary Fig. 13 [this file] . 
Since we see inter-individual differences of the mean standardized CSF protein levels not related to disease (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] and Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] ), this means that false positives (individuals with high biomarker levels not due to disease, but just because many protein concentrations in the CSF are relatively high) and false negatives (individuals with low biomarker levels but have the disease, but just because many protein concentrations in the CSF are relatively low) can occur from this commonly used method. 
This idea is strengthened by the fact that the top reference protein candidates showed high correlation with the main predictors in cognitively unimpaired Aβ-negative participants but were not predictive of the outcome when applied in models alone (AUCs between 0.62 and 0.67, as seen in Supplementary Note 1 [this file] : Reference Protein Candidate Profiles). 
As seen in Supplementary Note 1 [this file] : Reference Protein Candidate Profiles, the six reference protein candidates (NTRK3, NTRK2, BLMH, CBLN4, PTPRN2 and PTPRS) all had higher association with the mean standardized CSF protein level (partial correlations 0.62–0.80) than Aβ40 (partial correlation 0.48). 
To provide evidence that the results were not heavily dependent on the selection of K or random initialization, a robustness analysis is provided, see Supplementary Methods: K-means Robustness Analysis and Supplementary Figs. 14 [this file] – 16 [this file] . Additionally, a sensitivity analysis when only using proteins with missing frequency <75% can be seen in Supplementary Methods: LOD Sensitivity Analysis and Supplementary Figs. 17 [this file] – 20 [this file] , resulting in similar findings as when using all 2944 proteins.
