This cross-sectional group consisted of a convenience sample of 298 participants recruited from the Alzheimer Disease Research Center at University of California, San Francisco (UCSF, United States) or the Swedish BioFINDER study at Lund University between June 2014 and November 2017 ( eFigure 1 [this file] , eTable 1 [this file] ), and in the primary analyses ( eFigure 2A [this file] ), 239 participants were included ( Table 1 [rid=T1] ). Secondary analyses were performed using different groupings of participants to estimate the sensitivity and specificity of the PET visual read modalities in other scenarios ( eFigure 2B [this file] – F [this file] ). Patients fulfilled clinical diagnostic criteria for probable dementia-AD, MCI-AD, or other neurodegenerative clinical syndromes ( eMethods [this file] ). 
Additional amyloid- and FTP-PET dataset preparations were performed by a blinded, independent analyst (AS) to eliminate the normalization of each scan to its reference region, forcing the reader to manually rescale images, and to facilitate assessment of intra-rater reliability ( eMethods [this file] ). 
All were experienced and certified amyloid-PET readers ( eMethods [this file] ). They were trained to read FTP-PET scans using an algorithm developed at UCSF and University of California, Berkeley (UCB), which classifies scans as: tau positive with MTL binding (tracer binding in MTL, anterolateral, or inferior temporal lobe; eFigure 3 [this file] ), tau positive with AD-like binding (tracer binding extending beyond the MTL or independently involving the posterolateral temporal region, parietal cortex, or other extra-temporal cortical regions), or tau negative (normal or non-AD-like binding pattern) ( eFigure 4 [this file] ). Based on this classification, tau-PET scans were then assigned to two groups, AD tau positive with MTL binding as the minimum sufficient tracer uptake indicating presence of AD pathophysiology (tau-MTL+) and AD tau positive with posterolateral temporal lobe or extra-temporal cortical binding in an AD-like pattern (tau-CTX+) ( eFigures 4 [this file] – 5 [this file] ). Details of FTP-PET reader training and calibration are documented in the eMethods [this file] . 
Of the 52 UCSF patients with both fluid AD biomarkers, seven participants had discordant biomarkers, five of which were positive by CSF Aβ /Aβ and negative by plasma P-Tau217 ( eTable 2 [this file] ). 
Accuracy of PET visual reads for predicting fluid biomarker-supported diagnoses of MCI-AD and/or dementia-AD was evaluated in the primary and secondary analysis groups ( Table 1 [rid=T1] , eFigure 2 [this file] ) using diagnostic performance measures including sensitivity and specificity. 
UCSF participants were 88.9% Non-Hispanic White, 4.2% Hispanic White, 2.1% Non-Hispanic Black, and 4.8% other races/ethnicities ( eTable 3 [this file] ). 
Sensitivity and specificity of amyloid-PET and tau-CTX+ visual reads were evaluated for distinguishing fluid biomarker-confirmed MCI/dementia-AD patients from biomarker-negative patients and CN controls ( Fig 1 [rid=F1] , Table 2A [rid=T2] and D [rid=T2] , eFigure 2A [this file] ). 
Amyloid-PET and tau-CTX+ had similar sensitivity for fluid biomarker-confirmed dementia-AD (amyloid-PET 97.1% [91.6–99.4%] and tau-CTX+ 97.1% [91.6–99.4%], p=1), and amyloid-PET had higher, albeit statistically similar, sensitivity as tau-CTX+ for fluid biomarker-confirmed MCI-AD (amyloid-PET 92.7% [80.1–98.5%] and tau-CTX+ 80.5% [65.1–91.2%], p=0.18)( Table 2B [rid=T2] – C [rid=T2] , eFigure 2B [this file] – C [this file] ). 
When distinguishing fluid biomarker-confirmed MCI/dementia-AD patients from other biomarker-negative patients and controls ( eFigure 2A [this file] ), tau-MTL+ had similar sensitivity (97.2% [93.0–99.2%]) as amyloid-PET (p=0.69) and higher sensitivity than tau-CTX+ (p=0.02)( Fig 1 [rid=F1] , Table 2A [rid=T2] ). Tau-MTL+ had similar sensitivity (98.0 [93.1–99.8%]) as amyloid-PET (p=1) and tau-CTX+ (p=1) in dementia-AD ( Table 2B [rid=T2] , eFigure 2B [this file] ). Tau-MTL+ also had similar sensitivity (95.1% [83.5–99.4%]) as amyloid-PET (p=1) but higher sensitivity than tau-CTX+ (p=0.03) in MCI-AD ( Table 2C [rid=T2] , eFigure 2C [this file] ). 
In the most clinically-relevant secondary analysis, which evaluates the accuracy of PET visual read methods for distinguishing MCI/dementia-AD from clinically diagnosed MCI and dementia due to non-Alzheimer diseases ( eFigure 2D [this file] ), the specificity of tau-CTX+ was 85.7% (76.8–92.2%), tau-MTL+ was 74.7% (64.5–83.3%), and amyloid-PET was 80.2% (70.6–87.8%) ( eTable 4D [this file] ). When distinguishing MCI-AD patients ( eFigure 2F [this file] ), the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) for tau-CTX+ was 0.83 (0.76–0.90), tau-MTL+ was 0.85 (0.80–0.91), and amyloid-PET was 0.87 (0.81–0.92), reflecting the higher specificity but lower sensitivity of tau-CTX+ for MCI-AD compared to other methods ( eTable 4F [this file] ). Statistical comparisons are in eTable 4 [this file] . 
Characteristics of discordance between visual read methods are presented in eTables 5 [this file] and 6 [this file] . Diagnostic performance of individual readers is presented in eTable 7 [this file] . 
In CDR>0.5, sensitivity of tau-CTX+ increased (p=0.009), but specificity of tau-CTX+ (p<0.001) and amyloid-PET (p=0.036) decreased compared to the CDR≤0.5 subgroup ( eTable 8A [this file] ). 
Sensitivity of amyloid-PET was higher in the age≤65 subgroup (p=0.04)( eTable 8B [this file] ). 
Specificity of amyloid-PET and tau-CTX+ were also similar across the age quartiles, but specificity of tau-MTL+ could decrease with age (p=0.005 in age≥75 quartile compared to reference quartile)( eTable 9 [this file] ). 
In ε4 carriers, sensitivity of amyloid-PET increased and specificity of amyloid-PET and tau-CTX+ decreased, but these differences were not significant ( eTable 8C [this file] ). 
Combined visual reads had higher specificity than individual visual read methods, significant compared to amyloid-PET and tau-MTL+ (p<0.05 for all comparisons; eTable 10 [this file] ). They had similar sensitivity for dementia-AD compared to amyloid-PET, tau-MTL+, and tau-CTX+ (p>0.05 for all comparisons), but sensitivity for MCI-AD was slightly lower in amyloid-PET/tau-CTX+ compared to amyloid-PET and tau-MTL+ (p=0.016, 0.0078)( eTable 10A [this file] ). 
Inter-rater reliability of both tau-PET visual read methods was substantial to almost perfect and comparable to amyloid-PET visual reads (κ=0.77 [0.71–0.83] and 0.78 [0.73–0.84] vs. 0.83 [0.78–0.88], p>0.1 for all comparisons) ( Table 4 [rid=T4] , eTable 11 [this file] ). 
Amyloid-PET intra-rater agreement was 97.5–100% and reliability was κ=0.95–1.00 (p<0.0001) ( eTable 12 [this file] ). 
Comparing majority tau-CTX+ visual reads to manufacturer’s visual reads, there were three discordant reads (96.3% agreement; eTable 13A [this file] ). The manufacturer’s method uses neuroanatomical features to divide the temporal lobes into four quadrants, and with these strict boundaries, the temporal lobe signal in discordant cases extended from the anteromedial/anterolateral quadrants into the posterolateral temporal quadrant ( eFigure 6 [this file] ). 
Comparing majority tau-MTL+ visual reads to manufacturer’s visual reads, there were 17 discordant reads (78.8% agreement; eTable 13B [this file] ). All discordant cases had MTL tracer binding and were positive by tau-MTL+ but negative by the manufacturer’s method ( eFigure 7 [this file] ). The methods and analyses used for these comparisons are described in the eMethods [this file] .

Average completion time for BioCog was 11.2 min (s.d. 1.02 min), similarly across both cognitively unimpaired and cognitively impaired participants (Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ).

The Memory Lund replication cohort consisted of 59 Aβ- CN participants, 23 Aβ+ CN participants, 44 Aβ- MCI patients, and 53 Aβ+ MCI patients (see Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S6 for participant demographics). 
Three commercially available ProSeek® Multiplex panels were used to measure the concentrations of 270 proteins in human plasma and CSF (Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S1). 
For brevity, comparisons between clinical groups (AD versus Aβ+ MCI, Aβ+ MCI versus Aβ+ CN, AD versus Aβ+ CN) were omitted from the main text, but included in the Additional file 1 [this file] : (see Additional file 1 [this file] : Note 1 and Tables S23-S28). 
In a supplementary analysis, we employed a more complex LASSO model which adjusted for the standard covariates (Additional file 1 [this file] : Note 2). 
An additional 68 CSF proteins and 18 plasma proteins were excluded due to low detection rates (< 70%; Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S1). 
A single healthy elderly participant was identified as an outlier in plasma, due to a covariate-adjusted PCA value more than 3.5 standard deviations from the centroid (Additional file 1 [this file] : Figs. 
Compared to controls, ROBO2 ( = − 0.27, = 0.004, unadjusted) and RGMB protein ( = − 0.11, = 0.049, unadjusted) were decreased in the CSF of Aβ- MCI patients, whereas tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) was decreased ( = − 0.2, = 0.004, unadjusted) and STAM-binding protein (STAMBP) was increased ( = 0.09, = 0.03, unadjusted) in Aβ+ MCI patients (see Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] a and Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S7). 
Finally, plasma levels of urokinase-type plasminogen activator (uPA) were decreased in Aβ+ MCI patients ( = − 0.14, = 0.02, unadjusted), Aβ- MCI patients ( = − 0.16, = 0.043, unadjusted), and Aβ+ CN individuals ( = − 0.14, = 0.044, unadjusted) compared to Aβ- CN (see Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] b and Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S8). 
AD-signature cortical thickness [ 17 [rid=CR17] ] was negatively associated with four proteins in CSF, including MMP-10 and YKL-40 ( < 0.05), both of which were differentially regulated in the cross-sectional analyses, and two proteins in plasma, including elafin and lymphotoxin-beta receptor ( < 0.01; Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S9). 
Baseline CDR-SB scores were significantly associated with levels of sixteen proteins in CSF, including SMOC2, IL8, MMP-10, CCL3, TNF-R2, ezrin, RGMB and OPN, all of which were differential regulated in our univariate analysis ( < 0.05; Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S10). Baseline CDR-SB score was also associated with concentrations of eight proteins in plasma, including positive associations with IL-8 and TIMP4, and negative associations with JAM-B, THY1 and latexin, all of which were differentially regulated in our univariate analysis ( < 0.05; Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S11). Baseline MMSE scores negatively associated with levels of four proteins in plasma, including IL8 and PDF subunit alpha (− 0.1 < < − 0.05; < 0.05), and positively associated with levels of fifteen proteins in plasma, including THY1, RGMB, brevican, brorin, kallikrein-6, bone morphogenetic protein 4, TRANCE, and delta homolog 1 ( < 0.05; Additional file 1 [this file] : Tables S12-S13). 
Overall, the strongest protein-protein correlations were observed within fluids, as illustrated in Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] and Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S14. Weak-to-modest positive correlations were observed across an additional 123 proteins in CSF and their analogs in plasma, including 35 proteins showing evidence of differential regulation in our univariate cross-sectional analyses (0.08 < < 0.49; < 0.05; Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S14). 
AUCs for CSF models were non-significant for Aβ- MCI (AUC = 0.78, 95% CI = 0.46–0.98), and low for Aβ+ CN, in a model that included 14 biomarkers and gender (AUC = 0.64, 95% CI = 0.57–0.7; Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S2). 
Predictive accuracy was moderate for Aβ+ MCI, in a model that included 53 biomarkers and age (AUC = 0.78, 95% CI = 0.68–0.87; see Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S3). 
To address this possibility, we conducted a series of supplementary analyses, as detailed in Additional file 1 [this file] : Note 1. These analyses revealed that, with the exceptions of CHIT1, YKL-40 and SMOC2 in CSF, most differentially regulated proteins identified in Aβ+ patients may represent markers of disease diagnosis, rather than Aβ deposition alone, as they showed similar patterns of differential regulation when Aβ+ groups were compared with one another directly (see Additional file 1 [this file] : Tables S23-S32). 
To test this hypothesis, we conducted supplementary analyses in a small, independent cohort of Aβ- healthy elderly individuals compared with Aβ- patients with Parkinson’s disease (PD), multiple system atrophy (MSA), and progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP; see Additional file 1 [this file] : Note 1). This analysis indicated that MMP-10, STAMBP, LDL receptor, and EIF4EBP1 likely represent disease-specific biomarkers of AD, whereas CHIT1, ALCAM, CD200, OPG, ROBO2, and RGMB may serve as broader neurodegeneration biomarkers, potentially influenced by coexisting pathologies beyond Aβ- and tau (Additional file 1 [this file] : Tables S33-S38).

context_description:
Cortical thickness was determined across the whole cortex for the primary analyses and in frontal, temporal, parietal, and occipital regions of interest for secondary analyses (eTable 1 in the Supplement [this file] ). 
We calculated mean [ F]flortaucipir SUVR across the whole cortex for the primary analyses and in frontal, temporal, parietal, and occipital regions of interest for secondary analyses (eTable 1 in the Supplement [this file] ). 
We performed (separate) linear regression models between whole-cortex [ F]flortaucipir uptake and cortical thickness (eFigure 1 in the Supplement [this file] ) and used the standardized residuals as a measure of BR (ie, lower than expected cortical thickness based on [ F]flortaucipir SUVR reflects low BR). The same procedure was performed using whole-cortex [ F]flortaucipir uptake vs MMSE (CR ) (eFigure 1 in the Supplement [this file] ), delayed episodic memory recall (CR ), and category fluency (CR ) scores to obtain measures of CR (ie, a lower than expected cognitive score based on [ F]flortaucipir SUVR reflects low CR). 
The characteristics of the participants are presented in Table 1 [rid=noi190119t1] and eTable 2 in the Supplement [this file] . 
The simultaneous BR model yielded results comparable to those of the 2-step BR model (eTable 3 in the Supplement [this file] ). The multinomial logistic regression models were consistent with the linear regression approach (eTable 4 in the Supplement [this file] ). No significant interactions were found between sex and any of the other variables on BR (eTable 5 in the Supplement [this file] ). 
The simultaneous CR model yielded results comparable to those of the 2-step CR model (eTable 3 in the Supplement [this file] ). The multinomial logistic regression CR models were consistent with the linear regression approach (eTable 6 in the Supplement [this file] ). No interactions were found between sex and any of the other variables (eTable 5 in the Supplement [this file] ). 
Individuals with low CR and BR had the steepest slope (annual β coefficient = −2.55; 95% CI, −2.95 to −2.14), followed by high CR and BR (annual β coefficient = −1.79; 95% CI, −2.43 to −1.14), high CR and low BR (annual β coefficient = −1.47; 95% CI, −1.79 to −1.15), and low CR and high BR (annual β coefficient = −1.47; 95% CI, −2.02 to −0.91) ( Figure 3 [rid=noi190119f3] B and eFigure 3 in the Supplement [this file] ). 
Regional analysis of our data indicated that the association of sex with BR was most pronounced in the parietal cortex ( Figure 2 [rid=noi190119f2] ), but we found in a post hoc analysis that the main association of sex with [ F]flortaucipir uptake and cortical thickness was largely consistent across regions of interest (eFigure 2 in the Supplement [this file] ). 
The WMH volumes were also significant in the multivariable model (especially in occipitotemporal regions) ( Figure 2 [rid=noi190119f2] ), and their associations with CR were most pronounced in women (eTable 5 in the Supplement [this file] ).

Correlations with t-tau were stronger for p-tau181 than p-tau217 in the whole cohort and in different diagnostic groups (Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). Both biomarkers as well as their ratios to t-tau were increased in all three Aβ groups compared to Aβ CU and non-AD groups (Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] , Supplementary Figs. 1 [this file] and 2a [this file] ). 
First, we studied associations between the two p-tau isoforms and [ F]flortaucipir retention in three commonly used pre-defined brain regions including composites corresponding to Braak stage I–II, III–IV, and V–VI regions of interest (ROIs) (Supplementary Fig. 2b–d [this file] ) . However, correlation coefficients were consistently higher for p-tau217 compared with p-tau181 and the differences between the coefficients were statistically significant (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] , Table 2 [rid=Tab2] and Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] ). 
Increased levels of p-tau217 and p-tau181 were associated with decreased levels of CSF Aβ42 and with increased neocortical [ F]flutemetamol retention, and the correlations were stronger for p-tau217 and p-tau217/t-tau compared with p-tau181 (Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). The correlation coefficients and AUCs were lower for CSF t-tau and Tau PET measures than for p-tau181 (Table 4 [rid=Tab4] and Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). 
We corroborated the CSF biomarker findings in a previously described cohort of CU and MCI patients ( = 330) from the Swedish BioFINDER study (Table 4 [rid=Tab4] and Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). In addition, in this larger cohort, the correlations with CSF Aβ42 were significantly stronger for CSF p-tau217/t-tau than for p-tau181, p-tau217 and p-tau181/t-tau (Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ), and p-tau217/t-tau was a significantly better predictor of abnormal CSF Aβ42 status than p-tau181, p-tau217 and p-tau181/t-tau (Table 4 [rid=Tab4] ). 
Further, we observed significantly higher AUCs for p-tau217 and p-tau217/t-tau compared with p-tau181 when separating Aβ CU from Aβ CU and Aβ CU from AD dementia (Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). The AUCs were lower for t-tau compared with p-tau181 in all ROC analysis (Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). 
In addition, for exploratory group-wise analyses, we compared longitudinal changes in the CSF p-tau levels between individuals that were [ F]flortaucipir negative or had an abnormal uptake only in the Braak I–II ROI (Braak 0–II group) vs. study participants with abnormal [ F]flortaucipir retention in the Braak III–IV and V–VI ROIs (Braak III–IV and V–VI groups) using the SUVR cutoff of 1.3 (Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] ). We did not observe any differences between the groups in the rates of increase in CSF levels of t-tau (Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] ). 
To validate observations in the BioFINDER cohort, relationships between the two p-tau isoforms and [ F]flortaucipir signal were examined for amyloid positive mild AD participants of the EXPEDITION3 trial ( = 32, Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ). Specifically, we found a positive association between levels of p-tau217 and p-tau181 and flortaucipir SUVR (Fig. 2f [rid=Fig2] and Supplementary Fig. 3d [this file] ). 
Furthermore, in Aβ study participants ( = 132), p-tau217 better correlated with [ F]flortaucipir SUVR in all three regions (Spearman rho 0.705–0.798, = 4.2 × 10 –3.0 × 10 ) than p-tau181 (Spearman rho 0.615–0.731, = 4.3 × 10 –2.5 × 10 ) (Supplementary Fig. 5 [this file] ). 
The characteristics of those participants are given in Supplementary Table 4 [this file] . 
The assay performances across all p-tau217 and p-tau181 plates are summarized in Supplementary Table 5 [this file] with a 10 pg/ml and 50 pg/ml QC buffer spike and high, medium, and low control CSF samples. Selectivity and specificity were demonstrated across three experiments as described and shown in Supplementary Methods [this file] and Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] .

Two hundred and thirty-six participants from the Swedish BioFINDER-2 study were included (see Supplementary material [this file] for inclusion and exclusion criteria). 
Subsequent processing steps were performed with the combined multi-echo pipeline (see the Supplementary material [this file] for modifications) in QSMbox ( https://gitlab.com/acostaj/QSMbox (https://gitlab.com/acostaj/QSMbox) ), including the multi-scale dipole inversion (MSDI) algorithm described elsewhere ( Acosta-Cabronero[rid=awaa089-B4] ; Supplementary material [this file] and Supplementary Figs 1 and 2 [this file] ). 
QSM spatial standardization was achieved with a previously optimized method, which uses a combination of ANTs v2.1 ( http://stnava.github.io/ANTs (http://stnava.github.io/ANTs) ), SPM12 ( http://www.fil.ion.ucl.ac.uk/spm/software/spm12 (http://www.fil.ion.ucl.ac.uk/spm/software/spm12) ) and FSL-v5.10 (FMRIB Software Library) tools ( Acosta-Cabronero[rid=awaa089-B1] ) ( Supplementary material [this file] ). Results with QSM values referenced to a deep prefrontal white matter region are also included in Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] . 
However, a supplementary analysis with 1 mm for a randomly selected group of 191 participants was been performed ( Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] ). 
Mean regional cortical thickness was also calculated ( Supplementary material [this file] ). A mediation analysis to test the effect of QSM on the association between tau-PET tracer uptake and cortical thickness was performed and the statistical significance of the mediation effect was tested with bootstrapping (10 000 samples) ( Hayes, 2009 [rid=awaa089-B19] ; see also the Supplementary material [this file] ). Analyses were performed in Python 3.6. and RStudio v1.1.463 (see Supplementary material [this file] for a further analysis in which the cohorts have been divided in cognitively impaired participants and cognitively unimpaired participants.) 
In addition, although more sparse, QSM in parietal areas (especially the supramarginal gyrus), precuneus, posterior cingulate cortex, lateral occipital and frontal areas such as the middle frontal cortex and insular cortex also covaried with temporal lobe tau-PET tracer uptake ( Fig. 1 [rid=awaa089-F1] and Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). 
The regional pattern of statistically significant correlation between signed QSM and tau-PET values is shown as a 3D overlay in Fig. 2A [rid=awaa089-F2] (and further summarized in Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ; see also Supplementary Figs 5 and 6A [this file] ). 
In addition, both tau-PET and QSM values in the ITG were negatively associated with cortical thickness measures ( Supplementary material [this file] ). A regression model including age, sex and education level (in years) as nuisance covariate showed a significant negative correlation between QSM signal in the ITG and global cognition as quantified by the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) [QSM: β = −739, 0.001, CI: −1067 to −410; age: β=0.039, 0.3, CI: −0.050 to 0.128; sex: β = −0.63, 0.3, CI: −1.87 to 0.60; education: β=0.12, 0.1, CI: −0.03 to 0.27] ( Supplementary Figs 7 and 8 [this file] ). 
The age-split revealed that the association between QSM and tau-PET is more pronounced in younger amyloid-β-positive individuals (≤65 years old, 40) ( Fig. 3A, B, D and E [rid=awaa089-F3] , Supplementary Tables 3 and 4 [this file] , and Supplementary Fig. 6D and E [this file] ) [(regression model in the ITG): adjust-R = 0.48; tau-PET: β=0.0015, 0.001, CI = 0.001 to 0.002; Cog group: β=0.0002, 0.7, CI = −0.001 to 0.001; age: β = −0.0002, = 0.09, CI = 0 to 2.7 × 10 ; sex: β = −0.0005, 0.3, CI = −0.001 to 0.001] than in those who are older [ 196 (regression model in the ITG): adjust-R = 0.06; tau-PET: β=0.0007, 0.005, CI = 0 to 0.001; Cog group: β=0.0002, 0.5, CI = −0.001 to 0; age: β=3.8 × 10 , 0.1, CI = −1.3 × 10 to 8.9 × 10 ; sex: β=0.0002, 0.2, CI = 0 to 0.001]. The mediation effect by QSM on the association between tau-PET and cortical thickness was also stronger in the younger group (mediation effect = 38% versus 13% for the older group) ( Fig. 3C and F [rid=awaa089-F3] ) also when accounting for the different cognitive statuses of the participants (see Supplementary material, Supplementary Tables 3–7 [this file] and Supplementary Figs 6 and 9–11 [this file] for the results of the analyses stratified by cognitive status).

In this diagnostic study, we included participants in the prospective and longitudinal Swedish BioFINDER-2 study, including individuals without cognitive impairment and patients with mild cognitive impairment (MCI), AD dementia, and non-AD neurodegenerative disorders. eMethods 1 in the Supplement [this file] presents the inclusion and exclusion criteria. 
Full PET details are described elsewhere and included in eMethods 2 in the Supplement [this file] . We report findings uncorrected for partial volume error or corrected (geometric transfer matrix) (eTable 3, eTable 4, eFigure 5, and eFigure 6 in the Supplement [this file] ). 
These ROIs were originally developed using [ F]flortaucipir to approximate the Braak staging scheme for tau pathology and encompass I-II (entorhinal cortex), III-IV (inferior/middle temporal, fusiform gyrus, parahippocampal cortex, and amygdala), I-IV, and V-VI (widespread neocortical areas) (eFigure 1 in the Supplement [this file] ). For the head-to-head comparison between [ F]RO948 and [ F]flortaucipir in svPPA, owing to the focal nature of retention with [ F]flortaucipir in patients with svPPA (confined to the anterior temporal lobe, including the white matter), participant-specific ROIs were drawn encompassing voxels showing elevated SUVRs within the temporal lobes, including subcortical white matter (eMethods 3 in the Supplement [this file] ). 
Additional details can be found in eMethods 4 in the Supplement [this file] . 
Thresholds for tau PET positivity within composite ROIs were defined using the mean SUVR within a given ROI plus 2.5 SDs among 17 Aβ-negative young controls aged 20 to 40 years (eTable 1 in the Supplement [this file] ). Mean [ F]RO948 SUVR images and scatterplots for ROIs are shown in eFigure 2 in the Supplement [this file] for these participants. Group differences in the [ F]RO948 SUVR were compared across ROIs (analysis of variance and post hoc tests) and voxelwise (pairwise tests, < .001, ≥100) using SPM, version 12 software (eFigure 3 in the Supplement [this file] ). Familywise error–corrected maps are shown in eFigure 4 in the Supplement [this file] . 
Baseline characteristics are provided in Table 1 [rid=noi200021t1] and in the eResults and eTable 2 in the Supplement [this file] . Partial volume error–corrected [ F]RO948 PET SUVR data are presented in eTable 3 and eTable 4 in the Supplement [this file] . Details on both [ F]RO948 and [ F]flortaucipir in patients with svPPA are included in eTable 5 in the Supplement [this file] . 
Voxelwise comparisons are shown in Figure 1 [rid=noi200021f1] C and eFigure 3 in the Supplement [this file] . Familywise error–corrected results are shown in eFigure 4 in the Supplement [this file] . Compared with Aβ-negative cognitively unimpaired controls, [ F]RO948 retention was higher in patients with AD dementia (widespread), Aβ-positive MCI (temporal/parietal cortices), dementia with Lewy bodies (temporal/lateral parietal cortices), svPPA (temporal pole), and progressive supranuclear palsy (globus pallidus) (eFigure 3 in the Supplement [this file] ). Results were essentially the same when using partial volume error–corrected [ F]RO948 SUVR data (eFigure 5 and eFigure 6 in the Supplement [this file] ). The [ F]RO948 SUVRs using more liberal cutoffs and by age are shown in eFigure 7 and eFigure 8 in the Supplement [this file] , and [ F]RO948 SUVRs in primary sensory and motor cortices are shown in eFigure 9 in the Supplement [this file] . 
The diagnostic performance of [ F]RO948 when separating AD from different types of non-AD disorders was high except when distinguishing AD from dementia with Lewy bodies, where specificity was low (70.0%; 95% CI, 52.3%-87.0%) (eTable 6 in the Supplement [this file] ). Considering that mixed dementia with Lewy bodies and AD are common, results obtained when the dementia with Lewy bodies group is subdivided by Aβ status are shown in eFigure 10 and eFigure 11 in the Supplement [this file] . Furthermore, the diagnostic performance of [ F]RO948 using SUVRs in individual tau-imaging ROIs is summarized in eTable 7 in the Supplement [this file] . Diagnostic performance for tau-imaging ROIs using lower cutoffs for [ F]RO948 SUVRs (mean [SD] +1.5 [2] in Aβ-negative young controls) are summarized in eTable 8 and eFigure 7 in the Supplement [this file] . 
When comparing patients with AD dementia with both controls with no cognitive impairment and patients with non-AD disorders, [ F]RO948 SUVR measures also carried higher specificity ( Table 2 [rid=noi200021t2] ; eTable 9 in the Supplement [this file] ). Cerebrospinal fluid p-tau181 by diagnostic group and its association with the [ F]RO948 SUVR in tau-imaging ROIs are shown in eFigure 12 and eFigure 13 in the Supplement [this file] . 
Visual inspection of [ F]RO948 and [ F]flortaucipir SUVR images in the 3 patients with svPPA who underwent PET studies with both tracers suggested higher retention of [ F]flortaucipir (eFigure 14A in the Supplement [this file] ). This finding was confirmed by a voxelwise subtraction analysis that showed [ F]flortaucipir SUVRs to be higher than those for [ F]RO948 ([ F]flortaucipir − [ F]RO948), particularly within the anterior temporal lobe bilaterally (eFigure 14B in the Supplement [this file] ). The reverse operation ([ F]R0948 − ([ F]flortaucipir) showed higher SUVR values for [ F]R0948 only within the retina and skull/meninges (eFigure 14C in the Supplement [this file] ). Higher retention of [ F]flortaucipir was further supported by comparison of SUVR values within the anterior temporal lobe ROI (eTable 10 in the Supplement [this file] ). 
Elevated retention of [ F]R0948 in the skull/meninges (confluent signal on visual inspection, with SUVR>2.5) was seen in 4.4% of BioFINDER-2 participants (eTable 11 in the Supplement [this file] ). Resulting AUC values did not differ significantly from those including all participants (eTable 11 in the Supplement [this file] ). 
A single tau PET scan may preclude the need for Aβ PET or CSF AD biomarkers, as well as fluorodeoxyglucose F 18 PET, in the diagnostic workup of amnestic dementia (eFigure 15 in the Supplement [this file] ) given the finding that tau PET positivity was virtually confined to Aβ-positive cases and studies showing a high overlap between tau PET and hypometabolism.

Models performed best when SUVR data for the 66 cortical regions were converted to tau-positive probabilities as described above, with regression of age, sex, and non-specific choroid plexus binding from the data occurring beforehand (Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] A, B, F). Partial volume correction (PVC) (Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] C) and exclusion of A − MCI individuals (Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] E) did not appear to impact model performance, though the best-fitting model did not use PVC and excluded A − MCI individuals (Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] A). 
Model performance was better in ADNI (global pattern = 0.78) compared to BioFINDER ( = 0.6), though this difference was partially mitigated by subsampling BioFINDER to match ADNI based on demographic variables, and the difference disappeared entirely when subsampling BioFINDER to match ADNI based on mean cortical tau signal (Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] ). Model fit was good across cognitively normal, MCI and AD subjects, and expected increases in mean tau signal were observed as disease severity increased (Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] ). The ESM was particularly effective in predicting the early progression of tau, but diverged more from the observed tau pattern over time (Supplementary Fig. 5 [this file] , Fig. 4 [rid=Fig4] ). 
Once again, the ESM demonstrated good model fit, explaining 65.6% (null model mean [95% CI] = 0.107 [0.052, 0.217], < 0.01) of the overall spatial pattern of tau, and explained 44.8% (SD = 21.7%; null model mean [95% CI] = 0.104 [0.077, 0.147], < 0.01) of the spatial pattern within-individual subjects on average (Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] ). 
The ESM was fit once again using connectivity matrices composed of functional connections measured in separate samples of young healthy adults, and old healthy and impaired adults, respectively, using resting-state functional MRI connectivity (Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] , Fig. 4 [rid=Fig4] ). Models fit over functional connectomes performed quite well, though slightly worse than models using structural connectomes (YOUNG: Global = 0.565; null [95% CI] = 0.089 [0.031–0.187]; individual mean = 0.384, SD = 0.168, null [95% CI] = 0.103 [0.069–0.156]; OLD: Global = 0.586; null [95% CI] = 0.031 [0.000–0.087]; individual mean = 0.451, SD = 0.209, null [95% CI] = 0.063 [0.037–0.109]), a trend that was consistent across preprocessing strategies (Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] D). To test this hypothesis, a model was fit over a Euclidean distance matrix instead of a functional or structural connectome (Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] ). 
In our data, DTI tractography-based connectomes consistently showed superior model fit compared to models fit over other connectomes (Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] , Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] d), once again lending support to the cell-to-cell transmission hypothesis, though model fit was ultimately high and reproducible across both connectivity modalities. 
However, many different pre-processing combinations produced high-performing models (Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] A), so we are confident that our results are not dependent on our pre-processing decisions.

For the imaging and clinical variables that were significantly associated with baseline plasma biomarkers in the multivariate linear mixed effects models, we included the plots with the mean longitudinal trajectories ( Figs 1–4 [rid=awab163-F1] ) in addition to the spaghetti plots with the individual longitudinal trajectories ( Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] ). Finally, we also included the results of analyses performed in amyloid-positive non-demented individuals in Supplementary material [this file] and compare the results obtained in this group with the ones observed in the whole non-demented sample in the ‘Discussion’ section. 
These analyses showed that all baseline plasma biomarkers predicted greater longitudinal temporal tau accumulation ( Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). The model with plasma P-tau217 had a significantly better fit to the data compared to the other models, as reflected by the lowest AIC value (P-tau217: 270.6, P-tau181: 291.8, Aβ42/40: 305.3, NfL: 306.0) ( Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). In addition, it also displayed the largest effect size (P-tau217 Cohen’s : 0.87) compared to the other biomarkers (P-tau181: 0.60, Aβ42/40: −0.45, NfL: 0.44) ( Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). 
When the interactions between time and each plasma biomarker were included in the same multivariate model, only P-tau217 remained as a significant independent predictor of longitudinal temporal tau accumulation ( = 3.947, < 0.001) ( Fig. 1A [rid=awab163-F1] and Supplementary Fig. 1A [this file] ), after verifying there were no multicollinearity issues in this model ( Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). These results were also confirmed by the voxel-wise analyses, which showed that P-tau217 correlated with greater tau accumulation in temporal regions in addition to lateral parietal and medial parietal areas ( Fig. 1B [rid=awab163-F1] ), which overlapped with several brain areas showing increased longitudinal tau-PET deposition in our cohort ( Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] ). 
The results of significant interactions between all the predictors in the multivariate models can be found in the Supplementary material [this file] . 
These analyses showed that plasma Aβ42/40, P-tau217 and NfL, but not P-tau181, predicted longitudinal amyloid deposition, with the model including P-tau217 as a predictor having the lowest AIC values (P-tau217: 74.5, P-tau181: 97.6, Aβ42/40: 90.1, NfL: 90.7) ( Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). The analysis of the effect sizes showed that Aβ42/40 was the strongest predictor (Cohen’s : −0.81), followed by P-tau217 (Cohen’s : 0.73), NfL (Cohen’s : 0.65) and P-tau181 (Cohen’s : 0.42) ( Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). 
However, when all biomarkers were included in the same model, only plasma Aβ42/40 was a significant predictor of amyloid accumulation ( = −2.578, = 0.012), suggesting that this marker is the only one that is associated with amyloid pathology independently of the other biomarkers ( Fig. 2 [rid=awab163-F2] and Supplementary Fig. 1B [this file] ). There was no multicollinearity between all the predictors ( Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). 
The comparisons between the models showed that plasma P-tau217 was the best predictor of both temporal thinning (AIC P-tau217: 352.7, P-tau181: 372.6, Aβ42/40: 372.5, NfL: 365.1) and hippocampal atrophy (AIC P-tau217: 96.7, P-tau181: 116.3, Aβ42/40: 121.4, NfL: 102.0) ( Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). In line with this, P-tau217 had the largest effect size (Cohen’s : −0.63) in the predictions of temporal thinning compared to NfL (Cohen’s : −0.48), P-tau181 (Cohen’s : −0.21) and Aβ42/40 (Cohen’s : 0.11), whereas P-tau217 and NfL had the largest effects sizes (both with Cohen’s : −0.79) in the predictions of hippocampal atrophy compared to P-tau181 (Cohen’s : −0.53) and Aβ42/40 (Cohen’s : 0.39) ( Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). 
When all plasma biomarkers were included in the same model, P-tau217 was the only significant independent predictor of temporal cortical thinning ( = −3.048, = 0.003) ( Fig. 3A [rid=awab163-F3] and Supplementary Fig. 1C [this file] ), whereas both P-tau217 and NfL were significant predictors of hippocampal volume loss (P-tau217: = −2.958, = 0.004; NfL: = −2.794, = 0.006) ( Fig. 3B, C [rid=awab163-F3] and Supplementary Fig. 1D and E [this file] ). There was no multicollinearity between all the predictors ( Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). The results of significant interactions between all the predictors in the multivariate models can be found in the Supplementary material [this file] . 
The comparisons between the previous significant models showed that the one with P-tau217 had again the best fit to the data (AIC P-tau217: 166.4, P-tau181: 170.6, Aβ42/40: 178.0, NfL: 176.3) ( Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ), even after adjusting for the different cognitive profiles (amnestic, non-amnestic, single domain, multidomain) in individuals with mild cognitive impairment (AIC P-tau217: 154.6, P-tau181: 158.4, Aβ42/40: 165.7, NfL: 157.1). In line with this, P-tau217 showed the largest effect sizes (Cohen’s : −0.49) in the predictions of MMSE scores compared to P-tau181 (Cohen’s : −0.46), NfL (Cohen’s : −0.32) and Aβ42/40 (Cohen’s : 0.21) ( Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). 
When all biomarkers were included in the same multivariate model, only P-tau217 was a significant independent predictor of cognitive decline ( = −2.275, = 0.024) ( Fig. 4 [rid=awab163-F4] and Supplementary Fig. 1F [this file] ). There was no multicollinearity between all the predictors ( Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). The results of significant interactions between all the predictors in the multivariate models can be found in the Supplementary material [this file] . 
The other plasma markers did not predict longitudinal changes in brain imaging or cognitive measures in this non-Alzheimer’s group ( Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). 
These analyses revealed there were no significant differences between the models with CSF Aβ42/40 and plasma Aβ42/40 ( Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ). On the other hand, CSF P-tau181 was a worse predictor (higher AIC values) of cognitive decline than plasma P-tau181 but performed equally well in the prediction of all other outcomes ( Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ). Moreover, CSF P-tau217 was a worse predictor (higher AIC values) of tau accumulation, temporal cortical thinning and hippocampal atrophy compared to plasma P-tau217 but performed equally well in predicting amyloid accumulation or cognitive decline ( Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). Finally, CSF NfL was a worse predictor of temporal cortical thinning, amyloid accumulation and hippocampal volume (higher AIC values) but performed equally well in predicting tau or cognitive decline compared to plasma NfL ( Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ).

Participant characteristics across diagnostic groups are presented in Table 1 [rid=noi210030t1] (and stratified by discovery/replication sample and by cohort in eTables 1 and 2 in the Supplement [this file] , respectively). 
When comparing [ F]flortaucipir SUVR in the temporal meta-ROI against MRI-based AD-signature cortical thickness in linear regression models with annual change in MMSE as dependent variable ( Figure 1 [rid=noi210030f1] and eTable 3 in the Supplement [this file] ), greater [ F]flortaucipir uptake was more strongly associated with decline in MMSE over time than MRI across all participants ( , 0.35 [tau PET] vs 0.24 [MRI]; bootstrapped difference, = 80.3 [ < .001]), the Aβ-positive MCI group (R , 0.25 [tau PET] vs 0.15 [MRI]; bootstrapped difference, = 30.8 [ < .001]), the Aβ-positive CU group ( , 0.16 [tau PET] vs 0.08 [MRI]; bootstrapped difference, = 38.6 [ < .001]), and the Aβ-negative CU group ( , 0.06 [tau PET] vs 0.03 [MRI]; bootstrapped difference, = 13.6 [ < .001]). Comparable results were found in the [ F]RO948 replication cohort (eFigure 1 and eTable 3 in the Supplement [this file] ), with greater tau PET uptake being more strongly associated with annual decline in MMSE than MRI across all participants ( , 0.49 vs 0.34; bootstrapped difference, = 147.9 [ < .001]), the Aβ-positive MCI group ( , 0.34 vs 0.20; bootstrapped difference, = 23.1 [ < .001]), the Aβ-positive CU group ( , 0.53 vs 0.36; bootstrapped difference, = 16.7 [ < .001]), and the Aβ-negative CU group ( , 0.04 vs 0.03; bootstrapped difference, = 15.4 [ < .001]) and with better performance for MRI compared with PET in the Aβ-negative MCI group ( , 0.15 vs 0.16; bootstrapped difference, = −61.4 [ < .001]). In sensitivity analyses assessing entorhinal and Braak stages V and VI ROIs, tau PET was more strongly associated with MMSE change than MRI across all participants, the Aβ-positive MCI group, and the Aβ-positive CU group (eFigures 2-5 in the Supplement [this file] ). 
In the replication cohort (eTable 4 in the Supplement [this file] ), [ F]RO948 temporal meta-ROI SUVR always provided complementary information to models that only included AD-signature cortical thickness (all participants, χ = 176.2; AD dementia group, χ = 22.9; Aβ-positive MCI group, χ = 11.2; and Aβ-positive CU group, χ = 21.3 [ < .001]). 
In the replication cohort (eFigure 6 in the Supplement [this file] ), the association between baseline [ F]RO948 SUVR and decline in MMSE was only modestly mediated by AD-signature cortical thickness across all participants (21.0% [95% CI, 9.8%-35.0%]; < .001), but not in the AD dementia (13.0% [95% CI, −0.5% to 41.0%]; = .06), Aβ-positive MCI (9.0% [95% CI, −8.0% to 54.0%]; = .24), and Aβ-positive CU (19.8% [95% CI, −50.9% to 56.0%]; = .33) groups. 
Figure 1 [rid=noi210030f1] and eTable 5 in the Supplement [this file] indicate that [ F]flortaucipir-PET was more strongly associated with annual decline in MMSE than amyloid PET across all participants ( , 0.35 vs 0.17; bootstrapped difference, = 147.1 [ < .001]), the AD dementia group ( , 0.17 vs 0.02; bootstrapped difference, = 81.1 [ < .001]), the Aβ-positive MCI group ( , 0.25 vs 0.07; bootstrapped difference, = 63.3 [ < .001]), the Aβ-positive CU group ( , 0.16 vs 0.08; bootstrapped difference, = 47.0 [ < .001]), and the Aβ-negative CU group ( , 0.06 vs 0.04; bootstrapped difference, = 21.7 [ < .001]). Comparable results were found in the [ F]RO948 replication cohort (eFigure 1 and eTable 5 in the Supplement [this file] ). Tau PET always added information to models including amyloid PET ( for all participants, 0.49 vs 0.25; for Aβ-positive AD dementia group, 0.33 vs 0.20; for Aβ-positive MCI group, 0.39 vs 0.24; for Aβ-positive CU group, 0.18 vs 0.11) (all < .001) (eTable 6 in the Supplement [this file] ), whereas amyloid PET did not improve tau PET models in the AD dementia (χ , 0.1 [ = .82]), Aβ-positive MCI (χ , 0.01 [ = .97]), and Aβ-positive CU (χ , 0.2 [ = .69]) groups. 
In the [ F]RO948 cohort, modification by age was not replicated ( = −0.81; = .42) (eFigure 7 in the Supplement [this file] ). 
Because there were no major demographic differences between AD cases in the discovery vs the replication cohort (eTable 1 in the Supplement [this file] ), this discrepant finding may be explained by the slightly greater dynamic range of [ F]RO948 compared with [ F]flortaucipir that enables [ F]RO948 to slightly better capture cognitive change over time in more advanced clinical stages of AD.

We found steeper decline in cognition with higher age, less education, and male gender (supplementary table S7 [this file] ). The association between the model with APOE alone and the slope of MMSE was non-significant when adjusting for Aβ status ( = 0.8) and there was a considerable attenuation in the effect size (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] a, supplementary table S10 [this file] ). None of the PRS-Alz or APOE models showed any significant association with the random intercept after Bonferroni correction (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] b, supplementary table S11 [this file] ). 
After adjusting for Aβ status, PGS-Int 7 remained significantly associated with the slope of MMSE ( = 1.49e−02) (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] c, supplementary table S12 [this file] ) and PGS-Int 1, 2, 3 and 4 with the intercept ( = 3.06e−02, 2.55e−02, 1.86e−02 and 4.96e−02 respectively [Bonferroni corrected]) (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] d, supplementary table S13 [this file] ). 
For the APOE model, the interaction term was significant for the intercept (uncorrected value = 0.04) but not for the slope of MMSE (supplementary tables S14 [this file] – S19 [this file] ). 
Figure 3 [rid=Fig3] illustrates that the rate of change of MMSE that is significantly predicted by PRS-Alz 5 is partly but significantly mediated by Aβ pathology (20% mediation effect) (supplementary table S20 [this file] ). 
We also found 17 variants whose removal resulted in an increase in the value of association of PRS with Aβ relative to PRS-Alz 5 (indicating a less significant association), suggesting that these variants may be Aβ-dependent (supplementary table S21 [this file] ). Taken together, these findings support that a PRS consisting of these 23 variants is Aβ-independent (supplementary table S22 [this file] ). The PRS model (hereafter called as PRS-Alz 5-D, where D stand for dependent) with the top 10 variants (reverse order ranking) was the best Aβ-dependent model, as the association between the PRS model and slope of MMSE was lost when adjusting for Aβ (beta =− 0.06, = 8.5e−02) compared to when not adjusting for Aβ (beta =− 0.11, = 2e−03) (supplementary table S23 [this file] ) (this condition was not met for more extensive PRSs). Other inclusion criteria for the present study were: (i) cognitively unimpaired or experiencing mild cognitive impairment ; (ii) a valid baseline measurement of CSF amyloid-β , amyloid-β and p-tau not more than 12 months from the baseline tau-PET scan (to determine tau biomarker profiles, see the ‘Thresholds and grouping’ section; Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ); (iii) no known genetic variants associated with autosomal dominant forms of neurodegenerative diseases (e.g. , or variants); and (iv) not a current or past participant in a clinical trial aimed at affecting the Alzheimer’s disease pathological process. 
We performed Gaussian mixture modelling of CSF amyloid-β /amyloid-β ratios, CSF p-tau and temporal meta-region SUVRs to determine cut-offs for abnormal CSF amyloid-β, CSF p-tau and tau-PET ( Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] ). Thresholds were determined to be <0.078 for amyloid-β /amyloid-β ratios, >110 pg/ml for CSF p-tau and >1.40 SUVR for tau-PET ( Supplementary Fig. 1A–C [this file] ), and corresponded closely to thresholds used in previous publications. In accordance with studies showing that CSF p-tau positivity precedes tau-PET positivity in Alzheimer’s disease, there were no A+P−T+ individuals ( Supplementary Fig. 1D [this file] ). 
Longitudinal tau-PET was available for all subjects (by design; mean follow-up was 1.78 ± 0.19 years), cognitive follow-up was available for all but one subject (mean follow-up 2.18 ± 0.46 years) and follow-up MRI was available for 219/231 participants (95%; mean follow-up 1.74 ± 0.23 years; Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). 
Our group classification of amyloid-β-positive (A+) individuals yielded 30 in the tau-negative (A+P−T−) group, 48 in the tau-discordant (A+P+T−; i.e. CSF p-tau-positive, tau-PET-negative) group and 18 in the tau-positive (A+P+T+) group ( Supplementary Fig. 1D [this file] ). Differences between the groups in demographics and clinical characteristics at baseline are provided in Supplementary Table 3 [this file] . We also found that cortex in the entorhinal, AD-signature (intermediate) and late (temporoparietal) regions were all thinner at baseline in the tau-positive group than in the tau-discordant group, but there were no differences between the tau-discordant group and the control and tau-negative groups ( Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). 
Voxel-wise beta-maps, which are not dependent on sample sizes, are displayed in Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] .

Results obtained using these groups were similar to the main analyses using CSF p-tau and are provided in Supplementary Table 5 [this file] . To capture the entire spectrum of early Alzheimer’s Disease development from subthreshold Aβ levels to abnormal Aβ levels and finally cognitive symptoms, cognitively unimpaired participants and patients with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) with evidence of Aβ pathology were included (see Supplementary material [this file] for inclusion and exclusion criteria). 
A supplementary analysis using cortical mean diffusivity form the diffusion tensor model was also performed (see Supplementary material [this file] ). 
A further sensitivity analysis including both cortical thickness and tau-PET uptake when investigating the association with Aβ or Aβ-PET when investigating the association with tau is included in the Supplementary material (see Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] ). 
A further analysis restricting the cohort to Aβ-positive participants is reported in the Supplementary Material (see Supplementary material [this file] and Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] ). 
Parallel analysis employing RTOP have been also performed and are presented in the Supplementary material [this file] and Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] . 
The analysis focusing on the early-Aβ meta-region of interest provided converging evidence showing that MSD was associated with Aβ-PET uptake (MSD: standardized-β = 0.33, < 0.001; Fig. 3A [rid=awac343-F3] and Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). Cortical thickness was also associated with Aβ-PET uptake in the same meta-region of interest (cortical thickness: standardized-β = −0.18, < 0.001; Fig. 3B [rid=awac343-F3] and Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). The supplementary analysis restricted to Aβ-positive participants led to consistent results showing a significant association between MSD and Aβ-PET uptake (MSD: standardized-β = 0.14, < 0.05) but no association between cortical thickness and Aβ-PET uptake (cortical thickness: standardized-β = −0.06, > 0.3; see Supplementary material [this file] , Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] and Supplementary Tables 9 and 10 [this file] ). 
The analysis focusing on the temporal meta-region of interest provided similar results showing that MSD was associated with tau-PET uptake (MSD: standardized-β = 0.48, < 0.001; Fig. 3C [rid=awac343-F3] and Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). Cortical thickness was also associated with tau-PET uptake (cortical thickness: standardized-β = −0.35, < 0.001; Fig. 3C [rid=awac343-F3] and Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ). In this case the associations had a similar magnitude (see Supplementary material [this file] , Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] and Supplementary Tables 11 and 12 [this file] ). 
In the early-Aβ meta-region of interest, MSD was associated with performance in the trail making test (trail making B – trail making A), which reflects executive functions and has been previously related to early Aβ pathology (standardized-β = 0.33, < 0.001; Fig. 6A [rid=awac343-F6] and Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ). Cortical thickness was also associated executive functions (standard-β = −0.15, < 0.01; Fig. 6B [rid=awac343-F6] and Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ), but the comparison between standardized β-coefficients showed that the association between MSD and executive functions was stronger than the association between cortical thickness and executive functions ( < 0.001). Likewise, MSD in the temporal meta-region of interest was associated with the ADAS delayed recall score (standardized-β = 0.38, < 0.001; Fig. 6C [rid=awac343-F6] and Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ). A similar relationship was found between cortical thickness and ADAS delayed recall (standardized-β = −0.24, < 0.001; Fig. 6D [rid=awac343-F6] and Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ), but the standardized β-coefficients differed such that MSD was more strongly associated than cortical thickness to ADAS delayed recall score ( < 0.001). 
The inclusion of did not affect either the differences in cortical diffusion between groups or the associations between cortical diffusion and other markers of the Alzheimer’s disease pathological cascade (see Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] ). Also in this case, the supplementary analysis confirmed the main results (see Supplementary Tables 13–18 [this file] ). The results were very consistent with the results obtained employing MSD although both Aβ- and tau-PET uptake were more strongly associated with MSD than with MD, as the magnitude of the standardized β coefficients were significantly lower for MD than for MSD ( < 0.05; see Supplementary material [this file] and Supplementary Fig. 5 [this file] ). 
For example, our supplementary analysis using mean diffusivity (MD) from the diffusion tensor model showed that MD performed very similarly to MSD, although both Aβ- and tau-PET uptake were more strongly associated with MSD than with MD (see Supplementary material [this file] ).

Similar results as with p-tau217 was also observed with p-tau181 ( Table S4 [this file] ). Again, slightly more participants had better outcome prediction when including creatinine and BMI in logistic regressions (44% and 48% for p-tau217 and NfL respectively) compared to the number of cases where the model adjusted for confounding factors was worse than the basic model (33% and 40% for p-tau217 and NfL respectively, Figure S7 [this file] ). Here improvements in the models adjusted for creatinine and BMI were seen in participants with higher creatinine levels and higher BMI for both biomarkers (R=0.33 and 0.36 for associations between relative change between models and creatinine, and R=0.29 for same associations with BMI, Figure S7 [this file] ). Further, when assessed at the individual level very few participants exhibited clearly improved prediction of the CSF NfL concentration when plasma NfL was adjusted for either plasma creatinine or BMI ( Figure S3 [this file] ). Similarly, at the individual level very few participants exhibited improved prediction of dementia when adjusting for creatinine or BMI ( Figure S5 [this file] ).

The main results focusing on early AD were also validated in the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) database using [ F]flortaucipir PET, CSF p-tau181 as well as [ F]florbetapir or [ F]florbetaben Aβ-PET ( = 119: 52 CU Aβ-negative, 36 Aβ-positive CU and 31 Aβ-positive MCI participants; all figures and extended results in Supplementary information [this file] ). 
See Supplementary Table 1 [this file] for ADNI participants. 
In the BioFINDER-2 cohort, the baseline distribution of insoluble tau aggregates assessed via tau-PET recapitulated the AD-typical deposition in the medial and lateral temporal lobes in the controls and non-demented participants, and into lateral and medial parietal and lateral occipital regions at symptomatic AD stages (Fig. 1a [rid=Fig1] and Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] for CU and MCI separately). The longitudinal accumulation rate of tau aggregates (i.e., the annual tau-PET rate of change measured over a mean time of 2 years) was highest in temporal lobe regions in non-demented participants, and showed more extensive involvement mainly of medial parietal and lateral frontal regions in AD dementia (Fig. 1b [rid=Fig1] and Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] ). Between-group comparisons showing regions where accumulation of tau aggregates differ are also reported in Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] for complementary description of regional differences of tau-PET rate of change. 
In Supplementary Fig 1 [this file] , we show individuals above 50 years old, as well as dividing the non-demented group into CU and MCI. 
In ADNI (Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ), the spatial pattern of the main regions with highest tau-PET binding at baseline and the highest rate of change in tau aggregates per year mirrored the patterns found in BioFINDER-2 (Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] ). 
Of note, a similar effect of Aβ being no long significant after accounting for soluble p-tau was found on baseline tau aggregates (Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] ). These results were also consistent across different measures of Aβ, i.e. if using global Aβ load assessed by PET or the CSF Aβ42/40 ratio instead of regional Aβ aggregates in regression models (Supplementary Fig. 5 [this file] ). Further, investigating the same relations in the CU and MCI groups separately, the strong effect of soluble p-tau on subsequent tau aggregation rate, above the effect of Aβ, was clearly found in both groups (Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] ). When further adjusting for local baseline tau aggregates, soluble p-tau also remained a significant predictor in temporo-parietal regions in each group (Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] ). 
Statistical details of the mediation models are shown in Supplementary Fig. 8 [this file] . 
In ADNI, as in BioFINDER-2, soluble p-tau, measured with CSF p-tau181, was the main factor related to regional accumulation of tau aggregates over time (Supplementary Fig. 7 [this file] ). In both cases, soluble p-tau remained significant when accounting for Aβ and baseline tau-PET SUVR in temporo-parietal regions, although the regional pattern was more restricted than in BioFINDER-2 (Supplementary Fig. 7 [this file] ). 
The same associations were found in CU and MCI participants alone (Supplementary Fig. 9 [this file] ), suggesting that this effect is not only due to the MCI participants who tend to show greater association between connectivity to epicenter and tau-PET rate of change (more negative β-values on Fig. 3b [rid=Fig3] ). 
Results were also validated in the Aβ-positive non-demented participants from ADNI (Supplementary Fig. 10 [this file] ). 
We focused on tau-PET rate of change in regions most strongly connected to the epicenters (i.e. Q1), to capture individualized level of tau aggregates accumulation, and all results were also validated using a commonly used temporal meta-ROI (see Supplementary Fig. 11 [this file] ). We observe a full mediation effect of tau-PET rate of change, either in Q1 or in the temporal meta-ROI between soluble p-tau and cognitive decline on the cognitive composite score in CU (c’-c = −0.21 [−0.40, −0.06], = 0.002), and on decline on MMSE in MCI (c’-c = −0.24 [−0.46, −0.04], = 0.01), see Supplementary Fig. 12 [this file] for detailed statistics. 
Our motivation to focus on AD dementia patients separately was based on the plateau-phase reached by soluble p-tau species in more advanced disease stages (Fig. 5a [rid=Fig5] with CSF Aβ42/40 to include the full sample since AD dementia patients do not undergo Aβ PET, and Supplementary Fig. 13 [this file] with Aβ PET in a restricted sample). 
A similar association with Aβ-PET SUVR is shown in a restricted sample without AD dementia patients in Supplementary Fig. 13 [this file] . 
All findings in non-demented group also even held when analyzing CU and MCI groups separately (Supplementary Figs. 6 [this file] , 8 [this file] and 12 [this file] ). 
Correlations between baseline and longitudinal variables are also reported for descriptive purposes in Supplementary Table 2 [this file] .

The spike-in amount of each heavy peptide was adjusted to yield a light-to-heavy peak area ratio of approx. 0.1 – 0.2 in CSF from non-AD subjects (Supplementary Table S 1 [this file] ). 
The mass spectrometer was operated in the positive ion mode, with the following settings for the PRM scan: Activation Type: HCD; Collision energies were determined experimentally for each peptide and are listed in Supplementary Table S 1 [this file] ; Detector Type: Orbitrap; Orbitrap Resolution: 120 000; Scan Range: 150–1500; RF Lens: 60%; Easy-IC: On; Isolation Type: Quadrupole; Isolation Window: 1.2 m ; Maximum Injection Time: 400 ms; Normalized AGC Target: 1000%. 
Neat CSF samples were spiked with a mixture of heavy isotope-labeled peptide standards with amino acid sequences matching the trypsin proteolysis products containing the targeted phosphorylation sites (Supplementary Table S 1 [this file] ). Representative examples of PRM chromatograms are shown in Supplementary Figure S 1 [this file] . 
pS199, pS202, and pT205 were detected on isobaric tryptic peptides with identical amino acid sequence. pS199 (Supplementary Figure S 1 [this file] B) and pS202 (Supplementary Figure S 1 [this file] C) co-eluted in the LC separation but could be quantified separately by using distinct fragments ions formed by cleavage between the two phosphorylation sites (b and y , and corresponding fragments formed by neutral loss of phosphoric acid (-98 Da)). pT205 was resolved chromatographically from the other two isobaric peptides, and thus all prominent fragment ions detected from it could be used for quantification (Supplementary Figure S 1 [this file] D). 
The reproducibility of the method was determined by the analysis of eight aliquots of a CSF pool (Supplementary Table S 2 [this file] ). 
The performance of the pTau PRM method was evaluated by analyzing CSF samples from patients with AD-indicative and normal neurochemical biomarker profiles ( = 38), based on the core Alzheimer’s disease biomarkers (Supplementary Figure S 2 [this file] , Supplementary Table S 3 [this file] ). 
The PRM method showed strong correlation with the Simoa immunoassays for all three analytes (pT181: Spearman ( ) = 0.95, pT217: = 0.79, pT231: = 0.94, Supplementary Figure S 3 [this file] ). 
On this continuum, all measured pTau epitopes increased in both cohorts, with the best distinction between the different disease stages and the CU- group observed for pT231 (TRIAD: AUC = 93.61%, fold change = 5.72; BioFINDER-2: AUC = 84.44, fold change = 6.40), pT217 (TRIAD: AUC = 92.8%, fold change = 4.26), and pT205 (AUC = 85.07%, fold change = 3.35, Supplementary Table S 4 [this file] and Supplementary Table S 5 [this file] , Supplementary Figure S 4 [this file] and Supplementary Figure S 5 [this file] ). 
For the phosphorylated tau peptides for which it was possible to also measure the corresponding non-phosphorylated peptide (pS199, pS202, pT205 and pT217), we also calculated the ratios of phosphorylated to non-phosphorylated epitope (Supplementary Figure S 6 [this file] ). 
We found that the fold changes between Alzheimer’s disease and CU- patients for the phosphorylation ratios, pS199/S199, pS202/S202, pT205/T205, and pT217/T217, were all smaller compared with the fold changes for the concentrations of the corresponding peptides themselves, quantified using the isotope-labelled internal standards (Supplementary Figure S 6 [this file] ).

All participants in cohort 1 (eTables 1 and 2 in Supplement 1 [this file] ) had a clinical diagnosis of mild cognitive impairment. Cohort 2 (eTables 3 and 4 in Supplement 1 [this file] ) included a cognitively unimpaired group comprising cognitively healthy controls and individuals with subjective cognitive decline and another group of patients with cognitive impairment comprising those with mild cognitive impairment or dementia from the Swedish BioFINDER-2 study. 
Further details of cohort inclusion/exclusion criteria, sample collection, and analysis and tau-PET are described in the eMethods in Supplement 1 [this file] . 
Cohort 1 included 141 participants with mild cognitive impairment with a mean (SD) age of 72.2 (7.7) years; 82 (58.2%) were women, and 67 (47.5%) had abnormal CSF Aβ42/40 (eTables 1 and 2 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
We first tested correlations between eGFR and plasma p-tau biomarkers as shown in the Table [rid=noi230007t1] and eFigure 1 in Supplement 1 [this file] . 
We next compared the plasma p-tau levels between participants with CKD (CKD+) or without CKD (CKD−) (eTable 2 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). These results were verified when using the Lund-Malmö revised equation to calculate eGFR (eTable 5 and eFigure 2A in Supplement 1 [this file] ), except that there were no significant associations between CKD− status and pT181/T181 (eFigure 2A in Supplement 1 [this file] ). Finally, in line with already published data we found that eGFR was associated with plasma Aβ42 and Aβ40 but not with the Aβ42/40 ratio (eTable 6 and eFigure 3 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
The mean (SD) age in cohort 2 was 69.8 (9.4) years, 169 (50.9%) were women, and 172 (51.8%) had abnormal CSF Aβ42/40 (eTables 3 and 4 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). Correlations of eGFR with p-tau217, Tau212-221, p-tau181, and Tau181-190 were similar between the cognitive impairment groups in cohort 2 and cohort 1 ( Table [rid=noi230007t1] ; eFigures 1 and 4 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). For p-tau217, the correlations were somewhat stronger in cognitively unimpaired participants ( , −0.47 [95% CI, −0.59 to −0.34]; < .001) than patients with cognitive impairment (cohort 1: , −0.24 [95% CI, −0.41 to −0.07]; = .004; cohort 2: , −0.18 [95% CI, −0.32 to −0.02]; = .02) ( Table [rid=noi230007t1] ; eFigures 4 and 5 in Supplement 1 [this file] ).

Individuals in the tau PET cohort who were cognitively impaired (CDR ≥ 0.5) were included in Knight ADRC tau PET symptomatic AD subcohort ( = 55) (Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). 
For the intermediately abnormal CSF pool, pT231/T231 had higher variance (17.5%) compared with pT217/T217 (3.0%), pT181/T181 (5.8%) and pT205/T205 (9.1%) (see Appendix 1 [this file] for methodology, quality control and performance details of the MS assay). 
Concentrations of all phosphorylated and nonphosphorylated CSF tau species were higher in amyloid PET-positive compared with amyloid PET-negative individuals ( < 0.0001 for all) and the fold difference was largest for CSF p-tau231 concentration (7.79-fold) (Extended Data Table 4 [rid=Tab4] and Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). The phosphorylation occupancy at six sites (T217, T111, T231, T153, S208 and T181) and the concentrations of four p-tau species (p-tau217, p-tau231, p-tau208 and p-tau153) distinguished amyloid PET status with a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) area under the curve (AUC) > 0.90 (Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). 
CSF pT217/T217 had the highest correlation with amyloid PET Centiloid of all the measures (Spearman’s = 0.76 (95% CI 0.73–0.79), which was almost significantly higher than Lumipulse Aβ42/Aβ40 ( = −0.74 (−0.77 to −0.71), = 0.08) and was significantly higher than p-tau217 concentration = 0.71 (0.67–0.74), < 0.0001) (Supplementary Tables 4 [this file] and 5 [this file] ). Importantly, in amyloid PET-positive individuals, CSF pT217/T217 was strongly correlated with amyloid PET Centiloid ( = 0.69 (0.62–0.75)), whereas the correlation between Lumipulse Aβ42/Aβ40 and amyloid PET Centiloid was only modest ( = −0.42 (−0.52 to −0.32), < 0.0001; Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). 
The horizontal dashed lines denote the cut-offs that best distinguish amyloid PET status, based on combined sensitivity and specificity (Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). 
Concentrations of almost all CSF phosphorylated and nonphosphorylated tau species were higher in tau PET-positive compared with PET-negative individuals, with the highest fold difference again being in CSF p-tau231 concentration (7.16-fold) (Supplementary Tables 7 [this file] and 8 [this file] ). 
The phosphorylation occupancy at six sites (T217, T111, T181, T153, S208 and T231) and the concentrations of four p-tau species (p-tau217, p-tau208, p-tau231and p-tau153) that were strongly associated with amyloid PET status also distinguished tau PET status with an AUC ≥ 0.89 (Supplementary Table 9 [this file] ). 
In amyloid PET-positive individuals, only CSF measures related to T205 and T217 distinguished tau PET status with an AUC > 0.75: pT205/T205 (AUC = 0.88 (0.82–0.94), p-tau205 concentration (AUC = 0.87 (0.81–0.93)), pT217/T217 (AUC = 0.83 (0.76–0.90)) and p-tau217 concentration (AUC = 0.80 (0.72–0.88)) (Extended Data Fig. 2c [rid=Fig6] and Supplementary Table 10 [this file] ). Individuals who were both amyloid PET positive and tau PET positive could be distinguished from all other individuals by single measures, including CSF pT217/T217 (AUC = 0.96 (0.94–0.98)) (Supplementary Table 11 [this file] ). 
In the Knight ADRC tau PET cohort, CSF concentrations of p-tau208 ( = 0.52 (0.44–0.60)), p-tau205 ( = 0.51 (0.43–0.58), pT217/T217 ( = 0.47 (0.39–0.55)) and pT205/T205 ( = 0.47 (0.39–0.55)) had among the highest correlations with the tau PET summary measure (Supplementary Tables 12 [this file] and 13 [this file] ). In amyloid PET-positive individuals ( = 125), CSF pT205/T205 had the highest correlation with the tau PET summary measure ( = 0.72 (0.63–0.80)), which was not superior statistically to p-tau205 concentration ( = 0.65 (0.54–0.74)), but was superior to pT217/T217 ( = 0.55 (0.42–0.67), = 0.02) and p-tau217 concentration ( = 0.48 (0.33–0.60), = 0.0002) (Supplementary Table 14 [this file] ). 
The horizontal dashed lines denote the cut-offs that best distinguish tau PET status, based on combined sensitivity and specificity (Supplementary Table 9 [this file] ). 
CSF pT205/T205 had the highest correlation with tau PET standardized uptake value ratio (SUVR) in the amygdala and temporal regions (for example, inferior temporal gyrus, fusiform gyrus, parahippocampal gyrus, middle temporal gyrus and entorhinal), with partial Spearman’s values ranging from 0.68 to 0.61 for these regions (Supplementary Table 15 [this file] ). CSF pT217/T217 was also most highly correlated with regional tau PET in the amygdala and temporal regions, but the correlations were weaker, with partial Spearman’s values ranging from 0.55 to 0.49 for the top six most correlated regions of interest (ROIs) (Supplementary Table 16 [this file] ). The pattern of regional correlations with tau PET were similar for CSF pT181/T181 and pT231/T231, but the maximum partial Spearman’s value was 0.31 for both measures (Supplementary Tables 17 [this file] and 18 [this file] ). 
CSF pT205/T205 had the highest correlation with regional brain volumes in the hippocampus, amygdala and temporal regions (for example, temporal pole, middle temporal gyrus, fusiform gyrus and entorhinal), with partial Spearman’s values ranging from −0.50 to −0.37 for these regions (Supplementary Table 19 [this file] ). CSF pT217/T217 had the highest correlation with regional brain volumes in similar areas, with partial Spearman’s values ranging from −0.43 to −0.28 for the top six most correlated ROIs (Supplementary Table 20 [this file] ). After correction for multiple comparisons, CSF pT181/T181 and pT231/T231 were not significantly correlated with regional brain volumes (Supplementary Tables 21 [this file] and 22 [this file] ). 
Clinical status (cognitively unimpaired (CDR = 0) or cognitively impaired (CDR > 0, includes both MCI and AD dementia)) was predicted by biomarkers with and without the covariates of age, sex and years of education (Extended Data Fig. 1c [rid=Fig5] and Supplementary Table 23 [this file] ). In amyloid PET-positive individuals, the tau PET summary measure also had the highest correspondence with clinical status (AUC = 0.86 (0.78–0.94)), but again this was not statistically superior to pT217/T217 (AUC = 0.80 (0.74–0.85)) or pT205/T205 (AUC = 0.79 (0.73–0.84)) (Supplementary Table 24 [this file] ). 
The tau PET summary measure ( = 0.43 (0.35–0.51), CSF pT217/T217 ( = 0.43 (0.37–0.48)) and pT205/T205 ( = 0.39 (0.33–0.45)) had some of the highest correlations with CDR-SB (Supplementary Table 25 [this file] ). In amyloid PET-positive individuals, the CDR-SB had the highest correlations with the tau PET summary measure ( = 0.65 (0.54–0.74)), CSF pT217/T217 ( = 0.50 (0.41–0.59)) and pT205/T205 ( = 0.50 (0.40–0.59)), whereas correlations with Lumipulse Aβ42/Aβ40 were lower ( = −0.23 (−0.34 to −0.12); Supplementary Table 26 [this file] ). 
To evaluate the performance of these measures in a more clinically relevant cohort, CSF tau measures were examined in cognitively impaired (CDR ≥ 0.5) individuals from the Knight ADRC tau PET cohort ( = 55; Supplementary Table 27 [this file] ). There was a trend toward a higher correlation of amyloid PET Centiloid with CSF pT217/T217 ( = 0.77 (0.63–0.86)) compared with Aβ42/Aβ40 ( = −0.58 (−0.73 to −0.37), = 0.06; Supplementary Table 28 [this file] ). CSF pT217/T217 ( = 0.71 (0.55–0.82) and/or pT205/T205 ( = 0.67 (0.50–0.80)) had higher correlations with a tau PET summary measure compared with pT181/T181 ( = 0.42 (0.18–0.62), = 0.006 and = 0.04) or Lumipulse p-tau181 concentration ( = 0.44 (0.20–0.63), = 0.003 and = 0.07; Supplementary Table 29 [this file] ). 
CSF pT217/T217 ( = 0.55 (0.38–0.68)) was better correlated with amyloid PET Centiloid than CSF Aβ42/Aβ40 ( = −0.19 (−0.38 to 0.02), = 0.0007; Extended Data Fig. 3 [rid=Fig7] and Supplementary Table 30 [this file] ). CSF pT217/T217 ( = 0.76 (0.65–0.83)) and/or pT205/T205 ( = 0.72 (0.60–0.81)) had higher correlations with a tau PET measure for the Braak I–IV region compared with pT181/T181 ( = 0.59 (0.43–0.71), = 0.002 and = 0.14) and CSF p-tau181 concentration by immunoassay ( = 0.42 (0.23–0.57), = 0.0004 and = 0.02, respectively; Extended Data Fig. 4 [rid=Fig8] and Supplementary Table 31 [this file] ). CSF pT217/T217 ( = 0.59 (0.43–0.71)) and pT205/T205 ( = 0.66 (0.52–0.76)) were better correlated with a tau PET measure for the Braak V–VI region compared with pT181/T181 ( = 0.44 (0.25–0.59), = 0.004 and 0.02) and p-tau181 concentration by immunoassay ( = 0.23 (0.02–0.42), = 0.0003 and = 0.0007; Extended Data Fig. 5 [rid=Fig9] and Supplementary Table 32 [this file] ). 
CSF tau was immunopurified and digested, then phosphorylated and nonphosphorylated peptides were quantified using high-resolution MS (HRMS) as previously described and detailed in Appendix 1 [this file] (ref. ). 
Tau PET positivity was defined as a tau PET summary measure >1.52, based on Gaussian mixture modeling (Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] ).

A total of 391 participants were excluded (eMethods in Supplement 1 [this file] for details) and 878 participants met the inclusion criteria and completed the study. Participant characteristics are presented in the Table [rid=noi230028t1] and the eTable in Supplement 1 [this file] .

Once the form was filled out, the visual read of the [ F]RO948 PET was revealed together with a template for interpretation (eAppendix in Supplement 1 [this file] ) and the clinician was asked to fill out a follow-up report form, again stating the most likely etiology, their certainty, as well as if they planned changes in the medication regimen or patient management as a result of the [ F]RO948 PET information. The full forms, translated into English, are available in the eAppendix in Supplement 1 [this file] . 
Imaging acquisition details are provided in the eMethods in Supplement 1 [this file] . A detailed description of the visual read algorithm and example images are provided in the eMethods and eFigure 1 in Supplement 1 [this file] . 
Based on the pre-PET forms, 408 participants had an AD diagnosis and 470 had non-AD diagnoses (details in the eMethods and the eTable in Supplement 1 [this file] ). In the group with a non-AD diagnosis before PET, 39 of 470 had positive tau PET scan (8%) (eFigure 2 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
Significant changes in diagnoses were seen in participants with dementia (23 changed diagnosis, total n = 318; McNemar test, = .04) and MCI (33 changed diagnosis, total n = 419; McNemar test, = .01), whereas the number of changed diagnoses in the SCD group did not reach statistical significance (10 changed diagnosis, total n = 141; McNemar test, = .75; eFigure 3 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
The visual read results of the Aβ-positive group are presented in eFigure 4 in Supplement 1 [this file] . 
Graphs showing paired data of the changes in certainty in the AD diagnostic group are provided in eFigure 5 in Supplement 1 [this file] . 
The diagnostic certainty after the tau PET scan was lower in participants with a pre-PET non-AD diagnosis compared with a pre-PET AD diagnosis (6.7 [SD, 2.6] vs 8.2 [SD, 2.0]; < .001), but there was still a significant, yet subtle, increase in certainty in the non-AD group after receiving the tau PET result (6.3 [SD, 2.5] vs 6.7 [SD, 2.6]; < .001; eFigure 6 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
In a sensitivity analysis, only including changes in medication to enhance cognitive functions, the study team found similar results (eFigure 7 in Supplement 1 [this file] ).
