Initially, univariable linear regression analyses were conducted to determine the associations between each pathology (Aβ, tau and WMH, respectively; by using continuous measures) and each of the four dependent variables: step velocity variability, step length, step time, and stance time asymmetry, see Supplementary Tables 1–4 [this file] . 
Multivariable linear regression analyses with basic covariates ( Supplementary Tables 1–4 [this file] ) showed no significant associations between either WMH ( ≥0.135) nor Aβ pathology ( ≥0.090) with any of the dependent variables (i.e., the four gait parameters). In the models with step time and stance time asymmetry as dependent variables ( Supplementary Tables 3 and 4 [this file] ), none of the pathologies (tau, Aβ and WMH) showed any significant relationships with step time ( ≥0.222) or stance time asymmetry ( ≥0.219). 
If instead using dichotomized PET-values (see footnotes in Supplementary Tables 1–4 [this file] ), all univariable and multivariable analyses (adjusted for age and sex) remained similar except for the association between pathological Aβ and increased step length ( = 0.026). 
When controlling for leg length, the associations between tau and step velocity variability and step length remained statistically significant ( < 0.001), see Supplementary Table 5 [this file] . When controlling for gait speed, the previous significant association between increased tau and increased step length became non-significant ( = 0.168) whereas the association with step velocity variability remained significant ( < 0.001), see Supplementary Table 6 [this file] .

CSF levels of amyloid precursor protein (APP), syntaxin-1B (STX1B), neurogranin (Ng), neuronal pentraxin receptor (NPTXR), neuronal pentraxin 1 (NPTX1), β-synuclein (β-Syn), γ-synuclein (γ-Syn), 14-3-3ε, phosphatidylethanolamine-binding protein 1 (PEBP-1), cathepsin F (CTSF), GM2 activator (GM2A), neurosecretory protein VGF (VGF), secretogranin-2 (SgII) and chromogranin A (CgA) were all increased by 4.5-13.3% (95% CI, 1.7–7.2 to 4.4–22.1; < 0.048) in samples collected in the evening compared to those collected in the morning (Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] , Supplemental 1 [this file] , Table 4 [rid=Tab4] ). 
Data for all synaptic and endo-lysosomal proteins is shown in Supplementary Table 2 [this file] . 
Taken together these findings may explain the higher levels of synaptic proteins in evening samples in comparison to the morning seen in our study (See ﻿Supplementary Table 2 [this file] , Supplemental 1 [this file] , Table 4 [rid=Tab4] ).

Each year, participants undergo a uniform comprehensive evaluation, which includes a medical history interview, detailed cognitive testing, and a neurologic examination (see eMethods in Supplement 1 [this file] for details on the sample). 
Separately, continuous measures for β-amyloid and paired helical filament (PHF) tau tangles were obtained using immunohistochemistry (eMethods in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
Multiple cerebrovascular conditions including macroscopic and microinfarcts, CAA, atherosclerosis, and arteriolosclerosis were also assessed (eMethods in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
Ten neuropathologic indices (ie, β-amyloid, PHF tau tangles, Lewy bodies, LATE-NC, hippocampal sclerosis, atherosclerosis, arteriolosclerosis, macroscopic infarcts, microinfarcts, and CAA) were used in hierarchical clustering (eFigure 2 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). The optimal number of clusters was determined by following the cluster dendrogram to the point where no meaningful reduction of height could be obtained and verified using Gap statistic (eFigure 3 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
In total, 280 distinct copathologies were observed, and the numbers of participants with each distinct combination of pathologies ranged between 1 and 57 (eTable 1 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). With the exception of ADNC with CAA (57 participants), the distinct copathologies were present in less than 3% of deceased participants, reflective of a very complex nature of pathologic findings in aged brains (eFigure 1 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
Results from the hierarchical clustering analysis suggested that a 5-cluster model fit the data best (eResults in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
Results for other common AD/ADRD variants were less clear (eTable 2 in Supplement 1 [this file] ).

The joint mediator-adjusted model for prevalent T2D yielded an OR of 0.79 (95% CI 0.75-0.82), compared with 0.77 (0.73-0.80) after adjustment for lifestyle factors and BMI alone ( [xref] [this file] ). 
A prediction model incorporating educational attainment and standard clinical/lifestyle features yielded an AUC of 0.808 and Brier score of 0.182 ( [xref] [this file] ). 
The NHANES validation cohort included 21,750 adults from 2011-2018 ( [xref] [this file] ). In the adjusted weighted logistic model, college graduation or above was associated with lower odds of prevalent T2D (OR 0.69, 95% CI 0.61-0.78; n=20,502; [xref] [this file] ; [xref] [rid=f1] ).

Instrument diagnostics showed strong instruments for key analyses (minimum F statistic >29), and leave-one-out IVW analyses did not reverse the direction of educational-attainment estimates for BMI, T1D, or T2D ( [xref] [this file] ). Residual outlier diagnostics and stricter exposure P-value thresholds also retained inverse estimates for educational attainment on BMI and T2D ( [xref] [this file] – [xref] [this file] ; [xref] [this file] ).

However, individuals homozygous for the risk C allele of rs11787077 exhibited lower CLU levels ( Figure 1H [rid=F1] ), a trend observed across 12 of 16 CLU peptides spanning both α- and β-chains ( Figure S1E [this file] ). Strikingly, CLU levels were significantly elevated in later Braak stages only in individuals carrying the protective “T” allele ( Figures 1I [rid=F1] , S3K [this file] – M [this file] ). 
Using pseudobulk analysis of single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNAseq) from over 400 ROSMAP participants, we found that CLU is widely expressed but highest in astrocytes ( Figure S2A [this file] – B [this file] ). Human cellular models confirmed that astrocytes secrete the highest levels of CLU compared to neurons and microglia ( Figure S2C [this file] ). Several AD-associated CLU risk SNPs identified by GWAS were linked to lower CLU expression specifically in astrocytes, with no significant changes in neurons or microglia ( Figures 1J [rid=F1] , S2D [this file] – G [this file] ; Table 2). Notably, in individuals with high neuropathological burden, the strongest association was observed between lower CLU expression and the rs11787077-C risk allele ( Figure S2I [this file] ). 
Among individuals with amyloid pathology (as assessed by immunostaining, β-amyloid score>1), those with the rs11787077-C risk allele had worse global cognition ( Figure S2K [this file] ). 
To investigate CLU’s role in human cells, we used CRISPR/Cas9 to generate isogenic CLU wildtype (WT), heterozygous (HET), and knockout (KO) iPSC lines in two genetic backgrounds ( Figures S3A [this file] – B [this file] ). 
Example gene bar plots highlight CCL20, a top transcript upregulated by TNF + IL1β, and RRAD, the most differentially expressed protein in CLU KO astrocytes ( Figures S3D [this file] – E [this file] ). Consistent with our proteomics data, CLU loss led to increased secretion of IL-6, C3, SAA, and ICAM-1 ( Figures 2H [rid=F2] – I [rid=F2] , S4A [this file] – D [this file] ). WB further confirmed elevated intracellular ICAM-1 in CLU-deficient astrocytes ( Figure S4F [this file] ). 
WB analysis of CLU WT, HET, and KO iAs showed a reduction in IκBɑ levels after TNF + IL1β stimulation and a baseline decrease in CLU HET and KO iAs ( Figures S4G [this file] – H [this file] ). 
Baseline RNA and protein levels of C3 were elevated in CLU HET and KO vehicle-treated cultures ( Figures 3F [rid=F3] , S4J [this file] ), but NfκB inhibition significantly reduced C3 levels in these cells, with no effect in WT iAs. Similarly, elevated IL-6 and CCL2 expression in CLU HET and KO iAs was attenuated by NfκB inhibition ( Figures 3G [rid=F3] , S4K [this file] – L [this file] ). To assess whether NfκB activation regulates CLU expression, we measured CLU RNA and protein levels in iA cultures following NfκB stimulation ( Figures 3H [rid=F3] , S4M [this file] ). 
To investigate the non-autonomous effects of astrocytic CLU on neurons and microglia, we used transwell-based co-cultures ( Figures S5A [this file] – D [this file] ). After three days, neurons (iNs) and microglia (iMGs) co-cultured with CLU WT vs KO iAs were harvested for TMT-MS, showing minimal differences ( Figures S5A [this file] – L [this file] ; Table S4 [rid=SD5] ). Thus, we extended the co-culture to six days using a tri-culture system of iNs, iAs, and iMGs ( Figures S5M [this file] – N [this file] ). Immunostaining and WB confirmed the presence of TUJ1+ neurons, IBA1+ microglia, and CD44+ astrocytes ( Figures 4A [rid=F4] – B [rid=F4] , S5O [this file] ). As expected, CLU protein levels were reduced in CLU KO astrocyte tri-cultures ( Figure 4C [rid=F4] ), which also exhibited decreased APOE secretion ( Figure 4D [rid=F4] ), consistent with astrocyte-microglia co-culture findings ( Figures S5H [this file] ). Although CLU and APOE are expressed across multiple cell types, astrocytes are the primary source of their secretion ( Figures S5P [this file] – Q [this file] ). 
Tri-cultures with CLU KO astrocytes exhibited elevated phosphorylated tau relative to total tau ( Figures 4E [rid=F4] – H [rid=F4] , S6A [this file] – B [this file] ). Notably, CLU KO astrocytes had no significant impact on phosphorylated tau or APOE levels in these cultures ( Figures 4K [rid=F4] – L [rid=F4] , S6C [this file] ). 
UMAP clustering identified three major cell types—neurons, astrocytes, and microglia—across seven subclusters ( Figures S7A [this file] – B [this file] ). Despite astrocytes making up ~15% of the culture ( Figure S5N [this file] ), their recovery for scRNAseq was poor, a known challenge in the field. No significant shifts in neuron or microglia cluster membership were observed between CLU WT and KO conditions ( Figures 4M [rid=F4] , S7E [this file] – H [this file] ). The reduction in aligns with our previous transwell and tri-culture findings, which showed decreased APOE protein levels in CLU deficient conditions ( Figures 4D [rid=F4] , S5G [this file] – H [this file] ). Additionally, transwell proteomics revealed elevated C1q proteins in microglia co-cultured with CLU KO astrocytes ( Figures S5J [this file] – L [this file] ; Table S4 [rid=SD5] ), a finding validated at the protein level in tri-culture ( Figure 4O [rid=F4] ). Given TREM2’s reported role as a CLU receptor and its involvement in tau and complement activity, we measured TREM2 protein levels, which were reduced in CLU KO tri-cultures ( Figures S6F [this file] – G [this file] ), though the effect size was modest and varied across cell lines. 
In tri-cultures, C1q treatment significantly reduced TREM2 and APOE levels while increasing phosphorylated tau ( Figures 5B [rid=F5] – C [rid=F5] , S6D [this file] – I [this file] ). These effects were absent in neuron-astrocyte co-cultures and microglia monocultures, suggesting that C1q phenocopies CLU deficiency but still requires microglia-astrocyte interaction to influence phosphorylated tau levels ( Figure S6J [this file] ). 
GSEA revealed significant dysregulation of synaptic function pathways in CLU KO co-cultures ( Figure S7I [this file] ; Table S5 [rid=SD6] ). These inflammatory markers were also elevated in CLU HET and/or KO astrocytes in at least one genetic background ( Figures 2I [rid=F2] , S4C [this file] , Table S3 [rid=SD4] ), reinforcing the link between CLU genotype, expression, and inflammation. 
After culture establishment, we assessed AD-related pathology, including Aβ measures, tau phosphorylation, and the expression of proteins previously identified as dysregulated in CLU KO vs. WT conditions ( Figures 8B [rid=F8] – H [rid=F8] and S8A [this file] – I [this file] ; Table S8 [rid=SD9] ). Across the 14 lines, CLU protein levels were positively correlated with APOE and inversely with C3, C1q, and phosphorylated tau ( Figures 8H [rid=F8] – I [rid=F8] and S8J [this file] ). While grouping by CLU genotype alone showed no significant difference ( Figure S8I [this file] ), higher CLU levels correlated with increased spine density, while elevated C3 secretion was associated with reduced spine density ( Figures 8I [rid=F8] – K [rid=F8] , S8J [this file] ). 
Remarkably, these same inflammatory proteins were upregulated in CLU deficient astrocytes ( Figures 2I [rid=F2] , S4C [this file] , and Table S3 [rid=SD4] ). Additionally, tri-cultures with astrocytes carrying risk alleles also showed reduced CLU levels and elevated complement proteins ( Figures 7B [rid=F7] , 7D [rid=F7] , S8E [this file] ), mirroring CLU loss-of-function models. 
Although our analyses of human brain and iPSC models primarily focus on rs11787077 for visualization of results, this SNP—as well as many other LOAD-associated variants located in an intronic region ( Figure S1D [this file] )—are in high linkage disequilibrium (R > 90%; Figure 1J [rid=F1] ). 
Supporting this, C1q administration to tri-cultures phenocopies the loss of CLU, lowering TREM2 and APOE levels and increasing phosphorylated tau ( Figures 5A [rid=F5] – C [rid=F5] and S6H [this file] – K [this file] ).

Except for the “ ” gene enrichment term, which was equally up-regulated in Ctrl females and males ( Figures S4H [this file] and S4J [this file] ), all of the remainder terms were unique to each sex. Whereas only 17 and 29 DEGs were found in the same cell clusters of the female Ctrl group, when compared with Ctrl females ( Figures 2D [rid=F2] and S4G [this file] ). 
A closer look at the scRNA-seq cluster frequencies showed, once again, that females present higher proportions of meningeal dural macrophages than males, and that, as expected, the 4-week exposure to PLX efficiently reduced the macrophage frequencies in all the PLX groups ( Figure S4B [this file] ). Because the scRNA-seq technique is not designed for accurate profiling of tissue-resident immune cell frequencies, we employed flow cytometry to determine the effects of the employed PLX regimen on meningeal dural immune cells ( Figures S5A [this file] – S5I [this file] ). We observed a consistent and selective depletion of CD206 MHC-II macrophages in all female and male groups (~75–80% reduction compared with Ctrl groups), regardless of their genotype ( Figures S5D [this file] and S5H [this file] ). Discrete, but at times statistically significant, changes in the frequencies of the other meningeal dural immune cell populations (within total live CD45 cells) were also detected in the PLX groups, when compared with the Ctrl groups, which we interpreted as compensations for the reduced frequencies of the CD206 MHC-II macrophages ( Figures S5B [this file] and S5F [this file] ). 
Exposure to PLX led to reduced expression levels in the clusters of macrophages, fibroblasts, mast cells, and BECs, regardless of sex, in both the PLX and PLX groups ( Figure S6A [this file] ). Accordingly, we detected lower concentrations of APOE protein in the meningeal dura of mice of the PLX groups at 2 weeks, regardless of sex or genotype ( Figure S6B [this file] – S6D [this file] ). Differential gene expression analysis also pointed to a wide impact of innate immune cell depletion by PLX on the transcriptomes of different meningeal dural cell types ( Figures 2E [rid=F2] – 2J [rid=F2] and S7A [this file] – S7G [this file] ). As the cells expressing the highest levels of in the dura ( Figure S4E [this file] ), and most sensitive to CSF1R inhibition, macrophages were amongst the cell types presenting the highest number of DEGs across all the comparisons between the PLX and Ctrl groups ( Figure S7A [this file] ). The same was true for BECs and B cells of the female PLX group, which presented a total of 4,760 and 492 DEGs, respectively ( Figure S7A [this file] ). Of note, the two cell types showing the highest numbers of DEGs in the male PLX group (compared with male Ctrl) were also BECs and B cells, with a total of 1,076 and 257 DEGs, respectively ( Figure S7A [this file] ). However, in contrast to the female PLX and Ctrl group comparisons, the male PLX group also showed substantially higher number of DEGs in T & NK cells (126 DEGs), innate lymphoid cells (72 DEGs), dendritic cells (197 DEGs), and fibroblasts (89 DEGs), when compared with the male Ctrl group ( Figure S7A [this file] ). Contrarily to the NicheNet analysis where the LECs’ transcriptomes were used as “target genes” ( Figures 2G [rid=F2] and 2H [rid=F2] ), the BECs from the female Ctrl group established a limited crosstalk with macrophages ( Figure S8A [this file] ), whereas the opposite was observed in the male Ctrl group ( Figure S8B [this file] ). The BECs from the female Ctrl group seemed to establish a stronger crosstalk with LECs instead, via the genes , , and ( Figure S8A [this file] ), further substantiating the strong crosstalk between LECs and BECs observed before in this group ( Figure 2G [rid=F2] ). Increased signaling from T & NK cells to BECs also became prominent in the male PLX group ( Figure S8D [this file] ). Using data from participants in the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging (BLSA; = 196; age = 75.7 yrs. [SD = 8.3]) and the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities study (ARIC; = 272; age = 75.7 yrs. [SD = 5.2]) who had concurrent Aβ PET scans and plasma proteomic measurements on the SomaScan v4.0 (4,971 protein targets) and v4.1 (7,268 protein targets) platforms, respectively, we applied logistic regression models adjusted for demographic, physiological, and comorbid variables (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] a; sTable 1 [this file2] , 2 [this file2] ; sFigure 1 [this file] a). No proteins survived false discovery rate (FDR) correction for multiple comparisons, but seven displayed nominally significant ( < 0.05) associations across both cohorts, including four with directionally consistent relationships (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] b; sTables 3 [this file2] , 4 [this file2] ). Unlike other plasma proteins linked to Aβ PET status, which display low or undetectable expression in CNS tissue and cell types, OMG is preferentially expressed by oligodendrocytes and neurons in white matter and the cerebral cortex (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] c; sTable 5 [this file2] ; sFigure 1 [this file] b). Meta-analyzed results indicated > 40% lower odds of Aβ positivity (+) per each standard deviation increase in this protein’s plasma abundance (OR = 0.56, 95% CI: 0.39, 0.81; Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] b; sTable 6 [this file2] ). 
After confirming that external studies have validated OMG measurements on the SomaScan platform (sTable 7 [this file2] ), we leveraged publicly available data to demonstrate that OMG was lower at the RNA and protein level in AD-patient and -mouse brain tissue using bulk transcriptomics, mass spectrometry proteomics, and single-cell RNA-seq, where we found patterns of differential expression were most prominent in oligodendrocytes and neurons (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] d, e; sTables 8 [this file2] – 10 [this file2] ; sFigure 1 [this file] c) [ 16 [rid=CR16] – 23 [rid=CR23] ]. In addition, elevated plasma OMG was associated with higher CSF Aβ (indicative of lower cortical Aβ), lower CSF total tau, and lower CSF pTau-181 among Emory AD Research Center participants (Emory-ADRC; = 36, age = 66.5 yrs. [SD = 10.5]; Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] f; sTables 2 [this file2] , 11 [rid=MOESM8] ), and with lower Braak stages – but not CERAD scores – in BLSA participants who underwent autopsy ( = 40; Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] g; sTables 2 [this file2] , 12 [rid=MOESM8] ). Among participants with SomaScan and ADRD plasma biomarker data in the BLSA (Aβ , NfL, GFAP = 1,017; pTau181 = 690) and ARIC ( = 1,299), plasma OMG showed consistent associations with higher GFAP, an indicator of reactive astrogliosis (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] h; sTables 2 [this file2] , 13 [rid=MOESM9] ). In the full BLSA proteomic sample ( = 1,275), we also detected robust relationships between OMG and several other plasma proteins implicated in ADRDs, including complexins (CPLX1, CPLX2), neuronal pentraxins (NPTXR1, NPTXR2), and TREM2 (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] i; sTables 2 [this file2] , 14 [rid=MOESM9] ). OMG is a component of outer myelin sheaths whose age-related decreases in the BLSA were dependent on comorbidities (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] j; sTable 15 [this file2] ; sFigure 1 [this file] d). In addition to physical interactions with other mediators of neurodegeneration (e.g., tau, reticulons), OMG can regulate neurite growth and be released from its glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchor as a secreted protein, suggesting its higher circulating abundance in the absence of AD pathology may be an indicator of preserved axonal structural integrity (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] k; sTable 16 [this file2] ) [ 24 [rid=CR24] – 26 [rid=CR26] ]. 
Using plasma and CSF SomaScan data collected from the same participants at the same study visit in the Johns Hopkins Neurology cohort (JHN; = 194), the Knight-ADRC ( = 268), and the Stanford cohort ( = 212), we found OMG was higher in CSF compared to plasma and weakly correlated across biofluids (Spearman’s rho 0.07–0.17; sTable 2 [this file2] ; sTable 27 [this file2] ). Consistent with our previous observations of plasma OMG in the BLSA (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] j; sFigure 1 [this file] d), OMG displayed an inverse relationship with age; however, the statistical significance of this decrease tended to be more robust in plasma compared to CSF (sTable 27 [this file2] ). These results suggest that OMG is expressed in the CNS and migrates into peripheral circulation where its measurement is more sensitive to broader reductions in OMG protein levels, which could explain its superior predictive validity in plasma relative to CSF (sTable 17 [this file2] ).

Using data from participants in the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging (BLSA; = 196; age = 75.7 yrs. [SD = 8.3]) and the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities study (ARIC; = 272; age = 75.7 yrs. [SD = 5.2]) who had concurrent Aβ PET scans and plasma proteomic measurements on the SomaScan v4.0 (4,971 protein targets) and v4.1 (7,268 protein targets) platforms, respectively, we applied logistic regression models adjusted for demographic, physiological, and comorbid variables (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] a; sTable 1 [this file] , 2 [this file] ; sFigure 1 [rid=MOESM1] a). No proteins survived false discovery rate (FDR) correction for multiple comparisons, but seven displayed nominally significant ( < 0.05) associations across both cohorts, including four with directionally consistent relationships (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] b; sTables 3 [this file] , 4 [this file] ). Unlike other plasma proteins linked to Aβ PET status, which display low or undetectable expression in CNS tissue and cell types, OMG is preferentially expressed by oligodendrocytes and neurons in white matter and the cerebral cortex (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] c; sTable 5 [this file] ; sFigure 1 [rid=MOESM1] b). Meta-analyzed results indicated > 40% lower odds of Aβ positivity (+) per each standard deviation increase in this protein’s plasma abundance (OR = 0.56, 95% CI: 0.39, 0.81; Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] b; sTable 6 [this file] ). 
After confirming that external studies have validated OMG measurements on the SomaScan platform (sTable 7 [this file] ), we leveraged publicly available data to demonstrate that OMG was lower at the RNA and protein level in AD-patient and -mouse brain tissue using bulk transcriptomics, mass spectrometry proteomics, and single-cell RNA-seq, where we found patterns of differential expression were most prominent in oligodendrocytes and neurons (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] d, e; sTables 8 [this file] – 10 [this file] ; sFigure 1 [rid=MOESM1] c) [ 16 [rid=CR16] – 23 [rid=CR23] ]. In addition, elevated plasma OMG was associated with higher CSF Aβ (indicative of lower cortical Aβ), lower CSF total tau, and lower CSF pTau-181 among Emory AD Research Center participants (Emory-ADRC; = 36, age = 66.5 yrs. [SD = 10.5]; Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] f; sTables 2 [this file] , 11 [rid=MOESM8] ), and with lower Braak stages – but not CERAD scores – in BLSA participants who underwent autopsy ( = 40; Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] g; sTables 2 [this file] , 12 [rid=MOESM8] ). Among participants with SomaScan and ADRD plasma biomarker data in the BLSA (Aβ , NfL, GFAP = 1,017; pTau181 = 690) and ARIC ( = 1,299), plasma OMG showed consistent associations with higher GFAP, an indicator of reactive astrogliosis (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] h; sTables 2 [this file] , 13 [rid=MOESM9] ). In the full BLSA proteomic sample ( = 1,275), we also detected robust relationships between OMG and several other plasma proteins implicated in ADRDs, including complexins (CPLX1, CPLX2), neuronal pentraxins (NPTXR1, NPTXR2), and TREM2 (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] i; sTables 2 [this file] , 14 [rid=MOESM9] ). OMG is a component of outer myelin sheaths whose age-related decreases in the BLSA were dependent on comorbidities (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] j; sTable 15 [this file] ; sFigure 1 [rid=MOESM1] d). In addition to physical interactions with other mediators of neurodegeneration (e.g., tau, reticulons), OMG can regulate neurite growth and be released from its glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchor as a secreted protein, suggesting its higher circulating abundance in the absence of AD pathology may be an indicator of preserved axonal structural integrity (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] k; sTable 16 [this file] ) [ 24 [rid=CR24] – 26 [rid=CR26] ]. 
Given its enriched expression in the CNS and consistent associations with lower AD neuropathology, we asked if plasma OMG was related to prevalent dementia among participants with SomaScan proteomic data in the BLSA ( = 1,082, age = 66.4 yrs. [SD = 14.6]), the Stanford cohort ( = 607, age = 72.1 yrs. [SD = 8.1]), the Religious Orders Study/Rush Memory and Aging Project (ROSMAP; = 822, age = 86.0 yrs. [SD = 6.4]), the Knight AD Research Center (Knight-ADRC; = 1,952, age = 74.7 yrs. [SD = 9.9]), and the Emory-ADRC ( = 36; Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] a; sTable 2 [this file] ). Meta-analyzed results indicated that each standard deviation increase in plasma OMG abundance was associated with > 30% lower odds of dementia (OR = 0.68, 95% CI: 0.56, 0.80; Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] b; sTable 17 [this file] ). These findings were supported by cognitive domain-specific analyses among BLSA participants, where higher plasma OMG was associated with better executive functioning, attention, and processing speed (Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] c; sTable 18 [this file] ). As part of a cross-platform validation using Olink proteomic data (OMG Spearman’s rho = 0.88, < 0.001 across platforms), we also found plasma OMG was associated with lower odds of dementia in the Emory-ADRC and a Hong Kong AD cohort (HKADC; = 180; sTable 17 [this file] ) [ 7 [rid=CR7] , 8 [rid=CR8] ]. These findings on the Olink platform align with our previous Olink results from the Women’s Health Initiative (WHI; = 1,610), which reported higher plasma OMG abundance in cognitively resilient individuals at risk for AD (i.e., 80+ year-old carriers without cognitive impairment), and results from the UK Biobank (UKB; = 46,218), which reported plasma OMG’s associations with lower odds of dementia, stroke, cerebrovascular disease, neurodegenerative conditions (including MS), and higher fluid intelligence (semantic, numeric; sTable 19 [this file] ) [ 8 [rid=CR8] , 9 [rid=CR9] ]. CSF OMG abundance was not related to dementia status using SomaScan data from the AD Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI; = 655), the Stanford cohort ( = 438), or the Emory-ADRC ( = 36); however, CSF abundance of OMG in the Knight-ADRC (SomaScan; = 752) and the Alzheimer Center Amsterdam cohort (mass spectrometry; = 609) were related to higher and lower odds of dementia, respectively (sTables 2 [this file] , 17 [rid=MOESM8] ) [ 8 [rid=CR8] , 27 [rid=CR27] ]. 
To determine plasma OMG’s capacity for identifying individuals at risk for future cognitive impairment, we examined its relationship with incident dementia risk among ARIC participants who had SomaScan plasma proteomic data collected at baseline and were followed over 20 years beginning in mid-life ( = 11,595) and over 7 years beginning in late-life ( = 4,287) (sTable 2 [this file] ). Using Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for demographic, physiological, and comorbid variables, we found OMG abundance in mid-life (age = 57.1 [SD = 5.7]) was related to decreased dementia risk over the subsequent two decades (hazard ratio [HR] = 0.78, 95% CI 0.69, 0.89), while OMG levels in late-life (age = 75.2 [SD = 5.0]) were similarly related to decreased dementia risk (HR = 0.85, 95% CI 0.74, 0.97; Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] d; sTable 20 [this file] ; sFigure 2 [rid=MOESM2] a). In stratified ARIC analyses, we found OMG’s associations with lower dementia risk across mid- and late-life were more robust among 4 non-carriers, Black participants, non-obese participants, female participants, individuals with one or more cardiovascular diseases, and individuals with higher levels of education (sTable 20 [this file] ; sFigure 2 [rid=MOESM2] b). In a subset of participants with plasma measures of canonical ADRD biomarkers ( = 1,299), OMG’s association with 7-year dementia risk was not meaningfully affected by adjustment for Aβ , pTau-181, or NfL, suggesting that its link to dementia is independent of Aβ deposition, tau phosphorylation, and axonal injury, respectively; however, the incorporation of GFAP as a covariate in statistical models enhanced OMG’s associations with late-life dementia risk by more than two-fold (sTables 2 [this file] , 20 [rid=MOESM2] ). To further investigate the generalizability of OMG’s associations across races/ethnicities, we leveraged SomaScan plasma proteomic data from the National Institute for Longevity Sciences-Longitudinal Study of Aging (NILS-LSA) in Japan ( = 340; age = 66.7 [SD = 5.2]), where we did not detect OMG-dependent dementia risk over a 20 year follow up period (HR = 1.00, 95% CI 0.81, 1.24; sTables 2 [this file] , 20 [this file] ). 
OMG levels were not associated with all-cause dementia (ACD) risk in mid-life (HR = 0.96, 95% CI 0.84, 1.10), but were linked to decreased ACD risk in late-life (HR = 0.78, 95% CI 0.67, 0.91; Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] d; sTables 2 [this file] , 19 [this file] ; sFigure 2 [rid=MOESM2] c). Leveraging additional data from Whitehall II, along with covariate-adjusted linear mixed effects models, we found higher plasma OMG predicted slower rates of cognitive decline over an 18 year follow up period in mid-life, especially in the domain of executive function ( = 5,506; age = 55.4 [SD = 5.9]; Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] e; sTables 2 [this file] , 20 [this file] ). 
As part of a cross-platform validation to further investigate OMG’s association with etiology-specific dementia risk, we leveraged Olink proteomic data from the UKB ( = 47,362; age = 56.8 [SD = 8.2]), where we found that higher plasma OMG abundance was related to decreased risk of ACD, AD, and VaD over a 14-year follow up period (Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] f; sTables 2 [this file] , 20 [this file] ). OMG was associated with a similar reduction in 14-yr dementia risk regardless of etiology: 18–23% lower risk with each standard deviation increase in plasma OMG (Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] g; sTable 20 [this file] ; sFigure 2 [rid=MOESM2] d). 
Using BLSA SomaScan data ( = 1,003; age = 65.7 [SD = 14.9]) and covariate-adjusted linear regression models, we found plasma OMG abundance was related to higher regional brain volumes, especially gray matter in frontal, parietal, and occipital lobes, with voxel-based analyses showing OMG was also strongly associated with higher volume in the precuneus (i.e., where Aβ accumulation preferentially starts) and certain subcortical structures (e.g., thalamus, caudate; Fig. 4 [rid=Fig4] b, c; sTables 2 [this file] , 21 [this file] ; sFigure 4 [rid=MOESM4] , 4) [ 29 [rid=CR29] ]. Plasma OMG levels were also associated with lower white matter hyperintensity volume, and diffusion tensor imaging revealed this plasma protein’s relationship with preserved white matter microstructure (i.e., higher fractional anisotropy, lower mean diffusivity), especially in the anterior corona radiata, fornix, and tapetum (Fig. 4 [rid=Fig4] d; sTable 21 [this file] ). 
We observed similar OMG-related patterns using ARIC SomaScan data ( = 1,339; age = 76.1 [SD = 5.2]), namely higher regional brain volumes, greater cortical thickness, and preserved white matter microstructure (Fig. 4 [rid=Fig4] e; sTables 2 [this file] , 22 [this file] ). Previous ARIC results reported plasma OMG’s associations with lower white matter hyperintensity volume, microhemorrhages, and infarcts, as well as lower white matter hyperintensity volume when OMG is measured 18 years prior to MRI scan; similarly, plasma OMG in the Cardiovascular Health Study (SomaScan; = 765) has been linked to lower white matter lesions at baseline and slower increases in white matter lesions over 5 years (sTables 22 [this file] ) [ 10 [rid=CR10] ]. Using computed results from the Generation Scotland (GenS) cohort ( = 1,065; age = 59.9 [SD = 9.6]), where participants had SomaScan and 3T MRI data collected concurrently, we found plasma OMG was associated with higher total brain volume, gray matter volume, and fractional anisotropy, as well as lower machine learning-estimated brain age and white matter hyperintensity volume (Fig. 4 [rid=Fig4] f; sTables 23 [this file] ) [ 11 [rid=CR11] ]. 
Plasma OMG levels in the BLSA (SomaScan) and UKB (Olink) were associated with lower parieto-temporal atrophy, while OMG in UKB was additionally related to lower perisylvian atrophy (Fig. 4 [rid=Fig4] g; sTables 2 [this file] , 24 [this file] ). To compare the strength of OMG’s associations with structural neuroimaging when measured across different biofluids, we used data from a subset of Stanford participants who had 3T MRI and plasma ( = 402) or CSF ( = 173) SomaScan data collected at the same study visit; we found statistically insignificant but stronger relationships with brain structure when OMG was measured in CSF compared to plasma (sTable 25 [this file] ). 
Given evidence for the role of myelin-specific proteins in autoantibody-mediated neuroinflammatory conditions, along with its reported associations with lower odds and risk of MS in the UKB (Olink), we examined whether plasma OMG was associated with prevalent MS, structural neuroimaging, and neurological task performance among participants with SomaScan proteomic data from the Johns Hopkins Multiple Sclerosis Center (JHMSC; = 397; age = 51.6 [SD = 10.8]; sTable 2 [this file] ) [ 8 [rid=CR8] , 31 [rid=CR31] – 33 [rid=CR33] ]. In covariate-adjusted logistic regression models, plasma OMG was associated with lower odds of MS (MS: OR = 0.42, 95% CI 0.25, 0.71, = 0.001), a finding that was slightly more evident with progressive MS (OR = 0.37, 95% CI 0.20, 0.71, = 0.003) than with relapse-remitting MS (OR = 0.44, 95% CI 0.25, 0.78, = 0.005; sTable 26 [this file] ; sFigure 5 [rid=MOESM5] a). 
Using plasma and CSF SomaScan data collected from the same participants at the same study visit in the Johns Hopkins Neurology cohort (JHN; = 194), the Knight-ADRC ( = 268), and the Stanford cohort ( = 212), we found OMG was higher in CSF compared to plasma and weakly correlated across biofluids (Spearman’s rho 0.07–0.17; sTable 2 [this file] ; sTable 27 [this file] ). Consistent with our previous observations of plasma OMG in the BLSA (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] j; sFigure 1 [rid=MOESM1] d), OMG displayed an inverse relationship with age; however, the statistical significance of this decrease tended to be more robust in plasma compared to CSF (sTable 27 [this file] ). These results suggest that OMG is expressed in the CNS and migrates into peripheral circulation where its measurement is more sensitive to broader reductions in OMG protein levels, which could explain its superior predictive validity in plasma relative to CSF (sTable 17 [this file] ). 
To obtain a more reliable CSF proteomic signature of OMG, we incorporated data from the Stanford cohort, where SomaScan v4.0 data were available. 1,161 of these proteins were measured on the SomaScan v4 platform (4,830 protein targets) in CSF of Stanford cohort participants ( = 388), and 770 showed consistent directional associations with CSF OMG (625 and 145 positive and negative associations, respectively; FDR < 0.05; Fig. 5 [rid=Fig5] b; sTable 28 [this file] ; sFigure 6 [rid=MOESM6] a). 
In the CSF proteomic signature of CSF OMG (770 proteins), we confirmed enrichment of brain-, neuronal-, and oligodendroglial-specific proteins relative to other organs and CNS cell types, respectively (Fig. 5 [rid=Fig5] c; sTable 29 [this file] ). With publicly available databases and Ingenuity Pathway Analyses (IPA), we detected consistent upregulation of several biological processes including: axonal (e.g., axon guidance) and synaptic (e.g., synaptogenesis) integrity, cell adhesion (e.g., L1CAM signaling), and protein quality control (PQC; e.g., autophagy; sTable 30 [this file] ; sFigure 7 [rid=MOESM7] a, b). Results from IPAs causal network analyses revealed OMG’s CSF proteomic signature and its enriched biological processes were most dependent on upstream regulation by SORL1 (Sortilin Related Receptor 1), a CNS lipoprotein receptor whose loss of function AD-risk variants can impair endosomal trafficking of Aβ, and DSCAM (Down syndrome cell adhesion molecule), a trisomy 21-related neuronal cell adhesion molecule whose interactions with gamma secretase can modulate synapse formation (Fig. 5 [rid=Fig5] d; sTable 31 [this file] ) [ 34 [rid=CR34] , 35 [rid=CR35] ]. 
The CSF proteomic signature of plasma OMG was also examined using similar age and sex adjusted linear regression models, along with plasma and CSF SomaScan data collected at the same study visit from JHN ( = 194), the Knight-ADRC ( = 268), and the Stanford cohort ( = 212; sTable 2 [this file] ). 128 CSF proteins showed consistent directional associations with plasma OMG abundance across these three cohorts (all positive associations; FDR < 0.05; Fig. 5 [rid=Fig5] e; sTable 32 [this file] ). This pattern, as well as the differential frequency of CSF proteins associated with CSF OMG abundance (770 proteins) relative to plasma OMG abundance (128 proteins), may be attributed to OMG’s weak correlations across biofluids (sTable 27 [this file] ). Despite limited overlap, we observed similar enrichment of tissues (i.e., brain), cells (i.e., neurons, oligodenodrocytes), pathways (i.e., axon guidance, synaptogenesis) and upstream regulators (i.e., SORL1, DSCAM) in the CSF proteomic signature of plasma OMG (sTables 33 [this file] – 35 [this file] ). 
As part of a cross-biospecimen and cross-platform validation of OMG-related neurobiological processes, we applied age and sex adjusted linear regression models to determine whether CSF proteins linked to CSF OMG levels (SomaScan) were also associated with brain tissue OMG levels in BLSA participants who underwent autopsy (mass spectrometry; = 40; sTable 2 [this file] ). Of the 770 CSF proteins associated with CSF OMG abundance in preceding analyses, 388 were quantified in brain tissue, but only 25 (6%) showed consistent directional associations with OMG (23 positive and 2 negative associations; FDR < 0.05; sTable 36 [this file] ; sFigure 8 [rid=MOESM8] a), suggesting that the proteomic correlates of OMG are sensitive to assay type, sample preparation (i.e., soluble/insoluble), and/or vary across the parenchymal and CSF milieu. Despite limited overlap and orthogonal proteomic techniques, in OMG’s conserved brain tissue proteomic signature (25 proteins), we observed similar patterns of tissue-, cell-, and pathway-enrichment (e.g., axon guidance), along with additional enrichment of several immune processes (e.g., granulocyte adhesion; sTables 37 [this file] – 39 [this file] ; sFigure 8 [rid=MOESM8] b). OMG’s conserved brain tissue proteomic signature was most strongly and positively associated with mediators of structural stabilization (e.g., JAM3) and metalloproteases (e.g., ADAM23), several of which were also oligodendrocyte-specific, targets of existing drugs, and/or nominated AD therapeutic targets (Fig. 5 [rid=Fig5] f; sTable 40 [this file] ; sFigure 8 [rid=MOESM8] c). 
CSF pQTLs showed directionally consistent associations with dorsolateral prefrontal cortex OMG levels in a ROSMAP/Banner cohort (mass spectrometry; = 716), as well as plasma OMG levels in the deCODE cohort (SomaScan; = 35,559), the Fenland cohort (SomaScan; = 10,708), ARIC (SomaScan; = 7,597), and the UKB (Olink; = 54,219; sTable 41 [this file] ; sFigure 9 [rid=MOESM9] ) [ 37 [rid=CR37] – 41 [rid=CR41] ]. These SNPs have been associated with cognitive function and neurodegenerative conditions across multiple GWAS (sTable 42 [this file] ). Consistent with OMG’s neuroprotective associations in preceding analyses, several cis OMG variants (rs4263003, rs7212264, rs4795587) linked to lower protein levels in CSF, brain tissue, and plasma were also associated with a higher odds of dementia among BLSA participants with available genotyping data ( < 0.05; = 873; sTable 2 [this file] , 43; sFigure 9 [rid=MOESM9] ). 
Both of these variants have been linked to lower cortical OMG RNA levels in the Genotype-Tissue Expression project (GTEx; = 268) and higher odds of demyelinating diseases in the UKB ( = 395,464; sTable 42 [this file] ; sFigure 10 [rid=MOESM10] ) [ 37 [rid=CR37] ]. We found evidence supporting a causal relationship of higher cis-regulated CSF OMG abundance with lower odds of AD (2022 AD GWAS: OR = 0.84, 95% CI: 0.72, 0.98; 2019 AD GWAS: OR = 0.72, 95% CI: 0.54, 0.94), PD (OR = 0.68, 95% CI: 0.47, 0.97), ALS (OR = 0.72, 95% CI: 0.57, 0.90), and DLB (OR = 0.37, 95% CI: 0.18, 0.78), but not ACD (OR = 1.16, 95% CI: 0.75, 1.78), VaD (OR = 0.33, 95% CI: 0.07, 1.50), or MS (OR = 1.01, 95% CI: 0.74, 1.39; Fig. 5 [rid=Fig5] g; sTable 44 [this file] ). After pruning, the single retained cis pQTL (rs72815624) was in in LD ( = 1.0) with the pQTL used for CSF MR; this brain tissue pQTL showed similar associations with lower cortical OMG RNA levels and higher odds of demyelinating diseases (sTable 42 [this file] ; sFigure 10 [rid=MOESM10] ). We found consistent evidence supporting a causal relationship of higher cis-regulated brain OMG abundance with lower odds of AD (2022 AD GWAS: OR = 0.95, 95% CI: 0.90, 0.99; 2019 AD GWAS: OR = 0.89, 95% CI: 0.82, 0.98), PD (OR = 0.88, 95% CI: 0.79, 0.98), ALS (OR = 0.90, 95% CI: 0.84, 0.96), and DLB (OR = 0.74, 95% CI: 0.58, 0.93), but not ACD (OR = 1.05, 95% CI: 0.91, 1.21), VaD (OR = 0.72, 95% CI: 0.44, 1.18), or MS (OR = 1.00, 95% CI: 0.91, 1.11; Fig. 5 [rid=Fig5] g; sTable 44 [this file] ). 
These variants have been associated with lower cortical OMG RNA levels and neurocognitive phenotypes in multiple GWAS (sTable 42 [this file] ; sFigure 10 [rid=MOESM10] ). In meta-analyzed results, we found evidence supporting a causal relationship of higher cis-regulated plasma OMG abundance with lower odds of AD (2022 AD GWAS: OR = 0.82, 95% CI: 0.75, 0.89; 2019 AD GWAS: OR = 0.67, 95% CI: 0.59, 0.78), PD (OR = 0.64, 95% CI: 0.53, 0.77), ALS (OR = 0.68, 95% CI: 0.61, 0.77), DLB (OR = 0.33, 95% CI: 0.23, 0.48), and VaD (OR = 0.29, 95% CI: 0.13, 0.65), but not ACD (OR = 1.19, 95% CI: 0.95, 1.49) or MS (OR = 1.02, 95% CI: 0.86, 1.20; Fig. 5 [rid=Fig5] g; sTable 44 [this file] ).

Sex-stratified GWAS in a small African ancestry dataset (AFR; N=7,270; Tables-S7 [this file] – 8 [this file] , Fig.S6 [rid=SD2] ) showed 13/20 loci had consistent sex-heterogeneity or were unique to EUR subjects ( Table-1 [rid=T1] , Table-S9 [this file] ). 
We identified 37 proteins (28 female-brain, 5 female-CSF, 3 male-brain, 1 male-CSF) significant in one sex (P <0.05) but not the other (P>0.05) across 30 unique loci ( Fig. 2B [rid=F2] ; Tables-S10 [this file] – 17 [this file] , Figs.S9 [rid=SD2] – 10 [rid=SD2] ). While heritable proteins across brain and CSF showed limited overlap (9%; Fig.S12 [rid=SD2] ), 5/6 overlapping sex-biased proteins had consistent effect directions with 3 replicating nominally ( Table-S18 [this file] ). Out of 37 proteins, 20 also displayed consistent sex-heterogeneity in AFR PWAS ( Table-2 [rid=T2] , Table-S19 [this file] ). Importantly, when repeating PWAS after excluding Stage-2 from the sex-stratified GWAS to avoid potential biases due to proxy-AD samples , 34/37 genes showed consistent associations ( Table-S20 [this file] ). 
Out of 37 proteins, 33 were supported by at least one method, including 30 by SMR (P <0.05 and P >0.05), 23 by COLOC, and 20 by both ( Fig.2D [rid=F2] , COLOC Fig.S13 [rid=SD2] , SMR Table-S21 [this file] , locus plots Fig.S14 [rid=SD2] ). Annotations of the proteins’ lead pQTLs–and those in close linkage disequilibrium (LD)–further supported the genetic signals were likely to impact protein levels, marking many regulatory region or 5’/3’ untranslated region variants, while 4 proteins also had missense variants including 3 strongly predicted to be deleterious (GBA1, RTFN1, ARSA; Table-S22 [this file] ; Fig.S15 [rid=SD2] ). 
We therefore performed COLOC analyses for all identified sex-biased AD loci with extensive multi-tissue, multi-QTL (i.e. xQTL) datasets to comprehensively prioritize likely causal genes and epigenetic features (with strong colocalization support PP4>0.7; Tables-S23 [this file] – 25 [this file] ). 
Additionally, 27/49 (55%) prioritized proteins showed evidence of sex-biased differential abundance, reinforcing their relevance to AD sex-dimorphism ( Table-S26 [this file] ). 
In total, we prioritized 125 female-biased and 21 male-biased likely causal genes, with 62 assigned priority score-1 ( Table.S27 [this file] ). 
We next sought to gain a better biological understanding of the newly expanded, sex-biased genetic landscape for AD ( Table.S27 [this file] ). The mean sequencing coverage of the samples was 35.85 (range, 18.34–70.75, see Figure S9 [this file] ). 
The convenience control genomes obtained from the TOPMed consortium were called separately and merged with the study data for quality control checks ( Figure S1 [this file] ). 
A workflow diagram of the quality control steps is shown in Figure S1 [this file] . For sample-level quality control of the discovery dataset, we removed genomes based on the following criteria: (1) failed library preparations or sequencing, (2) abnormal heterozygosity (F-statistic outside of the −0.15 to 0.15 range), (3) low call rate (≤ 95%), (4) sex check failure (i.e., a discrepancy between reported sex and genotypic sex), (5) non-European ancestry (based on principal component analysis when compared to Hapmap3 data; Figure S3 [this file] ), (6) duplicate samples (pi-hat statistic > 0.8), (7) related samples (pi-hat statistic > 0.125), and (8) cases in whom the final diagnosis was changed. The final dataset included 91,594,360 variants in 888 cases and 7,128 controls, which were used for downstream common variant analyses ( Figure S1 [this file] ). 
For conditional analyses on GWAS loci identified in the additive and recessive models, we additionally included the respective index variants in the covariates ( Figure S4 [this file] ). To demonstrate the robustness of GWAS signals, we performed leave-one-out analyses by withholding samples based on their institutional source; there were twenty-four cohorts from the twenty different institutions at which samples were collected, meaning that twenty-four separate GWAS analyses were performed ( Figure S7 [this file] ).

To characterize microglia states, we analyzed the transcriptome of 152,459 single microglia nuclei from aged post-mortem brain samples of 217 AD (138 early and 79 late) and 226 control individuals ( Table S1 [this file1] , ) across 6 brain regions, consisting of prefrontal cortex, hippocampus, mid-temporal cortex, angular gyrus, entorhinal cortex, and thalamus, from ROSMAP study . We first collected 174,420 immune cells by sorting from brain snRNA-seq datasets using known marker genes ( STAR Methods [rid=S12] ) , which formed into 16 clusters, including 12 clusters of microglia (clusters 0–8 and 10–12, marked by , and ), one cluster of brain-associated macrophages (BAMs, cluster 9, marked by , and ), one cluster of T cells (cluster 13, marked by and ), and two clusters of potential doublets with other brain cell types (clusters 14 and 15) ( Figure S1A [this file] – B [this file] ). 
We defined these 12 clusters as distinct microglial states based on their molecular signatures and functions ( Figure 1A [rid=F1] – B [rid=F1] and Figure S1C [this file] – G [this file] , Table S1 [this file1] , ). We annotated homeostatic microglia (MG0) with high expression of well-known homeostatic markers and , and neuronal surveillance microglia (MG1) with high expression of neurotransmitter receptors ( Figure S1F [this file] ) . We found that MG3 showed strongest enrichment to ribosome biogenesis ( Figure S1G [this file] ). Of note, MG5 enrichment to phagocytic genes was relatively lower compared to the BAMs ( Figure S1C [this file] ). We next compared these 12 microglial states with a previously published dataset (Olah et al.) and found that MG3 (ribosome biogenesis), MG6 (stress-related), MG10 (inflammatory III), MG11 (antiviral) and MG12 (cycling) states show strongly and significantly alignment across studies, while MG0 (homeostatic) state shows weak but significant alignment ( Figure S1H [this file] – I [this file] , STAR Methods [rid=S12] ). In addition, comparison with mouse microglial transcriptional states yielded several well-aligned and conserved states across species ( Figure S1J [this file] ). 
We performed enrichment analysis to capture the expression of disease-associated microglia (DAM) genes across our dataset ( Figure S1D [this file] – E [this file] ). 
Count matrices, metadata and supplementary data [this file] in this study from the ROSMAP cohort are at http://compbio.mit.edu/microglia_states/ (http://compbio.mit.edu/microglia_states/) . 
The Jaccard score and significance were visualized by heatmap shown in Figure S1 [this file] . 
See also Figure S1 [this file] – 3 [rid=SD3] and Table S1 [this file1] , pages 1–4.

We found that lipid-processing MG4 and inflammatory MG8 showed significantly-increased fractions in AD, while neuronal surveillance MG1 showed a significantly-decreased fraction in AD ( Figure 1C [rid=F1] , Figure S2D [this file] , STAR Methods [rid=S12] ). We also performed correlation analysis between the microglial state proportions and multiple pathological variables in PFC to explore the association of those states with specific AD-relevant pathology and confounding factors ( Figure S2E [this file] , STAR Methods [rid=S12] ). We also observed that none of the microglial states were dominated by individuals and other covariates including batch, age, sex, or post-mortem interval (PMI) ( Figure S2F [this file] – K [this file] ). However, we found that the proportions of several microglial states were significantly different with age (MG5, MG4), PMI (MG1 and MG4), and sex (MG3) ( Figure S2K [this file] ), suggesting the importance of controlling these covariates when we evaluate the proportional changes between phenotypic groups.

Using the pan-macrophage marker IBA1 as a counterstain to label brain-resident macrophages, we performed immunohistochemistry for P2RY12 across 8 AD subjects which revealed high levels of P2RY12 immunoreactivity ( Figure 1D [rid=F1] and Figure S5 [this file] ). 
We obtained 41,832 nuclei of microglia with good quality and captured three epigenomic states including one homeostatic state (HOM) and two activated states (ACT1 and ACT2, Figure 3A [rid=F3] , Figure S5A [this file] – C [this file] , STAR Methods [rid=S12] ). We found that , the homeostatic marker, showed relatively low accessible signals in activated states although ubiquitous accessibility in all microglia( Figure S5B [this file] – C [this file] ). 
We also found that the nine transcriptomic clusters can recapitulate the microglial states we identified in the larger cohort ( Figure S5E [this file] ). 
We next called 179,534 accessible peaks and identified 16,800 epigenomic-state-specific peaks ( Figure S5F [this file] – G [this file] , STAR Methods [rid=S12] ). We annotated these peaks by the number of associated genes and their distance to TSS, and predicted their functions ( Figure S5H [this file] – I [this file] , STAR Methods [rid=S12] ). 
To investigate the regulatory machinery of these microglial states, we predicted transcription factors (TFs) through motif enrichment in the peaks of these epigenetically-defined states ( Figure S5J [this file] ). We also observed that the peaks from the two activated states were associated with very similar functions and shared many TFs even though the peaks themselves were distinct ( Figure S5G [this file] – J [this file] ). 
We also conducted single-cell TF activity analysis via DoRothEA , revealing significant motif/gene-enrichment ( Figure S5K [this file] ). 
We found that 13 TFs (including several ETS TF family members, SPI1 and CTCF) significantly shared their targets within the co-regulatory module ( Figure S5L [this file] ). 
For inflammatory state marker expression in multiplexed immunostaining experiments, values for each marker were visualized by creating expression gradients for each channel and superimposed onto IBA-positive surfaces using Imaris visualization tools, as presented in Supplemental Figure S5B [this file] . 
See also Figure S5 [this file] and Table S1 [rid=SD11] , pages 7–8.

From this experiment we were able to capture the transcriptome of 18,914 iMGL nuclei that formed 10 clusters, and that was largely segregated by treatment condition (i.e. baseline versus LPS enriched) ( Figure 4A [rid=F4] and Figure S6A [this file] ). Computing correlation scores across iMGL and MG states revealed a high degree of similarity between MG12 (a cycling state) and C9, a cell-cycle enriched cluster representing proliferating microglia ( Figure 4B [rid=F4] and Figure S6A [this file] ). As such, we conducted calcium imaging in monocultures of iMGLs at baseline and upon exposure of ATP, with or without LPS pre-treatment ( Supplemental Video 1 [rid=SD12] and Figure S6B [this file] ). 
After 8 days of lentiviral transduction, we observed that 58% of cells were successfully infected based on the expression of a mCherry reporter cassette ( Figure S6C [this file] ). Controls were infected with lentivirus carrying an empty cassette ( Figure S6D [this file] ). Through these orthogonal approaches, we found that overexpression of and (2 of the hits from our calcium imaging) reduced the adoption of ameboid-shaped in iMGLs compared to controls ( Figure 4G [rid=F4] and Figure S6D [this file] ). Co-staining for TMEM119 and P2RY12 confirmed overlapping microglial populations, as TMEM119 is a well-established homeostatic marker ( Figure S6D [this file] ). Through this analysis, we also determined that expression of SMAD3, IRF8 and ELF1 were not significantly correlated to microglial homeostasis in vivo although these were also hits from our calcium imaging screen ( Figure 4I [rid=F4] and Figure S6F [this file] – H [this file] ). 
We found that blocking MG10 TF regulators in the presence of LPS induced new clusters (C0 and C3) and was sufficient to prevent IL1B induction (MG10 state marker) without concomitant gain of homeostatic markers ( Figure S6I [this file] ). By modeling microglial state dynamics with iMGLs, we functionally assess the TF network activity prediction governing microglial state transitionings derived from our postmortem data analysis and provide a roadmap for TF-driven inflammatory state progressions ( Figure 4L [rid=F4] ) ( Figure S6J [this file] , STAR Methods [rid=S12] ). 
The result was visualized by the heatmap ( Figure S6J [this file] ), showing the score by color and significance by star.

To characterize microglia states, we analyzed the transcriptome of 152,459 single microglia nuclei from aged post-mortem brain samples of 217 AD (138 early and 79 late) and 226 control individuals ( Table S1 [this file] , ) across 6 brain regions, consisting of prefrontal cortex, hippocampus, mid-temporal cortex, angular gyrus, entorhinal cortex, and thalamus, from ROSMAP study . 
We defined these 12 clusters as distinct microglial states based on their molecular signatures and functions ( Figure 1A [rid=F1] – B [rid=F1] and Figure S1C [rid=SD1] – G [rid=SD1] , Table S1 [this file] , ). 
We then assessed the expression of inflammatory MG2, MG8 and MG10 markers over the course of 96 to 120 hours ( Figure 2H [rid=F2] and Table S1 [this file] , ). We found a rich transcriptional response that was enriched for inflammatory pathways and clustered by early (upon 4 hours) and late response (upon 24 hours) ( Table S1 [this file] , ). 
To investigate the upstream regulators that drive distinct microglial states, we leveraged the chromatin accessibility data measured by snATAC-seq using human postmortem brain tissues from a subset of individuals in the same cohort (100 individuals, Table S1 [this file] , ). 
We found 122,658 peak-to-promoter links, implicating 17,109 genes and 46,498 peaks ( Table S1 [this file] , ). 
We selected 25 TFs ( Figure 3E [rid=F3] ) to perform an overexpression screen in iMGLs and assay for increased sensibility to extracellular ATP (i.e. greater homeostatic states) ( Table S1 [this file] , ). 
We next classified 1,542 adDEGs into three major categories and 51 groups based on their effect size and state-specificity ( Figure 5A [rid=F5] , Figure S8 [rid=SD8] , STAR Methods [rid=S12] , Table S1 [this file] , ). 
We next performed Gene Ontology enrichment analysis per group and built a gene-gene network by function sharing ( Figure 5C [rid=F5] , Figure S9A [rid=SD9] , STAR Methods [rid=S12] , Table S1 [this file] , ). 
We identified 1,036 TWAS genes in microglia ( Table S1 [this file] , ) and found that 178 of them were also differentially expressed in AD progression ( Figure 6C [rid=F6] , Fisher’s exact test, p-value = 1.3e-12), suggesting that the differential expression of these genes may be directly regulated by genetic factors. 
We performed snRNA-seq in the prefrontal cortex for 423 individuals, and four other regions for a subset of 48 individuals, including mid-temporal cortex, angular gyrus, entorhinal cortex, thalamus, and hippocampus for a subset of 65 individuals and an additional 21 individuals ( Table S1 [this file] , . We sequenced DNA from the prefrontal cortex (PFC) samples of 190 AD patients and 121 matched controls from the Religious Orders Study/Memory and Aging Project (ROSMAP) cohort at an average sequencing depth of >1000X after UMI collapsing ( Figure 1A [rid=F1] , Table S2 [rid=SD2] , Figure S1A [this file] – B [this file] ). By generating a consensus sequence from multiple reads derived from the same original DNA molecule, UMI-based panel sequencing exponentially reduces base-calling errors and detects somatic variants with VAFs as low as 0.1% ( Figure S1C [this file] – D [this file] ), with much higher sensitivity and precision than previous methods not employing consensus error correction . Thirty-five of 39 (90%) tested sSNVs and 8 of 10 (80%) sIndels successfully validated in newly extracted DNA samples from the corresponding PFC samples, confirming the high accuracy of our somatic variant calling strategy even for those with VAFs as low as 0.1% ( Figure S1E [this file] – G [this file] ). The mutational spectrum of sSNVs is consistent with the cell division/mitotic clock signature SBS1 ( Figure S2A [this file] ; cosine similarity 0.92), suggesting that these variants predominantly occurred during cell division. 
With similar sequencing depth, coverage, and genic distribution between AD and control PFC samples ( Figures S1A [this file] – B [this file] and S2B [this file] ), we observed that AD brains harbored significantly more sSNVs among the 149 targeted genes than aged-matched controls ( Figure 2A [rid=F2] ; = 0.001, two-tailed proportion test; odds ratio (OR) = 1.3). 
In addition to an increased sSNV burden in AD, we also found age was an independent factor positively correlated with sSNV burden ( Figure 2C [rid=F2] ; = 0.002, linear regression) and the proportion of sSNV carriers ( Figure S2C [this file] ), suggesting a likely age-associated accumulation of somatic variants in cancer driver genes in both normal and diseased brains. 
Most AD somatic variants in were nonsense variants broadly distributed across the encoded protein, including two recurrent alleles observed in AD patients, similar to what is seen in variants in CH events of blood ( Figure S2D [this file] ). AD patients also showed missense variants in that clustered in its critical oxygenase domains ( Figure 2F [rid=F2] ), a similar mutational pattern to that seen in CH ( Figure S2D [this file] ) that was not observed in our aged controls. In addition to individual genes, AD patients showed significantly more somatic variants in PI3K-PKB/Akt pathway genes than controls ( Figure S2E [this file] ; < 0.05, one-tailed proportion test), a pathway that has been previously suggested to be enriched with somatic variants in AD brains . 
Somatic variants in AD brains also showed significantly higher VAFs than did variants in control brains, with the effect being more pronounced in TSG, CH-related genes, or AD-enriched genes ( Figure 2G [rid=F2] and S2F [this file] ). 
We further confirmed the enrichment of somatic variants in AD when considering only CHIP variants previously identified from blood whole-genome sequencing datasets ( Figure S3A [this file] – C [this file] ). Additional analyses suggested that this enrichment could not be explained by differences in age ( Figure S3D [this file] – H [this file] ) or sequencing depth ( Figure S3I [this file] – J [this file] ) between AD and control groups. Furthermore, logistic regression analysis confirmed a significant positive association between somatic variants—especially CHIP variants—and AD risk, after controlling for potential confounders such as sex, age, sequencing coverage, post-mortem interval, and e4 (APOE4) genotype ( Figure S3K [this file] ), suggesting that somatic variants could be an independent genetic factor in addition to the well-known APOE4 allele. 
To test this, we developed a fluorescence-activated nuclei sorting (FANS) method to selectively enrich microglial nuclei from frozen postmortem brain tissues using an antibody targeting CSF1R ( Figure S4A [this file] ), a well-known cell surface marker for microglia whose nuclear localization and function have been recently reported . Our subsequent single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNAseq) confirmed that >75% of sorted nuclei in both AD and control brains showed high expression of microglial marker genes including , , and ( Figures 3A [rid=F3] and S4B [this file] ). Interestingly, another 4-9% of the nuclei were classified as CNS-associated macrophages (CAMs; Figures 3A [rid=F3] and S4B [this file] ), a recently identified class of brain-resident macrophages with high expression of and , while the remaining cells represented various other brain cell types. 
All 10 AD somatic variants and 7 of 8 control variants in TSGs were enriched (2- to 438-fold) in the CSF1R+ cells compared to neurons from the same PFC samples ( Figures 3B [rid=F3] and S4C [this file] – D [this file] ). Interestingly, this same AD sample harbored a variant in a TSG gene ( (c.1429+1G>A)) that was almost exclusively present in CSF1R+ cells, suggesting that these two variants originated in different lineages ( Figure S4C [this file] ). 
Regional analysis of these somatic CHIP variants showed that all 7 profiled AD variants were globally present in CSF1R+ cells sorted from four distinct cerebral cortex regions and the cerebellum, but absent in neuronal populations across all brain regions ( Figures 3E [rid=F3] and S4E [this file] ). Analysis of matched blood DNA showed that all 10 AD variants enriched in CSF1R+ cells were also detected in blood, with a trend toward a positive correlation between VAFs in brain CSF1R+ nuclei and blood ( Figures 3F [rid=F3] and S4F [this file] ; = 0.052, Pearson correlation). We confirmed minimal blood contamination in both bulk brain tissue and sorted CSF1R+ nuclei ( Figures 3A [rid=F3] and S4B [this file] ). 
Quality control and cell type annotation ( Figure S5A [this file] – C [this file] ) yielded 14,928 high-quality MLBMs and 8,252 high-quality neurons, of which driver variants were successfully genotyped in 8,387 and 5,861 cells, respectively ( Figure 4B [rid=F4] - D [rid=F4] ). 
In contrast, mutant MLBMs from control brains were enriched in clusters C4 and C7 ( Figure 4F [rid=F4] ); while C7 did not show enrichment for a particular microglial state, C4 displayed strong activity of a proliferation-related microglial state gene module ( Figure S5D [this file] ). 
Consistent with other approaches, we confirmed that MLBMs carried the mutant allele ( Figure S5E [this file] – F [this file] ). 
We extracted microglia(-like)-CAMs that were either annotated as microglia-perivascular macrophages (a subtype of CAMs) in SEA-AD or identified as microglia-CAMs through automatic cell-typing with scType ( Figure S6A [this file] – B [this file] and Table S5 [rid=SD5] ). From all SEA-AD individuals with a consensus clinical diagnosis of AD (n = 31) or age-matched controls (n = 31) ( Table S6 [rid=SD6] ), we called mCAs using CONICSmat in microglia-CAMs as well as excitatory neurons (ExNs), astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs), and retained only mCAs that were not called in any other cell types from the same donor and that passed several stringent filtering criteria ( Figure S6C [this file] ; STAR Methods [rid=S12] ). Using whole-genome sequencing of sorted microglia-CAMs and neurons, we validated the presence and specificity of 3 of the 4 mCAs in microglia-CAMs for which we could access primary brain tissue ( Figure S6D [this file] ). 
Although the SEA-AD sample size is too small to demonstrate statistically significant enrichment of mCA in AD, the data enabled direct analysis of the transcriptional effects of mCA in microglia-CAMs. We created an integrated snRNAseq atlas of microglia-CAMs identified across AD cases and controls ( Figure S7 [this file] ) and identified differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between mutant and wild-type microglia-CAMs from mCA-carrying AD brains ( Figure 5D [rid=F5] and Table S7 [rid=SD7] ). 
We differentiated the three mutant and wild-type isogenic iPSC lines to induced microglia-like cells (iMGLs) using a modified protocol of McQuade and performed scRNAseq ( Figures 6B [rid=F6] and S8A [this file] – C [this file] ). We created an integrated scRNAseq atlas of these four genotypes and identified microglial states based on their transcriptional signatures ( Figures 6C [rid=F6] and S8D [this file] – E [this file] ). Using gene set enrichment analysis with the 50 Molecular Signature Databases Hallmark gene sets, we observed upregulation of pro-inflammatory and proliferation-associated pathways in mutant iMGLs ( Figures 6E [rid=F6] - F [rid=F6] and S8F [this file] and Table S8 [rid=SD8] ). 
Indeed, we confirmed that many variants with low VAF in the brain were undetectable in WES of matched blood samples ( Figure S9A [this file] ), and in our data, the enrichment of somatic variants in AD was largely driven by such lower-VAF variants ( Figure S9B [this file] – C [this file] ). 
In our study, the logistic regression model suggested that the burden of somatic driver variants is positively associated with AD, independent of the well-known germline genetic factor, the APOE4 allele ( Figure S3K [this file] ). 
Although transcriptomic differences between monocyte-derived macrophages and brain-resident microglia have been reported in mouse models , our snRNAseq data show that cells carrying CHIP variants express all classical microglial markers ( Figure S4B [this file] ) and are transcriptionally indistinguishable from brain-resident microglia. 
As a result, we achieved comparable depth and coverage between the AD and control samples, with more than 1000X average depth and more than 80% coverage of the targeted regions at >500X for consensus reads ( Table S2 [rid=SD2] and Figure S1A [this file] ). 
To note, the purity of our microglia-enriched brain macrophage sorting was slightly reduced in some AD samples, exhibiting a marginally higher proportion of non-microglia/CAM nuclei as determined by snRNAseq ( Fig. S3A [this file] ). Our subsequent single-cell multi-omic analyses showed that somatic driver mutations are generally absent in non-microglia/CAM brain cell types ( Fig. S5E [this file] – F [rid=SD1] ), indicating that they are unlikely to account for the observed VAF increase in CSF1R+ nuclei in AD brains. 
Cell clusters were manually annotated into different cell types based on the expression profile of marker genes ( Figure S4B [this file] ) for the major brain and blood cell types ( : red blood cell; : T-cell; : B-cell; : monocyte). We also observed minimal blood contamination in the sorted CSF1R+ population, with only 1% monocytes and the absence of other major blood cell types including red blood cells, T-cells, and B-cells ( Figures 3A [rid=F3] and S4B [this file] ). 
A candidate was considered validated as somatic variant ( Figure S1E [this file] – G [this file] ) if 1) the read fraction of the mutant allele was more than three times as high as the fractions of the other two error alleles in all three amplicons (somatic-I); or 2) the read fraction of the mutant allele in the corresponding brain sample was significantly higher than the fraction in an unrelated negative control brain sample for all three amplicons (somatic-II). 
The resulting subset of AD patients closely mirrored the age distribution of the control group ( Figure S3E [this file] ). We replicated our burden analyses using this matched subcohort and observed results that were highly consistent with those obtained from the full cohort ( Figure S3F [this file] – H [this file] ). 
We observed a significant positive association ( < 0.05) between somatic variant burden and AD risk, regardless of whether APOE genotype was modeled additively for the APOE4 allele ( Figure S3K [this file] ) or as categorical factors representing all genotypes (22, 23, 33, 34, 44). 
UMAP visualization of the integrated object showed no visible clustering by sample ID or individual ID, consistent with successful integration ( Figure S7 [this file] ).

To investigate the structures of complex interactions among the proteins in AD, we constructed a protein co-expression network through the multiscale embedded gene co-expression network analysis (MEGENA) of the entire profiled proteomes ( Figure 4A [rid=F4] ; Table S4 [this file] , pages 1–3). We identified 386 co-expressed protein modules, ranging in size from 10 to 3,118 proteins ( Table S4 [this file] , page 3). To identify the co-expression network modules that are associated with AD, we intersected these protein modules with the DEP signatures ( Figure 2C [rid=F2] ) and rank-ordered them based on a total enrichment score ( Figure 4B [rid=F4] , track 2), calculated as the sum of significance levels from multiple enrichment tests ( Table S4 [this file] , page 4; Figure 4B [rid=F4] , tracks 3–21). 
These AD-associated modules are cell-type specific based on their enrichment of human brain cell-type specific marker signatures ( Figure 4C [rid=F4] ; Table S4 [this file] , page 5). These brain cell-type-specific modules are involved in diverse biological functions ( Figure 4D [rid=F4] ; Table S4 [this file] , page 6). For example, the top-ranked module M3 ( Figure 4B [rid=F4] ), which is upregulated in AD ( Figure 4E [rid=F4] ), is involved in various critical biological pathways such as metabolic process, antigen presentation, signal transduction, and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) phagosome ( Figure 4D [rid=F4] ; Table S4 [this file] , page 6). For example, M39, the sixth highest-ranked module, which functions in astrocytes, is enriched for upregulated DEPs and is involved in cytokine signaling ( Figure S3A [rid=SD8] ; Table S4 [this file] , page 6). 
The neuron-specific module M2, ranked at 27 , is involved in chemical synaptic transmission and metal ion transport ( Figure 5D [rid=F5] ; Table S5 [rid=SD2] , page 6), while M31 is a child module to M2 ( Table S4 [this file] , page 3). 
Strikingly, the astrocytic modules M39 ( Figure S3A [rid=SD8] ), M210, M762, and M510 ( Table S4 [this file] , page 5) are enriched for the DAA gene signature ( Figure 5B [rid=F5] , track 6), while the microglia modules M245 ( Figure S3C [rid=SD8] ), M46 ( Figure 5C [rid=F5] ), M771, and M553 ( Table S4 [this file] , page 5) are enriched for the gene signatures of MG states ( Figure 5B [rid=F5] , tracks 7–13). 
The neuronal module M5 ( Table S4 [this file] , page 5) is enriched for the gene signatures of MG3 ( Figure 5B [rid=F5] , track 12). 
To uncover potential regulatory relationships among proteins, we constructed a global Bayesian causal network using the PHG proteomic data as well as the matched genetic data (details in STAR Methods [rid=S22] ; Figure 6A [rid=F6] ; Table S4 [this file] , page 7), followed by key driver analysis (KDA) to identify key driver proteins (KDPs). We identified 580 KDPs, corresponding to 471 genes (an average of 1.23 protein isoforms per gene) ( Table S4 [this file] , page 8). The moesin protein (MSN) and PRDX6 are the top two KDPs ( Table S4 [this file] , page 8), which are co-localized in a protein subnetwork that is upregulated in AD ( Figure 6B [rid=F6] ). 
Interestingly, 72% (340 out of 469) of KDPs have been understudied in AD, as they co-occur with “Alzheimer’s disease” in less than 5 papers ( STAR Methods [rid=S22] ; Data S1 [rid=SD7] , page 3), and 11 of these 340 proteins (AHNAK, RPH3A, EZR, PLEC, OLFM3, NUMA1, LIMS1, DTNA, PLCB1, NDUFS1, and PLCD1) are the top 30 KDPs ( Table S4 [this file] , pages 8 and 9; STAR Methods [rid=S22] ). 
Based on the KDP ranking scores ( Table S4 [this file] , page 8) and the availability of antibodies, and after the collapse of isoforms from the same proteins, we selected seven top-ranked KDPs for verification, which include MSN (#1, denoting its ranking order), PRDX6 (#2), VIM (#3), AHNAK (#5), RPH3A (#6), OLFM3 (#10), and NRN1 (#14). 
We selected AHNAK for further functional investigation for its high ranking in the KDP list and its biological significance in AD research, as it was the least studied among the top five KDPs ( Table S4 [this file] , page 9; STAR Methods [rid=S22] ).

We then investigated the association of each protein with the four AD neuropathological and clinical traits, including BS, CDR, CERAD, and PMD ( Figures 2A [rid=F2] and 2B [rid=F2] ; Table S2 [this file] , page 1). 
We identified over 1,000 DEPs from the comparisons of severe AD pathology vs. healthy control with respect to the clinical and neuropathological traits (e.g., DefiniteAD vs. NL) ( Figure 2C [rid=F2] ; Table S2 [this file] , page 1), accounting for ~10% of the total proteins evaluated. Similar results were found from the correlation analysis of protein expression and the clinical and neuropathological traits of AD ( Data S1 [rid=SD7] , page 1; Table S2 [this file] , page 2). 
As shown in Figure S1A [rid=SD8] , the DEP signatures were enriched for Gene Ontology (GO) pathways important in AD pathogenesis, such as neuronal and synapse functions in the downregulated DEP signatures and immune response in the upregulated DEP signatures ( Table S2 [this file] , page 3). These observations were consistent with our previous finding that downregulated DEP signatures were enriched in neuronal cells, while the upregulated DEP signatures were enriched in microglia and astrocytes ( Data S1 [rid=SD7] , page 2A; Table S2 [this file] , page 4).
