AD subjects for each cohort were selected based on a diagnosis of AD dementia and evidence of high Aβ/tau pathology, whereas control subjects exhibited no cognitive impairment along with low Aβ/tau pathology ( Figure S1 [this file] ; Table S1 [rid=SD2] ). 
IPAA identified 548 and 391 dysregulated pathways (FDR < 0.01) in TCX and PHG regions ( Figure 1C [rid=F1] ) between diseased and control subjects using a linear model adjusting for confounding covariates such as batch, sex, age at death, and post-mortem interval ( Figure S1B [this file] and S2C [this file] ). 
We performed bulk RNA-seq on the 3D AD cellular models and reference cells ( Figure S1D [this file] and S1E [this file] ). 
We also applied IPAA to human iPSC-derived neurons carrying familial AD mutations, or ( Figure S1G [this file] and S1H [this file] ). Intriguingly, correlative analysis did not show a strong, consistent positive correlation between these neurons and AD brains ( Figure S1H [this file] ). 
To ensure that the core pathways identified by IPAA are not artificially emphasized due to gene overlap among MSigDB pathways, we systematically refined the background list of pathways using the Jaccard index to minimize shared genes ( Figure S2 [this file] ). 
In keeping with this, IPAA also found fewer dysregulated DLPFC pathways than PHG and TCX ( Figures 2B [rid=F2] and S1F [this file] ). As a result, we used a less conservative threshold for the detection of dysregulated pathways (FDR < 0.1) in DLPFC compared to that of other brain regions and the cellular model ( Figure S1F [this file] ). 
To confirm IPAA pathway dysregulation at the protein level, we assayed changes in major regulator proteins of these pathways, including YAP, E-cadherin, cell division cycle protein 20 homolog (CDC20), the anaphase-promoting complex or cyclosome (APC/C), and cyclin B1 ( Figure S3 [this file] ). As predicted by the mRNA-based IPAA analysis, levels of these proteins were significantly altered in the 6-week differentiated 3D Aβ42-H model compared to control ( Figure S3 [this file] ). This supports the notion that advanced tau pathology is induced by substantial Aβ42 accumulation in our 3D human neural cultures ( Figures S3A [this file] and S3B [this file] ). We also observed increased phosphorylation of YAP and p38 MAPK, further indicating functional dysregulation of these pathways due to Aβ42 accumulation in 3D human neural cells ( Figures 4B [rid=F4] and 4C [rid=F4] , Figures S3C [this file] and S3D [this file] ). 
Immunofluorescence images also showed elevated p-p38 MAPK signals in brain sections of 5XFAD mice ( Figures 5C [rid=F5] – 5F [rid=F5] and S4A [this file] ). Interestingly, p-p38 MAPK signals mostly appeared in ring-like punctate structures ( Figures 5C [rid=F5] – 5E [rid=F5] and S4A [this file] ), which did not overlap with markers of microglia (Iba1) ( Figure 5C [rid=F5] ) or astrocytes (ALDH1L1) ( ) but strongly co-localized with synaptophysin and kinesin heavy chain ( Figures 5D [rid=F5] , 5E [rid=F5] , and S4A [this file] ). The level of the p-p38 MAPK also increased in protein extracts from the brains of human AD patients that exhibit high p-tau accumulation ( Figures S4B [this file] – S4D [this file] ). 
Upregulated phosphoproteins were enriched for kinases that were previously detected from similar phosphoproteomics analysis, including SRC, FYN, CDK5, GSK3B, MARK1, MAPAPK2 (MK2), MAPK14 (p38 MAPKα) ( Figure S5 [this file] and Table S6 [rid=SD2] ). Again, this unbiased analysis showed that p38 MAPK and MK2 were predicted as kinases significantly elevated by Aβ42 accumulation, as well as Glycogen Synthase Kinase-3β (GSK-3β), one of the major tau kinases that we have previously reported to regulate tau tangle pathology in our 3D AD cellular models ( Figure S5 [this file] and Table S6 [rid=SD2] ). 
To explore the impact of p38 MAPK activation on AD pathology induced by robust accumulation of Aβ42, we drugged multiple 3D AD cellular models, including the Aβ42-H model ( Figure 7 [rid=F7] and S6B [this file] – D [this file] ). p38 MAPK activity was modulated by Losmapimod, a clinically relevant p38α/β MAPK inhibitor. Losmapimod treatment effectively inhibited p38 MAPK activity in the 3D AD cellular models, as evidenced by decreased phosphorylated MSK1 and MK2, downstream substrates of p38 MAPK ( Figure 7B [rid=F7] and S6B [this file] ). In addition, decreased cleaved caspase-3 levels by Losmapimod treatment indicates that p38 MAPK inhibition interferes with Aβ42-induced neuronal death ( Figure 7D [rid=F7] and 7E [rid=F7] ). p38 MAPK inhibition also selectively reduced Aβ42 accumulation and Aβ42/40 ratio in Aβ42-H cultures ( Figure S6A [this file] ). 
Losmapimod treatments also reduced AD pathology in 3D AD cellular models expressing different familial AD mutations ( Figure S6B [this file] – S6D [this file] and S7A [this file] – S7D [this file] ). Consistent with observations with the Aβ42-H cells, Losmapimod treatments led to significant reductions in p-tau ( Figure S6B [this file] and S6C [this file] ) and active caspase-3 levels ( Figure S7A [this file] – S7D [this file] ), along with decreased Aβ42 levels ( Figure S6D [this file] ). Unbiased phosphoproteomic analysis of Aβ42-H cell cultures treated with Losmapimod also showed significant (FDR < 0.01) reversal of cell-death related pathways ( Figure S5D [this file] and Table S7 [rid=SD2] ). 
While Doramapimod treatment significantly decreased p-tau and tau levels, we observed widespread toxicity across all tested concentrations, manifested by dramatic reductions in control Tuj1 and actin levels ( Figure S8 [this file] ). VX-745, another clinically relevant p38 MAPK inhibitor, exhibited no sign of toxicity and significantly decreased the level of phosphorylated MSK1 (p-MSK1), a downstream substrate of p38 MAPK ( Figure S8A [this file] ). However, VX-745 treatment did not significantly affect p-tau or total tau levels ( Figure S8B [this file] ). 
We also found that the inhibition of p38 MAPK and MK2 by Losmapimod treatment displayed additional therapeutic benefits, as it attenuated LPS-induced neuroinflammatory activation of microglia ( Figure S9 [this file] ). 
Phosphoproteomics revealed alterations in phosphoproteins and kinase networks regulated by Aβ42 ( Figures 6 [rid=F6] , S5 [this file] , and Tables S3 [rid=SD2] – S7 [rid=SD2] ). Notably, Losmapimod, a p38α/β inhibitor, mitigated Aβ42-induced tau pathology and neuronal death ( Figure S5 [this file] , Tables S3 [rid=SD2] , S4 [rid=SD2] , and S7 [rid=SD2] ). Importantly, unbiased phosphoproteomic IPAA analysis reaffirms the robust activation of the p38 MAPK and MK2 pathways due to Aβ42 accumulation in our 3D human AD cellular models, closely aligning with the conclusions derived from the IPAA analysis of transcriptomic datasets ( Figures 6 [rid=F6] , S5 [this file] , Tables S4 [rid=SD2] , and S7 [rid=SD2] ). Kinase enrichment analysis with the same phosphoproteomics datasets also predicted that p38 MAPK and MK2 are significantly elevated by Aβ42 accumulation ( Figure S5 [this file] , Table S6 [rid=SD2] ). 
Accumulation of active p38 MAPK protein in dystrophic presynaptic neurites, but not in microglial cells, underscores its specificity in AD pathology in neurons ( Figures 5 [rid=F5] and S4 [this file] ). Losmapimod reduced Aβ42 accumulation, tau pathology, neuronal loss, and microglial activation in our 3D cellular model ( Figures 7 [rid=F7] , S6 [this file] , S7 [this file] , and S9 [this file] ), validating its potential. Losmapimod may have additional therapeutic benefits as it mitigates LPS-induced neuroinflammatory microglia activation ( Figure S9 [this file] ). 
Notably, inhibitors of p38 α (VX-745) and p38 α/β/δ/γ (Doramapimod) were not effective in lowering tau pathology ( Figure S8 [this file] ).

The final set of DC pairs includes pairs that are originally masked by cellular composition effects but revealed after CTC, and also DC pairs that are resilient to cellular composition effects (and hence found in both before- and after-CTC analyses; see Supplementary Table 11 [this file] ). 
This replication test has lent some confidence to proceed with further downstream analyses and reinforced the robustness of our methodology and findings (Supplementary Fig. 9 [this file] ). 
Partitioning each DC gene pair list from each inter-brain-region comparison resulted in multiple modules (see Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ). 
Total number of modules enriched in DC vs. random is represented in Supplementary Table 12 [this file] and Supplementary Fig. 10 [this file] a, 9b [this file] . Further, in Supplementary Fig. 10 [this file] c, 9d [this file] , empirical FDR of 2 representative modules reflects the robustness of DC module enrichment. Lastly, Supplementary Table 13 [this file] highlights that the functions enriched in random module are not related to brain or AD pathology except for one GO_BP “GO:0007628- adult walking behavior”. 
Only those that are enriched at FDR < = 0.05 cut-off are reported to be enriched (Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ).

Overall, removing the neurodegeneration screen hits removed the largest number of pathway enrichments compared to the final network solution ( Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ). context_description:
Each nucleus was assigned to one of seven major cell types, based on the RNAs it expressed ( Figure 1A [rid=F1] and S1 [this file] ). 
For analyses comparing donors (e.g. Figure 1 [rid=F1] ), to make rigorous comparisons of nuclei from many brain donors – while controlling for technical influences from extraction of nuclei, single-cell library construction, and sequencing – we processed sets of 20 brain specimens (each consisting of affected and control donors) at once as a single pooled sample, an approach we have previously described in which we make preparations of nuclei from sets (or “villages” ) of 20 donors at once ( Figure S1A [this file] ). Each set of 20 tissue samples was processed as a single sample through nuclei extraction, encapsulation in droplets, library creation, and sequencing ( Figure S1A [this file] ). This experimental approach ( Figure S1A [this file] ) allowed the data to be highly comparable donor-to-donor.

context_description:
Persons with CAP scores up to 300 – generally corresponding to the long latent period prior to clinical motor onset – tended to have SPN proportions just slightly lower than the average unaffected control brain donor ( Figures 1B [rid=F1] and S2A [this file] ). In contrast, SPNs appeared to be lost at a substantial rate in donors with CAP score greater than 350 (generally, donors with manifest HD symptoms), as evidenced by a steep downward slope in the relationship of SPN abundance to CAP score ( Figures 1B [rid=F1] and S2A [this file] ). 
Since iSPNs inhibit motor programs while dSPNs initiate such programs, the earlier average loss of iSPNs (which is consistent with stereological measurements ) may underlie the prominence of chorea (involuntary movements) as an early motor symptom in HD . (Relative losses of patch (striosomal) and matrix (extra-striosomal) SPNs were somewhat more variable across individuals, Figure S2B [this file] .) 
Individuals varied in expression levels, but accelerated SPN loss (relative to CAP score) did not associate with having higher expression levels ( Figures S2C [this file] – D [this file] ). 
These same data are shown on a log scale in Figure S2A [this file] . ( ) Decline in iSPNs (D2 SPNs, y-axis) and dSPNs (D1 SPNs, x-axis) with HD progression.

caption: Figure S3 . Determination of a consensus CAG-repeat length for individual HTT transcripts and allele specificity of somatic expansion, related to  Figure 2 .
description: 3  Figure  S3  .  Determination  of  a  consensus  CAG-repeat  length  for  individual  HTT  transcripts  and  allele  specificity  of  somatic  expansion,  related  to  Figure  2  .  (  A  )  Determination  of  consensus  CAG-repeat  length  from  sets  of  sequence  reads  derived  from  individual  HTT  RNA  transcripts.  Sequence  reads  (PCR  products)  originating  from  the  same  underlying  RNA  molecule  share  a  common  unique  molecular  identifier  (UMI)  that  was  applied  during  reverse  transcription.  The  histograms  show  representative  distributions  of  CAG-repeat  lengths  in  the  reads  for  individual  UMIs  for  (top  row)  short,  common  HD  alleles  (<35  repeats)  that  do  not  cause  HD;  for  HD-causing  alleles  with  modest  somatic  expansion  in  the  range  of  40–60  CAGs  (second  row);  for  longer  somatic  expansions  in  the  range  of  80–150  CAGs  (middle  row);  for  UMIs  with  somatic  expansions  in  the  range  of  150–300  CAGs  (fourth  row);  and  for  UMIs  showing  very  long  somatic  expansions  beyond  300  CAGs  (bottom  row).  Note  that  each  row  uses  a  different  x-axis  scale.  For  transcripts  with  long  somatically  acquired  CAG-repeat  expansions,  the  PCR  amplification  during  library  preparation  creates  a  left-tailed  distribution,  reflecting  the  way  that  PCR  errors  lead  to  the  generation  of  molecules  with  shorter  repeats  and  then  favor  these  smaller  molecules  over  longer  ones.  For  each  UMI,  we  use  the  mode  (the  Robertson-Cryer  half-sample  mode  estimator,  function  hsm()  from  the  R  package  modeest)  as  the  consensus  CAG-repeat  length  for  that  HTT  transcript.  The  accuracy  of  these  determinations  is  evaluated  in  Figure  2B  .  Cell  barcodes  on  the  same  sequence  reads  make  it  possible  to  then  connect  each  such  CAG-repeat  length  determination  to  the  wider  RNA-expression  profile  (cell  type  and  cell  state)  of  the  nucleus  from  which  it  was  sampled.  (  B  )  Allele  specificity  of  somatic  expansion.  Distributions  of  single-cell  CAG-repeat  length  measurements  for  each  donor/cell-type  combination,  showing  both  the  short,  non-HD-causing  allele  (<  35  repeats,  blue)  and  the  longer,  HD-causing  allele  (>35  repeats,  green),  here  zoomed  in  to  the  0–50  range  (beyond  which  most  SPNs  have  already  expanded  their  HD-causing  allele).  The  shorter  allele  (blue)  appears  to  be  somatically  stable  across  neuronal  and  glial  cell  types  in  all  six  persons  with  HD.  (  C  )  CAG-repeat  length  distribution  from  an  unaffected  control  donor  (homozygous  for  a  repeat  length  of  17  CAGs).  In  this  control  donor,  both  alleles  appear  to  be  somatically  stable.
context_description:
Despite the well-known distorting effects of PCR upon DNA repeats and molecular-size distributions, sets of sequence reads with the same cell barcode and molecular barcode (i.e. from the same RNA transcript) exhibited similar repeat lengths ( Figure S3A [this file] ), the consensus of which we used in downstream analyses. 
Astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, polydendrocytes (OPCs), microglia, and interneurons exhibited modest CAG-repeat instability, with almost all cells having a CAG repeat within a few units of the modal length ( Figures 2C [rid=F2] and S3 [this file] ). This pattern was present in all (6/6) of the persons with HD whose caudate we deeply sampled by this approach ( Figures 2C [rid=F2] – 2D [rid=F2] and S3B [this file] ). 
Somatic expansion was allele-specific, strongly affecting the HD-causing allele but not the other inherited allele ( Figures 2C [rid=F2] and S3B [this file] ), suggesting that somatic instability is affected in by an allele’s own CAG-repeat length. In an unaffected (control) donor, neither allele exhibited substantial somatic instability ( Figure S3C [this file] ). 
Figure S3 [this file] and Methods S1 [rid=SD13] , section 4 [rid=SD13] contain additional visualizations.

Genes  whose  expression  levels  change  significantly  with  repeat  expansion  in  at  least  one  of  the  donors  are  shown.
context_description:
This conclusion was supported by many kinds of analyses: simple correlations of gene-expression profiles ( Figures 3A [rid=F3] and S4A [this file] ); non-parametric statistical tests (as shown in volcano plots and genome-wide distributions of gene-level test statistics; Figures 3B [rid=F3] – C [rid=F3] and S4B [this file] – S4E [this file] ); and regression of gene-expression measurements against CAG-repeat length ( Methods S1 [rid=SD13] , section 3 [rid=SD13] ). None of these analyses detected any cell-autonomous consequences of repeat expansion to 150 CAGs, but all detected profound effects of CAG-repeat expansion beyond 150 CAGs ( Figure S4A [this file] – S4E [this file] ). 
We found that not only the high CAG-repeat-length threshold (~150), but also the ensuing gene-expression changes in SPNs with expansions beyond 150 CAGs, were highly similar from person to person ( Figures 3D [rid=F3] and S4F [this file] ). 
Analyses of the effect of CAG-repeat length on genome-wide gene expression in which we compared subsets of SPNs defined by CAG-repeat length ranges ( Figures 3B [rid=F3] – C [rid=F3] and S4B [this file] – S4E [this file] ) utilized a Wilcoxon rank-sum test (wilcox.test() function in R), in which the individual SPNs (in two groups of SPNs defined by CAG repeat-length ranges) were ranked by their expression level of a gene (as a fraction of all UMIs detected in a cell), and then the distribution of ranks were compared between the two groups. 
Figure S4A [this file] shows similar analyses of SPNs from six persons with HD. ( ) Comparisons (volcano plots) of gene expression between sets of SPNs, sampled from the same person with HD but with CAG-repeat lengths in different ranges. p-values (y-axis) are derived from a Wilcoxon test across the individual SPNs in each group. Analyses for all six donors are in Figure S4B [this file] – S4E [this file] . ( ) Consistency of long(150)-repeat-expansion associated SPN gene-expression changes among individual persons with HD. More analyses are in Figure S4F [this file] ; see also Methods S1 [rid=SD13] , section 3 [rid=SD13] .

description: 6  Figure  S6.  Expression  levels  of  example  genes  as  a  function  of  CAG-repeat  length,  related  to  Figure  4  .  (  A  )  Expression  levels  of  five  example  phase  C−  genes  in  the  individual  SPNs  of  four  persons  with  HD  (one  gene  per  row,  one  donor  per  column).  Gray  points  represent  individual  SPNs.  Colored  points  are  moving  averages  in  windows  of  width  log  2  (CAG-repeat  length)  to  reduce  the  measurement  noise  inherent  in  single-cell  measurement.  Point  color  indicates  window  width,  vertical  bars  denote  confidence  intervals.  The  genes  shown  (  PRKCB  ,  PHACTR1  ,  SLC35F3  ,  ATP2B1  ,  CELF2  )  are  genes  that  SPNs  normally  express  more  strongly  than  interneurons  do.  This  analysis  also  helps  explain  why  conventional  descriptive-genomics  analyses  (to  find  “differentially  expressed  genes”  in  case-control  comparisons)  generally  fail  to  recognize  such  effects  in  HD.  First,  these  effects  are  present  in  just  a  small  fraction  of  any  donor’s  SPNs  at  any  one  time  (those  SPNs  with  long  CAG-repeat  expansions),  and  are  pronounced  in  a  still-smaller  fraction  (those  in  which  the  CAG  repeat  has  expanded  even  further)  –  so  they  appear  as  small  and  often  insignificant  changes  in  bulk  and  sorted-cell-type  analyses.  Second,  most  of  these  genes,  like  most  human  genes,  exhibit  inter-individual  variation  in  expression  levels  (at  baseline),  further  obscuring  (in  case-control  comparisons)  effects  that  are  clear  in  within-tissue  comparisons  of  individual  cells.  (  B  )  Expression  levels  of  HTT  in  the  individual  SPNs  of  persons  with  HD.  Gray  points  represent  individual  SPNs.  Colored  points  and  vertical  bars  denote  moving  averages  and  confidence  intervals,  as  in  A  .

The distinction between SPNs and striatal interneurons was particularly notable, since all are inhibitory (GABAergic) neurons that share a developmental lineage. (Among interneurons, cholinergic interneurons exhibited more expansion than other interneurons, though much less expansion than SPNs ( STAR Methods [rid=S23] , Methods S1 [this file] , section 2 [this file] ).) 
This conclusion was supported by many kinds of analyses: simple correlations of gene-expression profiles ( Figures 3A [rid=F3] and S4A [rid=SD4] ); non-parametric statistical tests (as shown in volcano plots and genome-wide distributions of gene-level test statistics; Figures 3B [rid=F3] – C [rid=F3] and S4B [rid=SD4] – S4E [rid=SD4] ); and regression of gene-expression measurements against CAG-repeat length ( Methods S1 [this file] , section 3 [this file] ). 
Analysis identified more than 700 genes whose expression levels were affected by CAG-repeat length ( Table S2 [rid=SD8] , STAR Methods [rid=S23] , Methods S1 [this file] , section 3 [this file] ). 
These simulations are described in detail in Methods S1 [this file] , section 4 [this file] ; an animated rendering is in Video S1 [rid=SD9] . 
We estimate that an SPN takes 50 years (on average) to expand from 40 to 60 CAGs, then another 12 years to expand from 60 to 80, but with variability both cell-to-cell and person-to-person ( Methods S1 [this file] , section 4 [this file] ). 
An elaborated, expanded protocol, with illustrations and diagrams, helpful tips, potential modifications and pausing points, is in Methods S1 [this file] , section 5 [this file] . 
In Methods S1 [this file] , section 5 [this file] we provide diagrams illustrating a way to calibrate the number of PCR cycles using real-time quantitative PCR. 
As with the target-sequence enrichment step, the number of PCR cycles is ideally calibrated to the sample, with the PCR ended while in exponential (“log”) phase, as described in Methods S1 [this file] , section 5 [this file] . 
An extended protocol with diagrams and further discussions of each step’s optimization (to other biological samples), stopping points, and troubleshooting tips is in Methods S1 [this file] , section 5 [this file] . 
We found that, even with this conservative inferential approach, every caudate cell type – including all types of neurons and glia – exhibited thousands of DEGs whose expression levels differed (on average) between cases and controls, as described in more detail in Methods S1 [this file] , section 1 [this file] . Consistent with the idea that DEGs are largely responses to caudate atrophy, an HD-cases-only analysis found that the magnitude of these gene-expression changes was strongly correlated with the extent of a donor’s earlier SPN loss ( Methods S1 [this file] , section 1 [this file] ). Methods S1 [this file] , section 1 [this file] includes an extended discussion comparing the results of case-control and CAG-length analyses, and may be of interest to readers planning deeper work in this area or wondering how the results of the CAG-length analysis (which we emphasize here) intersect with the results of conventional case-control analysis. 
Each read was analyzed (“decoded”) based on the expected layout based on the library construction protocol (a schematic depiction of the layout is in Methods S1 [this file] , section 5 [this file] ). Based on the recognition of these landmarks, the read was divided into segments capturing features of the read used in downstream analysis, including index sequences used for multiplexing multiple experiments on the same flowcell, cellular barcodes and unique molecular identifiers, and the sequence of the CAG repeat itself ( Methods S1 [this file] , section 5 [this file] ). 
We then quantified the degree of somatic expansion among different cell types based both on (a) the overall distributions of repeat length and (b) using a somatic instability index ( Methods S1 [this file] , section 2 [this file] ). An extended discussion of these approaches and analyses is in Methods S1 [this file] , section 2 [this file] . 
Methods S1 [this file] , section 3 [this file] provides a detailed description and extended discussion of the wide range of models we considered (including simple models in which the CAG-repeat had a continuous effect on gene expression throughout its length range), and the analyses leading to our final choice of model; that extended discussion and set of analyses will be of interest to readers who want to consider alternative models or to apply these kinds of approaches in other scientific contexts. 
As described in Methods S1 [this file] , section 3 [this file] , these analyses pointed strongly toward a hinge-function relationship in which CAG repeat length had no effect on gene expression until the CAG repeat was longer than 150 CAGs. 
The final and most effective form of this model (m=150, n=500) that we tried involved a “hinge function” with a hinge at 150 CAGs – i.e., a model in which effects of CAG-repeat length commence at approximately 150 CAGs – and also included an additional term to capture phase D effects ( Methods S1 [this file] , section 3 [this file] ). 
Methods S1 [this file] , section 3 [this file] explains in detail the full set of alternative models that were evaluated, and the results of these evaluations. 
UMIs from these genes were used to recognize the phase D status of individual SPNs, a key input to the Negative Binomial Regression analyses of phase D gene expression in Methods S1 [this file] , section 3 [this file] . 
To better understand how these distributions might arise and evolve from the kind of simple, incremental, stepwise expansion-and-contraction process that biological studies have suggested is their primary mode of somatic mutation (reviewed in ), we developed stochastic models and simulations for the dynamics of the somatic expansion process (detailed in Methods S1 [this file] , section 4 [this file] ). 
We evaluated and compared a variety of different models (see Methods S1 [this file] , section 4 [this file] for an extended discussion). 
To create animated visualizations of repeat expansion dynamics, we first fitted a specific repeat expansion model (TwoPhasePowerModel/150, Methods S1 [this file] , section 4 [this file] ) to model the dynamics for a specific donor and potentially a specific scenario (e.g. a hypothetical inherited repeat length) and then simulated the random walks of a large number of cells (n=3000). 
An extended discussion of our modeling choices, their rationales and their critical evaluation is provided in Methods S1 [this file] , section 4 [this file] . 
Figure S3 [rid=SD3] and Methods S1 [this file] , section 4 [this file] contain additional visualizations. 
More analyses are in Figure S4F [rid=SD4] ; see also Methods S1 [this file] , section 3 [this file] .

For the purpose of this study, CSCs were classified into two main types, R-CSCs and D-CSCs, which correspond to the extremes of the whole morphological spectrum ( Figure S1 [this file] ); this suggests that D-CSCs and R-CSCs may represent different transient stages of the same structure. Both D-CSCs and R-CSCs were detected in cortical and subcortical brain regions, across multiple mammalian species (human, non-human primates, and rodents; Figure S2 [this file] ). This percentage was significantly lower (3%) in equivalent, adjacent areas outside the CSCs ( Figure 1D [rid=F1] ; Table S1 [this file] ). 
CS56 immunoreactivity was observed around dendritic spines, filling the synaptic cleft ( Figures 1 [rid=F1] E , S3 [this file] , and S4 [this file] ), as well as axodendritic and axosomatic boutons ( Figures 1E2 [rid=F1] , E3 [rid=F1] , and S3 [this file] ), thus implying an association with both excitatory and inhibitory contacts. 
Moreover, within CSCs, CS56 immunoreactivity was also enriched within glial endfeet and glial processes, predominantly overlapping with the intermediate filaments ( Figures 1F [rid=F1] , 1G [rid=F1] , and S3 [this file] ). No CS56 immunoreactivity was detected within neuronal cell bodies or dendrites ( Figure S3 [this file] ). 
Furthermore, the differential distribution of CS56 immunoreactivity accounts for the distinct morphology of CSCs, i.e., R-CSCs showing a predominance of large glial processes and D-CSCs presenting prevalent synaptic coatings, resulting in a punctate appearance ( Figure S1 [this file] ). 
No significant differences were found between dendritic spine densities within and outside of CSCs ( Figure S5 [this file] ; Table S2 [this file] ). These results show that dendritic spines are significantly larger, and putatively potentiated, within R-CSCs, while spines contained within D-CSCs present an intermediate morphology between R-CSCs and controls ( Figures 2H [rid=F2] and 2I [rid=F2] ; Table S3 [this file] ). 
First, we noted that, under standard conditions, R-CSCs are slightly more numerous in layer 2/3 compared to D-CSCs, while the density of both R-CSCs and D-CSCs is consistent across cortical layers ( Figure S6A [this file] ). More importantly, we established that there is no difference between left and right hemispheres ( Figures 3B [rid=F3] , 3C [rid=F3] , S6B [this file] , and S6C [this file] ). Conversely, in a group of whisker-deprived mice, the numerical densities (NDs) of CSCs were reduced in the BCx contralateral to whisker trimming compared to the ipsilateral side ( Figures 3B [rid=F3] , 3C [rid=F3] , S6B [this file] , and S6C [this file] ; Table S4 [this file] ). At 1 h, R-CSCs, but not D-CSCs, were significantly increased in layer 5 selectively ( Figures 3G [rid=F3] and S6D [this file] ; Table S5 [this file] ). Conversely, D-CSCs, but not R-CSCs, were significantly increased after 2 h in the same layer ( Figures 3H [rid=F3] and S6E [this file] ; Table S5 [this file] ). No significant changes in either category were observed when the post-stimulus interval was extended to 4 h ( Figure S6F [this file] ). Moreover, no interhemispheric difference was found in motor cortex layer 5, a brain region putatively unaffected by the stimulation, excluding the possibility of stimulus-independent interhemispheric biases ( Figure S6G [this file] ).

Among these, we identified synaptotagmins (SYT 1, 2, and 7), synapsins (SYN 1–3), synaptogyrins (SYG 1–3), synaptic vesicle glycoproteins 2 (SV2A and B) and synaptophysin (SYPH) ( Figure 4E [rid=F4] ; Table S8 [this file] ).

These data are also available as part of the supplemental material [this file] . 
Quantification of CSCs in layer 1 was not taken into account due to recurrent inconsistent results, likely a consequence of CS56 antibody accumulation into the pial surface (also see Figure S2 [this file] ). 
CSCs present with distinct morphological characteristics, such as a round shape with a diameter of 70–100 μm (in rodents) often enveloping several unstained cell bodies (examples in Figures S1A [this file] – S1C [this file] ). CSCs with negligible punctate labeling and predominant sharply labeled converging processes were classified as R-CSC ( Figures 1F [rid=F1] and S1A [this file] ). CSCs with a predominant pattern of diffuse immunolabeled puncta, lacking distinctive signs of immunolabeled processes, were categorized as D-CSC ( Figures 1G [rid=F1] and S1B [this file] ). CSCs presenting both sharply defined processes and dense punctate labeling simultaneously were classified as an intermediate category ( Figure S1C [this file] ). 
Glial processes were recognized according to Peters ( Figures S3 [this file] and 4 [this file] ). Each independent immunoreaction product within a glial cell process was quantified as a single element ( Figures 1F [rid=F1] , 1G [rid=F1] , S3 [this file] , and S4 [this file] ). When positive immunoreaction was observed within the edge of a glial cell process adjacent to a pre-or-post synaptic compartment the element was categorized as “glia endfoot” ( Figure S3 [this file] . Synapses, identified by their distinct pre- and post-synaptic elements, were counted as positive (CS56-coated) when showing clearly distinguishable black immunoreaction product within the synaptic cleft and/or coating the pre- and post-synaptic elements ( Figures 2 [rid=F2] and S4 [this file] ).

context_description:
Earlier work has found that genes expressed most strongly by neurons (relative to other cell types), but not genes expressed most strongly by glia, are enriched for the genes implicated by genetic analyses in schizophrenia ; we replicated these findings in our data ( Fig. 4a [rid=F32] and Supplementary Note [this file] ). 
We found that the genes dynamically recruited by SNAP-a in astrocytes were 14 times more likely than other protein-coding genes to reside at genomic loci implicated by common genetic variation in schizophrenia (p = 5 x 10 , 95% confidence interval (CI): 8.7–24, by logistic regression) and 7 times more likely to have strong evidence from rare variants in schizophrenia (95% CI: 2.3–21, p = 5 x 10 , by logistic regression) ( Supplementary Note [this file] ). 
As expected, the strongest neuron-identity genes (as defined in the earlier work) exhibited elevated schizophrenia association, while the strongest astrocyte-identity genes did not ( Fig. 4a [rid=F32] and Supplementary Note [this file] ). 
MAGMA Z-scores were then used for downstream analyses as described in the Supplementary Note [this file] . 
See also Supplementary Note [this file] .

To do this, we quantified the overlap between cis-eQTL SNPs and genomic features associated with functional cis-regulatory elements (CREs), including DHS sites, chromatin marks, and binding sites for transcription factors and other DNA associated regulatory proteins (see Table S3 [this file] for full list of data sets). 
We trained a random forest classifier on a large set of SNP features, including SNP position, effect size, cell type specific CRE overlap, and non-cell type specific genomic elements (CRE features listed in Table S3 [this file] ) to predict whether each eQTL SNP association would replicate in a second study or not (i.e., binary class). 
These data sets (fully listed in Table S3 [this file] ) were all downloaded directly from the ENCODE data coordination center at UCSC. 
For each pair of comparisons, we can train a random forest classifier to predict the binary replication outcome given a set of features about the genomic location of the eQTL and the CREs for the corresponding cell types (see Table S3 [this file] for complete set).

Almost universally, eQTL SNPs are enriched within regions of activating CREs ( Figure 3 [rid=pgen-1003649-g003] ; Tables S4 [this file] , S5 [rid=pgen.1003649.s024] , S6 [rid=pgen.1003649.s025] ) and depleted within repressive CREs ( Figure 4 [rid=pgen-1003649-g004] , Figures S12 [rid=pgen.1003649.s012] , S13 [rid=pgen.1003649.s013] , S14 [rid=pgen.1003649.s014] , Tables S4 [this file] , S5 [rid=pgen.1003649.s024] , S6 [rid=pgen.1003649.s025] ). 
We find that eQTL SNP-CRE overlap is frequently cell specific (see Figures 3 [rid=pgen-1003649-g003] – 5 [rid=pgen-1003649-g005] for examples, Tables S4 [this file] , S5 [rid=pgen.1003649.s024] , S6 [rid=pgen.1003649.s025] for full results). 
Notably, the canonical biochemical function of the CRE class is predictive of the pattern of cell type specific eQTL-CRE overlap. eQTL SNPs are more likely to overlap activating CREs and less likely to overlap repressive CREs derived from the same cell type as the eQTL discovery data (repeated measures logistic regression ; Tables S4 [this file] , S5 [rid=pgen.1003649.s024] , S6 [rid=pgen.1003649.s025] ). Consistent with previous observations [44] [rid=pgen.1003649-Kim1] , [45] [rid=pgen.1003649-Ngre1] , [48] [rid=pgen.1003649-Chen1] , the proportion of eQTL SNP - TSS pairs with intervening insulators is remarkably consistent across cell types, suggesting that CTCF binding sites do not substantially affect cell-specific eQTL function ( Figure 4I [rid=pgen-1003649-g004] , Figure S16 [rid=pgen.1003649.s016] , Tables S4 [this file] , S5 [rid=pgen.1003649.s024] , S6 [rid=pgen.1003649.s025] ). 
We next examined the hypothesis that the CRE landscape is a major determinant of eQTL specificity, and found that eQTL SNPs that overlap cell type specific CREs are more likely to be cell type specific than are eQTL SNPs that overlap shared CREs (Fisher's exact test ) for , , and CRE data sets in LCLs, liver, and cerebellum, respectively ( Tables S4 [this file] , S5 [rid=pgen.1003649.s024] , S6 [rid=pgen.1003649.s025] ). 
For Tables S4 [this file] , S5 [rid=pgen.1003649.s024] , and S6, eQTL SNPs ( ) were tested for overlap with CRE data sets, each listed in a separate row.

Statistical fine-mapping was performed using FINEMAP (see Supplementary material [this file] ), which revealed in each investigated loci a 95% credible set with candidate causal variants ( Supplementary Table 10 [this file] ).

Finally, despite not being included in the main systematic gene prioritization pipeline, we ran ancillary TWAS analyses using large-scale MetaBrain cortex, PsychENCODE DLPFC and eQTLGen blood datasets, whose detailed methodology (including reasons for exclusion from the main analyses) and results are available in the Supplementary material [this file] and Supplementary Table 11 [this file] .

Detailed information on these datasets and cohorts, including the PWAS significance thresholds and number of samples, can be found in Supplementary Table 2 [this file] . 
We first brought together all evidence for the candidate sCJD risk genes as a result of (i) variant annotation; (ii) eQTL-GWAS integration; and (iii) pQTL-GWAS integration domain analyses, each having various categories and subcategories with a predetermined weighting scheme for single hits and replicated hits (across different e/pQTL colocalization or TWAS/PWAS analyses), all described in detail in Supplementary Table 3 [this file] . 
Using the pipeline described by Bellenguez ., we then ranked all the protein-coding candidate genes in each locus based on their total weighted scores, determined the top-ranked genes and compared the relative score differences between the top-ranked genes and the other genes in each locus to classify them as tier 1 and tier 2 prioritized risk genes, representing higher and lower levels of confidence for being true risk genes in loci, respectively (see Supplementary material [this file] for detailed tier classification methodology). 
Our systematic gene prioritization pipeline identified 17 tier 1 prioritized risk genes and 15 tier 2 prioritized risk genes in 30 risk loci ( Fig. 1 [rid=awaf032-F1] and Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ).

For the mouse MEF cell line, FerroScore was applied to six experimental conditions, ranging from single amino acid starvation to combinatorial treatments ( Figs 2a [rid=f2] , S1 [this file] ). In the multi-method comparison, FerroScore maintained a strong phenotype concordant association and retained the ability to evaluate combinatorial perturbations such as Cys + CysAm and Cys + sh-CTNS ( Figs 2b [rid=f2] , bottom; S3A [this file] ). 
To further assess cross species applicability, we evaluated the same benchmark in the human A549 cell line treated with IKE or RSL3, each with and without PAOX/SMOX double knockout ( Fig. S2 [this file] ). For example, GSVA captured a negative trend in MEF cells but did not maintain comparable performance in A549 cells, while FPI and FPS showed context dependent associations under these perturbation settings ( Figs 2c [rid=f2] , bottom; S3B [this file] ). 
As detailed in the ( Figs S4 [this file] – S5 [this file] , S6A [this file] ), the inclusion of low-abundance genes under the relaxed threshold substantially altered the network topology and super-node composition, resulting in disrupted FerroScore values and loss of phenotypic correlation in both the MEF and A549 datasets. 
To assess sensitivity to PPI network construction, we evaluated alternative STRING confidence thresholds (300 and 500) in addition to the default cutoff of 400 ( Fig. S6B [this file] ). 
To examine potential scale effects of topological metrics, we applied min–max normalization to degree and intra-module density and recomputed the FerroScore in both the MEF and A549 datasets ( Tables S1 [this file] – S2 [this file] , Fig. S6C [this file] ). 
Finally, because FerroScore is initialized from DEGs defined relative to a control group, we further evaluated its sensitivity to the reference background by rerunning the complete pipeline under matched control leave-one-out and pooled control stress test settings ( Table S3 [this file] ). 
Stage-specific survival curves further revealed distinct nonlinear dynamics, with stage II presenting the broadest therapeutic window for ferroptosis-targeting interventions ( Fig. S7A [this file] ). To delineate the evolving molecular mechanisms, we identified high-frequency consensus genes ( Fig. S7B [this file] and C [this file] ), enriched KEGG pathways ( Fig. S7D [this file] ), and GO terms ( Fig. S7E [this file] ) for each stage. This enabled the construction of a mechanistic map ( Fig. S8 [this file] ), which revealed a dynamic evolution of ferroptosis: from simplicity in stage I, to high activity in stage II (driven by lipid peroxidation, GSH synthesis, and ROS), and stage III (sustained by iron metabolism with emerging resistance), culminating in suppression in stage IV alongside decreased free iron. 
Finally, decision curve analysis demonstrated that our ferroptosis index provided a higher net benefit than traditional tumor staging across a wide threshold probability range ( ), supporting its potential clinical utility ( Fig. S7F [this file] ). 
Cell annotation identified 20 immune cell subtypes ( Figs 4b [rid=f4] , S9A [this file] ) (see for details). For non-immune cells, initial classification into five broad types ( Figs 4d [rid=f4] , S9B [this file] ) revealed limited discriminative capacity of ferroptosis index ( Fig. S10A [this file] ). To resolve this, we subclustered the Epithelial, Endothelial, Fibroblast, and Stellate populations based on functional characteristics and marker specificity ( Figs S9C–F [this file] , S10B–E [this file] ) (see for details) and re-assessed ferroptosis activity at this refined resolution ( Fig. 4e [rid=f4] ). 
In addition, a parallel analysis of CD8 Trm and exhausted T cells revealed that exhausted cells upregulated a KLF2-mediated antioxidant program, reducing ferroptosis susceptibility to promote survival ( Fig. S11A–B [this file] ). 
To elucidate the underlying regulatory mechanisms, we constructed a transcription factor (TF)–target gene regulatory network ( Figs 4h [rid=f4] , S11C [this file] ), which identified TXN, EGFR, and NOX4 as core drivers modulated by TFs including NFKB1, STAT1, RELA, STAT3, and JUN. We also observed divergent ferroptosis susceptibility between EMTEn and EMTEp cells ( Fig. S11D–E [this file] ), which reflected their distinct microenvironmental niches. 
GSEA of ferroptosis- and immune-related pathways ( Fig. S12A [this file] and D [this file] ), combined with TF–target network analysis ( Fig. S12B–C [this file] , E [this file] ), revealed distinct immunoregulatory mechanisms. 
We identified active signaling pathways and categorized them by their relevance to ferroptosis ( Fig. 5a [rid=f5] , Table S4 [this file] ). We focused on five key pathways—MIF, GALECTIN, SPP1, PLAU, and MK—for in-depth analysis, examining their network structures, gene expression, ligand–receptor contributions, and key communicating cells ( Figs 5c–f [rid=f5] , S13A–D [this file] ). 
Finally, to delineate how ferroptosis signals are transmitted across the TME, we constructed a “Cell–Gene–Signal” multilayer network ( Figs 5g–h [rid=f5] , S13E–F [this file] ) by integrating cell-specific ferroptosis genes, intercellular communication data, and gene–pathway associations. 
Taking AD as an example, we identified an “inverted–checkmark” relationship between ferroptosis score and age at death, linking elevated ferroptosis to accelerated mortality ( Fig. S14A [this file] ). Correlation analyses with AD pathological markers revealed positive associations between ferroptosis score and both APOE genotype and Thal phase, implicating the APOE4 risk variant and Aβ deposition in promoting ferroptosis ( Fig. S14B–D [this file] ). Furthermore, a stage-progressive map of ferroptosis mechanisms across Braak stages ( Fig. S14E [this file] ) nominated stage V.5 as a potential intervention window. 
To further assess its scalability, we extended FerroScore to independent datasets including Liver Hepatocellular Carcinoma (LIHC), Kidney Renal Clear Cell Carcinoma (KIRC), cardiomyopathy cohorts (ischemic cardiomyopathy, ICM, and dilated cardiomyopathy, DCM), and Nonalcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD) ( Fig. S15 [this file] ).

We generated TMEM106B null mice using embryonic stem cells from the KnockOut Mouse Project (KOMP), which were crossed with ubiquitous Cre and Flp recombinase lines to remove the lacZ cassette and delete the essential exon 4 ( Supplementary Fig. 1a [this file] , online resource). Unlike past work with KOMP mice in which both the lacZ and exon remained intact [ 22 [rid=R22] , 32 [rid=R32] ], our strategy produced nearly complete loss of TMEM106B protein ( Supplementary Fig. 1b [this file] , online resource). KO:tau animals were hyperactive in the open-field arena ( Supplementary Fig. 2a [this file] - b [this file] , online resource) but swam at the same speed and efficiency as other genotypes in the straight swim test ( Supplementary Fig. 2c [this file] - d [this file] , online resource), which allowed for cognitive testing using water-based tasks. 
We performed a cognitive test battery that started with Morris water maze (MWM) to assess spatial reference memory ( Supplementary Fig. 3a [this file] - c [this file] , online resource), followed by repeated reversal learning (RRL) to assess cognitive flexibility ( Supplementary Fig. 3d [this file] , e [this file] , online resource), and ended with radial arm water maze (RAWM) to assess spatial working memory ( Supplementary Fig. 3f [this file] , g [this file] , online resource). 
KO:tau mice developed paralysis as early as 5.9 mo, while tau animals first showed hind limb weakness at 8.4 mo ( Fig. 1a [rid=F1] ,), and the effect was more pronounced in females than in males ( Supplementary Fig. 4a [this file] , online resource). 
We focused these experiments on tau and KO:tau groups because we had seen no significant differences between WT and KO tested at 8 mo of age ( Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] , online resource). Further, KO:tau mice swam as well as tau animals in the cued test ( Supplementary Fig. 2e [this file] , f [this file] , online resource). 
We confirmed the mouse T186S variant by Sanger sequencing of the full exon and high-resolution melting point analysis to check for off-target mutations ( Supplementary Fig. 5a [this file] , online resource). Because past work had suggested that the in vitro expression of the human T185S variant reduced TMEM106B protein half-life and steady-state levels [ 30 [rid=R30] ], we tested TMEM106B expression in our T186S mice but found no differences from WT at any age examined ( Supplementary Fig. 5b [this file] , online resource). All four genotypes expressed similar levels of monomeric and presumptive dimeric TMEM106B protein ( Supplementary Fig. 5c [this file] , online resource). 
Initial assessment in the open field and straight swim showed no difference between genotypes ( Supplementary Fig. 6a [this file] , b [this file] , online resource), so we proceeded to the cognitive test battery. Both KI:tau and tau mice learned the escape location equally well in the Morris water maze; however, there were pronounced differences in both short- and long-term memory for the trained location ( Fig. 2a [rid=F2] - c [rid=F2] , see Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] , online resource, for graphs including all four genotypes). 
In contrast to the accelerated phenotype observed in KO:tau animals, expression of the T186S allele slowed the onset of hind limb paralysis from a median survival of 9.7 mo in the tau animals to 11.9 mo in KI:tau mice, with a stronger effect in females than males ( Fig. 2h [rid=F2] , Supplementary Fig. 4b [this file] , online resource). 
Even at 6 mo of age when phospho-tau accumulation was just beginning, KO:tau mice harbored twice as much AT8 signal as tau siblings ( Supplementary Fig. 8 [this file] , online resource). Neurofibrillary tangles identified by Gallyas staining were also more frequent in the KO:tau mice (data not shown), and appeared as early as 6 mo of age in both male and female KO:tau animals ( Supplementary Fig. 8 [this file] , online resource). 
Conversely, overexpression of pathogenic tau did not affect TMEM106B levels ( Supplementary Fig. 5c [this file] , online resource). 
This analysis revealed enrichment in the TYROBP causal network associated with microglia, which also included synapse pruning genes ( Fig. 6d [rid=F6] , Supplementary Fig. 9 [this file] and Supplementary Table 5 [rid=SD2] , online resource). In line with TMEM106B function in autophagy and endo-lysosomal trafficking, we observed enrichment in pathways related to lysosomal lumen peptidases and hydrolases, chaperone mediated autophagy, and exosome/secretory granules ( Fig. 6d [rid=F6] and Supplementary Fig. 9 [this file] , online resource). Many of these genes were also concordant with single cell AD data, suggesting that expression changes caused by TMEM106B deletion were not due solely to differences in cell type proportions within our bulk RNA datasets ( Fig. 6d [rid=F6] , Supplementary Fig. 9 [this file] , online resource; [ 25 [rid=R25] ]). 
We again found that TMEM106B deletion increased the correlation between mouse tau and human AD both overall and within several of the individual brain regions tested ( Supplementary Fig. 10 [this file] , online resource).

GO-MF analysis revealed enrichment in ATP binding, protein binding, and RNA binding, highlighting their roles in molecular interactions and energy-related functions ( Figure S2D [this file] ). To assess disease-specific changes, we quantified the relative abundance of common interactors in AD vs. control brains, identifying 48 differentially abundant proteins (11 upregulated, 37 downregulated) ( Figure S2E [this file] ). Upregulated interactors were enriched in endocytic recycling pathways, suggesting increased endocytosis in AD, whereas downregulated interactors were linked to cellular biosynthesis, particularly translation, indicating impaired protein synthesis in AD ( Figure S2F [this file] ). 
Specifically, phosphorylations at T181, T231, T235, and S262 were detected in the AD Tau-seed interactome, while pS404 was detected in both AD and control HMW-Tau interactomes ( Figure S3A [this file] ). No Tau phosphorylation sites were exclusively detected in the control HMW-Tau interactome ( Figure S3A [this file] ). Notably, pT231 exhibited a distribution pattern that strongly resembled the distribution of seeding activity in AD, as highlighted by the gray overlay in the plot, suggesting a potential association between pT231 phosphorylation and Tau-seed pathogenicity ( Figure S3D [this file] ). Surprisingly, we did not find significant differences in pT217 levels between AD and control SEC fractions, including those HMW AD fractions with seeding activity ( Figure S3E [this file] ).

Five cohorts of LOAD2 and control mice fed either a HFD (high‐fat diet) or CD (control diet) were evaluated at JAX (Cohort 1: biometrics, behavior, plasma biomarkers, neuropathology, transcriptomics, proteomics), IU (Cohort 2: MRI, plasma biomarkers and cytokines, biochemistry, neuropathology; Cohort 3: PET/CT, autoradiography), and PITT (Cohorts 4 and 5: longitudinal plasma biomarkers, Touchscreen cognitive testing) (Figure S1 [this file] ). 
For full details see Supplemental Methods (Figure S1 [this file] ). 
Specifically, total distance traveled decreased significantly only in LOAD2+HFD animals (Figure S2A [this file] ), but performance was not affected by sex or genotype alone. Differences in rearing behavior as measured by total vertical activity were only observed in males, of both genotypes, to be decreased by HFD (Figure S2B [this file] ). Rotarod performance was decreased in a HFD‐dependent manner only (Figure S2C [this file] ). 
One hemisphere (right) from each brain was prepared for transcriptomics and proteomics, while the other hemisphere (left) was evaluated for neuronal cell loss, microglia number, astrocyte reactivity, and amyloid plaques in the cortex and hippocampus by immunofluorescence (Figure S3 [this file] ). 
Differential expression analyses identified very few significantly differentially expressed genes (DEGs) ( < 0.05) at 4 and 18 month old LOAD2 mice compared to age‐ and sex‐matched LOAD1 mice (Table SA [this file] ). At 12 months, there were 57 DEGs (38 upregulated, 19 downregulated; < 0.05) in male LOAD2 mice, and 17 DEGs (3 upregulated, 14 downregulated; < 0.05) in female LOAD2 mice (Table SA [this file] ). KEGG functional enrichment analysis identified enrichment of “protein processing in ER” in upregulated DEGs in 12 month old LOAD2 male mice and “MAPK signaling pathway” in downregulated DEGs in 12 month old LOAD2 female mice (Table SB [this file] ). At 24 months, there were only five significantly differentially upregulated genes ( < 0.05) in male LOAD2 mice, and 30 DEGs (12 upregulated, 18 downregulated; < 0.05) in female LOAD2 mice (Table SA [this file] ). Upregulated DEGs in male and female LOAD2 mice were enriched for the “motor proteins” KEGG pathways (Table SB [this file] ). 
In females, we observed only 9 significant DEGs (3 upregulated, 6 downregulated) ( < 0.05) in LOAD2 mice on control diet (CD), while 2988 genes were significantly differentially expressed (1565 upregulated, 1423 downregulated) ( < 0.05) in LOAD2+HFD (Table SA [this file] ). We observed 44 significantly DEGs (19 upregulated, 25 downregulated) ( < 0.05) in female LOAD1+CD, while 164 genes were significantly differentially expressed (117 upregulated, 47 downregulated) ( < 0.05) in female LOAD1+HFD (Table SA [this file] ). In males, we observed a total of 7 and 23 significant DEGs ( < 0.05) in LOAD1 and LOAD2 mice on CD, respectively, while 39 and 98 genes were significantly expressed ( < 0.05) in LOAD1 and LOAD2 mice on HFD, respectively (Table SA [this file] ). 
Functional enrichment analyses of DEGs in female LOAD2+HFD identified enrichment of multiple KEGG pathways such as “glutamatergic synapse,” “dopaminergic synapse,” and “MAPK signaling pathway” in upregulated genes, while downregulated genes were enriched for KEGG pathways such as “lysosome,” “fatty acid metabolism,” “TCS cycle,” and “valine, leucine and isoleucine degradation.” Differentially upregulated genes in female LOAD1+HFD were enriched for “circadian entrainment,” while downregulated genes were enriched for “phagosome” KEGG pathway (Table SB [this file] ). 
We observed 260 significant DEGs (154 upregulated, 106 downregulated) ( < 0.05) in female LOAD2+HFD compared to female LOAD2+CD, while 45 significant DEGs (9 upregulated, 36 downregulated) ( < 0.05) in male LOAD2+HFD compared to male LOAD2+CD (Table SA [this file] ). In LOAD1 male mice, we observed a total of 12 DEGs ( < 0.05) on HFD compared to CD, while only two DEGs ( < 0.05) on HFD compared to CD in female LOAD1 mice (Table SA [this file] ). Upregulated genes in female LOAD2 female mice on HFD compared to CD were enriched for KEGG pathways such as “glutamatergic synapse,” “dopaminergic synapse,” and “MAPK signaling pathway,” while downregulated genes in female LOAD2+HFD compared to CD were enriched for “motor proteins” pathway (Table SB [this file] ). 
WGCNA identified 30 distinct modules of co‐expressed genes (Table SB2 [this file] ). 
To understand the functional significance of these modules, we correlated each module eigengene with age, sex, diet, genotype, and measured behavioral assays such as cumulative frailty score, body weights, NfL, plasma cytokines, GFAP, Iba1, and NeuN counts (Figure S4 [this file] ). Two modules (greenyellow and sienna3) were significantly correlated with the Apoe4.Trem2*R47H allele combination in both LOAD1 and LOAD2 ( < 0.05), while five modules were significantly correlated with humanized Aβ specific to LOAD2 ( < 0.05) (brown, thistle3, greenyellow, blue, and orange) (Figure S4 [this file] ). 
We observed that HFD was strongly significantly correlated with the lightyellow module ( = 0.45; = 9 × 10 ), while age was strongly significantly correlated with both the turquoise ( = 0.81; = 2 × 10 ) and lightyellow modules ( = 0.52; = 1 × 10 ) (Figure S4 [this file] ). 
We also observed that the diet and age driven lightyellow module was significantly correlated ( < 0.05) with multiple assays such as NfL, frailty score, plasma cytokines (interleukin [IL]1β, IL10, IL5, IL6, KC‐GRO) (Figure 3B [rid=alz13828-fig-0003] , Figure S4 [this file] ). In contrast, the age driven turquoise module was significantly correlated ( < 0.05) with effect of age on behavior and weakly correlated with a few plasma cytokines (IL2, interferon gamma [IFN‐γ]) and inflammatory cell counts (Iba1 and GFAP counts) (Figure 3B [rid=alz13828-fig-0003] , Figure S4 [this file] ). 
We found that genes in lightyellow modules were significant enriched for the Apoptosis (odds ratio = 1.90, = 2.11 × 10 ), Immune Response (odds ratio = 1.63, = 3.67 × 10 ), Lipid Metabolism (odds ratio = 2.01, = 3.64 × 10 ), Oxidative Stress (odds ratio = 1.76, = 3.32 × 10 ), and Vasculature (odds ratio = 2.14, = 1.14 × 10 ) AD biological domains (Figure 3C–D [rid=alz13828-fig-0003] ; Table SB3 [this file] ). We also identified GO‐terms associated with these biological domains that are significantly enriched in lightyellow gene modules (Figure 3C–D [rid=alz13828-fig-0003] , Table SB3 [this file] ). On the other hand, genes in the turquoise module were prominently enriched for the Immune Response biological domain (odds ratio = 2.39, = 1.8 × 10 ) (Table SB3 [this file] ). 
To focus on effects in aged mice, we assessed protein expression changes in 18 month old LOAD1 and LOAD2 mice on CD and HFD compared to age‐matched B6J mice on CD by one‐way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with post‐hoc Tukey significance testing (Table SC [this file] ). In LOAD1 mice on CD, we observed 1666 significantly differentially expressed proteins (838 upregulated, 828 downregulated) (padj < 0.05), while a total of 2590 proteins were significantly differentially expressed (1237 upregulated, 1353 downregulated) (padj < 0.05) in LOAD1+HFD compared to B6J mice on CD (Table SC [this file] ). 
These included M1_Synapse_Neuron, M3_Oligo_Myelination, and M12_Cytoskeleton (Figure 4A [rid=alz13828-fig-0004] ; Table SD [this file] ). The M2_Mitochondria module exhibited significant positive correlation ( < 0.05) with all mouse models except LOAD2 mice on HFD, for which a positive correlation did not reach significance ( = 0.06) (Figure 4A [rid=alz13828-fig-0004] ; Table SD [this file] ). Additional correlations reaching significance included LOAD1 mice on HFD and LOAD2 mice on both diets with M22_Post‐Synaptic_Density and M38_Heat_Shock_Folding modules (Figure 4A [rid=alz13828-fig-0004] ; Table SD [this file] ). LOAD2+HFD additionally showed significant positive correlations with M4_Synapse_Neuron, M7_MAPK_Metabolism, and M43_Ribonucleoprotein_Binding modules (Figure 4A [rid=alz13828-fig-0004] ; Table SD [this file] ), whereas other mice (LOAD1+CD, LOAD1+HFD and LOAD2+CD) were positively correlated but below the significance threshold. 
Proteins that showed mouse‐human directional coherence in the M1_Synapse_Neuron module were enriched for biological functions including “synaptic vesicle cycle,” “vesicle‐mediated transport in synapse,” and “synapse organization” (Figure 4B [rid=alz13828-fig-0004] ; Table SE [this file] ). Proteins that showed directional coherence in the M4_Synapse_Neuron module were enriched for “synaptic vesicle cycle” and “exocytosis” biological functions (Figure 4B [rid=alz13828-fig-0004] ; Table SE [this file] ). In the M22_Post‐Synaptic_Density module, coherent mouse‐human proteins were enriched for biological functions including “synapse organization,” “postsynapse organization,” and “dendrite development” (Figure 4B [rid=alz13828-fig-0004] ; Table SE [this file] ). 
For non‐synaptic modules, we found coherent proteins in the M3_Oligo_Myelination module were enriched for biological functions including “oligodendrocyte differentiation,” “myelination,” and “microtubule organization” (Figure 4B [rid=alz13828-fig-0004] ; Table SE [this file] ). Proteins with directional coherence in the M7_MAPK_Metabolism module were enriched for biological functions such as “regulation of transforming growth factor beta production” and “carbohydrate metabolic process” (Figure 4B [rid=alz13828-fig-0004] ; Table SE [this file] ). In the M28_Ribosome_Translation module, protein abundances mostly increased (logFC > 0) and were enriched for “ribosome biogenesis” and “cytoplasmic translation” (Figure 4B–C [rid=alz13828-fig-0004] ; Table SE [this file] ). Finally, coherent proteins in the M38_Heat_Shock_Folding module were enriched for “protein folding” and “chaperone‐mediated protein folding” biological functions (Figure 4B [rid=alz13828-fig-0004] ; Table SE [this file] ). 
Statistical analysis revealed a significant reduction in brain volume was observed at 4 and 18 months in LOAD2+HFD male mice (4 months, = 0.0225 and 18 months, = 7.88e‐6; Table SF [this file] ), while no significant difference was observed at 12 months ( = 0.5134; Table SF [this file] ). For LOAD2 female mice on a HFD, a significant difference was observed at 18 months ( = 0.0186), but no significant disparities at 4 months ( = 0.812; Table SF [this file] ) or 12 months ( = 0.4911; Table SF [this file] ). 
Notably, the analyses unveiled a progressive increase in the number of significant areas with advancing age of the mice (Figure 5A,B [rid=alz13828-fig-0005] ; Table SF [this file] ). 
Similar to cohort 1, neurodegeneration and gliosis were also measured in the cortex and subiculum (Figure S5 [this file] ). 
In addition to biomarker analysis through aging, the cohort were also evaluated for cognitive function assessed by a touchscreen testing battery as well as evaluating the effects of food restriction necessary for touchscreen testing and its impact on cytokine levels (Figure 8 [rid=alz13828-fig-0008] and Figure S6 [this file] ). 
In cohort 5, the middle‐aged (6–12 months old) start for HFD (Figure S6A [this file] ) produced a more modest effect on plasma TNFα with LOAD2+HFD males showing higher concentrations of plasma TNFα at 4 months on diet relative to WT males on CD ( = 0.0241) and at 5 months on diet relative to LOAD2 and WT males on CD ( = 0.0451 and = 0.0034), LOAD2+HFD females showing higher concentrations of TNFα relative to LOAD2+CD females only at 5 months on diet ( = 0.0291), and WT males but not females on HFD showing higher concentrations of TNFα relative to WT+CD mice also only at 5 months on diet ( = 0.0091 males and = 0.998 females, Figure S6B [this file] ). In all other cytokines measured—IL‐6, IL‐10, IL‐1β, IFNγ, IL‐5, KC‐GRO and IL‐2 (Figure S6C–I [this file] )—there was no significant effect of diet on LOAD2 or WT males or females, though we did again observe a sex‐effect in plasma IL‐5 with concentrations being higher in LOAD2 females compared to LOAD2 males regardless of diet ( < 0.01 at 2 months on diet and < 0.05 at 3 months on diet, Figure S6G [this file] ). 
Concentrations of plasma Aβ40 and 42 were also altered by HFD in cohort 4 (Figure 8J–K [rid=alz13828-fig-0008] ) and by genotype but not diet or sex in cohort 5 (Figure S6J,K [this file] ) consistent with the observation that HFD started earlier in life (cohort 4) produces a more robust phenotype than when initiated midlife (cohort 5). As demonstrated in Figure S7A [this file] LOAD2 mice beginning HFD at 6+ months of age (cohort 5) failed to demonstrate increases in plasma Aβ40 relative to LOAD2+CD (Figure S6J [this file] ). Plasma Aβ42 was significantly increased in LOAD2+HFD females from cohort 4 compared to LOAD2+CD females at 18 months of age ( < 0.0001, Figure 8K [rid=alz13828-fig-0008] ) and compared to age‐matched WT+CD females ( = 0.0319, Figure S6K [this file] ). 
During the initial associative learning, pretraining phase of the task in which subjects were required to demonstrate the ability to pair the presentation and touch response to the visual stimuli with the presentation of the reward, all subjects irrespective of age, genotype, diet, or sex, demonstrated intact associative learning and completed the pretraining steps (Figure S7 [this file] ). 
The lack of ability to learn the task in HFD mice is unlikely to be explained by food motivation, as both HFD and CD groups were sufficiently restricted, and all groups independent of diet or genotype acquired the initial touch‐reward association (Figure S6 [this file] ). Figure S6M [this file] illustrates performance of aged (18+ month) LOAD2 mice on CD (purple diamonds) and age‐ and sex‐matched C57BL/6J (WT) mice on control diet ( = 3–5 per genotype) on the LD task for both large (easy) and small (hard) separation conditions (mean ± s.e.m.). 
While both modules were enriched for immune response, this enrichment was more significant in the turquoise ( = 1.8 × 10 ) than the lightyellow ( = 3.7 × 10 ) module (Table SB3 [this file] ). 
Interestingly, across two separate cohorts, advanced aged mice conditioned on a HFD either from 2 months of age or from 6+ months of age failed to meet learning criteria with daily performance at or below chance levels (Figure 8 [rid=alz13828-fig-0008] and Figure S7 [this file] ). 
While there was robust cross‐cohort and cross‐laboratory replicability for plasma cytokines irrespective of the different laboratory environments, we observed divergent results for plasma Aβ for cohort 2 (Figure 5D,E [rid=alz13828-fig-0005] ) versus cohorts 4 and 5 (Figure 8J,K [rid=alz13828-fig-0008] and Figure S7J,K [this file] ).

context_description:
Altogether, we built predictive models for 50,000 to 80,000 isoforms across 8,000 to 12,000 unique genes per tissue that met CV cutoffs ( Methods [rid=Sec9] , Extended Data Figs. 3 [rid=Fig9] – 5 [rid=Fig11] and Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). 
At the isoform level (criterion 1), through multivariate modeling, we trained 2.3- to 2.5-fold more models at CV > 0.01 across the 48 tissues, compared to univariate approaches (Fig. 3a [rid=Fig3] ). isoTWAS improved prediction for 79–82% of isoforms with a median increase of ~1.8- to 2.4-fold increase in adjusted (Extended Data Fig. 3a,b [rid=Fig9] and Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). Concordant with simulations, multivariate elastic net outperformed other methods, indicating that leveraging the shared genetic architecture between isoforms aids in marginal prediction of each isoform (Extended Data Fig. 3c [rid=Fig9] and Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). 
The number of unique genes with >1 isoTWAS model at CV > 0.01 (inclusion criterion for isoTWAS trait mapping) was 1.9–2.5 times larger than the number of unique genes with TWAS models achieving CV > 0.01 for gene expression prediction (Fig. 3c [rid=Fig3] , Extended Data Fig. 4a [rid=Fig10] and Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). Multivariate isoTWAS models outperformed univariate TWAS models in predicting total gene expression, with a 15.2% median percent increase in adjusted when training in GTEx and testing in PsychENCODE/AMP-AD and 23.9% vice versa (Fig. 3e [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). 
As genes differ in the number and expression patterns of their constituent isoforms, gene length, SNP density, quantification accuracy, and other relevant factors, we characterized their impact on isoTWAS performance ( Methods [rid=Sec9] , Supplementary Note [this file] , Extended Data Fig. 6 [rid=Fig12] and Supplementary Data 3 [rid=MOESM7] and 4 [rid=MOESM8] ). We discuss these evaluations in detail in Supplementary Note [this file] . 
In the developing cortex, despite a smaller sample size, 16,504 and 10,535 models for genes were successfully trained using isoTWAS and TWAS, respectively ( Methods [rid=Sec9] and Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). 
Across a combined 1,149 GWAS loci, isoTWAS identified significant associations within 323, compared with 201 detected by TWAS, a ~ 60% increase in discovery (Fig. 5b [rid=Fig5] , Methods [rid=Sec9] and Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ). Finally, to explore whether these isoTWAS-specific associations were capturing true disease signal, we compared the rate at which each method prioritized constrained genes (probability of loss-of-function intolerance, pLI ≥ 0.9; Supplementary Tables 5 [this file] – 8 [this file] ), which are known to be substantially enriched for disease associations . 
Using a heuristic to estimate increases in effective sample size ( Methods [rid=Sec9] ), we observed an approximate increase in effective sample size of 10–20% when using isoTWAS compared to TWAS (Fig. 5e [rid=Fig5] and Supplementary Table 9 [this file] ). 
In the Supplementary Note [this file] , we discuss several examples of trait associations for which isoTWAS prioritized a highly constrained gene within a GWAS locus (Supplementary Tables 5 [this file] – 8 [this file] ) . 
We illustrate several examples of isoTWAS-prioritized isoforms, all in the adult cortex, for genes with limited or distinct expression QTLs (Fig. 6 [rid=Fig6] , Extended Data Fig. 10b [rid=Fig16] and Supplementary Data 14 [this file7] ), with exon/intron structure shown in Supplementary Figs 1 [this file] – 4 [this file] . 
Further mathematical details are provided in Supplemental Methods [this file] .

Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] summarizes the workflow and data used for this project. The total number of subjects across all cohorts was 23 885, of which 13 190 were cases ( Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). For this analysis, 1000 cases for each disease were randomly sampled to ensure even representation, resulting in a final sample size of 5000 cases ( Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). 
Variant level QC included call rate pruning (<0.05) and pruning SNPs with a minor allele frequency (MAF) < 0.05 for exclusion ( Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). The merged data were then passed through an ancestry prediction and pruning method to ensure all samples were of European descent ( Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). 
Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] summarizes the dimensionality reduction and clustering analyses performed. 
Across the different splits and iterations, mean shift consistently identifies the main cluster that contains the majority (>4000 out of 5000 individuals) of the samples ( Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ). More information on the iterative clustering approach can be found in the Supplementary material, ‘Methods’ section [this file] . 
To account for the increased variability that comes with running the pipeline on a reduced sample size, individuals were grouped into C0 or C2 (C1 if only two clusters were identified in a disease subset) if they were consistently inside or outside the main cluster for at least 12 of the 15 70:30 (training:testing) splits ( Supplementary material, ‘Methods’ section [this file] ). 
Using the iterative clustering approach, C0 contained 2863 samples, C1 contained 2074 samples and C2 contained 63 samples ( Fig. 1A [rid=awad161-F1] and Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] ). 
All specified variants, aside from rs41290102, show significant associations with low density lipoprotein cholesterol levels as well as high cholesterol in the Open Targets PheWAS look up ( Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ). In addition, of the top 20 variants associated with each cluster, 13 were consistent across clustering iterations for C0 and C1, and nine were consistent for C2 ( Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). 
The individual SNP regressions reveal variants localized with , and are significantly associated with all clusters ( Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ). Given its importance in determining NDD and AD risk, it should be noted that the variant itself is not significantly associated with membership in any of the clusters ( Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ). 
For the NDD-specific clusters, only AD and FTD had a group of samples that were consistently outside the main cluster across all iterations (i.e. a presence of C2), containing 14 and 25 samples, respectively ( Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] ). Interestingly, across all single-disease clustering analyses, the AD PRS is significantly associated with differentiating subsets of samples ( Table 2 [rid=awad161-T2] and Supplementary Table 9 [this file] ). 
Supplementary Table 10 [this file] compares the multi-disease cluster counts from the iterative clustering approach with the four conditional analyses described previously. Hierarchical clustering also identifies three clusters that show a similar pattern to the iterative clustering approach ( Supplementary Fig. 5 [this file] ). Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] contains a dendrogram to visualize the hierarchical relationship between the clusters formed. However, when looking at the disease enrichments per cluster the only changes in significance are the presence of PD in C1 and ALS in C2 ( Supplementary Table 11 [this file] ). 
The proportion of samples in C2 increased for the analysis with the locus removed when compared to the original analysis ( Supplementary Fig. 7 [this file] ). C2 is significantly enriched with LBD, but not to the point of significance in the regressions, revealing that the increase in C2 size is largely due to LBD cases ( Supplementary Table 12 [this file] ). The PRS regressions revealed a similar trend, with PRS for AD, PD, ALS and LBD having significant negative associations with membership in C0 and significant positive associations with membership in C1 ( Supplementary Table 13 [this file] ). 
The proportion of samples in each cluster is very similar for the downsampled analysis when compared to the 5000 sample analysis ( Supplementary Fig. 8 [this file] ). Again, none of the clusters show significant enrichment of LBD ( Supplementary Table 14 [this file] ). The same trend in PRS regressions was observed, with PRS for AD, PD, ALS and LBD having significant negative associations with membership in C0 and significant positive associations with membership in C1 ( Supplementary Table 15 [this file] ). 
Of the 1000 controls included as a negative control, 991 are grouped into C0 ( Supplementary Fig. 9 [this file] ). Because of this, C0 is most significantly enriched with controls (OR = 108.690, = 6.1 × 10 , beta = 4.688, SE = 0.450) and is significantly depleted for all NDDs except ALS ( Supplementary Table 16 [this file] ). Once again, C0 shows significant negative associations with PRS for each NDD besides FTD, which is expected as nearly every control is contained within the cluster ( Supplementary Table 17 [this file] ). 
The LDSC analysis showed that AD and PD ( = 0.197, SE = 0.084, = 0.019), AD and LBD ( = 0.385, SE = 0.188, = 0.040), and PD and LBD ( = 0.599, SE = 0.166, = 3.0 × 10 ) were the only pairs of NDDs to have significant genetic correlations ( Supplementary Table 18 [this file] ). This is less genetic overlap than is seen in the NDD-specific clustering analysis, where significant associations were seen between the AD PRS and cluster membership in all studied NDDs, as well as the ALS PRS and cluster membership for AD and FTD ( Supplementary Table 9 [this file] ).
