Expression data was collected as part of two independent studies (studies 1 and 2, Table S1 [this file] ). 
After quality control (QC), a total of 22,560 unique genes were detected in both studies, the majority (67%) of which are protein-coding (Table S2 [this file] , Figure S1 [this file] ). Importantly, a secondary model that adjusted for cell proportions (Figure S2 [this file] ) showed congruent expression dysregulation, indicating that the expression perturbations are not confounded by neuropathology-induced differences in cell populations. 
Also see Supplementary Table 1 [this file] . 
We observed biologically congruent gene expression associations with both diagnosis and neuropathology such that genes that are higher in PSP than controls are also positively correlated with tau neuropathologies and those that are down in PSP have negative neuropathology correlations (Fig. 1b [rid=Fig1] , S3 [this file] ). In contrast, many of the PSP down-regulated genes are oligodendrocyte-specific ( < 0.001, 77 genes) (Figs. 1b, c [rid=Fig1] , S4 [this file] ). 
One of the top perturbed genes is the antisense RNA which is significantly lower in PSP brains (logFC = −1.00, FDR = 8.790E-5, Figs. 1d, e [rid=Fig1] , S5 [this file] , Table S3 [this file] ). 
These consensus network modules were robust with high agreement between the gene expression clusters and module assignments (Figure S6a [this file] ) and high preservation of modules between the two studies (Figure S6b [this file] ). These associations were consistent across both studies (Figure S7 [this file] ). 
Gene ontology (GO) terms enriched in co-expression modules were broadly consistent with their cell types (Fig. 2d [rid=Fig2] , S8 [this file] , Supplementary Data 3 [rid=MOESM6] ). 
We sought to further replicate the glial gene expression changes from bulk brain RNAseq detected in our two independent studies by conducting snRNAseq experiments in brain tissue samples from the TCX of PSP and control patients (Table S4 [this file] ). After QC (Figure S9 [this file] ), we obtained 26,241 nuclei from 34 brain samples comprising 18 PSP and 16 controls. There was no statistically significant enrichment of nuclei from either sex or diagnosis in any cluster (Figures S10, [this file] 11 [this file] ). 
We annotated each cluster based on the overlap of their highly overexpressed cluster-marker genes and a list of (see Methods) well-known cell-type marker genes curated from the literature (Fig. 3b [rid=Fig3] ) or via published databases Figure S12 [this file] , 13 [this file] ) , which yielded consistent annotations. 
We detected significantly up- or down-regulated DEGs in both neuronal and glial clusters (Table S5 [this file] , Supplementary Data 4 [rid=MOESM7] ). 
We subsequently evaluated the overlap between the snRNAseq DEGs in each nuclear cluster with genes from the three modules (Fig. 3e [rid=Fig3] , S14 [this file] ). 
The subset of these module genes that are also significant snRNAseq DEGs in the same glial cell clusters still constitute a large number for experimental validations (Figure S14 [this file] ). 
We analyzed brain gene expression data from 24 transgenic (rTg4510) mice and their wild-type control littermates sacrificed at 4.5 or 6 months of age (Table S6 [this file] ), available on the AD Knowledge Portal . 
Of the 21 high-confidence PSP glial DEGs, 11 have a ortholog and available RNAi stocks (Tables S7, [this file] 8 [this file] ). 
Three of the 11 screened genes, , , have the strongest suppressive effect on the tau eye phenotype (Score < −1.5) when down-regulated with RNAi (Fig. 4c, d [rid=Fig4] ). is a hub gene in the astrocyte-enriched M4, whereas and are hubs in the microglia/endothelia-enriched M6 (Fig. 5 [rid=Fig5] , Figures S15, [this file] 16 [this file] ). The three genes are up-regulated even after adjusting for differences in cell proportions (Table S7 [this file] ), indicating that the expression perturbations are not driven by this but are likely associated with disease pathogenesis. Pseudobulk DEG analysis using the snRNAseq datasets also supported the up-regulation of the three genes in astrocytes (Table S8 [this file] ). Interestingly, the subclustering analysis (Figure S17 [this file] ) indicated and are up-regulated in specific populations of astrocytes including reactive astrocytes, whereas the up-regulation of is universal to all astrocytes. 
With brain snRNAseq of PSP and control donors, we further filtered down these 550 hub bulk DEGs by selecting the subset of 155 that are snRNAseq DEGs with concordant expression changes in the cell cluster corresponding to the bulk module cell type (Figure S18 [this file] ). 
We have collected RNAseq from bulk brain tissue of 408 frozen, post-mortem, temporal cortex (superior temporal gyrus) tissue samples consisting of 127 control and 281 PSP patients from two independent study cohorts (Table S1 [this file] ). 
Examples of the gating strategy are shown in Figure S19 [this file] . 
Based on the bimodal expression distribution, genes with low CQN values (CQN < 2 for study 1, CQN < −1 for study 2) were filtered out (Figure S1 [this file] ). 
A t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE) plot (Figure S6 [this file] ) was made for final modules using gene expression of the combined cohort of study 1 and 2 through R package Rtsne as described in other studies . In addition, statistics were calculated regarding the preservedness of final modules in studies 1 and 2 separately (Figure S6 [this file] ). 
Modules were manually annotated with the top GO terms from the list. (Figures S7, [this file] 8 [this file] ). 
We obtained an average of 924 nuclei (standard deviation: 469, = 36) per sample and performed quality control for each individual (Figure S9 [this file] ). First, nuclei with an extreme number of mapped UMIs (lower bound 1000, upper bound 98th percentile, or >=85,906.5, Figures S9a, b [this file] ) or detected genes (lower bound 500, upper bound 98 percentile >=9,648.8, Figures S9c, d [this file] ) were removed. Nuclei with more than 10% mitochondrial genes were also excluded (Figure S9e, f [this file] ). At a sample level, PSP sample 12117 was removed from the analysis because it has an abnormal distribution in terms of the number of mapped UMIs and the number of detected genes (Figure S9g [this file] ). PSP sample 12051 was removed due to the low number of nuclei ( = 117, Figure S9h [this file] ). Genes that are only expressed (defined as having a count of greater than 0) in less than 6 nuclei are excluded (Figure S9i [this file] ). The recorded sex for each individual was compared against that of the median expressions of 4 chromosome Y genes , , , and to identify any potential mislabeled samples (Figure S9j [this file] ). 
We checked if there was significant enrichment (fold-enriched > 5, unadjusted -value < 0.05) of nuclei from any diagnosis, sex, or sample in each cluster (Figures S10 [this file] , 11 [this file] ). 
Additional cluster cell type assignment was performed with published databases Figure S12 [this file] , 13 [this file] ) , which yielded consistent annotations. 
Pseudobulk DEG comparing the expression between PSP and control participants was performed for each cell type separately (Supplementary Data 4 [rid=MOESM7] , Table S9 [this file] ). 
To elucidate additional cell population, the astrocyte nuclei were subjected to subclustering analysis (Figure S17 [this file] ). 
Using the RNAseq data from the 4.5- and 6-month-old (Table S6 [this file] ) mice, we normalized the gene expression values using CQN, followed by QC to check for outliers or mismatched sex (Figures S20, [this file] 21 [this file] ). 
We obtained all available RNAi lines against the homologues of the high confidence PSP glial DEGs (Fig. 4a [rid=Fig4] ) from the Bloomington Drosophila Stock Center (BDSC), Transgenic RNAi Project (TRiP) collection or requested from laboratories within the fly research community (Tables S9 [this file] , 10 [this file] ).

Six of the 29 candidates have been previously nominated by AMP-AD investigators, and there is a mix of genes with transcripts and proteins that are both up and down in AD brains postmortem ( Figure S1A [this file] ). We confirmed the expression of the candidate target genes in publicly available gene expression datasets from BV2 cells (GEO accessions: GSE162526 (GSE162526) , GSE132739 (GSE132739) , and GSE137741 (GSE137741) ) by averaging the log2 transformed expression values from each dataset and plotting a heatmap ( Figure S1B [this file] ). 
A custom library of siRNAs against BioHyV targets (ON-TARGETplus siRNA) was purchased from Horizon Discovery, which consisted of a pool of four siRNA per target ( Supplementary Table S1 [this file] ). 
Knockdown efficiency of the siRNAs was confirmed with real-time PCR ( Figure S1C [this file] ). The sequences of primers used for RT-PCR are listed in ( Supplementary Table S2 [this file] ). 
All results are reported ( Supplemental Table S3 [this file] ). 
An average of 6,576 proteins were identified per sample ( Figure S2B [this file] - C [this file] ), and some samples had fewer proteins identified with one sample having only 565 proteins identified ( Figure S2B [this file] - C [this file] ). The samples with fewer protein IDs tend to also have higher median log2 protein intensity ( Figure S2B [this file] ), which may reflect protein degradation. To limit the potential for these samples to influence downstream analyses, we excluded 11 samples with fewer than 6,100 proteins identified per sample, which resulted in 3 to 6 replicates per siRNA and BV2 cell line ( Figure S2A [this file] ). A large proportion of proteins (4,850) were identified in over 300 samples ( Figure S2D [this file] ). Principal components analysis on the 310 samples ( Figure S2E [this file] - G [this file] ) revealed BV2 cell line (i.e., psen2_kd vs scramble) was the biggest contributor to intra-sample variance, and explained 41% of that variance ( Figure S2F [this file] ). Specific target knockdowns contributed less to sample variance, but can be appreciated ( Figure S2G [this file] ). Protein differential abundance was assessed using one-way ANOVA followed by post hoc correction using Tukey’s HSD as previously described [ 15 [rid=R15] ] ( Supplementary Table S4 [this file] ). The log2 fold change for each protein was used as a ranking statistic for GSEA and significantly enriched Gene Ontology (GO) terms were mapped onto the TREAT-AD biodomains (syn25428992.v10; [ 5 [rid=R5] ]) ( Supplementary Table S5 [this file] ). 
Significantly correlated terms and phenotype effects are listed ( Supplemental Table S6 [this file] ). 
Mutations in both PSEN1 and PSEN2 are causal for autosomal dominant forms of AD [ 27 [rid=R27] ] and in bulk transcriptomic meta-analyses of AMP-AD data the PSEN2 transcript is significantly decreased in AD brains relative to control brains ( Figure S3A [this file] ). 
The Psen2 knockdown condition affects the expression of nominated target genes ( Figure S1C [this file] ), and in particular Ifih1 which is 37-fold up-regulated in the Psen2 knockdown cells. We tested microglial proteomic co-expression modules [ 19 [rid=R19] ] and found that the proteins up-regulated in the Psen2 knockdown cells are significantly enriched for a module related to “Macrophage cytokine production”, while proteins that are down-regulated in Psen2 knockdown cells are significantly enriched for an “RNA processing” module ( Figure S3B [this file] ). 
We confirmed over 50% knockdown for most targets, with many as high as 70–80% knockdown ( Figure S1C [this file] ). Two targets had knockdown levels below 50%; TICAM1 knockdown averaged a 46% reduction in expression while DHX58 knockdown averaged a 19% reduction ( Figure S1C [this file] ). 
A summary of all results from cell phenotype assays is shown ( Figure 3C [rid=F3] ) and more detailed results are contained in the supplemental figures [this file] (alamarBlue, Figure S4 [this file] ; MitoTracker, Figure S5 [this file] ; NFkB Figure S6 [this file] ; phagocytosis Figure S7 [this file] ). 
We examined the proteomic effect on the target of each knockdown and found that for all but five proteins (Ifih1, Traf3, Tlr4, Ticam1, and Kat5) there was a negative log fold change for the targeted protein ( Figure S2H [this file] ). 
Protein level correlation by biological domain supports the reversal of Mitochondrial Metabolism disease associated signatures by knockdown of Ap2a2, Arhgef2, Dlat, Dld, and Pdhb ( Figure S8 [this file] ). 
Decreased expression and function of genes and proteins involved in mitochondrial bioenergetics, including PDH subunits, is an early and consistent hallmark of AD associated neurodegeneration ( Figure S1A [this file] , [ 29 [rid=R29] ]). 
Using Psen2 knockdown BV2 cells revealed heightened baseline phagocytosis and AD-relevant proteomic signatures ( Figure 2 [rid=F2] , Figure 3 [rid=F3] , Figure S2 [this file] ). 
Another limitation is the reliance on siRNA-mediated target knockdown, which introduces variability in the levels of target suppression (e.g. Figure S1C [this file] ) and may include off-target effects that confound interpretation.

We conducted an analysis of KRAB-ZNF genes and TEs expression patterns and networks using two independent RNA-seq datasets: and ( Figure 1A [rid=fig1] , Supplementary file 1, tables S1–S3 [this file] ). 
For example, there were 12 upregulated and 42 downregulated KRAB-ZNF genes, along with 31 upregulated and 22 downregulated TEs in humans compared to chimpanzees in the primary and secondary cortices ( Figure 2B [rid=fig2] ; see Supplementary file 1, table S2 [this file] for information on Brodmann areas included in the group ‘primary and secondary cortices’). 
To systematically analyze the putative functional relationships between TEs and KRAB-ZNF genes, we conducted pairwise Pearson’s correlation analysis using normalized expression levels in seven clustered brain regions ( Supplementary file 1, table S2 [this file] and Figure 1 in Khrameeva et al., 2020 [rid=bib43] ). There were 324 KRAB-ZNFs and 895 TEs (subfamily level) expressed in Primate Brain Data (copy number provided in Supplementary file 1, table S4 [this file] ). In humans, we found 100,987 positive and 26,810 negative significant correlations between TEs and KRAB-ZNFs in the primary and secondary cortices and 38,295 positive and 11,475 negative significant correlations in the limbic and association cortices (adjusted p-value<0.01), while the other clusters have fewer or no correlations detected ( Supplementary file 1, table S5 [this file] ). 
For a fair comparison across species, we required that a correlation between KRAB-ZNFs and TEs in humans needed to be significantly detected in all human leave-one-out combinations ( Figure 4A [rid=fig4] , Supplementary file 1, table S6 [this file] ). 
However, it is important to note that such an analysis would have been limited by the detectable correlations of only 3 out of 9 KRAB-ZNF genes and 9 out of 92 TE subfamilies in our dataset ( Supplementary file 1, table S7 [this file] ). 
More details about samples and the preparation steps can be found in Supplementary file 1, table S1 [this file] and Khrameeva et al., 2020 [rid=bib43] .

Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) is a neurodegenerative disease characterized by the accumulation of tau in the brain along with symptoms such as postural instability and ocular motor abnormalities.[rid=mds30150-bib-0001] ,[rid=mds30150-bib-0002] ,[rid=mds30150-bib-0003] Despite a number of other loci identified through association studies in the last decade,[rid=mds30150-bib-0004] ,[rid=mds30150-bib-0005] ,[rid=mds30150-bib-0006] ,[rid=mds30150-bib-0007] the 17q21.31 of human genome, which presents two haplotypes H1 and H2 (distinguished by a ~1 Mb inversion, Figure S1A [this file] in Data S1 [this file] ), remains the most prominent genetic risk factor for PSP. 
At least 10 structural forms within 17q21.31 can be characterized by H1 and H2 along with three large duplications (ie, α, β, γ; Figure S1B [this file] in Data S1 [this file] ).[rid=mds30150-bib-0012] ,[rid=mds30150-bib-0013] However, the impact of these structural forms and copy number variations (CNVs) on PSP risk has not been systematically assessed. To assess the impact of these structural forms and CNVs on PSP risk, the copy numbers of α, β, and γ and structural forms of 17q21.31 were called from whole genome sequencing (WGS) data (Figure S1C [this file] in Data S1 [this file] ). 
WGS were performed at 30× coverage (Table S1 [this file] in Data S2 [rid=mds30150-supitem-0002] ). 
Among 4618 samples, we filtered 183 samples with abnormally low reads mapped (aligned read depth <1.7×) to α, β, or γ region (Figure S2 [this file] in Data S1 [this file] ) and 10 samples with high genotyping missing rate (>0.05). Given the specification of H1/H2 genotype, determined by the 238‐bp deletion, and the copy numbers of α, β, and γ, we can ascertain the 10 structural forms (Figure S1B [this file] in Data S1 [this file] ) in each individual. We removed 30 individuals (Figure S3 [this file] in Data S1 [this file] ) since their structural forms could not be decided based on the copy numbers of α, β, and γ. 
Clinical diagnosis criteria are outlined in the Supplementary Methods in Data S1 [this file] . 
The genomic coordinates on HG38 for α (chr17:46,135,415–46,289,349), β (chr17:46,087,894–46,356,512), and γ (chr17:46,289,349–46,707,123) were obtained from two previous studies[rid=mds30150-bib-0012] ,[rid=mds30150-bib-0013] (Figure S1A [this file] in Data S1 [this file] ). Segmental duplications can introduce mapping challenges and thus inaccurate calling of the number of copies.[rid=mds30150-bib-0020] ,[rid=mds30150-bib-0021] ,[rid=mds30150-bib-0022] To address this, we removed segmental duplicated regions inside the α, β, and γ (Figure S4 [this file] in Data S1 [this file] ) when calculating aligned read depth. Each individual was found to have up to six copies of α or β and up to eight copies of γ (Figure S1 [this file] in Data S1 [this file] ). On the H1 background, the β region, which includes α, can duplicate up to four copies, whereas on the H2 background, only the α region duplicates, with a maximum of two copies of γ (Figure S1 [this file] in Data S1 [this file] ). 
Overall, the copy number of α, β, or γ inferred by aligned read depth from WGS were highly consistent (α, R = 0.87; β, R = 0.85; γ, R = 0.96) with that from TaqMan assay (Figure S5 [this file] in Data S1 [this file] ). The experimental procedure is detailed in the Supplementary Methods in Data S1 [this file] . 
For approximately 60% of the samples, only one combination of the structural forms (Figure S1B [this file] in Data S1 [this file] ) was possible based on the H1 and H2 genotypes, determined by the 238‐bp deletion, and the copy numbers of α, β, and γ. The expectation–maximization (EM) algorithm[rid=mds30150-bib-0012] (Supplementary Methods in Data S1 [this file] ) were employed to infer the two structural forms of 17q21.31 in each individual. The allele frequency of each structural form of 17q21.31 after EM convergence are shown in Figure S1B [this file] in Data S1 [this file] . 
We also tested the models when the allele count of H2 was added as an additional covariate, as the β region can only duplicate in the H1 haplotype, the smaller α region but not the entire β duplicates in the H2 haplotype, and the γ region usually duplicates only once in the H2 haplotype (Figure S1B [this file] in Data S1 [this file] ). 
We found that each additional copy of γ was associated with 1.08‐fold (95% CI 1.02–1.15; = 0.014) of increased risk of PSP in H1H1 individuals and 1.29‐fold (95% CI 1.06–1.56; = 0.0096) of increased risk of PSP in H1H2 individuals (Table 2 [rid=mds30150-tbl-0002] ; Figure S6 [this file] in Data S1 [this file] ). 
This finding reaffirmed that the copy number of γ was associated with increased risk of PSP, and β was not associated with the risk of PSP (Table 2 [rid=mds30150-tbl-0002] ; Figure S6 [this file] in Data S1 [this file] ). On the H2 background, it was not practical to evaluate the effect of γ as H2α2γ2 dominates (Figure S1B [this file] in Data S1 [this file] ). 
Furthermore, 96% of H1c sub‐haplotypes corresponded to structural forms of 17q21.31 with more than one copy of γ (H1β1γ2, H1β1γ3, and H1β1γ4) (Figure S7 [this file] in Data S1 [this file] ). When compared with structural forms of 17q21.31 with exactly one copy of γ (H1β1γ1 and H1β2γ1), structural forms with additional copies of γ (H1β1γ2, H1β1γ3, and H1β1γ4) were more likely to be H1c or other sub‐haplotypes associated with increased risk of PSP (ie, H1o, H1d, H1g, and H1g) (Figure S7 [this file] in Data S1 [this file] ). Based on RNA‐seq of the cerebellum, we observed that the expression of three genes located on γ region, ie, (β = 0.63; = 1.16 × 10 ), (β = 0.48; = 4.21 × 10 ), and (β = 0.81; = 4.31 × 10 ) showed the strongest correlation with the copy number of γ (Fig. 2B [rid=mds30150-fig-0002] ; Figure S8A [this file] in Data S1 [this file] ; Table S9 [rid=mds30150-supitem-0002] in Data S2 [rid=mds30150-supitem-0002] ). This increased expression with higher γ copy numbers was also observed from RNA‐seq of the temporal cortex (Fig. 2C [rid=mds30150-fig-0002] ; Figure S8B [this file] in Data S1 [this file] ; Table S9 [rid=mds30150-supitem-0002] in Data S2 [rid=mds30150-supitem-0002] ). One of the most developed resources describing AD‐relevant endophenotypes is the Common Alzheimer's and Related Dementias Research Ontology (CADRO).[rid=trc212461-bib-0002] As CADRO is already in standard use for drug development classification, we leveraged this resource to help guide the initial stages of identification of relevant biological domains of AD (Table S1 [this file] ). Based on these criteria, we elected to use an exhaustive elaboration of GO terms associated with each biological domain as the core definition (Figure S2 [rid=trc212461-supitem-0001] and Table S2 [this file] , see supplemental methods for more details). 
The genetic component of AD risk, or genetic risk score, queries all ensemble gene loci for genetic associations with AD‐relevant traits across a range of studies (both GWAS/GWAX and quantitative trait locus [QTL]; see Table S3 [this file] for all studies queried). The genetic risk score for a target (Table S4 [this file] ) is calculated as the sum of the inverse rank for each of the following evidence categories, scaled to a total of three points: number of GWAS studies, minimum GWAS value across studies, mean rank of minimum GWAS value across studies, number of QTL studies, minimum QTL false discovery rate (FDR) across studies, mean rank of minimum QTL FDR across studies, coding variant summary, non‐coding variant summary, human phenotype score, model organism phenotype score, and MODEL‐AD strain and correlation. 
A ratio of means meta‐analysis with a random effects model[rid=trc212461-bib-0013] was applied separately to both transcriptomics (Table S5 [this file] ) and proteomics (Table S6 [this file] ) datasets; modality‐specific weights were subsequently generated (see supplemental methods for details). To harness weights into a single value, a weighted adjustment by modality was applied (Table S7 [this file] ). For genes with no statistically significant RNA or protein values, this weight was set to zero and the weight was then multiplied by 2 to attain the points value of the multi‐omic risk score component (Table S8 [this file] ). 
The list of AD GWAS hits is derived from integrating genes identified from three sources: the supplementary table that accompanies Neuner et al. (2020),[rid=trc212461-bib-0015] Table S5 [this file] from Bellenguez et al. (2022), which identifies all genome‐wide significant loci,[rid=trc212461-bib-0006] and the list of AD loci with genetic evidence compiled by the ADSP Gene Verification Committee ( adsp.niagads.org/index.php/gvc‐top‐hits‐list/ (https://adsp.niagads.org/index.php/gvc-top-hits-list/) ). For our investigation of clinical trial target genes, we obtained the list of “known drugs” from the Open Targets API (Table S9 [this file] ). 
Leveraging the CADRO ontology, with augmentation through literature curation and biological alignment with the employed multi‐omic datasets (see methods), we established 19 biological domains that covered the AD endophenotypic space (Table S1 [this file] ). The number of terms annotated to each domain varies enormously (Figure 1A [rid=trc212461-fig-0001] , Table S2 [this file] ); the Synapse domain requires 1379 terms to define, while Tau Homeostasis only requires 10 terms. 
The genetic risk score component is a summary of genetic evidence supporting the target gene's association with late‐onset AD (LOAD), drawing from GWAS and quantitative trait locus (QTL) studies.[rid=trc212461-bib-0019][rid=trc212461-bib-0021] In total, 27 different association studies were queried (Table S3 [this file] , Figure S4 [rid=trc212461-supitem-0001] ). Gene‐level results for all evidence sources were summed to generate the genetic risk score (Figure 2A [rid=trc212461-fig-0002] , Table S4 [this file] ). 
GSEA using the genetics score to rank genes identifies significant GO terms from 17 biological domains; the biological domains with the largest number of enriched GO terms are Synapse, Lipid Metabolism, and Structural Stabilization (Figure 2C,D [rid=trc212461-fig-0002] , Table S10 [this file] ). 
The score makes use of proteomic and transcriptomic datasets generated as part of AMP‐AD consortium efforts (Tables S5 and S6 [this file] ). 
The calculated weights for each modality are combined using a scoring harness (Table S7 [this file] ) that yields a higher score for targets with evidence for both, followed by targets with evidence for protein only, followed lastly by targets with evidence for RNA only (Figure 3E [rid=trc212461-fig-0003] ). 
We compare the distribution of all scored targets (Table S8 [this file] ) to those scored by the Open Targets platform[rid=trc212461-bib-0016] ,[rid=trc212461-bib-0022] and those nominated for follow‐up by the AMP‐AD consortium.[rid=trc212461-bib-0005] ,[rid=trc212461-bib-0024] The AMP‐AD nominated targets tend to have higher multi‐omic scores than the population of all targets (Figure 3F [rid=trc212461-fig-0003] ), and there is a very weak correlation between the multi‐omic score and the number of nominations received by a given target ( = 0.153; Figure S8E [rid=trc212461-supitem-0001] ). 
The domains with the largest number of enriched terms include Synapse, Immune Response, Structural Stabilization, and Mitochondrial Metabolism (Figure 3G,H [rid=trc212461-fig-0003] , Table S11 [this file] ). 
The TRS is derived by summing the component risk scores (ie, genetic and multi‐omic), and the highest ranked target scores 4.74 out of a maximum possible score of 5 (Table S12 [this file] ).

Our gene set enrichment analysis further supports MTCH2 involvement across a wide array of metabolic processes (Additional file 1 [this file] : Fig. S.10). 
This preliminary evidence aligns with the KNOP1 expanded gene set enrichment which shows a strong signal for mitotic cell phase transition and regulation of DNA-binding transcription factor activity (Additional file 1 [this file] : Fig. S.11).

Iterative normalization was performed to regress significant covariates for individual studies including, but not limited to, diagnosis, age at death, sex, and post mortem interval (Additional file 2 [this file] : Table S1). 
An iterative normalization model was deployed to identify significant covariates and regress them from the expression data before scaling the data (Additional file 2 [this file] : Table S2). 
Correction for 18 multiple comparisons was applied for replication of associated genes (Additional file 2 [this file] : Table S2). COLOC analysis was carried out to examine the probabilities that the expression-AD phenotype signals for the remaining targets were driven by the same underlying genomic variant etiology [ 24 [rid=CR24] – 26 [rid=CR26] ] (Additional file 2 [this file] : Table S6). 
Wilcoxon rank-sum tests were performed comparing value distributions between SNPs near genes with trained weights versus those without, as well as within and intergenic regions (Additional file 2 [this file] : Fig. S6). 
Association of all remaining genes was further supported by SMR (Additional file 2 [this file] : Table S3). 
Colocalization analysis resulted in a 99% probability that GWAS association signal and functional TWAS signal for CD2AD originate from shared causal variants (Additional file 2 [this file] : Table S6). 
While there is a non-zero probability (H2 = 0.18), our signal arises only due to GWAS association, which may be a function of EED risk variants being in linkage with PICALM risk variants (Additional file 2 [this file] : Table S6). 
Colocalization analysis yielded a high probability that GWAS and functional associations were driven by shared genetic risk factors (H4 = 0.809) (Additional file 2 [this file] : Table S6). 
This is likely a result of LD within this region (Additional file 2 [this file] : Table S6). 
While this speaks to the high LD within this window and the dominating signal from APOE, there remains evidence for a distinct regulatory schema for CLPTM1 (Additional file 2 [this file] : Table S6).

Contrary to the ~4–16 h needed for EV isolation with other technologies, SECrifuge can be performed in ~60 min with >10-fold enrichment ( < 0.05) than SEC (Supplementary Fig. 1A, B [this file] ). Compared to UC, SECrifuge replicates were highly correlated (Rho = 0.97 vs 0.6, < 0.05) (Supplementary Fig. 1C, D [this file] ). When compared with other approaches, is rapid (<60 min), highly reproducible ( > 96%), cost-effective (<$10/prep), requires no specialist equipment, and is amenable to clinical settings (Supplementary Fig. 1E [this file] ). SECrifuge replicates displayed relatively low variability, while UC replicates introduced considerable additional variability, indicating highly expressed genes detected at significantly different expression levels (Fig. 1P [rid=Fig1] , Supplementary Fig. 1F [this file] ). Finally, we compared a list of brain-derived RNA markers in each individual serum EV sample (Supplementary Fig. 1F [this file] ). SECrifuge demonstrated reproducible identification of brain-derived markers in all six samples, while UC isolated samples displayed low reproducibility (Supplementary Fig. 1F [this file] ). 
Schematic drawing of integrative methodology used in this study to isolate diverse EVPs from brain and blood (described in detail in Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] ). Unprocessed TEMs are provided in Supplementary Fig. 2F, H [this file] . 
Small EVs mostly displayed a frequently reported round cup-shaped morphology associated with ~100–150 nm particles , while SECmeres mostly displayed sub-50 nm electron dense morphologies (Fig. 1D, E [rid=Fig1] , unprocessed TEMs are provided in Supplementary Fig. 2A–F [this file] ). 
To address this, we treated each EVP subpopulation (10 human subjects’ tissue and blood, EVP = 60) with RNase (Supplementary Fig. 3A–D [this file] ). We found that most of the small EVs and SECmeres associated RNAs were resistant to RNase treatment (Supplementary Fig. 3A–D [this file] ). 
In contrast, the non-EV markers, cytochrome C, Ecadhrin, and HSP90 were not significantly ( > 0.05) different between large EVs, small EVs, and SECmeres (Supplementary Fig. 4A–D [this file] ). The debris exclusion marker HMGB, a nonhistone nuclear protein, was below the detection limits in our assay (Supplementary Fig. 4C, D [this file] ). Common adhesion proteins, Perforin and EpCAM, were not significantly enriched in EVPs ( > 0.05) (Supplementary Fig. 4C, D [this file] ). 
The lipoproteins (ApoA, ApoB, ApoC), which are commonly associated with HDL, LDL, vLDL, and Chylomicrons, were consistently depleted in the proteome of small EVs (Fig. 2D, E [rid=Fig2] , and Supplementary Fig. 4E, F [this file] ). We also investigated other common co-isolates (Argonaute proteins, nuclear proteins, calnexin, golgimatrix130, and histones), none of which were significantly ( < 0.05) enriched in large EVs, small EVs, and SECmeres (Supplementary Fig. 4G, H [this file] ). 
Finally, we curated a list of brain-specific protein markers (Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ) from the Human Protein Atlas, GTEx Portal, and Allen Brain Atlas . Over 95% of the select proteins in our curated list were enriched in the brain, reflecting brain lineage specific markers (Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). 
Using unsupervised clustering of the RNA-seq data, we were reassured that brain and blood samples displayed distinct enrichment of the RNA molecules within each EVP subtype (large EVs, small EVs, and SECmeres) (Supplementary Fig. 5A, B [this file] displays brain blood RNAs). We next compared our curated list of brain-specific transcripts with the EVP transcriptomes and found that EVs from brain and blood are enriched ( < 0.05) in neuronal (SYT1, KIF5A) and microglial (VSIG, PROS1, PLXDC2, CX3CR1) transcripts (Fig. 4H, J [rid=Fig4] ) and (Supplementary Fig. 5A, B [this file] ). SECmeres, on the other hand, show enrichment for a different set of neuronal (L1CAM, ENO2) and microglial transcripts (CSF1R) (Fig. 4H, J [rid=Fig4] ) and (Supplementary Fig. 5A, B [this file] ). 
In this new batch, we isolated EVPs ( = 115) from the brain and blood of 26 (10 AD and 16 controls) human subjects (Fig. 6A [rid=Fig6] , detailed information is provided in Supplementary Fig. 6A, B [this file] , and “methods”). Next, we performed variance partition analysis to determine the effect of AD confounding factors (demographics, age, race, sex, PMI, ApoE genotype, comorbidities, batch effect, and technical variables) in our study (Fig. 6C [rid=Fig6] , Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). This data indicates that most variance is due to enrichment of different RNAs in different EVP-subpopulations (Supplementary Fig. 6C [this file] ). While small EVs and SECmeres yielded significant (FDR < 0.05) differences, large EVs did not display differential RNA expression between AD and controls (Fig. 6D–F [rid=Fig6] , Supplementary Fig. 6D [this file] ). Overall, small EVs and SECmeres from brain and blood were able to distinguish neuropathologically confirmed AD from controls (Supplementary Fig. 7 [this file] ). Next, we aligned and harmonized the scale of clinical variables to facilitate annotation of both datasets (as described by Donghoon et al. ) and found that 9 and 4 RNA biomarkers associated with Serum AD-EPs and -EVs, respectively, we positively correlated with measures of the severity of AD neuropathology, namely diagnostic certainty of AD, CERAD, and Braak stage (Supplementary Fig. 8 [this file] ). 
To ensure that our findings provide an unbiased outcome that is not dependent upon a small number, EVP isolation methods, and is reproducible across sites/institutions, and protocols applied for RNA-seq, we have increased our QC reproducibility and RNA-seq reproducibility in our own datasets and curated external datasets from Johns Hopkins University (details provided in Supplementary table 2 [this file] ). Our combined analyses have included new brain homogenates and iPSCs from living subjects (total samples 62, with 40 AD and 22 controls) presenting a set of overlapping 45 brain-derived RNA molecules which were represented across experiments, batches, and institutions (Supplementary Fig. 9 [this file] ). 
Here, we addressed the EVP heterogeneity, which displayed the highest variance contribution as AD cofactor (Supplementary Fig. 10 [this file] ).

Since different brain regions may have different cell-type composition and biological functions, we tested for sex-biased expression in five additional regions: parahippocampal gyrus, temporal cortex, premotor, precuneus and middle frontal gyrus (Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). Within each region, about half of the proteins had higher abundance in males, while the other half had higher abundance in females at FDR < 0.05 (Supplementary Tables 2 [this file] and 3 [this file] ), which was consistent with findings from the dPFC. 
Sex-biased gene expression was observed in each of the six brain regions examined (Supplementary Tables 2, [this file] 3 [this file] ). We found 13.2% (1,354 of 10,198) proteins with sex-biased protein expression in at least one brain region at MASH LFSR < 0.05 and, among those, 4.7% were encoded by genes on the X chromosome (Supplementary Tables 2 [this file] and 3 [this file] ).

Of the index sb-pQTLs, 5.4% were pQTLs in both sexes with concordant direction of association, 2.4% were pQTLs in both sexes with discordant direction of association, 51.2% were pQTLs in males only and 37.9% were pQTLs in females only (Supplementary Tables 4 [this file] – 6 [this file] ). Among the 150 proteins with sb-pQTLs, nine were encoded by genes on the X chromosome and none were in the pseudo-autosomal region of the X chromosome (Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ).

GSEA showed that the knockout of SRGN in MES GSCs reduced the expression of genes involved in nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB) signaling, tumor necrosis factor (TNF) signaling, and IL6-JAK-STAT3 signaling (Supplementary Fig. 8c [this file] ). Analysis of Hallmark, KEGG, and Reactome pathway genesets in GSCs RNA-seq and scRNA-seq datasets (GSC-like tumor cells) revealed that these signals were characteristically enriched in MES/MES-like GSCs, indicating their important roles in MES/MES-like GSCs (Supplementary Fig. 8d, e [this file] ). Among them, NFKB1, a vital protein of the NF-κB signaling pathway, binds with SRGN (Supplementary Fig. 8g [this file] ), suggesting that SRGN plays a crucial role in MES GSCs by modulating the NF-κB signaling pathway. 
Gene expression analysis revealed that NFKB1 has a similar expression pattern as SRGN, which was also explicitly overexpressed in MES GSCs (Supplementary Fig. 8h [this file] ). The same expression distribution of NFKB1 was also verified by scRNA-seq data (Supplementary Fig. 8i [this file] ). However, SRGN knockdown did not alter NFKB1 mRNA levels (Supplementary Fig. 8j [this file] ). In contrast, the depletion of endogenous SRGN led to a drastic decrease in NFKB1 protein levels in two MES GSCs (Supplementary Fig. 8k [this file] ), indicating that SRGN may regulate NFKB1 protein stability. 
NFKB1 was gradually degraded within 8 h of CHX treatment in control cells (Supplementary Fig. 8l [this file] ). Treatment of cells with the proteasome inhibitor MG-132 resulted in a significant increase in NFKB1 protein levels (Supplementary Fig. 8m [this file] ). Blocking proteasomal degradation with MG-132 restored NFKB1 expression caused by SRGN knockdown (Supplementary Fig. 8n [this file] ), but cycloheximide-chase analysis revealed that NFKB1 half-life was reduced by half in SRGN-depleted GSCs (Supplementary Fig. 8o [this file] ).

context_description:
Cardiovascular sub‐score on the SCOPA‐AUT was negatively correlated with MSE‐ADL response ( = −0.388, < 0.001), (Table S4 [rid=mdc370291-supitem-0002] ; Fig. S1 [this file] ). 
Alongside depression and fatigue symptoms, the contribution of cardiovascular dysfunction on functional dependence may be overshadowed, as there is a significant relationship between functional dependence and cardiovascular decline, shown in Figure S1 [this file] . 
However, there was a significant positive correlation between SCOPA‐AUT cardiovascular score and GDS from 1 year follow‐up, onwards, as well as with MSE‐ADL at 6 and 7 years (Fig. S1 [this file] ), suggesting that there are associations between mood and cardiovascular function, which we have identified already as individual contributors of functional decline.

A lower GM volume was observed in the bilateral fusiform gyrus (FG) (Brodmann area, BA 19/37) and brainstem in females relative to male PD patients ( Supplementary Table S1 [this file] ). Then, while ALFF is more susceptible to physiological noise than fractional ALFF (fALFF), our GSR analysis ( Supplementary Figure S1 [this file] ) confirmed the spatial stability of these sex-divergent patterns against global artifacts.

Out of the total of 8099 patients represented in the 24 cohorts, 7745 participants had the genetic and covariate data available for inclusion in the downstream analyses (Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] ). 17% (1330) of PD patients carried thehaplotype, 8.5% (662) carried the variant, 7.9% (610) carried variants, 2.4% (187) carried the variant, and 1.9% (151) carried the variant. 
It was well correlated with the number of progression loci present ( = 0.96), yielding comparable results to the unweighted multi-locus burden (Supplementary Fig. 5 [this file] ). 
Exploratory analyses of heterozygous and homozygous carriers of the ε4 haplotype showed elevated risk of dementia for PD patients homozygous for the ε4 allele, as expected (Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] ). Subgroup analysis limited to homozygous haplotype carriers was consistent with a monotonic increase in dementia risk in association with the number of progression loci carried for the limited subset of patients homozygous for (Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] ). 
Subgroup analysis tailored to biomarkers, population-based incidence cohorts, and clinical trials showed statistically significant associations between three or more loci and decline in MMSE scores over time in all three study design types (Supplementary Table S3 [this file] ). 
For , meta-analysis of 20 cohorts yielded a summary HR of 2.05 (95% CI: 1.33–3.15; Supplementary Fig. S2 [this file] , Table 3 [rid=Tab3] ). 
Finally, for , meta-analysis of 21 cohorts identified a significant association with dementia risk (HR = 1.56, 95% CI: 1.17–2.07; Supplementary Fig. S3 [this file] , Table 3 [rid=Tab3] ). 
Compared to non-carriers, carriers of each of the five individual genotypes had an extra annual decline in MMSE score of 0.06-0.16 points (Supplementary Table S3 [this file] ). 
Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] shows an overview of the workflow. The clinical characteristics of the 24 cohorts are summarized in Supplementary Tables S2 [this file] – S4 [this file] and delineated in detail in Refs. 
Supplementary Table S2 [this file] and Refs. list the specific dementia criteria used for each of the 24 cohorts. 
Genotyping and sample quality control steps are listed in Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] . 
We considered progression loci nominated by prior reports that met all of the following criteria: (i) Peer-reviewed original articles evaluating associations between genetic variants and cognitive decline in patients with PD; (ii) only studies using longitudinal study designs, which account for the critical time dimension, were included; (iii) variants showing associations with at least nominal statistical significance were considered. 15 loci met the three criteria and are shown in Supplementary Table 1 [this file] .

As expected for this developmental period, the prevalence of risky behaviours ( ., substance use) increased from ages 14 to 19 (Table S1 [this file] ). 
This hierarchical clustering procedure identified 18 DNAm clusters ( ., C1-C18) that showed consistent patterns of coordinated methylation change across adolescence, and spanning all 22 autosomal chromosomes (Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] ; Fig. S2 [this file] ; Table S2 [this file] ). 
Importantly, the identified DNAm clusters were technically robust, with consensus-based longitudinal clustering demonstrating significantly higher internal consistency across array platforms and batches than non-consensus approaches (see Methods and Fig. S3 [this file] ), supporting that the observed patterns reflect biological rather than methodological signal. 
We further tested the robustness of the DNAm pattern in two independent datasets of older adults (PPMI and ADNI; Table S1 [this file] ). 
Table S3 [this file] summarises DNAm levels within each cluster at ages 14 and 19, the magnitude of developmental change, and associations with sex, pubertal development (PD), and socioeconomic stress (SES). No DNAm cluster showed significant associations with pubertal development (Table S3 [this file] ). 
To infer the biological systems represented within each DNAm cluster, we performed tissue-specific gene expression enrichment (Table S4 [this file] ), Gene Ontology (GO), and KEGG pathway analyses (Table S5 [this file] , Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] ). 
These clusters were characterised by their differing overall DNAm levels and consistent patterns of change across adolescence (Table S3 [this file] ). 
At the cortical level, the majority of brain regions showed significant reductions in cortical thickness (CT) over time (Table S6 [this file] ). 
We therefore focused on the interpretation of the first canonical components of the ΔCT and ΔSubCortVol analyses (Tables S7 [this file] – S8 [this file] ; Fig. 4g, h [rid=Fig4] ). 
C12 -which showed a moderate decrease in methylation (Table S3 [this file] )– loaded negatively, indicating that greater decreases in methylation in this cluster were associated with greater cortical thinning. 
Descriptive data (Table S1 [this file] ) show significant increases in lifetime substance use from ages 14 to 19 (all < 0.0001). Accordingly, we next examined whether changes in depressive symptoms and lifetime frequency of substance use across adolescence were associated with the coordinated patterns of DNAm and cortical and subcortical changes identified in the first CCA components (Table S9 [this file] ). 
As shown in Table S10 [this file] and Fig. 5c, d [rid=Fig5] , associations with substance use differed across clusters and ages. Notably, C6 and C11, which showed an overall decrease in methylation from ages 14 to 19, were negatively associated with smoking and cannabis use (Table S10 [this file] ); associations with cannabis use, remaining significant even after controlling for smoking. 
Two clusters displayed significant associations with depressive symptoms ( < 0.05; Fig. 5e [rid=Fig5] ; Table S10 [this file] ). 
The present study included 506 participants with DNAm and behavioural data available at both ages 14 and 19 (Table S1 [this file] ). A detailed participant flow diagram for each analytical step is provided in Fig. S4 [this file] . 
To evaluate whether the longitudinal DNAm pattern identified in adolescence generalises across the lifespan, we examined two independent adult cohorts: (i) the Parkinson’s Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) cohort [ 25 [rid=CR25] ] ( = 513; 32.9% female; mean age = 61.57 ± 10.04 years), consisting of individuals with Parkinson’s disease (PD, = 329), PD and scans without evidence for dopaminergic deficit (SWEDD, = 53), or neurologically healthy controls ( = 131) (Table S1 [this file] ), and (ii) the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) cohort ( = 606; 44.1% female; mean age = 73.16 ± 7.07 years), including participants with Alzheimer’s disease (AD, = 72), mild cognitive impairment (MCI, = 329), or healthy controls ( = 205) (Table S1 [this file] ). 
A two-stage dimensionality reduction procedure was used for the DNAm data (workflow in Fig. S5 [this file] ). 
For adjacency matrices, soft-thresholding (β = 5) was selected using scale-free topology criteria for both age 14 and age 19 networks (Fig. S6 [this file] ). 
First, we compared our consensus-based clustering approach (modules required to be present at both ages 14 and 19) with a non-consensus approach in which WGCNA was applied directly to ΔDNAm values (Fig. S7 [this file] ). Specifically, correlation matrices derived from the full cohort (450 K → 850 K data) and the subset of 61 adolescents measured on the same platform and wave (850 K → 850 K) showed higher similarity for the consensus structure than for the non-consensus structure ( = 0.86 vs. = 0.79; Z = 2.24; = 0.025; Fig. S3 [this file] ), indicating that consensus-based clustering is more robust to technical heterogeneity. 
Prevalence rates of each behaviour at ages 14 and 19 are provided in Table S1 [this file] . 
Sensitivity models additionally controlled for pubertal development, socioeconomic status [ 80 [rid=CR80] ], and co-use of other substances to evaluate potential confounding (see Table S10 [this file] ).
pub_title: A longitudinal DNA methylation atlas and its link to brain structure and mental health

Additionally, after adjusting the regression for age, sex, and PC1-5, a statistically significant association between the H1 haplotype and PD was only observed in the EUR population (OR = 1.33, 95%CI = 1.24–1.43, = 2.4E-15) and the LARGE-PD cohort (OR = 1.51, 95%CI = 1.19–1.93, = 0.000745) (Supplementary Data 6 [this file] and Supplementary Fig. 2 [rid=MOESM1] ). No differences were observed for PD AAO between H1 and H2 haplotype carriers in any ancestry group (Supplementary Data 8 [this file] ). A nominal association (not passing Bonferroni significance) between the H1 haplotype and AAO was observed in a linear regression adjusted for sex and 5PCs in the AJ and LARGE-PD groups (Supplementary Data 9 [this file] ), with the H1 haplotype being associated with a ~ 1.3 and ~3.2 years earlier AAO compared to the H2 haplotype (AJ: beta = −1.368, SE = 0.657, = 0.0374, LARGE-PD: beta = −3.175, SE = 1.253, = 0.0115). 
The variants were in HWE in all populations with a few exceptions (chr17:45908813:G:A in AFR, chr17:45942346:G:A in AJ, chr17:46003698:A:G in AAC and MDE, and chr17:46028029:A:G in LARGE-PD) (Supplementary Data 10 [this file] ). 
A large variation in the H1 subhaplotype frequencies was observed between several ancestry populations (Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Data 11 [this file] ). 
After ranking the subhaplotypes by Gini importance score, none of the subhaplotypes with the highest importance scores overlapped between the ancestries (Supplementary Data 12 [this file] ). 
The breakdown of the numbers of PD patients and controls is listed in Table 2 [rid=Tab2] , and a summary of demographics can be found in Supplementary Data 1 [this file] . 
Additionally, the estimated number of samples needed to reach 80% power at the effect size (odds ratio [OR]) observed in the EUR population was calculated for the observed MAF in the different ancestry groups (Supplementary Data 2 [this file] ). 
The resulting output is a per-ancestry list of the input subhaplotypes, and their corresponding Gini importance score (Supplementary Table 12 [this file] ).

Demographic data, main clinical diagnosis, primary pathology and co-pathology were provided by brain banks ( eTable 1 [this file] ). 
For statistical power, LB staging systems were collapsed into neocortical, limbic, and brainstem LBD subtypes ( eTable 2 [this file] ). 
We used the PanelAPP neurodegenerative disease panel ( eTables 3 [this file] and 4 [this file] ) to define genes of interest for neurodegenerative disease. Variants were extracted using bcftools and annotated with ANNOVAR ( eMethods [this file] ) and defined by ClinVar as pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants. 
Individuals of South Asian (SAS) ancestry died at a significantly younger age than individuals of European or Ashkenazi Jewish (AJ) ancestry (p < 0·001, eTable 5 [this file] ). 
LB pathology was present in 33/745 (4·4%) clinical controls, including neocortical involvement in 10/33 (30·3%), of whom 2/10 (20·0 %) carried an ε4 allele ( eTable 6 [this file] ). 
AD pathology was most frequent, present in 426/1064 (40·0%) LBD cases ( eTable 7 [this file] ) and associated with more extensive LB distribution (OR = 2·61, 95% CI = 1·79 – 3·80, p = 5·8e-07). 
Similar gradients were observed in Braak NFT, CERAD, and Thal phase, supporting a cumulative increased burden of AD and LBD pathology from PD to PDD to DLB ( eTable 8 [this file] ). 
Individuals with pathologically defined LBD were more likely than pathological controls to carry GD-causing variants (OR = 5·65, 95% CI=1·35 – 23·66, p = 5e-03), and PD risk variants (OR = 1·58, 95% CI=1·07 – 2·34, p = 0·02) ( eTable 9 [this file] ). 
We identified 19 individuals with clinically diagnosed movement disorders who carried mutations ( eTable 10 [this file] ). 
We found a significant association between ancestry and pathological diagnosis (X = 35·5, df =2, p= 1·95e-08, eTable 5 [this file] ). LBD was more common in individuals of AJ ancestry compared to the SAS population, whereas PSP was more frequent in SAS ( eFigure 1 [this file] ).

To build a molecular atlas that resolves previously underappreciated rare cell types and aid in the interpretation of noncoding variant effects in PD, we performed paired single-nucleus multiomic profiling of chromatin accessibility and gene expression from postmortem brain tissue derived from five brain regions across 101 donors (80 PD patients and 21 controls) ( Fig. 1a [rid=F1] , Supplementary Fig. 1a [this file] ). These individuals were volunteers in the Arizona Study of Aging and Neurodegenerative Disorders community aging study and have detailed clinical and neuropathologic annotation ( Supplementary Fig. 1b [this file] – c [this file] , Supplementary Table 1 [rid=SD2] ). We selected cases across the neuropathological spectrum of Lewy body formation, which follows a stereotypical progression from brainstem, then limbic, and finally neocortical neurons ( Supplementary Fig. 1b [this file] , Supplementary Table 1 [rid=SD2] ). To mitigate batch effects across this large cohort, we mixed nuclei from different donors together prior to droplet generation and leveraged 30x WGS from each donor to perform genetic demultiplexing ( Supplementary Fig. 1a [this file] ). After strict quality control, we created three different atlases: (i) 4.2 million nuclei with high-quality snATAC-seq data, (ii) 4.5 million nuclei with high-quality snRNA-seq data, and (iii) the intersection, 3.3 million nuclei with high-quality multi-omic data (snATAC-seq and snRNA-seq) ( Fig. 1a [rid=F1] , Supplementary Fig. 1d [this file] – g [this file] ). In our multi-omic atlas, we retained an average of 32,956 nuclei per individual (across all brain regions), and 92% of the 505 brain samples were represented by over 3,500 nuclei that passed quality control filters in both snATAC-seq and snRNA-seq assays ( Fig. 1b [rid=F1] , Supplementary Fig. 2a [this file] ). 
Dimensionality reduction and clustering revealed seven broad cell types (astrocytes, excitatory neurons, inhibitory neurons, microglia/immune cells, oligodendrocytes, oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs), and vascular/endothelial cells), with many neurons showing brain region specificity ( Supplementary Fig. 2b [this file] – c [this file] ). These cell types showed minimal detectable bias due to covariates, including biological sex, disease status, donor, and batch ( Supplementary Fig. 2d [this file] – g [this file] ). We further subclustered these broad cell classes based on refined marker genes to identify 30 distinct cell types ( Fig. 1c [rid=F1] – f [rid=F1] , Supplementary Fig. 3a [this file] – d [this file] ). 
Subclustering of dopaminergic neurons revealed transcriptionally distinct populations ( Fig. 1g [rid=F1] , Supplementary Fig. 4a [this file] – b [this file] ). Additionally, we uncovered substantial evidence for the existence of three distinct populations of MSNs within the putamen ( Supplementary Fig. 4c [this file] ). As expected, we identified the canonical MSN subtypes marked by expression of dopamine receptor D1 ( ) or D2 ( ) but we also identified a third population that expresses both and in addition to other previously unappreciated marker genes ( Supplementary Fig. 4d [this file] – f [this file] ). 
We further subclustered the most abundant non-neuronal cell types, uncovering varying degrees of regional specificity ( Supplementary Fig. 5a [this file] – b [this file] ). Differential expression analysis identified subpopulation-specific markers, such as + astrocytes in the substantia nigra (Astrocyte Subcluster 1) and + microglia in the substantia nigra (Microglia Subcluster 2), suggesting that non-neuronal cells adopt regionally specialized transcriptional programs tailored to local environments ( Supplementary Fig. 5c [this file] ). 
For each test, we corrected for age at death, biological sex, and postmortem interval if those covariates showed a correlation (Pearson’s -value < 0.05) with any of the first five principal component values for pseudobulked expression of that cell type ( Supplementary Fig. 6a [this file] ). We also performed a permutation-based assessment of the reliability of those differentially expressed genes (DEGs) by shuffling the case/control labels and determining the background number of DEGs that would occur by chance within our dataset, an approach that explicitly accounts for the imbalanced sample sizes of PD and control individuals in our cohort ( Supplementary Fig. 6b [this file] ). This analysis highlighted oligodendrocytes, MSNs, excitatory neurons, and astrocytes as the cell types with the greatest changes in transcriptional profile ( Fig. 2a [rid=F2] , Supplementary Fig. 6c [this file] ). We note that, as expected, the total number of DEGs detected is impacted by the number of cells of the given cell type captured per sample and thus some cell types may remain underpowered even in this large dataset ( Supplementary Fig. 6D [this file] ). Excitatory neurons similarly showed enrichment for monoamine and catecholamine response pathways, together implicating dysregulated neurotransmitter signaling as a central mechanism in PD pathogenesis ( Supplementary Fig. 7a [this file] , Supplementary Table 3 [rid=SD2] ). 
Across astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and excitatory neurons, these DEGs showed greater overlap than expected by chance between brain regions based on permutation testing ( Fig. 2b [rid=F2] , Supplementary Fig. 7b [this file] ), suggesting that a subset of transcriptional responses in PD is coordinated across regions and reflecting shared injury or response to injury mechanisms. Specifically, among oligodendrocytes, the strongest overlap occurred between the substantia nigra and putamen ( Supplementary Fig. 7c [this file] – d [this file] ). Enrichment analysis further revealed that Oligodendrocyte Subclusters 0 and 1 were most strongly enriched for regional DEGs ( Supplementary Fig. 7e [this file] ). Pathway analysis of these overlapping regional DEG sets highlights nitric oxide–cGMP signaling, perisynaptic extracellular matrix organization, and non-integrin membrane-extracellular matrix interactions, pointing to shared alterations in synaptic plasticity and neuron–glia communication across these disease-relevant brain regions ( Supplementary Fig. 7f [this file] ). 
Whereas the majority of our differential expression results were identified in glial cells, all of the cell populations that showed significant differences in cellular proportions were neuronal, including multiple types of inhibitory neurons showing increased proportion in PD ( Fig. 2c [rid=F2] , Supplementary Fig. 8a [this file] ). Within the two brain regions profiled that contain these neuronal types, the cellular proportion differences were more pronounced in the cingulate gyrus than in the middle temporal gyrus ( Supplementary Fig. 8b [this file] ). 
Stratifying across this progression, we observe that the same cell types showing changes in cell proportion between disease and control in the cingulate gyrus also show progressive changes across disease stages ( Fig. 2d [rid=F2] and Supplementary Fig. 8c [this file] ). We also identified chromatin accessibility peaks from astrocytes that mapped to that showed stage-associated changes, suggesting that its transcriptional upregulation may be driven by dynamic regulatory mechanisms ( Supplementary Fig. 8d [this file] ). To further resolve cell type-specific stage-associated transcriptional patterns, we classified these genes based on their trajectories through the pathological progression of PD ( Supplementary Fig. 8e [this file] , Supplementary Table 5 [rid=SD2] – 6 [rid=SD1] ). MSNs were particularly enriched for genes showing monotonic upregulation across Lewy body stages, highlighting progressive, stage-linked transcriptional activation in this neuronal population ( Supplementary Fig. 8f [this file] ). 
We quantified the ML-predicted impact of each variant using the Jensen–Shannon Divergence (JSD) between the predicted chromatin accessibility profile of the reference and alternate alleles, allowing us to create a prioritized list of variants predicted to increase or decrease chromatin accessibility ( Fig. 4b [rid=F4] – c [rid=F4] , Supplementary Fig. 9a [this file] ). Pearson’s = 0.73; range 0.68–0.82), with no clear relationship between model performance and number of cells used for training ( Supplementary Fig. 9b [this file] ). 
To do so, we generated cell type-specific chromatin conformation data (Micro-C) from neurons, oligodendrocytes, microglia, and astrocytes isolated by fluorescence-activated nuclei sorting of middle temporal gyrus tissue ( Supplementary Fig. 10a [this file] – c [this file] ). Given the high depth of the data, we called “loops” at 10-kb resolution, identifying 120,512 total loops ( Supplementary Fig. 10d [this file] – e [this file] ). As expected, the majority of loops spanned distances less than 500 kb, with 57–70% of anchors overlapping with a called ATAC-seq peak in the respective cell type ( Supplementary Fig. 10f [this file] – l [this file] ). 
We then employed a tiered approach to link regulatory elements to their putative target genes ( Supplementary Fig. 11a [this file] ). This hierarchical strategy yielded comprehensive regulatory element annotations while prioritizing evidence-based functional connections over simple proximity-based assignments ( Supplementary Fig. 11b [this file] – d [this file] ). 
This revealed several genes involved in protein trafficking and the ubiquitin–proteasome system, including , , and , as well as , which contributes to peptide turnover ( Supplementary Fig. 11e [this file] ). This analysis revealed that 3,230 of 13,944 genes (23.2%; 95% CI, 22.5–23.9%) exhibited significant cell type-restricted enrichment of effect variants ( Supplementary Fig. 11f [this file] ), indicating that approximately one-fifth of genes concentrate their regulatory variation within specific cell types which is substantially higher than would be expected if effect variants were randomly distributed across cell types. 
This approach identified genes with significantly elevated effect variant burdens in particular cell types, with the majority showing enrichment in only a single cell type ( Supplementary Fig. 11g [this file] ). Across all tested cell types, genes enriched for cell type-specific effect variants converged on pathways regulating protein depolymerization, ubiquitination, and DNA repair, highlighting mechanisms of proteostasis and genome integrity that are increasingly implicated in PD pathogenesis ( Supplementary Fig. 11h [this file] ). 
The variant, observed in an individual from the GP2 cohort, is predicted to reduce chromatin accessibility in GABAergic interneurons in the putamen and in excitatory and SST+ interneurons across the brain by disrupting a JUNB-binding motif ( Supplementary Fig. 11i [this file] – j [this file] ). 
Using ML-prioritized variants within these testing sets from the 3,611 PD cases and 350 controls available in the GP2 Release 8, we performed rare variant association tests using SKAT , weighting each variant by its allele frequency and its ML-predicted effect (JSD) with well-calibrated test statistics across cell types (genomic inflation factor λ = 0.80–0.87, Supplementary Fig. 12a [this file] ). On average, we tested associations for 14,773 genes per cell type ( Supplementary Fig. 12b [this file] ), identifying 46 genes with statistically significant associations within at least one cell type ( Fig. 5b [rid=F5] , large dots; Supplementary Table 7 [rid=SD2] ). 
Of the initial 78 cell type-significant associations, four remained significant in the validation cohort ( in DRD1/2 MSNs, in DRD1 MSNs, in LAMP5 neurons, and in Chandelier cells) ( Fig. 5b [rid=F5] , red gene names; Supplementary Fig. 12c [this file] ). Further supporting a role for LRFN2 in PD pathogenesis, we find a significant decrease in expression across the neuropathological progression of PD ( Supplementary Fig. 12d [this file] ). 
Beyond having statistical power to associate novel genes with PD, our rare variant association testing methods also enable statistical association of rare noncoding variants within individual regulatory elements with PD ( Supplementary Fig. 12e [this file] ). Moreover, the number of peak regions tested varied across the different cell types, with no clear correlation between the number of peaks tested and the number of significant hits uncovered ( Supplementary Fig. 12b [this file] ).

Demographics for each cohort separated by ancestry, including age at sample collection, age at onset, sex, and number of cases/controls, are presented in Supplementary Table 1 [this file] . The p.A419V variant was in HWE across all ancestry groups in all the cohorts (Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). 
Power calculations indicated that only the EAS and EUR cohorts in GP2 had an 80% power to detect an association with an OR > 2.0 and a value < 0.05 (Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ), while the AMP-PD, UKB, and AOU cohorts were underpowered for association analysis of the p.A419V variant. 
Logistic regression analyses conducted in the GP2 EAS and EUR ancestry groups indicated that a significantly higher frequency of the p.A419V variant was observed in cases compared to controls in both the EAS (MAF cases = 1.15% vs. MAF controls = 0.57%; OR = 2.908; 95% CI = 1.659–5.098, = 0.0002) and EUR (MAF cases = 0.06% vs. MAF controls = 0.02%; OR = 5.754; 95% CI = 1.399–23.66, = 0.015) groups (Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ). In the Singapore-EAS exome dataset , the p.A419V variant was present in 107 of 3967 cases (1.4%) and 70 of 5457 controls (0.6%), with a significant risk association (OR = 1.51, 95% CI = 1.103–2.068, = 0.012, Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). In the Juntendo EAS-Japanese replication cohort, the p.A419V variant was significantly associated as a risk factor in Japanese PD patients (MAF = 3.20%) than in the controls (MAF = 1.58%); (OR = 2.06; 95% CI: 1.76–2.42; = 1.301 × 10⁻16, Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). 
In the GP2 cohort, there was minimal LD (r² < 0.01) between p.A419V and other coding variants across all ancestries studied (Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ), suggesting that the observed risk association is unlikely to be confounded by nearby coding variation. Six rare haplotypes (MAF < 0.01) were identified in the GP2 EAS cohort, with one (Haplotype 9) observed in 1.2% PD cases and 0.34% controls (Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ), but further analysis lacked sufficient power to assess association. 
Based on ADMIXTURE analysis, the GP2 EUR p.A419V carriers were found to be highly admixed, with 29/35 carriers having relatively lower EUR ancestry (median: 13.86%, range: 4.68–70.8%, Supplementary Table 9a [this file] ) compared to EUR non-carriers (median: 65.75%, range: 4.09–82.30%, Supplementary Table 9b [this file] ). In contrast, all the EAS p.A419V carriers demonstrated high EAS ancestry (median: 91.68%, range: 71.9–94.1%, Supplementary Table 9c [this file] ) similar to EAS non-carriers (median: 91.83%, range: 44.24–94.91%, Supplementary Table 9d [this file] ), lending greater confidence to the observed associations within this population. 
Six p.A419V carriers also carried a concomitant p.G2385R variant (mean AAO: 51.3 ± 13 years), and one patient with young onset, unknown monogenic PD status (AAO: 35 years), was found to have a concomitant p.R1628P variant (Supplementary Table 10 [this file] ).

Similarly, there is a higher proportion of phased UMIs when we include intronic reads in our analysis ( Fig. S1a [this file] ). For each gene with significant ASE, comparing the allelic imbalance effect size between the two approaches with introns and without introns, however, there was very high agreement overall ( Fig. S1b [this file] ). 
As expected, longer reads yielded a higher proportion of phased UMIs ( Fig. 2e [rid=F2] ) and allowed us to detect more allelically imbalanced genes in aggregated data from all cells ( Fig. 2e [rid=F2] ) or from most cell types individually ( Fig. S2 [this file] ). 
Of the peaks identified by Sierra ( Fig. S4a [this file] ), 79.5% were in introns and 28.9% were in exons – with some overlap between the different classes, thus adding up to >100% ( Methods [rid=S17] ). 
Compared to the gene-level approach, the peak-level analysis resulted in slightly fewer genes with ASE, with a fair amount of overlap between the genes identified at the peak level and at the gene level ( Fig. S4b [this file] ), such that 32.3% of genes with significant imbalance had at least one significant peak and 38.6% of peaks with significant imbalance were in a gene with significant imbalance ( Supplementary Table 2 [rid=SD2] ). 
To investigate this, we looked at the frequency of mismatches, insertions, and deletions in each technology relative to the reference genome, scaled by the number of aligned bases ( Fig. S3 [this file] ). 
Consistent with our intron . exon analysis in short reads ( Fig. 2b [rid=F2] , Fig. S1a [this file] ), a higher percentage of UMIs were phased in unspliced isoforms than spliced isoforms (25.0% 17.4%). The vast majority of phased UMIs were assigned to isoforms from pre-mRNA for most genes ( Fig. S4c [this file] ). On a per-nucleus basis ( Fig. S4d [this file] ), there were relatively few (11 on average) phased UMIs assigned to spliced isoforms, with many more phased UMIs (450 on average) assigned to unspliced isoforms. 
With varying lengths for read 2, there were very few phased UMIs for spliced transcripts (1–2 per cell), but hundreds for the unspliced transcripts ( Fig. S4e [this file] ). This was much fewer spliced transcripts per cell than for the MAS-Seq data ( Fig. S4d [this file] ) – suggesting MAS-Seq has a major advantage over short-read data for isoform-level ASE analysis. 
As might be expected, many more of the genes with known eQTLs are found to be allelically imbalanced than those without known eQTLs in both hybrid-selected and non-hybrid-selected data ( Fig. S5a [this file] ). Analysis at a finer level revealed that with selection reads were much closer to the baits ( Fig. S5b [this file] ), with ~80% of uniquely mapping reads overlapping a bait in the selected data, but >90% of uniquely mapping reads being >10,000 bp away from the closest bait without selection. 
For each gene, we also compared the enrichment (total number of phased UMIs with selection divided by the total number of phased UMIs without selection) to QC metrics from the data without selection ( Fig. S5c [this file] ). Similarly, there was not a strong association between the reason genes were chosen and the enrichment score ( Fig. S5d [this file] ). 
In general, the selected libraries were sequenced less deeply than the non-selected libraries, as measured by reads per cell for each individual, ( Fig. S6a [this file] ), with a median of 42% of the sequencing depth in the selected data compared to the non-selected data and with 86 of 91 samples having more sequencing in the non-selected data than the selected data. 
To investigate in a more systematic way, we determined the number of significant SNP/gene pairs in each cell type after downsampling the selected data to a depth of 5,000 reads per cell ( Methods [rid=S17] , Fig. S6b [this file] , c [this file] ). 
There is very high agreement in the estimated effect size between the selected (without downsampling) and non-selected data ( Fig. S6d [this file] ) (Pearson correlation = 0.86, p-value < 2.2*10 ). 
First, we tested how many peaks had significant ASE in excitatory neurons ( Fig. S7a [this file] ). We also checked for peaks in which the ASE ratio in that peak differs from the ASE ratio of the rest of the gene ( Methods [rid=S17] ), which is similar to differential transcript usage (DTU), and observed similar results ( Fig. S7b [this file]. 
To explore this, we compared each isoform peak’s estimated allelic imbalance levels to that for the associated gene and observed very high concordance, with many being significant in both (83.3% of genes with at least one significant peak were significant at the gene level; 25% of genes significant at the gene level had at least one significant peak in that gene), and with only 16.6% being significant at the peak level but not the gene level ( Fig. S7c [this file] ). The gene stands out visually because it has 37 peaks, 28 of them tested for allelic imbalance, (once for each of two SNPs), with points for each of the two SNPs forming a vertical line ( Fig. S7d [this file] ). 
In terms of runtime, unsurprisingly the pseudobulk approach is by far the fastest (median of 2.25 seconds over all cell types), followed by our mixed model approach (median of 82.0 seconds over all cell types), followed by DAESC (median of 1772 seconds over all cell types) ( Fig. S8a [this file] ). In terms of performance, the effect sizes ( Fig. S8b [this file] ) and p values ( Fig. S8c [this file] ) estimated by all three methods showed very high agreement, particularly between the DAESC and glmmTMB mixed models, as expected. 
Additionally in the future, long-read sequencing could be used to better understand isoform-level ASE — we showed that long reads could be used to quantify isoform-level ASE by assigning long reads to their isoform of origin and examining transcriptional regulation at a finer level of detail ( Fig. S4 [this file] ). By contrast, short-read analysis had to use Sierra peaks ( Fig. S4b [this file] , S7a [this file] – d [this file] ) or similar methods, a less easily interpretable and less powerful measure of isoform-level ASE. 
We also developed a novel approach that shows that allelic imbalance can be extended beyond the gene level ( Fig. S7a [this file] – d [this file] ), opening the possibility of isoform-level analysis even in droplet-based single-cell and single-nucleus transcriptomic data. 
We loaded nuclei of each GTEx sample onto three channels, with each pair named as channel 1, 2, or 3 ( Fig. S9 [this file] ) of a Chromium Single Cell 3’ Chip B (10x Genomics, 1000073) aiming to recover 10,000 cells per channel.

The external validation results showed the same trends as the internal results, with RETFound Plus showing significantly higher c-indexes for all tasks in all datasets (all < = 0.014) Supplementary Table 4 [this file] , and especially better performance on predicting the 5-year incidence of stroke (up to 0.127 higher c-index when comparing with RETFound), MI (up to 0.109 higher c-index when comparing with RETFound), and hypertension (up to 0.091 higher c-index when comparing with RETFound).

Similar results can be found in external validation datasets, both for major cardiovascular diseases and other chronic diseases (Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). 
A similar trend was also found in disease progression prediction tasks, including DME progression (from non-centre to centre-involved DME [ciDME]), and any DR progression (all < 0.001, Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ). 
For the prediction of 5-year incidence of eye diseases across external tests, RETFound Plus achieved c-indexes between 0.727–0.799, significantly outperforming RETFound (c-indexes between 0.646–0.717, all < = 0.006, Supplementary Table 8 [this file] . It significantly outperformed both RETFound and MAE in most external validation datasets Supplementary Table 8 [this file] . 
Notably, for stroke incidence, RETFound Plus achieved a comparable c-index with only 20% of training data (0.733, 95%CI 0.711–0.756) to RETFound with 100% proportion of training data (0.725, 95%CI 0.694–0.756) (Supplementary Table 9 [this file] ). While for hypertension and diabetes incidence Supplementary Table 9 [this file] , as well as for DR incidence prediction (Supplementary Table 11 [this file] ), RETFound Plus, with only 50% of training data, achieved a comparable c-index with RETFound with 100% of training data.
