Among the remaining cognitive and visual variables, the majority did not exhibit significantly different rates between PD and controls (Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ), except for Salthouse Perceptual Comparison Test and high-contrast visual acuity measured with digital software, which progressed faster in PD patients. 
On average, PD patients (76.7 [8.6] years old) and controls (75.7 [9.4] years old) were older than in test dataset (Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). 
In the test dataset, the group effect at baseline was not significant for pfGCIPL thickness (group PD, [SE] = 1.28 [1.11], = 0.251), but pfGCIPL consistently correlated with disease-related outcomes, showing a significant correlation with global cognition, H&Y stage, and disease duration at baseline (Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] ). 
Further adjusting the models for disease duration at baseline did not lead to different outcomes (Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). No differences were observed in controls according to the pfGCIPL subgroup (Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ). 
Similarly, in the validation cohort PD patients with low pfGCIPL were, on average, 4 years older ( = 0.003; Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ). Furthermore, in PD patients with slow progressing pfGCIPL pattern, baseline global cognition was significantly worse after adjusting for the age at entry, sex, and years of education, whereas baseline H&Y stage was higher (Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). They also showed worse baseline cognitive scores in tests assessing visual attention and processing speed and visual executive functions, whereas primary visual function was comparable among fast and slow pfGCIPL progressing PD subgroups (Table 3 [rid=Tab3] and Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). In controls, we did not observe statistically significant differences in baseline cognitive scores according to pfGCIPL subgroup (Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ). Finally, PD patients with slow progressing pfGCIPL pattern not only exhibited lower macular thickness but also reduced pRNFL thickness across all its sectors at baseline (Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ). 
Longitudinally, the changes in pfGCIPL thickness did not temporally correlate with changes in clinical scores (Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] ). Nonetheless, individual cognitive and visual tests revealed that the differences between pfGCIPL thinning patterns were non-significant (Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). 
A similar trend was observed for non-motor symptoms and the motor-related activities of daily living parts of the UPDRS (Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). 
Despite these trends, the covariances of pRNFL thickness (both average and by sectors) and clinical scores - including MoCA, UPDRS III, or H&Y - were not significantly correlated (Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] ). 
However, there were no significant differences in the rate of pRNFL thinning over time between PD subgroups (Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ). 
Some participants had visits at baseline, 1-year, and 2-years, while others had visits at baseline, 3-years, and 5-years, or baseline and 2-years as indicated in Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] . 
The majority (>70%) belonged to the white racial group (Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). The inclusion and exclusion criteria for the validation dataset are described in Supplementary Methods (Supplementary Fig. 5 [this file] ). 
For the validation dataset (AlzEye project), OCTs were acquired by several graders and with different Topcon OCTs (Topcon Corporation, Tokyo, Japan) as indicated in Supplementary Table 8 [this file] . AlzEye OCT data curation is detailed in Supplementary Fig. 5 [this file] . 
However, our results revealed that: (1) The atrophy rate in PD versus control groups was most noticeable in the GCIPL; (2) Within the GCIPL, the parafoveal area exhibited a more pronounced rate of thinning; (3) Among the parafoveal concentric rings in the GCIPL, the 1- to 2-mm and 2- to 3-mm thicknesses showed the strongest correlation with clinical outcomes (see Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] for an illustration); (4) Dividing the parafoveal rings into quadrants did not yield sufficient evidence of a distinct trend (in terms of atrophy rate or correlation with clinical outcomes) to justify splitting the macular parameters and analyzing them separately. 
The selected cut-off value for this classification derived from the thickness distribution of a reference control sample with a comparable age range (Supplementary Methods, Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] ), and the upper limit of the lowest quartile of pfGCIPL thickness was used as the cut-off value .

To ensure that predictive ability is not compromised to achieve specificity, we repeated our meta-analyses to compare system scores to previously trained epigenetic clocks ( Fig. 4 [rid=F4] , Extended Data Figs. 4b [rid=F11] , 5 [rid=F12] and 6 [rid=F13] and Supplementary Tables 2 [this file] – 5 [this file] ).

We also performed an analysis among never smokers ( Extended Data Figs. 5c [rid=F12] and 8c [rid=F15] and Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ), finding that system scores retained strong associations compared to existing clocks.

Within each organ system, we defined disease states, and their severities based on accepted medically pre-defined disease criteria (Table S1 [this file] ), using combinations of medical history, medical laboratory and physical examinations. The related health questions are listed in the Table S2 [this file] , and the disease definitions and their levels are also summarized in Table S1 [this file] . 
Pathology at the specific organ level was established based on predefined disease/impairment criteria, either deviating from normal or as used for disease diagnoses in clinical practice (Table S1 [this file] ). The questions and medical examinations are summarized in Tables S1 [this file] and S2 [this file] . The definition of BODN, reflecting progressive system morbidities, using the 11 organ systems was then extended to include cerebrovascular accidents (CA), and cancer (Can) (Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] , S1 [this file] , Tables S1 [this file] , S2 [this file] ), because CA involves multiple mechanisms, such as hypertension, coagulopathy and genetics, and cancers have both shared and distinct mechanisms across organs. 
Moreover, ordinal numbers were assigned to the disease levels as covariates of the models, representing the severity of each organ-specific pathology, serving as lagged predictors of BODN (e.g., no hypertension, hypertension with no treatment, and hypertension with treatment would be coded 1, 2, and 3, respectively; Table S1 [this file] ). 
Using Gamma distribution models with a log link function, we regressed chronological age against BSCs and the Body Clock to obtain Bodily System-Specific Age and Body Age, as proxies for organ-specific and whole-body systems rates of aging, respectively (Table S3 [this file] ). 
We developed a Disability Index (DI) by applying the Zero Inflated Beta Binomial (ZIBB) approach in a probability theory framework (Formula [S1] and [S2] in the Supplemental Methods), combining information on physical and cognitive function, falls, and urinary or bowel incontinence (Table S4 [this file] ). The equations and description of each model are summarized in Table S3 [this file] . 
The characteristics of the BLSA study by age group are summarized in Table S5 [this file] . 
We then sequentially added diseases within a single organ system (organ-specific diseases are defined in Table S1 [this file] ), multi-system diseases, and, ultimately, whole entropy, incorporating all organ-system diseases as covariates. 
Analyses of the BLSA data and then InCHIANTI as replication revealed significant and varied effects of single diseases and organ system-specific diseases on the accumulation of system multimorbidity, as expressed by the longitudinal BODN (Table S6 [this file] ). For example, in the BLSA study, peripheral artery disease (PAD) contributed to BODN with posterior estimate [b]=3.43, 95% CI: 2.05–4.8, while the cardiovascular (CV) system’s contribution was = 1.21, 95% CI: 0.03–2.46 (Table S6A–B [this file] ). Similarly, in the InCHIANTI data, the effect size of PAD as a single disease was b = 1.56, 95% CI: 1.06–2.06 (Table S6G–H [this file] ), which was attenuated within the organ system ( = 0.8, 95% CI: 0.8–1.26) (Table S6G–H [this file] ), indicating the link between diseases within the same organ system and potential shared mechanisms. Comparing model performance weights, called average model weight stacking (Supplemental Methods), indicated that the model including the chronological age as only predictor, the age-only model, outperformed individual disease or single organ-system models (Fig. 2A–D [rid=Fig2] ; Table S7 [this file] ), highlighting the necessity of developing models that explain the variability of health entropy with aging beyond what is explained by a single disease. 
The detailed weights are reported in Table S7 [this file] . 
This was evident in the superior model performance (larger ELPD: expected log pointwise predictive density) and greater model weights compared to chronological age-only models (Fig. 2E, F [rid=Fig2] , Table S7 [this file] ). Furthermore, the full models, including all systems, outperformed chronological age in predicting longitudinal BODN in both the BLSA and InCHIANTI datasets (Fig. 2E, F [rid=Fig2] , Table 1 [rid=Tab1] , Table S7 [this file] ). 
Indeed, examination of correlations among the 13 organ-system BSAs revealed varying degrees of correlation between each pair of BSA values, indicating disparate aging rates among organ systems and suggesting that organs do not age synchronously (Fig. S3A, B [this file] ). 
Notably, a similar trend emerged in the InCHIANTI dataset, confirming the replication of this approach (Fig. S3C [this file] ). 
However, for some organ-system diseases, such as peripheral artery disease, hyperthyroidism, thrombocytopenia, adult-onset asthma, and Parkinson’s disease, there was substantial uncertainty in the estimate, reflected by wider 95% credible intervals, possibly because the prevalence of these conditions in the population is relatively low (Fig. 4A, B [rid=Fig4] , Fig. S4 A, B [this file] , Table S6C [this file] , S6F, I [this file] ). Interestingly, milder states of organ system diseases (e.g., transitional ischemic attack, impaired glucose tolerance, mild anemia, subclinical hypothyroidism, cataract, mild liver disease, gingivitis without edentulous, osteopenia, mild osteoarthritis, and poor hearing that improves with a hearing aid) had larger estimates contributing to longitudinal BODN compared to more severe states of these diseases (Figs. 4A, B [rid=Fig4] , S4 A&B [this file] , Table S6C, F, I [this file] ). Similarly, diseases without pharmacological treatment (e.g., hypertension [HTN], type-2 diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, chronic bronchitis, gastrointestinal disease, depression, and Parkinson’s) had larger posterior coefficient estimates for predicting BODN (Fig. S4A, B [this file] Table S6 [this file] ). Arrhythmias, such as sinus bradycardia, elongated QTc, and atrial fibrillation, also significantly affected BODN (Fig. S4A, B [this file] ; Table S6C, F, I [this file] ). Similar results were observed in the InCHIANTI study for stage-1 CKD (Table S6 [this file] ). These patterns were also observed in the time-2 full model BLSA, where hyperthyroidism and Parkinson’s significantly incorporated into BODN (Fig. S4A, B [this file] , Table S6 [this file] ). Overall, as pointed out above, model assessments using LOO-CV approach indicated that full entropy models, incorporating all disease severities, with larger ELPD (Table 1 [rid=Tab1] ) had the best performance in predicting longitudinal BODN (Fig. S5 [this file] ). 
For the values of mean posterior estimates and 95% CI, please see the values in Table S6C, F [this file] for full models. 
In the BLSA, peripheral artery disease (PAD) showed significant incorporation into BODN either as a single disease or as part of a single-organ system, but its significance was not retained in the full model; while in the InCHIANTI study, PAD retained its significance in the full model, albeit with a smaller magnitude (Fig. S4A, B [this file] , Table S6C, F, I [this file] ). 
These trajectories exhibit varying slopes and magnitudes, underscoring the unique maximum intrinsic aging experienced by different individuals (Fig. S6A, B [this file] ). The Body Clock increases with each successive 10-year age interval, and its values are heterogeneously distributed within each age group, as depicted in both the BLSA and InCHIANTI studies (Fig. S7A, B [this file] ). 
We obtained the post hoc prediction for each individual using posterior predict, termed Body Age (Eq. 4 [rid=Equ4] , Fig. S7C, D [this file] ). 
To assess the influence of the Body Clock on walking speed, we predicted longitudinal changes of walking speed by the Body Clock, adjusting for height using a Gaussian regression and modeled the walking speed variance (sigma) over the Body Clock to develop another health metric that we called Speed-Body Clock (equation [5] and [6]; Fig. S8 A, B [this file] ). 
At the population level, for each unit increase in the Body Clock, the posterior coefficient of walking speed decreased by 0.062 m/s (0.065–0.062) in men and 0.064 m/s (0.063–0.061) in women (Fig. S8A [this file] ). Again, women exhibited a smaller Speed-Body Clock than men, with values of 1.29 ± 0.15 for women and 1.56 ± 0.14 for men (Fig. S8B [this file] ). 
This heterogeneity in the aging rate is captured by regressing chronological age on the Speed-Body Clock using a Gamma distribution and the predicted value was denoted as Speed-Body Age (equation [7] and [8]; Fig. S8 C, D [this file] ). 
The data revealed increasing heterogeneity in Speed-Body Age after age 70 as depicted in Fig. S8C, D [this file] . 
We incorporated a total of 47 measured components as the total number of trials in the DI (Table S4 [this file] ). 
This approach enabled us to explore how the Body Clock predicts the model-based physical and cognitive DI, based on events within the total 47 measured (trials) components (Table S3 [this file] ).

The median Disability-Body Clock was 1.2 (range 0.12–9.48) and not different between men and women (women: 1.5 ± 1.04; men: 1.52 ± 1.08) (Fig. S9.A [this file] ). The median Disability-Body Clock was 6.3 (range: 1.45–12.8) with a larger mean in women (6.5 ± 1.82) than men (6.17 ± 1.74) (Fig. S9B [this file] ). 
In the InCHIANTI data, the median Disability-Body Age was 67.3 (range 43.5–120.2) with women exhibiting a higher average biological age compared to men (69.56 ± 11.55 vs. 67.2 ± 10.7) (Fig. S9C [this file] ). 
We used the same list of diseases described in Table S1 [this file] to manually develop disease-based FI scores, which is a common metric used to capture age-related deficits . 
It is important to note that while the FI and Body Clock exhibit strong correlation ( = 0.83, 95% CI: 0.816–0.84), the Body Clock more effectively captures health heterogeneity, as evidenced by instances where identical FI values correspond to varying Body Clock values (Figs. 6 [rid=Fig6] , S10A, B [this file] ). The AUC values consistently indicate that the Body Clock provided stronger predictions for all these outcomes across both the BLSA and InCHIANTI studies (Figs. 7 [rid=Fig7] , S11A [this file] ). 
As chronological age increased, the Body Clock demonstrated heightened heterogeneity after age 60, mirroring the pattern observed in the BLSA and InCHIANTI studies (Fig. S12A [this file] ). In addition, in NHANES data, Body Clock outperformed FIs specifically in predicting mortality, with an accuracy of 80% (Fig. S13 [this file] ). 
Similar to the BLSA and InCHIANTI data, the Disability-Body Age surpassed the reported ceiling in humans (Fig. S12B [this file] ). 
The predicted and observed values in both studies were matched as depicted using posterior predicted check in the Bayesian framework (Fig. S14 A, B [this file] ).

However, cell proliferation was inhibited after exposure to 7.5 and 10 Gy as seen by reduced incorporation of 5-ethynyl-2’-deoxyuridine (Edu) in the treated cells ( Fig. 2a [rid=F2] – b [rid=F2] ; Fig S1g [this file] ). Further, the expression levels of a panel of senescence marker mRNAs ( mRNA, ( ) mRNA and ( ) mRNA) and mRNAs encoding SASP factors (e.g., and mRNAs) were significantly higher in IR-treated cells than proliferating controls ( Fig. 2c [rid=F2] ; Fig. S1b [this file] – e [this file] ). Elevated levels of SPiDER β-gal in IR-treated cells further confirmed the stable induction of senescence 7 days after exposure to 7.5 Gy ( Fig. 2d [rid=F2] ; Fig. S1f [this file] ). 
Additionally, even though protein expression was positively correlated on the peptide and protein level between neat and nanoparticle-processed samples ( Fig. S2a [this file] , b [this file] ), the reproducibility of protein measurements was improved after processing ( Fig. S2c [this file] ). 
After adjusting for covariates, the size of the regression coefficient for the SASP proteins in the elastic net model did not change substantially ( Fig. S3a [this file] ), suggesting that ENSPs are not simply demonstrating association with clinical traits due to their association with age and might have age-independent clinical implications. 
ENSPs were identified for several clinical traits in both BLSA ( Fig. S4a [this file] ) and InCHIANTI ( Fig. S4b [this file] ). These linear models, when trained on the BLSA cohort, significantly predicted several clinical traits in InCHIANTI ( Fig. S4c [this file] ), and when trained on the InCHIANTI cohort, significantly predicted many clinical traits in the BLSA ( Fig. S4d [this file] ). 
Ranking the BLSA and InCHIANTI cohorts by their compositive senescence burden and plotting linear trends of the clinical traits walking pace, HDL, BMI, and CRP reveals that increasing senescence burden score shows the expected association with trait trending in the direction of poorer health (positively associated with BMI and CRP, negatively associated with walking pace and HDL), in both BLSA ( Fig. 7d [rid=F7] ) and InCHIANTI ( Fig. S5b [this file] ). 
ANOVA testing revealed that including ENSPs in linear models significantly improved the accuracy of covariate-only linear models ( Table S4 [rid=SD4] ) Additionally, including ENSPs in covariate-only linear models substantially increased correlation coefficients ( Fig. S3a [this file] ), and ENSP-only models produced similar correlation coefficients to ENSP with covariates models ( Fig. S3a [this file] ). ANOVA testing again revealed that ENSPs added significant additional predictive accuracy to models using only body fat and other covariates ( Table S4 [rid=SD4] ), and adding ENSPs to body fat percent with other covariate-only linear models again increased the correlation coefficient for many clinical traits, particularly triglycerides, HDL, LDL, CRP, and fasting glucose ( Fig. S3b [this file] ). Permutation tests (100,000 repetitions per trait) revealed that ENSPs often demonstrated better out-of-sample trait prediction potential than randomly selected proteins ( Fig S5a [this file] , Table S5 [rid=SD5] ). 
The associations of monocyte SASP and body fat and related outcomes is notably independent of age and other covariates ( Fig S3a [this file] , Table S4 [rid=SD4] ).

The KOLF2.1J reference cell line, which is the reference clonal cell line for the iNDI consortium and contains 18 and 20 uninterrupted CAGs followed by a CAACAG that encodes 20 and 22 uninterrupted glutamines (Q), was used to create an allele-specific CAG isogenic series using CRISPR/Cas9 technology ( Table S1 [this file] ). The primers used for the CAG tract amplification were polyCAG_Fw and polyCAG_Rv ( Table S1 [this file] ). Four knock-in clones for each CAG length were confirmed by PCR amplification and Sanger sequencing using PCR primers HTT_PF3 and HTT_PR3 with sequencing primer HTT_SF1 ( Table S1 [this file] ). 
Genomic integrity was confirmed by Array Comparative Genomic Hybridization (aCGH). sgRNA, primer, and donor sequences are provided in Table S2 [this file] . 
Expanded alleles were amplified and sequenced to confirm repeat length ( Figure S1 [this file] ). Western blot confirmed protein expression of HTT and mHTT ( Figure 1C [rid=F1] , S2A [this file] - C [this file] ). All lines maintained pluripotency and parental karyotype , evidenced by qPCR for standard markers ( Figure S2D [this file] ) and SNP analysis ( Figure S3 [this file] , Table S3 [this file] ), respectively. 
For all three lines (21Q, 56Q, and 79Q), there was a significant increase in fluorescence in our PHrodo cultures after 12, 18, and 24 hours ( Figure 4C [rid=F4] , S4 [this file] ) suggesting that all three lines can engulf the S. particles and introduce them to an acidic environment for degradation as would occur in normal phagocytosis. 
Three homozygous KO clones were identified by PCR and Sanger sequencing, and two were chosen for Western blot to confirm lack of protein expression ( Figure 5B [rid=F5] , S5A [this file] - C [this file] ); both KO_1, KO_2 showed absence of HTT protein. Both clones were further confirmed pluripotent by qPCR for standard markers ( Figure S5D [this file] ) and karyotypically normal by aCGH analysis ( Figure S6 [this file] ). 
At Day 37, all lines produced a high percentage of mature neurons as evidenced by 70-90% expression of the mature neuron marker NeuN ( Figure 6B [rid=F6] , 6C [rid=F6] , S7A [this file] ), and high MAP2 expression ( Figure S7B [this file] ). There were no significant differences, although the KO_2 appears to have lower co-localization of SYP and PSD95 compared to 21Q which will need to be further investigated ( Figure S8A [this file] - B [this file] ). 
Differential gene analysis was performed and identified 96 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) for the 56Q vs 21Q, 389 DEGs in 79Q vs 21Q, and 1441 DEGs in KO vs 21Q comparisons ( Figure 7B [rid=F7] , S9A [this file] - C [this file] , Table S4 [this file] ). From this analysis, we observed that the DEGs in the 79Q and KO striatal neurons compared to controls are more similar than the 56Q line compared to controls at the pathway level. All lines were comprehensively characterized using Sanger sequencing, transcriptomic profiling, quantitative PCR (qPCR), and immunoblotting, as well as immunostaining to confirm pluripotency ( Figures 1C [rid=F1] - 1F [rid=F1] ; S1A [this file] and S1B [this file] ). Interestingly, in the KO CRISPR-edited lines, there was upregulation of the few residual exons both upstream and downstream of the CRISPR-targeted site, suggesting a compensatory transcriptional response to loss of TBK1 ( Figures 1C [rid=F1] ; S2A [this file] ). We confirmed that the TBK1 G217R variant was associated with reduced TBK1 levels in a gene dosage-dependent manner compared to the isogenic “revertant” control in iPSCs, consistent with this variant contributing to haploinsufficiency for TBK1 function in affected carriers ( Figures S4A [this file] - S4C [this file] ). Finally, we validated that the CRISPR-mediated KO resulted in a complete loss of expression ( Figures S2B [this file] - S2D [this file] ). 
There was no detectable induction of the cryptic exon, which is a sensitive readout for loss of TDP-43 nuclear function in neurodegeneration, while levels were unchanged across genotypes ( Figure S3A [this file] ). Additionally, TDP-43 localization was predominantly nuclear in both control and TBK1 KO neurons ( Figure S3B [this file] ). 
TANK, another TBK1 adapter, was trending toward reduced abundance in TBK1 KO iPSCs ( Figure 2C [rid=F2] ), and TANK was significantly decreased in isogenic TBK1 G217R iPSCs compared to G217R iPSCs ( Figures S4D [this file] and S4E [this file] ). 
Transcriptomic analysis confirmed that the corresponding transcripts of these adapters were unchanged ( Figure S2E [this file] ), suggesting that TBK1 promotes the stability of these three proteins in human neurons. 
In TBK1 KO cells, Gene Ontology (GO) analysis of the top decreased phospho-peptides revealed enrichment for autophagy-related processes (GO:0006914, adj. = 6.01 × 10 ), especially selective autophagy cargo receptors (SACRs; Figure 3B [rid=F3] ), in contrast to modest-to-absent changes in their protein abundance ( Figure S5 [this file] ). 
However, our approach was sensitive enough to detect a lower level of IRF3 pS173 in TBK1 G217R variant cells, despite the absence of applying inflammatory stimuli ( Figure S4F [this file] ), suggesting that TBK1 may act in additional roles in certain cell types. 
Therefore, we compared the number of phospho-peptides detected in the phospho-proteome of control iPSCs and iNeurons, in the absence of any stressors, focusing on 29 proteins implicated in various neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer’s disease (AD), frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD), ALS, Huntington’s disease (HD), Parkinson’s disease/dementia with Lewy bodies (PD/DLB), and neurofilaments, which are generally used as disease biomarkers ( Figure 4A [rid=F4] ; Tables S6 [rid=SD8] ; S7 [rid=SD9] and S8 [this file0] ). Interestingly, TDP-43 pS409/S410, a phospho-site used as a common marker for TDP-43 pathology in ALS/FTLD and additional TDP-43 proteinopathies, was detected in both iPSCs and iNeurons ( Figure S6 [this file] ). 
To better define the function of TBK1 in neurons, we generated isogenic neurons for phospho-proteome-wide profiling, where TMT-based analysis identified 66,278 normalized phospho-peptides, providing even greater coverage than for iPSCs ( Figure 5A [rid=F5] ; Tables S7 [rid=SD9] ; S8 [this file0] ). Nonetheless, we detected an intriguing increase in the phosphorylation of TDP-43 (pS409/pS410), which is a neuropathological hallmark of ALS and FTD, in both TBK1 and OPTN variant excitatory neurons compared to controls ( Figure S6 [this file] ). 
Similarly, complete loss of OPTN was associated with increased abundance of lysosomes and lysosomal proteases, cathepsins ( Figures 2B [rid=F2] ; S7A [this file] and S7B [this file] ). 
Of note, we identified a novel phosphorylation site on NCOA7 (nuclear receptor coactivator 7), a putative estrogen receptor-binding protein, that was regulated by TBK1 ( Figure S8A [this file] ). pS441 of NCOA7 corresponded to a TBK1 consensus phosphorylation motif with a phospho-site prediction model highlighting TBK1 as the top kinase for this residue ( Table S11 [this file1] ). Overexpression of NCOA7 resulted in increased fluorescence intensity for LysoTracker, similar to the TBK1 LoF phenotypes ( Figure S8B [this file] ). 
Nonetheless, we did observe a trend toward increased TDP-43 phosphorylation in neurons with loss of TBK1 function ( Figure S6 [this file] ).

that expression of and between microglia within the iAssembloids and patient microglia were comparable
( Fig. S3C [this file] ). 
Many of the hits fell
into categories related to metabolism, neuronal activity, cell adhesion, lipid
and lipoprotein function, immune response, stress response, and endocytosis
( Fig. 3B [rid=F3] , Fig.S4A [this file] , Table S3 [rid=SD4] ). We confirmed that our
screen was highly reproducible across two different time points ( Fig. S4B [this file] ). CRISPRi screens using the shorter protocol for astrocytes yielded similar
results to screens using the more laborious protocol ( Fig. S4C [this file] ). 
We compared our findings to those of screens previously performed in
neuron monocultures in our lab . iAssembloid screens conducted
at two different timepoints were highly correlated with each other, but not as
highly correlated with the original 2D neuron screen ( Fig. S4D [this file] ). 
We conducted a focused validation screen targeting the 68 curated genes
from the primary screen. and found that the results were highly correlated
(r=0.9) with the primary screen ( Fig. S5A [this file] , Table S3 [rid=SD4] ). We
also compared iAssembloids with neurons co-cultured with microglia and 3D
neuronal monocultures and found that with 3D neuron monoculture clustered more
closely to the screen conducted in BrainPhys media ( Fig. S5B [this file] , Table S3 [rid=SD4] ). To understand the
downstream effects on neuronal function after perturbation of these genes, we
selected hits that maintained a phenotypic difference between monoculture and
iAssembloid culture for a focused screen with single-cell transcriptomic readout
( Fig. S5B [this file] ). 
Knockdown of did not influence the level of ROS in neurons in 2D
or 3D culture ( Fig. 5D [rid=F5] , Fig. S6A [this file] ), suggesting that it does
not drive oxidative stress but activates NRF2 downstream of oxidative
stress. 
Indeed, addition of rotenone to 2D
neurons, which increases ROS levels ( Fig. S6B [this file] ), increased
GSK3 activity ( Fig.
5F [rid=F5] ). Furthermore, ROS levels in 3D neurons were consistently higher
than in 2D ( Fig. 5G [rid=F5] , Fig. S6C [this file] ). 
Knockdown of decreased the level of peroxidated
lipids in neurons ( Fig. 5J [rid=F5] – K [rid=F5] , Fig. S6D [this file] ), which is a downstream
effects of increased ROS that
can drive neuronal death via ferroptosis . We found that ROS levels
of neurons in iAssembloids, which contains glia, are lower when compared to
those of 3D neuronal monocultures ( Fig. S6E [this file] ). 
We conducted this screen in two different cell line background pairs:
one where the neurons and astrocytes were not isogenic, with astrocytes
generated from the TCW 1E33 and 1E44 background , and neurons from WTC11
background ( Fig. S7A [this file] , Table S5 [rid=SD6] ), and another where the
neurons and astrocytes were isogenic with cells from the iNDI project
(KOLF2.1) ( Fig. S7B [this file] , Table S5 [rid=SD6] ). 
We conducted snRNA-seq on nuclei isolated from 3D neuron-astrocyte
co-cultures with neurons and astrocytes at 1:1 or 2:1 ratio ( Fig. S7C [this file] ). We separated the neurons
and astrocytes based on cell type-specific markers and focused mainly on
neuronal gene expression ( Fig. S7D [this file] – E [this file] ). 
We then performed unbiased clustering of this population
of cells, and we found that clusters 1 and 7 consisted of cells with lower expression ( Fig S7F [this file] ). We found that
cells within these clusters also expressed other markers such as for cluster 1, and for cluster 7
( Fig S7E [this file] , Table S6 [rid=SD7] ). (Cux2 cut-like homeobox 2) is a transcription factor
that is highly expressed in upper layers of the brain, particularly in the
pyramidal neurons of layer II-IV. In these clusters, we find that clusters 1 contain a
higher proportion of neurons from patients with no disease as opposed to those
diagnosed with AD ( Fig. S7F [this file] – G [this file] ). For both these clusters, we also found that these clusters contain more
APOE- 3 neurons than APOE- 4
AD patient neurons ( Fig. S7G [this file] ).

Wild type TDP-43-specific interactors were strongly enriched in splicing factors, consistent with the well-known and prominent role of TDP-43 in RNA splicing and in line with previous interactome studies ( Fig. 1h [rid=F1] ; Table S1 [this file] , S2 [this file] ) . In addition, our analysis uncovered previously known TDP-43 molecular functions, such as transcription regulation and DNA binding ( Fig. S1 [this file] ) . Validating our approach, the differences in the pathway-specific enrichment and interaction networks between TDP-43WT and TDP-43mNLS proteomes ( Fig. S1 [this file] ), pointed to a shift from nuclear interactomes in the wild type ( Fig. 1h [rid=F1] ) to cytoplasmic ones in the mutant NLS variant, which were enriched in translation regulation, RNA catabolic processes and the assembly of membraneless organelles, such as stress granules ( Fig. 1i [rid=F1] ). 
To characterize the pathological protein burden in each sample, we performed immunoblotting and quantified the total ( Fig. 2a [rid=F2] - b [rid=F2] ), or phosphorylated TDP-43 at positions 409/410 (pTDP-43) ( Fig. 2c [rid=F2] , d [rid=F2] , Fig. S2a [this file] ). All exogenous seeds, regardless of the source exhibited high internalization rate at 6 d.p.i, maintained similar levels at 10 d.p.i., and then showed a marked decline afterwards when assessed at 18 d.p.i. ( Fig. 2f [rid=F2] , Fig. S2b [this file] ). Despite some individual variability per condition ( Fig. S2c [this file] ), the FTLD patient seeds displayed an overall higher rate of retention within cells compared to the extracts from the non-neurodegenerative control brains, with the FTLD-TDP-A seeds showing the highest cell retention ( Fig. 2f [rid=F2] ). The internalization rate was largely unchanged in our BioID-TDP-43mNLS cell line with a subset of patient-seeds ( Fig. S2d [this file] ). 
Confocal immunofluorescence images from seeded cells were processed in Imaris to reconstruct three-dimensional objects for quantification ( Fig. 2g [rid=F2] , Fig. S3 [this file] ). In the BioID2-TDP-43mNLS line, seeding with the same SarkoSpin extracts produced higher rates of neoaggregates in both patient groups and both timepoints, likely driven by the higher cytoplasmic substrate availability ( Fig. S4a [this file] - c [this file] ). 
After monitoring the internalization rates and seeding efficiencies of all individual brain-derived SarkoSpin extracts ( Fig. 2 [rid=F2] , Fig. S3 [this file] - S4 [this file] ), we proceeded in the identification of changes in TDP-43 interactomes upon seeding to illuminate potentially distinct molecular pathways between the CTRL and patient groups as well as between the two FTLD subtypes. PCA analysis of the enriched interactomes showed that PC1 primarily separates samples based on the d.p.i., while both PC1 and PC2 allowed sample separation according to their treatment ( Fig. S4d [this file] ). This was supported by the common FTLD-TDP-A and FTLD-TDP-C biological processes identified via GO enrichment analysis, which pointed to decreased nuclear interactions of TDP-43 with partners in ribonucleoprotein biogenesis and other processes involving binding to nucleic acids ( Fig. 3c [rid=F3] , d [rid=F3] and Fig S5a [this file] ). Interestingly, at this later timepoint, FTLD-TDP-A-seeded cells showed increased interactions with spectrin-binding proteins ( Fig. S5c [this file] ), specifically ADD1 (Adducin 1, alpha subunit), which maintains the actin-spectrin cytoskeleton, KIF3A (Kinesin family member 3A), a motor protein important for axonal transport, and EPB41 (Erythrocyte membrane protein band 4.1), which anchors membrane proteins to cytoskeleton in neurons. 
SH-SY5Y cells stably expressing TDP-REG were incubated with Atto-488-labeled patient-derived seeds and analyzed by immunofluorescence and high-content confocal imaging at 10 and 18 d.p.i. ( Fig. 4a [rid=F4] and Fig. S6 [this file] ). Notably, large inclusions with filamentous or compact morphology were evident in seeded cells, containing both the exogenous, patient-derived material and recruited endogenous TDP-43 ( Fig. 4a [rid=F4] and Fig. S6 [this file] ), resembling the morphologies previously reported in patient brains . 
Using all available biochemical variables ( Fig. 2a [rid=F2] - d [rid=F2] and Fig. 5a [rid=F5] - d [rid=F5] ) and clinical data for these patients ( Table S3 [this file] ), we applied multiple linear regression to determine whether any variables showed a linear association with the seeding outcomes. In the final model, the load of pTDP-43 and TMEM106B fibrillar core showed a significant positive contribution to neoaggregate formation ( Fig. 5e [rid=F5] , f [rid=F5] and Fig. S7 [this file] ). Surprisingly, the same analysis using TDP-43 loss of function as the outcome, identified TMEM106B fibrillar core as the only significant variable in the final model, independently accounting for 80% of the variability in the data ( Fig. 5e [rid=F5] , f [rid=F5] and Fig. S7 [this file] ). 
TDP-43 recruitment and consequent loss of function occurred exclusively in neurons exposed to LCD fibrils but not α-synuclein or tau K18 species ( Fig 6e [rid=F6] , Fig. S8a [this file] , b [this file] ). 
In agreement with what we previously reported in neuron-like cells , most neurons (~90%) internalized LCD-488 fibrils, yet only a small population (~0.1%) developed loss of TDP-43 function and activated the TDP-REG to generate mScarlet-positive neurons ( Fig. S8b [this file] ). Moreover, another predominantly nuclear RNA-binding protein, FUS was unaffected in mScarlet-positive neurons ( Fig. S8c [this file] , d [this file] ), confirming the specificity of this induced cytoplasmic localization of TDP-43. A first set of affected neurons showed cytoplasmic TDP-43 aggregates, while a second one contained intranuclear inclusions ( Fig. 6l [rid=F6] , m [rid=F6] and Fig. S8e [this file] , f [this file] ). 
To verify that the measured mScarlet signal was not affected by the intrinsic autofluorescence of brain-derived material, we applied the same treatment to non-TDP-REG human neurons using as seeds our best FTLD-TDP-A seeder (FA 11) and one CTRL, confirming the specificity of the mScarlet signal to the activation of the reporter and the clear distinction with the detectable autofluorescence of the SarkoSpin extracts ( Fig. S9a [this file] - c [this file] ). Importantly, also in this case the combination of seeding with LLME increased the occurrence of cytoplasmic TDP-43 deposits ( Fig. 7d [rid=F7] , e [rid=F7] , Fig. S9d [this file] ). Image-based quantification of mScarlet-positive seeded neurons showed incomplete or absent LIMP2 signal surrounding those SarkoSpin aggregates that efficiently recruited endogenous TDP-43 (recruiters) compared to inactive ones that were fully sequestered within lysosomal membranes ( Fig 7f [rid=F7] , g [rid=F7] , Fig. S9e [this file] ). Interestingly, FTLD-TDP-A seeders in the absence of LLME-mediated lysosomal permeabilization showed higher percentages of mScarlet-positive neurons (ranging from ~2 to 15%) ( Fig. 7b [rid=F7] ) compared to neurons exposed to recombinant LCD fibrils (0.1%) ( Fig. 6k [rid=F6] , Fig. S8b [this file] ), indicating that patient-derived seeds possess different properties and are more potent than pure -obtained LCD fibrils.

We conducted cluster analysis to investigate the global impact of viral infections on the proteomic landscape, revealing distinct clustering patterns of proteomic data based on the viral infection conditions ( Figure S1B [this file] ). 
Using WGCNA, we identified 18 distinct modules of human proteins highly correlated with one another across all the conditions ( Figure 4A [rid=F4] , Figure S2A [this file] , Table S5). Among these, module 10 (1407 proteins), module 11 (854 proteins), and module 5 (578 proteins) contained the largest number of proteins ( Figure S2B [this file] ).

Moreover, the five viruses we tested caused unique changes in the trajectories of module 11 proteins, suggesting that viral infections may contribute to neurodegenerative processes in different ways ( Figure 4E [rid=F4] , Figure S2C [this file] ). A protein–protein interaction network of NDD-related genes highlighted interactions among proteins dysregulated during viral infections ( Figure S2D [this file] ). 
The module 16 was significantly enriched in pathways related to wound healing, emphasizing its role in tissue repair and regeneration ( Figure S3A [this file] ). The module 10 was associated with protein degradation pathways, including lysosome and ubiquitin-proteasome systems, which are crucial for cellular protein turnover ( Figure S3B [this file] ). The module 5 was enriched in pathways involved in DNA repair and cell cycle regulation, emphasizing its role in maintaining genomic stability and cellular integrity ( Figure S3C [this file] ). The module 2 showed enrichment in pathways related to mRNA splicing and processing, focusing on RNA metabolism and regulation ( Figure S3D [this file] ), which viruses often manipulate to control host gene expression and optimize conditions for their replication .

Ontology analysis of the secretomes of LRRK2 and wild type confirmed that proteins associated with secretion, including those associated with exosome formation, e.g., multivesicular body (MVB) proteins, were readily released ( Figure 2D [rid=F2] and Supplemental Figure 1E [this file] ). Interestingly, we noted that proteins associated with synaptic function, mitochondria and autophagy were also enriched in the secretomes from both LRRK2 and wild type neurons ( Figure 2D [rid=F2] and Supplemental Figure 1E [this file] ). 
In line with previous work, we detected 5 of 6 ATG8s in both the LRRK2 and control samples, with the highest detected being LC3B ( Figure 2E [rid=F2] , Supplemental Figure 1D [this file] ). 
Ontology analysis of the differentially expressed proteins suggests that mitochondrial proteins are the most prominent cargo upregulated in LRRK2 EVs ( Supplemental Figure 1F [this file] ). 
We next asked whether any miRNAs were differentially expressed, and detected no miRNAs significantly upregulated in either genotype ( Supplemental Figure 2A [this file] ). While no individual miRNA was significantly upregulated in LRRK2 EVs, the average levels of the top 50 detected miRNAs were all elevated in LRRK2 compared to wild type ( Figure 2I [rid=F2] , Supplemental Figure 2B [this file] ). 
Changes in the relative enrichment of these proteins were not due to changes in protein expression as no significant changes were observed by immunoblot analysis of neuronal lysates ( Supplemental Figure 3 [this file] ). 
We used the RNA specific dye, SYTO RNASelect (Thermo), to measure relative levels in fluorescence across our different conditions and observed that RNA could be readily detected in both wild type and LRRK2 P100 fractions ( Supplemental Figure 2C [this file] ), suggesting that RNAs are likely cargos within released exosomes. 
We confirmed that this signal could be detected in TIRF ( Figure 4D [rid=F4] , F [rid=F4] ) and was distinct from LC3/GABARAP localization in permeabilized cells ( Supplemental Figure 3B [this file] ). 
To determine if the LRRK2-mediated secretion of exosomes was similarly dependent on LC3 conjugation, we knocked down ATG7 using siRNA ( Supplemental Figure 4A [this file] – B [this file] ) and tracked CD63-pHluorin fusion events in LRRK2 neurons. We determined that ATG7 activity was required for LRRK2 mediated exosome release as we observed a nearly 50% reduction in the number of CD63 secretion events in neurons expressing the ATG7 siRNA ( Supplementary Figure 4C [this file] ). When compared to the non-coding siRNA control, ATG7 knockdown had no effect on exosome secretion from wild type neurons ( Supplemental Figure 4D [this file] ), suggesting that LC3 conjugation was required for the increased exosomal release induced by hyperactive LRRK2. 
Previous reports suggest that an acute prevention of autophagosome degradation via Bafilomycin A 1 (BafA1) ( 56 [rid=R56] , 57 [rid=R57] ) can also initiate the upregulation of secretion in several different cell types ( 58 [rid=R58] , 59 [rid=R59] ) ( Supplemental Figure 5A [this file] ). Consistent with previous reports, we observed significantly more particles secreted by BafA1 treated neurons as measured via NTA ( Supplemental Figure 5B [this file] – C [this file] ). We next isolated Large EVs/P20 and Small EVs/P100 released from DMSO and BafA1 treated neurons for immunoblot analysis ( Supplemental Figure 5D [this file] ). We observed that BafA1 treatment significantly increased the release of CD81 in small EVs ( Supplementary Figure 5G [this file] ), but, in contrast to LRRK2 neurons, CD63 was not detected in small EVs in either condition ( Supplemental Figure 5J [this file] ). BafA1 treated neurons did release more TSG101 and LC3 selectively within large EVs ( Supplementary Figure 5E [this file] – F [this file] , I [this file] – J [this file] ). 
We observed no change in the number of CD63-pHluorin events in neurons treated with DMSO or BafA1 ( Supplementary Figure 6G [this file] ). We tracked CD9-pHluorin fusion events in primary cortical neurons and observed significantly more fusion events in neurons following BafA1 incubation ( Supplementary Figure 6A [this file] – F [this file] ). In contrast, LRRK2 neurons exhibited no change in CD9-pHluroin events compared to wild type ( Supplementary Figure 6H [this file] – I [this file] ). 
In isolated plasma, we observed a significant increase in CD81 in LRRK2 plasma ( Figure 6C [rid=F6] , G [rid=F6] ), but failed to detect any change in CD63 ( Supplemental Figure 6A [this file] – B [this file] ).

We analyzed their lipidome by comprehensive, quantitative shotgun lipidomic analysis and found that iPSC-derived neurons, astrocytes and microglia had very distinct lipid profiles ( Fig 1D [rid=F1] – G [rid=F1] , individual lipid species in Sup Fig 1 [this file] ) that resembled lipotypes of freshly isolated cells from mouse brain tissue . 
First, we explored regional differences in lipid composition between brain regions in the control brains ( Fig 2B [rid=F2] – C [rid=F2] , Sup Fig 2A [this file] ). The frontal cortex white matter had high levels of ceramides (CER, HexCER) and sphingomyelin (SM), consistent with the enrichment of these lipids in oligodendrocytes ( Fig 2C [rid=F2] , Sup Fig 2A [this file] ) . On the contrary, phospholipid and storage lipid (e.g. CE, TG) levels were relatively higher in cerebellum and frontal cortex gray matter ( Fig 2C [rid=F2] , Sup Fig 2A [this file] ). Principal component analysis (PCA) largely separated control and AD samples in the frontal cortex gray and white matter, but less so in the cerebellum ( Fig 2D [rid=F2] , Sup Fig 2B [this file] – C [this file] ). At the class level, we found that cholesterol esters were significantly upregulated in AD in frontal cortex gray and white matter ( 2E [rid=F2] – G [rid=F2] , Sup Fig 2J [this file] – Q [this file] ) and trended towards increased levels in cerebellum. Analysis at the level of individual lipid species also showed an increase for most CE species ( sup 2D [this file] – F [this file] ), but no single CE species reached significance, likely reflecting high variation in fatty acid tails of CEs in individual human subjects. However, no consistent changes in phospholipid or TG saturation were observed ( Sup Fig 2G [this file] – I [this file] ). 
ApoE genotype of the iPSCs was confirmed by sanger sequencing on receipt and after differentiation to astrocytes, as well as after each experiment to verify sample identity ( Sup Fig 3A [this file] ). Successful differentiation to astrocytes was validated by astrocyte marker staining and expression of astrocyte markers by RNAseq ( Fig 3B [rid=F3] , Sup Fig 3B [this file] – C [this file] ). We performed lipidomics on two biological replicates (with 3 replicate samples per experiment) for both isogenic sets using our standardized iPSC-lipidomic pipeline (see Fig 3D [rid=F3] – G [rid=F3] and Sup Fig 3D [this file] – E [this file] for individual replicates, and Fig 3H [rid=F3] and Sup Fig 3F [this file] for group level results). Strikingly, and consistently across experiments and lines, we observed a strong ApoE4-dependent increase in CE (individual species Fig 3D [rid=F3] – G [rid=F3] , Sup Fig 3D [this file] – E [this file] , and class level Fig 3H [rid=F3] , Sup Fig 3F [this file] ). SM levels were significantly downregulated in ApoE4 astrocytes at both the species and class level, while LPE levels were only increased at the class level ( Fig 3D [rid=F3] – H [rid=F3] , Sup Fig 3D [this file] – F [this file] ). The (female) BIONi037 ApoE4 astrocytes also showed a strong and consistent increase in LacCER, HexCER and ceramide (CER) species, which was not found in the (male) Kolf2.1J ApoE4 astrocytes ( Fig 3D [rid=F3] – H [rid=F3] , Sup Fig 3D [this file] – F [this file] ). We did not find evidence for increased saturation of phospholipids in our ApoE4 astrocytes, as is typical for activated astrocytes ( Sup Fig 3G [this file] ) . 
To be able to compare our results to previous transcriptomic studies with different ApoE4 iPSC-derived astrocytes , we also performed transcriptomic analysis on our BIONi037 isogenic set ( Sup Fig 4C [this file] – E [this file] ). Through unbiased gene set enrichment analysis, the MHC class I antigen presentation pathway was shown to be downregulated by ApoE4 also at the transcriptome level ( Fig 4K [rid=F4] , Sup Fig 4E [this file] ). Our transcriptomic analysis additionally showed downregulation of interleukin and interferon immune signaling pathways, the complement cascade and ER phagosome transport, while translation related terms were upregulated ( Fig 4K [rid=F4] , Sup Fig 4E [this file] ). When looking at ApoE4 dependent gene expression changes in the complete Interferon reactome pathway ( Sup Fig 4G [this file] ) we found that similar to the proteomic results, specifically all genes in the MHC class I pathway and immune specific subunits of the proteasome, were downregulated by ApoE4 in our isogenic sets ( Fig 4L [rid=F4] ) as well as in all isogenic sets and case-control sets from Lin . 2018 and TCW . 2022 ( Fig 4G [rid=F4] , L [rid=F4] ). 
In contrast to the ApoE4 astrocytes, CEs and TGs were strongly downregulated in reactive astrocytes at the species ( Fig 5B [rid=F5] , Sup Fig 5A [this file] – E [this file] ) and class level ( Fig 5C [rid=F5] , J [rid=F5] , Sup Fig 5B [this file] – D [this file] ), whereas HexCER were increased in reactive astrocytes as well as in the BIONi037 ApoE4 astrocytes ( Fig 5C [rid=F5] , J [rid=F5] ). As expected, phospholipid saturation was increased in activated astrocytes ( Fig 5D [rid=F5] , Sup Fig 5F [this file] ) , but not in ApoE4 astrocytes ( Sup Fig 3G [this file] ). We focused our analysis on proteins that were upregulated or downregulated by reactivity in both lines ( Figure 5H [rid=F5] – I [rid=F5] , Sup Fig 6A [this file] ). Overrepresentation analysis did not identify any significant downregulated pathways ( Sup Fig 6A [this file] ). Beyond these terms, analysis showed that virtually all immune upregulated proteins in reactive astrocytes were down in the ApoE4 astrocytes ( Fig 5K [rid=F5] , Sup Fig 6B [this file] – C [this file] ). 
We also found that a specific cluster of cholesterol synthetic genes was upregulated in reactive astrocytes ( Sup Fig 7A [this file] ). Combined addition of cholesterol with the ACAT inhibitor avasimibe further increased IL-6 secretion, indicating that CE formation buffered the immune activation by cholesterol treatment ( Sup Fig 7B [this file] ). Moreover, the addition of cholesterol to astrocytes is sufficient to increase saturated phospholipid levels ( Fig 6E [rid=F6] ) and the LPC lipid class level ( Sup Fig 7C [this file] – D [this file] ) typical for activated astrocytes ( Fig 5C [rid=F5] – D [rid=F5] ). 
We have uploaded our data presented above, as well as (un)published lipidomics data generated together with a large group of collaborators, totaling a current number of 50 datasets over four neurodegenerative diseases and multiple treatment conditions ( Sup Table S1 [this file] ). 
Importantly, ApoE4 astrocytes do not show the increase in saturated phospholipids typical for reactive astrocytes ( Sup Fig 3G [this file] ). 
Similarly, our proteomics analysis ( Sup Fig 4A [this file] – B [this file] ) revealed several differences between ApoE4 effects in the different parental lines with stronger overall effects in the female BIONi037 ApoE4 line. 
All donor information, including postmortem (PM) delay, age, sex, APOE genotype and pathological information is listed in table S1 [this file] . 
Main figure 3 [rid=F3] shows lipidomic analysis on Kolf2.1J set II and BIONi037 set II, while supplementary figure 3 [this file] shows lipidomic analysis of Kolf2.1J set I and BIONi037 set I. 
The comparison of proteomic and transcriptomic analysis shown in Sup Fig 4C [this file] , as well as all transcriptomic data are from the BIONi037 iAstrocytes (set I) cultured in 2% FBS. 
All lipid values in this figure are plotted as % of total lipids, raw concentration can be found in Supplementary figure 2 [this file] .

Genotypes for both cell lines were confirmed by DNA sequencing ( Figures S1 [this file] A and S2 [this file] A). A normal karyotype was confirmed for parental lines ( Figures S1 [this file] B and S2 [this file] B). Wild-type and mutant iPSCs were indistinguishable from each other in colony morphology, the ability to form embryoid bodies, and the expression of pluripotency markers ( Figures 1 [rid=fig1] B, S1 [this file] C, S2 [this file] C, and S2D). After 3 days, retinoic acid (RA) and smoothened agonist (SAG, an activator of the SHH pathway) were added to create NES+, SOX2+, PAX6+ neural precursor cells (NPCs) ( Figures 1 [rid=fig1] D, 1E, S1 [this file] D, S2 [this file] E, and S2F). Twenty-one days of maturation produced >90% class III β-tubulin (TUJ1), neurofilament heavy chain (SMI32), choline acetyltransferase (CHAT)-positive motor neurons ( Figures 1 [rid=fig1] D, 1E, S1 [this file] E, and S2 [this file] G). 
See also Figures S1 [this file] and S2 [this file] . 
See also Figure S3 [this file] . 
We investigated TDP-43 localization in our iPSC lines using confocal microscopy and found that both mutant 392.1 and KOLF2.1 motor neurons had depleted levels of TDP-43 in the nucleus compared with wild-type ( Figures 2 [rid=fig2] D and S3 [this file] A). However, total TDP-43 levels were equivalent between lines suggesting that nuclear depletion was not due to loss of protein ( Figures 2 [rid=fig2] E and S3 [this file] B). 
In our models, we found no change in several markers of ER stress including the transcription factor ATF4 or the ER chaperone BIP ( Figures 2 [rid=fig2] E and S3 [this file] B). Furthermore, we found no significant change in total ubiquitin conjugates or autophagy markers p62 or LC3B ( Figures 2 [rid=fig2] E and S3 [this file] B). We measured cell viability and found that KOLF2.1 and 392.1 p97 R155H motor neurons had decreased survival relative to wild type in agreement with previous studies ( Hall et al., 2017 [rid=bib28] ; Wang et al., 2022 [rid=bib63] ) ( Figures 2 [rid=fig2] F and S3 [this file] C). 
Peptides from day 30 motor neurons from wild-type and R155H (KOLF2.1 or 392.1) were labeled with TMTs and analyzed by liquid chromatography and mass spectrometry (LC/MS-MS) ( Figure 3 [rid=fig3] A and Table S1 [this file] ) ( McAlister et al., 2014 [rid=bib44] ; Ting et al., 2011 [rid=bib60] ). Gene ontology (GO) analysis of differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) found different pathways altered in KOLF2.1 and 392.1 mutant motor neurons despite the same R155H mutation ( Figures S4 [this file] A–S4C). KOLF2.1 homozygous motor neurons showed significant depletion of mitochondrial proteins ( Figure S4 [this file] B) that are part of complexes regulating import of proteins into mitochondria, and subunits of electron transport chain complexes I-IV was observed ( Figure S4 [this file] D). These results were further validated by immunoblot ( Figure S4 [this file] E). Notably, KOLF2.1 mutant motor neurons had significantly decreased mitochondrial membrane potential as measured using MitoTracker red ( Figures S4 [this file] F and S4G). No significant changes were observed in mitochondrial morphology ( Figure S4 [this file] H). Interestingly, these mitochondrial changes were not seen in the 392.1 mutant motor neurons ( Figure S4 [this file] C, and data not shown). This methodology uses a dynamic branch-cutting algorithm to separate clusters identified via a topological overlap matrix into distinct modules ( Figure S5 [this file] A and Table S2 [this file] ). Inspection of module eigenprotein expression revealed agreement between KOLF2.1 and 392.1 wild-type lines, but a divergence in the mutant neurons ( Figure S5 [this file] B). To identify modules that represented proteins changing in a similar manner between cell lines, modules were ranked by a composite score based on concordance between genetic backgrounds and average log fold change ( Figures S5 [this file] D–S5F and Table S2 [this file] ). Multiple GO terms related to autophagy and lysosomal homeostasis were enriched ( Figures S5 [this file] D and S5E middle panels). 
See also Figures S4 [this file] and S5 [this file] . 
See also Figure S6 [this file] . 
We assessed viability following LLOME treatment and found that mutant motor neurons had increased cell death following release while wild-type neurons had no change ( Figures 6 [rid=fig6] A and S6 [this file] A). Following subthreshold LLOME or bafilomycin-A1 (inhibitor of lysosomal vacuolar H+ ATPase) treatment, we found that the LysoSensor fluorescence was significantly decreased demonstrating compromised pH ( Figures 6 [rid=fig6] B and S6 [this file] B). Notably, mutant motor neurons had decreased fluorescence at basal levels compared with wild-type ( Figures 6 [rid=fig6] B and S6 [this file] B). 
We found that LGALS8 puncta colocalized with ubiquitin in both wild-type and mutant motor neurons ( Figures S6 [this file] C and S6D). 
We attempted to prevent the persistence of damaged lysosomes in mutant motor neurons using a low dose of CB-5083, a highly specific p97 ATP-competitive inhibitor ( Zhou et al., 2015 [rid=bib72] ) ( Figure 7 [rid=fig7] A). p97 inhibition by itself did not cause LGALS8 or p62 puncta formation in CB-5083-treated cells ( Figures 7 [rid=fig7] B, S7 [this file] A, and S7E). Notably, CB-5083 treatment caused mutant neurons to accelerate the clearance of damaged lysosomes in a manner that was comparable to wild-type neurons ( Figures 7 [rid=fig7] B, 7C, and S7 [this file] A). LGALS8 puncta in mutant motor neurons were larger than those in wild-type during CB-5083 treatment, similar to the pattern seen in non-CB-5083-treated neurons ( Figure S7 [this file] B). We asked whether higher doses of CB-5083 were also able to rescue lysophagy defects; however, at 2-μM and 4-μM CB-5083, we found that CB-5083 was unable to rescue the phenotype and LGALS8 puncta persisted in both wild-type and mutant motor neurons up to 24 h ( Figure S7 [this file] C). 
See also Figure S7 [this file] . 
While wild-type neurons treated with CB-5083 were able to clear LGALS8 puncta at a similar rate to untreated neurons, they showed persistent and elevated levels of p62 puncta 24 h after LLOME ( Figures S7 [this file] D–S7F). Indeed, increased p62 puncta were observed upon LLOME-CB-5053 co-treatment compared with LLOME alone ( Figure S7 [this file] F). CB-5083 treatment restored basal lysosomal pH in mutant motor neurons to that of wild-type neurons ( Figures 7 [rid=fig7] D, 7E, and S7 [this file] G). Furthermore, CB-5083 treatment prevented cell death in mutant motor neurons during release from LLOME ( Figures 7 [rid=fig7] F and S7 [this file] H). 
While the KOLF2.1 cell line with R155H displayed mitochondrial deficits ( Figures S4 [this file] B and S4D), the 392.1 patient cell line had no significant alterations to the mitochondrial proteome ( Figure S4 [this file] C). 
While mutant was recruited to ubiquitylated lysosomes, it did not increase in association with UBXD1 and presumably the ELDR complex ( Figures 6 [rid=fig6] and S6 [this file] ). 
In wild-type and mutant neurons, p97 inhibition increased p62 accumulation ( Figure S7 [this file] ). The additional rescue of lysosomal pH and viability suggests that p97 inhibition may afford therapeutic benefit ( Figure 7 [rid=fig7] and S7 [this file] ). 
Once iPSCs reached 80% confluency, the media was replaced with freshly made induction media ( Table S1 [this file] ). 
Media composition can be found in the supplementary methods [this file] . 
For all experiments, n ≥ 3 or more biological replicates for each condition examined except immunofluorescence characterization experiments in Figures 4 [rid=fig4] , S1 [this file] , and S2 [this file] (n = 2).

More specifically, glutamate receptor subunits such as and as well as ion-channel subunits ( ) were more highly expressed in neurons cultured in iAssembloids ( Fig. 2C [rid=F2] , Fig. S1D [rid=SD8] , Table S1 [this file] ). 
These functions include BDNF signaling ( ), axon guidance ( ), as well as synaptic transmission ( ) ( Fig. S2B [rid=SD8] – C [rid=SD8] , Table S1 [this file] ). Single-nucleus RNA sequencing also revealed that some astrocytes expressed higher levels of genes associated with glycolysis ( ) as well as the unfolded protein response ( ) ( Fig. S2B [rid=SD8] – C [rid=SD8] , Table S1 [this file] ). Very few (0.4–0.5%) of the iAssembloid-derived astrocytes expressed markers of reactive astrocytes such as , , , , or , suggesting that astrocytes in iAssembloids do not spontaneously become inflammatory ( Fig. S2D [rid=SD8] , Table S1 [this file] ). 
These clusters, which we named “iAssembloid +”, “iAssembloid chemokine”, and “iAssembloid proliferative”, have profiles like the monocultured microglia +, chemokine, and proliferative clusters, but are characterized by expression of MHC class II proteins such as and ( Fig. S3B [rid=SD8] , Table S1 [this file] ), which were either not expressed or not captured by microglia in the monoculture dataset.

We first assayed whether neurons in iAssembloids had higher levels of c-FOS, an immediate early gene whose expression is triggered by neuronal activity, Indeed, we saw that there was a higher level of c-FOS in neurons with iAssembloids as compared to 2D monoculture neurons ( Fig. S1G [this file] ). 
Compared to 2D monocultured astrocytes previously generated in our lab , astrocytes cultured in iAssembloids developed distinct transcriptional profiles ( Fig. S2A [this file] ). As astrocytes within iAssembloids matured, astrocytes had transcriptional profiles more strongly associated with supporting neuronal function based on EnrichR pathway and gene ontology analysis of the upregulated genes ( Fig. S2B [this file] ). These functions include BDNF signaling ( ), axon guidance ( ), as well as synaptic transmission ( ) ( Fig. S2B [this file] – C [this file] , Table S1 [rid=SD1] ). Single-nucleus RNA sequencing also revealed that some astrocytes expressed higher levels of genes associated with glycolysis ( ) as well as the unfolded protein response ( ) ( Fig. S2B [this file] – C [this file] , Table S1 [rid=SD1] ). Very few (0.4–0.5%) of the iAssembloid-derived astrocytes expressed markers of reactive astrocytes such as , , , , or , suggesting that astrocytes in iAssembloids do not spontaneously become inflammatory ( Fig. S2D [this file] , Table S1 [rid=SD1] ). Imaging showed a lower number of processes between astrocytes induced by IL1a+TNF+C1q as compared to those found without stimulation ( Fig S2E [this file] ). 
To characterize transcriptional changes that occur in microglia cultured in iAssembloids, we compared single-nucleus RNA-sequencing data for microglia in iAssembloids to those for monocultured iPSC-derived microglia ( Fig. S3A [this file] ). These clusters, which we named “iAssembloid +”, “iAssembloid chemokine”, and “iAssembloid proliferative”, have profiles like the monocultured microglia +, chemokine, and proliferative clusters, but are characterized by expression of MHC class II proteins such as and ( Fig. S3B [this file] , Table S1 [rid=SD1] ), which were either not expressed or not captured by microglia in the monoculture dataset. We mapped our dataset onto an existing human patient dataset and found that expression of and between microglia within the iAssembloids and patient microglia were comparable ( Fig. S3C [this file] ).

[xref] [rid=bib73] Although these data are derived from bulk brain tissue and therefore reflect signals across multiple cell types rather than microglia alone, and assess a more limited set of TFs compared to the broader motif set analyzed by motifbreakR, the strongest ASB signals were observed for CTCF and RAD21, a cohesin complex component that frequently colocalizes with CTCF. The c.1306 G>A mutation introduces a frameshift resulting in a functional knockout of ATP13A2 and is causally associated with Kufor-Rakeb syndrome, an autosomal recessive form of juvenile Parkinsonism ( Fig. S1a [this file] – b [this file] ). Importantly, expression of canonical midbrain specification markers ( , , and ) was comparable between genotypes, indicating intact early midbrain patterning and enabling downstream analyses of disease-relevant phenotypes independent of developmental specification defects ( Fig S1c [this file] ). 
Consistent with intact early neuronal development, dopaminergic neuron marker TH was present at similar levels in ATP13A2 and ATP13A2 organoids by day 25, before astrocyte appearance (p = 0.5513) ( Fig S1d [this file] ). In contrast, by day 100, after the appearance of astrocytes, ATP13A2 organoids exhibited a significant reduction of immunoreactivity for dopaminergic neurons markers including TH and GIRK2 compared to isogenic ATP13A2 midbrain organoids (TH: Clone1: p = 0.0038, fold change 0.264±0.397; Clone2: p =0.0004, fold change 0.132±0.322) (GIRK2: p = 0.0149; fold change 0.652±0.373) ( Fig 1a [rid=F1] and S1e [this file] ). 
Isolated astrocytes exhibited comparable morphologies and homogenous expression of midbrain and astrocytic markers (S100b, SOX9, and FOXA2) ( Fig S1f [this file] – g [this file] ). Across co-culture conditions, the total astrocyte abundance, quantified as CD44-normalized area, did not differ significantly, suggesting that astrocyte abundance was not a confounding variable (vs. all-ATP13A2 : ATP13A2 neurons p = 0.9908; ATP13A2 astrocytes p = 0.3627; all-ATP13A2 p = 0.2367) ( Fig S1h [this file] ) However, notably, co-cultures containing ATP13A2 astrocytes exhibited a significant increase in GFAP, even when co-cultured with WT-neurons, indicating that ATP13A2 loss promotes an astrocyte-autonomous reactive state (p = 0.0024; fold change 5.549±3.143) ( Fig 1e [rid=F1] ). 
Across all midbrain co-culture conditions, the number of MAP2 immunoreactive cells did not differ significantly, suggesting that ATP13A2 astrocytes may be selectively toxic to dopaminergic neurons rather than inducing a generalized neuronal toxicity (vs. all-ATP13A2 : ATP13A2 neurons p = 0.8136; ATP13A2 astrocytes p = 0.7970; all-ATP13A2 p = 0.1136) ( Fig S1h [this file] ). In this context, ATP13A2 astrocytes again exhibited significantly increased GFAP immunoreactivity, consistent with a cell-autonomous reactive phenotype (staining p = 0.0198, fold change 1.694±0.647; immunoblot p = 0.0164, fold change 5.245±2.745) ( Fig 1f [rid=F1] , Fig S1i [this file] ). Notably, this reactive state did not impair cortical neuron survival, as indicated by no significant change in the number of MAP2-positive neurons, and protein levels for the pan-neuronal marker β-neuronal tubulin (TUJ1) were modestly increased compared to isogenic controls (MAP2: p = 0.7821; TUJ1: p = 0.0347, fold change 1.444±0.450) ( Fig 1f [rid=F1] and S1i [this file] ). 
Gene ontology and pathway enrichment analysis of the upregulated genes showed significant enrichment of pathways associated with cytokine signaling and extracellular matrix remodeling, consistent with a pro-inflammatory reactive astrocyte phenotype ( Fig S2a [this file] ) . This treatment led to significant upregulation of key transcriptional signatures found in ATP13A2 astrocytes, inducing , and , thereby establishing polyamine lysosomal retention of polyamines as a causal upstream driver of astrocyte reactivity ( Fig S2b [this file] ). 
Pharmacologic inhibition of lysosomal polyamine export using AMXT-1501 in ATP13A2 astrocytes also reduced both DQ-BSA proteolysis and LysoSensor signal ( Fig S2c [this file] – d [this file] ), establishing that impaired ATP13A2-dependent polyamine transport disrupts lysosomal acidification and impairs proteolytic function in astrocytes. Notably, despite impaired lysosomal function, ATP13A2 astrocytes, and AMXT-1501-treated ATP13A2 both exhibited a significant increase in lysosomal mass, as assessed by LAMP1 immunostaining (vs. ATP13A2 UT, ATP13A2 p = 0.114, fold change 1.482±0.093; ATP13A2 AMXT-1501 p = 0.114, fold change 1.492±0.146) ( Fig S2e [this file] ). 
Immunofluorescence and immunoblot analyses revealed a significant increase in α-synuclein protein in ATP13A2 astrocytes compared to isogenic controls (p = 0.0034, fold change 1.393±0.313) ( Fig 2f [rid=F2] , S2f [this file] ). However, increased α-synuclein occurred without changes in transcripts abundance, as assessed by RNA-seq and qPCR, suggesting that increased α-synuclein in astrocytes was a result of impaired degradation rather than transcriptional upregulation ( Fig S2g [this file] ). To directly assess intracellular trafficking to the lysosomal compartment, we performed live-cell imaging of mCherry-LAMP1-labeled lysosomes following exposure to fluorescently tagged α-synuclein monomers ( Fig S2h [this file] ). 
We observed a time-dependent increase in cell death; while no significant changes were detected at earlier time points ( Fig S3a [this file] ), four weeks of exposure to ATP13A2 ACM resulted in a significant elevation of extracellular lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), indicating a loss of membrane integrity (p = 0.0346, fold change 1.596±0.916) ( Fig 3c [rid=F3] ). 
We validated this increase quantitatively via ELISA, confirming that CXCL1 protein levels are significantly higher in ATP13A2 ACM compared to control ACM ( Fig S3b [this file] ). 
We observed a clear dose-dependent trend in apoptotic activation indicated by a significant increase in cleaved caspase-3 immunoreactivity at 50 and 100 ng/ml of CXCL1 ( Fig 3h [rid=F3] , S3c [this file] ). In contrast, the 100 ng/ml dose resulted in broad, non-selective neurotoxicity ( Fig S3d [this file] )To assess whether CXCL1 is a soluble factor associated with ATP13A2 LOF in vivo, we employed Atp13a2 knock-out (−/−) mice. 
Complementary uptake assays using labeled BODIPY-SPM and BODIPY-SPD showed a modest but significant increase in polyamine influx in ATP13A2 astrocytes (SPM: p = 0.0276; SPD: p = 0.0276) ( Fig S4a [this file] ). 
Consistent with this, RNA-seq analysis of the polyamine biosynthetic pathway (schematized in Fig 4a [rid=F4] ) revealed coordinated induction of polyamine synthesis and transport genes in ATP13A2 LOF astrocytes, including , along with , which encodes the SAM-synthesizing enzyme required to sustain elevated polyamine demand ( Fig 4d [rid=F4] , orange label). qPCR validation confirmed upregulation of key pathway nodes ( 1.521±0.104; 1.921±0.252) ( Fig s4b [this file] ). 
Volcano plot highlighted a few neuroinflammatory genes among the hypomethylated promoters, including ( Fig S4c [this file] ). 
Although ATP13A2 astrocytes showed a small reduction in overall promoter accessibility genome-wide (39.6% vs 43.25% in ATP13A2 , Fig S4d [this file] ), regions that became differentially accessible in the mutant condition were disproportionately enriched at promoters (approximately 40% vs. 20% in ATP13A2 ), indicating preferential promoter opening rather than uniform chromatin relaxation ( Fig S4e [this file] ). 
Locus-level inspection further validated these findings, revealing increased accessibility specifically at core inflammatory chemokines ( ) and astrocyte reactivity genes ( ) ( Fig S4f [this file] ). 
Critically, MGBG also reversed the reactive astrocyte phenotype, reducing GFAP expression at both the transcript and the protein levels (ATP13A2 MGBG vs control fold change 0.23±0.144, p = 0.0281) ( Fig 5c [rid=F5] , S5a [this file] ). 
Similar to MGBG, shRNA knockdown of significantly increased lysosomal proteolytic activity in ATP13A2 astrocytes, achieving similar levels as seen in ATP13A2 astrocytes (vs ATP13A2 shScr, shAMD1#1 fold change 1.317±0.206, p = 0.0432; shAMD1#2-fold change1.514±0.259, p = 0.0046) ( Fig S5b [this file] ). Likewise, shRNA knockdown of AMD1 significantly reduced reactive astrocyte marker GFAP compared to scramble control, again achieving similar levels of GFAP expression as WT control astrocytes (vs ATP13A2 shScr, shAMD1#1 fold change 0.144±0.026, p < 0.0001; shAMD1#2-fold change 0.168±0.062, p < 0.0001) ( Fig S5c [this file] ).

The estimated progression speeds appeared correlated with the slope of the regression line to the total score of ALSFRS-R , but a distinct difference between them was observed in a certain number of patients (Supplementary Figs. 2 [this file] , 3) [this file] . Using posterior state probabilities computed during model fitting and the learned emission probabilities, the model demonstrated high agreement between observed and reconstructed total ALSFRS-R scores (R² = 0.801; Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). First, we compared patient-specific progression speeds obtained under joint estimation of the transition rate matrix and speeds with patient-specific progression speeds obtained under re-estimation of speeds while holding a pre-estimated transition rate matrix fixed (Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] ). Second, we evaluated sensitivity to the scale of the transition rate matrix by perturbing off-diagonal transition rates by (recomputing diagonal entries to preserve row-sum constraints) and re-estimating patient-specific progression speeds with the perturbed fixed (Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] ). 
To aid clinical interpretation, we provide illustrative patient pairs with similar baseline total ALSFRS-R and the same trajectory cluster but markedly different inferred progression speeds, showing divergent subsequent decline in total ALSFRS-R (Supplementary Fig. 5 [this file] ). We additionally illustrate an example in which two patients have similar total-score slopes yet substantially different estimated speeds (Patient D and F, Supplementary Fig. 5b, c [this file] ). 
Cluster #6 began with functional levels similar to Cluster #1 but experienced a slightly faster and more generalized functional decline overall (Fig. 2e [rid=Fig2] , Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] ). 
We found that speed estimation remained stable (Pearson’s correlation = 0.81–0.83), and pathway recovery was high (accuracy was 0.84 at mean interval 10 and 0.97–0.98 at mean intervals 20–40) across all conditions, supporting that the model can reliably infer its key latent quantities under irregularly sampled longitudinal data (Supplementary Fig. 7 [this file] ). 
Pathways stratified the timing of these milestone events (Supplementary Fig. 8 [this file] ), indicating that pathways capture heterogeneity in the domain-specific pattern and timing of severe functional deterioration beyond overall progression speed. Consistently, in Cox multivariable model analysis, standardized speed remained associated with risk, while pathways provided complementary prognostic stratification for clinically interpretable endpoints (Supplementary Fig. 8 [this file] ), supporting the added clinical value of the pathway classification beyond speed alone. 
Following the same criteria used in AnswerALS to select patients, 2,565 individuals were included in the analysis (Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). We observed similarly high agreement between observed and reconstructed total ALSFRS-R scores in PRO-ACT as in AnswerALS (R² = 0.800; Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). However, one notable exception was observed: patients in Cluster #2 of the AnswerALS cohort showed a decline in respiratory function, whereas such a pattern was not observed in the corresponding cluster of PRO-ACT cohort (Fig. 3b [rid=Fig3] , Supplementary Fig. 9 [this file] ). 
Total-score prediction errors were lower under IPS-CT-HMM (MAE 4.04 vs 4.17; RMSE 5.43 vs 5.56), with higher variance explained (R² 0.398 vs 0.368) (Supplementary Fig. 10 [this file] ). 
We performed a multivariable regression analysis to predict the estimated progression speed by the presence and absence of each gene mutation as explanatory variables, and also covariates of gender, age at onset, and prior exposure to riluzole (Supplementary Fig. 11a–c [this file] ). No significant associations were also found in the patients with ATXN2 mutations (Supplementary Fig. 11d, e [this file] , ). No clear linear relationship was observed (Pearson’s correlation ) and no significant association was observed in the regression analysis (Supplementary Fig. 11f, g [this file] , ). 
In GO CC analysis, we observed downregulation of gene clusters associated with mature ribosomes, such as polysomes (Fig. 5b [rid=Fig5] , Supplementary Fig. 12a, b [this file] ). 
However, GSEA analysis revealed upregulation of protein groups related to ribosome biogenesis in GO BP category (Fig. 5c [rid=Fig5] , Supplementary Fig. 12c [this file] ). 
Gene expression levels in patient iPSC-derived motor neurons did not contribute to predicting progression speeds or progression pathway clusters (Supplementary Fig. 13 [this file] ). 
However, a certain number of patients showed relative difference between the two measures (Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] ). Although survival information was available for only a limited subset, age at death tended to be slightly lower in the discordant group (Supplementary Figs. 2 [this file] , 3 [this file] ). 
Basic characteristic values for each cohort are shown in Supplementary Table 1 [this file] . 
We set the standard deviation of progression speed to a broad value ( , unless otherwise noted) to avoid excessive shrinkage of individual speeds. (Sensitivity analyses for are provided in Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ).
