After blocking, primary antibodies were added at 50 μL per well at different dilutions in the block solution as listed in the Supplementary Table 2 [this file] , and the cells were incubated at 4°C overnight. 
We also created an isogenic series of TDP-43 variant-containing lines by introducing the Q331K and M337V mutations (TDP-43 , TDP-43 ) in the PGP-CTRL background via CRISPR editing ( Figure 1B [rid=F1] , blue panel and Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). 
We observed robust MAP-2 staining indicating high numbers of mature neurons, robust expression of neurofilament H (NFH), and low numbers of proliferating cells as stained by KI67 ( Figure 2A [rid=F2] and Supplementary Figures 1 [this file] – 4 [this file] ). We also observed typical expression of TDP-43 with no gross changes in localization of TDP-43 in the TDP-43 iMNs ( Supplementary Figure 5 [this file]. 
The expression of motor neuron markers ISLET1 and NKX6.2 were moderate and variable across control and TDP-43 iMNs ( Supplementary Figure 6 [this file] ). We found no significant differences in the proportion of ISLET1-positive or NKX6.2-positive cells between all controls and TDP-43 , with an average of ~33% ISLET positive and 38% NKX6.2-positive cells per image tile ( Supplementary Figure 6A [this file] , C [this file] ). However, there were subtle differences across the gene-edited clones and gene-corrected lines compared to parental controls ( Supplementary Figure 6B [this file] , D [this file] ). Similarly, we did not observe differences in the number of KI67-positive cells in the TDP-43 lines compared to the controls ( Supplementary Figure 6E [this file] , F [this file] ). We also did not detect significant differences in TDP-43–expressing cells ( Supplementary Figure 6 G [this file] , H [this file] ). 
Combined with RM, RGEDI allows us to monitor tens to hundreds of thousands of cells at a time. iMNs were transduced with RGEDI on differentiation day ~DIV20 and subjected ~ 1 week later (~DIV27) to daily time-lapse imaging using RM in both the red and green channels for 9 days ( Supplementary Figure 7 [this file] ). In the green channel, iMNs displayed typical neuronal morphology with dendrites and branching processes ( Supplementary Figure 8A [this file] ), and quantification of neuron length and structure on ~DIV31 using previously described methods revealed no significant differences in neurite length, number of processes or branch ends in the TDP-43 lines compared to their isogenic controls ( Supplementary Figure 8 B [this file] – G [this file] ). 
To determine whether this was true in our TDP-43 iMNs as well, we evaluated the RGEDI ratio of red-fluorescing (dying) cells to the total number of green-fluorescing (live) cells in mutant and control cells over time ( Supplementary Figure 7B [this file] ). 
iMNs displayed a higher proportion of dead and dying cells than their isogenic controls (OR-CD of 2.4) ( Figure 2B [rid=F2] , Supplementary Figure 9 [this file] ), even though two of the control lines displayed different death rates ( Supplementary Figure 9A [this file] ). The TDP-43 iMNs displayed the highest death rate compared to controls (OR-CD = 2.6), followed by TDP-43 iMNs (OR-CD= 1.7) ( Supplementary Figure 9 B C [this file] ). The iMNs from the patient with the TDP-43 mutation displayed an OR-CD of 1.4 compared to its gene-corrected control (GC-CTRL ), which was similar to our previous reports ( Supplementary Figure 9D [this file] ). While we did not observe significant changes collectively in ISLET1or NXK6.1 iMNs across the controls and all TDP-43 iMNs, there were significantly fewer NKX6.2-positive cells among the TDP-43 and TDP-43 iMNs compared to their parental controls ( Supplementary Figure 6B [this file] ). 
To uncover these features, we subjected images acquired from RM to shallow fully connected ML algorithms (SML) in a custom-built pipeline we developed ( Supplementary Figure 10 [this file] ). Images from TDP-43 and control cell lines in the EGFP channel were processed in our Galaxy software and cropped so that only the cell body and immediate processes were captured for each cell at two timepoints: T1 (~ DIV27) and T6 (~ DIV33) ( Figure 3A [rid=F3] , Supplementary Figure 9 [this file] ). We used a feature extraction that captures cellular properties such as cell size, shape, complexity and texture ( Supplementary Figures 11 A [this file] – P [this file] ). 
The True Positive (TP) and True Negative (TN) rates at T1 were twice as high as False Positive (FP) and False Negative (FN) rates at T6, but slightly less than that at T1 ( Supplementary Figures 12A [this file] , D [this file] ). However, there were fewer misclassification counts and the identification of TDP-43 cells improved subtlety at the later time point ( Supplementary Figures 12 A [this file] , D [this file] ). To confirm that the SML models use signals from the iMNs that reflect mutation class and are not just classifying based on artifacts, leakage, or structure in the data, we randomized the labels and found no true relationship between features and the labels exists ( Supplementary Figures 12 B [this file] , C [this file] , E [this file] , F [this file] ). Upon scrambling the labels, we find that the ratio of correctly classified crops, regardless of if they are control or TDP-43, is comparable to incorrectly classified crops, show that the models perform no better than chance ( Supplementary Figures 12 B [this file] , C [this file] , E [this file] , F [this file] ). 
The ResNet18d classifier demonstrated the most robust performance, with high prediction accuracy at T1 (AUC = 0.83) and T6 (AUC = 0.81) ( Figure 3D [rid=F3] , E [rid=F3] ) and high discriminative abilities at both timepoints ( Supplementary Figures 12 G [this file] , H [this file] , K [this file] , L [this file] ). Confusion matrices for both T1 and T6 showed that TN and TP rates were much higher than the FP and FN rates ( Supplementary Figures 12 G [this file] , K [this file] ). We scrambled the labels across both timepoints and there was a complete loss of classification ( Supplementary Figures 12 I [this file] , J [this file] , M [this file] , N [this file] ). 
The Res-Net50 DNN achieved higher precision across a wide range of recall values than did the SML models at both T1 (AUC = 0.79) and T6 (AUC = 0.81), but not as high as the Res-Net18 DNN ( Supplementary Figures 12 P [this file] , U [this file] ). The ROC curves were 0.79 for both T1 and T6 models ( Supplementary Figures 12 Q [this file] , V [this file] ), indicating a robust ability to identify true positive TDP-43 samples while minimizing false positives, though not as reliably as the ResNet18 model. The confusion matrices at both T1 and T6 showed that the ResNet50 model exhibited slightly less sensitivity and specificity than both the ResNet18 the SML models however was still robust ( Supplementary Figures 12 O [this file] , T [this file] ). Furthermore, the predictive models again lost all predictive capacity when labels were scrambled, confirming that the learned signal reflects genuine biological structure rather than technical artifact. The antibodies recognized NEUN (nucleus and perinucleus ), GM130 (Golgi ), Calnexin (ER ), SUN-2 (inner nuclear membrane (INM ), Lamin B1 (nuclear envelope ) and DAPI (nucleus ) ( Supplementary Figure 13 A [this file] , B [this file] , C [this file] , D [this file] ). We observed that there was an increased reliance on the nuclear label NEUN and to a lesser degree DAPI and Calnexin and Lamin B1 ( Supplementary Figure 15 F [this file] ). 
We also confirmed the relative contribution of cellular and subcellular markers to variance across control and TDP-43 mutant conditions, by visualizing the computed partial R values as a clustered heatmap ( Supplementary Figure 15 G [this file] ). 
We quantified the spatial occupancy of each fluorophore within GFP- and RFP-positive iMNs ( Figure 5B [rid=F5] and Supplementary 16A [this file] ). The RFP/GFP ratio was higher in TDP-43 than control iMNs ( Figure 5C [rid=F5] and Supplementary 16B [this file] ). While we observed some difference in nuclear size between the TDP-43 iMNs and their controls, and between the patient derived TDP-43 iMNs and their gene-corrected control ( Supplementary 16C [this file] ), those differences did not reach significance when cells from the 3 mutant lines combined were compared to cells from the 3 control lines ( Figure 5D [rid=F5] ). These differences were also not found across gene-corrected iMNs compared to the TDP-43 nor in the gene-edited lines compared to the parental control ( Supplementary 16C [this file] ). 
We chose lines from ALS patients that had early to typical age of onset (AO) (45 to 68 years old) and age-matched controls ( Figure 1 [rid=F1] and Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). We observed robust MAP-2 staining and moderate expression of motor neuron markers such as ISLET1 and NKX6.2 across all lines ( Supplementary Figures 17 [this file] , 18 [this file] ). In addition, the cultures contained very low numbers of KI67-positive cells ( Supplementary Figure 19 [this file] ). For both ISLET1 and NKX6.2, the overall number of stained cells averaged 25% and ranged between cell lines from ~15 to 50% ( Supplementary Figure 20 [this file] , A [this file] , B [this file] , D [this file] , E [this file] ), indicating that a subset of the cells patterned toward a motor neuron-like fate, consistent with previous reports . The C9 line showed a higher number of NKX6.2-positive cells than the CTRL control ( Supplementary Figure 20 D [this file] ). Consistent with this notion, when we combined the C9orf72 and sALS lines and compared them to controls, we did not observe significant differences in the number of ISLET1 and NKX6.2 iMNs across the groups ( Supplementary Figure 20 C F [this file] ). We also observed TDP-43 staining in C9orf72 and a subset of sALS compared to controls ( Supplementary Figure 21 [this file] ). The average frequency of TDP-43–positive cells ranged from ~35 to 60% ( Supplementary Figure 20 G [this file] , H [this file] ). We observed a subtle but significant increase in the number of TDP-43–expressing cells in sALS compared with controls ( Supplementary Figure 21 H [this file] ), consistent with similar reports in sALS patients . 
At DIV~30, we observed no significant differences in neurite length, number of processes or branch ends between the C9orf72 , sALS iMNs and controls ( Supplementary Figure 22 A [this file] , B [this file] , D [this file] , E [this file] , F [this file] ). We observed a very subtle increase in the number of trunks per neuron in the C9orf72 but not sALS iMNs compared to control iMNs ( Supplementary Figure 22 C [this file] ). 
The two C9orf72 displayed a greater OR-CD than the controls (OR-CD = 1.6; Figure 6B [rid=F6] ), and a slightly different OR-CD from one another ( Supplementary Figure 23A [this file] ). OR-CDs were highly variable among sALS lines but proved overall subtly yet significantly higher than those of controls ( Figure 6C [rid=F6] , Supplementary Figure 23 B [this file] , C [this file] ). By this secondary metric, we observed a significant increase death rate in a subset of the sALS iMNs compared to controls (HR = 1.4) ( Supplementary Figure 23 D [this file] ). 
On the other hand, we found a significant negative correlation between the overall fraction of dead cells and the proportion of ISLET1-positive iMNs found at the conclusion of live cell imaging (Spearman r = −0.81, p = 0.0011) ( Supplementary Figure 24 A [this file] ), suggesting that the ISLET1-positive iMNs are the cells most susceptible to degeneration. We did not observe a similar correlation for the NKX6.2-positive iMNs ( Supplementary Figure 24 B [this file] ). 
In both groups, sALS iMNs exhibited a significantly higher OR-CD than did control iMNs ( Supplementary Figure 24C [this file] , D [this file] ). 
The SML model showed a moderate performance at T1 (AUC = 0.60) ( Figure 7A [rid=F7] ) with CMs indicating near-balanced classification of CTRL and C9orf72 iMNs ( Supplementary Figure 25 A [this file] ). However, when trained and tested on scrambled images, classifier performance deteriorated to be no better than chance-level performance ( Supplementary Figure 25 B [this file] ). Consistent with this the ROC for the scrambled condition yielded an AUC = 0.49 which was entirely flat ( Supplementary Figure 25 C [this file] ). In contrast, the ResNet-50 model at T1 demonstrated improved classification accuracy ( Figure 7B [rid=F7] ) with ROC = 0.68 with and an improved separation between CTRL and C9orf72 ( Supplementary Figure 25 D [this file] ). The PRC analysis showed an AP of 0.64, well above the no-skill baseline ( Supplementary Figure 25 E [this file] ). Notably, performance metrics for the ResNet-50 model trained on scrambled images indicate a loss of discriminatory ability ( Supplementary Figure 25 F [this file] , G [this file] ). suggesting features that capture C9orf72 pathology are present at subtle, but genuine levels. 
At the later T6 time point, SML classifiers trained on control and C9orf72 iMNs also showed moderate classification capability ( Figure 7D [rid=F7] ) but displayed improved correct classification of C9orf72 iMNs relative to CTRL ( Supplementary Figure 25 H [this file] ). Again, scrambling the images completely abolished this signal, resulting in a collapsed ROC AUC of 0.49 ( Supplementary Figure 25 I [this file] , J [this file] ). The ResNet-50 model at T6 trained on the same images achieved a more robust classification performance with an AUC = 0.69 ( Figure 7E [rid=F7] ), with CMs showing strong prediction accuracy for both classes ( Supplementary Figure 23 H [this file] ). PRC yielded an AP of 0.64 ( Supplementary Figure 25 H [this file] ), consistent with the performance observed at T1 and indicating sustained discriminative capacity over time. Image scrambling again reduced classification to random levels ( Supplementary Figure 25 M [this file] , N [this file] ). 
SML performance remained modest to classify sALS from control at T1 (AUC = 0.60) ( Figure 7 F [rid=F7] ) and the CM displayed limited class separation, with substantial overlap between control and sALS predictions ( Supplementary Figure 26 A [this file] ). However, scrambling the images completely reduced classification ability as shown by the collapsed ROC ( Supplementary Figure 26 B [this file] , C [this file] ). The ResNet DNN models demonstrated improved predictive capacity to classify sALS from control at T1 (AUC = 0.66) ( Figure 7G [rid=F7] ) showing with higher correct classification rates for both CTRL and sALS iMNs ( Supplementary Figure 26 D [this file] ). PRC yielded an AP of 0.63, exceeding the no-skill baseline ( Supplementary Figure 26 E [this file] ). Performance metrics for the ResNet-50 model trained on scrambled images flatlined and the models classified no better than chance ( Supplementary Figure 26 F [this file] , G [this file] ). 
At the T6 time point, SML classifiers again showed modest performance when trained on sALS versus control images ( Figure 7G [rid=F7] ), however with a slightly better discrimination towards sALS ( Supplementary Figure 26 H [this file] ). Image scrambling abolished this trend ( Supplementary Figure 26 I [this file] , J [this file] ). By contrast, the ResNet-50 model at T6 exhibited more robust classification (AUC = 0.69) ( Figure 8 I [rid=F8] ) and more consistent discrimination correctly identifying a large fraction of both CTRL and sALS samples ( Supplementary Figure 26 K [this file] ). PRC analysis revealed an AP of 0.66 ( Supplementary Figure 26 L [this file] ), indicating enhanced discriminative power at later stages of differentiation. The model flatlined upon image scrambling ( Supplementary Figure 26 M N [this file] ). 
Using the features extracted from our SML models ( Supplementary Figure 10 A [this file] – P [this file] ) for each image described above, we estimated the change in these morphological readouts from T1 to T6 (T1 →T6) for each group of cropped images for TDP-43mut, C9orf72 and sALS compared to control iMNs differentiated in parallel ( Figure 8 A [rid=F8] ). 
We grouped the SML features based on various characteristics such as those that capture size, shape, texture or brightness of objects within each crop ( Figure 8 [rid=F8] and Supplementary Figure 10 [this file] and methods [rid=S2] section). For example, the area and perimeter of all control iMNs increased from T1 to T6 while in all ALS groups, they remained more static ( Figure 9B [rid=F9] and Supplementary Figure 27 A [this file] , B [this file] ). The change in cell perimeter displayed similar trends ( Figure 8B [rid=F8] and Supplementary Figure 27 B [this file] ). 
The TDP-43 iMNs demonstrated the most widespread decreases across multiple feature classes and displayed the largest number of changes that were consistent in the other ALS groups ( Figure 9B [rid=F9] and Supplementary Figure 27 [this file] , 28 [this file] ). There was an extremely large difference between T1 and T6 in the HOG MCOT in the TDP-43 iMNs, whereas the controls were much more static ( Figure 8B [rid=F8] and Supplementary Figure 27 D [this file] ). 
Other features that were most disrupted in TDP-43 compared to controls are features that capture complexity such as such as Minkowski-Bouligand Fractal Dimension (Mink Dim) , which has been used to detect differences in complexity in human tissues , and Corners and Voronoi clustering , which has been used to capture information about neuronal structure ( Figure 8B [rid=F8] and Supplementary Figure 27 F [this file] – J [this file] ). Interestingly, the only “complexity” MCOT that was significantly different in the C9orf72 was the “radial distance” MCOT, which had the largest difference of all features and was 20 times larger (2000% change) in C9orf72 than in controls ( Figure 8B [rid=F8] and Supplementary Figure 27 E [this file] – J [this file] ). The Mink Dim decreased across all ALS groups ( Supplementary Figure 28 F [this file] ), suggesting that a decrease in complexity over time is a unifying hallmark of ALS. Although the direction of the MinkDim appears to differ across TDP-43 compared to controls (~−230%) vs. C9orf72 and sALS compared to controls (~+250%, +338% respectively) this case the change over time is in the control MCOTs and not the ALS MCOTs, which all decrease from T1 →T6 ( Figure 8B [rid=F8] and Supplementary Figure 27 F [this file] ). 
This decline is much faster in the TDP-43 and sALS iMNs (~+30% for both groups) compared to controls whereas it is similar in C9orf72 versus controls ( Figure 8B [rid=F8] and Supplementary Figure 27 H [this file] ). The Voronoi MCOT differed across all groups but increased in both the C9orf72 and sALS iMNs compared to controls, with the largest change in the sALS (~+420%) ( Figure 8B [rid=F8] and Supplementary Figure 27 J [this file] ). 
Other texture features include Gray-Level Co-occurrence Matrix (GLCM) , which measures the spatial relationships between neighboring pixel intensities while the Variance feature measures variance of the object/cell ( Figure 8B [rid=F8] and Supplementary Figure 28 A [this file] – C [this file] ). The “texture” MCOT changed most significantly in the TDP-43 compared to controls, followed by C9orf72 , and while the changes were in the same direction in sALS, they were much subtler ( Figure 8B [rid=F8] and Supplementary Figure 28 A [this file] – C [this file] ). The largest changes were in C9orf72 versus controls followed by the TDP-43 with the least robust changes in the sALS ( Figure 8B [rid=F8] and Supplementary Figure 28 D [this file] – F [this file] ). 
The iMNs with mutations died at the highest rate ( Figure 2 [rid=F2] , Supplementary Figure 8 [this file] ), followed by those with mutations. In sALS iMNs, the rate of cell death was variable across lines, but was overall higher than in controls ( Figure 6 [rid=F6] , Supplementary Figure 23 [this file] ). 
We found that reproducible morphological patterns are present and apparent in iMNs and sufficient to distinguish cells carrying known ALS-causing mutations from controls, with the strongest signal detected in TDP-43 lines ( Figures 3 [rid=F3] , 7 [rid=F7] , Supplementary Figures 12 [this file] , 25 [this file] , 26 [this file] ). 
Using the interpretable algorithm SmoothGrad in conjunction with immunohistochemistry allowed us to triangulate the predictive signal in TDP-43 iMNs to the nuclear/perinuclear region ( Figure 4 [rid=F4] , Supplementary Figure 15 [this file] ). Further, assessment of NCT with a shuttling biosensor revealed nuclear reporter leakage or mislocalization in TDP-43 iMNs, consistent with impaired NCT fidelity ( Figure 5 [rid=F5] , Supplementary Figure 16 [this file] ). 
Using a novel approach, MCOT, to quantify changes in cell size, shape or complexity between 2 timepoints, we uncovered robust shared and subtype-specific phenotypic trajectories ( Figure 8 [rid=F8] , Supplementary Figures 27 [this file] , 28 [this file] ). 
For example, the ALS iMNs changed little in size between the two timepoints, whereas their control counterparts grew larger, suggesting a neurodevelopmental delay in the ALS cells ( Figure 8 [rid=F8] , 9 [rid=F9] , Supplementary Figure 27 [this file] ). 
While stunted growth was observed in all mutant iMNs, complexity, another feature that could reflect development or neurodegeneration, declined in TDP-43 and sALS relative to controls over time but curiously not in C9orf72 ( Figure 8 [rid=F8] , 9 [rid=F9] , Supplementary Figure 27 [this file] ). 
Both SML and DNNs distinguished TDP-43 from control simply from live EGFP signal, but the ResNet DNNs outperformed the SML models ( Figure 3 [rid=F3] , Supplementary Figure 12 [this file] ). ResNet DNNs also outperformed SML models for C9orf72 ( Supplementary Figure 25 [this file] ) and sALS ( Supplementary 26 [this file] ) models. Likewise, when scrambling labels for C9Orf72 we also observe chance-level performance for both T1 and T6 ( Supplementary 25 B [this file] ), and for sALS ( Supplementary 26 B [this file] ). 
The comparatively lower performance of the shallow connected ML algorithms model ( Figure 3B [rid=F3] – C [rid=F3] , Supplementary Figure 12 [this file] , 25 [this file] , 26 [this file] ) relative to the DNNs can be attributed to limitations in feature representation (the model’s ability to capture meaningful patterns from raw data) as well as inductive bias (the built-in assumptions that a model makes about how to generalize from training examples). 
The superior performance of the ImageNet-pretrained ResNet18 ( Figure 3D [rid=F3] – E [rid=F3] , Supplementary Figure 12 [this file] ) over the SimCLR-pretrained ResNet50 for the TDP-43 model, suggests that transfer learning from large, labeled natural image datasets can provide more task-relevant inductive priors than self-supervised representations learned on a potentially mismatched or limited domain. 
Individual death plots are shown in Supplementary Figure 9 [this file] . 
See also Supplementary Figure 14 [this file] .

The cohort was roughly evenly split by sex (339 male, 255 female, Figure S1a [this file] - b [this file] ), mostly of European ancestry ( Figure S1c [this file] ), and iPSCs for most lines were derived from T-cells ( Figure S1a [this file] - b [this file] ). Only 63 reported a family history of the disease ( Figure S1d [this file] - e [this file] ). 
After regressing out known and hidden covariates from the processed sequencing data in Section 3.1 [rid=S3] , we generated tables of QTLs: genomic variants whose genotype is significantly associated with gene expression (eQTLs), splicing (sQTLs), and chromatin accessibility (caQTLs) ( Figure 1b [rid=F1] ) (see Methods [rid=S13] , Figure S2a [this file] , Table S2 [rid=SD1] - 4 [rid=SD1] ). 
In comparisons to eQTLs generated from 48 tissues by the GTEx consortium , our eQTLs were most similar to brain tissues in terms of correlation of effect sizes and number of gene-variant pairs in common ( Figure S2b [this file] - c [this file] ). Many genes were regulated by more than one QTL ( Table S5 [rid=SD1] - 7 [rid=SD1] , Figure S2e [this file] , see Methods [rid=S13] ). As expected, these higher order QTLs were located progressively farther away from omic features (example for eQTLs shown in Figure S2f [this file] ). 
Variants were generally located within 10 kb of the omic feature they were most strongly associated with; most top eQTLs, sQTLs, and caQTLs were located within 5kb, 2.5kb, and 1 kb of their top feature, respectively ( Figure S2d [this file] ). 
Importantly, we find that they are also sQTLs for exon 2 skipping; the only sQTL that falls within the introns adjacent to exon 2 is rs229190 ( Figure 3b [rid=F3] , Figure S3a [this file] ). A prior study examining truncated isoforms of the G2E3 protein suggests that exon 2 skipping would result in a truncated protein missing a nucleolar localization sequence, while exon 11 skipping would result in a truncated protein missing a nuclear localization sequence ( Figure S3a [this file] ). 
We identified highly significant sQTLs (corresponding to alternative 5’ splicing at exon 1a/1b) and eQTLs ( Figure S3b [this file] ), and less significant caQTLs ( Table S11 [rid=SD1] - 13 [rid=SD1] ). Significant QTLs spanned the locus and formed roughly a dozen linkage-disequilibrium (LD) blocks (correlation heatmap of a subset of significant QTLs is shown in Figure S3c [this file] ). Although the local LD limits our ability to computationally identify causal variants, our analysis revealed that variation in expression was most likely driven by the combined genotypes of two common variants (rs2492816, gnomAD MAF 0.41, and rs13691, gnomAD MAF 0.22) and one rare variant with a particularly large effect size (rs113860022, gnomAD MAF 0.011) ( Figure 4a [rid=F4] , Figure S3d [this file] ). 
At the same time, no genotype-dependent trend was detected in non-C9-ALS patients ( Figure S3e [this file] ). 
To confirm that the WTA haplotype was modifying the effects of the mutant allele, we compared the difference in survival between C9- and non-C9 ALS patients in ALS Compute who shared the same WTA haplotype ( Figure 4g [rid=F4] , S3e [this file] ). Notably, C9-ALS patients carrying the C9-high haplotype on their WTA had a 8+/−2 month (standard error, p < 6e-5) shorter survival than non-C9 ALS patients with the same genotype, whereas C9-ALS patients carrying the C9-super-low haplotype on their WTA had a 18 +/−5 month (standard error, p < 3e-4) shorter survival than non-C9 ALS patients. ( Figure 4g [rid=F4] , S3e [this file] ). 
For each of the 112 C9-ALS patients, we estimated the time from disease onset for a patient to reach an ALSFRS-R score of 24 using linear interpolation ( Figure S3f [this file] , see methods [rid=S13] ). A range of other ALSFRS-R thresholds were tested to verify the robustness of our method ( Figure S3g [this file] ).

However, for many patient lines, the magnitude of individual mRNA alterations increased over time and for a small subset some displayed a slight restoration back towards control levels (Supplementary Figs. 3 [this file] , 4 [this file] and Supplementary Data 1 [rid=MOESM3] ). As iPSN culture composition did not change over time (Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] ), the time dependent emergence of molecular hallmarks associated with TDP-43 loss of function does not merely reflect alterations in neuronal/glial populations but instead is suggestive of a maturation of pathophysiologic events in patient iPSNs. 
For example, , originally identified as one of the most altered mRNA targets following artificial TDP-43 knockdown in SH-SY5Y cells and iPSNs , was variably altered in this large population of patient iPSNs, with a substantial number of patients showing only modest changes in expression and splicing, with other TDP-43 loss of function associated mRNA changes (e.g. , CE) more dramatically altered in some patient lines (Figs. 1 [rid=Fig1] – 4 [rid=Fig4] and Supplementary Figs. 3 [this file] , 4 [this file] , Supplementary Data 1 [rid=MOESM3] ). In addition, decreased mRNA expression was only moderately correlated with an increase in truncated detection in our patient iPSNs (Supplementary Fig. 5 [this file] ). Nonetheless, we were able to detect a decrease in STMN2 protein expression in a subset of patient iPSC lines (Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] ) that displayed the largest change in mRNA expression suggesting that at least some of the detected RNA level alterations are associated with altered protein expression. 
No other TDP-43 loss of function associated gene expression or mRNA splicing alterations were observed in mutant TDP-43 patient iPSNs at the time points evaluated (Figs. 1 [rid=Fig1] , 2 [rid=Fig2] , and Supplementary Figs. 3 [this file] , 4 [this file] , Supplementary Data 1 [rid=MOESM3] ). 
By day 60 of differentiation, we observed multiple distinct histologic patterns of TDP-43 immunoreactivity across sALS and C9orf72 patient iPSC lines (Supplementary Fig. 7 [this file] ). We next correlated the nuclear/cytoplasmic distribution of TDP-43 with magnitude of detection of each molecular hallmark of TDP-43 loss of function examined (Supplementary Figs. 8 [this file] and 9 [this file] ). Overall, these analyses yielded moderate correlations (Supplementary Figs. 8 [this file] and 9 [this file] ) suggesting that presumed changes in gene expression and splicing may not be accurately assessed by histological analyses of cytoplasmic mislocalization of TDP-43. 
Employing a qRT-PCR based panel of gene expression and mRNA splicing alterations associated with TDP-43 loss of function, we observed a strikingly similar magnitude of dysregulation of individual mRNA processing events in day 60 iPSC derived spinal neurons compared to cervical spinal cord and multiple motor cortex samples from the same patients (Fig. 5a–d [rid=Fig5] , and Supplementary Fig. 10 [this file] ). We did not detect TDP-43 loss of function associated mRNA misprocessing events in the occipital cortex (Fig. 5a–d [rid=Fig5] and Supplementary Fig. 10 [this file] ) which is pathologically and clinically unaffected in ALS. In fact, with the exception of truncated and cryptic exon containing , cryptic exon containing mRNAs were not detected in control (average value across 4 control cases represented by horizontal dashed line) or ALS postmortem occipital cortex (Fig. 5a–d [rid=Fig5] and Supplementary Fig. 10 [this file] ). 
Next, similar to our iPSN studies (Supplementary Figs. 7 [this file] and 9 [this file] ), we wanted to examine how TDP-43 loss of function may relate to histologic TDP-43 pathology in end-stage CNS autopsy tissues. 
Nuclear intensity moderately correlated with nuclear/cytoplasmic distribution of TDP-43 in postmortem motor and occipital cortex (Supplementary Fig. 11 [this file] ).

No change in gene expression and splicing was observed in SOD1 motor cortex compared to control (Fig. 7a [rid=Fig7] and Supplementary Fig. 12 [this file] ). Additionally, we examined our panel of molecular hallmarks of TDP-43 loss of function in postmortem spinal cord tissues from control, sALS, and C9orf72 ALS patients (Fig. 7b [rid=Fig7] and Supplementary Fig. 13 [this file] ). Similar to motor cortex, we observed extensive heterogeneity in molecular signatures associated with TDP-43 loss of function in sALS and C9orf72 ALS spinal cord tissue (Fig. 7b [rid=Fig7] and Supplementary Fig. 13 [this file] ). Interestingly, the magnitude of truncated detection was substantially higher in ALS patient spinal cord (Supplementary Fig. 13s [this file] ) compared to motor cortex (Supplementary Fig. 12s [this file] ). Consistent with our observations in iPSNs (Figs. 1 [rid=Fig1] – 4 [rid=Fig4] ), we did not detect changes in expression or splicing in postmortem patient spinal cord tissue (Fig. 7b [rid=Fig7] and Supplementary Fig. 13f,t [this file] ). Moreover, in motor cortex, minor alterations in expression and splicing were detected and in only a small number (<5) of patients (Fig. 7a [rid=Fig7] and Supplementary Fig. 12f,t [this file] ). However, we did detect changes in gene expression and splicing in frontal cortex, but not motor cortex or spinal cord tissue from ALS/FTD patients compared to controls (Fig. 7c [rid=Fig7] and Supplementary Fig. 14 [this file] ). We note that gene expression or splicing changes were not observed in every ALS/FTD patient examined (Fig. 7c [rid=Fig7] and Supplementary Fig. 14 [this file] ) consistent with the notion of patient to patient variability. 
To address the extent to which a larger population-like cohort of C9orf72 and sALS patient lines displayed nuclear accumulation of CHMP7, reduction of POM121, and a readout of impaired nucleocytoplasmic transport capacity, the abnormal nuclear/cytoplasmic distribution of Ran GTPase compared to molecular hallmarks of TDP-43 loss of function, we performed immunostaining and confocal imaging for CHMP7 and Ran GTPase and immunostaining and super resolution imaging for POM121 at days 18, 25, 32, 46, and 60 of differentiation (Fig. 8a–c [rid=Fig8] , Supplementary Figs. 15a–c [this file] , 16a–c [this file] ). We also measured the nucleocytoplasmic distribution of TDP-43 at days 18, 25, 32, 46, and 60 of differentiation in all 180 iPSC lines evaluated (Fig. 8d [rid=Fig8] , Supplementary Figs. 15d [this file] , 16d [this file] ). For all measures, we observed that the magnitude of nuclear/cytoplasmic redistribution or immunoreactivity was stable overtime once the measured pathologic/histologic alteration reached maximal magnitude in cultured iPSNs (Fig. 8 [rid=Fig8] and Supplementary Figs. 15 [this file] , 16 [this file] ). Maximal detected changes were reached at day 18 for CHMP7 nuclear accumulation (Fig. 8a [rid=Fig8] and Supplementary Figs. 15a [this file] , 16a [this file] ), day 32 for POM121 reduction (Fig. 8b [rid=Fig8] , and Supplementary Figs. 15b [this file] , 16b [this file] ), and day 46 for redistribution of Ran GTPase (Fig. 8c [rid=Fig8] , and Supplementary Figs. 15c [this file] , 16c [this file] ). 
Following 3 weeks of treatment with CHMP7 ASOs yielding sufficient reduction in CHMP7 protein (ref. and Supplementary Fig. 17 [this file] ), we observed a near complete restoration of TDP-43 function across all mRNA targets and lines evaluated (Supplementary Fig. 17 [this file] ). 
Albeit subtle, induction of NPC injury in an otherwise wildtype iPSN was sufficient to cause an increase in cytoplasmic TDP-43 immunoreactivity, ultimately leading to reduced TDP-43 N/C ratio (Supplementary Fig. 18a [this file] ). Moreover, using qRT-PCR, we observed a significant dysregulation of TDP-43 mRNA targets across our panel of gene expression and mRNA splicing changes associated with TDP-43 function (Supplementary Fig. 18b [this file] ) in control iPSNs following 7 days of POM121 reduction. 
Given our previous report that replenishment of POM121 via overexpression following initial POM121 reduction was sufficient to re-establish NPC composition and active nuclear import in C9orf72 iPSNs , we hypothesized that POM121 overexpression may alleviate TDP-43 loss of function which we have now established (Supplementary Fig. 18 [this file] ) is one of likely many consequences of NPC injury. Two weeks later, consistent with CHMP7 nuclear accumulation occurring upstream of NPC injury in ALS, we did not observe a reversal of CHMP7 nuclear accumulation (Supplementary Fig. 19 [this file] ). The restoration of TDP-43 function corresponded with a repair of active nuclear import (Supplementary Fig. 20 [this file] ) as examined by the localization of a previously described and utilized S-tdTomato NCT reporter as well as an increase in nuclear and concomitant decrease in cytoplasmic TDP-43 immunoreactivity (Supplementary Fig. 21 [this file] ). 
Our study revealed a significant time dependent emergence of molecular hallmarks associated with TDP-43 loss of function (Figs. 1 [rid=Fig1] – 4 [rid=Fig4] and Supplementary Figs. 3 [this file] – 4 [this file] ) in sALS patient iPSNs. However, not all gene expression or splicing alterations previously linked to TDP-43 depletion were observed at the time points evaluated (Figs. 1 [rid=Fig1] – 4 [rid=Fig4] and Supplementary Figs. 3 [this file] – 4 [this file] ). However, we also did not detect alterations in postmortem ALS patient motor cortex or spinal cord tissues (Fig. 7a, b [rid=Fig7] and Supplementary Figs. 12f [this file] , t [this file] , 13f,t [this file] ). In contrast, changes in expression and splicing were detected in postmortem frontal cortex tissue from ALS/FTD patients (Fig. 7c [rid=Fig7] and Supplementary Fig. 14 [this file] ). 
Our iPSN model revealed an extensive variability in the magnitude of gene expression and cryptic exon containing mRNA detection both across mRNAs examined in individual patient iPSC lines and amongst patient iPSC lines for individual mRNAs (Figs. 1 [rid=Fig1] – 4 [rid=Fig4] and Supplementary Figs. 3 [this file] , 4 [this file] ). This was variability was also observed in postmortem ALS patient motor cortex and spinal cord tissues (Fig. 7a, b [rid=Fig7] and Supplementary Figs. 12 [this file] , 13 [this file] ). In our study, similar to these prior reports, we also identified a subset of sALS patient iPSNs where we were unable to detect molecular signatures of TDP-43 loss of function, at least amongst the 18 gene expression and splicing changes evaluated (Figs. 1 [rid=Fig1] – 4 [rid=Fig4] and Supplementary Figs. 3 [this file] , 4 [this file] ). In fact, our POM121 overexpression (Fig. 10 [rid=Fig10] ) or CHMP7 knockdown (Supplementary Fig. 17 [this file] ) studies suggest that at least targeting the nuclear pore complex or nuclear pore complex surveillance pathways may restore proper expression of multiple hallmarks of TDP-43 loss of function. 
However, we demonstrate that TDP-43 loss of function associated molecular can be robustly detected in bulk cellular and tissue lysates (Figs. 1 [rid=Fig1] – 5 [rid=Fig5] , 7 [rid=Fig7] and Supplementary Figs. 3 [this file] , 4 [this file] , 10 [this file] , 12 [this file] , 13 [this file] ) in the absence of overt histological nuclear clearance in the majority of cells even in postmortem tissues (Figs. 5e–m [rid=Fig5] , 6 [rid=Fig6] ). 
In this current study, we now provide evidence that NPC injury itself can directly contribute to altered TDP-43 functionality in sALS iPSNs (Supplementary Fig. 18 [this file] ).

In our NLuc reporter assays these 22 nt gRNAs successfully targeted the sense and antisense repeat-containing transcripts (Supplementary Fig. S1j, k [this file] ). 
In our initial NLuc reporter assays (Supplementary Fig. S1a–d [this file] ) the gRNAs were supplied as a separate plasmid, in a 5:1 molar ratio to CasRx. 
We confirmed that after 5 days of dox treatment these cells expressed neuronal markers using immunocytochemistry and RT-qPCR (Supplementary Fig. S2 [this file] ). We also performed RT-qPCR analysis for CasRx expression in these samples (Supplementary Fig. S3a [this file] ) and found that, for our most efficacious guide 17, CasRx levels were highest in C9 line 3, the line with the greatest reduction of antisense repeat transcripts. 
We observed no significant reduction in viable cells after a 5-day treatment with CasRx plus gRNA expressing lentiviruses (Supplementary Fig. S3b, c [this file] ), though there was a downward trend in C9 line 2 (Supplementary Fig. S3c [this file] ). 
Using the same experimental paradigm, we performed RNA sequencing of three independent inductions of C9 line 1 iPSC-neurons 5 days post-transduction with lentiviruses expressing CasRx and either non-targeting guide, sense transcript targeting guides 8 or 10 (Fig. 2h [rid=Fig2] and Supplementary Fig. S3d [this file] ), or antisense transcript targeting guides 11 or 17 (Supplementary Fig. S3e, f [this file] ). Guides 8 and 10 significantly reduced repeat-containing transcripts but not transcripts that do not contain the repeat expansion (Fig. 2h [rid=Fig2] and Supplementary Fig. S3d [this file] ). We were not able to detect the antisense repeat-containing transcripts in our RNA-sequencing dataset, likely due to the relatively low number of transcripts and so were not able to confirm target engagement using RNA-seq (Supplementary Fig. S3e, f [this file] ). We did not observe any DEGs with guide 11 or guide 17 (Supplementary Fig. S3e, f [this file] ), indicating that they did not lead to detectable off-target transcriptional changes when using our standard sequencing depth. 
We next tested whether CRISPR-CasRx-mediated lowering of C9 sense and/or antisense transcripts could prevent neurotoxic phenotypes and TDP-43 loss of function-associated splicing alterations, in iPSC-spinal neurons (iPSC-SNs), either individually or in dual-targeting configuration (Supplementary Fig. S4a–c [this file] ). We used a nucleofection paradigm in 6 different patient iPSC-SNs, which resulted in ~80% reduction of sense or antisense RNAs without loss of variant 2 when treated with CRISPR-CasRx and either guide 10 or 17, respectively, in single vectors (Supplementary Fig. S4d, e [this file] ). We observed that either guide 10 or guide 17 could significantly reduce cell death upon glutamate exposure (Fig. 3a–c [rid=Fig3] ), while guide 17 could prevent the inclusion of cryptic exons in and (Supplementary Fig. S4g–i [this file] ). As with the guides by themselves, we observed robust knockdown of sense and antisense RNAs (Supplementary Fig. S4j, k [this file] ), no reduction in variant 2 (Supplementary Fig. S4l [this file] ), significant protection from excitotoxicity (Fig. 3d–f [rid=Fig3] ), and reduced cryptic exon expression (Supplementary Fig. S4m–o [this file] ). 
Having established efficacy in vitro, we tested CRISPR-CasRx in vivo using zebrafish larvae (Supplementary Fig. S5a [this file] ), which express 45 pure G C repeats and generate DPRs . Using an MSD immunoassay, we confirmed that G C larvae produce polyGP (Supplementary Fig. S5b [this file] ). Compared to wild-type siblings, G C larvae were markedly hyperactive (Supplementary Fig. S5c [this file] ), spending on average 1.7× more time performing swimming bouts each day (Supplementary Fig. S5d [this file] ). As this model does not contain any of the endogenous human sequence upstream or downstream of the repeats, we designed new gRNAs specifically to target the zebrafish G C transcripts (Supplementary Fig. S5e [this file] ). We screened larvae for high expression of the construct (Supplementary Fig. S5f [this file] ) and video-tracked them (Supplementary Fig. S5h [this file] ). As expected, control-injected G C larvae were hyperactive, 1.3× more time active each day compared to wild-type larvae expressing CasRx and non-targeting gRNAs (Supplementary Fig. S5i [this file] ). In contrast, expression of CasRx and targeting gRNAs reduced the amount of polyGP DPRs (Supplementary Fig. S5g [this file] ) and hyperactivity (Supplementary Fig. S5i [this file] ). 
In either wild-type or BAC transgenics, sense and antisense targeting CasRx AAVs did not significantly alter weight (Supplementary Fig. S6a, b [this file] ), induce overt symptoms of sickness (Supplementary Fig. S6c, d [this file] ), or cause evident microgliosis or astrocyte activation (Supplementary Fig. S6e–l [this file] ). There was also no change in C9orf72 protein levels via Western blot (Supplementary Fig. S6m, n [this file] ), although we note that this band contains both mouse (which is not targeted by CasRx) and human C9orf72. DPR levels were more variable, but were also reduced, with a significant reduction in polyGP (Fig. 5f, g [rid=Fig5] ), however surprisingly we observed no change in RNA foci load, assessed in the retrosplenial cortex (Supplementary Fig. S7 [this file] ). 
We observed that transduction efficiency in this paradigm is only ~5–10% of all cells across the cortex and hippocampus and that transduction is largely confined to neurons and astrocytes (Supplementary Fig. S8 [this file] ).

C9orf72 and non-neurological control iPSC lines were obtained from the Answer ALS repository [ 3 [rid=R3] ] at Cedars-Sinai (see Supplemental Table 1 [this file] for demographics) and maintained and differentiated into spinal neurons using a modified version of the direct induced motor neuron (diMNs) protocol recently described in detail [ 2 [rid=R2] ]. 
Previously described primer/probe sets (see Supplemental Table 2 [this file] for sequences) [ 24 [rid=R24] ] were used to detect G C and G C repeat containing transcripts. Previously described primer sets (see Supplemental Table 2 [this file] for sequences) [ 30 [rid=R30] , 32 [rid=R32] , 40 [rid=R40] , 43 [rid=R43] ] were used to detect truncated STMN2 and cryptic exon containing mRNA transcripts. TaqMan Gene Expression Assays (see Supplemental Table 2 [this file] for probe information) were used to detect mRNA targets. 
In addition, immunostaining and confocal imaging revealed a small but statistically significant number of G C , but not G C expressing neurons that contained observable new cytoplasmic TDP-43 immunoreactivity ( Supplemental Fig. 1 [this file] ). Notably, we did not detect TDP-43 aggregation in G C or G C expressing iPSNs ( Supplemental Fig. 1 [this file] ) consistent with prior reports from our group and others that cytoplasmic aggregation of TDP-43 does not occur in the majority of iPSN models of C9orf72 disease despite subtle cytoplasmic mislocalization [ 9 [rid=R9] , 14 [rid=R14] , 19 [rid=R19] , 47 [rid=R47] , 48 [rid=R48] ]. Although expression of either G C and G C led to increased susceptibility to glutamate induced neuronal death ( Supplemental Fig. 2 [this file] ), our data demonstrate that G C repeat RNA expression is sufficient to induce TDP-43 dysfunction in human neurons and suggest that perhaps our prior observations of molecular hallmarks of TDP-43 loss of function in endogenous C9orf72 iPSNs [ 8 [rid=R8] ] could be predominantly linked to endogenous antisense G C and not G C repeat RNA expression. 
We observed a significant strand specific decrease in G C and G C repeat RNA expression as early as 5 days after treatment ( Supplemental Fig. 3 [this file] ), an observation that is supported by prior reports that G C repeat RNA knockdown happens significantly faster than DPR reduction [ 9 [rid=R9] , 14 [rid=R14] , 17 [rid=R17] ]. Important for evaluation of biological specificity, the G C targeting ASO had no impact on G C expression and the ASO targeting G C containing RNA had no impact on G C expression ( Supplemental Fig. 3 [this file] ). 
In doing so, we found that 5 and 10 day treatment with either G C or G C repeat RNA targeting ASOs was not sufficient to repair TDP-43 function ( Supplemental Figs. 4 [this file] – 7 [this file] ). In contrast, consistent with a time-dependent therapeutic efficacy, 15 and 20 day treatment with G C antisense, G C sense, repeat RNA targeting ASOs was sufficient to restore the expression and splicing of TDP-43 mRNA targets ( Figs. 3 [rid=F3] – 4 [rid=F4] , Supplemental Figs. 8 [this file] – 9 [this file] ) thereby alleviating TDP-43 dysfunction. We also observed a significant reduction in the percentage of C9orf72 iPSNs with observable cytoplasmic TDP-43 immunoreactivity following 20 days of treatment with G C but not G C repeat RNA targeting ASOs ( Supplemental Fig. 10 [this file] ). Again, consistent with prior reports [ 9 [rid=R9] , 14 [rid=R14] , 19 [rid=R19] , 25 [rid=R25] , 36 [rid=R36] , 47 [rid=R47] , 48 [rid=R48] ], the percentage of neurons with detectable cytoplasmic TDP-43 immunoreactivity was low and we did not observe cytoplasmic TDP-43 puncta of aggregates ( Supplemental Fig. 10 [this file] ). Moreover, despite our data that only treatment with G C repeat RNA targeting ASOs repairs TDP-43 function ( Figs. 3 [rid=F3] – 4 [rid=F4] , Supplemental Figs. 8 [this file] – 9 [this file] ), both G C and G C repeat RNA targeting ASOs alleviated C9orf72 neuronal death in response to glutamate stress ( Supplemental Fig. 11 [this file] ). Interestingly, using immunoprecipitations for TDP-43 followed by qRT-PCR for repeat RNAs, we found that that G C antisense, but not G C sense, repeat RNA is enriched in TDP-43 complexes in C9orf72 patient iPSNs ( Supplemental Fig. 12 [this file] ) further underscoring the relationship between G C antisense repeat RNA and TDP-43 in C9orf72 ALS/FTD pathogenesis. 
Importantly, the efficacy of repeat RNA knockdown was essentially unchanged following simultaneous treatment with both repeat RNA targeting ASOs ( Supplemental Fig. 13 [this file] ). Additionally, simultaneous treatment with G C and G C targeting ASOs provided no additional protection against glutamate-induced neuronal death in C9orf72 patient iPSNs compared to either ASO alone ( Supplemental Fig. 14 [this file] ). 
Our RNA immunoprecipitation experiments ( Supplemental Fig. 12 [this file] ) suggest that TDP-43 may be at least partially sequestered away from it’s multiple RNA targets by G C repeat RNA. Further, our data highlight the possibility that G C repeat RNA induced TDP-43 dysfunction occurs in the absence of and perhaps prior to overt TDP-43 nuclear clearance and mislocalization to the cytoplasm ( Figs. 1 [rid=F1] – 2 [rid=F2] , Supplemental Fig. 1 [this file] ). 
In this manuscript, we demonstrate that treatment with G C , but not G C , ASOs after the onset of TDP-43 loss of function associated molecular changes, is sufficient to restore molecular signatures of TDP-43 function ( Figs. 3 [rid=F3] – 4 [rid=F4] , Supplemental Figs. 8 [this file] – 9 [this file] ). Importantly, this is a time dependent phenomenon ( Figs. 3 [rid=F3] – 4 [rid=F4] , Supplemental Figs. 4 [this file] – 9 [this file] ) suggesting that a neuronal “recovery” period is needed following ASO initiated degradation of antisense repeat RNA species. Nonetheless, treatment with either G C or G C repeat RNA targeting ASOs was sufficient to alleviate neuronal death in response to exogenous glutamate stress ( Supplemental Fig. 11 [this file] ) suggesting that both repeat RNA species can disrupt neuronal survival perhaps via distinct mechanisms.

However, not all gene expression or splicing alterations previously linked to TDP-43 depletion were observed at the time points evaluated ( Figures 1 [rid=F1] – 4 [rid=F4] , Supplemental Figures 1 [this file] – 2 [this file] ). Strikingly, we observed an extensive variability in the magnitude of gene expression and cryptic exon containing mRNA detection both across mRNAs examined in individual patient iPSC lines and amongst patient iPSC lines for individual mRNAs ( Figures 1 [rid=F1] – 4 [rid=F4] , Supplemental Figures 1 [this file] – 2 [this file] ).. 
However, we clearly demonstrate that TDP-43 dysfunction can be robustly detected in bulk cellular and tissue lysates ( Figures 1 [rid=F1] – 6 [rid=F6] , Supplemental Figures 1 [this file] – 2 [this file] ) in the absence of overt histological nuclear clearance in the majority of cells even in postmortem tissues ( Figure 6 [rid=F6] , Supplemental Figure 3 [this file] ). 
In this current study, we now provide evidence that NPC injury itself can directly contribute to altered TDP-43 functionality in sALS iPSNs ( Supplemental Figure 10 [this file] ).

When CUG was mutated to CGG in the intron, the GA-NLuc was significantly reduced, while there was no decrease in GP and GR (Supplementary Fig. 1e [this file] ).

To validate that the two tags can faithfully represent the translation of two reading frames, we first constructed a negative control reporter with no repeats between HA-tag and the +1 SunTag (Supplementary Fig. 2a [this file] ) and a readthrough reporter in which HA-tag and SunTag sandwiching the 70× (GGGGCC) repeats were both placed in the GA frame (Supplementary Fig. 2a, b [this file] ). For the readthrough reporter, the vast majority (85%) of translating mRNAs (red) colocalized with both HA-tag (magenta) and SunTag (green) signals (Supplementary Fig. 2c, d [this file] , Supplementary Movie 4 [rid=MOESM7] ). 
We analyzed individual translating mRNAs and quantified the frequencies of frameshift by calculating the percentage of mRNAs showing both SunTag and HA-tag signals within the imaging window (Fig. 2f [rid=Fig2] , Supplementary Fig. 3a–c [this file] ). However, when frameshift did happen, it occurred more often for GR to GA (6.4%), followed by GA to GP (4.3%) and lastly GA to GR (2.3%) (Supplementary Fig. 3d [this file] ). 
We placed stop codons in all three reading frames between HA-tag and repeats, such that the SunTag signal arose only from the cap-independent RAN translation in the GA frame (Supplementary Fig. 4a [this file] ). We observed rare RAN SunTag TLS (Supplementary Fig. 4b, c [this file] , Supplementary Movie 6 [rid=MOESM9] ), with a frequency similar to the SunTag-only events in the frameshift reporters (about 2%, Fig. 2g [rid=Fig2] ). 
In agreement with the ribosome runoff experiment, we observed the TLS fluorescence in the control NLuc and GA reporters recovered rapidly, whereas the recovery was significantly slower in GP and GR reporters (Supplementary Fig. 5a, b [this file] , Supplementary Movie 8 [this file1] ). 
Similarly, we observed a slower ribosome runoff in GP frame encoded by the antisense repeats (Supplementary Fig. 5a, c [this file] ). The FRAP experiment also showed consistent results (Supplementary Fig. 5b [this file] ). Similarly, we observed that the ribosome runoff was significantly slower than the NLuc control and similar to the repeat-encoded poly-GR (Supplementary Fig. 5c [this file] ).

The in vitro transcribed reporter mRNAs (Supplementary Fig. 6h [this file] ) were capped and translated in rabbit reticulocyte lysate. The translation yield from the GA reporter was comparable to the no repeat control (Supplementary Fig. 6i [this file] ), consistent with the in vivo translation measurement that the elongation in GA frame was similar to the NLuc. There were multiple shorter protein bands, likely representing truncated translation products (Supplementary Fig. 6i [this file] ).

A schematic of the procedures and computational tools used in this study are diagrammed in Supplementary Figure 1 [this file] . Briefly, to “pan” stain all cellular proteins, lysines across the proteome were labeled with a fluorophore conjugated N-hydroxysuccinimide (NHS), DNA was labeled with SYTOX Green, and proteins of interest were labeled with antibodies ( Supplementary Figure 1a [this file] ). As expected ( M’Saad and Bewersdorf, 2020 [rid=R41] ), cellular organelles like nucleoli, mitochondria, Golgi and centrioles were identifiable by their characteristic ultrastructural morphologies revealed by the pan-stain ( Supplementary Figure 1b [this file] ). NPCs were likewise visible at the edge of the nucleus ( Supplementary Figure 1b [this file] ). We developed an image analysis pipeline using Imaris software and the Fiji ( Schindelin et al., 2012 [rid=R57] ) plugin LABKIT ( Arzt et al., 2022 [rid=R4] ), a machine-learning based random forest classifier, to segment cellular structures in 3D ( Supplementary Figure 1c [this file] ). 
The latter were normalized to an expansion factor calculated for each sample by measuring the mean distance between mitochondria cristae ( Supplementary Figure 2a [this file] ) and centriole diameters ( Supplementary Figure 2b [this file] ); the average of these two was then taken as the expansion factor for assigning pre-expansion scale ( Supplementary Figure 2c [this file] ). There was remarkable consistency in sample-to-sample expansion that ranged from 13.94 to 16.69-fold ( Supplementary Figure 2d [this file] ). 
The anti-nup antibodies specifically labeled one or more of the three substructures of the expanded NPCs in a manner congruent with their established locations ( Figure 3b [rid=F3] , c [rid=F3] , Supplementary Figure 3a [this file] , b [this file] ). For example, we observed anti-NUP107 and anti-NUP96 staining at both pan-stained rings, confirming these to be the CR and NRs ( Supplementary Figure 3c [this file] , d [this file] ). 
This result was consistent with a recent super-resolution microscopy study (using a different antibody)( Andronov et al., 2022 [rid=R3] ) and was not unique to HeLa NPCs, as we observed the identical asymmetry in the POM121 labeling of A549 and SH-SY5Y cells as well ( Supplementary Figure 3e [this file] , f [this file] ). 
Consistent with this, although recent work indicates that some molecules of NUP93 and NUP62 reside at CRs ( Bley et al., 2022 [rid=R7] ; Huang et al., 2020 [rid=R30] ; Mosalaganti et al., 2022 [rid=R46] ; Zhu et al., 2022 [rid=R67] ), these pools are only rarely observed in the immunolabeling of the pan-stained samples ( Supplementary Figure 3g [this file] ). 
These results were consistently reproduced in an independent expansion experiment and mirrored in HeLa cells ( Supplementary Figure 4a [this file] – d [this file] ). 
To investigate whether the measured biases in NPC diameter reflected the functional integration of NPCs within a mechanoresponsive network (and to rule out expansion-induced artifacts), we performed pan-ExM and measured NPC diameters in CRISPR-edited A549 cells lacking and ( Supplementary Figure 4e [this file] – k [this file] ). Strikingly, the ablation of LINC complexes completely disrupted the observed bias for larger NPC diameters on the basal surface of the nucleus in cell populations from two independent expansion experiments ( Figure 4d [rid=F4] , Supplementary Figure 4l [this file] ), which were now also found to be uniformly distributed. Further, we no longer detected a bias for the largest NPCs to cluster ( Figure 4e [rid=F4] , f [rid=F4] , Supplementary Figure 4m [this file] ). 
In contrast, the change between the WT and SUN1/2 dKOs A549 cells was ~5% ( Supplementary Figure 4n [this file] ).

Control and ALS patient iPSCs were differentiated using a standardized 32-day direct induced motor neuron protocol in 6-well plates in 50 batches of 5–14 patients using a method based on dual SMAD inhibition and ventral patterning ( Figure S1A [this file] ). Further quantification and separation into male and female lines showed that the higher percentage of ISL1 in ALS samples was primarily due to a significantly higher percentage of ISL1+ cells specifically in male ALS samples versus all other groups ( Figure S1B [this file] ). Additionally, the motor neuron progenitor marker NKX6–1 ( Figure S1C [this file] ) and the general neuronal marker TUBB3 ( Figure S1D [this file] ) were also similarly enriched in male ALS samples versus all other groups. Quantification of SMI-32, Nestin, and S100B staining showed no significant differences between ALS and control groups or between male and female participants ( Figures S1E [this file] – S1G [this file] ). Temporal analysis of a subset of lines (n = 8) revealed S100B+ cells to be present as early as day 18 and significantly more abundant at day 32 and day 46 in motor neuron cultures ( Figure S1H [this file] ). 
Gene ontology (GO) analysis of the HVGs in the BTCs ( Table S2 [rid=SD2] ) showed significant enrichment for mitochondrial-associated GO terms ( Figure S2A [this file] ). Interestingly, these highly variable batches coincided with the BDC samples having the highest percentage of S100B+ cells by staining ( Figure S2B [this file] ), suggesting that the high variability in these genes and pathways is likely attributable to differences in cell composition. 
Unsupervised hierarchical clustering revealed that 9 of the repeat sample pairs clustered most closely together while the remaining pairs were more distant ( Figure S2C [this file] ). Multidimensional scaling revealed that many of the repeat samples clustered together as nearest neighbors ( Figure S2D [this file] ), and additional estimates of similarity by Spearman’s correlation ( Figure S2E [this file] ) or simple error ratio estimate (SERE) scores ( Figure S2F [this file] ) showed that gene expression for the intra-individual (self) repeats was significantly more correlated than inter-individuals (non-self). 
We next examined genes that correlate with S100B staining and identified several in which the percent of S100B+ cells could explain over 50% of the variation in gene expression ( Figure S3A [this file] ). Interestingly, several genes including were more highly correlated with %S100B+ staining than the expression of itself ( Figure S3B [this file] ), suggesting that the RNA-protein relationship for this gene and many others is not always tightly correlated. For other staining markers, NKX6–1 protein was also highly correlated with its own RNA, whereas Nestin protein staining was most correlated with genes such as , and TUBB3 staining with and gene expression ( Figure S3C [this file] ). Interestingly, mutation status best-explained variance in gene expression ( Figure S3D [this file] ), and patients with hexanucleotide repeat expansion (HRE) had significantly less overall gene expression ( Figure 4G [rid=F4] ), supporting previous studies showing a loss of function due to the expanded repeats. Comparing patients with healthy controls or all other ALS patients revealed only a small number of DEGs ( Figure S3E [this file] ). The sample batch explained significant amounts of variation in ribosomal and small nucleolar RNA genes ( Figure S3F [this file] ) that overlapped with many of the HVGs present in the BTC and BDC samples. A large proportion of variation in several genes could be explained by sequencing depth ( Figure S3G [this file] ), and notably, sex could explain nearly all the variation in a number of genes, many being X- and Y-linked ( Figure S3H [this file] ). The disease status of the participant (ALS versus control) only explained an average of 0.22% of the variation in total gene expression ( Figure 4A [rid=F4] ) and a maximum of approximately 15% of the variation of any single gene ( Figure S3I [this file] ). Lastly, correlating the age of the patients at iPSC sample collection with day 32 motor neuron gene expression showed very little association, with age at sample collection only able to explain a maximum of 5.7% of variation in any individual gene, the lowest of any of the covariates we tested ( Figure S3J [this file] ), supporting that age of the patient at iPSC production only minimally affects downstream gene expression of iPSC-derived tissues. 
The distinct clustering of male versus female samples appeared to be driven mainly by X- and Y-linked genes; however, PCA using only autosomal genes revealed weaker but still significant correlations between sex and PC clustering ( Figure S4A [this file] ). Plotting samples along the two highest correlated autosomal-only PCs (PC4 and PC7) revealed significantly more overlap between sexes ( Figure S4B [this file] ) compared with PCA including sex-linked genes ( Figure 5A [rid=F5] ); however, differential gene expression testing between male and female samples uncovered 1,016 DEGs, the majority of which were autosomal ( Figure 5D [rid=F5] ; Table S4 [rid=SD5] ). However, an analysis of XCI status confirmed that nearly all female samples display normal XCI with X-linked gene dosage comparable to males ( Figure S4C [this file] ), which is in line with previous reports assessing XCI in human iPSCs and their differentiated progeny. By comparing the expression level of each X-linked gene in females with the average expression in male samples ( Figure S4D [this file] ), we identified a small number of female samples (n = 4) that display aberrant expression of X-linked genes and have an XX:XY expression ratio >1.2, indicating some erosion of XCI. As expected, XX:XY expression ratios were negatively correlated with levels ( Figure S4E [this file] ), but surprisingly, several female samples maintained normal X-linked gene dosage despite expressing low levels of ( Figure S4F [this file] ). Conversely, many Y-linked genes such as were significantly enriched in male samples ( Figure 5G [rid=F5] ); however, the gene most often associated with sex determination, , was very lowly expressed and only detectable in 78 of 252 male samples ( Figure S4G [this file] ), suggesting alternative drivers of sexual dimorphism in motor neurons. Mapping of the DEGs between males and females shows they are distributed across all chromosomes with several interesting genes displaying sex-specific differences ( Figure S4H [this file] ). 
We therefore performed a random 80/20 split of the ALS patient samples into training (n = 264) and validation (n = 66) groups and performed variance partitioning in the training group using revised ALS Functional Rating Scale (ALSFRS-R) progression rate, age at symptom onset, and site of disease onset as covariates ( Figure S5A [this file] ). This allowed us to identify several genes in which a portion of the variation of expression in day 32 iPSC-derived motor neurons could be explained by the patient clinical data, including a number of genes related to ALSFRS-R progression rate ( Figure S5B [this file] ). Several of these genes such as and were positively correlated with ALSFRS-R slope, with lower expression correlating with faster disease progression ( Figure S5C [this file] ). Several genes were also negatively correlated with ALSFRS-R slope ( Figure S5D [this file] ). ALSFRS-R progression rates ranged from approximately −3.0 to + 0.8 in the training set ( Figure S5E [this file] ), with the median value of −0.54 used to delineate fast and slow progressors. Using the top 7 genes that most highly correlated with ALSFRS-R slope, we generated PCA plots of ALS samples in the training set ( Figure S5F [this file] ) and used ROC curves to estimate the performance of the model to separate fast and slow progressors along PC1. Using this approach, we obtained a borderline acceptable classifier model for predicting disease progression rates from day 32 motor neuron gene expression (AUC = 0.66, p = 3e–4; Figure S5G [this file] ). The distribution of ALSFRS-R progression rates was similar in the validation set ( Figure S5H [this file] ) and patients were plotted along PC1 ( Figure S5I [this file] ) according to the expression of the 7 genes identified in the training group. Applying the classifier model to this set confirmed the significant, but borderline acceptable predictive ability of the model to separate fast and slow progressors using an independent cohort of patients (AUC = 0.68, p = 0.042; Figure S5J [this file] ). We also analyzed several genes that have been previously identified by GWAS and expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) studies to correlate with disease progression ( ) or disease onset ( and ) and found no correlation in our dataset ( Figure S5K [this file] ). 
Differentiation to motor neurons was performed using an optimized 32-day protocol summarized in Figure S1A [this file] and detailed in Baxietal.

The enrolled participant population for the AALS program (Fig. 1a [rid=Fig1] , Extended Data Fig. 1 [rid=Fig7] , Supplementary Information [rid=MOESM1] and Supplementary Tables 1 [this file] – 5 [this file] ) had clinical characteristics comparable to past large sALS population demographics, with a slightly higher number of male than female participants, site of disease onset predominantly a limb rather than bulbar and a mean age of disease onset of approximately 57 years. Non-ALS motor neuron disease (MND) included patients with predominantly upper MND, not formally categorized as ALS (for example, primary lateral sclerosis), and their demographic information is included in Supplementary Table 4 [this file] . 
This differentiation protocol (Extended Data Fig. 3 [rid=Fig9] ) generates a mixed population of neurons consisting of ~75% (±8%) β -tubulin- (TuJ1-) and ~70% (±10%) NF-H-positive cells, ~19% (±6%) Islet-1- and ~34% (±9%) Nkx6.1-positive spinal motor neurons, and ~18% (+/13%) S100B-positive progenitors 32 d after the onset of differentiation (Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). 
We also investigated the number of P/LP variants called by Intervar (IP), in in silico prediction (ISD variants) and a new combination of ACMG gene criteria as well as the in silico prediction and family-based segregation data, a list of high-confidence causal variants in 12 genes— , , , , , , , , , , and —which have been curated and designated as the HP (Harms P/LP, Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ) variants. 
The AALS data portal ( http://data.answerals.org (http://data.answerals.org/) ; Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ) was designed to provide information about the various types of biological and clinical data generated by the AALS partners and to allow easy visualization/access to the metadata and data, along with links to obtain biofluids and iPS cell lines. 
A web portal for downloading filtered datasets, for example, proteome, whole genome, etc., has been set up with minimal but appropriate requirements for data access (Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). Biospecimens (for example, CSF and plasma) longitudinally collected from patients are also available (Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). 
The eight enrolling neuromuscular clinics were distributed across the USA and included Johns Hopkins University, Massachusetts General Hospital, Ohio State, Emory University, Washington University, Northwestern University, Cedars-Sinai and Texas Neurology (Supplementary Table 1 [this file] and Extended Data Fig. 1 [rid=Fig7] ). 
Measures of ALS progression included: deep tendon reflexes, Ashworth Spasticity Scale, Hand Held Dynamometry, ALSFRS-R and pulmonary slow vital capacity (Supplementary Tables 2 [this file] and 3 [this file] and Supplementary Information [rid=MOESM1] ). 
Serum, plasma and CSF samples were shipped on dry ice to a centralized biofluid repository to be stored at −80 °C (Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). 
Clones were isolated, expanded and maintained according to standard feeder-free protocols and characterized extensively as described in Supplementary Table 6 [this file] . Rigorous quality control (QC) (Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ) was performed on each AALS iPS cell line, similar to previously publications . The cell line authentication (STR) is performed on the original donor blood/PBMC sample, then performed on the reprogrammed iPS cell line and the differentiated neurons (Supplementary Tables 6 [this file] and 19 [this file] ). 
The iPS cells were differentiated into motor neurons according to the direct iPS cell diMN protocol, which comprises three main stages (Extended Data Fig. 3 [rid=Fig9] and Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ), as described previously . 
All of the clinical datasets, the various omics results, including whole-genome, proteome, transcriptome and epigenome, along with the data integration have been posted to a portal for data sharing and crowd sourcing ( https://data.answerals.org (https://data.answerals.org) ; Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). 
Finally, precise definitions are provided for our data levels, which are ways to stratify all the various omics data coming from our analyses (Supplementary Table 20 [this file] ). 
The AALS data portal ( http://data.answerals.org (http://data.answerals.org) ; Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ) provides all raw and processed data including longitudinal clinical data and biological data generated by the AALS program, along with visualization/access to the metadata, data and biosamples released. 
Data levels (Supplementary Table 20 [this file] ) were employed as a categorization schema to group similar types of omics data products together. Supplementary Table 21 [this file] describes examples of these data levels in action with each experimental assay that our program collects.

Phasing starts with assignment of SNV alleles to FGLs for the individuals with homozygous SNV genotypes (Figure 2A [rid=gepi70039-fig-0002] and Supporting Information S1: Figure S2A [this file] ). 
Individuals with heterozygous SNV genotypes are phased to FGLs if at any point in the process, there is already an SNV allele assignment to one of their FGLs from phasing other individuals, (Figure 2A [rid=gepi70039-fig-0002] and Supporting Information S1: Figure S2A [this file] ): the FGL without an allele assignment in the heterozygous individual is then assigned the remaining allele from the SNV genotype of the individual. Phased alleles for an individual with a missing genotype can be imputed if the individual's FGLs have allele assignments from genotype phasing in other individuals (Supporting Information S1: Figure Figure S2B [this file] ). It is also possible that some heterozygous individuals end up with their genotypes unphased for a particular SNV if there are no allele assignments to FGLs in these individuals from phasing other genotypes (Supporting Information S1: Figure S3A [this file] ). 
Inconsistencies between allele assignments to the same FGL in different individuals at a SNV position can occur in real data (Figure 2B [rid=gepi70039-fig-0002] and Supporting Information S1: Figure S3B [this file] ).

Variants were scored separately using three WatershedSV models for RNA expression, plasma protein levels, and CSF protein levels as each model prioritizes different annotations ( Supplementary Figures 1 [this file] – 3 [this file] ) We identified 365, 545, and 202 prioritized rare SV-gene pairs from RNA expression, plasma protein levels, and CSF protein levels, respectively (Watershed posterior probability > 0.6) ( Table S2 [rid=SD2] , Figure 3d [rid=F3] ). 
At an FDR threshold of 0.05, we discovered 60,177 SV-QTLs for 16,201 unique features (molQTL targets) over our 4 molecular traits ( Figure 4a [rid=F4] , Extended Data Figure 6a [this file] , Table S3 [rid=SD2] ) (methylation: 53,112 SV-QTLs in 13,397 regions; expression: 3,202 SV-QTLs in 1,216 genes; plasma: 2,904 SV-QTLs in 1,149 aptamers; CSF: 959 SV-QTLs in 439 aptamers). Similarly, a typical molQTL target had 2.5 associated SVs across expression or protein, and an average of 4 SV-QTLs for methylation ( Extended Data Figure 6b [this file] ). By overlapping QTL-associated SVs across molecular traits, we discovered SVs with effects across multiple molecular traits, including over 100 SVs which had a significant QTL in all 4 traits. ( Extended Data Figure 6c [this file] ) 
62.1% of our SV-QTLs included a lrGS-specific SV, particularly for insertions where a majority (76%) of QTLs were lrGS-specific ( Extended Data Figure 6d [this file] ). In addition to allele frequency, we also observed that longer variants had larger absolute effect sizes (Length>10Kb, beta=0.11, p-value<1E-32) ( Extended Data Figure 6e [this file] ). QTLs for methylation had closer-range effects compared to the other omes (p-value=9.4E-18), and across all molecular traits, closer SVs had significantly higher effects (log-distance slope=−0.022, p-value<1E-32), particularly those for SVs directly overlapping their molecular target ( Extended Data Figure 6f [this file] , g [this file] ). 
With our lrGS SV calls, we observed 12% of QTL associations having an SVs in the credible set, with 6% having an SV as the lead variant ( Figure 5a [rid=F5] , Table S4 [rid=SD2] ). 54% of these SVs contained in credible sets were novel to lrGS ( Extended Data Figure 7a [this file] ). 
Across SV types, deletions and duplications were most enriched to be fine-mapped in credible sets ( Extended Data Figure 7b [this file] ), and longer SVs that disrupt more sequence were also more likely to be included ( Extended Data Figure 7c [this file] ). Credible sets with a lead SV tended to be smaller than those containing a lead SNV ( Extended Data Figure 7d [this file] ). Comparing fine-mapped SVs to other SV-QTLs not included in credible sets, we found lead SVs tended to be in lower LD with nearby SNVs (p-value<1E-32, Extended Data Figure 7e [this file] ). Fine-mapped SVs in QTL credible sets were also more likely to disrupt functional regions compared to background SVs, as evidenced by a higher non-coding constraint score from Gnocchi for these variants ( Chen et al. 2024 [rid=R10] ) ( Extended Data Figure 7f [this file] ). 
All together, these represent 8 unique risk loci for AD and 4 for PD that are colocalized with a fine-mapped SV association, representing candidate GWAS signals that are driven by an SV ( Extended Data Table 2 [this file] ). 
We additionally colocalized GTEx-QTLs with high-tagging SVs to capture associations in tissues not profiled in this study ( Supplementary Figure 4 [this file] – 5 [this file] ). QTL variants for NBEAL1 expression in the GTEx Tibial Artery tissue colocalized with Alzheimer’s GWAS (PP4=0.81) and across all neurovascular GWASs (small vessel disease PP4=0.74, stroke and white matter hyperintensities PP4=0.84) ( Extended Data Figure 8 [this file] ). 
Also present in the credible sets is an Alu element insertion in ACE (chr17:63488532; 291 bp insertion) ( Supplementary Figure 6 [this file] ), which has been shown to affect isoform splicing ( Wu et al. 2013 [rid=R50] ) and may be a relevant locus for AD (R =0.4 with rs4277405 reported in AD-GWAS, R =0.62 with rs4309 in CSF proteomics GWAS) ( Cruchaga et al. 2023 [rid=R16] ). The SAMS/ADRC CSF protein levels of the corresponding SNVs in both genes showed strong colocalization with AD GWAS signals (PP4=0.96 ACE CSF protein levels, Supplementary Figure 7 [this file] ), TMEM106B protein levels (PP4= 0.81 CSF, PP4= 0.91 plasma), as well as GTEx expression (PP4=0.85 brain cortex, and Figure 6c [rid=F6] ). 
SVs are also present within the fine-mapped credible set—for example, LRRC37A2 (ENSG00000238083) shows strong colocalization with PP4 = 0.79 for AD and PP4 = 0.98 for PD ( Supplementary Figures 8 [this file] ), with a lead SV (37 bp insertion) in the LRRC37A2 eQTL fine-mapped credible set ( Supplementary Figures 9 [this file] ).
