Data from participants with longitudinal plasma %p-tau217 measurements collected at least 1 year apart were considered for potential inclusion in developing the clock models (Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). 
Similar clock models were constructed using all longitudinal data (Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] ). 
Additionally, we performed cross-cohort comparison of the models and found that the estimated ages at plasma %p-tau217 positivity based on TIRA models implemented on either the Knight ADRC or ADNI cohorts were highly correlated (adjusted of 0.978), and ages based on SILA models from the two cohorts were almost perfectly aligned (adjusted of 0.999) (Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] ). The estimated ages at plasma %p-tau217 positivity based on the TIRA or SILA models were also highly correlated in the Knight ADRC cohort (adjusted of 0.942) but were less correlated in the ADNI cohort (adjusted of 0.863) (Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] ). 
Cox models for both the Knight ADRC and ADNI cohorts are shown in Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] . 
Additional analyses incorporating left-censored participants for those with cognitive impairment at study enrollment confirmed these associations with better discrimination and addressed potential survivor bias (Supplementary Fig. 5 [this file] ). 
For the Knight ADRC cohort, models included 59 individuals using TIRA and 61 individuals using SILA clock models; for the ADNI cohort, models included 20 individuals using TIRA and 22 individuals using SILA (see Supplementary Table 2 [this file] for cohort characteristics). The age at onset of AD symptoms was moderately associated with the estimated age at plasma %p-tau217 positivity for both TIRA-based (Knight ADRC adjusted of 0.599; ADNI adjusted of 0.337) and SILA-based (Knight ADRC adjusted of 0.612; ADNI adjusted of 0.470) estimates (Fig. 4 [rid=Fig4] and Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). Comprehensive model diagnostics confirmed the appropriateness of linear modeling across all cohort−method combinations (Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ). Consistent with findings from the Cox models, these models demonstrated that older individuals had a much shorter interval from plasma %p-tau217 positivity to symptom onset (Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] ). 
The effects of ε4 carrier status, sex and years of education were also examined, but these variables were either not significant or had minimal effects and, thus, were not included in the models (Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ). Associations between estimated age at plasma %p-tau217 positivity and age at symptom onset were lower when individuals who developed cognitive impairment before %p-tau217 positivity were included, likely because these individuals had non-AD causes of cognitive impairment (Supplementary Fig. 7 [this file] ). 
For initially cognitively unimpaired individuals in the Knight ADRC cohort with an estimated age at plasma %p-tau217 positivity by the TIRA-based model (Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ), individuals who became %p-tau217 positive at age 60 were estimated to develop symptomatic AD after 14.0 years, whereas individuals who became %p-tau217 positive at age 80 were estimated to develop symptomatic AD after only 6.2 years (Figs. 4 [rid=Fig4] and 5 [rid=Fig5] Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ). Similar analyses were performed for individuals with an estimated age at plasma %p-tau217 positivity by TIRA or SILA in both the Knight ADRC and ADNI cohorts, including only those who were initially cognitively unimpaired (Supplementary Fig. 8 [this file] ) and all individuals regardless of initial cognitive status (Supplementary Tables 7 [this file] – 9 [this file] and Extended Data Fig. 3 [rid=Fig9] ). 
Similar analyses are shown for SILA-based models in the Knight ADRC dataset (Supplementary Fig. 9 [this file] ) and for TIRA-based and SILA-based models in the ADNI dataset (Supplementary Figs. 10 [this file] and 11 [this file] ). 
Plasma trajectories by age or estimated years from positivity are shown for each plasma measure (Extended Data Figs. 5 [rid=Fig11] − 7 [rid=Fig13] and Supplementary Figs. 12 [this file] and 13 [this file] ). 
The associations between age at symptom onset and age at plasma positivity were examined: Fujirebio Lumipulse p-tau217/Aβ42, TIRA adjusted of 0.276 and SILA adjusted of 0.584 (Extended Data Fig. 5 [rid=Fig11] ); Janssen LucentAD Quanterix p-tau217, TIRA adjusted of 0.041 and SILA adjusted of 0.211 (Extended Data Fig. 6 [rid=Fig12] ); ALZpath Quanterix p-tau217, TIRA adjusted of 0.082 and SILA adjusted of 0.258 (Extended Data Fig. 7 [rid=Fig13] ); C2N Diagnostics p-tau217, TIRA adjusted of 0.084 and SILA adjusted of 0.301 (Supplementary Fig. 12 [this file] ); and Fujirebio Lumipulse p-tau217, TIRA adjusted of 0.239 and SILA adjusted of 0.450 (Supplementary Fig. 13 [this file] ).

In a post-hoc analysis, CSF oligomeric amyloid β was measured with an oligomeric amyloid β-preferring immunoassay platform that allows increased sensitivity compared with traditional immunodetection systems ( appendix [this file] pp 3–4). 
A graph-based testing procedure was used to ensure the family-wise type I error was controlled at a two-sided α of 0·05 ( appendix [this file] p 13).

The null results for the primary outcomes by amyloid status are shown in the appendix [this file] (p 16). 
The Kaplan–Meier curve for time to MCI or dementia due to Alzheimer’s disease, p=0·48 (log-rank) and HR 0·79 (95% CI 0·41–1·51), presented in the appendix [this file] (p 14) are exploratory in nature. CSF total Aβ40 concentrations did not change in mutation non-carriers and increased more in crenezumab-treated versus placebo-treated carriers (unadjusted p<0·0001; appendix [this file] p 15). Baseline CSF oligomeric amyloid β concentrations were not significantly different between the mutation carrier and non-carrier groups, did not change in mutation non-carriers, and increased more in crenezumab-treated carriers versus placebo-treated carriers (unadjusted p<0·0001; appendix [this file] p 21). No participants received or were recruited with the intent of receiving or being recommended for disease-modifying treatments or therapies, nor were participants referred to our study for treatment (previously published exclusionary criteria are provided in the supplement [this file] for reference). 
Additional details on medications can be found in the Supplementary Material [this file] . 
WF ADRC participants (n=238) who received cognitive diagnoses at adjudication (see Cognitive Status) by June 1st, 2025, and had an MRI and both amyloid and tau PET within one year (see Figure S1 [this file] for greater details) were selected for the ARTS ATN sub-study. 
Demographics were comparable to and representative of the larger WF ADRC cohort (see Table S1 [this file] ). 
ARTS scores were higher on average in females, participants with HTN, and participants with a history of smoking (all <.05; see Table 1 [rid=T1] and Figure S2 [this file] ). Consistent with ARTS as an aging vascular biomarker, ARTS scores were strongly positively associated with age ( =0.62, <.001; Figure S3 [this file] ). Raw unadjusted Spearman correlation matrices are presented in Figure S4 [this file] . 
Higher ARTS score was significantly associated with greater levels of amyloid deposition and greater tau PET deposition in unadjusted models ( Table 2 [rid=T2] , Model 1; Figure 1 [rid=F1] ; also see Figure S5 [panel a] [this file] and S6 [this file] ), and in models adjusted by sex, race, education, -ε4 carriership, and the interval in days between PET and MRI (Model 2). Results were nearly identical using gamma regression (see Table S2 [this file] ). Associations of ARTS with PET positivity of A+ and T+ are presented in the Supplemental Material [this file] (also see Table S3 [this file] ). 
ARTS was not significantly associated with cerebral blood flow in white matter before or after adjustment (all >.05; Table 3 [rid=T3] ; also see Figure S5 [panel a] [this file] and S6 [this file] ). 
Higher ARTS scores were significantly associated with elevated plasma biomarker levels in unadjusted models (Model 1; Table 4 [rid=T4] , Figure 1 [rid=F1] ) and models adjusted for age, sex, race, education, APOE genotype, BMI, eGFR, and the time interval between blood draw and MRI acquisition (Model 2; Table 4 [rid=T4] , Figure 1 [rid=F1] ; also see Figure S5 [panel b] [this file] and S7 [this file] ).

First, using independent DNAm data from neonatal buccal swabs and cord blood we verified that our 371 stemTOC CpGs retain ultra-low DNAm levels, as required (“Methods” section, Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] ). Second, we used 3 separate age-matched DNAm datasets of sorted cells (including adult neutrophils, monocytes, naïve CD4+ T-cells, B cells, neurons, adipocytes, endothelial cells, lung- epithelial, colon-epithelial, hepatocytes, exocrine and endocrine pancreas), as well as the age-matched multi-tissue eGTEX dataset , to confirm that stemTOC CpGs are not cell-type specific markers of adult cell types (“Methods” section, Supplementary Figs. 2 [this file] and 3 [this file] ). Indeed, any cell-type specific DNAm differences in these aged cell and tissue-types were exclusively restricted to comparisons involving colon-epithelial cells, the tissue with the highest turnover rate, thus clearly indicating that these DNAm differences are likely due to differences in cell-type specific mitotic rates (Supplementary Figs. 2 [this file] and 3 [this file] ). Applying eFORGE2 to the 371 stemTOC CpGs, we observed strong and exclusive enrichment for DNase Hypersensitive Sites (DHSs) as defined in hESCs (Supplementary Fig. 4a [this file] ). Among chromatin states, we observed strong enrichment for bivalent transcription start sites (TSS), which was strongest for those also defined in hESCs (Supplementary Fig. 4b [this file] ). Correspondingly, we observed strong enrichment for both H3K27me3 and H3K4me3 marks, although notably stronger for the repressive H3K27me3 mark (Supplementary Fig. 4a [this file] ), consistent with previous observations that H3K4me3 is moderately protective of age-associated DNAm accrual . 
Applying stemTOC to the normal-adjacent tissue data from the TCGA confirmed this: tissues with a high stem-cell division rate like the colon and rectum displayed strong correlations between mitotic and chronological age, whilst slower-dividing and hormone-sensitive tissues like breast and endometrium did not, despite these being appropriately powered (Fig. 2a, b [rid=Fig2] , Supplementary Fig. 5 [this file] , Supplementary Data 2 [rid=MOESM4] . Similar results were obtained when estimating mitotic age in the enhanced GTEX (eGTEX) DNAm dataset, encompassing 987 samples from 9 normal tissue-types (Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] , Supplementary Data 3 [rid=MOESM4] ). For instance, the colon displayed a clear correlation, whilst the ovary and breast did not (Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] ). 
Associations of mitotic age with chronological age remained significant and even displayed a marginal increase after adjustment for CTH (Supplementary Fig. 7 [this file] ). Similar findings were obtained in the eGTEX normal tissue datasets for which we could infer cell-type fractions using our EpiSCORE DNA-atlas (“Methods” section, Supplementary Fig. 8a, b [this file] ). 
CpGs making up each clock displayed relatively little overlap except for the epiTOC1 and epiTOC2 clocks (Supplementary Fig. 9 [this file] ). Similar patterns were observed in the normal-tissue EPIC DNAm data from eGTEX (Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] ) as well as in the sorted immune-cell subsets (Fig. 2d [rid=Fig2] ). 
We observed that hypermethylated counters displayed less sensitivity to the underlying CTH of the tissue, as compared to the hypomethylated ones (Supplementary Figs. 7 [this file] , 8 [this file] , 10 [this file] ). It is also noteworthy that stemTOC’s mitotic age displayed stronger correlations with chronological age than those of all hypomethylated clocks, including RepliTali (Supplementary Figs. 8b [this file] , S10b [this file] ). For instance, in a high-turnover-rate tissue (colon eGTEX EPIC dataset), RepliTali’s association with chronological age was only significant upon adjustment for CTH, whilst stemTOC’s association was stronger and independent of CTH adjustment (Supplementary Fig. 8b [this file] ). Moreover, the effect of beadarray technology seemed to be relatively minor as RepliTali’s mitotic age estimates on EPIC data were very robust upon restricting to 450k probes (Supplementary Fig. 8c [this file] ). 
It is worth stressing that for each tumor-type, the strongest correlation with mitotic age was attained by the presumed tumor cell-of-origin Supplementary Fig. 11a, b [this file] ). stemTOC’s mitotic age also displayed strong correlations with other tumor purity indices as estimated by Aran et al. , although the correlations with EpiSCORE’s tumor cell fraction were generally higher than for gene-expression or IHC-based tumor purity estimation methods (Supplementary Fig. 11c [this file] ). For instance, in low-grade glioma (LGG) and glioblastoma multiforme (GBM), mitotic age correlated most strongly with astrocyte fraction (Fig. 3c [rid=Fig3] , Supplementary Fig. 11b [this file] ), favoring an astrocyte-like progenitor as the putative cell of origin . Our analysis is consistent with the known luminal-cell expansion associated with PRAD (Fig. 3c [rid=Fig3] , Supplementary Fig. 11b [this file] ), and the prevailing view that the cell-of-origin of human PRAD is a luminal progenitor cell . 
Moreover, none of the other 6 mitotic counters achieved 100% accuracy in predicting the putative cell-of-origin (Supplementary Fig. 11d [this file] ). We also combined epiCMIT-hyper and epiCMIT-hypo into epiCMIT following Duran-Ferrer et al. , but in line with epiCMIT-hypo’s worse performance, stemTOC and epiCMIT-hyper also outperformed epiCMIT (Supplementary Fig. 12 [this file] ). However, all mitotic counters were universally accelerated in TCGA cancer types, as compared to their respective age-matched normal-adjacent tissue (Supplementary Fig. 13 [this file] . To further explore the relationship between mitotic counters, we computed correlations between each pair of counters across all sorted immune cell subsets, the normal tissues from GTEX and the normal-adjacent and tumor samples from TCGA, demonstrating that the hypermethylated counters are well-correlated with each other and to a lesser extent also with RepliTali (Supplementary Fig. 14 [this file] − 16 [this file] ), which is noteworthy given the aforementioned relatively little CpG overlap between them (Supplementary Fig. 9 [this file] ). 
Some of the other counters did not provide the expected discrimination, and a formal comparison of all counters across the 9 datasets revealed an overall improved performance of stemTOC (Supplementary Fig. 17 [this file] ). Using EpiSCORE we next estimated cell-type fractions in these datasets, and broadly speaking, for most tissue-types we observed correlations of the mitotic age with tumor cell-of-origin fraction in the precancerous lesions and in cancer itself, but not in the histologically normal tissue, although in many cases the number of samples with normal histology was much lower, which limits power to detect associations in this subgroup (Supplementary Fig. 18 [this file] ). For instance, in colon adenoma there was a clear correlation ( = 0.75, = 3e-8, = 39) but not so in normal colon ( = 0.44, = 0.27, = 8), likely due to the much lower number of normal samples (Supplementary Fig. 18 [this file] ). In premalignant cholangiocarcinoma (CCA) lesions, there was a strong correlation with cholangiocyte fraction ( = 0.45, < 0.001, = 60), which was not observed in normal liver samples ( = 0.16, = 0.25, = 50), probably because the cholangiocyte fraction is much lower in these normal samples (Supplementary Fig. S18 [this file] ). Correlations between stemTOC’s mitotic age with tumor cell-of-origin fraction in normal-adjacent tissue from the TCGA was broadly speaking also observed (e.g. COAD, BRCA, PRAD), but there were also exceptions (e.g. KIRP, LUAD) (Supplementary Fig. 19 [this file] ). Of note, using an upper quantile over the 371 stemTOC CpGs to define the mitotic age generally resulted in larger effect sizes as well as stronger correlations with cancer-status and tumor cell-of-origin fraction compared to taking an average, highlighting the importance of taking the underlying stochasticity of DNAm patterns into account (Supplementary Fig. 20 [this file] ). 
We verified that this saturation effect is also observed if we define stemTOC in terms of an average DNAm over the 371 CpGs (as opposed to taking the upper quantile), indicating that this is not a technical artifact of our stemTOC definition (Supplementary Fig. 21 [this file] ). 
Of note, stemTOC correlated with MS1 within most TCGA cancer types, even after adjusting for chronological age (Supplementary Fig. 22 [this file] ). However, in some cancer types (e.g. lung squamous cell carcinoma) no correlation was evident (Supplementary Fig. 22 [this file] ). Of note, a strong correlation with tumor cell-of-origin fraction is not seen if one were to use the MS1-load as a proxy for mitotic age (Supplementary Fig. 23 [this file] ), and correlations of MS1-load with CPE-based tumor purity estimates were weaker than with EpiSCORE-derived tumor cell-of-origin fractions (Supplementary Fig. 24 [this file] ).

Cohen’s , which estimates effect sizes by comparing one cell-type to all others, also proved suboptimal as it fails to guarantee specificity, i.e., it frequently selected probes with high effect size but negative GSS (SI Fig. S1b [this file] , Supplementary Data 1 [rid=MOESM3] ). In contrast, ranking features by positive GSS values ensures specificity (SI Fig. S1c [this file] , Supplementary Data 1 [rid=MOESM3] ). A concrete example of a marker for memory CD4+ T-cells selected using Cohen’s illustrates how its GSS is negative, since T-regulatory cells display even lower DNAm levels than memory CD4+ T-cells (SI Fig. S1d [this file] ). 
To confirm that low effect size DMCs can negatively impact downstream cell-type deconvolution, we built DNAm reference matrices using the two different approaches (Fig. 1b [rid=Fig1] ), subsequently applying them to deconvolve twelve experimental mixtures, each being a mixture of 12 immune-cell-types with known cell type proportions (Supplementary Data 2 [this file] ). Furthermore, this improvement was not dependent on the optimization algorithm, as it consistently outperformed the -statistic-ranked panel when fractions were evaluated using two other optimization methods (Constrained Projection and Support Vector Regression ) (SI Fig. S2 [this file] , Methods, Supplementary Data 1 [rid=MOESM3] ). 
Surprisingly, comparing the effect sizes of markers before and after IDOL optimization showed that IDOL has a tendency to select DMCs with lower effect sizes (SI Fig. S3a, b [this file] , Supplementary Data 1 [rid=MOESM3] ), irrespective of whether we started out using the T-Both or GSS-Hypo reference panel. To explore this further, we assessed the performance of the four reference matrices in the experimental mixtures from the training set as well as those of an independent validation set (Methods, see Supplementary Data 2 [this file] for known cell-type proportions). Interestingly, the IDOL-optimized references demonstrated comparable PCCs in the training set but somewhat higher RMSEs (SI Fig. S3c [this file] , Supplementary Data 1 [rid=MOESM3] ). Moreover, IDOL-optimized references performed worse in terms of both PCC and RMSE in the independent validation set (SI Fig. S3d [this file] , Supplementary Data 1 [rid=MOESM3] ). 
As before, effect sizes of selected features using EN or RF were substantially smaller compared to GSS-Hypo (Fig. 4a, b [rid=Fig4] , Supplementary Data 1 [rid=MOESM3] ), translating into a lower accuracy for the cell-type deconvolution on experimental mixtures (Fig. 4c, d [rid=Fig4] , Supplementary Data 1 [rid=MOESM3] ), as well as on an independent DNAm dataset with matched FACS counts for 4 cell-types (Methods, Fig. 4e, f [rid=Fig4] , Supplementary Data 1 and 2 [this file] ). 
Performing a meta-analysis across 15 adult blood cohorts, while adjusting for sex, we observed that for all 3 reference panels (i.e., GSS-hypo, T-hypo and T-both), naive B-cell, naïve CD8+ T-cell and naïve CD4+ T-cell fractions decreased with age, whilst corresponding memory fractions increased (Fig. 5a [rid=Fig5] , Methods, Supplementary Data 3 [this file] ). 
This result was robust to additional adjustment for chip and position, as well as top principal methylation components (SI Fig. S4 [this file] , Supplementary Data 1 [rid=MOESM3] ). In Hannon2, we observed a strong batch effect, which we successfully adjusted for using Combat (SI Fig. S5 [this file] , Supplementary Data 1 [rid=MOESM3] ). Indeed, in all 3 cases, we observed enrichment for the steroid biosynthesis pathway, which has been implicated in SZ (SI Fig. S6 [this file] , Methods, Supplementary Data 1 [rid=MOESM3] ) . Interestingly, in the case of GSS-hypo, the 20 SZ-DMCs were enriched for inflammation-related pathways, whilst this enrichment was absent or less evident for T-Both or T-Hypo (Fig. 6c [rid=Fig6] , Supplementary Data 4 [this file] , Supplementary Data 1 [rid=MOESM3] ). Supporting their biological significance, among the 20 SZ-DMCs, were CpGs mapping to the chemokine , consistent with reports of elevated CCL18 chemokine levels in the serum of SZ patients , and to the chemokine receptor gene , a gene implicated in neuroinflammation and schizophrenia (Fig. 6d [rid=Fig6] , Supplementary Data 4 [this file] , Supplementary Data 1 [rid=MOESM3] ). Another CpG mapped to the gene (Fig. 6d [rid=Fig6] , Supplementary Data 4 [this file] , Supplementary Data 1 [rid=MOESM3] ), which is known to promote IL-6 production and inflammatory responses through chromatin remodeling . 
The specific covariates adjusted for in each of the 15 cohorts are detailed in Supplementary Data 3 [this file] .

To assess any biases that heparin enrichment may have caused, and to compare the differences in proteome coverage to traditional immunodepletion methods [ 59 [rid=CR59] , 60 [rid=CR60] ], we benchmarked the Hp-enriched proteome against the immunodepleted proteome from the same 36 samples in Set 1 (Supplemental Fig. 3 [this file] A). Among these, 432 proteins were increased in AD and 383 were decreased (Supplemental Fig. 3 [this file] B and Supplemental Table 8 [rid=MOESM9] ). We found that 804 out of the 1,129 proteins (71%) in the immunodepletion dataset overlapped with the Hp-enriched dataset, with 325 proteins not detected by heparin enrichment (Supplemental Fig. 3 [this file] C and Supplemental Table 9 [rid=MOESM9] ). These include many members of the M42 matrisome module, such as SMOC1, SMOC2, OLFML3, SPON1, FRZB, and MDK (Supplemental Fig. 3 [this file] D). Additionally, significant protein levels (AD vs. Control) measured following either heparin enrichment or immunodepletion exhibited a strong correlation regarding the directional changes observed in AD plasma (Supplemental Fig. 3 [this file] E). 
Given that the significant protein levels ( -value < 0.05) measured following either heparin enrichment or immunodepletion exhibited strong correlation regarding the directional changes observed in AD plasma (Supplemental Fig. 3 [this file] E), this discrepancy may be attributed to the methodology. 
This number is more than twofold greater than the coverage generated with immunodepletion method followed by TMT-MS (Supplemental Fig. 3 [this file] C), supporting the depth and sensitivity of the heparin enrichment approach when coupled to TMT-MS.

All proteins along with corresponding -value and fold-change were listed in Supplemental Table 21 [this file] . Same correlations performed for SomaScan ( = 35 samples) and Olink ( = 35 samples) were listed in Supplemental Table 24–25 [this file] . 
Additional ROC curve characteristics including sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy were calculated with the reportROC R package and listed in Supplemental Table 27 [this file] . 
To assess the consistency of the Hp-enriched MS proteomic approach, measurements of proteins with no missing values across all three replicates within each fraction were listed in Supplemental Table 1 [this file] along with their coefficient of variation (CV). To evaluate the depth of protein identification across the fractions, we assessed the overlap of proteins that were detected in at least two out of three replicates of each fraction (Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] E and Supplemental Table 2 [this file] ). 
In total, 518 proteins exhibited significant changes in their abundance levels across the two fractions (Supplemental Fig. 1 [rid=MOESM1] A and Supplemental Table 3 [this file] ), with 338 increased and 180 decreased. 
After successfully demonstrating enrichment of HBPs from human plasma, we aimed to both enhance the depth and determine the differences in the plasma proteome between AD ( = 18) and control ( = 18) individuals using discovery Set 1 (Supplemental Table 4 [this file] ). Following heparin-affinity enrichment, we employed tandem mass tag mass spectrometry (TMT-MS) in conjunction with high-pH off-line fractionation to identify a total of 3284 proteins (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] A and Supplemental Table 5 [this file] ). To enhance data completeness, we considered only those proteins quantified in at least 50% of the samples for subsequent analyses, culminating in the final quantification of 2077 proteins (Supplemental Table 6 [this file] ). The complete list of differentially abundant proteins is provided in Supplementary Table 7 [this file] . 
Among these, 432 proteins were increased in AD and 383 were decreased (Supplemental Fig. 3 [rid=MOESM3] B and Supplemental Table 8 [this file] ). We found that 804 out of the 1,129 proteins (71%) in the immunodepletion dataset overlapped with the Hp-enriched dataset, with 325 proteins not detected by heparin enrichment (Supplemental Fig. 3 [rid=MOESM3] C and Supplemental Table 9 [this file] ). 
The protein measures were obtained from these two platforms following cross-platform median-centered normalization as previously described [ 30 [rid=CR30] ] and are provided in Supplemental Table 10 [this file] and 11 [this file] . We used gene symbols from each output to calculate the number of measurements and their overlap across the various platforms (Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] A and Supplemental Table 12 [this file] ). However, consistent with our previous results [ 30 [rid=CR30] ], we observed a notable bias towards decreased protein levels in AD plasma on the SomaScan and Olink platform even following median-centered normalization (Supplemental Fig. 4 [rid=MOESM4] A-B and Supplemental Tables 13–14 [this file] ). 
To demonstrate the reproducibility of the Heparin-MS approach in plasma, we analyzed a separate set of samples (Set 2) involving 49 controls and 36 AD individuals (Supplemental Table 15 [this file] ), which included 13 overlapping controls with the discovery Set 1. TMT-MS was employed for the analysis of the Hp-enriched fraction, carried out across five batches, resulting in the identification of 2618 proteins measured in 50% or more of the samples. (Supplemental Table 16 [this file] ). Impressively, this encompassed proteins across 10 orders of magnitude in concentration within the plasma, even extending to those with the lowest concentration (1.47 pg/ml), as evidenced by inclusion of proteins such as LAG3 and RNF213 as well as many M42 matrisome members based on The Human Protein Atlas Database (Fig. 4 [rid=Fig4] C and Supplemental Table 17 [this file] ). In total, 1829 out of 2866 (64%) proteins overlapped between the two independent TMT-MS datasets (Fig. 4 [rid=Fig4] D and Supplemental Table 18 [this file] ). Differential expression analyses were performed on all 2618 proteins within Set 2, resulting in 826 proteins being increased and 795 proteins decreased in AD (Supplemental Table 19 [this file] ). 
As a result of this selection process, 12 non-overlapping samples were excluded from Set 2, resulting in a total of 109 samples (Set 1 = 36 samples, Set 2 = 73 samples) for further analysis (Supplemental Table 20 [this file] ). This -analysis revealed a substantial increase in differentially abundant proteins in the Hp-enriched AD plasma, with 945 proteins showing an increase and 923 proteins showing a decrease in AD, as compared to analyzing either dataset alone (Fig. 5 [rid=Fig5] A and Supplemental Table 21 [this file] ). To assess the relationship between Hp-enriched plasma proteins and AD biomarkers and cognitive measures, we conducted correlation analyses between Z-transformed protein abundance (Supplemental Table 22 [this file] ) and MoCA scores, as well as immunoassay values of CSF (Aβ , tTau, pTau181, tTau/Aβ ) and plasma pTau181 (Supplemental Table 23 [this file] ). Correlation between SomaScan or Olink protein abundance and MoCA scores, as well as immunoassay values of CSF (Aβ , tTau, pTau181, tTau/Aβ ) and plasma pTau181 were also provided in Supplemental Table 24–25 [this file] . To ensure that the observed changes in these proteins in AD were not influenced by age, sex, or race, we performed regression analyses for these traits within Set 1 and Set 2, followed by the same -analysis described earlier (Supplemental Fig. 6 [rid=MOESM6] and Supplemental Table 26 [this file] ). 
ROC curve statistics for highly significant proteins, including AUC, -value, 95% DeLong confidence interval, accuracy, specificity, and sensitivity for AD vs CTL, are provided in Supplemental Table 27 [this file] . 
This analysis used plasma pTau181 measurements and only included plasma proteins with no missing values and those that were highly significant ( -value < 0.0001, = 536 proteins) across 34 control and 61 AD individuals (Supplemental Table 27 [this file] ). 
To ensure the consistency of protein overlap analysis, we employed the same Uniprot database and utilized the FragPipe search algorithm we used for Heparin-MS plasma analysis to re-analyze 456 dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) tissues from control, asymptomatic AD (AsymAD) and AD brains from the ROSMAP and the Banner cohorts (Supplemental Fig. 7 [rid=MOESM7] A and Supplemental Table 28 [this file] ) [ 11 [rid=CR11] ]. By applying a data normalization approach similar to the one used for the Hp-enriched plasma samples, we successfully identified 8,956 proteins detected in 50% or more of the samples from brain tissues corresponding to 8,904 unique gene symbols (Supplemental Table 29 [this file] ). When compared to a previous brain proteome dataset generated using Proteome Discoverer (PD) and an older 2015 Uniprot protein database [ 11 [rid=CR11] ], it was found that 7,476 of these unique gene symbols overlapped between the two outputs, while 1,428 were exclusive to the FragPipe, representing an approximately 18% increase in the number of identifications (Supplemental Fig. 7 [rid=MOESM7] B and Supplemental Table 30 [this file] ). Furthermore, to ensure the consistency of the direction of change in the AD brain proteome compared to controls, we correlated the differentially abundant proteins across these two sets of results (Supplemental Table 31–32 [this file] ), revealing a correlation coefficient of 0.9 between AD and control groups and a correlation coefficient of 0.84 between AsymAD and control groups (Supplemental Fig. 7 [rid=MOESM7] C). This mapping was achieved by recalculating the kME (bicor correlation to module eigenprotein) for each protein and assigning it to the module with the highest correlation (Supplemental Table 33 [this file] ). When comparing the proteins identified in plasma with those in the brain proteome, we discovered that a substantial portion, approximately 77% (2211 out of 2685) of the plasma-identified proteins were also quantified in the brain (Fig. 7 [rid=Fig7] B and Supplemental Table 34 [this file] ). This represents a significant improvement compared to the immunodepletion approach, which only detected 5 out of 35 members (APOE4, APP, DAG1, GPNMB, and LRP1), reflecting a mere 14% of the module (Supplemental Tables 8 [this file] and 33 [this file] ).

To assess the presence of cdsRNA in neurons of patients with AD pathology, we stained formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) amygdala sections of human postmortem brains of healthy individuals ( = 9) and of patients who met the pathologic diagnosis of AD ( = 10) (Fig. 1a [rid=Fig1] ; Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). In contrast, whenever pTDP-43 inclusions were absent, our immunostainings were negative for cdsRNA as well (Supplementary Fig. 1a,b [this file] ). However, pTDP-43 and cdsRNA were spatially coincident (enriched two-fold in AD cases; Supplementary Fig. 1c [this file] ), paralleling our previous observations in ALS brains . If this cdsRNA acts as a damage-associated molecular pattern (DAMP) in neurons, then we anticipate it would trigger an IFN-I response through the activation of the PRRs RIG-I and MDA5 (Supplementary Fig. 1d [this file] ). To test whether cdsRNA is immunogenic in brains with AD pathology, we immunostained amygdala sections for phosphorylated protein kinase R (PKR), another PRR that binds to cdsRNA and activates autophosphorylation (Supplementary Fig. 2a [this file] ). We observed phosphorylated PKR (pPKR) only in cdsRNA-positive AD brains, close to 66% of it being coincident with cdsRNA (Supplementary Fig. 2b [this file] ), indicating a potential direct link between cdsRNA and the activation of PRRs. 
This experiment included nine controls brains and ten AD patients (Supplementary Fig. 1a [this file] ). CyCIF was done on a single brain section of the same healthy control as the IHC images, but of a different AD patient (also see Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). This experiment included nine controls brains (one used for multiplexed staining) and ten AD patients (two used for multiplexed staining; Supplementary Fig. 1a [this file] ). Patient information of depicted brains is available in Supplementary Table 1 [this file] . 
Through this pipeline, we previously identified baricitinib, ruxolitinib, and tofacitinib, which are FDA-approved JAK inhibitors that inhibit interferon signaling, as drug candidates for repurposing in AD (Supplementary Fig. 3a [this file] ). 
We confirmed that neuronal nuclei with loss of nuclear TDP-43 into cytoplasmic aggregates have higher reads of the CEs STMN2 short (log2 fold change (LFC) = 3.55; < 0.0001), UNC13A-CE1 (LFC = 4.20; = 0.0002) and UNC13A-CE2 (LFC = 4.05; = 0.0006) relative to control neuronal nuclei that contain TDP-43 (Supplementary Fig. 3b [this file] ). 
We reasoned that the single-end sequencing protocol to generate the MSBB RNA-sequencing data was less sensitive for CE detection, relative to the paired-end reads in the ROSMAP data (Supplementary Fig. 4a [this file] ). For this purpose, we mapped out CE expression in all 546 analyzed cases and could not identify any form of link in their occurrence (Supplementary Fig. 4b [this file] ). To determine whether predicted TDP-43 positivity was associated with later Braak stages, we used an ordinal regression model and found no significant difference in Braak staging ( = 0.27) between “positive” and “negative” cases (Supplementary Fig. 5a [this file] ), indicating that CE production was orthogonal to the stage of tau progression. 
We assessed the predicted efficacy of baricitinib, ruxolitinib, and tofacitinib in AD patients with two or more CEs (as a proxy of TDP-43 dysfunction) relative to AD patients with one or no CEs (Fig. 3e [rid=Fig3] ; further replicates in Supplementary Fig. 5b [this file] ). These findings and the observation that the expression of ISGs is significantly increased in cases that we deemed TDP-43-positive based on cryptic exon expression (Supplementary Fig. 5c [this file] ) support our hypothesis that cdsRNA associated with TDP-43 dysfunction contributes to IFN-I-mediated neuroinflammatory processes occurring in AD patients’ brains. 
These differentiated human neural cells contain markers for neurons, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes, but not microglia and are not sensitive to other common stressors such as DNA-damaging agents and reactive oxygen species (Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] ), perhaps because this cell line does not express STING . Analysis of downstream target genes associated with expression found such genes to be significantly enriched in immune-related and inflammation pathways (Additional file 2: Figure S3 [this file] ), supporting that reduced expression due to this SNP-methylation interaction could influence immune function in AD patients. 
Our findings indicate that expression could be regulated by a combination of the SNP rs55829688 and the methylation site cg13489958 (Fig. 5 [rid=Fig5] and Additional file 2: Figure S4 [this file] ). 
For example, although transcript expression of was associated with genotype at rs73058141 (Additional file 2: Figure S6 [this file] A), the regulatory effect was also impacted by methylation: that is, the SNP genotype is significantly associated with increased expression under high methylation, but not low methylation (Additional file 2: Figure S6 [this file] ).

[xref] [rid=bib49] [xref] [rid=bib50] [xref] [rid=bib51] Integration of the 18-month CRND8 TMT-MS data with these AD genetic studies shows that many established AD risk genes and prioritized GWAS loci (e.g., , , , , , , , , and ) are DEPs in CRND8 mice. 
For this integration, we chose a dataset in which AD and control CSF were compared using a highly similar proteomic pipeline for both data generation and analysis. [xref] [rid=bib58] These data show significant overlaps with other large-scale proteomic analyses of AD CSF. [xref] [rid=bib58] [xref] [rid=bib59] [xref] [rid=bib60] [xref] [rid=bib61] [xref] [rid=bib62] [xref] [rid=bib63] [xref] [rid=bib64] [xref] [rid=bib65] [xref] [rid=bib66] [xref] [rid=bib67] [xref] [rid=bib68] Of the 1,839 in the human CSF proteomes, 257 of these are significantly altered, and of these, 62 are significantly changed in the 18-month CRND8 mice brains. 39 of these changes are congruent in directionality between the mouse brain and human CSF and 23 are discordant in directionality ( Figure S11 [this file] B; Table S13 [this file4] ). 
There is ongoing debate as to how amyloid or Aβ aggregate pathology drives cellular dysfunction and degeneration in AD. [xref] [rid=bib2] [xref] [rid=bib6] [xref] [rid=bib7] More generally, this debate extends to all amyloid disorders and how amyloid accumulation causes tissue damage and organ dysfunction. [xref] [rid=bib39] [xref] [rid=bib47] [xref] [rid=bib100] Indeed, extensive efforts have been made to identify toxic species or conformers. [xref] [rid=bib101] Our current data and previous studies of proteins that co-accumulate with amyloid offer an alternative hypothesis to the concept that amyloid or amyloid-like aggregate is directly toxic. [xref] [rid=bib75] [xref] [rid=bib102] We term this the “amyloid scaffold” hypothesis ( Figure S12 [this file] ) and posit that if amyloid deposits scaffold the accumulation of numerous proteins, then perhaps the accumulation of these proteins mediates downstream pathophysiology.

The dlPFC yielded 4,871 by MS, with no postmortem brain datasets available from the affinity platforms ( Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). The organoid model again detected almost all these clinical DAPs, recovering 98.8% of plasma and 96.4% of CSF DAPs in the conditioned media and 96.1% of dlPFC DAPs in the lysate ( Supplementary Table 3 [this file] , Fig. 3a [rid=F3] ).

We confirmed that BMP(22:6/22:6) levels were significantly increased in KO mouse kidney by quantifying BMP levels from dissected renal cortex and medulla using LC-MS/MS, with higher levels of BMP observed in the renal medulla consistent with our findings using IMS (Supplementary Figure S1 [this file] A). 
In contrast, we observed a significant accumulation of multiple species of GSLs and components of the BMP pathway, including hemi-BMP, lysophosphatidylglycerol (LPG) and phosphatidylglycerol (PG), in both kidney regions examined from KO mice (Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] D and Supplementary Table S1 [this file] ). Both pharmacokinetics (unbound concentration of the MLi-2) and LRRK2 pS935 analysis demonstrated a high level (> 90%) of LRRK2 kinase inhibition (Supplementary Fig. S1 [this file] B and C). In kidney, we observed a significant reduction in BMP and GSL levels in LRRK2 G2019S mice compared to WT littermates (Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] E and Supplementary Fig. S1 [this file] D), and LRRK2 inhibition increased levels of BMP-related lipids and several classes of GSL (Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] E and Supplementary Figure S1 [this file] D, and Supplementary Table S1 [this file] ). The levels of urine BMP were significantly reduced compared to vehicle treated mice following LRRK2 kinase inhibition in both LRRK2 G2019S KI and WT mice (Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] F, Supplementary Fig. S1 [this file] E, Supplementary Table S1 [this file] ), consistent with previous findings in both preclinical and clinical studies [ 14 [rid=CR14] , 31 [rid=CR31] , 53 [rid=CR53] ]. Beyond changes in BMP, several species of GlcCer were also reduced following LRRK2 kinase inhibition in mouse urine (Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] F, Supplementary Table S1 [this file] ). 
In models adjusting for sex, age, disease status and principal components derived from the WGS data, urine levels of BMP(22:6/22:6) were significantly increased in carriers of the PD risk variant G2019S ( = 5.78E-82; Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] G and Supplementary Table S2 [this file] ), consistent with previous studies [ 32 [rid=CR32] , 54 [rid=CR54] ]. We next assessed whether the LRRK2 N551K protective variant impacted BMP levels in urine and observed a significant decrease in urine BMP(22:6/22:6) levels in carriers of the PD protective variant N551K ( = 7.33E-4; Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] G and Supplementary Table S2 [this file] ). These relationships were maintained (consistent direction of effect and < 0.05) in sensitivity analyses that removed the adjustment by disease status or additionally adjusted for GBA N370S/N409S status, N551K status (for the G2019S effect) or G2019S status (for the N551K effect) (Supplementary Table S2 [this file] ). 
Overall, we did not observe gross differences in brain BMP levels between WT and KO mice, in contrast to the effects observed in the kidney (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] A and Supplementary Fig. S2 [this file] A-C). We observed the most profound lipid changes in astrocytes from KO mice compared to other CNS cell types, with reductions in several classes of GSLs (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] B and C, Supplementary Fig S2 [this file] D and E, and Supplementary Table S2 [this file] ). 
Many GSLs accumulated in astrocytes and microglia from LRRK2 G2019S mice in both age groups assessed (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] E and H and Supplementary Table S3 [this file] ), including several species of GlcCer and GalCer (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] F and I). The changes in GSLs observed in neurons were comparatively modest (Supplementary Fig. S2 [this file] F), which may be attributable to the relatively low expression of LRRK2 reported in mouse neurons compared to glial cells [ 58 [rid=CR58] ]. 
Using LC-MS/MS, we found that the levels of several species in the BMP pathway, including BMP(22:6/22:6), were significantly elevated in LRRK2 R1441G KI cells compared to WT cells (Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] A and Supplementary Fig. S3 [this file] A). We treated LRRK2 R1441G cells with DNL151, a selective LRRK2 kinase inhibitor currently being assessed in late-stage clinical studies for the treatment of PD (Supplementary Fig. S3 [this file] B), for 72 h and demonstrated DNL151 treatment fully normalized the levels of GlcCer(d18:1/24:1), the most significantly elevated GlcCer species observed in LRRK2 R1441G cells compared to WT cells (Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] C). These data are consistent with recent clinical findings with a related LRRK2 inhibitor (DNL201) (Supplementary Fig. S3 [this file] B), which show that > 80% LRRK2 kinase inhibition is needed to reduce BMP levels in human urine and suggest that this level of inhibition may be necessary to correct lysosomal dysfunction mediated by LRRK2 hyperactivity [ 14 [rid=CR14] ]. 
The LRRK2 R1441G variant also led to a significant reduction in endolysosomal pH and cathepsin activity as assessed using a pan-cathepsin activity-based probe (Supplementary Fig. S3 [this file] C and D), consistent with previous work suggesting LRRK2 pathogenic variants can lead to hyperacidification of the endolysosomal compartment [ 27 [rid=CR27] ]. Assessment of endolysosomal cathepsin B and D activity using additional live-cell probes did not show any effect of the LRRK2 R1441G variant on cathepsin B or D activity, suggesting the activity of a different cathepsin may be impacted by LRRK2 hyperactivity (Supplementary Fig. S3 [this file] E and F). 
Similar to our observations from whole cell extracts, lysosomes isolated from LRRK2 R1441G cells showed broad elevations in GlcCer species compared to lysosomes from WT cells (Fig. 4 [rid=Fig4] A and B, Supplementary Fig. S4 [this file] A and B). DNL151 treatment reduced levels of BMP and all GlcCer species examined, including GlcCer(d18:1/24:1), in lysosomes isolated from LRRK2 R1441G cells to WT levels, demonstrating that LRRK2 kinase inhibition can rescue lysosomal lipid accumulation (Fig. 4 [rid=Fig4] B and C and Supplementary Fig. S4 [this file] A-C). 
GCase protein levels were not changed in lysosomes isolated from LRRK2 R1441G cells and were significantly elevated in lysosomes isolated from KO A549 cells (Supplementary Fig. S4 [this file] D). 
We showed that LRRK2 G2019S KI iMicroglia had an approximately two-fold increase in LRRK2 kinase activity, as assessed by levels of phosphorylated Rab10 per molecule of LRRK2 (Fig. 5 [rid=Fig5] A and Supplementary Fig. S5 [this file] A-C). Unlike in our A549 cell studies, we did not observe alterations in GlcCer(d18:1/24:1) with expression of a pathogenic LRRK2 variant in iMicroglia (Supplementary Fig. S5 [this file] D) which may reflect that these cells have greater levels of acid ceramidase (ASAH1) activity, an enzyme that converts GlcCer to GlcSph. 
Imiglucerase treatment attenuated GlcCer accumulation in isolated lysosomes from LRRK2 R1441G cells (Fig. 6 [rid=Fig6] B and Supplementary Fig. S6 [this file] A). Interestingly, imiglucerase treatment also significantly reduced BMP(20:4/20:4) levels in lysosomes isolated from one clone of LRRK2 R1441G cells (Fig. 6 [rid=Fig6] C and Supplementary Fig. S6 [this file] B), suggesting that BMP accumulation is a secondary consequence of reduced GCase activity. 
We confirmed that knockdown of GBA1 significantly reduced LysoFQ-GBA signal in these cells as expected and validated previous data suggesting that Rab10 can regulate GCase activity (Fig. 6 [rid=Fig6] G and Supplementary Fig. S6 [this file] C) [ 63 [rid=CR63] ]. We also assessed the impact of additional Rabs that have not been shown to be direct LRRK2 substrates but have been recently implicated in PD risk, Rab21 and Rab32 [ 66 [rid=CR66] – 68 [rid=CR68] ], and found that knockdown of both of these Rabs also significantly impaired endolysosomal GCase activity (Supplementary Fig. S6 [this file] D and E). 
To gain insight into the potential relevance of these LRRK2-dependent lipid changes in the CNS of PD subjects, we measured the levels of various GSLs and BMP in CSF from healthy control and PD subjects with or without variants using samples collected from the LRRK2 Cohort Consortium (Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ) [ 49 [rid=CR49] ]. BMP and GSL levels were comparable in healthy subjects that carry a variant compared to non-variant carrier controls (Supplementary Fig. S7 [this file] A). Within the GSL lipid class, GlcCer(d18:1/24:1) increased by 15% (unadjusted = 0.07), and lactosylceramide (LacCer) (d18:1/24:1) decreased by 53%, (unadjusted = 0.07) in variant PD subjects compared to PD patients that do not carry a variant in (Fig. 7 [rid=Fig7] A and B, Supplementary Fig. S7 [this file] B). 
Exploratory analyses of CSF samples revealed a trend toward reduced levels of GalCer and GlcCer in LRRK2-PD patients following DNL201 treatment, while BMP levels did not show a significant treatment response in CSF (Fig. 7 [rid=Fig7] E and Supplementary Fig. S7 [this file] C).

We generated a multi-regional single-nucleus transcriptomic atlas of PD using postmortem brain tissue from 97 donors enrolled in the Accelerating Medicines Partnership for Parkinson’s Disease (AMP-PD) consortium ( Fig. 1a [rid=F1] , Supplementary Fig. 1a [this file] – b [this file] , ), including preclinical, clinically defined PD and control cases, capturing a broad spectrum of Lewy body (LB) pathology, as measured by Braak LB staging (range 0–6). The cohort spans late adulthood (ages 57–102 years) and includes a balanced distribution of male and female donors, and diverse ancestry groups ( Extended Data Fig. 1a [rid=F8] – b [rid=F8] , Supplementary Fig. 1a [this file] – c [this file] ). 
Taxonomy annotations were aligned and validated against previously published datasets from the PsychAD cohort and the Alzheimer’s disease (AD) dataset from Mathys et al. (2023) ( Extended Data Fig. 1Ff [rid=F8] – g [rid=F8] , Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] , ), and demonstrated robust expression of canonical marker genes ( Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] ). 
Region-specific mapping across the class, subclass, and subtype levels of the taxonomy revealed substantial neuronal heterogeneity across brain regions ( Fig. 1d [rid=F1] – e [rid=F1] , Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] ). 
The effect of biological and technical covariates that contribute to gene expression variability is estimated based on variance partition analysis ( Supplementary Fig. 5a [this file] – c [this file] ). Of these, 7,219 DEGs (64% of unique DEGs) were dysregulated across multiple cell types, while 4,057 DEGs (36% out unique DEGs) were cell-type specific ( Supplementary Fig. 5d [this file] – e [this file] ), reflecting both shared and cell-type–specific transcriptional alterations in PD. 
We observed strong concordance between differential expression results from PD vs. Control and Braak LB staging analyses ( Supplementary Fig. 6a [this file] ), indicating consistent disease-associated transcriptional signatures across comparisons; for subsequent analyses, we focused on PD vs. Control results, which exhibited greater log FC magnitudes and clearer case-control contrasts. The distribution of DEGs across cell types revealed a relatively even balance between up- and down-regulated genes ( Supplementary Fig. 6b [this file] ). While cluster size may contribute to DEG counts to some extent, the observed transcriptional responses likely reflect cell-type-specific vulnerabilities in PD ( Supplementary Fig. 6c [this file] ). 
For each gene, we assigned a putative cell type based on the highest absolute t-statistic across taxonomy classes, a strategy supported by strong concordance between DE comparisons (Spearman ρ = 0.91, p < 0.05 for PD vs. control and Braak LB staging comparisons; Supplementary Fig. 7a [this file] ). 
Functional grouping revealed enrichment in biological categories highly relevant to PD pathophysiology, including vesicle trafficking, RNA processing, synaptic signaling, mitochondrial dynamics, and immune-related pathways ( Supplementary Fig. 7b [this file] – c [this file] ). 
Several TFs demonstrated strong cell-type-specific enrichment and formed interconnected TF-TF protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks ( Supplementary Fig. 8a [this file] ). We incorporated 3,293 individuals from 8 different datasets ( Table 1 [rid=T1] , Supplementary Figure 1 [this file] ). 
Balancing data fit and generalizability, our model selection procedure identified 4 amyloid factors and 7 tau factors after manual removal of white matter and reference tissue components ( Supplementary Figure 2 [this file] , Supplementary Figure 3 [this file] ). 
The largest discrepancies arose when validation factors reflected combinations of training factors ( Supplementary Figure 4 [this file] ). PAC-Frontal and PAC-Parietal appeared as a single validation factor, capturing areas typically used for amyloid quantification ( 23 [rid=R23] ) ( Supplementary Figure 5 [this file] ). Factors were also largely reproducible in fixed-tracer subsets of the validation data, with differences again due to hierarchical merging of factors ( Supplementary Figure 6 [this file] , Supplementary Figure 7 [this file] ). 
The positivity-defined ordering of PACs and PTCs in the validation data was consistent with that of the training set, indicating a similar estimated temporal ordering of regions (Friedman test, χ =22, df=2, p<0.001; Supplementary Figure 8A [this file] & B [this file] ). The derived staging model also indicated a similar pathological cascade, though the number of stages and specific grouping of PACs and PTCs differed ( Supplementary Figure 8C [this file] ). Despite these differences, individual stage assignments were consistent across models (ARI=0.60; Supplementary Figure 8G [this file] ). Results were similarly consistent when models were derived from fixed-tracer subsets of the validation data ( Supplementary Figure 8D [this file] – G [this file] , ARI>0.57). 
We used longitudinal imaging data to test whether staging assignments progressed in accordance with the inferred pathological cascade ( Supplementary Figure 9 [this file] ). 
Correspondingly, CDR Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB) scores worsened with increasing disease stage (one-way ANOVA, F(7, 1236)=50.98, p<0.001; Figure 5B [rid=F5] , Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). Similarly, Mini Mental State Examination MMSE scores worsened with increasing stages (one-way ANOVA, F(7, 1343)=174.97, p<0.001; Figure 5C [rid=F5] , Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ) with significant decline first observable at A2T0 (Tukey test, p<0.001). Similar patterns were observed in validation data ( Figure 5D [rid=F5] – F [rid=F5] , Supplementary Table 4 [this file] , Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ). 
In the training dataset, baseline stages were associated with longitudinal CDR-SB trajectories (F=31.9, p<0.001; Figure 5G [rid=F5] , Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). MMSE decline also varied across stages (F=22.8, p<0.001; Supplementary Figure 10A [this file] , Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ). CDR-SB trajectories differed by stage (F=45.5, p<0.001; Figure 5I [rid=F5] , Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ), with significant differences first emerging at A2T0 (t-ratio=−5.225, df=619.4, p<0.001). MMSE trajectories similarly varied by stage (F=23.6, p<0.001; Supplementary Figure 10B [this file] , Supplementary Table 9 [this file] ), with accelerated decline first observable at A2T2 (t-ratio=4.5, df=495.7, p<0.001). 
NS presentations were subdivided into the following subgroups: individuals without amyloid but with tau (A0T+), individuals with first stage amyloid and tau (A1T+), and individuals with both amyloid stages and late-stage tau without medial temporal involvement (MTL-) ( Supplementary Figure 11 [this file] ). 
We ran additional models to compare stageable and NS individuals ( Supplementary Table 12 [this file] ). Similar results were observed in validation data ( Supplementary Table 13 [this file] ). 
Leveraging the AA2024 framework ( 1 [rid=R1] ), we categorized individuals as expected, vulnerable (worse clinical stage than biologically predicted), and resilient (better clinical stage than biologically predicted; Figure 6C [rid=F6] , Supplementary Table 14 [this file] ). Replication in validation-ADS ( Figure 6 [rid=F6] , Supplementary Table 15 [this file] ), confirmed that vulnerable individuals were older (difference=4.3 years, p<0.01) and had lower education (difference=1.1 years, p<0.001). 
Details on PET image acquisition from each dataset are provided in the Supplementary Material [this file] . All PET images (amyloid and tau) were preprocessed with a volumetric pipeline to generate SUVR images in a common space (see Supplementary Material [this file] ). Measures of global amyloid and tau burden were derived from volume-weighted averages of meta-ROIs using regions suggested by the ADNI Imaging Core (listed in Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). 
If available (91.2% of included individuals), we selected the assessment of amyloid-positivity provided by the dataset (see Supplementary Material [this file] ). 
For purposes of clinical staging (described below), we computed a modified version of the Preclinical Alzheimer Cognitive Composite (PACC) ( 40 [rid=R40] ) for subjects with available neuropsychological assessments (see Supplementary Material [this file] ). 
A detailed description of NMF formulation is provided in Supplementary Methods [this file] . 
Further details on W-score computation are provided in the Supplementary Material [this file] . Further details about this method are described in the Supplementary Material [this file] . 
The longitudinal stability of stage assignment was evaluated with a permutation test (see Supplementary Material [this file] ).

The associations between age and the sleep parameters stratified by sex are shown in Figure 2 [rid=F2] , and the detailed model outcomes of the results are listed in Supplementary Table S4 [this file] . We found a significant linear effect of age on TST only in women ( Supplementary Table S4 [this file] ). 
The cross-sectional associations between age and sleep parameters stratified by race are shown in Figure 3 [rid=F3] , and the detailed model outcomes are listed in Supplementary Table S5 [this file] . A significant linear association of age with TST was observed in White but not minoritized participants ( Supplementary Table S5 [this file] ). 
As shown in Supplementary Figure S1 and Table S6 [this file] , there were no meaningful differences in the findings from the main analyses, in terms of statistical significance. We only found that the nonlinear effect of age on TST was changed from nonsignificant to significant ( Supplementary Figure S2 and Table S7 [this file] ). As shown in Supplementary Table S8 [this file] , adjusting for either self-reported physical activity, years of education, or number of hours worked per week did not substantially alter the age-TST association in terms of effect sizes and statistical significance. In participants who did not work for pay, we found that older age was still associated with longer TST from age 40 through the 70s ( Supplementary Figure S3A [this file] ), although the effect was smaller compared to the main results. On the other hand, in participants who did work for pay, we found a steeper increasing trend in TST from age 40 to the 60s ( Supplementary Figure S3B [this file] ). 
In addition, working status may have played a role, supported by our findings that there was a flatter increasing trend in TST from ages 40 to 70s, among participants who did not work for pay, compared to the results observed in all participants or participants who worked for pay ( Supplementary Figure S3A [this file] ).

context_description:
Physical activity history was ascertained by questionnaire: participants were asked to categorize their activity level in each decade from adolescence, age 10–19 years old, through their current age as minimal (mostly sitting some walking), light (low intensity exercise 2–4 h/week), moderate (low intensity exercise ≥5 h/week or medium intensity exercise ≥3 h/week) or intense (medium to high intensity exercise ≥5 h/week) (Appendix S1 [this file] ). 
Levels of activity reported on the physical activity history questionnaire were associated with both questionnaire‐based and accelerometer‐based current physical activity assessed at the index visit (Figure 2 [rid=acel14078-fig-0002] ; Table S1 [this file] ). Reported moderate or intense activity level in a decade was positively associated with all concurrently ascertained activity measures (Table S2 [this file] ). For example, the model estimating accelerometer based active min/day suggests that participants who reported moderate activity had approximately half an hour more active time than participants reporting minimal activity ((se) = 33.4 (14.8)) However, a significant interaction between activity level and the time between assessments suggests that the reliability of recalled activity levels was attenuated over time, e.g., the estimated difference in concurrently measured active time for participants reporting minimal and moderate activity is approximately nine minutes smaller with each year prior to the index visit ((se) = −9.3 (4.7)) (Table S2 [this file] ). 
In linear regression models, LCPA appears consistent with the trajectory of physical activity over time: while LCPA was not associated with individual time slope estimates for total kcal, it was positively associated with individual time slope estimates for minutes of high intensity exercise per week, total activity count per day and active minutes per day: ‐value <0.01 for all three analyses (Figure S1 [this file] ; Table S3 [this file] ). To evaluate whether LCPA and physical activity trajectory had similar relationships to selected clinical characteristics, coefficients from separate multivariable linear regression models for measures of clinical characteristics, body composition and physical performance (assessed at the index visit) were qualitatively compared: coefficients for LCPA were mostly similar in magnitude and direction to the effect estimates for physical activity trajectory as estimated by individual slopes (Figure 3 [rid=acel14078-fig-0003] ; Table S4 [this file] ). For example, when standardized usual gait speed was the dependent variable the coefficient for standardized LCPA was 0.17 ( < 0.001) while in the comparable model the coefficient for standardized total kcal was 0.04 ( = 0.331) (Table S4 [this file] ). 
Higher LCPA was consistent with higher HDL, hemoglobin, peak VO , FEV1/FVC, thigh muscle area, thigh muscle intensity, usual gait speed and Health ABC PPB, while triglycerides, RDW, fasting glucose, fasting insulin, abdominal subcutaneous fat, visceral fat, and multimorbidity were all lower (Figure 4 [rid=acel14078-fig-0004] ; Table S5 [this file] ). Among participants a standard deviation higher LCPA was associated with an estimated difference of 1.95 cm ( = 0.005) in thigh muscle area and 0.03 m/s ( < 0.001) difference in gait speed (Table S5 [this file] ). In these models, minutes of high intensity exercise at the index visit was associated with HDL, peak VO , measures of body composition except thigh muscle area and usual gait speed (Table S5 [this file] ). Results were similar when models were adjusted for total kcal, minutes of high intensity exercise, total activity count, or active minutes (Table S5 [this file] ).

In comparison with the global longitudinal phenotypic score, associations of epigenetic clocks with changes in physical and cognitive functions were much weaker, indicating that these epigenetic age clocks may provide some information on the biological age of an individual but are poor metrics of longitudinal rates of aging in a relatively healthy population (Supplementary Fig. 10 [this file] ). 
Concordant with this hypothesis, we found that the domain-specific scores using longitudinal phenotypes were robustly and significantly associated with various measures of physical and cognitive function (Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] ). The associations between global longitudinal phenotypic score and changes in physical and cognitive functions remained strong across different age groups (Supplementary Figs. 8 [this file] and 9 [this file] ).

Adjusting for sex, baseline age, height, weight, interactions between sex and time, and baseline age and time, a global longitudinal phenotypic score (that is, decelerated decline in aging phenotypes) one point lower was associated with (1) slower (0.0032 m s ) annual decline in gait speed (95% confidence interval (CI): 0.0004, 0.0059), (2) 2.57 s less annual increase in time to finish a 400-m walk (95% CI: 1.51, 3.64) and (3) 0.0177 less annual decline in HABC SPPB score (95% CI: 0.0113, 0.0240) (Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). In our study population, gait speed declined at an average annual rate of 0.014 m s , and 1 year older in chronological age was associated with faster decline in gait speed with an annual increment of 0.0008 m s (Supplementary Tables 3 [this file] and 4 [this file] ). 
Adjusting for baseline age, sex, race, years of education and interactions between sex and time, and baseline age and time, one point higher in global longitudinal phenotypic score (that is, accelerated decline in aging phenotypes) was associated with 0.236 faster annual decline in DSST score (95% CI: 0.138, 0.334) and with significantly faster annual decline in executive function, attention, memory, language and visuospatial ability (Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). In our study population, DSST declined at an average annual rate of 1.159, while 1 year older in chronological age was associated with faster decline in DSST, with an annual increment of 0.021 (Supplementary Tables 3 [this file] and 4 [this file] ). 
Adjusting for baseline age, sex and interactions between sex and time, and baseline age and time, one point lower in global longitudinal phenotypic score (that is, decelerated decline in aging phenotypes) was independently associated with 0.025 fewer morbidities accumulated per year (95% CI: 0.004, 0.046) (Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). In our study population, the multimorbidity index increased at an average annual rate of 0.199, and 1 year older in chronological age was associated with faster increase in multimorbidity index, with an annual increment of 0.008 (Supplementary Tables 3 [this file] and 4 [this file] ). Adjusting for age, sex and education, among those surviving to at least 60 years, one point ‘higher’ in global longitudinal phenotypic score was associated with 12% shorter survival time (adjusted time ratio: 0.88, 95% CI: 0.81, 0.96) (Supplementary Fig. 7 [rid=MOESM1] and Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ). 
When we ranked the importance of domain-specific longitudinal phenotypic scores based on their ability to explain the variability in changes of functions (Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ), some results were unexpected (for example, the body composition domain being ranked higher than the neuroplasticity/neurodegeneration domain for changes in attention), indicating that relationships between phenotypic and functional aging constructs are not always obvious.

To understand the relationships between CSF and plasma protein levels, we used the SomaScan platform to perform proteomics on paired CSF and plasma samples from 2,171 people, including 931 healthy controls and 1,240 participants with neurodegenerative disease and cognitive impairment (Extended Data Fig. 1 [rid=Fig6] and Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). Some 2,304 proteins were robustly detected in both CSF and plasma ( Methods [rid=Sec8] ) and were included in analyses for the present study (Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). 
Pearson’s correlations were performed in the Stanford cohort ( = 304) and replicated in the Knight-ADRC and GNPC cohorts (Extended Data Fig. 2a,b [rid=Fig7] and Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). 
Only participants who were cognitively unimpaired and free from neurodegenerative disease diagnoses were included in aging analyses (Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ). Discovery analysis was performed in the Knight-ADRC ( = 180) and Stanford ( = 200) cohorts and cohort-level results were combined through meta-analysis using fixed-effect models (Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ). 
Next, we examined how CSF to plasma ratios differ between men and women in healthy control (HC) participants, with age as a covariate (Fig. 3a [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). 
To understand how relationships between CSF and plasma protein levels change with cognitive impairment, we used linear modeling to examine the associations between CSF to plasma ratios and the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) score in 1,280 individuals from the GNPC (Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ), controlling for age and sex. We identified 160 proteins with ratios that were significantly associated with MMSE scores, including 35 peripherally derived proteins (Fig. 4a [rid=Fig4] , Extended Data Fig. 7a [rid=Fig12] and Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ). 
Using genetic data from 208 individuals in the Stanford cohort and 243 individuals in the Knight-ADRC cohort (Supplementary Table 9 [this file] ), we performed GWASs to identify variants linked to each of 2,304 protein ratios. We identified 320 quantitative trait loci (QTLs) associated with CSF to plasma ratios of 241 proteins, using a stringent genome-wide and multiple comparison-corrected significance threshold of < 2.17 × 10 (Fig. 5b [rid=Fig5] and Supplementary Table 10 [this file] ). 
Of the 127 ratio QTLs, 56 included a protein-coding or splice-site mutation (Fig. 5f [rid=Fig5] and Supplementary Table 11 [this file] ), suggesting a particular residue or region that may be important for protein uptake across the blood–CSF barrier.

Grey matter volumes were calculated as the bilateral average for 13 regions segmented in native MRI space (prefrontal cortex, insula, cingulate gyrus, fusiform, lingual gyrus, entorhinal cortex, middle inferior temporal gyrus, superior temporal gyrus, inferior parietal cortex, superior parietal cortex, amygdala, hippocampus and striatum [see Supplementary Materials [this file] for region of interest or ROI definitions]). 
Given that every individual has microglia, TSPO positivity across a composite brain region was simplistically defined as above the mean in amyloid-negative cognitively unimpaired adults by binding affinity groups ( Supplementary Materials [this file] ; Supplementary Fig. S1 [this file] ). 
By definition, individuals with ADRD had lower MMSE and cognitive domain scores, with the greatest impairment in visuospatial ability, followed by delayed episodic memory, immediate episodic memory, attention, executive function and language ( Supplementary Table S1 [this file] ). Out of 25 individuals with ADRD, 44% were amyloid-positive, tau-positive and TSPO-positive; 4% were amyloid-positive, tau-positive and TSPO-negative; 8% were amyloid-negative, tau-positive and TSPO-positive and 20% were amyloid-negative, tau-negative and TSPO-positive (for biomarker positivity profile by ADRD diagnosis, see Supplementary Fig. S1 [this file] ). 
Early tau mediated the association between composite TSPO and intermediate tau (0.47 [0.24, 0.71], < 0.001), while intermediate tau mediated the association between composite TSPO and late tau (0.59 [0.36, 0.83], < 0.001; Supplementary Table S2 [this file] ). 
In sensitivity analyses, we assessed the role of TSPO in the context of amyloid-positive ADRD and amyloid-negative ADRD separately ( Supplementary Table S1 [this file] ). 
When accounting for specific pathways, TSPO mediated amyloid-associated tau in the superior (0.25 [0.07, 0.43], = 0.05) and inferior (0.24 [0.06, 0.42], = 0.05) parietal cortex as well as tau spreading across progressive Braak regions (early to middle: 0.12 [0.02, 0.21], = 0.03; middle to late: 0.09 [0, 0.18], = 0.05) in amyloid-positive ADRD ( Table 6 [rid=fcag242-T6] ; Supplementary Table S3 [this file] ). Testing the alternative pathways, earlier-stage tau mediated associations between TSPO and later-stage tau (middle to late: 0.62 [0.39, 0.84], < 0.001; early to middle: 0.51 [0.28, 0.74], < 0.001; Supplementary Table S4 [this file] ). 
After transformation, elevated TSPO was now colocalized with elevated tau in 11 regions total and with elevated neurodegeneration in 5 regions total in all participants ( Supplementary Table S5 [this file] ). In amyloid-positive ADRD, elevated TSPO was colocalized with elevated neurodegeneration in seven regions total, while in amyloid-negative ADRD, elevated TSPO was colocalized with elevated neurodegeneration in seven regions total and elevated tau in five regions total ( Supplementary Table S5 [this file] ). TSPO-tau associations in the superior parietal cortex and TSPO-neurodegeneration association in the entorhinal cortex and middle inferior temporal cortex did not remain significant after transformation in all participants ( Supplementary Table S6 [this file] ). TSPO-tau associations in the entorhinal cortex and middle inferior temporal gyrus did not remain significant in amyloid-positive ADRD ( Supplementary Table S6 [this file] ). All mediation results were unchanged after transformation ( Supplementary Tables S7 [this file] and S8). 
After assessing TSPO associations with amyloid, tau or neurodegeneration in separate, univariate models ( Supplementary Table S9 [this file] ), greater TSPO was additionally associated with greater tau in the hippocampus, amygdala, entorhinal cortex, middle inferior temporal cortex, fusiform gyrus and prefrontal cortex, as well as greater neurodegeneration in the lingual gyrus, insula, superior temporal gyrus, superior parietal cortex, inferior parietal cortex and prefrontal cortex in all participants. 
After investigating regions across the brain ( Supplementary Fig. S2 [this file] ), similar patterns of elevated TSPO, tau and amyloid were observed with additional involvement of occipital cortex, sensorimotor cortex and medial structures; however, using individual subregions for neurodegeneration attenuated the difference in prefrontal, temporal and limbic regions, but greater neurodegeneration persisted in parietal regions.

To test the predictions of the rhythmic architecture hypothesis, we developed a phase-based tool to measure rhythmicity over the frequency spectrum (Figs. 1 [rid=Fig1] and S1 [this file] , and online methods). The canonical bands are typically identified by measuring spectral power at different frequencies (Fig. S2A-C [this file] ). 
As a measure of phase-consistency, it is influenced by the rate of phase-shift occurrence (Fig. S1 [this file] ). Leveraging this property, we define the median across frequencies as baseline rhythmicity and the surrogate range as the noise ribbon (see Methods and Supplementary Text [this file] ; Fig. S6 [this file] ). 
Importantly, within the universal framework, individual subjects showed considerable variability, with some frequencies classified as high- or low-rhythmicity depending on the subject (Figs. 2D–E [rid=Fig2] and S2G [this file] ). 
Dotted lines mark troughs; arrows indicate phase shifts, likely due to neighbouring high-rhythmicity bands (see Fig. S5 [this file] for control analyses). See Supplementary Table 1 [this file] for ANOVA including pink-noise simulations. 
At the population level ( = 37 subjects; see also Fig. S3 [this file] for analysis across six EEG datasets (total of 178 subjects), bursts in high-rhythmicity bands lasted significantly longer (3.5 vs. 2.9 cycles), a pattern amplified when using Within-Trial Phase-Lock (WTPL ), a time-resolved measure of phase-consistency (5.3 vs. 3.6 cycles; Fig. 3B-C [rid=Fig3] . See Supplementary Table S1 [this file] for full statistical details). Moreover, although instantaneous frequencies can drift within bursts (Fig. S4 [this file] ), in both modes over 80% of peak frequencies during bursts were confined within the LAVI-defined frequency band (Fig. 3G [rid=Fig3] ). 
Bursts shorter than 3.81 cycles yielded rhythmicity below chance levels, while bursts longer than 5.45 cycles exceeded it (Figs. 3H–I [rid=Fig3] and S4 [this file] ), resembling WTPL-based burst durations and supporting a distinction between transient and sustained rhythmicity. 
To assess the statistical significance of these bands efficiently, and based on characterization of the parameters affecting the noise ribbon (Fig. S6 [this file] ), we first generated 200 random-phase surrogate datasets to construct a reference table of null distributions, matched to a range of 1/ power profiles and acquisition parameters. 
See Supplementary Table 1 [this file] for full statistical details. 
We observed age-related reductions in rhythmicity magnitude and frequency not only in alpha but also in other sustained (delta, theta, and beta2) and transient bands (theta/alpha and beta1; Pearson correlation per participant and ANOVA per age decade group, Fig. 6A-B [rid=Fig6] and Table S1 [this file] ). 
We observed that high-rhythmicity bands can attenuate rhythmicity in adjacent frequency ranges via phase interference at the level of the measured signal (Fig. 3A [rid=Fig3] ; see Fig. S5 [this file] ). 
For low frequencies, LAVI’s noise levels are influenced by session duration (Fig. S6 [this file] ); thus, for frequencies below 3 Hz, we recommend using recordings of at least several minutes.

The median of the rhythmicity profiles of noise also depends of and τ, and their dispersion range depends on the sampling frequency, session duration, and the aperiodic slope (for further discussion, see Supplementary Text [this file] , parametrical effects on rhythmicity, and Fig. S6 [this file] ).

For all simulations presented in Figs. 3 [rid=Fig3] , S1 [this file] , S4 [this file] , and S5 [this file] , we generated 180 s “pink” surrogate data using IAAFT, with aperiodic exponent of -1, range of ~100 μV, mean 0 μV and SD ~ 12.5 μV. 
To simulate bursts with varying degrees of frequency drift (Fig. S4A–B [this file] ), we defined each burst as a sinusoid of the form y = sin(2π ), where the instantaneous frequency linearly drifted from 15+drift/2 to 15-drift/2 Hz. 
In the transient input simulations (Fig. S4C-F [this file] ), the initial conditions were identical to the oscillatory burst duration simulation. In the rhythmic condition (Fig. S4C-D [this file] ), the distance between each impulse in a “burst” was set to 66.6 ms (one cycle of a 15 Hz oscillation). In the arrhythmic condition (Fig. S4E-F [this file] ), the last impulse in a “burst” was set to 66.6*( -1) ms after the first pulse, with the number of impulses in a “burst”. 
To implement phase shifts (Fig. S1 [this file] ), we flipped the sign of the signal by multiplying it by −1 every 2 to 20 cycles (in logarithmic steps). To investigate the effect of power on rhythmicity (Fig. S5A-B [this file] ), we multiplied the data filtered at 15 Hz by values ranging between 0.1 and 2, in steps of 0.1. 
As can be observed in Figs. 3I [rid=Fig3] , S1B [this file] , and S5B [this file] , increasing (decreasing) the rhythmicity in one band decreases (increases) rhythmicity in neighbouring bands. We used the coefficients of the regression to calculate the expected beta1 troughs based on data alpha peaks, and compared them to beta1 troughs observed in data (Fig. S5C-D [this file] ). Finally, we compared the LAVI values at theta/ alpha and beta1 troughs of the data to the troughs of surrogates generated with aperiodic components and power in alpha matching the observed data, using filter arrays (Fig. S5E [this file] ). 
Complete details of all statistical tests are presented in Table S1 [this file] .
