We first examined the association of each presurgical clinical variable with response by applying ordinary least squares regression (Fig. 1d [rid=Fig1] ; Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] ). No clinical features were significantly associated with VNS outcome after false discovery rate correction (Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). This was corroborated by principal component analysis which revealed low explained variance (<12% for PC1) and no systematic response associated differences (Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] , Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). 
However, conventional approaches to dimensionality reduction, such as region-based parcellation, are insufficient to model the relationship between structural alterations and response following VNS (Supplementary Tables 3 [this file] - 4 [this file] ). 
The VQ-VAE’s reconstructions preserved anatomical details and captured biologically meaningful variation (Fig. 3a [rid=Fig3] , Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] ). The VQ-VAE demonstrated strong performance (Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ), with a mean (SD) MS-SSIM of 0.97 (0.01), FID of 1.5 × 10 (1.2 × 10 ), and an MSE of 3.7 × 10 (8.6 × 10 ). The VQ-VAE reconstructions demonstrated high correlation with true volumes across all four classes, with Pearson correlation coefficients ranging from 0.96 to 1.00 (Fig. 3b [rid=Fig3] ); furthermore, the reconstructions exhibited strong spatial overlap, yielding mean Dice-Sørensen coefficients ranging from 0.78 to 0.91 (Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). Reconstruction fidelity was lower in subjects with significant structural abnormalities (Fig. 3a [rid=Fig3] ; Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] ) with a mean (SD) SSIM of 0.95 (0.01), FID of 4.1 × 10 (9.8 × 10 ), and MSE of 4.7 × 10 (9.2 × 10 ), consistent with the VQ-VAE being trained primarily on anatomically typical brains. 
We encoded each subject’s image from the training subset of children who underwent VNS in the CONNECTiVOS cohort (199 of 263 images, Supplementary Fig. 5 [this file] ), computed the median latent representations separately for responders and non-responders, quantized these representations, and decoded them to generate synthetic archetypal brains (Fig. 3c [rid=Fig3] ). 
We then applied two-sided t-test-based feature selection on the training data ( = 199) to retain 27 of the 32 latent features (Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ), which were used to train several classifiers for comparison. The SVM demonstrated the strongest predictive performance (Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] ). 
The resulting model achieved an AUC of 0.73 in predicting response to VNS (permutation = 0.007; Fig. 3f [rid=Fig3] ; Supplementary Fig. 7 [this file] ; Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ). The VQ-VNS model maintained its predictive capacity across diverse age groups and treatment centres (Supplementary Fig. 7C [this file] ). Model performance remained robust with the inclusion of subjects with ambiguous outcomes binarized at the 50% seizure reduction threshold ( = 53; AUC = 0.67, permutation = 0.02; Supplementary Fig. 8 [this file] ). To evaluate the classifier’s ability to generalize across acquisition sites, we performed site hold-out validation, in which all images from one site were excluded during training and used exclusively for testing (Supplementary Table 9 [this file] ). 
We first demonstrated that cortical thickness measurements did not contain site-specific batch effects (Supplementary Fig. 9 [this file] ) and that group-level spatial patterns of atrophy alone did not clearly distinguish responders from non-responders (Supplementary Fig. 10 [this file] ). Regional brain atrophy maps converged upon large-scale structural (Fig. 4d [rid=Fig4] , Supplementary Fig. 11 [this file] ) and functional (Fig. 4e [rid=Fig4] ) networks that were preferentially disrupted in non-responders to VNS. The VQ-VNS model’s saliency map showed significant spatial concordance (Supplementary Fig. 12a [this file] ) with these structural ( < 0.001, Supplementary Fig. 12b [this file] ) and functional ( = 0.04, Supplementary Fig. 12c [this file] ) networks following spin permutation tests. 
Rather, a pattern of brain atrophy characterized by the VQ-VNS salience map predicts response across development (Supplementary Fig. 7c [this file] ). 
This may limit generalizability to grossly abnormal brains, which represented <10% of our datasets (45 out of 489 images screened, Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] ). This does not discount the established mechanistic role of the LC-NE pathway ; which may be underrepresented within our latent space due to its highly focal concentration within the brainstem (Supplementary Fig. 13 [this file] ). 
Counts of missing values for each clinical variable are presented in Supplementary Table 10 [this file] . 
During training, we employed a composite loss function incorporating voxel-wise accuracy, spectral alignment, perceptual similarity, encoder-quantizer alignment (commitment), and adversarial objectives (Summarized in Supplementary Table 11 [this file] ) . 
Subjects with significant anomalies, prior neurosurgical intervention (Supplementary Fig. 4a–d [this file] ), or conflicting outcome assessments, were excluded. After filtering, the final dataset comprised 263 subjects (Supplementary Fig. 5 [this file] ). The 263 patients included in model training did not differ significantly from the excluded cohort in terms of demographic or clinical characteristics (Supplementary Table 12 [this file] ). 
Latent features were evaluated via two-sided t-tests, and only those showing significant group-level differences ( < 0.05) were retained (27 of 32, Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ). 
Embeddings were visualized by site (Supplementary Fig. 9a [this file] ), outcome, and age (Supplementary Fig. 9b, c [this file] ). Age showed the strongest correlation with t-SNE component 1 (Supplementary Fig. 9d [this file] ). 
Subjects were excluded if the atrophic vertex count exceeded 5% (Supplementary Fig. 10a [this file] ) of the total brain surface ( = 5) to minimize the confounding effects of global atrophy. 
To test whether the spatial concordance was statistically significant, we leveraged the aforementioned latent-space spin permutation procedure, adapted from methods for rotating cortical surface maps to maintain spatial autocorrelation (Supplementary Fig. 12a [this file] ).

Following a stepwise conditional analysis, we identified 25 independent secondary signals in 16 loci ( Figure 1 [rid=F1] , Supplementary Table 3 [this file] , Supplementary Figures 3 [rid=SD2] – 55 [rid=SD2] ). Of note, in addition to the 91 Tier 1 loci, we detected 5 loci where the significance dropped after conditional analyses (P > 1×10 ) within or across loci, suggesting a slight inflation of the unconditional analysis ( Figure 1 [rid=F1] , Supplementary Tables 2 [this file] , 3 [this file] and 4 [this file] ). Finally, four loci identified in the two previous largest ADRD GWAS meta-analyses on European ancestry samples were not genome-wide significant in the EADB-IGAP-PGC meta-analysis: , , and ( Supplementary Table 5 [this file] , Supplementary Figure 56 [rid=SD2] ). 
Overall, the genetic correlation among the three AD phenotypes thus defined was above 0.97 ( Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). Among the 91 Tier 1 loci, 75 (82.4%) were genome-wide significant in the no-proxy meta-analysis, and 56 (61.5%) in the no-biobank meta-analysis focusing on clinically diagnosed AD cases ( Figure 1 [rid=F1] , Supplementary Tables 2 [this file] and 7 [this file] ). We additionally checked for putative signals only detected in the sensitivity meta-analyses: nine loci were only identified in the no-proxy meta-analysis, while four loci were only identified in the no-biobank meta-analysis ( Figure 1 [rid=F1] , Supplementary Tables 2 [this file] and 7 [this file] , Supplementary Figures 57 [rid=SD2] – 61 [rid=SD2] ). The Supplementary Information [rid=SD1] further describes the GWAS results and provides putative secondary signals at a more lenient significance threshold of 1×10 ( Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). 
Among the index variants of the main or secondary Tier 1 signals, three were missense variants with a REVEL score above 0.25 (in the , and loci); only seven index variants were rare, with minor allele frequency or MAF below 1%, in the , , , , and loci ( Supplementary Tables 2 [this file] and 3 [this file] ). In the gene, loss-of-function variants and missense variants with a REVEL score above 50 were jointly associated with AD risk (OR=4.23 (2.04–8.79), P=1.06×10 , Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ) in the ADES-ADSP summary statistics . 
As in previous GWASs, genes enriched in ADRD or AD association signal in the main, no-proxy, and no-biobank meta-analyses were over-expressed in microglia in four different datasets spanning different brain regions ( Supplementary Information [rid=SD1] , Supplementary Tables 9 [this file] and 10 [this file] , Supplementary Figures 62 [rid=SD2] – 64 [rid=SD2] ). Similarly to previous GWAS results, association signals were significantly enriched in pathways related to Tau, amyloid, lipids, immunity or endosome/lysosome, in the main, no-proxy, and no-biobank meta-analyses ( Supplementary Table 11 [this file] ). By performing a phenome-wide association study, we also linked some of the new loci (both Tiers) to pathways related to tau, lipids or immunity ( Supplementary Tables 12 [this file] , 13 [this file] and 14 [this file] ). After exclusion of , the no-proxy ADRD phenotype was significantly (P≤3.13×10 ) genetically correlated with Lewy body dementia (r=0.64, 95% confidence interval (CI) [0.37, 0.92]), amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (r=0.29, 95% CI [0.18, 0.40]), Parkinson’s disease (r=0.16, 95% CI [0.06, 0.27]) and educational attainment (r=−0.12, 95% CI [−0.17, –0.07]) ( Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). 
Genetic correlation with ADRD could not be assessed reliably for most of the 11 neuropathological endophenotypes (NPE) we considered due to the low study samples sizes or heritability of those traits ( Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). To better study the genetic link between ADRD and NPEs, we constructed three polygenic scores (PGS) based on the Tier 1 main and secondary signals (except ) detected in the main, no-proxy and no-biobank meta-analyses respectively ( Supplementary Table 15 [this file] ). We then assessed their association with the 11 NPEs in the Adult Changes in Thought (ACT) cohort (N=677 including 12.9% with dementia) and in the Alzheimer Disease Centers /National Alzheimer’s Coordinating Center (ADC/NACC) dataset (N=5,808 including 82.7% with dementia) ( Supplementary Table 16 [this file] ) . None of the scores was significantly associated with the cerebrovascular NPEs, nor with hippocampal sclerosis or Lewy body ( Figure 2a [rid=F2] , Supplementary Table 17 [this file] ) while the genetic correlation between ADRD and Lewy body dementia was significant after exclusion of ; this may indicate common pathological pathways underlying conversion from the pathology to AD or Lewy body dementia, although we can not exclude other explanations, such as a lack of statistical power of the PGS analysis or misdiagnoses among AD and Lewy body dementia cases impacting genetic correlation. Results were similar across the main, no-proxy and no-biobank PGS ( Supplementary Table 17 [this file] ). After adjustment on the (other) AD NPEs, only the associations with Braak stage and CERAD score remained significant in ADC/NACC ( Figure 2b [rid=F2] , Supplementary Table 17 [this file] ). The association with LATE-NC remained significant at the nominal level only (P=3.78×10 , Supplementary Table 17 [this file] ); a larger sample size is required to assess if the association with LATE-NC is due or not to the frequent co-occurrence of LATE-NC and AD NPEs ( Supplementary Information [rid=SD1] ). There was no significant interaction (P≤2.27×10 ) between the PGS and the number of APOE ε4 and ε2 alleles for Braak stage and CERAD score ( Supplementary Table 17 [this file] ). In the ADC/NACC dataset, compared to the individuals with a main PGS in the median quintile (40 to 60%), individuals in the 10 decile had a risk increased by 2.05-fold (95% CI=[1.47–2.85]) and 1.96-fold (95% CI=[1.39–2.78]) for Braak stage above 5 and moderate/severe neuritic amyloid plaque pathology at death respectively, while individuals in the 1 decile had a risk decreased by 0.47-fold (95% CI=[0.37–0.61]) and 0.43-fold (95% CI=[0.33–0.56]) respectively ( Figure 3 [rid=F3] , Supplementary Tables 18 [this file] and 19 [this file] , Supplementary Figure 67 [rid=SD2] and Supplementary Information [rid=SD1] ). The discriminative power as measured by AUC was similar for the main, no-proxy and no-biobank PGS (P > 0.05, Supplementary Table 21 [this file] ).

removing the per-study variant filtering on effective allele count, except in the FHS study ( Supplementary Information [rid=SD1] , Supplementary Table 23 [this file] ).

For males, only the mother’s status was used to define the proxy status ( Supplementary Material [this file] ). 
In addition to the classical autosomal QC, an X-chromosome specific QC was performed prior to imputation for each study ( Supplementary Material [this file] and Supplementary Table S4 [rid=MOESM2] ). 
The approaches are described briefly below, while additional details are provided in the Supplementary Material [this file] . Dosage or genotype probabilities were used for all studies but FinnGen, where best guessed genotypes were considered ( Supplementary Material [this file] ). 
To account for differences in genotypic variance between sexes, we considered a robust estimate of the variance (or Huber-White Sandwich estimator, accounting for heterogeneity of variance within a regression model, Supplementary Material [this file] ) for case-control studies [ 61 [rid=CR61] , 62 [rid=CR62] ] and an adjustment on sex for family studies and biobanks (Supplementary Table S5 [rid=MOESM2] ). The association test on proxy status in UKB was performed separately for males and females, and a correction factor of 2 was applied to the association statistics (effect sizes and standard errors) of the female-only model ( Supplementary Material [this file] ) [ 51 [rid=CR51] , 63 [rid=CR63] ]. 
The sex-stratified models were adjusted on PCs and/or the genotyping center only, except for two ADGC studies (PFIZER and TGEN2) and the CHARGE studies (FHS, RS and CHS), where models were additionally adjusted on age (Supplementary Table S6 [rid=MOESM2] and Supplementary Material [this file] ). 
The variant effect sizes of males and females were then compared with a Wald test ( Supplementary Material [this file] ).

The novel synSAA was developed by modifying previously reported synSAA conditions, using larger Si N beads, a higher temperature, more frequent fragmentation cycles, sarkosyl, and reducing the total reaction volume ( appendix [this file] p 2). CSF samples from people with Parkinson’s disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, and isolated rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder (IRBD) produced three replicates with high (≥45 000 relative fluorescence units [RFU], defined as type 1); multiple system atrophy samples presented two or three replicates with intermediate (3000–45 000 RFU, defined as type 2); and control samples presented two or three replicates with below threshold (<3000 RFU, defined as negative; appendix [this file] pp 5–6). Determination criteria with dual output for specimens were, thus, defined: the first output established the detection or non-detection of α-synuclein seeds; the second output established the type of seeds present in synSAA-positive samples ( appendix [this file] pp 2–3). The novel synSAA yielded consistent results across batches of substrate, with synSAA-positive type 2 results obtained for multiple system atrophy samples, synSAA-positive type 1 results obtained for Parkinson’s disease samples, and synSAA-negative results obtained for healthy control samples ( appendix [this file] p 6). Thus, the modifications made to develop the novel synSAA resulted in higher reproducibility, improved detection of multiple system atrophy, and a reduction in runtime, compared with the previous synSAA ( appendix [this file] pp 5–6). To this end, a masked cohort of pathology-confirmed brain samples (obtained from the NYBB cohort) were homogenised ( appendix [this file] p 3) and analysed with the novel synSAA. The EKUT cohort included CSF samples from people with Parkinson’s disease and dementia with Lewy bodies that were independently prescreened to lack α-synuclein seeding activity, using an alternative synSAA ( appendix [this file] pp 3–4). 
Neurofilament light chain has been proposed to be elevated in multiple system atrophy compared with Parkinson’s disease and was available for analysis in some cases ( appendix [this file] pp 4–5). 
Primary pathologies consisted of 4R-tauopathies (nine progressive supranuclear palsy, six corticobasal degeneration, and one argyrophilic grain disease), two with Lewy bodies, and three with glial cytoplasmic inclusions ( appendix p 8 [this file] ). The five cohorts that were enriched for multiple system atrophy cases (BARMSA, EKUT, KAMSA, UGOT, and KIMSA) also included some samples from people with Parkinson’s disease and dementia with Lewy bodies ( table [rid=T1] ; appendix [this file] pp 3–4). Under optimized conditions, 10 min of incubation with 0.1% Sudan Black led to a 93% reduction in background autofluorescence for 561 nm laser excitation (26 W cm illumination intensity), corresponding to a decrease in median detected photon counts from 4,400 ± 1,040 photons ± median absolute deviation (MAD) to 333 ± 47 photons (Fig. 2b [rid=Fig2] ) (the background reduction for other excitation colours (488, 561 nm), treatment times and concentrations are shown in Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] ). Next, we repeated this background suppression step on antibody-labelled samples and evaluated various antibodies against multiple forms of α-synuclein for specificity and detectability (Supplementary Figs. 2 [this file] and 3 [this file] and Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). 
Given this link between p-syn and pathology in synucleinopathies, we tested a variety of antibodies (Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ), including two complementary antibodies targeting the pS129 epitope of α-synuclein raised in two species (rabbit, AB_2270761, and mouse, AB_2819037). The AB_2819037 antibody showed characteristic Lewy pathology in both DAB and immunofluorescence staining and were shown to be specific through substantial co-localization with a second antibody for total α-synuclein (AB_2832854) (Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] ). These recombinant p-syn protein aggregates can be detected by the same AB_2819037 antibody (Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] ). 
Using a high NA objective lens has two main impacts: first, the NA scales with the collection angle of collected light (Fig. 2d [rid=Fig2] and Supplementary equation ( 3 [this file] )), and thus, more photons from the sample are collected at high NA. Second, increasing the NA improves the image resolution (Supplementary equation ( 8 [this file] )). 
Applying the ASA–PD protocol within tissue revealed hundreds of detectable fluorescent puncta per field of view (FOV) (55 × 55 µm ) in both PD and HC samples (Supplementary Fig. 5 [this file] ). 
A detailed description of the analysis is provided in Supplementary Information Note 3.1 [this file] and Supplementary Figs. 6 [this file] – 12 [this file] . These objects can be segmented with a simple intensity threshold after a background subtraction step (large-object pipeline in Fig. 3b [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Fig. 7 [this file] ). To do so, we applied a bandpass filter to each image which selects features on the scale of the diffraction limit (Supplementary Figs. 6 [this file] and 9 [this file] ). 
To evaluate the performance of the pipeline for detecting and characterizing nanoscale assemblies, we simulated images of puncta on noisy backgrounds at various signal-to-noise levels based on empirically determined parameters (Supplementary Note 3.2 [this file] , Simulations). 
To characterize the distributions of α-synuclein in brain tissue, we selected three PD brains (Braak stage 6) and three HC brains for imaging (Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). Negative control samples, lacking primary antibodies, were also tested using PD tissue to quantify the degree of false positives caused by residual autofluorescence and unbound secondary antibodies (Supplementary Fig. 12 [this file] ). 
These aggregates were distributed over a broad range of sizes from 0.04 to 100 µm in PD and 0.04 to 1 µm in HC (Fig. 4g [rid=Fig4] ), where the aggregate sizes associated with Lewy pathology essentially exclusively found in PD samples, consistent with the original tissue classifications (Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). 
At this scale, the resolution obscures aggregate sizes; however, for larger aggregates, where the size and brightness can be measured, the two were strongly linearly proportional, > 0.99 (Supplementary Fig. 13a [this file] ). The brightness distributions for all measured objects are shown in Supplementary Fig. 13b [this file] together with the estimated number of bound secondary antibodies, assuming each antibody contributes ~700 photons in our imaging conditions (Supplementary Fig. 14 [this file] ). The existence of this bright, disease-specific shift in the nanoscale population was highly robust by ASA–PD and was observed consistently when testing different α-synuclein antibodies, two different brain banks (Queen Square Brain Bank for Neurological Disorders (QSBB) and Multiple Sclerosis and Parkinson’s Brain Bank (Imperial), 12 individuals (6 PD and 6 HC), and using different antigen retrieval methods (formic acid and heat mediated epitope retrieval) (Supplementary Note 3.3 [this file] , Supplementary Figs. 15 [this file] – 17 [this file] and Supplementary Tables 2 [this file] and 3 [this file] ). 
When these probes are adjacent, they produce an amplified signal that can be visualized using fluorescence microscopy (Supplementary Fig. 19a [this file] ). PLA was performed on 13 brain sections from the anterior cingulate gyrus, comprising six late Braak stage 5–6 PD and seven HC samples (Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ), and imaged (20× magnification, NA 0.75). Representative images and the puncta density is shown in Supplementary Fig. 19b,c [this file] plotted per sample. 
Next, brain lysates were fractionated using SEC to separate soluble α-synuclein species by apparent molecular weight from the Braak stage five or six PD, and HC donors (three PD and three HC; Supplementary Fig. 20a [this file] ). 
The SEC-ELISA analysis revealed that total α-synuclein concentrations differed across high and low molecular weight fractions by two orders of magnitude but did not reveal statistical differences in the total α-synuclein in PD compared with controls, suggesting a similar amount of total protein (Supplementary Fig. 20b [this file] ). Physiological (low molecular weight) fractions, in contrast, showed no statistical differences in lag times between PD and HC samples (Supplementary Fig. 20d,e [this file] ). 
Finally, we validated the presence of Proteinase K-resistant fluorescent puncta to assess whether the observed aggregates exhibited distinct chemicophysical properties (Supplementary Fig. 21 [this file] ). 
The detection of small protein assemblies in post-mortem tissue is sensitive to many experimental fluctuations, and therefore ASA–PD was tested in a range of conditions, including the source of the brains (from two independent brain banks, Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ) and the traditional antigen retrieval methods (formic acid and heat mediated epitope retrieval). We found that the most consistent detection of oligomers was obtained using formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) Braak stage 6 tissue sections from a single brain bank, without any formic acid antigen retrieval; however, broadly similar trends were observed in all conditions tested (Supplementary Note 3.3 [this file] and Supplementary Fig. 15 [this file] ). 
Braak stage 3/4 PD cases ( = 3) were obtained from Imperial, Braak stage 6 PD cases ( = 4; 1 for technical controls, 3 for main study) from QSBB and three HCs from each brain bank to control for brain bank processing effects ( = 6; 3 from Imperial, 3 from QSBB) as highlighted in Supplementary Table 2 [this file] . Case demographics for each case are described in Supplementary Table 3 [this file] . 
Then, 8-µm-thick FFPE tissue sections from the cingulate cortex were cut from the cases summarized in Supplementary Table 2 [this file] and described in detail in Supplementary Table 3 [this file] . 
For specific details of values used, see Supplementary Information Note 3.1 [this file] .

No significant differences in pS129‐α‐syn and the pS129‐α‐syn/t‐α‐syn ratio were observed between patients and controls in unadjusted analysis (Table 1 [rid=ene70167-tbl-0001] , Figure 1 [rid=ene70167-fig-0001] ). pS129‐α‐syn was significantly correlated with age (Figure S3 [this file] ). 
In brief, the developed assay is highly sensitive with an LLOQ well below the observed native levels in PD and control CSF samples, and specific for pS129‐α‐syn, as demonstrated by no reactivity with nonphosphorylated t‐α‐syn (Figure S1 [this file] ). Parallelism experiments showed a trend of decreasing recovery with increasing dilution factor, as concentrations approached the limit of quantification (Figure S2 [this file] ). Spike‐recovery experiments showed small overestimates of lower concentrations and underestimates of higher concentrations (Table S1 [this file] ).

caption: Supplementary Figure 1. Cognitive footprint of medication according to results from UK Biobank cohort, on the following domains and outcomes: Abstract Nonverbal Reasoning, Verbal Memory, Visual Processing, Strategic Planning, Trail Making Tests 1 & 2 (Tmt1 & 2). For each cognitive outcome, the leftward panel presents medications classified according to the last level of the Anatomical Therapeutic Classification (ATC level 5: chemical substances, e.g., ‘ibuprofen’), while the rightward panel groups medications according to the ATC level 4 (pharmacological subgroups, e.g., propionic acid derivatives). Note than while the ATC codes are official, the accompanying terms may have been abbreviated (e.g., ‘tertiary anticholinergics’ for ‘anticholinergics with tertiary amino group’). The cognitive footprint of a medication on a specific cognitive outcome represents the estimated effect of medication use in the UK population (ages 40 to 70), according to the individual effect estimated by modeling UK Biobank data and assuming UK‐wide prevalence of consumption is the same as in the cohort. Units are Z‐scores of the distribution of the cognitive outcome score (RT, FI) across UK Biobank participants. Error bars represent 95% credible intervals. Only medications with over 50% credibility for a non‐zero effect are presented in the graph (i.e., the 50% credible intervals of the corresponding regression coefficient do not contain zero). Negative values and red color indicate the medication is associated to worse cognitive score, while positive values indicate association to better score. The dashed vertical bars represent the cognitive footprint of other covariates in the model or potential interventions (demographic, medical or environmental conditions, etc.). For instance, the cognitive footprint of multiple sclerosis is calculated as the individual effect of the disease according to the model presented in the same graph (e.g., ATC level 5‐medications and RT), multiplied by the estimated prevalence of the condition in the UK population (ages 40 ‐ 70), extrapolated from the prevalence in the UK Biobank cohort. The cognitive footprint of a hypothetical intervention consisting on reducing air pollution by a certain amount is calculated according to the individual effect of the condition (pollution in this case) according to the model, if it was applied to the entire UK population by the amount indicated (e.g., 1 mcg/m 3  NO 2 ). context_description:
Principal component analysis was performed and the results confirm no clustering of samples by cohort could be observed in the first two principal components (Figure S1 [this file] ). The distribution of nontransformed values in the 98 metabolic variables were broadly normal, as determined through inspection of histograms and quantile‐quantile plots (Figure S2 [this file] and S3 [this file] ). 
Pairwise Pearson's correlations of the 24 metabolic variables, both within the training cohort set and within UKB, are presented in Figure S4 [this file] . 
Further details of the multivariable aging models are provided in the Appendix S1 [this file] . 
Cohort‐specific Cox proportional hazards regression models were adjusted for age, sex, BMI, and ethnicity, and fixed‐effect meta‐analysis was performed to pool together individual cohort effect estimates (Figure S5 [this file] , Figure 2c [rid=acel14164-fig-0002] ). Forty‐nine metabolic biomarkers were negatively associated with all‐cause mortality, and PUFA, omega‐6, omega‐3 fatty acids, and cholesterols and cholesterol esters in IDL were found to be most negatively associated with mortality in our study sample (Figure S5 [this file] , Table S5 [rid=acel14164-supitem-0002] ). Our biomarker‐mortality associations study results are in good agreement with results reported by Deelen et al. ( 2019 [rid=acel14164-bib-0008] ), with coefficients of mortality associations of individual metabolites of our analysis strongly correlated to the results reported (Figure S6 [this file] ). 
The overall Pearson's correlation coefficients ( ) between CA and the CV predicted age were 0.57, 0.65, and 0.47, and the correlations ( ) with the LOCO predictions were 0.38, 0.37, and 0.23, respectively, for the elastic net, MARS, and phenotypic age models. (Figure S7 [this file] ). 
However, adjusting for BMI did not significantly affect study models associations with adverse health outcomes (Figure S8 [this file] ). 
Generally, associations were stronger in the youngest age band: for those aged under 55 years, each additional year of MARS age was associated with a 4% increase in mortality risk, compared to a 2% increase among those aged over 65 years (Figure S9 [this file] ).

Details on individual cohort characteristics are listed in Table S1 [this file] . 
The remaining 98 well quantified metabolic variable signals were considered in the main part of this study (Table S2 [this file] ). 
This yielded 24 variables (Table S2 [this file] ), which were then used as input predictors in our multivariable CA models. 
Summary of biological aging markers data by cohort are shown in Table S1 [this file] . 
Individual cohort characteristics can be found in Figure 1a [rid=acel14164-fig-0001] and Table S1 [this file] . 
For example, albumin, histidine (His), leucine (Leu), phospholipids in small HDL (S_HDL_PL), and diameter for VLDL particles (VLDL_size) were found to decrease with higher CA; whilst citrate, glucose, creatinine, β‐hydroxybutyrate (bOHbutyrate), docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), omega‐3 fatty acids, glutamine (Gln), tyrosine (Tyr), phenylalanine (Phe), total free cholesterol (Total_FC), and sphingomyelins were among those found to increase with CA the most. (Figure 2a [rid=acel14164-fig-0002] , Table S3 [this file] ). 
Significant metabolic associations against both age and mortality after correcting for FDR ( < 0.05) were highlighted according to whether they shared the same direction of associations: red (same direction) or green (opposing direction).The list of full names of the abbreviated metabolic variables can be found in Table S2 [this file] . 
Whereas the increase in citrate levels with age appeared to be driven by older populations, the increases in many cholesterols/cholesterol esters and lipoprotein subfraction measurements appeared to be more prominent in those aged <60 years (Figure 2b [rid=acel14164-fig-0002] , Table S4 [this file] ). 
Forty‐nine metabolic biomarkers were negatively associated with all‐cause mortality, and PUFA, omega‐6, omega‐3 fatty acids, and cholesterols and cholesterol esters in IDL were found to be most negatively associated with mortality in our study sample (Figure S5 [rid=acel14164-supitem-0001] , Table S5 [this file] ). 
Using Cox proportional regression models adjusted for CA and sex, we studied associations of metabolomic aging models with all‐cause mortality (= 6645), CVD (= 2585), T2DM (= 3850), cancer (= 8192), dementia (= 450), and COPD (= 1814) incidences in the UKB samples (Figure 5b [rid=acel14164-fig-0005] , Table S8 [this file] ).

Missing data on covariates were imputed using multiple imputations with a chained equation, [xref] [rid=R32] following established protocols as previously described. [xref] [rid=R33] The rates of missing data for covariates are summarised in online supplemental table 2 [this file] . 
Across all cohorts, frail individuals were older, more likely to be female, with a lower prevalence of high education level, and had a higher level of BMI and a higher prevalence of chronic conditions, as compared with robust individuals ( online supplemental table 3 [this file] ). Baseline characteristics stratified by depression status are presented in online supplemental table 4 [this file] . 
As shown in online supplemental table 5 [this file] , frail participants had a significantly higher risk of incident all-cause dementia than robust participants (pooled HR: 2.55, 95% CI 2.36 to 2.76; I =72.3%). 
In the analysis of estimating the importance of physical frailty and depression in predicting incident all-cause dementia, we found these two factors ranked among the top predictors in relative strength compared with traditional risk factors ( online supplemental figure 2 [this file] ). 
In sex-specific subgroup analyses, the individual associations between physical frailty, depression and the risk of incident all-cause dementia remained consistent in both males and females (p-difference>0.05; online supplemental table 6 [this file] ). Similarly, the joint effect of physical frailty and depression on dementia risk was consistent across sex groups (p-difference>0.05; online supplemental table 7 [this file] ). 
When we mutually adjusted for physical frailty and depression, the individual associations remained robust ( online supplemental table 8 [this file] ). In analyses using different definitions to assess depression, the associations were consistent with those using the original definitions ( online supplemental tables 8–10 [this file] ). We observed similar associations with the primary analyses after conducting the competing risk analyses between mortality and incident dementia ( online supplemental tables 8,9 and 11 [this file] ). Additional exclusion of incident dementia cases within the first 5 years of follow-up did not alter the observed associations ( online supplemental tables 8,9 and 12 [this file] ). The findings were consistent when we restricted the analyses to participants without heart disease ( online supplemental tables 8,9 and 13 [this file] ) or without missing data on covariates ( online supplemental tables 8,9 and 14 [this file] ).

Using this definition, the results follow the same pattern as the main analysis, where at low social advantage (≤ 1 favorable SDH), no statistically significant differences between APOE alleles were observed (APOE-ε2 HR = 0.68, 95%CI = 0.35–1.34; APOE-ε4 HR = 1.34, 95%CI = 0.90–2.01), while at the greater level of social advantage (≥ 4 favorable SDH), the differences between APOE-ε2 and APOE-ε4 were statistically significant in the expected direction (APOE-ε2 HR = 0.29, 95%CI = 0.19–0.43; APOE-ε3ε3 HR = 0.47, 95%CI = 0.35–0.62; APOE-ε4 HR = 0.75, 95%CI = 0.55–1.01) (S2 Fig and S2 Table in S1 File [this file] ). 
Results indicated that the impact of social adversity on increasing dementia risk remained similar across different polygenic risk profiles, as observed in the main analyses (S3 Table in S1 File [this file] ). 
The results obtained were similar to the main analyses, confirming a low possibility of reverse causality in our findings (S4 Table in S1 File [this file] ). 
Fourth, to assess whether the results are influenced by the outcome assessment method, we included cases of dementia based solely on cognitive scores and functional limitations, finding that the results followed the same direction that those obtained in the main analyses (S5 Table in S1 File [this file] ). 
As expected, the association effect’ sizes were slightly reduced, but all the analyses presented the same direction and statistically significant association as the main analysis (S6 Table in S1 File [this file] ). 
Observed results from the weighted analysis did not differ from those obtained in the primary analyses, confirming a low chance of selection bias in our findings (S7 and S8 Tables in S1 File [this file] ). 
Subgroup analysis by sex showed that, in both males and females, the same pattern of APOE allele impact was observed: the effect was more evident among individuals living with low social adversity, whereas among those exposed to greater social adversity, the influence of the APOE allele was less pronounced (S9.a Table in S1 File [this file] ). We also observed that the effect of social adversity on male APOE-ε2 carriers was less pronounced than in female carriers, whereas the opposite pattern was found for APOE-ε4, with a stronger effect among female carriers compared to male carriers (S9.b Table in S1 File [this file] ). 
Regarding racial differences (Black and White individuals), the same effect was observed: people at high social disadvantage presented the greatest risk of dementia, regardless of APOE allele (S10.a Table in S1 File [this file] ). Among White participants, APOE-ε2 carriers at social advantage presented a lower risk of dementia, and APOE-ε4 carriers at social advantage had a greater risk of dementia than APOE-ε3ε3 carriers at social advantage (S10.b Table in S1 File [this file] ). In contrast, among Black participants, APOE-ε2 carriers at social advantage did not present a lower risk of dementia, and APOE-ε4 carriers at social advantage showed no difference in dementia risk compared to APOE-ε3ε3 carriers at social advantage (S10.b Table in S1 File [this file] ). 
Regarding individual social determinants, having a lower education level and lower family income presented the strongest interactions and were associated with a greater risk of dementia, regardless of APOE allele group (S11.a Table in S1 File [this file] ). Interestingly, among APOE-ε4 carriers, only having less than upper secondary education was associated with greater dementia risk, whereas dementia risk remained elevated across all income levels (intermediate and low) when compared to those with high family income (S11.a Table in S1 File [this file] ). 
In terms of healthcare-related factors, lower access to and quality of healthcare were associated with increased dementia risk among APOE-ε3ε3 and APOE-ε4 carriers (S11.b Table in S1 File [this file] ). Meanwhile, lower perceived social support and higher levels of neighborhood physical disorder were linked to greater dementia risk among APOE-ε2 and APOE-ε3ε3 carriers (S11.b and 11.c Tables in S1 File [this file] ). Finally, lower neighborhood social cohesion was associated with increased dementia risk, but only among APOE-ε3ε3 carriers (S11.c Table in S1 File [this file] ).

Further details are provided in the appendix (Table A in S1 Appendix [this file] ). 
Further details of the assessments of physical function, depressive symptoms, and cognitive performance are provided in the appendix (Table A in S1 appendix [this file] ). 
Harmonized covariate classifications are shown in the appendix (Table A in S1 Appendix [this file] ). 
A total of 10,990 participants, including 5,495 matched pairs of participants who experienced falls and those who did not, were included to investigate trajectories of physical function, depressive symptoms, and cognitive performance before and after incident falls over 10 years of follow-up, of whom 3,038 (27.6%) from China, 3,540 (32.2%) from the UK, and 4,412 (40.1%) from the USA (Table B in S1 Appendix [this file] ). The characteristics of participants by fall-related characteristics are shown in the appendix (Tables C–E in S1 Appendix [this file] ). 
Figs A–D in S1 Appendix [this file] show the raw trajectories of physical function, depressive symptoms, and cognitive performance before and after falls and fall-related characteristics. Among participants with incident falls, physical (difference in mean: −0.14, 95% CI [−0.19, −0.09]) and cognitive functioning (difference in mean: −0.07, 95% CI [−0.12, −0.01]) were poorer than among participants without reported falls, beginning 3–5 years before the fall, whereas depressive symptoms (difference in mean: −0.15, 95% CI [−0.23, −0.08]) was more severe beginning 5–7 years before the fall (Table F in S1 Appendix [this file] ). These differences persisted up to 5 years after the fall and were more pronounced among those with injurious falls, hip fractures, and recurrent falls (Tables G–I in S1 Appendix [this file] ). 
Results were generally similar across cohorts (Tables J–M in S1 Appendix [this file] ). Subgroup analyses showed that the differences in physical function, depressive symptoms, and cognitive performance at t0 between participants who experienced falls and those who did not were more pronounced among participants with lower socioeconomic status (both lower education level and lower household wealth) (Table N in S1 Appendix [this file] ). In addition, among participants aged ≥75 years, the differences in the rates of decline in physical function between participants who experienced falls and those who did not, both before and after t0, were greater than among participants aged <75 years (Table N in S1 Appendix [this file] ). Similar findings were observed when fall severity was further differentiated (Tables O–Q in S1 Appendix [this file] ). Sensitivity analyses supported the robustness of our findings (Tables R–V and Fig E in S1 Appendix [this file] ). 
A total of 8,675 participants with at least three repeated measurements of physical function, depressive symptoms, and cognitive performance during follow-up, including 4,366 participants who experienced falls and 4,309 who did not, were included in the joint trajectory analysis (Table W in S1 Appendix [this file] ). The fitted parameters of the GBMTM are presented in the appendix (Table X in S1 Appendix [this file] ), and the baseline characteristics according to the identified trajectory groups are shown in the appendix (Table Y in S1 Appendix [this file] ). 
Similar results were observed across cohorts (Table Z in S1 Appendix [this file] ) and in subgroups defined by age, sex, and socioeconomic status (Tables AA–DD in S1 Appendix [this file] ). Sensitivity analyses supported the robustness of the findings (Tables EE–FF in S1 Appendix [this file] ).

Following previous studies, [xref] [rid=hcaf333-B15] we pooled data from 16 countries ( Supplementary Table S1 [this file] ) derived from three harmonized cohort studies: the Health and Retirement Study (HRS), the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA) and the Survey of Health, Ageing, and Retirement in Europe (SHARE). [xref] [rid=hcaf333-B16] These surveys were developed using a shared methodological framework originally modeled on the US HRS. 
Follow-up data were used up to the final wave before the COVID-19 pandemic (wave 9 for ELSA, wave 14 for HRS and wave 7 for SHARE) ( Supplementary Table S2 [this file] ). After excluding participants younger than 50 years, those diagnosed with cancer at baseline, those without follow-up data, and those missing information on handgrip strength test results, BMI, cancer status, or other covariates, the primary analysis included 3162 participants from ELSA, 127 from HRS and 26 635 from SHARE ( Supplementary Figures S1–S3 [this file] ). 
Compared to participants in the lowest quartile of relative handgrip strength, those in the highest quartile were younger, more likely to have a higher education level, be married, have a lower BMI, greater household wealth, fewer chronic conditions, and engage in more physical activity ( Supplementary Table S3 [this file] ). 
When analyses were conducted separately within each cohort (HRS, ELSA and SHARE) and combined using a random-effects meta-analysis, the pooled estimate [HR (95% CI): 0.92 (0.88–0.95)] remained stable and consistent with the main findings ( Supplementary Figure S4 [this file] ). The other three sensitivity analyses (excluding individuals with a follow-up duration of <2.5 years, excluding participants with absolute handgrip strength > 55 or <16 kg, and using multiple imputations to account for missing data) also showed results consistent with the main analysis ( Supplementary Table S4–S6 [this file] ). 
The significant inverse association between relative handgrip strength and cancer incidence persisted across lifestyle stratifications ( Supplementary Table S7 [this file] ), with a more pronounced protective effect observed in individuals with healthier lifestyles ( Figure 2 [rid=hcaf333-F2] ). Additionally, individuals in the highest quartile of relative handgrip strength (Quartile 4) consistently exhibited a lower cancer risk compared with those in the lowest quartile (Quartile 1), although this association was not statistically significant among participants aged 80 years and older, those living alone, or those with a primary school education or below ( Supplementary Table S8 [this file] ).

Longitudinal data from 22 countries came from six nationally representative cohort studies ( appendix [this file] p 2): the Survey of Health, Ageing, and Retirement in Europe (SHARE), the Health and Retirement Study (HRS), the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA), the Mexican Health and Aging Study (MHAS), the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS), and the Korean Longitudinal Study of Aging (KLOSA). The dataset comprised 212 904 individuals aged 50 years and older, with comparable pain measures across countries and over time ( appendix [this file] p 2). 
Pain prevalence across all timepoints and countries was 43⋅21% (297 035/687 369; 95% CI 43⋅10–43⋅33) and was higher for females, those with less education, and older respondents ( table [rid=T1] ; country-specific demographic statistics are provided in the appendix [this file] p 3). 74% of respondents reporting pain also did so in the previous or following wave, indicating substantial continuity. 
Regression models 1–5 included a dummy for site-specific ( general) pain questions to account for instrument-induced bias ( appendix [this file] pp 4–8). Priming respondents to consider pain in specific body parts resulted in pain prevalence of 14⋅56 percentage points higher than asking about pain in general (see appendix [this file] pp 9–13 for diagnostics and sensitivity analyses, supporting robustness). 
Pain increased in 15 of 22 countries (as indicated in the appendix [this file] [p 14] by non-overlapping 2006 and 2016 95% CIs in Belgium, the Czech Republic, England, Estonia, France, Greece, Israel, Italy, South Korea, the Netherlands, Poland, Portugal, Slovenia, Spain, and the USA), with a mean annual increase of 1⋅21 percentage points, totalling 12⋅1 percentage points over a decade (from 37⋅11% in 2006 to 49⋅16% in 2016). These trends are unlikely to be fully explained by demographic shifts, as changes in sex composition, education levels, and population ageing were minimal over the observed period ( appendix [this file] p 3). 
We classified disparities as remaining stable if the gap changed by less than 1 percentage point over the decade ( appendix [this file] p 15). 
The overall disparity landscape for 2016, showing lower disparities in western and northern European countries (Austria, Denmark, France, Germany, and the Netherlands) and greater disparities in southern European countries (Greece, Italy, Portugal, and Spain) and South Korea, compared with countries in other regions is shown in the appendix [this file] (p 17). The intersectoral disparities for females with low levels of education aged older than 60 years shows the widest gaps in South Korea and the smallest in Denmark ( appendix [this file] p 18). 
In 2016, Germany, Greece, and Italy had the largest population share of those aged 65 years and older; from 2000–24 China, Israel, and the Netherlands were ageing fastest, shaping pain projections ( appendix [this file] p 16). 
For baseline years and country–specific descriptives see the appendix [this file] (p 3).

The predictive performance of the HbA1c/HDL-C ratio for incident CMM was assessed by ROC curve analysis, NRI, and IDI ( Figure 5 [rid=fig5] , Supplementary Table S14 [this file] ). 
After adjusting for covariates, BMI was identified as a mediator between the trajectory of HbA1c/HDL-C ratio and CMM risk in HRS, with the total effect of −50.9182, ADE of −50.0776, ACME of −1.8463, and a relatively low proportion mediated of 3.33% ( = 0.034) ( Supplementary Table S15 [this file] ). 
Figure 6 [rid=fig6] and Supplementary Figures S2, S3 [this file] present the associations of HbA1c/HDL-C ratio and CMM risk stratified by age, gender, education levels, marital status, smoking status, drinking status, BMI, hypertension, and dyslipidemia. 
Generally, the positive associations between HbA1c/HDL-C ratio and incident CMM observed in the primary analysis remained largely consistent when using logistic regression models ( Supplementary Tables S16, S17 [this file] ), excluding participants with missing covariates ( Supplementary Tables S18, S19 [this file] ), excluding those receiving medications for certain conditions (heart disease, stroke, diabetes, hypertension, or dyslipidemia) at baseline ( Supplementary Tables S20, S21 [this file] ), or excluding participants with less than 2 years of follow-up ( Supplementary Tables S22, S23 [this file] ). Based on fully adjusted models, the E-value suggested that this association was relatively robust to unmeasured confounding factors ( Supplementary Table S24 [this file] ).

The participant selection process for each cohort is outlined in eFigures 1 to 4 in Supplement 1 [this file] . 
Detailed descriptions of the cognitive assessment tasks for each cohort are elaborated in eMethods and eTable 1 in Supplement 1 [this file] . 
The detailed classification for each cohort was presented in eTables 2 and 3 in Supplement 1 [this file] . 
These classifications were based on the rationale that both parental education at or above the primary level and participants’ education at or above the upper secondary level were associated with slower decline rates in cognitive state across cohorts, although statistical significance was not always reached (eTable 4 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
Consistent patterns for both maternal and paternal education were observed in the episodic memory and mental status domains across cohorts, except for episodic memory in HRS (eTables 5 and 6 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
Compared with those excluded because of missing data or loss to follow-up, included participants were generally younger, less likely to be from minoritized racial and ethnic groups, and more likely to have highly educated parents and higher own educational level, with some exceptions in CHARLS (eTables 7 to 10 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). Results from imputed datasets were consistent with main analyses, showing that higher parental education was associated with slower cognitive decline across domains and cohorts (eTables 11 and 12 in Supplement 1 [this file] ).

They were self-reported and included age at wave 10, and the following baseline measures: sex (male or female), educational attainment (equivalent to less than high school, high school, or above high school), household non-pension wealth standardized by year, smoking status (current smoker or not), alcohol consumption (consumes alcohol or not), physical activity level (engages in MVPA less than weekly, weekly, or more than weekly), self-rated hearing (excellent, very good, good, fair, or poor), depressive symptoms (eMethods 3 in Supplement 1 [this file] ), and diagnosis of the following long-term conditions (yes or no): high blood pressure, diabetes, cancer, heart disease, stroke, and psychiatric conditions. 
Detailed statistical methods are available in eMethods 4 in Supplement 1 [this file] . 
Details of additional analyses are provided in eMethods 5 in Supplement 1 [this file] . 
Compared with ELSA participants with cognitive data collected at least once during waves 1 through 9 who were excluded from the analytic sample (eg, who exited the study or died before wave 10 or did not participate in the accelerometer substudy), included participants were similar with respect to sex (1394 of 2529 [55.1%] vs 8619 of 15 872 [54.3%] female; = .46) but younger at baseline (mean [SD] 56.1 [5.4] years vs 62.5 [10.3] years; < .001), of higher socioeconomic position (eg, educated above high school level: 660 of 2529 [26.1%] vs 2252 of 15 872 [14.2%]; < .001; mean [SD] standardized wealth: 0.13 [1.2] vs −0.02 [1.1]; < .001), and generally had a more favorable health behavior and chronic disease profile (eTable 1 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). Compared with the 3622 wave 10 participants who did not participate in the accelerometer substudy, the 3860 substudy participants were similar with respect to age (mean [SD] 68.3 [9.3] years vs 68.2 [10.4] years; = .62) and sex (2143 [55.5%] vs 1978 [54.6%] female; = .44), and were broadly similar across chronic conditions but were of slightly higher socioeconomic position (eg, 1120 [29.0%] vs 971 [26.9%] educated above high school level; < .001), and had a more favorable health behavior profile (eTable 2 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
The median follow-up duration of the cognitive assessment period was 12 (IQR, 8-16) years, with a maximum follow-up period of 17 years (eFigure 1 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
The median individual-specific cognitive change was −0.004 (IQR, −0.011 to 0.004) SD per year for memory and 0.010 (IQR, 0.000 to 0.021) SD per year for fluency (eFigure 2 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). Illustrative trajectories at these values are shown in eFigure 3 in Supplement 1 [this file] . 
After adjustment for covariates, both individual-specific memory and fluency change were associated with the overall movement behavior composition (eTable 3 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). 
There was no evidence of effect modification by sex (eTable 4 in Supplement 1 [this file] ), or by age group for fluency (eTable 5 in Supplement 1 [this file] ). However, there was evidence of effect modification by age group for memory (eTable 5, eFigure 4 in Supplement 1 [this file] ): for participants older than 70 years at wave 10, the more favorable memory trajectory was associated with 2 (95% CI, 1 to 3) more minutes of MVPA, 20 (95% CI, 11 to 30) more minutes of LPA, 16 (95% CI, −27 to −5) fewer minutes of SB, and 6 (95% CI, −13 to 1) fewer minutes of sleep time compared with a less favorable trajectory. Results were substantively unchanged when nonlinear terms were included at the population-level for estimation of individual-specific cognitive change (eTable 6, eFigure 5 in Supplement 1 [this file] ) and when adjusted for baseline self-reported sleep duration (eTable 7, eFigure 6 in Supplement 1 [this file] ) or baseline mobility limitations (eTable 8, eFigure 7 in Supplement 1 [this file] ).

The phrasing of IQCODE items was equivalent across settings; appropriate translations and back‐translations were conducted for LASI‐DAD.[rid=alz13895-bib-0035] Each study imputed missing data using similar methods based on information from other informant interview questions, objective cognitive testing, demographics, and information from the prior wave of the broader HRS‐IPS study.[rid=alz13895-bib-0036] The proportion of imputed responses by item and study is available in Supplemental Materials 1 [this file] ; proportions are below 10% in all cases except items with high proportions of “doesn't do” responses in LASI‐DAD. 
In all three studies, cognitive functioning of respondents was assessed using neuropsychological batteries covering multiple cognitive domains, including orientation, memory, executive functioning, language, and visuospatial functioning (full list Supplemental Materials 2 [this file] ). 
Second, we created independent (internally scaled) classifications of low, medium, and high levels of education in each country based on the distributions of the data, which reflects differences between those with relative advantage or disadvantage in each setting (details in Supplemental Materials 3 [this file] ). 
We used scree plots with parallel analysis using polychoric correlations for ordinal data to confirm the unidimensionality of the IQCODE battery in each country (Supplemental Materials 4 [this file] ) and calculated as a measure of scale reliability.[rid=alz13895-bib-0039] We then used exploratory factor analysis with a single factor to assess construct validity and compare item loadings across settings. 
Comparison of model Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) confirmed this visual assessment; BIC was either lower or similar for models with a piecewise linear spline compared to models with flexible spline fits (Supplemental Materials 5 [this file] ). 
We did re‐calculate descriptive statistics presented using sampling weights (Supplemental Materials 6 and 7 [this file] ); application of weights did not change paper conclusions or descriptions included in the results. 
Parallel analysis revealed a unidimensional underlying trait in all three studies (Supplemental Materials 2 [this file] ). Factor loadings were highest across items in ELSA‐HCAP, indicating stronger intercorrelations between items in this setting (Supplemental Materials 8 [this file] ). 
Differences between studies for informant generation, caregiver status, and how long the informant has known the participant were statistically significant (Supplemental Materials 9 [this file] ).

Follow‐up extended to wave 15 in the HRS, wave 9 in the ELSA, and wave 5 in the CHARLS (Figure S1 [this file] ). 
After applying these criteria, the final analytical sample comprised 15,229 participants from CHARLS, 9287 from ELSA, and 14,374 from HRS (Figure S2 [this file] ). 
Substantial differences were observed (Table S1 [this file] ), which should be considered when interpreting the findings. 
Those with BRI > 5.06 were more likely to be older and to have hypertension, CMD, and cancer (Table S2 [this file] ), while individuals with BRI ≤ 5.06 were designated as the reference group. 
RCS analyses in both CMD subgroups revealed a similar non‐linear association between BRI and cancer risk, consistent with the overall population findings (Figure S3 [this file] ). 
When participants with a follow‐up duration of < 2 years were excluded, the association remained significant, with individuals having a BRI > 5.06 showing a higher risk of cancer (HR: 1.13; 95% CI: 1.03–1.24) (Table S3 [this file] ). Similarly, in a complete‐case analysis limited to participants with no missing covariate data, the association persisted and was stronger (HR: 1.49; 95% CI: 1.29–1.73) (Table S4 [this file] ). Additionally, a meta‐analysis synthesizing results across the three cohorts showed that individuals with a BRI > 5.06 had a 12% increased risk of cancer incidence compared to those with a BRI ≤ 5.06 (HR: 1.12; 95% CI: 1.04–1.21) (Figure S4 [this file] ). No significant associations were observed in other subgroups (Figure S5 [this file] ). 
Individuals with BRI < 5.06 (blue) generally exhibited lower cancer risk, whereas those with BRI ≥ 5.06 (orange) showed higher cancer risk (Figure S6 [this file] ).

In other words, older adults can be categorized as having 1) no cognitive impairment, 2) mildly impaired cognitive functioning (e.g., MCI), or 3) severely impaired cognitive functioning (e.g., dementia) (see Supplementary Text 1 [this file] for a Glossary of cognitive terms and mapping of cognitive status categories to cognitive terms). 
The current study was completed via secondary analysis of existing datasets that were either public and de-identified prior to our access to them or we completed a data use agreement that provided access to the requisite data to complete the analyses (see Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). 
Our study addresses four primary research questions (RQs), and corresponding hypotheses , examining the relationships between loneliness, social isolation, cognitive status, and mortality risk (see Table 1 [rid=T1] and Supplementary Text 2 [this file] for a full description). 
Thus, to maximize harmonization across analyses, we did not examine racial differences; however, we report prevalence of race within each dataset when race data were available (see Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). The SHARE datasets do not have race data; instead, we report country of birth as the closest possible proxy (see Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ). 
These datasets are either publicly available or access can be requested directly from the study sites, with the exception of ELSA death data (see Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). 
Specific information about accessibility for each dataset is included in the text and in Supplementary Table 1 [this file] . See Supplementary Table 2 [this file] for all deviations and decisions that were made after seeing the data ( Willroth & Atherton, 2024 [rid=R162] ). 
To increase transparency regarding prior exposure to these data, Supplementary Table 5 [this file] reports existing publications and manuscripts ( =103) that included co-authors of the current project using the same dataset(s). 
Specifically, the highest preference of cognitive status information was based on a clinical diagnosis of MCI and dementia, followed by the Clinical Dementia Rating scale, followed by traditional assessments used by medical professionals to screen for cognitive impairment (e.g., the Mini Mental State Examination), followed by composites of cognitive test scores (see Supplementary Text 3 [this file] for more details). Supplementary Table 6 [this file] provides a comprehensive overview of how cognitive status is assessed and harmonized across all included datasets, including operation definition of each cognitive status category. 
See Supplementary Table 7 [this file] for available loneliness items and operational definition for each included dataset. 
To address the limitation of differing contact frequency measures, we report the specific contact frequency measure used for each dataset in our supplementary materials [this file] and include this as a limitation in our discussion, explicitly addressing how differences in contact frequency measurement may impact our findings and interpretations. See Supplementary Table 8 [this file] for available social isolation items for each included dataset, as well as explanations of our operational definition of social isolation. 
Next, to tease apart the inconsistencies in the field, we used Cox Proportional Hazard models, logistic regression models, and multi-state survival models to examine the (i.e., independent; not adjusting for competing risks) and (i.e., adjusting for competing risks) associations among social disparities, cognitive aging, and mortality by addressing four primary research questions (see Footnote 1 [rid=FN1] , Table 1 [rid=T1] , and Supplementary Text 2 [this file] ). 
All datasets are publicly available for researchers, and access can be requested directly from the study sites (see Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). 
Therefore, we registered an extensive analytic contingency plan (see Supplementary Text 4 [this file] ). 
This report therefore includes two sets of supplementary results: a series of tables, figures, and text shared as a PDF document (see Supplementary Materials [this file] ), and a series of tables based on the individual and meta-analytic results shared on OSF (titled HTML Supplement [this file] ). Correlation matrices of primary study variables for each study are reported in Supplementary Figure 1 [this file] , while Table 2 [rid=T2] summarizes the primary synthesized results across modelling techniques. 
All individual study unconditional and conditional estimates for the Cox models (HTML Tables 2a1–3c3) and Logistic regression models (HTML Tables 4a1–5c3), as well as meta-analytic results (HTML Tables 6a/6b and 7a/7b, respectively) are reported in the HTML Supplement [this file] , while forest plots for logistic regression results are reported in Supplementary Figures 2 [this file] – 5 [this file] . 
Overall, synthesized results from the logistic regression models were consistent with those from the Cox models (also see Supplementary Text 5 [this file] ), with one exception: social isolation was not associated with severely impaired cognitive functioning in the logistic regression model (when loneliness was not included in the model) but was in the Cox model. 
Although point estimates tended to be slightly smaller, the direction and significance of nearly all estimates across both the Cox models (see HTML Supplement 2a3 [this file] , 2b3 [this file] , 2c3 [this file] , 3a3 [this file] , 6b [this file] , 7b [this file] ) and multistate survival models (see HTML Supplement 10a [this file] – 10c [this file] ) were consistent when additionally adjusting for depressive symptoms, with only four exceptions. See Supplementary Text 6 [this file] for the complete results from models additionally adjusting for depressive symptoms. 
Together, these findings suggest that social isolation and loneliness likely overlap to some extent (also see Supplementary Figure 1 [this file] ), but loneliness is the more proximal risk factor for death. 
By providing accessibility information about each dataset (see Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ) and detailed harmonization tables (see Supplementary Tables 6 [this file] – 8 [this file] ), this project contributes to ongoing efforts to develop more standardized methods for assessing cognitive status and social isolation across diverse longitudinal aging studies. 
As shown in Supplementary Tables 6 [this file] – 8 [this file] , there were notable differences in variable harmonization based on available data. 
Although all datasets were selected and preregistered in advance, three had to be excluded after data access due to unforeseen issues related to variable availability and research design structure (e.g., loneliness and isolation were administered at alternating occasions; see Supplementary Table 2 [this file] for more details). 
A full written explanation of the research questions and hypotheses are included in Supplementary Text 2 [this file] . This content was originally included in the Registered Report that was accepted in principle, but to streamline the primary manuscript, was moved to the supplement [this file] as the content overlaps directly with the information reported in Table 1 [rid=T1] .

Following a recently published study that examined multimorbidity based on 14 health outcomes available in ELSA [ 40 [rid=CR40] ], our study selected seven health outcomes or NCDs that have been found to be associated with both obesity and psychological well-being related measures: hypertension, heart disease, stroke, diabetes mellitus, arthritis, cancer, and dementia or memory-related disease (see Table A1 [this file] in Supplementary Materials). Table A2 [this file] presents how each NCD was determined in ELSA and HRS. 
Table A3 [this file] presents a list of psychological well-being related measures available at baseline in ELSA ( = 7) and HRS ( = 15). 
No risk differences in developing stroke, cancer, and memory-related disease were observed between participants with obesity vs. normal weight (Models 1 and 2), or between those with Class II & III obesity vs. normal weight (Table B1 [this file] ). 
Individual psychological well-being related measures (e.g., depressive symptoms, enjoyment of life) were also independently associated with those NCDs ( < 0.01) (Table B2 [this file] ). We found stronger associations between obesity and psychological well-being related measures when Class II & III obesity and normal weight were compared (Table B3 [this file] ), as opposed to when all obesity and normal weight were compared. 
However, findings from causal mediation analysis consistently indicated no evidence of mediation by the index of overall psychological well-being (Table 4 [rid=Tab4] ) or by individual psychological well-being related measures of which preconditions for mediation analysis were satisfied (Table B4 [this file] ). 
Obesity (vs. normal weight) was also associated with the cumulative number of NCDs across the follow-up period (IRR = 1.35; 95% CI = 1.26, 1.44) (Table B5 [this file] ). For psychological well-being related measures, none were associated with the cumulative number of NCDs at < 0.01 (Table B6 [this file] ). No mediation analysis was conducted for the number of NCDs because not all preconditions for successful mediation were satisfied (see Tables B3 [this file] , B5 [this file] and B6 [this file] for more information). Furthermore, we did not find associations between psychological well-being related measures and weight change (Table B7 [this file] ) and weight change were not associated with the incidence of any NCDs (Table B8 [this file] ), and therefore, mediation by weight change was not examined. When the incidence of NCDs in ELSA was classified on the basis of hospital admissions data, results were largely consistent with obesity being a risk factor for NCD incidence but there being no mediation by psychological well-being related measures; obesity (vs. normal weight) was associated with hypertension (HR = 2.23; 95% CI = 1.63, 3.04) and diabetes incidence (HR = 3.80; 95% CI = 2.38, 6.09) with no evidence of mediation (Tables B9 [this file] – B17 [this file] ). The exception was memory-related disease (Table B18 [this file] ), whereby the association between obesity status and disease development risk was higher among participants with lower overall psychological well-being (a higher index score). 
For most of the NCDs, findings remained when Class II & III obesity and normal weight were compared (Table C1 [this file] ). 
These findings were largely consistent when individual psychological well-being related measures were examined (Table C2 [this file] ). In addition, stronger associations between obesity and psychological well-being related measures appeared when Class II & III obesity and normal weight were compared (Table C3 [this file] ), as opposed to all obesity vs. normal weight. The associations between obesity and increased risk of some NCDs were not mediated by index of overall psychological well-being (Table 7 [rid=Tab7] ) and individual psychological well-being related measures that satisfied pre-mediation conditions (Table C4 [this file] ). 
When the outcome was assessed as the cumulative number of NCDs, obesity (IRR = 1.13; 95% CI = 1.11, 1.16) and psychological well-being related measures (e.g., index of overall psychological well-being measures, life satisfaction, anxiety) were associated with the cumulative number of NCDs (Tables C5 [this file] and C6 [this file] , respectively). Psychological well-being related measures did not mediate the association between obesity and the number of NCDs (Table C7 [this file] ). Furthermore, we did not assess mediation by change in BMI between waves on the association between baseline psychological well-being related measures and NCDs as preconditions were not satisfied (see Tables C8 [this file] and C9 [this file] ). In HRS, no evidence for the interaction between obesity and index of overall psychological well-being was observed in predicting NCDs (Table C10 [this file] ).

Details of the patterns of missingness are provided in Table S1 [this file] and of the imputation procedure in Supplementary methods. 
Analyses in 2015–2018 were based on 152,856 respondents aged ≥ 50 years, including 16,069 from HRS, 38,121 from SHARE, 7040 from ELSA, 6940 from KLoSA, 15,858 from MHAS, 52,393 from LASI, and 16,435 from CHARLS (flow chart in Figure S1 [this file] ); corresponding numbers from 2002 to 2006 are also shown in Figure S1 [this file] . At the 2002–2006 wave, completeness of data varied between 66.9% in MHAS and 97.7% in SHARE; at the 2015–2018 wave, completeness varied between 63.0% in ELSA and 98.5% in KLOSA (Table S1 [this file] ). 
Mean BMI in all BMI categories (underweight, normal weight, overweight, and obese) in 2002–2006 and 2015–2018 is shown in Table S2 [this file] , and the characteristics of the participants at the two time periods are shown in Tables S3 [this file] and S4 [this file] . 
The prevalence of IADL limitations across BMI categories in 2002–2006 and 2015–2018 is shown in Table S5 [this file] . No significant differences were found between the two time periods in the association between BMI (in categories) and IADL limitations (Table S6 [this file] ). Analyses of subgroups (HIC/MIC) suggested differences in associations ( values < 0.01 for men and women) with associations in HIC (OR, 95% CI: 2.86, 1.78–4.59 in men; 2.86, 1.87–4.38 in women) being stronger than those in MIC (OR, 95% CI: 1.37, 1.25–1.51, in men; 1.25, 1.15–1.36 in women) (Figure 1 [rid=obr70054-fig-0001] and Table S6 [this file] ). Analyses of individual IADL revealed a consistent pattern, with underweight being associated with higher odds of all limitations in both men and women (all for overall estimates < 0.05; Figure S2 [this file] ). 
Among men, obesity was associated with lower odds of IADL limitations (OR, 95% CI: 0.80, 0.67–0.96), with no difference in estimates from HIC and MIC ( value = 0.83; Figure 1 [rid=obr70054-fig-0001] and Table S6 [this file] ). This association was mainly due to fewer difficulties in managing money in men with obesity (OR, 95% CI: 0.68, 0.53–0.88; Figure S2 [this file] ). In women, obesity was not associated with IADL limitations in the overall pooled analyses (OR, 95% CI: 1.18, 0.94–1.49), but in HIC, it was associated with higher odds of IADL limitations (OR, 95% CI: 1.40, 1.11–1.77), with a value of 0.02 for the Q test (Figure 1 [rid=obr70054-fig-0001] and Table S6 [this file] ). In women from HIC, these results were mainly due to difficulties in activities such as shopping for groceries (OR, 95% CI: 1.55, 1.32–1.82) and preparing hot meals (OR, 95% CI: 1.25, 1.03–1.53; Figure S2 [this file] ). 
The prevalence of ADL limitations in 2002–2006 and 2015–2018 was higher in the extreme BMI categories (underweight and obesity) in both men and women, except CHARLS where obesity in men had the lowest level of ADL limitations compared with the other BMI categories (Table S7 [this file] ). The results of logistic regression, using the normal weight group as the reference, for the association between BMI and ADL limitations in both time periods are shown in Figure 2 [rid=obr70054-fig-0002] and Table S8 [this file] . In analyses of individual ADL items, underweight was consistently associated with higher odds of all limitations in both men and women (all for overall estimates < 0.05; Figure S3 [this file] ). 
At the 2015–2018 wave, obesity in men was associated with higher odds of ADL limitations in the pooled analyses (OR, 95% CI: 1.38, 1.14–1.65) with some heterogeneity (I = 34.4%) reflected in associations in HIC (OR, 95% CI: 1.57, 1.28–1.91) but not MIC (OR, 95% CI: 1.12, 0.90–1.41), with Q‐test showing differences between the two groups ( value = 0.03) (Figure 2 [rid=obr70054-fig-0002] and Table S8 [this file] ). These results in men were mainly due to higher odds of difficulty in dressing (OR, 95% CI: 1.59, 1.29–1.97; Figure S3 [this file] ). These associations were primarily driven by higher odds of difficulty in bathing (OR, 95% CI: 1.42, 1.13–1.79), dressing (OR, 95% CI: 1.68, 1.32–2.15), getting in/out of bed (OR, 95% CI: 1.41, 1.24–1.59), and using the toilet (OR, 95% CI: 1.41, 1.25–1.60; Figure S3 [this file] ). 
Additional analyses using the 2015–2018 data to examine whether age modified the association between BMI and IADL/ADL limitations suggested no differences in association in those < 65 years or ≥ 65 years in men and women (Table S9 [this file] ). Analyses using Asia‐Pacific WHO thresholds to categorize BMI in KLoSA, LASI, and CHARLS yielded similar results to those in the main analysis, with the direction of the associations remaining unchanged for overall and MIC estimates (Figures S4 [this file] and S5 [this file] ), but differences between HIC and MIC in the association of obesity with ADL limitations in women were attenuated ( value = 0.21; Figure S5 [this file] ).
pub_title: Cross‐Sectional Associations of Body Mass Index With Disability Across High‐ and Middle‐Income Countries in 2002–2006 and 2015–2018
