We adjusted for covariates associated with hypertension or cognitive function, which included age, sex, education level, marital status, current smoking, alcohol drinking, body mass index, physical activity, depressive symptoms, diabetes, cancer, chronic lung diseases, and heart failure.[rid=jah311035-bib-0023] Details of covariates and handling of missing covariates are provided in Supplementary Data S1‐S2 [this file] and Supplementary Tables S2‐S3 [this file] . 
A methodological study has reported that, in an interrupted time series analysis, when the effect size exceeds 0.3, a sample size of 500 and 8 time points are sufficient to ensure adequate statistical power.[rid=jah311035-bib-0027] A detailed description of this model is shown in Supplementary Figures S1–S3 [this file] .[rid=jah311035-bib-0010] ,[rid=jah311035-bib-0011] ,[rid=jah311035-bib-0028] Figure 2 [rid=jah311035-fig-0002] illustrates the cognitive trajectories of the 2 groups, comprising the following kinds of trajectories: the average decline rate from baseline to the end of the follow‐up of the entire hypertension‐free group, and the average difference in (1) baseline scores between the 2 groups, (2) slope during the whole follow‐up period for the hypertension‐free group versus slope of the hypertension group before hypertension onset, and (3) slopes before and slope after hypertension onset. 
In the subgroup analysis, the primary analyses were repeated and stratified by age at hypertension onset, baseline age, BP control status, sex, and education level.[rid=jah311035-bib-0029] An additional linear mixed model further explored whether age and other risk factors modified the effects of hypertension on posthypertension cognitive change (Supplementary Figure S2 [this file] ). 
Supplemental Method 3 and Supplementary Figure S3 [this file] describe the reasons and details of the sensitivity analysis. 
Supplementary Table S4 [this file] shows the number of new‐onset hypertension cases in each wave. At any given time point, 26% to 28% of hypertensive participants were taking anti‐hypertensive medications (Supplementary Table S4 [this file] ). Hypertension occurred at a mean of 4.6 years ±SD: 3.2 after baseline; 55.8% of the participants completed cognitive tests in the final wave (Supplementary Table S5 [this file] ). The 483 participants who were lost to follow‐up tended to be older, less educated, unmarried, smoking, depressive, have chronic lung disease and heart failure, have lower body mass index and baseline cognitive scores, and are less likely to drink or participate in physical activity (Supplementary Table S1 [this file] ). 
Difference in baseline characteristics between those included in the final analysis and those excluded during the sample selection is shown in Supplementary Table S6 [this file] . 
Detailed description for variables is shown in Supplementary Figures S1–S3 [this file] . 
These findings remained consistent after applying IPTW (Supplementary Table S7 [this file] and Supplementary Figure S4 [this file] ). 
Compared with participants developing hypertension between 55 and 64 years, those developing hypertension between 65 and 74 years experienced a more pronounced decline in global cognition after hypertension (β, −0.046 SD/y [95% CI, −0.077 to −0.014];0.004; Supplementary Table S8 [this file] and Figure 3 [rid=jah311035-fig-0003] ). 
Older baseline age (70–99 versus 50–59) was associated with steeper cognitive decline in orientation ( for interaction = 0.002) and global cognition scores ( for interaction 0.005, Supplementary Tables S9–S12 [this file] ). 
While comparing the mean cognitive slope from baseline to the end of the follow‐up between the hypertension group and the hypertension‐free group, the hypertension group had higher baseline scores in all cognitive domains (global cognition; 0.101 SD [95% CI, 0.046–0.166];0.022; Supplementary Table S13 [this file] and Supplementary Figure S5 [this file] ). The “acute cognitive change” at the time of hypertension onset was not significant (Supplementary Table S14 [this file] and Supplementary Figure S6 [this file] ). The primary findings were consistent when taking “acute cognitive change” into consideration or restricting participants to those who attended all follow‐up interviews (Supplementary Tables S14 and S15 [this file] ).

Detailed information on the three cohorts is provided in Additional file 1 [this file] : Methods. An illustrative summary of this study is provided in Additional file 1 [this file] : Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] . 
Depressive symptoms were assessed at each follow-up wave using different versions of the Centre for Epidemiologic Studies of Depression scale (CES-D): the eight-item CES-D (CESD-8) was used in HRS and ELSA, while the ten-item CES-D (CESD-10) was used in CHARLS (Additional file 1 [this file] : Methods). 
Additional information related to the covariates is provided in the Additional file 1 [this file] : Methods. The missing data of covariates were described in Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S1. 
Mean eCRF levels were 9.51 METs in HRS, 8.82 METs in ELSA, and 10.18 METs in CHARLS (Additional file 1 [this file] : Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] ). In addition, we compared the baseline characteristics of participants who were included and those who were excluded in Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S2. 
Baseline characteristics stratified by eCRF levels are presented in Additional file 1 [this file] : Tables S3–S5. 
In all three cohorts, the Schoenfeld residual tests indicated no evidence of violation of the PH assumption for the core variable eCRF (all > 0.05, Additional file 1 [this file] : Tables S6–S8). The cumulative incidence analyses across eCRF levels showed a similar trend to the main results, with higher eCRF associated with reduced depressive symptoms risk in the HRS and ELSA cohorts, while an increased risk was observed in the CHARLS cohort (Additional file 1 [this file] : Figs. 3 [rid=Fig3] –5). 
In the sensitivity analyses, the results did not significantly change after excluding individuals who developed depressive symptoms in the first follow-up wave (Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S9). Similar results were observed after excluding individuals who reported a history of lung diseases, cancer, or CVD at baseline (Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S10). After excluding participants with missing covariate data considered in this study, the association between eCRF and depressive symptoms remained consistent in direction and magnitude (Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S11). Additionally, the results remained consistent with the primary analysis after using multiple imputation, suggesting minimal bias from missing data (Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S12). 
To reduce reverse causality, we excluded individuals who reported depressive symptoms during the first wave of follow-up in sensitivity analyses and the association remained stable (Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S9).

Our exclusion criteria were as follows: (1) age < 45 years old; (2) participants with cognitive-related disorders (see Additional file 1: Table S 1 [this file] )[ 42 [rid=CR42] ]; (3) cases of missing, unclear responses, and rejections both in baseline and follow-up surveys. For the population from ELSA, HRS, and MHAS cohorts, the European and American criteria were utilized for classification, and obesity is defined as BMI ≥ 30 kg/cm [ 45 [rid=CR45] ] (cut-off values of BMI under different standards were shown in Additional file 1: Table S 2 [this file] ) [ 44 [rid=CR44] ]. 
Additional file 1: Table S 3 [this file] [ 20 [rid=CR20] , 51 [rid=CR51] – 55 [rid=CR55] ] provides more information about each scale.

Details of cognitive assessments for each cohort and the method for calculating z-score are provided in the Additional file 1: Table S 4 [this file] and Supplementary Methods 1 [this file] [ 20 [rid=CR20] , 42 [rid=CR42] , 56 [rid=CR56] – 61 [rid=CR61] ]. 
The definition of covariates is reported in the Additionalfile 1: Supplementary Methods 2 [this file] . 
Further explanations on this methodology are provided in the Additionalfile 1: Supplementary Methods 3 [this file] [ 66 [rid=CR66] , 67 [rid=CR67] ]. 
Moreover, Additionalfile 1: Fig. S 4 [this file] and Fig.S 5 [this file] shows basic characteristics of the dynamic transition of depression-obesity status from baseline to outcome wave. 
No matter which obesity indicator was adopted, compared to participants in “Neither condition,” individuals in “Depression alone” and “Comorbidity” at baseline exhibited significantly poorer performance in subsequent cognitive assessments (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] and Additional File 1: Table S 5 [this file] ). 
Therefore, we identified different numbers of trajectories for different cohorts respectively (Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] , Additional file 1: Table S 6 [this file] and S 7 [this file] ). Furthermore, after randomly excluding 20% of participants and repeating the cluster analysis, no substantial differences were found in the newly divided trajectory group (Additionalfile 1: Fig. S 6 [this file] , Table S 6 [this file] and S 7 [this file] ). 
Figure 4 [rid=Fig4] and Additional file 1: Table S 8 [this file] –S 9 [this file] summarize the association between joint trajectories (BMI/WHtR and depressive symptoms) and changes in cognitive function. 
In CHARLS, although no “Abdominal obesity and Depression” group was divided, the group containing depression (Group 2: No abdominal obesity (II) and Depression) also had poorer cognitive development than the reference group ( =− 0.31, 95% CI − 0.39 to − 0.23, < 0.001); meanwhile, participants in this group exhibited a higher WHtR compared to those in the reference group (Additionalfile 1: Table S 9 [this file] ). 
We further stratified the population into different subgroups according to main demographic variables (such as age, gender, education status and so on) to assess the heterogeneity of joint trajectories (BMI and Depressive symptoms and WHtR and Depressive symptoms) on changes in cognitive function (Additional file 2: Fig. S 7 [this file] –S 8 [this file] , and Table S 10 [this file] ). 
The results indicated that compared to those who maintained neither depression nor obesity, participants in other transition groups may have had worse cognitive function (Additional file 3: Table S 11 [this file] –S 13 [this file] and Fig. S 9 [this file] ). (2) We included Weight-Adjusted Waist Index (WWI) as another measure of obesity. It was observed that individuals in the joint trajectory groups with higher WWI and/or depression had poorer cognitive development compared to the reference group (Low WWI and No depression) (Additional file 3: Fig. S 10 [this file] and Table S 14 [this file] –S 15 [this file] ). We also conducted a sensitivity analysis (removed 566 underweight participants) and obtained results that accorded closely with those of the main analyses (Additional file 3: Fig. S 11 [this file] andTable S 16 [this file] ).

This study followed the STROBE (Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology) guidelines (See Supplementary Section 5 in S1 Appendix [this file] ) [ 28 [rid=pone.0297422.ref028] ]. 
To assess the potential impact of excluding participants with missing data, we compared the included and excluded samples (for details, see Supplementary Section 2 in S1 Appendix [this file] ). 
Therefore, an online survey was used to gather consensus from experts on how SNAP behaviours should be for the present analysis (i.e. which measure to choose) and into risk groups (i.e. how many categories to divide each behaviour into and what cut-offs to use; see Supplementary Section 1 in S1 Appendix [this file] ). 
However, across Waves 5 to 8, participants were asked ‘how many portions of vegetables–excluding potatoes–do you eat on a given day?’ and ‘how many portions of fruits do you eat on a given day?’ To make fruit and vegetable intake consistent across waves, we used an established method to match Wave 4 and Waves 5 to 8 responses (see Supplementary Fig S1 in S1 Appendix [this file] ) [ 30 [rid=pone.0297422.ref030] , 31 [rid=pone.0297422.ref031] ]. 
More details on the evaluation of model fit are provided in Supplementary Section 3 in S1 Appendix [this file] . To assess the reliability of the class solution, we conducted a split-half replication where the sample was randomly split in half, and the above RMLCA was performed separately on these split samples to see if the solution for the full sample was replicated between these smaller splits. (for details, see Supplementary Section 4 in S1 Appendix [this file] ). 
The body system disorders with the highest prevalence were: multimorbidity (57.9%), circulatory disorders (50.3%), and disorders of the musculoskeletal and connective system (47.5%) (see Supplementary Table 3 in S1 Appendix [this file] ). 
As the decline in information criteria plateaued around seven classes (screeplot shown in Supplementary Fig S2 in S1 Appendix [this file] ), we opted for the seven-class model. Furthermore, analysis on the split-half samples also indicated that the 7-class solution was the optimal solution, as identical classes were uncovered in each split-half (full details can be found in Supplementary Section 3 in S1 Appendix [this file] ). 
Results were adjusted for disease status and socio-demographic variables at baseline Wave 4 (see Table 6 [rid=pone.0297422.t006] ; for unadjusted results, see Supplementary Table S5 in S1 Appendix [this file] ).

As an initial validation of the method’s ability to uncover novel biological signals within our data, SDA revealed a previously unreported eQTL regulating a cluster of olfactory receptor genes, with the signal being driven predominantly by neuronal and oligodendroglial cells (Component 21 as shown in Figure S1 [this file] ). 
From the 546 components, we first generated a comprehensive annotation, summarized in Supplementary Table 1 [this file] , that details each component’s primary cell-type drivers, top multi-omic features, pathway enrichments, and significant associations with clinical phenotypes (such as cognitive decline and biological sex). 
Notably, microglial transcripts associated with immune-inflammatory responses, such as , , , and , show strong contributions to this component ( Figure 2B [rid=F2] ), suggesting robust microglial activation in the aged brain ( Figure S2A [this file] ). 
Additional evidence comes from H3K9ac ChIP-seq peaks ( Figure S2B [this file] ) enriched for a -like motif. 
Parallel analysis in the independent SEA-AD dataset revealed a correlated transcriptional signature (Component 21) that marks a principal immune axis in aged cortex ( Figure S2C [this file] – E [this file] ). In both cohorts, a few outlier samples display exceptionally high expression ( Figure 2F [rid=F2] ; Figure S2E [this file] ), consistent with sporadic B-cell-driven inflammation. 
This signature is also correlated with SEA-AD Component 21 ( Figure S3B [this file] ). 
Sample scores for this component were significantly higher in females (two-sided Mann-Whitney; = 6808, = 5.3 × 10 , FDR-adjusted = 0.0097) ( Supplementary Figure 4A [this file] ). The cell-type loadings reveal a dynamic axis of opposition between oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs), which contribute positively, and mature oligodendrocytes, which contribute negatively ( Supplementary Figure 4B [this file] ). The biological basis of this axis is underscored by the enrichment of genes involved in canonical growth and differentiation pathways, including RAS, PI3K-Akt and MAPK signaling ( Supplementary Figure 4E [this file] ), providing a cell-type-specific example of the broader pluripotency theme identified in Component 74. 
A second distinct axis of glial variation is captured by Component 177, a program driven almost exclusively by microglia ( Supplementary Figure 5A [this file] ). The transcriptional signature of this component is defined by a coherent set of genes related to mitochondrial bioenergetics ( Supplementary Figure 5B [this file] ), with top hits including (a core subunit of Complex I) and (a subunit of Complex IV). This bioenergetic theme is reinforced at the protein level, where the component’s top hit is Metadherin (MTDH), a protein implicated in cell metabolism and stress ( Supplementary Figure 5C [this file] ). This component’s multi-omic signature is further defined by a coordinated program of DNA methylation changes linked to cellular quality control, including sites near the autophagy initiator ATG9B, the lysosomal enzyme , and the oppositely regulated cell adhesion gene ( Supplementary Figure 5D [this file] ). 
For example, we identified a purely inhibitory neuron component (Component 172) enriched for MAPK signaling and is associated with Alzheimer’s diagnosis (two-sided Mann-Whitney; = 6726, = 0.0004, FDR-adjusted = 0.017) ( Figure S6A [this file] – D [this file] ) ( Munoz & Ammit, 2010 [rid=R27] ; Kim & Choi, 2010 [rid=R17] ), and an excitatory neuron component (Component 277) enriched for GABAergic synapse genes and is associated with cognitive decline (Kruskal-Wallis; = 21.9, = 1.77 × 10 , FDR-adjusted = 0.002) ( Figure S6E [this file] – H [this file] ) ( McQuail et al., 2015 [rid=R24] ; Rozycka & Liguz-Lecznar, 2017 [rid=R32] ).

Tissue preparation, quality control and data preprocessing for snRNA and bulk RNA-seq are described in the Supplementary material [this file] . 
A bimodal distribution was observed in the gene Spearman correlation distribution across cell types for the human MTG model ( Supplementary Fig. 1A [this file] ). The number of genes for the human MTG model ranges from 10 344 to 12 800 genes per cell type for this threshold and from 3920 to 8945 for a very conservative threshold of 0.7, while for the human brain model more than 12 500 genes can be predicted across all the cell types with a Spearman correlation of 0.5 ( Supplementary Fig. 1B [this file] ). 
To enhance the correlation between synthetic bulk RNA from snRNA samples and the corresponding actual bulk RNA and to improve the model's performance, snRNA samples were normalized by total count and log transformed ( Supplementary Fig. 1C [this file] ). Spearman correlations were higher than Pearson correlations in the presence of outliers ( Supplementary Fig. 1D [this file] ). 
Cellformer enables accurate deconvolution of more than 20% genes per cell type than the previous state-of-the-art method at different thresholds ( Supplementary Fig. 1E [this file] ). Especially for highly similar cell types such as OLD and OPCs, BayesPrism accurately predicts less than 5000 genes for a threshold of 0.3, which is two times less than Cellfomer and less than 50 genes at a more stringent threshold ( Supplementary Fig. 1E [this file] ). 
As expected, cell type was the dominant source of variation in the deconvoluted data from both bulk tissue and bulk nuclei RNA-seq (adjusted ANOVA < 0.0001) ( Fig. 1C [rid=awaf285-F1] and Supplementary Fig. 1F [this file] ). 
Overall, the classifiers accurately separated AD from healthy controls with a mean cross-validated AUROC ranging from 0.60 to 0.85 and AUPRC ranging from 0.72 to 0.89 across experiments and cell type, which are significantly superior to a random baseline across all the cell types ( Fig. 1G [rid=awaf285-F1] and Supplementary Fig. 1G [this file] ). 
Additionally, we observed that RNA quality correlates with model performance, while the model remains robust to random computational noise ( Supplementary Fig. 1H [this file] ). 
For validation in another tissue type, we applied Cellformer to peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) using data from different snRNA probing methods ( Supplementary Fig. 2A and B [this file] ). 
Again, we observed that the within-individual gene-wise variation was significantly lower than the total across cell types (Wilcoxon test, < 0.05) ( Supplementary Fig. 2C [this file] ). We then investigated the effect of low expressed genes on gene-wise correlation and found that gene-wise correlation using only highly expressed genes leads to similar results as sample-wise correlation with mean Pearson correlation superior to 0.83 and a mean Spearman correlation superior to 0.78 ( Supplementary Fig. 2D [this file] ). 
Interestingly, the model appears sensitive to data quality and batch effect ( Fig. 3C [rid=awaf285-F3] and D [rid=awaf285-F3] and Supplementary Fig. 3E [this file] ). 
Interestingly, protein phosphatase 3 catalytic subunit alpha ( ) encoding the protein calcineurin A, which plays a crucial role in synaptic plasticity by regulating the activity of N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor channel gating, was found upregulated in AD resilience in EXC. was also found significantly differentially expressed in most of the cerebral cortical excitatory neuron subtypes in the external validation snRNA SEA-AD dataset ( Supplementary Fig. 3A [this file] ). Cross-validated multivariate analysis suggests that not only AST but also EXC, Endo-Mural, MIC and INH might contribute to AD resilience ( Supplementary Fig. 3B [this file] ). 
Cross-validated multivariate analysis suggests the most significant transcriptional signals to separate AD resilience from AD resistance are in AST and EXC ( Supplementary Fig. 3C [this file] ). 
While Cellformer does not output cell proportions, we investigated potential changes in cell type proportions between ADD, AD resilience and AD resistance by comparing the relative content proportion differences among the different groups ( Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] ). 
Despite the high similarity in cell type-specific profiles and marker genes between deconvoluted tissue data and both deconvoluted nuclei and snRNA data ( Fig. 5C [rid=awaf285-F5] , Fig. S5 [this file] ), we observed 100 times more differentially expressed (DE) genes in the deconvoluted tissue compared with nuclei-based RNA data ( Fig. 5E [rid=awaf285-F5] ). 
Interestingly, this discrepancy between RNA content in the nucleus and in the cytoplasm or dendroplasm accounts for more variability than computational errors or technical dropout (see Supplementary Fig. 1H [this file] ). 
For future applications, we recommend focusing on genes that can be predicted with high confidence for downstream analyses ( Supplementary Fig. 1A [this file] ). 
Cellformer performance can vary up to 0.2 Spearman correlation with extreme cell type proportion change ( Supplementary Fig. 2C [this file] ). We anticipate this sensitivity to decrease with larger training datasets, as both gene-wise and sample-wise prediction performance increase with more data (see Fig. 2B [rid=awaf285-F2] and Supplementary Fig. 1A [this file] ).

First, in human tissues this score was tightly associated with the protein abundance and modification status of the DREAM-subunits MuvB and p107/p130, whose phosphorylation status controls DREAM assembly (Pearson r = 0.70, p = 6.8 × 10 , n = 160 human individuals, Supplementary Fig. 1a [this file] – b [this file] , Methods [rid=S10] ). Fourth, increased DREAM activity was associated with lower expression of the proliferative marker MKI67 across cell types (Spearman ρ = −0.56, p = 4.37 × 10 , n = 120 cell types, Supplementary Fig. 1c [this file] ) and tissues (Spearman ρ = −0.45, p = 0.03, n = 23 tissues, Supplementary Fig. 1d [this file] ) – as would be expected given the DREAM complex’s role as a negative regulator of the cell cycle . 
For this purpose we analyzed the dataset (TMS, Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ) , which includes full-length RNA sequencing of single cells collected from 21 organs in 18 C57BL/6JN mice at young (3 months), middle (18 months), and old (24 months) age. DREAM activity was scored in the single-cell RNA-seq data of each of 110,824 cells, revealing a broad range of values that varied significantly across organs and individual mice, and decreased with age ( Supplementary Fig. 2a [this file] – c [this file] ). 
Notably, in the vast majority of tissues, cells with high DREAM activity had significantly greater mutation burdens than those exhibiting low activity ( Fig. 2b [rid=F2] – e [rid=F2] , Supplementary Fig. 2d [this file] – e [this file] ). For instance, liver hepatocytes with greater DREAM activity had significantly greater mutation burdens at each age ( Fig. 2f [rid=F2] ), and this was the case for the majority of cell types ( Fig. 2g [rid=F2] ) and tissues ( Fig. 2h [rid=F2] ) even when correcting for cell proliferation rate ( Supplementary Fig. 2f [this file] – g [this file] ). 
Negative associations were observed across all tissues profiled ( Fig. 3c [rid=F3] ) and became even stronger after controlling for the adult weight (AW) of each species (Spearman ρ: liver = −0.59, p = 6.23 × 10 ; brain = −0.46, p = 1.26 × 10 ; kidney = –0.30, p = 6.23 × 10 ; Fig. 3d [rid=F3] , Supplementary Fig. 3a [this file] – b [this file] ). 
Comparing the DREAM activity of liver, brain, and kidney tissues to previous measurements of species-specific somatic mutation rates (n = 11 species), we found that DREAM complex activity in the liver and brain was positively correlated with somatic mutation rate across species (Liver: ρ = 0.61, p = 6.0 × 10 ; Brain: ρ = 0.49, p = 0.008; Kidney: ρ = −0.31, p = 0.12; Fig. 3f [rid=F3] , Supplementary Fig. 3c [this file] – g [this file] , Methods [rid=S10] ). Further linking DREAM complex activity to species-specific DNA repair capacity, we observed that fibroblasts from species with lower DREAM complex activity exhibited greater resistance to various stress-inducing agents including the mitochondrial respiration inhibitor rotenone; the oxidative damage inducing agents cadmium and paraquat; the alkylating agent methyl methanesulfonate (MMS); UV radiation; and heat (n = 37 cell lines from 6 species , Supplementary Fig. 4a [this file] – h [this file] , Methods [rid=S10] ). 
Using a large cohort of mice from 50 distinct inbred strains (n = 882 mice, Supplementary Fig. 5a [this file] ), half fed a high-fat diet (HFD; 60% calories from fat) and half fed a regular chow diet (CD; 6% calories from fat), we investigated whether strains with lower DREAM activity were protected from the harms of HFD leading to extended survival. 
Lifespan and DREAM activity varied greatly across strains (median lifespan: 704 ± 147 days, mean ± std; Methods [rid=S10] ), with HFD mice having markedly shorter lifespans than CD mice (median survival: HFD = 640 days, CD = 730 days; Supplementary Fig. 5b [this file] – f [this file] ). Controlling for sequencing depth and physiological factors – including weight, weight gain on diet, and blood lipid levels ( Supplementary Fig. 5g [this file] , Methods [rid=S10] ) – a one standard deviation increase in DREAM activity was associated with a 36% increase in risk of death for HFD mice (Hazard ratio = 1.36, p = 9.0 × 10 ; Fig. 4b [rid=F4] ). When fed the CD, there was no significant difference in survival associated with DREAM activity (Hazard ratio = 0.93, p = 0.27; Fig. 4b [rid=F4] , Supplementary Fig. 5h [this file] ). 
Somatic mutations accumulated in tissues at varying rates: from approximately 5 per cell per year in bladder and lung cells, to 10 in brain cells ( Fig. 5b [rid=F5] ), and 22 in fat cells ( Fig. 5c [rid=F5] , Supplementary Fig. 6a [this file] – f [this file] ). 
Unlike DREAM-target genes, the expression of randomly selected sets of genes did not exhibit a significant association with AD diagnosis risk (mean HR = 1.0, Supplementary Fig. 6h [this file] – i [this file] ). However, DREAM activity was not associated with the duration of AD before death ( Supplementary Fig. 6j [this file] ). 
Although the observed relationship between DREAM activity and lifespan does not appear to be confounded by species size ( Fig. 3d [rid=F3] , Supplementary Fig. 3a [this file] – b [this file] ), the possibility of other confounding factors, such as lower metabolic rate – or additional, yet unidentified mechanisms – warrants further investigation. 
DNA- and RNA-based mutation estimates were generally consistent though the rates we now observed were marginally lower ( Supplementary Fig. 6b [this file] – f [this file] ). 
To serve as background distributions for the association of DREAM activity with somatic mutation rate ( Fig. 2g [rid=F2] – h [rid=F2] ), species maximum lifespan ( Fig. 4c [rid=F4] ), and age at AD onset ( Supplementary Fig. 6h [this file] – i [this file] ), the association between the expression of random gene sets and these measures was calculated. 
To do so, we performed an allometric regression of each trait (DREAM activity and ML) on log -transformed AW and compared the resulting residuals (i.e., partial regression of DREAM activity vs. ML with respect to AW, Fig. 5d [rid=F5] , Supplementary Fig. 3a [this file] – b [this file] ). Finally, integrating a previously published estimate of somatic mutation rates for a subset of the same species, we performed analogous cross-species comparisons of DREAM complex activity and somatic mutation rate, both with and without adjusting for AW ( Fig. 4f [rid=F4] , Supplementary Fig. 3c [this file] – g [this file] ). 
Covariates in the Cox model included: the mean DREAM activity value within each strain on each diet; the mean sequencing depth in each strain, to account for any confounding of DREAM activity by differences in sequencing depth between strains; the first principal component (PC1, 25.2% of variance explained, Supplementary Fig. 5g [this file] ) from an analysis of normalized clinical biomarkers and organ weights (variables listed in Supplementary Fig. 5g [this file] ); diet group (chow or high fat diet); and change in body weight since starting the respective diet. 
Model 3 showed the best fit across all mutation types as measured by log-likelihood ( Supplementary Fig. 7a [this file] – f [this file] ) and was therefore used for all statistical comparisons of mutation frequency. One outlier sample – identified by having a Cook’s distance > 1 and total mutation count |Z-score| > 3 across both mutation classes – was removed ( Supplementary Fig. 7g [this file] – i [this file] ). 
Other data can be accessed through the respective publications (see Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ).

The distribution of categorical and quantitative measures of AD- and other pathologies, as well as quantitative clinical phenotypes in the cohort of 427 study participants ( Figure 1C [rid=F1] ) closely reflected that of the entire ROSMAP cohort ( Data S1 [this file] , page 1A [this file] - 1Q [this file] ). 
Based on Leiden clustering, marker gene analysis, and comparisons with previously published data we annotated 54 high-resolution cell types in 12 major groups ( Figure S1 [rid=SD2] and Data S1 [this file] , page 1R [this file] and 1S [this file] ). Transcriptomic cell types were largely conserved across individuals, as most of the identified cellular subsets contained nuclei from the large majority of donors ( Data S1 [this file] , page 1R [this file] and 1S [this file] ). 
One notable exception was diabetes, which exhibited a remarkably cell-type-specific association with gene expression alterations in oligodendrocytes ( Figures 2A [rid=F2] and Data S1 [this file] , page 2 [this file] ). We also observed sex-specific responses to AD pathology ( Data S1 [this file] , page 2H [this file] ), consistent with previous observations . 
The overlap of AD-associated genes between excitatory neuron subtypes was also indicated by self-organizing map (SOM) analyses of gene-trait correlations ( Methods S1 [this file1] , page 1A [this file1] ), was broadly observed across the expression level spectrum ( Data S1 [this file] , page 3A [this file] ), and was further confirmed using a permutation test ( Data S1 [this file] , page 3B [this file] and 3C [this file] ). 
To validate our differential expression results, we compared them to those of previously published single-nucleus RNA sequencing studies of Alzheimer's disease and found a significant positive correlation for gene expression changes across multiple cell types, with particularly high concordance between our results and those of other studies analyzing the PFC ( Data S1 [this file] , page 3D [this file] - 3G [this file] ). To further test the robustness and generalizability of our results, we divided the full cohort into two non-overlapping random subsets and found a highly significant overlap of differentially expressed genes between the results of the original analysis across the entire cohort and both random sub-cohorts ( Data S1 [this file] , page 4A [this file] ). Furthermore, the association scores and effect sizes of significant DEGs were strongly correlated between the full cohort and both sub-cohorts ( Data S1 [this file] , page 4B [this file] and 4C [this file] ). We also confirmed that the observed associations between gene expression and global AD pathology remained significant after accounting for additional potential confounding factors such as technical variability, sex, diabetes, and after removing ambient RNA using DecontX ( Data S1 [this file] , page 4D [this file] - 4F [this file] ). 
A permutation test revealed a highly significant overlap of global AD pathology associated DEGs between the two datasets ( Data S1 [this file] , page 5A [this file] ). Interestingly, we observed that a large fraction of genes confirmed to be altered in the prefrontal cortex by both our dataset and the De Jager dataset were also significantly associated with the continuous pseudo-progression score of AD severity in the MTG dataset ( Data S1 [this file] , page 5B [this file] and 5C [this file] ). 
Consistent with this hypothesis, genes negatively associated with multiple measures of AD pathology across multiple excitatory neuron subtypes were confirmed to be decreased in AD brains based on quantitative proteomics ( Figures S3H [rid=SD4] - S3K [rid=SD4] ) , a finding that was further supported by cell type-specific RT-qPCR ( Data S1 [this file] , page 6A [this file] ) and multiplex RNA in situ hybridization ( Data S1 [this file] , page 7A [this file] - 7C [this file] ). A significant upregulation of HNRNPA2B1 in individuals with a pathologic diagnosis of AD was corroborated using RT-qPCR ( Data S1 [this file] , page 6B [this file] and 6C [this file] ) and multiplexed RNA in situ hybridization ( Data S1 [this file] , page 7D [this file] and 7E [this file] ). 
Consistent with these results, RT-qPCR on neuronal nuclei confirmed a significant downregulation of BDH1 and GPCPD1 in individuals with a pathologic diagnosis of AD ( Data S1 [this file] , page 6D [this file] and 6E [this file] ). While the consensus signature is based on gene expression differences in excitatory neurons, dysregulation of lipid metabolism and cholesterol biosynthesis genes was also evident in astrocytes ( Figure 3F [rid=F3] ), an observation that was further supported by immunohistochemical analysis of postmortem prefrontal cortex tissue ( Data S1 [this file] , page 8A [this file] - 8C [this file] ). Alterations in lipid metabolism were accompanied by widespread changes of genes encoding the mitochondrial electron transport chain components and individuals with a high level of AD pathology exhibited a decreased expression of several genes encoding components of the mitochondrial intermembrane space bridging complex (MIB), a complex that is of central importance for the maintenance of mitochondrial inner membrane architecture ( Figures 3G [rid=F3] , 3H [rid=F3] , and Data S1 [this file] , page 8D [this file] ) . 
The gene expression differences related to synaptic signaling, RNA splicing, lipid metabolism, and mitochondrial function observed in the PFC were largely confirmed in a separate dataset derived from the middle temporal gyrus ( Figures 3D [rid=F3] and Data S1 [this file] , page 6F [this file] - 6I [this file] ), and were further supported by bulk RNA sequencing data from the ROSMAP cohorts (n = 638), quantitative proteomics data ( Data S1 [this file] , page 6J [this file] - 6O [this file] ), and a group-based differential expression analysis ( Methods S1 [this file1] , page 2 [this file1] and page 3 [this file1] ). 
Many of these genes were themselves positively associated with multiple measures of AD pathology across multiple excitatory neuron subtypes and were also positively correlated with cohesin complex expression in excitatory neurons in other brain regions ( Figures S4F [rid=SD5] - S4H [rid=SD5] and Data S1 [this file] , page 9A [this file] - 9C [this file] ). A coordinated increase in the expression of the cohesin complex and DNA damage response genes in AD was also observed in oligodendrocytes ( Figures 4E [rid=F4] - 4G [rid=F4] and Data S1 [this file] , page 9D [this file] ). 
We observed a convergence in gene expression changes associated with different types of AD pathology, as well as a significant overlap of DEGs between excitatory neuron subtypes, at both the early and late stages of disease progression ( Data S1 [this file] , page 10A [this file] - 10C [this file] ), consistent with the results based on the entire cohort of individuals. 
Additional synaptic genes positively associated with global cognitive function included NUMB and VGF ( Figures 6D [rid=F6] and 6E [rid=F6] ), a finding that was further corroborated through RT-qPCR ( Data S1 [this file] , page 11 A [this file] ) and immunohistochemical analysis ( Data S1 [this file] , page 11B [this file] and 11C [this file] ). 
First, we assessed whether the proportions of major cell types change with the progression of AD pathology and found that the relative abundance of most major cell types did not significantly change ( Figures 7A [rid=F7] and 7B [rid=F7] , and Data S1 [this file] , page 12A [this file] and 12B [this file] ). One exception was the population of microglial cells that exhibited a significant increase in its relative abundance in individuals with the highest levels of global AD pathology, neuritic plaque burden, and overall amyloid level ( Figures 7A [rid=F7] and 7B [rid=F7] , and Data S1 [this file] , page 12A [this file] - 12D [this file] ). By contrast, excitatory neurons trended towards a subtle decrease in their relative abundance with the progression of AD pathology, reaching significance when considering the neocortex-specific measure of global AD pathology ( Figures 7A [rid=F7] and 7B [rid=F7] , and Data S1 [this file] , page 12B [this file] ). 
Consistent with the results of the overrepresentation analysis, the relative abundance of the entire subclass of SST inhibitory neurons, as well as the relative abundance of individual subtypes of the group of selectively vulnerable SST neurons, was significantly decreased in the subset of individuals with the highest levels of global AD pathology, neurofibrillary tangle burden, and tangle density, a finding that was further confirmed using a quasi-binomial regression model ( Figures 7E [rid=F7] and 7F [rid=F7] , and Data S1 [this file] , page 13A [this file] - 13D [this file] ). The relative abundance of many excitatory neuron subtypes trended towards a decrease with the progression of AD pathology but did not reach significance ( Data S1 [this file] , page 13E [this file] and 13F [this file] ). 
Analyzing the combined dataset using quasi-binomial regression we confirmed a decrease in the relative abundance of the entire subclass of SST inhibitory neurons and all three vulnerable SST neuron subtypes in individuals with higher levels of AD pathology ( Data S1 [this file] , page 13G [this file] and 13H [this file] ). 
The relative abundance of inhibitory neurons trended to be highest in the subset of individuals with the highest level of global cognitive function and was significantly decreased in the subset of individuals with the lowest scores in the cognitive domains perceptual orientation and semantic memory ( Data S1 [this file] , page 14A [this file] - 14D [this file] ). Likewise, the relative abundance of excitatory neurons was significantly decreased in the subset of individuals with the lowest scores in the cognitive domain perceptual orientation ( Data S1 [this file] , page 14B [this file] and 14D [this file] ). 
The relative abundance of the entire LAMP5 RELN group of inhibitory neurons and the entire subclass of SST inhibitory neurons was significantly decreased in individuals scoring low on tests of global cognitive function, episodic memory, perceptual orientation, and semantic memory ( Figures 7H [rid=F7] and Data S1 [this file] , page 15A [this file] ). These findings were further supported by additional group-based analyses comparing individuals with high versus low cognitive function and by quasi-binomial regression analysis (Data S1 [this file] , page 15B [this file] - 15D [this file] ). In general, we did not find a significant association between the relative abundance of excitatory neuron subtypes and cognitive function, except for layer 2/3 (L2-3) excitatory neurons (Exc L2-3 CBLN2 LINC02306), which were positively associated with the measure of perceptual orientation ( Data S1 [this file] , page 16A [this file] and 16B [this file] ). 
These findings were further supported by a quasi-binomial regression analysis of the combined snRNA-seq dataset encompassing 615 individuals ( Data S1 [this file] , page 16C [this file] - 16E [this file] ). 
These findings were further supported by quasi-binomial regression analysis ( Data S1 [this file] , page 17A [this file] - 17C [this file] ), RT-qPCR ( Data S1 [this file] , page 17D [this file] ), chromogenic RNA in situ hybridization ( Data S1 [this file] , page 17E [this file] - 17G [this file] ), immunohistochemical analysis ( Data S1 [this file] , page 18A [this file] - 18C [this file] ), a quasi-binomial regression analysis of the combined dataset across 615 individuals ( Data S1 [this file] , page 18D [this file] - 18F [this file] ), and multiplex RNA in situ hybridization analysis of post-mortem prefrontal cortex tissue ( Data S1 [this file] , page 19 [this file] ). 
Overall, we found that the results of our original analysis were largely confirmed after removing ambient RNA contamination ( Data S1 [this file] , page 4F [this file] ).

Cohesin, a protein complex that regulates sister chromatid cohesion, homologous recombination, and DNA looping, was most consistently and significantly elevated across excitatory neuron subtypes from the PFC of individuals with high levels of AD pathology ( Figures 4A [rid=F4] and S4A [this file] - S4C [this file] ) and was also positively associated with global AD pathology in PFC oligodendrocytes ( Figure 4A [rid=F4] ). Increased expression of the cohesin complex in individuals with high levels of AD pathology was also observed in a subset of excitatory neuron subtypes in other brain regions ( Figure 4A [rid=F4] ) and further confirmed based on bulk RNA sequencing data from the ROSMAP cohorts (n = 638) ( Figure 4B [rid=F4] ), RT-qPCR analysis ( Figure S4D [this file] ), and quantitative proteomics data ( Figure 4C [rid=F4] ) . 
Interestingly, many genes positively correlated with the cohesin complex including the chromatin regulators ATRX, ZBTB1, SIRT1, CHD1, BPTF, and ZBTB7A have been reported to play a critical role in the cellular response to DNA damage ( Figures 4D [rid=F4] and S4E [this file] ) . Other genes positively correlated with the cohesin complex are recruited to sites of DNA damage (NIPBL) , regulate base excision repair (USP47) , promote DNA damage recovery (BAZ1B) , regulate the DNA damage response (CDKN2AIP) , and play a critical role in DNA damage repair (MACROD1) ( Figures 4D [rid=F4] and S4E [this file] ). Many of these genes were themselves positively associated with multiple measures of AD pathology across multiple excitatory neuron subtypes and were also positively correlated with cohesin complex expression in excitatory neurons in other brain regions ( Figures S4F [this file] - S4H [this file] and Data S1 [rid=SD1] , page 9A [rid=SD1] - 9C [rid=SD1] ).

The overlap of AD-associated genes between excitatory neuron subtypes was also indicated by self-organizing map (SOM) analyses of gene-trait correlations ( Methods S1 [this file] , page 1A [this file] ), was broadly observed across the expression level spectrum ( Data S1 [rid=SD1] , page 3A [rid=SD1] ), and was further confirmed using a permutation test ( Data S1 [rid=SD1] , page 3B [rid=SD1] and 3C [rid=SD1] ). 
The gene expression differences related to synaptic signaling, RNA splicing, lipid metabolism, and mitochondrial function observed in the PFC were largely confirmed in a separate dataset derived from the middle temporal gyrus ( Figures 3D [rid=F3] and Data S1 [rid=SD1] , page 6F [rid=SD1] - 6I [rid=SD1] ), and were further supported by bulk RNA sequencing data from the ROSMAP cohorts (n = 638), quantitative proteomics data ( Data S1 [rid=SD1] , page 6J [rid=SD1] - 6O [rid=SD1] ), and a group-based differential expression analysis ( Methods S1 [this file] , page 2 [this file] and page 3 [this file] ). 
We defined cell-type-restricted DEGs as genes significantly altered in no more than two cell types and found that a considerable fraction of DEGs fell within this category ( Methods S1 [this file] , page 4A [this file] - 4C [this file] ). We successfully identified cell type-restricted AD-associated gene expression changes not only at the level of major cell types but also among excitatory subtypes and inhibitory neuron subclasses ( Methods S1 [this file] , page 4D [this file] - 4F [this file] ) and confirmed a large fraction of these alterations in the SEA-AD dataset ( Methods S1 [this file] , page 4G [this file] and 4H [this file] ). 
To determine the genes linked to cognitive resilience in the aged human brain, we analyzed differential gene expression in excitatory neuron subtypes with regard to the cognitive resilience (CR) and cognitive decline resilience (CDR) measures (see methods) ( Methods S1 [this file] , page 5A [this file] and 5B [this file] ). DEGs significantly associated with cognitive resilience were identified in multiple excitatory neuron subtypes ( Methods S1 [this file] , page 5C [this file] ). We identified 5 genes (HES4, PDE10A, RPH3A, ST6GAL2, and UST) that were differentially expressed relative to at least one cognitive resilience measure in at least 8 excitatory neuron cell types ( Methods S1 [this file] , page 5D [this file] and 5E [this file] ). These genes were also robustly differentially expressed relative to all the cognitive resilience measures in at least 1 excitatory cell type ( Methods S1 [this file] , page 5D [this file] and 5E [this file] ). Greater expression of these genes in resilient individuals was further confirmed based on an overrepresentation analysis ( Methods S1 [this file] , page 5F [this file] - 5K [this file] ), bulk RNA-sequencing data from the ROSMAP cohorts ( Methods S1 [this file] , page 5L [this file] - 5O [this file] ), RT-qPCR analysis of RNA isolated from PFC post-mortem tissue ( Methods S1 [this file] , page 5P [this file] ), and a group-based differential expression analysis comparing individuals with both pathologic and cognitive diagnoses of AD versus individuals with no cognitive impairment despite a pathologic diagnosis of AD ( Methods S1 [this file] , page 5Q [this file] ). 
A simulation-based power analysis revealed considerably lower statistical power estimates for less abundant cell types such as those associated with the vasculature and inhibitory neuron subtypes ( Methods S1 [this file] , page 6A [this file] ). And our empirical investigation revealed a positive association between the number of cells evaluated per participant and the number of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) identified ( Methods S1 [this file] , page 6B [this file] and 6C [this file] ). 
We found that the factors estimated by RUV-seq effectively captured the variance attributable to known technical covariates ( Methods S1 [this file] , page 7 [this file] ). 
To quantify cognitive resilience, we computed a cognitive resilience score (CR score) as the difference between the observed cognition and the cognition predicted by a linear regression model, given the level of pathology ( Methods S1 [this file] , page 5A [this file] and 5B [this file] ). Using this approach, we computed Cognitive Resilience (CR) scores based on the measure of global cognitive function and Cognitive Decline Resilience (CDR) scores based on the measure estimating the rate of change of global cognitive function over time ( Methods S1 [this file] , page 5A [this file] and 5B [this file] ). 
For each individual, a score was calculated as the difference between the observed cognition (y) and the predicted cognition (y) by the model based on their level of pathology (x) ( Methods S1 [this file] , page 5A [this file] and 5B [this file] ).

Fragment formation was independent of genotype, as treatment with rotenone also induced this fragment in WT neurons ( Figure S3A [this file] ). Surprisingly, we did not observe the complementary C-terminal fragment, suggesting that this fragment is degraded ( Figure S3C [this file] ). 
Treatment with antimycin A, an ETC complex III inhibitor, but not CCCP, a proton-gradient uncoupler, or oligomycin, an ATP Synthase inhibitor, led to 25kD fragment formation ( Figure S3D [this file] ). 
The antioxidant N-acetyl-cysteine (NAC) partially counteracted the rotenone-induced formation of the 25kD fragment ( Figure 6K [rid=F6] ). 25kD fragment formation was not due to cell death via apoptosis or ferroptosis, as treatment with the pan-caspase inhibitor ZVAD-MVK, the ferroptosis inhibitor ferrostatin, or the ferroptosis inducer RSL3 did not change fragment levels ( Figure S3E [this file] - H [this file] ). 
To identify the cellular protease that induces the 25kD fragment, we treated neurons with rotenone and inhibitors of common tau proteases: cathepsins (E-64), calpain (calpastatin), and the proteasome (MG132) ( Figure S3I [this file] - J [this file] ). Proteasome activity measured by native gel revealed a decrease in activity of 30S, 26S and 20S proteasomes upon rotenone treatment without changes in levels of proteasomal proteins ( Figure 7B [rid=F7] and C [rid=F7] , Figure S3K [this file] ). Synaptosomal proteasomes showed the same changes in activity as the overall pool of proteasomes ( Figure S3L [this file] - N [this file] ). Treatment with a membrane-impermeable proteasome inhibitor ruled out the involvement of membrane-bound proteasomes in the production or extracellular release of the 25kD fragment ( Figure S3O [this file] ). 
Knockdown of the PA28 subunit PA28β increased 25kD fragment levels ( Figure 7C [rid=F7] , right, Figure S3P [this file] - Q [this file] ). 
We next asked whether direct oxidation of tau contributes to 25kD fragment formation. 0N3R tau only has one cysteine, C291, and expression of GFP-0N3R tau C291A did not change fragment levels compared to a WT transgene ( Figure S3R [this file] - S [this file] ).

We annotated 1,197,032 snRNA-seq cells from 84 matched individuals into eight major cell types based on known marker genes ( Fig. 2 [rid=GR280436RENF2] B; Supplemental Fig. S1A [this file] ). We further annotated 18 neuronal cell subtypes based on the classifications described in the original paper ( Supplemental Fig. S2 [this file] ; Gabitto et al. 2024 [rid=GR280436RENC24] ). Among these, we observed that the L2/3 IT subtype of excitatory neurons showed a significant decrease in cell counts at the high ADNC stage compared with other stages, whereas the L4 IT subtype of excitatory neurons exhibited a significant increase at the high ADNC stage ( Supplemental Fig. S3 [this file] ). Notably, microglia cell counts showed a significant increase at the high ADNC stage compared with the non-AD and intermediate ADNC stages ( Supplemental Fig. S4 [this file] ). 
For snATAC-seq, we identified 740,875 cells distributed across six major cell types using the same marker genes as for snRNA-seq annotation ( Fig. 2 [rid=GR280436RENF2] C; Supplemental Fig. S1B [this file] ). 
Notably, ADNC strongly correlated with the continuous pseudoprogression score in their study ( = 0.75, = 2.08 × 10 ) ( Supplemental Fig. S5 [this file] ; Gabitto et al. 2024 [rid=GR280436RENC24] ). 
In microglia, significantly enriched pathways included hypoxia response, chemotaxis, antigen presentation via MHC-II, and lipid/lipoprotein metabolism ( Supplemental Fig. S6 [this file] ), overall consistent with a previous study ( Gabitto et al. 2024 [rid=GR280436RENC24] ). 
The analysis revealed that the nine candidate drugs—galantamine, resveratrol, imatinib, deferoxamine, captopril, staurosporine, quercetin, procaine, and probucol—were predominantly enriched in the high stage ( Supplemental Table S9 [this file2] ; Supplemental Fig. S7 [this file] ), indicating that these compounds primarily target gene programs associated with later stages of AD progression. 
In addition, we visualized the top enriched drugs across the low, intermediate, and high stages to highlight their stage-specific activity patterns ( Supplemental Fig. S8 [this file] ). 
Major cell types were annotated according to established marker genes ( Morabito et al. 2021 [rid=GR280436RENC49] ; Mathys et al. 2023 [rid=GR280436RENC47] ; Xiong et al. 2023 [rid=GR280436RENC79] ; Emani et al. 2024 [rid=GR280436RENC21] ; Gabitto et al. 2024 [rid=GR280436RENC24] ) and verified for consistency with prior studies ( Supplemental Fig. S1 [this file] ; Gabitto et al. 2024 [rid=GR280436RENC24] ).

To automatically annotate cells, we utilized differentially expressed genes for specific cell populations, obtained from a publicly available reference atlas of human peripheral mononuclear blood cells (PBMC Atlas) [ 23 [rid=CR23] ], We chose the PBMC Atlas as the reference for our study due to its comprehensive and accurate annotation of human peripheral blood cell types, which includes a variety of well-characterized immune cell populations at both transcriptomic and proteomic levels (Figure S1 [this file] A). 
The function also assessed their statistical significance (Figure S1 [this file] B). 
The heatmaps with median signature scores clearly showed that higher median signature scores corresponded to the correct population (Figure S1 [this file] C). 
However, since for each distribution, there is only a cell group in which values are significantly higher than all the other groups, the simple inspection of PBMC3k UMAP showing the different signature scores was sufficient to annotate the expected cell populations (Figure S1 [this file] D). 
The evaluation was conducted on three benchmark datasets of increasing complexity (Table S1 [this file] ): PBMC3k; NEURO_test [ 28 [rid=CR28] ], comprising 119,152 nuclei from the human middle temporal gyrus, used to assess CIA’s scalability and robustness on large, granular transcriptomic data; KUL3 [ 29 [rid=CR29] ], a colorectal cancer dataset from six patients (Katholieke Universiteit Leuven) containing 27 distinct cell types, representative of high tissue heterogeneity. 
This setup ensured that all classifiers, whether signature-based or model-based, relied on the same biological sources (see Methods and Supplementary Table S1 [this file] and repository https://github.com/ingmbioinfo/CIA_benchmark/ (https://github.com/ingmbioinfo/CIA_benchmark/) for full reproducibility). 
When comparing classifier performance on the PBMC3k dataset, CIA reached the highest accuracy and F1 score while also achieving the shortest runtime (Figs. 2 [rid=Fig2] B, 3 [rid=Fig3] A, Figure S2 [this file] , one-sided t-test, -value < 0.01 for running time). 
Importantly, CIA outperformed all other methods in terms of speed (Figs. 2 [rid=Fig2] D, 3 [rid=Fig3] B, Figure S4 [this file] , one-sided t-test, -value < 0.01), classifying approximately 120,000 cells in one minute or less than one second using 8 CPUs (CIA Python). 
For the KUL3 dataset, where high tissue complexity generally reduced classification accuracy, CIA still ranked among the best-performing tools, with an F1 score of 0.78 compared to Celltypist, the top performer (F1 = 0.79) (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] F, Figure S6 [this file] ). 
First, the 'GOMF_STRUCTURAL_CONSTITUENT_OF_MYELIN_SHEATH' (GO:0019911) signature was significantly enriched in oligodendrocytes within the neuro training dataset, consistent with their established role in myelination (Figure S7 [this file] A, B, one-sided t-test < 0.01). 
To harmonize biological priors across methods, we explicitly documented the knowledge sources used by each tool (Supplementary Table S1 [this file] ). In addition, to broaden the benchmarking we included deep learning–based methods such as scANVI and scBalance, which were trained or applied on the same reference datasets used for the other tools (Table S1 [this file] ).

context_description: To investigate Lrp4+ cells in the brain, we crossed Lrp4‐CreER mice with Ai9 mice to generate an Lrp4 reporter mouse line, Lrp4‐CreER; Ai9, in which the Lrp4‐CreER mice express CreER under the control of the Lrp4 promoter, and the Ai9 allele expresses a Cre‐dependent tdTomato (tdTom) reporter (Figure S1A [this file] ). We injected tamoxifen (TAM) into Lrp4creER; Ai9 mice at P10, P30, and P60, respectively, and examined and compared Lrp4+ cells (tdTom positive) at the P70 cortex (Figure S1A [this file] ). The number of Lrp4+ cells incrementally increased along the pia and in the cortex from P10–P60 TAM‐injected mice (Figure S1B,C [this file] ), whereas GFAP+ astrocyte density is largely unchanged (Figure S1D [this file] ). Interestingly, 15%–20% of tdTom+ cells at the pia are positive for GFAP from P10–P30 but then drop to 0%–10% by P60 (Figure S1E [this file] ).

context_description:
To determine whether these GFAP‐ Lrp4+ cells are truly astrocytes, we used RNAscope and co‐immunostaining analysis to address if these Lrp4+ (tdTom+) cells (TAM injected at P60 and examined at P90) (Figure S2A [this file] ) co‐expressed Glast1, a marker of astrocytes. Moreover, these Lrp4+ cells were negative for IBA1 (a marker for microglia), Oligo2 (a marker for oligodendrocytes), or NeuN (a neuronal marker) (Figure S2B,C [this file] ). This view was further supported by analyzing the scRNAseq database of Allen's Brain Institute, which showed abundantly expression of Lrp4 in astrocytes in both mouse (Yao et al. 2021 [rid=glia70114-bib-0077] ) and human brains (Hodge et al. 2019 [rid=glia70114-bib-0029] ; Bakken et al. 2021 [rid=glia70114-bib-0004] ) (Figure S2D [this file] ). 
Morphologically, both GFAP+ and Lrp4+ pial membrane‐associated cells appeared to be elongated, exhibiting features of “fibrotic” astrocytes described in white matter, in contrast to those inside of the cortex (Figure S3 [this file] ), or astrocytes described in gray matter (Miller and Raff 1984 [rid=glia70114-bib-0051] ; Zhou et al. 2019 [rid=glia70114-bib-0086] ).

We crossed LSL‐DTR mice, in which DTR is expressed in a Cre‐dependent manner, with Lrp4‐creER; Ai9 mice to generate an inducible Lrp4+ cell ablation/reporter mouse line (LSL‐DTR; Lrp4creER; Ai9) (Figure S4A [this file] ). Mice received TAM at 2 MO of age, followed by DT treatment at a non‐toxic dose [30 μg/kg, administered every other day via intraperitoneal (i.p.) injection for three doses], or saline at 3 MO, and were sacrificed at 4 MO (Figure S4A [this file] ). Under these conditions, ~50% ablation was achieved in the pia and top cortical layers (L1‐4) (Figure S4C [this file] ). 
Given that Lrp4+ astrocyte ablation was most effective in cortical layers 1–4 (Figure S4 [this file] ), we focused our subsequent analyses on these regions.

Moreover, in the iDTR ablation mice, Lrp4+ astrocytes along the pia did not upregulate GFAP, whereas Lrp4+ astrocytes in the cortex did (Figure S5A,B [this file] ). These findings suggest that Lrp4+ astrocytes negatively influence GFAP+ astrocytes in the cortex, but positively affect pial GFAP+ astrocytes (Figure S5C [this file] ). 
Supporting this, ablation of Lrp4 astrocytes leads to increased densities of GFAP astrocytes and CD11b /IBA1 microglia (Figures S5 [this file] and S6 [rid=glia70114-supitem-0006] ), both of which are markers commonly associated with heightened inflammatory responses.

Among midlife retirees ( = 1021), alcohol consumption at Phase 9 was associated with increased pain severity at Phase 12 (β = 0.15, 95% CI: 0.04–0.25), corresponding to a 49.3% increase in above-moderate-pain probability per SD increase ( Supplementary Fig. S10 [this file] ). Among high-SEP participants ( = 2739), only association from Phases 7 to 9 reached borderline significance (β = 0.06, 95% CI: 0.00–0.13), corresponding to a 13.3% increase per SD increase ( Supplementary Fig. S12 [this file] ).

Baseline characteristics of low-SEP participants matched the social disadvantages described in the “alcohol-related harm paradox,” such as higher proportions of adverse health indicators (obesity, current smoking, hypertension, CVD) and lower mental wellbeing compared to higher SEP groups ( Supplementary Table S16 [this file] ), but limited power undermined the robustness of this association ( Katikireddi et al. 2017 [rid=ref22] ).

Fourth, though we acquired poor model fit from analyses with scalar measurement invariance for ordinal pain outcomes, acceptable model fit was achieved under approximate invariance with relaxed Bayesian priors, suggesting that threshold deviations across phases were modest ( Supplementary Table S18 [this file] ).

Since these subjects were under increased risk of death and their adherence to the SEAD differed from that of their disease-free counterparts at the pooled sample and country levels ( , Supplementary material online [this file] , ), this could have biased the study results if illness had led individuals to change their dietary habits. 
This convergence towards the pooled estimates was especially marked for all-cause mortality ( for country interaction = 0.77), as even the one-time outliers (i.e. United Kingdom) reached significance (see Supplementary material online [this file] , ). 
Moreover, the study associations were not significantly different between countries, even if the distribution of potential confounders (both measured and unmeasured) between SEAD categories was likely unequal (see Supplementary material online [this file] , ).

The study population consisted of 10,216 participants who had complete data on covariates and were free of dementia at baseline in 1985–1988 (Figure S1 [this file] ). Figure S1 [this file] also shows the derivation of the study populations at age 55, 60, 65, and 70 years. 
Of the 3275 participants who developed CVD over the 31.6‐year span of the study, we had data on the four lifestyle factors after CVD diagnosis on 1536 participants (Figure S1 [this file] ). Mean age at CVD diagnosis was 61.2 years (SD 10.5) and 22.5% were female (Table S1 [this file] ). The 391 participants with CVD excluded from these analyses due to missing data on lifestyle factors post‐CVD were less educated, more often had type 2 diabetes and hypertension prior to or at CVD onset, and had poorer lifestyle factors compared to those included in the analyses (Table S2 [this file] ). 
After removing physical activity, the association between number of lifestyle factors and incident dementia was no longer statistically significant (HR 0.80, 95% CI 0.60–1.06), Table S3 [this file] ). Excluding participants with prevalent diabetes ( = 133, Table S4 [this file] ) or participants whose lifestyle factors were assessed >6 years after CVD diagnosis ( = 114, Table S5 [this file] ) yielded results consistent with those obtained in the main analysis. There was no evidence of sex differences in these analyses (all values for interaction >.10; Table S6 [this file] ), although there was some evidence of race/ethnicity differences in the number of lifestyle factors and body mass index at recommended levels ( ‐values for interaction .028 and .033, respectively; Table S6 [this file] ). Among participants of White ethnicity, the HR for dementia was 0.65 (95% CI 0.51–0.83) per additional lifestyle factor at recommended levels (Table S7 [this file] ). In addition, all individual lifestyle factors, except guideline‐recommended levels of dietary habits, were associated with incident dementia among participants of White ethnicity (Table S7 [this file] ). Analysis using inverse‐probability weighting to account for missing data on the lifestyle factors led to results that were consistent with those in the main analysis (Table S8 [this file] ).

Components of the metabolic-obesity phenotypes were measured six times (1991, 1997, 2002, 2007, 2012, and 2015) for each participant and data were extracted from measurements taken at < 60 (range: 40 to 59.9 years), 60 to < 70 (range: 60 to 69.9 years), and ≥ 70 (range: 70 to 84 years) using multiple waves of the study (Additional file 1 [this file] : Fig. S1). 
We also excluded 1274 (12.4%) participants with missing data on metabolic-obesity phenotypes, three participants with missing data on covariates, and 55 (0.5%) participants with BMI < 18.5 kg/m , leading to 7109 (69.0%) participants free of dementia in the analyses of exposures measured before 60 years (mean age at clinical examination 55.1 years, standard deviation [SD] 3.0 years; Additional file 1 [this file] : Fig. S1). 
Additional file 1 [this file] : Fig. S1 describes the sample selection in the analysis for metabolic-obesity phenotypes measured at ages < 60 years, 60 to < 70 years, and ≥ 70 years. 
Obesity and unhealthy metabolic status measured before 60 years, and considered separately, were associated with dementia; the mutually adjusted hazard ratios (HR) being 1.31 (95% CI: [1.00, 1.73]) and 1.27 (95% CI: [1.02, 1.57]), respectively (Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S1). 
Analyses using inverse probability weighting to account for missing data (Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S2), as well as the exclusion of non-white participants (Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S3) and prevalent cases of CVD (Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S4), yielded results similar to that in the main analyses. Further analyses with an alternative threshold (≥ 1 instead of ≥ 2 unhealthy metabolic components) show a similar pattern to that in the main analyses (Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S5). 
The change in MHO status across the 3 age groups is shown in Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S6. 
Of the 8097 participants at the 1997 wave (the baseline in these analyses), data were missing for 406 (5.0%) participants on metabolic-obesity phenotypes, for 531 (6.6%) participants on cognitive tests, for one participant on covariates, resulting in 7156 (88.4%) participants in the analyses on cognitive decline (Additional file 1 [this file] : Fig. S2), their characteristics at baseline are shown in Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S7. 
Five trajectories of metabolic-obesity phenotypes were identified (Additional file 1 [this file] : Tables S8 and S9): persistent MHNO (45% of participants were in this group), transition from MUNO to MHNO (5%), transition from MHNO to MUNO (9%), persistent/transition to unhealthy metabolic status and/or transition to obesity (32%), and transition to obesity or persistent obesity (9%). 
Redefining MHO using no adverse metabolic parameters, a stricter definition of metabolically healthy obesity supports the hypothesis that obesity before the age of 60 is associated with a higher risk of dementia, irrespective of metabolic health components (Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S5).

The hypothesized biological pathway connecting KB metabolism and cognitive functions is shown in Additional file 1 [this file] : Fig. S1. 
To assess the association between KBs and cognitive functions, we used the Whitehall II study (WHII) including 5506 participants from the University College London-London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine-Edinburgh-Bristol (UCLEB) Consortium [ 19 [rid=CR19] ] (Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] , Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S1). Both KB and cognitive functions were measured at baseline (details in Additional file 1 [this file] : Supplementary Method). 
We obtained genetic instruments and their summary statistics from our in-house KB meta-analysis between the UCLEB Consortium [ 19 [rid=CR19] ] and Kettunen et al. [ 25 [rid=CR25] ] involving 45,031 participants (Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] , Additional file 1 [this file] : Supplementary Method). 
The details of demographics and GWAS analyses for cognitive performance and AD were provided in Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S1. 
Descriptive statistics on the characteristics of the WHII are shown in Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S2. 
Little evidence of association was shown in general cognitive function ( = 0.318, = 0.15), verbal meaning ( = 0.292, = 7.28 × 10 ), verbal fluency ( = 0.097, = 0.591), and word memory ( = 0.156, = 0.412) (Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S3). 
Little evidence can be observed in verbal fluency ( = 0.716, = 0.113) and word memory ( = 0.253, = 0.596) (Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S3). 
For ACACE, three independent SNPs were shown at a genome-wide significance level (Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S4) with the variance explained by the genetics of 0.5% and the -statistic of 72.24. For the suggestive set of instrumental variables ( < 1 × 10 ), 19 and 14 independent SNPs were identified for BOHBUT and ACACE, respectively (Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S5 and S6). 
All instrumental SNPs were not associated with potential confounders, except for rs6982502, which was shown to be associated with smoking (ever/never) ( -value = 8.95 × 10 ) (Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S7 and S8). 
Using the strong set of instrumental variables, we observed a positive association of genetically predicted BOHBUT with cognitive performance using the IVW and W-median methods (IVW: = 7.89 × 10 , = 1.03 × 10 , W-median: = 8.65 × 10 , = 9.60 × 10 , W-mode: = 0.126, = 8.56 × 10 ) (Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] , Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S9). Evidence of causality between BOHBUT and cognitive performance was consistent by using a suggestive set of instrumental SNPs ( = 6.11 × 10 , = 2.03 × 10 ; = 5.68 × 10 , = 2.30 × 10 ; = 4.35 × 10 , = 0.367) (Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S10). In addition, no evidence of directional pleiotropy or outliers was observed using MR-Egger intercept ( > 0.05) and MR-PRESSO ( > 1 × 10 ) (Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S11). 
We did not find evidence of causality between ACACE and cognitive performance (Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S12 and S13). Directional pleiotropic effects were not observed in the MR-Egger regression, and no outlier SNP was detected in the MR-PRESSO test (Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S14). 
However, we did not observe evidence of causality under a suggestive set of instrumental SNPs (Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S10). No significant causal association was observed between ACACE and AD (Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S12 and S13), and evidence of directional pleiotropy and outliers was not observed (Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S14). 
Evidence of neither directional pleiotropy nor outliers was observed using MR-Egger intercept and MR-PRESSO (Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S15). 
Three -acting SNPs ( < 1 × 10 and < 0.4) were identified close to the region with the variance explained of 0.19% and -statistic of 28.40 (Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S16). Accounting for the remaining residual correlation, -MR suggested little evidence of therapeutic modulation of on either cognitive performance ( = 0.038, = 0.312) or AD ( =− 0.331, = 0.290) while the direction of effect estimates was consistent with those previously shown (Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S17). 
A complete list of the UCLEB Consortium members can be found in Additional file 1 [this file] . 
GWAS summary statistics used and/or analyzed in this study are publicly available and accessible (Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S1).

Of the 8,815 participants at the 1991 to 1993 wave, the baseline of the present study, nine were excluded as they did not consent to follow‐up, 988 due to missing data on lipids ( = 952) or covariates ( = 37), and 145 because of prevalent CHD at baseline, leading to a final analytic sample of 7,672 participants (see the flow‐chart in Figure S1 [this file] ). Sample characteristics at baseline of participants as a function of sex and dementia status at the end of follow‐up are shown in Table 1 [rid=alz13140-tbl-0001] , and as a function of sex and mortality status and CHD status in Table S1 [this file] and Table S2 [this file] , respectively. All lipid levels except ApoA1 at baseline differed as a function of mortality status at follow‐up in men and women (all 0.01, Table S3 [this file] ); this was the case for all lipids when examined as a function of CHD at follow‐up in men and women (all 0.001, Table S4 [this file] ). 
The proportional hazards assumption was not supported in these analyses, but splitting the follow‐up at year 20 resolved this issue for all lipids apart from triglycerides (Table S5 [this file] ). As there were sex differences in the association of several lipids with all three outcomes (Table S6 [this file] ), subsequent analyses were split according to length of follow‐up and stratified by sex. 
Figure 1 [rid=alz13140-fig-0001] and Table S7 [this file] show the association of lipids with all three outcomes in men. 
Figure 2 [rid=alz13140-fig-0002] and Table S8 [this file] show the corresponding analyses in women. 
Adjusting for cardiovascular risk factors (hypertension and diabetes) did not substantially change the results in men (Table S9 [this file] ) or women (Table S20 [this file] ). In analyses of participants without 4 alleles, the results were similar to those in the main analyses for men (Table S11 [this file] ) and women (Table S12 [this file] ), apart from an unexpected lower dementia risk found for higher TC, LDL‐C, and non‐HDL‐C for ≥20 year follow‐up in men. Similarly, in further analyses of participants without 2 alleles the associations were contrary to expectations with high levels of TC, LDL‐C, non‐HDL‐C, and ApoB associated with lower risk of dementia in men in the < 20 year follow‐up (Table S13 [this file] ), but results in women were similar to those in the main analyses (Table S14 [this file] ). In analysis with lipids‐lowering drugs treated as a time‐varying covariate, the results did not significantly differ from those in the main analyses in men (Table S15 [this file] ) or women (Table S16 [this file] ). Adjustment for menopausal status in analyses of women did not modify the main findings (Table S17 [this file] ). 
Backward lipid trajectories over 28 years before dementia, mortality, and CHD for men and women are shown in Figure 3 [rid=alz13140-fig-0003] ; the accompanying differences in lipids between cases and non‐cases at time 0 and 5, 10, 15, 20, and 25 years prior to the date of the event are shown for each outcome in Table S18 [this file] . Additional adjustment for menopausal status in women did not change the findings (Figure S2 [this file] ). 
Differences in lipid levels between cases and non‐cases for mortality and CHD were observed in both men and women (Figure 3 [rid=alz13140-fig-0003] and Table S18 [this file] ), and were characterized by an adverse profile in midlife.
