In total, we analyzed 10 primary brain RNA-seq datasets ( Table S1 [this file] ). 
All omics datasets used in this study, including RNA-seq and snATAC-seq, are listed in Table S2 [this file] . 
We obtained GWAS summary statistics for 14 brain-related traits from the public domain, including intelligence (IQ), [xref] [rid=bib38] educational attainment (EA), [xref] [rid=bib39] smoking initiation (SmkInt), [xref] [rid=bib40] neuroticism, [xref] [rid=bib41] age at menarche (AAM), [xref] [rid=bib42] schizophrenia (SCZ), [xref] [rid=bib43] Alzheimer disease (AD) [xref] [rid=bib44] Parkinson disease (PD), [xref] [rid=bib45] insomnia, [xref] [rid=bib46] bipolar disorder (BIP), [xref] [rid=bib47] amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), [xref] [rid=bib48] cognitive performance (CP), [xref] [rid=bib49] major depression (MD), [xref] [rid=bib50] and anorexia nervosa (AN) [xref] [rid=bib51] ( Table S3 [this file] ). 
We obtained RNA-seq data from 2,865 cortical tissue samples collected from 2,443 unrelated individuals of European descent across seven cohorts (BrainGVEx, LIBD, CMC, HBCC, MSBB, Mayo, and ROSMAP) through the PsychENCODE [xref] [rid=bib63] [xref] [rid=bib64] and AMP-AD [xref] [rid=bib65] [xref] [rid=bib66] data portals ( Table S1 [this file] ). This process identified 38,441 lncRNAs, which can be classified into three categories according to their genomic positions relative to PCGs: 13,621 lincRNAs, 14,217 intronic RNAs (exclusively in the intronic regions of PCGs), and 10,603 antisense lncRNAs ( Figure S1 [this file] A). Among these lncRNAs, 96.7% were expressed (≥0.5 TPM in at least one sample) in at least two cohorts ( Figures S2 [this file] A and S2B). Notably, 71.4% (27,453 out of 38,441) of the expressed lncRNAs identified in this study are not annotated by GENCODE, highlighting the critical importance of high-quality transcriptomic data with sufficient sequencing depth and the integration of multiple samples to detect and validate previously unrecognized lncRNAs, particularly those that are context dependent ( Figure S1 [this file] B). We further compared these lncRNAs with those in the lncRNAKB database, which integrates annotations from six databases. [xref] [rid=bib67] This comparison revealed that 35.1% (13,481 out of 38,441) of our identified lncRNAs were not present in lncRNAKB ( Figure S1 [this file] B), and these newly identified lncRNAs showed higher expression levels than those cataloged in GENCODE or lncRNAKB ( Figure S1 [this file] E). Their characteristics, including lower expression levels relative to PCGs ( Figure S1 [this file] F), greater inter-individual expression variability ( Figure S1 [this file] G), and numerical properties such as exon count ( Figure S1 [this file] C) and isoform number ( Figure S1 [this file] D) were similar to those identified in previous studies. [xref] [rid=bib19] [xref] [rid=bib67] Moreover, these key characteristics were consistently observed across both poly(A)-based cohorts (LIBD and Mayo) and rRNA-depleted cohorts (BrainGVEx, CMC, HBCC, MSBB and ROSMAP). 
In addition to lncRNAs, we identified 355,415 circRNAs from the same data ( Figure S3 [this file] A), of which 86.9% were exonic ( Figure S3 [this file] B). However, we noted that a relatively low proportion of circRNAs showed robust expression across samples, defined as being present in 20% or more of the samples in each cohort ( Figure S3 [this file] A), indicating that circRNAs have either low expression levels or high variability among samples. Such a trend is expected, especially in poly(A)-selected RNA-seq libraries optimized for polyadenylated RNAs (e.g., mRNAs) rather than for non-polyadenylated circRNAs ( Figures S3 [this file] A and S3C). Of these, approximately 75% (18,241 out of 24,243) of the circRNAs were detected in at least two cohorts ( Figure S3 [this file] D), and over 90% of them could be identified using the find_circ method ( Figure S3 [this file] C). 
This analysis yielded 1,519,782 unique -eQTL SNPs for 15,362 lncRNAs, 101,203 for 1,312 circRNAs, and 1,370,398 for 10,609 PCGs, which will be referred to as eLncRNAs, eCircRNAs, and ePCGs, respectively ( Figures 2 [rid=fig2] B, S4 [this file] A, and S4B). Note that ∼70% (625 out of 892) of the eCircRNAs previously identified using the CMC data were also detected in our analysis of this dataset [xref] [rid=bib16] ( Figure S4 [this file] B). 
Here, a “case” denotes a lncRNA-PCG -pair where both genes exhibited significant -eQTLs within a shared ±1-Mb window, and one COLOC test was performed per pair ( supplemental methods [this file] ). The COLOC analysis indicated distinct causal variants (PP3 ≥ 0.8) in 83.3% (67,976 out of 81,644) of cases and a shared causal variant (PP4 ≥ 0.8) in only 4.7% (3,812 out of 81,644) of cases ( Figures S5 [this file] A and S5B), consistent with the relatively low LD between the lead lncRNA-eQTL and PCG-eQTL SNPs ( Figure S5 [this file] C). The results remained consistent across the three categories of lncRNAs (lincRNAs, intronic RNAs, and antisense lncRNAs), classified according to their genomic positions relative to PCGs ( Figure S5 [this file] B). Similar results were obtained when we performed a colocalization analysis of lncRNA-eQTLs with previously published PCG-sQTLs [xref] [rid=bib18] ( Figures S6 [this file] A and S6C). Because COLOC assumes a single causal variant per locus, we performed an additional colocalization analysis using eCAVIAR, which allows multiple causal variants ( supplemental methods [this file] ); the results were largely consistent with those from COLOC ( Figures S6 [this file] D and S6E). 
The COLOC analysis suggested a shared causal variant between circRNA-eQTLs and PCG-sQTLs in 30.6% of cases (2,294 out of 7,499; PP4 ≥ 0.8) ( Figure S6 [this file] F), slightly higher than that between circRNA- and PCG-eQTLs (24.7%), and much higher than the proportions for lncRNAs reported above, likely due to shared genetic regulation between back-splicing in circRNAs and linear splicing of their parental genes. It is consistent with the relatively low LD between the lead circRNA-eQTL and PCG-sQTL SNPs ( Figure S6 [this file] F). Nevertheless, in 57.8% (4,332 out of 7,499) of cases, the circRNA causal variant appeared distinct (PP3 ≥ 0.8) from either the eQTL or sQTL causal variant of its parental PCG at the locus level despite extensive SNP-level overlap ( Figure S6 [this file] F). Additional analysis using eCAVIAR [xref] [rid=bib68] again yielded broadly consistent results ( Figures S6 [this file] G and S6H). 
To further investigate the characteristics of lncRNA and circRNA-eQTLs, we annotated the lead SNP for each of the 15,362 eLncRNAs and 1,312 eCircRNAs by overlapping these SNPs with functional annotation data, including canonical splicing sites, RNA-binding protein (RBP)-binding sites, transcription factor (TF)-binding sites, seven histone marks, and 18 chromatin states ( Table S2 [this file] ). We performed an enrichment analysis using Torus, [xref] [rid=bib69] which uses full -eQTL summary statistics without SNP selection ( supplemental methods [this file] ). Similar to PCG-eQTLs, lncRNA-eQTLs were predominantly located around TSSs, with notable enrichment in TFs, RBPs and splicing sites, although to a lesser extent than PCG-eQTLs ( Figures 2 [rid=fig2] C, 2D, 2F, and S5 [this file] D–S5H). The unannotated lncRNAs showed comparable enrichment in TF- and RBP-binding sites to the annotated lncRNAs, yet they exhibited lower enrichment in splice sites ( Figures S5 [this file] F and S5G). In contrast, circRNA-eQTLs were highly enriched in canonical splice sites ( Figures 2 [rid=fig2] D and S5 [this file] G), consistent with the critical role of back-splicing in circRNA biogenesis. [xref] [rid=bib70] Furthermore, compared to PCG-eQTLs, circRNA- and lncRNA-eQTLs exhibited larger effect sizes ( Figure 2 [rid=fig2] E), and lncRNA-eQTLs displayed higher density around TSSs ( Figure 2 [rid=fig2] F), in line with previous work [xref] [rid=bib15] that suggests potentially simpler mechanisms of gene expression regulation for ncRNAs. 
Specifically, we obtained GWAS summary statistics for 14 traits, including SCZ, AD, and PD ( Table S3 [this file] ). Regardless of whether the three types of QTLs were analyzed with a joint or single-annotation model, lncRNA-eQTLs were consistently significantly enriched for heritability across most traits, albeit at slightly lower levels than PCG-eQTLs on average ( Figures S7 [this file] A–S7F). 
Across the 14 traits, lncRNA- and circRNA-eQTLs accounted for an average of 11.14% and 3.20% of SNP-based heritability, respectively, while PCG-eQTLs and -sQTLs contributed 17.19% and 7.60% of the SNP-based heritability, respectively ( Figures 3 [rid=fig3] B and S7 [this file] F), noting that there were overlapping SNPs among these eQTL/sQTL sets. After Bonferroni correction ( < 0.05/(3 × 14)), the enrichment of lncRNA-eQTLs remained significant in 11 of the 14 traits ( Figures S7 [this file] A and S7B). 
A full list of the prioritized genes and lncRNAs for the 14 traits is available in Table S5 [this file] . For SCZ specifically, the 176 prioritized lncRNAs and 173 PCGs were located in 104 of the 282 non-MHC autosomal SCZ GWAS loci as defined by PLINK clumping [xref] [rid=bib71] ( supplemental methods [this file] ), and, among these 176 prioritized lncRNAs, 81 and 44 were not annotated in GENCODE and lncRNAKB, respectively. 
Through PLINK clumping analysis ( supplemental methods [this file] ), we identified 1,038 quasi-independent GWAS signals across the 14 traits. This indicates that 72 of the colocalized GWAS signals (11.2%) were exclusively associated with lncRNA-eQTLs ( Table S4 [this file] ), with no evidence of colocalization with PCG-eQTLs/sQTLs identified in the same dataset ( Figure 3 [rid=fig3] E). A complete list of lncRNA- and circRNA-eQTLs that colocalize with GWAS signals can be found in Tables S5 [this file] and S6 [this file] . 
First, the -eQTL signal of the GENCODE-annotated lncRNA ( , lead variant rs12063329) colocalized with a GWAS signal for SCZ, and it demonstrated a higher gene prioritization score compared to that of its adjacent gene, , whose -eQTL signal did not reach genome-wide significance ( Figure 4 [rid=fig4] A). was negatively co-expressed with , suggesting a potential role in repressing expression ( Figures S8 [this file] A and S9 [this file] A). Notably, exhibited higher expression levels in neuronal cells compared to non-neuronal cells ( Figure S8 [this file] B), consistent with a previous finding that knockdown of can alter neural cellular phenotypes in human iPSC-derived neural cell lines. [xref] [rid=bib73] 
Our results suggest a potential effect of the circRNA on SCZ through DNA methylation and circRNA abundance showed no correlation with the expression or splicing phenotype of ( Figures S9 [this file] B–S9D), although these results do not preclude that the effect of circRNA may also be mediated through other genes. 
This lncRNA is predominantly expressed in neurons across various brain regions, particularly in glutamatergic neurons during crucial phases of human neocortical development ( Figures S10 [this file] A–S10C). Moreover, was highly enriched in total RNA-seq libraries compared to poly(A) RNA-seq libraries, suggesting it lacks a poly(A) tail ( Figure S10 [this file] C). This interpretation aligns with the observed lower expression levels of in SCZ patients relative to controls ( Figures 5 [rid=fig5] B and S10 [this file] D). 
Moreover, it is likely that lacks a poly(A) tail, as indicated by its strong enrichment in total RNA-seq libraries compared to poly(A) RNA-seq libraries ( Figure S11 [this file] C). The specific expression of in non-neuronal cells, particularly oligodendrocytes, along with its differential expression between individuals with SCZ and controls, suggests its potential role in SCZ ( Figures 5 [rid=fig5] C, 5D, S11 [this file] A, S11B, and S11D). 
One such example is the lncRNA AC244033.2, which colocalized with an SCZ GWAS signal ( Figure 4 [rid=fig4] A) and also showed colocalization with a BIP GWAS signal ( Table S5 [this file] ). The SMR-estimated effects of on these three traits were in the same direction ( Table S5 [this file] ). A further example is lncRNA , which was associated with AAM, neuroticism, CP, IQ, insomnia, and MD ( Figure S12 [this file] ). Interestingly, although the genetic correlations among three of these traits (AAM, neuroticism, and CP) were negative ( Figure S13 [this file] ), the SMR-estimated effects of on these traits were all in the same direction. By estimating the local genetic correlation in this locus using LAVA, [xref] [rid=bib76] we found that the effects of this lncRNA on these traits were consistent with a positive local genetic correlation ( Figure S13 [this file] ), suggesting heterogeneous genetic sharing among traits across the genome. 
A full list of acknowledgments to these datasets can be found in the supplemental note [this file] .

These observations were validated as disease-specific changes in female LOAD subjects rather than inherent biological sex differences between male and female ND participants (Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] ). 
Despite these findings, the log2-fold change (log2FC) in transcript expression between the LOAD and ND groups was minimal (≤ |0.07 | ) but statistically significant ( < 0.05) (Supplementary Fig. 2b [this file] ). These results were confirmed via quantitative PCR analysis (Supplementary Fig. 2a [this file] ). 
This reduction was more pronounced in female subjects, particularly at advanced ages (Fig. 1f [rid=Fig1] and Supplementary Fig. 2c, d [this file] ), and was further exacerbated in those with LOAD (Fig. 1f [rid=Fig1] ). 
VCD-treated animals showed no significant changes in motor function, as assessed by the rotarod test and open-field test (Fig. 2h [rid=Fig2] and Supplementary Fig. 3e–g [this file] ). However, significant declines in spatial learning and memory, as evaluated by the Morris water maze (MWM) (Fig. 2f [rid=Fig2] and Supplementary Fig. 3a–c [this file] ), and in short-term working memory, as assessed by the Y-maze, were observed beginning at Cycle 7 (Fig. 2g [rid=Fig2] and Supplementary Fig. 3d [this file] ). Furthermore, the animals displayed mild anxiety-like behaviour, as indicated by the significantly reduced time spent in the centre zone during the open-field test (Fig. 2i [rid=Fig2] and Supplementary Fig. 3g [this file] ). Importantly, the decline in behavioural performance at the onset of the perimenopausal state transition (Cycle 7) was most strongly correlated with the E2:P4 ratio (Figs. 2f–g, i [rid=Fig2] ) rather than with the circulating levels of E2 or P4 alone (Supplementary Fig. 3b [this file] –d, g [this file] ). Immunohistochemical analysis further supported the negative impact of elevated E2:P4 ratios (≥2.5 pg/ng) on brain cellular integrity, revealing significant neurite loss in the Cornu Ammonis area 1 (CA1) of the hippocampus (Fig. 2j [rid=Fig2] and Supplementary Fig. 3h–j [this file] ). 
However, with the VCD-induced increase in the oestradiol-lower progesterone imbalance, the nuclear localisation of ERRα and PGC1α was significantly reduced (Fig. 3f [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] ). 
Using previously reported but incomplete, open structures of the ERRα LBD (PDB: 7E2E and 2PJL) , we generated a complete open conformation of the ERRα LBD by reconstructing the missing alpha-helix segment with AlphaFold2 (Supplementary Fig. 5a, b [this file] ), which allowed us to model the effect of cholesterol ligand binding on the interaction with another AlphaFold2-simulated 3rd LXXLL motif (amino acids 208–216) of PGC1α using the HADDOCK 2.4 algorithm . In contrast, docking simulations with the closed ERRα LBD structure (PDB: 1XB7) , which is incompatible with cholesterol binding, failed to reveal similar interactions (Supplementary Fig. 5c [this file] ). 
These metabolic changes were neuron-specific, as demonstrated by cell-specific metabolomic analyses (Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] ). 
Quantifications in Supplementary Fig. 7c [this file] . Quantifications in Supplementary Fig. 10 [this file] . 
Furthermore, on the basis of initial predictions made with the ENCODE, CHEA and ChIP-Atlas databases (Supplementary Fig. 7a [this file] ), chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) analysis confirmed that five dysregulated metabolic genes identified in the VCD-induced AOF model were bona fide ERα targets, including (encoding a component of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex), , and (both involved in cholesterol biosynthesis) (Fig. 4e [rid=Fig4] ). ChIP–PCR revealed robust E2-induced ERα binding to the promoter regions of these receptor genes, which was blocked by the ERα antagonist MPP dihydrochloride (Fig. 4f [rid=Fig4] and Supplementary Fig. 7a–c [this file] ) . In support of neuronal specificity, mouse SMART-seq data from the Allen Brain Atlas confirmed the enrichment of these genes in neurons (Supplementary Fig. 8 [this file] ). In the ROSMAP brain transcriptomics dataset, the expression of these genes (except for ) was selectively reduced in female patients and correlated with cognitive impairment (Fig. 4g [rid=Fig4] and Supplementary Fig. 9 [this file] ). 
Reanalysis of ChIP-sequencing data from the hormone-sensitive breast cancer cell line MCF7 ( GSE68359 (GSE68359) ) revealed that cotreatment with E2 and natural P4, but not E2 alone or with synthetic P4 (R5020), induced the co-occupancy of ERα, PR, and p300 histone acetyltransferase at the promoters of cholesterol biosynthesis genes (Supplementary Fig. 7d [this file] ). Conversely, supplementation with additional P4 further enhanced the E2-induced upregulation of cholesterol biosynthesis-related gene expression (Fig. 4h–i [rid=Fig4] and Supplementary Fig. 7e [this file] ). Downstream of these events, the relative abundance of ERRα-bound cholesterol (Fig. 4k [rid=Fig4] ), protein–protein interactions between ERRα and PGC1α (Fig. 4l [rid=Fig4] and Supplementary Fig. 10 [this file] ), and ERRα nuclear transcriptional activity (Fig. 4m [rid=Fig4] ) were regulated in a similar manner. 
To investigate this interaction, an adeno-associated virus (AAV) expressing a microRNA-30 (miR30)-based short hairpin RNA (shRNA) under the control of a human synapsin promoter was injected into the prefrontal cortex of C57BL/6 mice to specifically knock down neuronal (Fig. 5a, b [rid=Fig5] and Supplementary Fig. 11a [this file] ). Validation of the knockdown results revealed reduced expression at both the mRNA and protein levels, along with significant neurite loss in regions where the shRNA was robustly expressed (Fig. 5b [rid=Fig5] and Supplementary Fig. 11a–d [this file] ). Behaviourally, this knockdown led to mild impairments in memory and cognitive function (Supplementary Fig. 11e–h [this file] ). 
Transcriptomic and metabolomic profiling of microdissected GFP-positive neurons revealed that the TCA cycle was the most affected pathway, followed by “alanine, aspartate, and glutamate metabolism” (Fig. 5c–f [rid=Fig5] and Supplementary Fig. 12 [this file] ). 
In support of these findings, the VCD-induced AOF mouse model, characterised by diminished ERRα signalling, also displayed reduced succinate, fumarate, NAA, and NAAG levels (Supplementary Fig. 13 [this file] ). 
Compared with males, female subjects exhibited more dramatic changes in amino acid, phospholipid, and cholesterol-related metabolites, even when sample sizes were adjusted via permutation analysis (Fig. 5j [rid=Fig5] and Supplementary Fig. 14 [this file] ). 
Transcriptomic data further revealed decreased expression of and , which encode key SDH subunits, in both -knockdown and XCT-790-treated neurons (Fig. 5c, d [rid=Fig5] and Supplementary Figs. 12c [this file] –e and 15b [this file] ). In agreement with the predictions from the ENCODE and ChIP-atlas (Supplementary Fig. 15a [this file] ) databases, ChIP–PCR confirmed that these genes were direct ERRα targets (Supplementary Fig. 15c [this file] ), and enzyme activity assays verified the reduced SDH function in ERRα-deficient neurons (Fig. 6j [rid=Fig6] ). 
Measurements of the mitochondrial oxygen consumption rate (OCR) revealed that both basal respiration and reserve respiratory capacity were significantly impaired in ERRα-deficient neurons (Fig. 6k [rid=Fig6] and Supplementary Fig. 15d [this file] ). 
Similar to findings in C57BL/6 mice (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] ), VCD-induced AOF treatment in 3xTg-AD mice led to increased plasma FSH levels (Supplementary Fig. 16a [this file] ) and prolonged oestrous cycles beginning around the 6th–7th cycle posttreatment (Fig. 7a [rid=Fig7] , right panel). These changes were absent in vehicle-treated 3xTg mice, confirming that the observed effects were not influenced by the three transgenes (Fig. 7a [rid=Fig7] and Supplementary Fig. 16a [this file] ). 
Pathway enrichment analysis of upregulated DEGs presented in Supplementary Fig. 20a, b [this file] on Enrichr (two-tailed Fisher’s exact test with correction). 
However, around Cycles 6–7, some mice exhibited a pronounced increase in E2 or a decrease in P4 levels, resulting in an elevated E2:P4 ratio (≥2.5 pg/ng), indicating a high oestradiol-low progesterone imbalance (Fig. 7b [rid=Fig7] and Supplementary Fig. 16a [this file] ). This hormonal imbalance was associated with impaired spatial learning (Fig. 7c [rid=Fig7] and Supplementary Fig. 16b [this file] , d [this file] ) and short-term working memory (Fig. 7d [rid=Fig7] and Supplementary Fig. 16c [this file] ). Transcriptomic analysis of the cerebral cortex from mice with an E2:P4 concentration ≥ 2.5 pg/ng revealed significant downregulation of genes involved in cholesterol homoeostasis, oestrogen responses, and glycolysis (Fig. 7e–g [rid=Fig7] ), which was consistent with findings in C57BL/6 mice (Figs. 3 [rid=Fig3] and 4 [rid=Fig4] and Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] ). These changes were accompanied by a reduction in the expression of cholesterol-bound ERRα during Cycle 7 (Fig. 7h [rid=Fig7] ) and a subsequent decrease in the expression of OXPHOS pathway genes during Cycle 14 (Supplementary Fig. 17a, b [this file] ). 
The 3xTg mice exhibited a high E2:P4 ratio, and a decreased ERα–PR interaction was accompanied by increased levels of Aβ monomers, dimers, and oligomers, as well as phosphorylated tau (S202/T205), in cortical tissues (Fig. 7i [rid=Fig7] and Supplementary Fig. 17c [this file] ). Pharmacokinetic profiling after P4 administration revealed a short plasma half-life following intraperitoneal (i.p.) injection (4–8 mg/kg), with peak levels occurring at 15 min and a rapid decline thereafter [Supplementary Fig. 18a [this file] (2), b(2)]. Although P4 injections had no effect on endogenous E2 levels [Supplementary Fig. 18a [this file] (3), b(3)], they effectively reduced the E2:P4 ratio below the defined imbalance threshold (≥2.5 pg/ng) for approximately 8 h [Supplementary Fig. 18a, b [this file] (4)]. Using a protocol combining i.p. injection (4 mg/kg) followed by subcutaneous infusion (11.7 ± 0.7 mg/kg over 48 h), we found that P4 treatment normalized plasma E2:P4 ratios (Fig. 7k [rid=Fig7] and Supplementary Fig. 18c [this file] ) and restored P4 levels in brain tissues (Fig. 7k [rid=Fig7] and Supplementary Fig. 18d [this file] ). Subsequent extended P4 supplementation over 60 days, which coincided with Cycles 14–15, improved memory and cognitive functions in 3xTg mice with an initial high E2:P4 ratio, whereas no significant effects were observed in vehicle-treated mice with balanced E2:P4 ratios (Fig. 7l [rid=Fig7] and Supplementary Fig. 19a, b [this file] ). Brain tissues harvested from P4-treated 3xTg mice showed significant improvements in neurite length (Fig. 7m [rid=Fig7] ), reduced levels of phosphorylated tau (Fig. 7m, n [rid=Fig7] and Supplementary Fig. 19c [this file] ), and decreased Aβ immunoreactivity, accompanied by enhanced ERα–PR interactions (Fig. 7n [rid=Fig7] and Supplementary Fig. 19d [this file] ). Transcriptomic and metabolomic profiling revealed that P4 supplementation restored cholesterol and NAAG biosynthetic networks (Fig. 7o [rid=Fig7] and Supplementary Fig. 20a–g [this file] ). Neurophysiological analyses further demonstrated that P4 supplementation improved the maximal respiratory capacity and ATP-linked respiration in the brain (Supplementary Fig. 20h [this file] ). 
This hypothesis was supported by our pilot data (Fig. 1f [rid=Fig1] and Supplementary Fig. 2c, d [this file] ), which showed that compared with noncarriers, samples from carriers exhibited greater depletion of nuclear PGC1α and ERRα. This decrease in cholesterol availability is linked to reduced nuclear localisation and activity of ERRα, as evidenced by the lower number of MAP2+ nuclear ERRα+ neurons in the brains of females with and without dementia than in the brains of their male counterparts (Fig. 1f [rid=Fig1] and Supplementary Fig. 2c, d [this file] ). 
For the VCD study (Fig. 2j [rid=Fig2] and Supplementary Fig. 3i, j [this file] ), five cohorts of mice were tested. The number of mice in each cohort showing signs of neurite loss—characterised by fragmentation and/or reduced MAP2 signal density within the same unit area compared to the vehicle control group—was counted (Supplementary Fig. 3i [this file] ) to determine which CA region was most severely affected. Additionally, the normalised ratio of total neurite length in VCD-treated groups relative to the control treatment group was calculated and presented (Supplementary Fig. 3j [this file] ). 
Similarly, for the knockdown study (Fig. 5b [rid=Fig5] and Supplementary Fig. 11c, d [this file] ), four cohorts of mice were tested. The number of mice in each cohort exhibiting neurite loss—characterised by fragmentation and/or reduced densities of cytosolic GFP signals within the same unit area compared to the scramble shRNA control group—was counted (Supplementary Fig. 11c [this file] ) in the prefrontal cortex and CA1-2 hippocampal regions. Additionally, the normalised ratio of total neurite length in the knockdown group relative to the scramble shRNA control group was calculated and presented (Supplementary Fig. 11d [this file] ).

Together, the stratified analyses leaves 21 proteins of the 55 proteins identified in the overall analysis including VGF, SYT1, CEND1, MENT, NPTXR, LDLR, IL1RL1, RBP7, EBI3-IL27, TNFRSF6B, SLC13A1 and PSG1 which were significantly associated with AD only in APOE 4 , LTBP2, SHISA5, CST5, VEGFB, LMOD, TGFBR1 and FRMD7 which were significantly associated with AD in APOE 4 carriers, and GFAP and NEFL, which were associated with AD in both APOE 4 and APOE 4 carriers ( Supplementary Figure 2 [this file] ). 
CELSR2 belongs to the flamingo family of cadherins and is encoded by the gene , which hosts the genetic variant (rs12740374_T, 3’UTR) that determines the plasma levels of progranulin (GRN, effect=−0.664, p-value=0) ( Supplementary Figure 3 [this file] ). CELSR2 localizes to the same chromosomal region as SORT1 ( Supplementary Figure 3 [this file] ), which encodes sortilin 1 protein that is primarily responsible for the degradation of GRN . In contrast, most of the proteins associated with AD in APOE 4 individuals localize to the extracellular region and do not cluster in any specific pathway ( Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ). 
VaD showed a significant association (FDR < 0.05) with 49 proteins in plasma, including GFAP, NEFL, CHI3L1, PVR, GDF15, SPON2, SMOC2, C7, CKB, ASAH2 and BSG among others ( Figure 4 [rid=F4] , Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). Pathway enrichment analysis suggests that the proteins with the future risk of VaD are enriched in the virus receptor, cytokine activity, matrix metalloproteinases and regulation of Insulin-like Growth Factor (IGF) transport and uptake pathways ( Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ). 
However, among significant ones 13/49 proteins including GFAP, NEFL, IL27, IGFBP2, LTBP2, APOE, KLK4, PVR, CKB, SPP1, CHI3L1, GDF15 and TIMP4 overlap with that of AD. 11/13 overlapping proteins are localized to the extracellular region, of which 3 cluster in elastic fibre formation and matrix metalloproteinases pathway ( Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ). 
Proteins PVR and EPHA2 were associated with seropositivity of VZV, while HAVCR1 was associated with seropositivity of HSV1 ( Supplementary Table 9 [this file] ). All six proteins were significantly associated with the two established markers of neurodegeneration, i.e., GFAP and NEFL ( Supplementary Table 10 [this file] ). 
To evaluate the relevance of plasma proteins associated with AD and VaD in neurodegeneration in the brain, we tested their association with neuritic plaques based on the Consortium to Establish a Registry for Alzheimer’s Disease (CERAD) score, tau pathology as measured with the Braak stage, mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and AD in the ROSMAP cohort ( Supplementary Table 11 [this file] ). Several proteins, including GFAP, NEFL, VGF, APOE, SNAP25, PVR, VCAN, LMOD1, DCN, PEPD, PALM, CHI3L1, TINAGL1, ACTA2 and SYT1, were associated with at least one trait tested ( Supplementary Table 12 [this file] ). Of the 36 unique proteins associated with VaD in plasma, 15 were assessed in the ROSMAP dataset, of which IGFBP7, RGCC, IMMT, BSG, SPON1, RNASE4 and SNAPIN showed association with at least one of the tested traits ( Supplementary Table 13 [this file] ). 
Among the proteins significantly associated with AD in the Cox regression analysis, APOE, SNAP25, PVR and PALM showed significant association in MR ( Supplementary Tables 14 [this file]15 [this file] ). The MR association with APOE, SNAP25 and PALM was driven by the APOE 4 variant rs429358-C ( Supplementary Table 16 [this file] , Supplementary Figure 8 [rid=SD1] ). MR-Egger showed a significant causal association of SNAP25 with AD (Beta = 2.12, P-value = 1.6*10 ; Supplementary Table 14 [this file] ) after correcting for directional pleiotropy. Further, the results of MR methods, e.g., weighted median and mode, were also significant and consistent with that of the inverse variance weighted method ( Supplementary Table 14 [this file] ). 
Interestingly both proteins were also causally associated with VZV seropositivity ( Supplementary Tables 14 [this file]15 [this file] ).

For the WT experiment, no samples were excluded ( Figure S1C [this file] – E [this file] ). Three samples (TDP43-Soma-NT_6, TDP43-Soma-KD_6, HNRNPA1-Neurite-NT_2) were excluded due to their low numbers of protein groups ( Supplementary Figure S4I [this file] ), intensity values that did not respond to median-normalization ( Supplementary Figure S4K [this file] ), or unexpected pairwise sample correlation patterns ( Supplementary Figure S4J [this file] ). 
Proteins with low intensity ( Supplementary Figure S3A [this file] , B [this file] , F [this file] , G [this file] ) were excluded from further analysis. 
GFP-tagged end binding protein 1 (EB1) shows primarily unidirectional growth, demonstrating that most processes on the bottom of the membrane are axons, which have unipolar microtubules ( 42 [rid=R42] ) ( Supplementary Figure S1A [this file] – B [this file] ). Principal component analysis shows clear separation of neurite and whole cell samples ( Supplementary Figure S1F [this file] ). Pathway analysis on proteins enriched in the neuritic fraction shows terms related to axon health and function, including axon guidance, actin regulation, and various signaling pathways ( Supplementary Figure S1G [this file] ). Conversely, terms enriched in the whole cell fraction shows pathways related to nuclear functions, like the spliceosome, DNA repair, and nucleocytoplasmic transport ( Supplementary Figure S1G [this file] ). 
Principal component analysis (PCA) reveals that 97% of the variance in the samples comes from its cellular fraction, vastly outweighing the sample-to-sample variance (1%) ( Supplementary Figure S2A [this file] ). Quality control metrics show similar expression efficiencies and number of genes identified between neurite and whole cell fractions ( Supplementary Figure S2B [this file] – C [this file] ). Percent alignment to rRNA was higher in neurites, but snoRNAs were depleted from neurite fractions ( Supplementary Figure S2B [this file] , D [this file] ). KEGG pathway analysis of the transcripts enriched in the neuritic fraction reveals ribosomal protein transcripts among the most overrepresented terms ( Figure 2B [rid=F2] ), while GO Biological process shows terms related to transport, metabolism, and cytoskeleton ( Supplementary Figure S2E [this file] ). 
Comparing the intensity of the heavy and light mass spec channels, there were few proteins found in the flow through and the QuanCAT samples were enriched for heavy labeled peptides ( Supplementary Figure S3A [this file] ). However, the number of protein groups identified is drastically reduced in the QuanCAT samples compared to the input or flow through, demonstrating enrichment of the small number of proteins that are labeled with heavy amino acids ( Supplementary Figure S3B [this file] ). In comparison, we only identified 26 heavy labeled proteins in the input fraction and 34 in the flow through fraction ( Supplementary Figure S3C [this file] – E [this file] ). 
As expected, due to the lack of enrichment and short pulse, fewer heavy labeled proteins were detected than light proteins ( Supplementary Figure S3F [this file] – G [this file] ). However, in comparing the heavy labeled proteins identified in the neurite and whole cell fractions, we were able to detect heavy labeled proteins significantly enriched in both fractions ( Supplementary Figure 3H [this file] ). Pathway analysis of neurite versus whole cell enriched proteins shows many nuclear and cell body related pathways and functions, reflective of the increased abundance of newly synthesized proteins in those compartments ( Supplementary Figure S3I [this file] – J [this file] ). 
Western blots and immunofluorescence both confirm RBP KDs compared to a non-targeting (NT) control guide ( Supplementary Figure S4A [this file] – D [this file] ). Most of the variance between samples can be explained by the neurite versus whole cell separation, rather than RBP KD ( Supplementary Figure S4E [this file] – F [this file] ). Pathway analysis identified pathways related to the extracellular matrix in TDP-43 KD neurites and RNA processing in hnRNPA1 KD neurites ( Supplementary Figure S4G [this file] – H [this file] ). 
Overall, samples show similar percent expression efficiencies, but neurite samples tend to have higher percentages of reads aligning to ribosomal RNA (rRNA) ( Supplementary Figure S5A [this file] – B [this file] ). Samples had similar numbers of genes detected within an experiment, although the hnRNPA1 experiment typically had more genes detected ( Supplementary Figure S5C [this file] – D [this file] ). As expected, higher snoRNA expression was observed in whole cell samples, but some snoRNAs and pre-mRNAs were detected in neurites, with more detected in the hnRNPA1 experiment compared to the TDP-43 experiment ( Supplementary Figure S5E [this file] – F [this file] ). 
Interestingly, most of the difference in the samples (81% and 79% for TDP-43 KD and hnRNPA1 KD, respectively) comes from the cellular fraction, not the KD itself ( Supplementary Figure S6A [this file] – B [this file] ). Pathway analysis identifies axon guidance related transcripts decreased in TDP-43 KD neurons and neurodegeneration transcripts in hnRNPA1 KD neurons ( Supplementary Figure S6C [this file] – E [this file] ). 
We observe over 500 novel splice junctions in the TDP-43 KD dataset and almost 150 in the hnRNPA1 KD neurons ( Table S1 [this file] and 2 [this file] ). 
However, the sphere area did not change in size substantially across the time course for any genotype, indicating neurons are not dying ( Figure S7A [this file] ). These results were confirmed by a two-dimensional neurite outgrowth assay, where 1% of cells were labeled with a cytoplasmic marker ( Supplementary Figure S7B [this file] – F [this file] ).

We transduced the iPSCs with lentiviral sgRNAs targeting to knock down tau or non-targeting control (NTC) sgRNAs for further mechanistic characterization (Fig. S1A–C [this file] ). 
Knocking down tau in Het neurons resulted in only five differentially expressed genes (Fig. S1D [this file] ). Differentially expressed genes in Hom and * Het neurons compared to isogenic controls were also significantly enriched for regulators of axonogenesis, even at one week of differentiation (Fig. S1E–G [this file] ). While many of the same transcripts relevant to axonogenesis are perturbed in * Het and Het, we did not see a high level of concordance in direction of change (Fig. S1E [this file] ). 
ATAC-seq at 2 and 4 weeks of differentiation showed similar patterns as the RNA-seq (Figs. 1D [rid=Fig1] , S2A [this file] ), and genes with differentially accessible peaks proximal to their transcription start site (TSS) were enriched for axon-related genes (Fig. S2B [this file] ). Transcription factor motif analysis showed that motifs for the AP-1 Transcription factor network, which includes the cJun family of transcription factors, were consistently more accessible in Het and WT tau knockdown neurons compared to controls (Figs. 1E [rid=Fig1] , S2C [this file] ). Supporting the validity of the ATAC-seq results, we found that both p-cJun and cJun are increased in Het, Hom, and Het neurons vs. isogenic controls (Figs. 1F, G [rid=Fig1] , S2D [this file] ). 
There was significant overlap in the proteins with differential phosphorylation between Hom, Het, and Het neurons vs. isogenic controls (Fig. 2B [rid=Fig2] ), though the identities of the differential phosphosites varied between conditions (Fig. S3A [this file] ). S3B-D [this file] , S9 A–C [this file] ). 
When we performed gene set enrichment analysis on proteins with differential phosphorylation in WT tau knockdown neurons, the only significantly enriched term was “Regulation of microtubule-based process,” with many of these proteins being involved in axonogenesis (Fig. S3E [this file] ). Gene set enrichment analysis of proteins with differential phosphorylation in Het tau knockdown neurons compared to Het showed that splicing factors were predominantly affected, whereas cytoskeletal and axonogenesis proteins were not perturbed (Fig. S3F [this file] ). 
We validated these results in the patient-derived neurons and found a consistent axonogenesis defect (Fig. S4A–C [this file] ). 
We observed that V337M neurons had lower tau phosphorylation compared to WT across all domains of the protein at many sites (Fig. 4 [rid=Fig4] A and 4B [rid=Fig4] ) and validated these changes by western blot (Figs. 4C [rid=Fig4] , S5D, E [this file] ). Many of the differential phosphorylation sites are known to be hyperphosphorylated in Alzheimer’s disease and other tauopathies (Fig. S5A [this file] ). Intriguingly, V337M tau hypophosphorylation is transient, approaching WT levels after two to four weeks of differentiation (Figs. 4D [rid=Fig4] , S5F–I [this file] ). 
V337M tau consistently had lower pS202/T205 tau levels when compared to WT or R406W tau at two and four weeks of differentiation when overexpressed (Fig. S6A–C [this file] ). To test if the V337M mutation directly impaired susceptibility to phosphorylation, we purified WT and V337M tau and tested phosphorylation by GSK3B and PKA in vitro (Fig. S6D–G [this file] ). 
Proline-directed phosphorylation sites were decreased in V337M neurons, many of which serve as priming sites for additional sites of decreased tau phosphorylation (Fig. S5B, C [this file] ). 
To directly test which kinases perturb tau phosphorylation in WT and V337M neurons, we employed CRISPRi and CRISPRa screens to test the effects of gene knockdown or overexpression on tau phosphorylation using the AT8 antibody, which detects the tau pS202/pT205 phosphoepitope (Figs. 5A [rid=Fig5] , S7A–D [this file] ). We filtered out hits for enrichment analysis that also modified T22 levels in previously published work (Fig. S7E [this file] ) . Cytoskeleton genes and genes involved in neuron projection development modified tau phosphorylation in both WT and V337M neurons (Fig. 4A,B [rid=Fig4] ) without altering T22 levels (Fig. S7E [this file] ). Intriguingly, several kinases in the p38 MAPK pathway altered tau phosphorylation specifically in V337M neurons (Fig. S8A [this file] ). Other kinases predicted to have differential activity that may have regulated tau phosphorylation in V337M neurons did not affect tau pS202/pT205 levels, including , , and (Fig. S7F [this file] ). Another fascinating signature emerged when we looked at proteins involved in arginine/citrulline/nitric oxide metabolism that were very consistently differentially expressed (Fig. S8A [this file] ). Nitric oxide activates guanylate cyclases, which in turn activate cGMP-dependent kinases . knockdown increased AT8 levels specifically in Het neurons (Fig. S8A [this file] ).

To understand the impact of Tau phosphorylation on Tau degradation in lysosomes, we used patient-derived iPSC-derived neurons harboring a doxycycline-inducible neurogenin-2 (NGN2) cassette stably integrated in the AAVS1 locus (Supplementary Figs. 1 [this file] and 2 [this file] ). These neurons express the neuronal markers Microtubule-Associated Protein 2 (MAP2) and β-tubulin III (Tuj1) by DIV7 and synapsin by DIV14 (Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] ). 
To understand where endogenous Tau localizes within the endolysosomal compartments of human neurons, we visualized total Tau (Tau5) and phosphorylated Tau (AT180; pThr231; pTau) in LAMP1-positive (LAMP1 + ) vesicles of DIV14 neurons using immunocytochemistry and Airyscan super-resolution microscopy (Fig. 1A [rid=Fig1] and Supplementary Fig. 4A [this file] ). LAMP1+ vesicles appeared as donut-shaped structures (Supplementary Fig. 4A [this file] ). LAMP1+ vesicles were Cathepsin D positive (74.2%; Supplementary Fig. 4B [this file] ) and lysosomal membrane protein 2 (LIMP2) positive (95.2%; Supplementary Fig. 4C [this file] ) . Signal intensity measurements illustrate that total Tau localization was enriched within the lysosomal lumen (Fig. 1B, C [rid=Fig1] and Supplementary Fig. 4D [this file] ), while pTau localization was enriched at the lysosomal membrane (Figs. 1 [rid=Fig1] B, D [rid=Fig1] and Supplementary Fig. 4D [this file] ). 
See Supplementary Fig. 4D [this file] for individual traces. 
NGN2 was engineered into the AAVS locus of iPSC lines from patients carrying the FTD-causing p.R406W mutation and its isogenic, WT pair (Fig. 2A [rid=Fig2] ; Supplementary Figs. 1 [this file] and 2 [this file] ). p.R406W neurons (DIV14) produced significantly more total Tau (Tau5), Tau phosphorylated at pThr231 (AT180; Fig. 2B-D [rid=Fig2] ), and Tau phosphorylated at pSer202/pThr205 (AT8; Supplementary Fig. 5A, B [this file] ) compared to isogenic control neurons. The ratio of pTau/total Tau was also significantly higher in mutant neurons using immunofluorescence (Fig. 2E [rid=Fig2] ) and immunoblotting (Supplementary Fig. 5C–F [this file] ). 
Total Tau was enriched in the lysosomal lumen in both p.R406W and isogenic control neurons (Fig. 3A, B [rid=Fig3] ); however, mutant neurons exhibited significantly more Tau in the lumen compared to isogenic controls (p.R406W: 69.6% vs. WT: 19.41%; = 0.002; Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] A, B, E [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Fig. 5G [this file] ). We also observed a modest increase in membrane-bound Tau in the mutant neurons compared to the controls (p.R406W: 26.7% vs. WT: 11.8%; = 0.017; Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] A, B, E [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Fig. 5G [this file] ). p.R406W neurons exhibited significantly more pTau in the lysosomal membrane than isogenic controls (p.R406W: 70.3% vs. WT: 26.2%; = 0.016; Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] C, D, F [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Fig. 5G [this file] ). Strikingly, p.R406W neurons had fewer lysosomes free of total Tau (p.R406W: 3.6% vs. WT: 68.7%; = 0.002) and pTau (p.R406W: 10.3% vs. WT: 51.2%; = 0.015; Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] C, D, F [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Fig. 5G [this file] ) compared to isogenic controls. 
The significantly differentially expressed genes in p.R406W neurons were enriched in protein degradation pathways associated with phagosome maturation ( , , ), regulation of autophagy ( , , , , ), autophagosome ( , ), and vesicle transport along the microtubule ( , Fig. 4A [rid=Fig4] ; Supplementary Fig. 6A [this file] ). We also discovered that a number of lysosomal genes, including vATPases and autophagy genes, are significantly reduced in p.R406W neurons (Supplementary Fig. 6B–D [this file] ; Supplementary Data 1 [rid=MOESM3] ). 
LysoTracker+ vesicles were also significantly larger in mutant neurons (Supplementary Fig. 7A, B [this file] ). Interestingly, the mean intensity of LysoTracker was significantly lower in p.R406W neurons compared with isogenic controls (Supplementary Fig. 7A, [this file] C [this file] ). 
To determine whether p.R406W contributes to defective autophagy, we assessed the overall abundance of autophagosomes in p.R406W and isogenic controls using CYTO-ID (Fig. 6B [rid=Fig6] and Supplementary Fig. 8A [this file] ). Compared to DMSO-treated neurons, Rap/CQ treatment significantly enhanced CYTO-ID intensity and CYTO-ID positive vesicle density in both mutant and isogenic control neurons (Fig. 6B–D [rid=Fig6] and Supplementary Fig. 8B [this file] ). Consistent with our CYTO-ID findings, LC3B intensity was significantly elevated in mutant neurons (Fig. 6E, F [rid=Fig6] and Supplementary Fig. 8C [this file] ). Immunoblotting also revealed an increase in the ratio of LC3BII to LC3BI in p.R406W neurons (Supplementary Fig. 8D–F [this file] ). 
We observed significantly more lipid droplet content in mutant neurons relative to controls based on the overall BODIPY fluorescence per cell (Fig. 6H, I [rid=Fig6] and Supplementary Fig. 8G [this file] ). 
We observed the more enlarged yellow puncta in transduced mutant neurons (Fig. 6K, L [rid=Fig6] and Supplementary Fig. 8H [this file] ), representing more autophagosomes and consistent with our CYTO-ID findings. 
G2-567 treatment also restored the proportion of pTau-free lysosomes in p.R406W neurons to control levels, without significantly altering the localization of pTau in the lumen (p.R406W-DMSO: 27.2% vs. p.R406W-G2-567: 40.3%; Supplementary Fig. 9 [this file] ). LAMP1+ vesicle size in p.R406W neurons was restored to sizes observed in controls upon G2-567 treatment (Fig. 7H, I [rid=Fig7] and Supplementary Fig. 10 [this file] ). 
We replicated the same phenotype in a second donor line, further confirming the robustness of our findings (Supplementary Fig. 11 [this file] ). 
Engineered cell lines were verified using Sanger sequencing for the mutation and the NGN2 cassette, karyotyping for chromosomal stability, and immunocytochemistry for pluripotency markers (Supplementary Figs. 1 [this file] and 2 [this file] ). 
Neurons typically show neuronal identity 7 days after plating based on immunocytochemistry for β-tubulin III (Tuj1) and microtubule-associated protein 2 (MAP2), a marker of mature neuronal dendrite (Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] ). 
CYTO-ID selectively probes the autophagosome membrane, and vesicles appear as round-shaped structures detectable under fluorescence excitation/emission of 495/519 nm (Supplementary Fig. 8A [this file] ). 
This analog has been subjected to chemical modification to derive the G2-567 compound. p.R406W and isogenic control iPSC-neurons were treated with 0.5 µM G2-567 (resuspended in DMSO) on DIV7, a time point where neurons are positive for neuronal markers MAP2 and Tuj1 (Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] ). 
The reproducibility and uniformity of differentiation are demonstrated in Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] .

Finally, we repeated all analyses based on non-partial volume corrected FTP PET data and found overall similar results, suggesting that partial volume correction did not fundamentally drive the observed pattern of longitudinal tau spread in PCA (Supplementary Figs. 8 [this file] – 11 [this file] ).

For this study, we included interview transcripts from 12 “rapid-type” and 15 “slow-type” bereaved caregivers ( Supplementary Table S1 [this file] ). 
Reflexive thematic analysis has six recursive phases (see Supplementary Appendix [this file] for details). 
During phases 5–6 of reflexive thematic analysis that used poetic analysis, we iteratively engaged in three “deceptively simple” steps., KLH reviewed coded data to select poignant or illustrative units (e.g., paragraphs or pages of transcript) that reflected common or divergent experiences to become “poem seeds” ( Supplementary Tables S1 [this file] and S3 [this file] ). KLH gathered context and complexity from reviewing the transcript of the poem seed ( Table S1 [this file] , S3 [this file] ). , KLH created poems from transcript selections. She then combined or re-arranged sections of text that spoke to similar topics or experiences ( Table S3 [this file] ), creating line breaks and removing but not adding words. Analysis iteratively engaged the question of how each poem validated or challenged our understanding of each theme (including pruning as part of recursive engagement with phase 4 of analysis) and the core comparisons across dementia types ( Table S4 [this file] ). In the final step of phase 5, we refined theme names to highlight comparisons and the role of time ( Table S5 [this file] ). 
We use these findings to develop a conceptual model of end-of-life dementia care ( Supplementary Figure S1 [this file] ).

In contrast, the mean biological variance across patient samples was 68%, allowing for straightforward extraction of biological pathway alterations from the technical variation (Appendix Fig. S1C [this file] ). Principal component analysis (PCA) revealed tight clustering of the pooled reference samples, further indicating high technical consistency and overall data quality (Appendix Fig. S1D [this file] ). Across multiple plates, UMAP visualization showed no evidence of plate-associated heterogeneity, indicating minimal batch effects (Appendix Fig. S1E [this file] ). To maintain high data quality, we evaluated each sample in the three studies for blood contamination and technical variation, leading to the exclusion of 54 samples in total: seven from the Columbia cohort, four from the LCC cohort, and 43 from the PPMI cohort (Appendix Fig. S1F,G [this file] ). Given the differences in instrumentation, sample collection and preparation, and data acquisition protocols across cohorts, we considered the possibility that batch effects could influence the outcome of our ML analysis combining the three cohorts (Appendix Fig. S10A [this file] ; Dataset EV5 [rid=MOESM7] ). Feature selection yielded consistent results, with the top discriminative proteins–such as NEU1, ALPI, CTSB, ENPEP, and CTSH - shared between corrected and uncorrected datasets (Appendix Fig. S10B [this file] ; Dataset EV4 [rid=MOESM6] ). Model performance remained the same after batch correction (Appendix Fig. S10C [this file] ), underscoring the robustness of our results and confirming that batch effects did not compromise feature selection or predictive accuracy. 
Using library-free DIA proteomics on urine from BAC- rats ( = 8) and controls ( = 10), we reproducibly identified 2486 proteins (Appendix Fig. S11A [this file] ), with ~11% significantly altered at values <5% (Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] A, Appendix Fig. S11A,B [this file] ; Dataset EV6 [rid=MOESM8] ). 
Western blotting of kidney and brain tissues confirmed successful deletion and pharmacological inhibition (Appendix Fig. S12A,B [this file] ). 
Our MS-based proteomic analysis reproducibly identified 2635 proteins in the KO dataset and 2852 in the inhibitor dataset (Appendix Fig. S11A [this file] ). In line with LRRK2’s diverse roles, exhibited the most significant differences compared to controls, with >50% of proteins significantly regulated (Fig. 3B [rid=Fig3] ; Appendix Fig. S11B [this file] ; Dataset EV6 [rid=MOESM8] ). Fold-changes in KO vs. WT were strongly inverse to G2019S vs. WT (Pearson = −0.72; Appendix Fig. S13A [this file] ). Regression analysis revealed changes induced by PF-475 and MLi-2 were highly concordant (Pearson = 0.71; Appendix Fig. S13A [this file] ), consistent with on-target Lrrk2 kinase inhibition. Inhibitor-induced urinary proteomics alterations resembled KO (Pearson = 0.50) and anticorrelated with G2019S (Pearson = −0.20) (Appendix Fig. S13A [this file] ). 
On these, the model achieved even better performance with ROC AUCs of up to 0.9 (Appendix Fig. S14 [this file] ). 
Across tissues, we identified over 9000 proteins (Appendix Fig. S12C [this file] ). BAC- and inhibitor-treated rats exhibited changes that were more modest than in knockouts yet consistent (Appendix Fig. S12D [this file] ). 
Fold-changes were negatively correlated between KO vs. WT and G2019S vs. WT, indicating that gain- and loss-of-function perturbations induce opposing molecular phenotypes (Appendix Fig. S13B [this file] ). Both inhibitors elicited consistent alterations (Appendix Fig. S13B [this file] ), with enrichment for lysosomal and mitochondrial pathways (Fig. 5E [rid=Fig5] ) and substantial overlap with G2019S-associated urinary protein changes in humans (Fig. 5F [rid=Fig5] ). 
Both inhibitors produced robust but partially overlapping changes (Appendix Fig. S13C [this file] ). 
Correlation analyses mirrored the kidney, showing opposing alterations between KO and G2019S, with both inhibitors positively correlating with KO and strongly with each other (Appendix Fig. S13D [this file] ). 
Together, these findings demonstrate tissue-specific proteomic signatures of perturbations, with the kidney showing a stronger response among the tissues examined and the largest overlap of significantly regulated proteins with urine, as expected (Appendix Fig. S12E [this file] ). Notably, urine exhibited an even stronger aggregated effect than the corresponding tissues (Appendix Fig. S12F [this file] ). 
In the unpublished targeted urinary proteomics analysis of the PPMI cohort, total RAB10 and LRRK2 seemed to be elevated in G2019S carriers while phosphosite signals were sparse, consistent with detection limits rather than absence of biology (Appendix Fig. S15 [this file] ). 
This analysis revealed the strongest phenotypic similarity shared with the kidney (278 proteins) (Appendix Fig. S12E [this file] ), consistent with high LRRK2 expression in renal tissue, particularly in proximal tubule cells (Baptista et al, 2013 [rid=CR11] ; Kluss et al, 2021 [rid=CR39] ; Thévenet et al, 2011 [rid=CR69] ). Yet, lung (137) and brain (117) signals were also detectable in rat urine (Appendix Fig. S12E [this file] ). 
Notably, aggregate fold-changes were often more pronounced in urine than in individual tissues (Appendix Fig. S12F [this file] ), suggesting that urine acts as a sensitive integrator of LRRK2-linked biology across compartments. 
Our research focuses on PPMI Project 190, which includes three groups: 477 PD patients with early untreated PD or genetic and variants, 362 prodromal participants at risk of developing PD based on clinical features, genetic variants, or other biomarkers, and 141 healthy controls with no neurological disorders or family history of PD (Appendix Fig. S16 [this file] ).

Expression of pluripotency stem cell-specific markers was confirmed by immunostainings for SSEA4, Nanog, and TRA-1-60 (Supplementary Fig. 1A [this file] ). The pluripotency of the iPSC lines was also validated by their ability to differentiate into endodermal, mesodermal, and ectodermal origin cells upon immunostaining of Brachyury (Mesoderm marker), Sox17 (endoderm marker), and Nestin/Sox2 (ectoderm marker) (Supplementary Fig. 1B [this file] ). The iPSC lines maintained a normal karyotype after reprogramming (Supplementary Fig. 1C [this file] ). 
We found no significant differences in the expression of GFAP and Tuj1 at week 12 between the first and second round of experiments (Supplementary Fig. 9 [this file] ). 
Cerebral organoid size was monitored and there were no evident differences observed among different groups at 2 and 12 weeks (Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] ). In contrast, on week 4, reverse transcription-quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) revealed that cerebral organoids from AD patients exhibited higher mRNA levels of mature neuronal markers including , , and , but not , an astrocyte marker (Supplementary Fig. 3A–D [this file] ). Synaptophysin and PSD95 were also upregulated in AD organoid groups by week 4 (Supplementary Fig. 3E–G [this file] ). While synaptophysin levels were increased in AD-E4 organoids (Supplementary Fig. 3F [this file] ), did not influence PSD95 levels (Supplementary Fig. 3G [this file] ). 
Higher levels of Aβ40 at week 8 (Supplementary Fig. 4A [this file] ) and Aβ42 at weeks 4 and 8 (Supplementary Fig. 4B [this file] ) were observed in the RIPA-soluble fraction from AD organoids as compared to those from healthy subject-derived cerebral organoids. 
While RIPA-soluble p-tau increased in all groups in time, or AD patient-derived organoids showed higher p-tau levels as early as week 4 (Supplementary Fig. 4C [this file] ). 
Both and AD status were associated with the increased soluble apoE levels at week 4 (Supplementary Fig. 4D [this file] ). No significant differences in GFAP/Tuj1 ratio were observed among the four groups of cerebral organoids by immunostaining (Supplementary Fig. 5A–B [this file] ), RT-qPCR (Supplementary Fig. 5C [this file] ), and western blotting (Supplementary Fig. 5D [this file] ), suggesting that or AD status leads to the higher apoE level without increasing astrocyte population in the cerebral organoids.

The top-ranked pathways enriched by DEGs were “Actin filaments” in Con-E3 vs. Con-E4 comparison (Supplementary Fig. 6D [this file] ), “Regulation of epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition” in AD-E3 vs. AD-E4 comparison (Fig. S6E), “Axonal guidance” in Con-E3 vs. AD-E3 comparison (Supplementary Fig. 6F [this file] ), and “Endoplasmic reticulum stress pathway” in Con-E4 vs. AD-E4 comparison (Supplementary Fig. 6G [this file] ). “Innate inflammatory response” also showed up in all of the top 10-ranked pathways, suggesting a potential involvement of inflammation in effects and AD pathogenesis (Supplementary Fig. 6D–G [this file] ). The control cases were on average younger (65.4 +/− 8.9 years) than those with disease (PD=78.1 +/− 8.7; PDD=76.9 +/− 7.7; DLB=73.2 +/− 6.7 years) ( Table S1 [this file] ). 
All three Lewy body disorders demonstrated a robust number of significantly altered proteins ( <0.05) ( Fig. 1B [rid=F1] , Table S2 [this file] ). 
These 8,517 proteins were clustered into 33 co-expression modules, with M1 representing the largest module ( proteins=601) and M33 the smallest module ( proteins=39) ( Fig. 1D [rid=F1] , Table S3 [this file] ). In addition, each module was further characterized by cell type enrichment and gene ontology (GO) analyses ( Fig. 1E [rid=F1] , Table S4 [this file] ), as previously described [ 16 [rid=R16] – 18 [rid=R18] ]. 
The presynaptic compartment and related functions (vesicular signaling / transport, cell localization) were most strongly reflected among the top GO terms for these elevated modules ( Table S4 [this file] ). 
Two LBD-associated modules (M17, M19) were significantly enriched in PD GWAS targets ( Fig. 2I [rid=F2] , Table S5 [this file] ). Meanwhile, M8 was the only LBD-associated module enriched with AD GWAS targets ( Fig. 2I [rid=F2] , Table S6 [this file] ). 
Yet, we noticed that SNCA harbored kMEs of similar strength to other modules beyond M19, including M7 (kME=0.6245), M17 (kME=0.5820), and M26 (kME=0.5688) ( Table S3 [this file] ). This analysis revealed SNCA as the strongest bottleneck ( =0.003089) among the 242 members of M19, highlighting this protein as central to flow of information between the four modules ( Fig. 3B [rid=F3] , Table S7 [this file] ). 
Accordingly, the same presynaptic modules were also highly represented among individual proteins with strong positive correlations to SNCA abundance levels ( Fig. 3C [rid=F3] – D [rid=F3] , Table S8 [this file] ). 
Like the UPenn cohort, those Emory cases with dementia were on average in their mid-70s (PDD=75.3 +/− 10.7, DLB=74.6 +/− 7.9) and predominantly male ( Table S9 [this file] ). 
The resultant network comprised 7,829 proteins organized into 39 Emory (E) modules with the largest (E-M1) featuring 431 proteins and the smallest (E-M39) harboring 90 proteins ( Fig. 4B [rid=F4] , Table S10 [this file] – 11 [this file] ). 
Accordingly, synaptic signaling ontologies were featured among the top GO terms for these Emory modules ( Table S11 [this file] ). Furthermore, E-M24 harbored SNCA among its module members ( Fig. 4E [rid=F4] , Table S10 [this file] ). 
We used available clinical and pathological traits to classify these cases into control ( =42), asymptomatic LB pathology (AsymLB, =21), and Lewy body dementia (LBD, =40) groups ( Table S12 [this file] ). 
The first AD network was also derived from the UPenn ADRC, comprising 49 DLPFC tissues from pathologically defined AD cases and the same 47 control tissues analyzed in the LBD network ( Table S1 [this file] ). 
Differential expression analysis of these low- and high-amyloid LBD cases revealed >700 proteins significantly altered between these two groups ( Fig. 6A [rid=F6] , Table S13 [this file] ).

MS identified multiple homocysteinylated lysine residues throughout the α‐syn sequence (Table S1 [this file] ), with lysine 80 (K80) as the major modified residue (Figure 2a [rid=acel13745-fig-0002] ). Dot blots showed that anti‐K80Hcy antibody preferentially recognized α‐syn K80Hcy peptide (Figure S1 [this file] ). 
ELISA showed that K80 modification in standard was recognized by anti‐K80Hcy antibody in a concentration‐dependent manner, while the anti‐K80Hcy antibody did not react with the α‐syn K80R mutant or unmodified α‐syn (Figure S2a [this file] ). ELISA showed that the percentage of α‐syn K80Hcy in control subjects was 1.63%, while that in PD patients was about 5.57% (Figure S2b [this file] ). ELISA showed that 1.99%, 3.47%, and 6.05% of α‐syn was modified in TgA53T mice at 8, 10, and 12 months of age, respectively (Figure S2c [this file] ). 
However, the fibrillization of K80R mutant α‐syn was not affected by HTL (Figure 4a [rid=acel13745-fig-0004] , Table S2 [this file] ). HTL‐modified α‐syn PFFs were more resistant to digestion with protease K or pronase than control α‐syn PFFs (Figure 4c,d [rid=acel13745-fig-0004] , Figure S3a [this file] ). 
ELISA analysis using the anti‐K80Hcy antibody showed that 4.94% of α‐syn was modified in α‐syn‐HEK293 cells exposure to 0.1 mM HTL (Figure S3b [this file] ). The aggregates colocalized with ubiquitin, a marker of Lewy bodies (Figure S3c [this file] ). Moreover, HTL induced α‐syn phosphorylation in the absence of α‐syn PFFs in α‐syn‐HEK293 cells and neurons (Figure S3d‐g [this file] ). Similar to HTL, Hcy also resulted in an elevation of α‐syn aggregation in α‐syn‐HEK293 cells (Figure S4a‐d [this file] ). Knocking down of MARS in α‐syn‐HEK293 cells prevented the elevation of α‐syn aggregation induced by Hcy treatment, but not by HTL (Figure S4e‐h [this file] ), indicating that the conversion of Hcy to HTL is required for it to promote α‐syn aggregation in cells. 
Hcy and HTL promoted the aggregation of wild‐type α‐syn, but not the K80R mutant α‐syn (Figure S5a,b [this file] ). The results were further validated by Western blot analysis of the soluble and insoluble α‐syn species (Figure S5c‐f [this file] ). 
ELISA assay showed that 10.63% of α‐syn was modified by K80Hcy in α‐syn PFFs generated from wild‐type α‐syn in the presence of HTL (Figure S6a [this file] ). Coomassie Blue staining confirmed that equal amounts of fibrils were used (Figure S6b [this file] ). 
Compared with α‐syn PFFs, HTL‐PFFs induced more deposition of pS129 (Figure S7a [this file] ). HTL‐α‐syn PFFs caused an increased accumulation of high molecular weight α‐syn species (Figure S7b‐g [this file] ). Furthermore, the expression of the microglial marker IBA1 and astrocyte marker GFAP in the striatum was higher in mice injected with HTL‐α‐syn PFFs than these in mice injected with α‐syn PFFs (Figure S7h‐j [this file] ). The number of tyrosine hydroxylase (TH)‐positive neurons in the SNpc ipsilateral to the injection site was slightly decreased compared with that in mice injected with α‐syn PFFs (Figure S7k,l [this file] ). Moreover, the loss of TH‐positive nerve terminals in the striatum was also more drastic in mice injected with HTL‐α‐syn PFFs (Figure S7k,m [this file] ). Western blot analysis found that the levels of TH in the striatum were decreased in mice injected with HTL‐α‐syn PFFs compared with mice injected with α‐syn PFFs (Figure S7n,o [this file] ). Consistently, the mice injected with HTL‐PFFs showed more severe motor deficits in behavioral tests including the rotarod test, wire hang test, pole test, and balance beam test (Figure S7p‐t [this file] ). 
The percentage of α‐syn K80Hcy increased from 3.58% in vehicle‐treated TgA53T mice to 6.88% in Met‐treated TgA53T mice (Figure S8a [this file] ). Met did not trigger the appearance of pS129 in wild‐type mice (Figure S8b [this file] ). Met administration also induced an increased IBA1 and GFAP immunoreactivity in TgA53T mice, but not in wild‐type mice (Figure S8c‐j [this file] ). 
The expression of exogenous α‐syn in the SN was confirmed by immunostaining with an antibody specific to human α‐syn (Syn211) (Figure S9a [this file] ). Immunofluorescence confirmed that TH‐positive neurons in the SN were efficiently infected by AAVs (Figure S9b [this file] ). The results were further confirmed by immunostaining (Figure 6e [rid=acel13745-fig-0006] and Figure S10a [this file] ). The deposition of α‐syn K80Hcy and pS129 was accompanied by increased IBA1 and GFAP immunoreactivity (Figure S10b‐e [this file] ). Met exacerbated the loss of TH‐positive neuronal terminals and the decrease of TH levels in the striatum in mice expressing α‐syn A53T, but not in mice expressing α‐syn A53T K80R (Figure 6h,i [rid=acel13745-fig-0006] and Figure S10f,g [this file] ).

All three F1 crosses share key features of the disease , including decreased survival ( Fig. 1b [rid=F1] ) and body weight ( Supplementary Fig. 1a [this file] – b [this file] ), progressive accumulation of hyperphosphorylated tau in the cortex and hippocampus (AT8 staining; Fig. 1c [rid=F1] ), and prominent astrogliosis and microgliosis ( Fig. 1d [rid=F1] – f [rid=F1] ). Consistent with previous reports that FVB mice can be more vulnerable to neurodegeneration, we observed that F1 Tau transgenics on the FVB/C57 (TPR50xFVB/NJ) background had decreased survival and increased pathological tau as compared to the C57/C57 (TPR50xC57BL/6J) and DBA/C57 (TPR50xDBA/2J) progeny ( Fig. 1b [rid=F1] ) ( Supplementary Fig. 1c [this file] – h [this file] ). Importantly, no significant decrease in the weight of any of the affected brain areas was detected in transgenic animals at six months ( Supplementary Fig. 1i [this file] ), consistent with previous data showing no cell loss at this stage . 
The differentially expressed genes from transgenic and wild type mice clearly separate tau mutant from wild type genotypes within affected brain regions ( Supplementary Fig. 2a [this file] – c [this file] ), but not in the cerebellum ( Supplementary Fig. 2a [this file] ), and are consistent are across strains ( Supplementary Fig. 2d [this file] , e [this file] ). There was significant overlap in differential expression ( Online Methods [rid=S19] ; Supplementary Fig. 3a [this file] ) between the cortex and hippocampus, and significant correlation between fold changes in differentially expressed genes (Rank-rank hypergeometric test; p<0.05) from these two regions (R =0.76, slope=0.92, Supplementary Fig. 3a [this file] ). We find lesser, but significant correlation in gene expression between the cortex and brain stem (R =0.33, slope=0.82, Supplementary Fig. 3a [this file] ). Consistent with the absence of significant cell loss at six months in this model , positive regulators of apoptosis (GO ID:0043065) do not show significant changes across all 3 strains ( Supplementary Fig. 3b [this file] – e [this file] ) and negative regulators of apoptosis (GO ID :0043066) show modest, more significant changes ( Supplementary Fig. 3f [this file] – i [this file] ).We note that although we do not observe frank apoptosis, we do see evidence for initial activation of cellular pathways associated with inflammation in cerebral cortex by six months, including increases in GFAP and Iba-1 immunoreactivity in cortex ( Fig. 1d [rid=F1] – f [rid=F1] ). 
We observed no significant overlap in gene expression between the cortex and cerebellum ( Supplementary Fig. 3j [this file] – k [this file] ) and no correlation between differentially expressed genes in cortex and cerebellum (R =0.01, slope=0.14, Supplementary Fig. 3a [this file] ). Even more striking is that the expression changes of the top upregulated genes in the cerebellum are reversed in the cortex ( Supplementary Fig. 3l [this file] ), implying that protective changes may potentially occur in the cerebellum, as has been previously suggested . 
To place gene expression changes in a systems level framework, we performed consensus Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis (cWGCNA ) across all three heterozygous F1 mouse strains to identify relationships not observed in only a single background ( Supplementary Fig. 4a [this file] , Supplementary Table 1 [rid=SD3] ). Cell-type enrichment analysis demonstrated that the salmon module is enriched in neuronal markers, the magenta module for oligodendrocyte markers, and the turquoise module for microglial, astrocyte and endothelial markers ( Fig. 2b [rid=F2] ) across multiple different cell type specific gene expression datasets ( Supplementary Fig. 4b [this file] ). Gene ontology (GO) analyses is consistent with the cell type enrichments, showing that the salmon module is enriched for synaptic pathways, magenta for DNA repair and transcription, while the turquoise module is enriched for immune and inflammatory categories ( Supplementary Fig. 4c [this file] – d [this file] ). 
Genes correlated highly with phospho-tau levels (R >0.6; Online Methods [rid=S19] ) were found to be significantly enriched in the salmon (42-fold) and turquoise modules (9.5-fold), but not in the magenta and pink modules ( Supplementary Fig. 4e [this file] ). Given the consistent cell type enrichments and strong gene ontology enrichments ( Fig. 2b [rid=F2] , d-g; and Supplementary Fig 4b [this file] – d [this file] ) we relabel the salmon module, the Neurodegeneration-Associated Synaptic (NAS) module, and the turquoise module, the Neurodegeneration-Associated Inflammatory (NAI) module, so as to provide more intuitive names for these core disease-associated modules. 
Moreover, both the NAI and NAS module eigengenes show changes across affected brain regions (cortex, Fig. 2e [rid=F2] , h [rid=F2] ; hippocampus, Supplementary Fig. 4f [this file] – g [this file] ; brain stem, Supplementary Fig. 4h [this file] – i [this file] ) but not cerebellum ( Fig. 2i [rid=F2] , j [rid=F2] ), prior to decreases in brain weight that would be indicative of cell loss ( Supplementary Fig. 1i [this file] ). This is further supported by analysis of expression profiles from sorted neurons and glia from the Tg4510 and PS2APP AD model which show cell intrinsic changes in the NAI and NAS module trajectories ( Supplementary Fig. 5a [this file] – d [this file] ). The NAI module is highly preserved in both microglia and astrocytes and significantly upregulated in these populations in transgenics ( Supplementary Fig. 5a [this file] , c [this file] , d [this file] – l [this file] ), while the neuronal NAS module is highly preserved in sorted neurons and downregulated in transgenics ( Supplementary Fig. 5b [this file] , e [this file] – l [this file] ). 
Functional annotation of the NAS module with GO and KEGG terms, confirms its broader relationship to synaptic function ( Fig. 2d [rid=F2] and Supplementary Fig. 4c [this file] ). In contrast, functional annotation of the NAI module highlights pathways associated with astrogliosis and inflammatory changes , including T cell activation and Toll-like receptor signaling pathways ( Fig. 2g [rid=F2] and Supplementary Fig. 4d [this file] ). 
Further analysis of 4 independent datasets from mouse models harboring pathological tau mutations including a replication dataset that we generated using the Tg4510 tau model (Methods, Supplementary Fig 5f [this file] ) confirm the preservation of the NAI and NAS modules ( Supplementary Fig 5e [this file] ), and the expected changes in gene expression early in the disease course ( Supplementary Fig. 5f [this file] - h [this file] , l [this file] ). The NAS and NAI models are highly preserved and their disease associations are maintained and both the NAI and NAS module expression changes occur with similar temporal profiles across each of these models ( Supplementary Fig. 5e [this file] , i [this file] – l [this file] ). 
The NAS and NAI modules are dysregulated in patient cortex, but not in cerebellum, both in the previously published microarray-based data and in our newly generated RNA-seq dataset ( Fig. 3a [rid=F3] – d [rid=F3] and Supplementary Fig. 5e [this file] , m [this file] – n [this file] ) consisting of both tau-positive and tau-negative FTD ( Fig. 3c [rid=F3] ). Moreover, the NAS module and its disease-trait relationship are preserved in iPSC-derived neurons from human FTD patients carrying GRN mutations ( Supplementary Fig. 5e [this file] , o [this file] ). 
We also performed mass-spectrometry-based, label-free, quantitative proteomics in an independent set of GRN-positive and GRN-negative FTD frontal cortex ( Supplementary Fig. 5p [this file] , Supplementary Table 2c [rid=SD4] – d [rid=SD4] , Online Methods [rid=S19] ). 
Examination of RNA sequencing and proteomic post mortem brain datasets from AD patients showed preservation of both the NAI and the NAS modules at the mRNA ( Supplementary Fig. 5e [this file] , Fig. 3g [rid=F3] – h [rid=F3] , Supplementary Table 4a [rid=SD6] ), and at the protein level ( Fig. 3i [rid=F3] ). 
We identified two miRNA modules associated with the transgenic condition (Bonferroni corrected P < 0.05, Fig. 4a [rid=F4] , Supplementary Table 3 [rid=SD5] ): the miM12 module that is anti-correlated, and the miM16 module ( Fig. 4b [rid=F4] ), which is positively correlated with the transgenic condition in affected regions, but not cerebellum ( Fig. 4c [rid=F4] and Supplementary Fig. 6a [this file] – e [this file] ). The miM16 module eigengene is strongly anti-correlated with the NAS module eigengene ( Fig. 4d [rid=F4] and Supplementary Fig. 6f [this file] ), and predicted targets of miR-203, an miM16 hub, are highly enriched (see Online Methods [rid=S19] ) in the NAS module ( Fig. 4e [rid=F4] and Supplementary Fig. 6g [this file] , h [this file] ). Consistent with its potential regulatory role, miR-203 is robustly upregulated in transgenic mice at six months in disease-affected areas ( Fig. 4f [rid=F4] and Supplementary Fig. 6i [this file] – k [this file] ), and in the frontal cortex in both tau-positive and tau-negative FTD ( Fig. 4g [rid=F4] , h [rid=F4] ). 
To test the predicted causal relationship between miR-203 expression and NAS module down-regulation, we acutely over-expressed miR-203 ( Fig. 5a [rid=F5] ) in primary cortical mouse neuronal cultures ( Online Methods [rid=S19] , Supplementary Fig. 7a [this file] ), observing downregulation of its predicted targets ( Fig. 5b [rid=F5] ) and the NAS module more broadly ( Fig. 5c [rid=F5] , Supplementary Fig. 7b [this file] , Supplementary Table 4a [rid=SD6] ). We further experimentally validated several predicted direct targets of miR-203 ( , , , ) by luciferase reporter assays ( Fig. 5f [rid=F5] ) and western blot (BCL2L2 and VSNL1l; Fig. 5g [rid=F5] , see Supplementary Fig 9 [this file] for uncropped blots). 
To control for potential confounding by supra-physiological over-expression in vitro, we moderately overexpressed miR-203 (approximately 2-fold; Online Methods [rid=S19] ) or a scrambled miRNA control (sc-miRNA) ( Fig. 5h [rid=F5] ) targeting neurons in wild-type mice in vivo ( Supplementary Fig. 7c [this file] – f [this file] ). The NAS module is highly preserved ( Supplementary Fig. 7g [this file] , Supplementary Table 4a [rid=SD6] ) and down-regulated in neurons overexpressing miR-203 after six weeks ( Fig. 5i [rid=F5] ). Strikingly, the level of miR-203 expression correlates remarkably well with downregulation of both miR-203 predicted targets (R =0.81, slope=−2.3; Supplementary Fig. 7h [this file] ) and NAS module genes (R =0.81, slope=−2.2; Supplementary Fig. 7i [this file] ). Furthermore, apoptotic pathways are altered in miR-203-overexpressing neurons (, Figure 5j [rid=F5] , Supplementary Table 4b [rid=SD6] ), confirmed by Casp8 protein expression ( Figure 5k [rid=F5] , Supplementary Fig. 7j [this file] ). Additionally, miR-203 over-expression in one-month-old Tg4510 Tau transgenic cortex ( Supplementary Fig. 8a [this file] – b [this file] ) causes downregulation of predicted miR-203 targets ( Fig. 5l [rid=F5] ), the NAS module ( Fig. 5m [rid=F5] ), a significant increase in CASP8 protein ( Fig. 5n [rid=F5] ) and apoptotic pathways ( Supplementary Fig. 8c [this file] – d [this file] ) and genes involved in calcium signaling and neuroactive ligand receptors ( Supplementary Fig. 8e [this file] – f [this file] ). 
Both short term (6-weeks, Supplementary Fig. 8g [this file] – h [this file] ) and longer term (4-months, Supplementary Fig. 8i [this file] – j [this file] ) inhibition of miR-203 oppose the pathologic transcriptional changes in predicted miR-203 targets ( Supplementary Fig. 8k [this file] , Fig. 5o [rid=F5] ) and the NAS module broadly ( Supplementary Fig. 8l [this file] , Fig. 5p [rid=F5] ) including genes involved in calcium signaling and neuroactive ligand receptor pathways ( Supplementary Fig. 8m [this file] – n [this file] ), and apoptosis ( Fig. 5q [rid=F5] , Supplementary Fig. 8o [this file] – p [this file] ). Reducing miR-203 did not affect phospho-tau immunostaining ( Supplementary Fig. 8q [this file] – r [this file] ), consistent with its acting downstream of tau pathology. C-fos intensity was also significantly increased in mutant neurons expressing the miR-203 TuD construct, as compared to those expressing the control construct ( Fig. 5q [rid=F5] , Supplementary Fig. 8s [this file] , p-value <0.0001), suggesting functional rescue. 
It is noteworthy that modules identified in the initial individual F1 crosses that are not conserved and dysregulated across all three strains, are also not conserved in other mouse models, or human brain ( Supplementary Fig 10a [this file] – c [this file] ), supporting the approach that we have taken. 
As we show, long-term inhibition of miR-203 in the Tg4510 model, while upregulating anti-apoptotic pathways, downregulating pro-apoptotic pathways and increasing neuronal activity as measured by c-fos activation, does not reduce the phospho-tau burden ( Supplementary Fig. 8q [this file] – r [this file] ).

Scriptaid treatment does not alter miR-203 overexpression levels ( Supplementary Fig. 9 [this file] , indicating that the decrease in cell death is not a result of changes in viral infection, miRNA processing or regulation of miR-203 by scriptaid.
