Overall, neocortical brain regions (i.e., AG, MTC, and PFC) show greater cell fractions of excitatory neurons ( Figures 1D [rid=F1] and S1F [rid=SD3] ), and we identified 12 excitatory subtypes primarily found in various neocortical brain regions and 6 excitatory subtypes enriched in the entorhinal cortex, 6 in the hippocampus, and 1 thalamic-specific subtype (Exc NXPH1 RNF220) ( Figure 1D [rid=F1] ; Data S1 [this file] , pages 2A [this file] – 2F [this file] ). The entorhinal cortex-specific subtypes were marked by genes associated with the lateral or medial entorhinal cortex, e.g., , , and ( Figure 1D [rid=F1] ; Data S1 [this file] , pages 2A, 2B [this file] , and 2E [this file] ). In the hippocampus, identified neuronal subtypes included cells from the structured hippocampal formation, such as CA1 and CA2/CA3, as well as the dentate gyrus (DG) and subiculum ( Figure 1D [rid=F1] ; Data S1 [this file] , pages 2A, 2B [this file] , and 2E [this file] ). In contrast to the greater regional diversity of excitatory neuron subtypes, most inhibitory neuron subtypes (21 out of 22) were shared across brain regions, with the exception of Inh MEIS2 FOXP2, which was more specific to the thalamus ( Figure 1D [rid=F1] ; Data S1 [this file] , pages 2C, 2D [this file] , and 2F [this file] ). 
We identified 7,520 cell-subtype-specific genes shared between snATAC and snRNA datasets across the 67 subtypes, with 3,335 genes specific to excitatory and inhibitory neuron subtypes ( Figure 1D [rid=F1] ; Data S1 [this file] , page 2G [this file] ; Table S1 [rid=SD2] ). We observed substantial cross-modality concordance between cell-subtype-specific transcriptional expression and epigenomic activity ( Figure 1D [rid=F1] ; Data S1 [this file] , page 1C [this file] ). 
Further analysis revealed a strong enrichment of core circadian regulators (NR1D1/REV-ERBα, NR1D2/REV-ERBβ) and retinoic acid receptors (RORs: RORA, RORB, RORC) in both thalamic excitatory and inhibitory neurons, with inhibitory thalamic neurons additionally enriched for PITX and GSC family TFs ( Figures S2C [rid=SD3] and S2D [rid=SD3] ; Data S1 [this file] , pages 3A [this file] and 3B [this file] ). 
To systematically characterize large-scale epigenomic dynamics during AD progression, we inferred active and repressive compartments in major cell classes across 6 brain regions using hidden Markov model and ATAC signals from 27,993 high-quality genome-wide 100-kb bins and further grouped them into 25 epigenomic compartment groups (ECGs), based on their active or repressive status, using K-means clustering ( Figure 3A [rid=F3] ; Data S1 [this file] , pages 4A [this file] – 4F [this file] ; STAR Methods [rid=S21] ). We validated the inferred epigenomic compartments using multiple genetic and epigenetic features, including CpG density, A/T content, enrichment in nuclear domains (active speckle-associated domains [SPADs] and repressive lamina-associated domains [LADs]), and EpiMap chromatin states ( Figures 3A [rid=F3] and S4A [rid=SD3] – S4D [rid=SD3] ; Data S1 [this file] , pages 4A [this file] – 4E [this file] ; STAR Methods [rid=S21] ). 
Microglia and oligodendrocytes exhibited a higher proportion of repressive compartments, whereas excitatory and inhibitory neurons showed fewer repressive regions ( Data S1 [this file] , page 4D [this file] ). These patterns coincide with the activation of cell-type-specific gene expression programs ( Data S1 [this file] , page 4G [this file] ). 
We observed that genes in repressive compartments showed overall increased expression in lateAD, while genes in active compartments exhibited decreased expression ( Figure S4J [rid=SD3] ; Data S1 [this file] , page 5A [this file] ). Motivated by the coordinated epigenomic and transcriptomic changes in AD, we then analyzed the relationship between gene expression in repressive and active compartments and various variables of AD pathology and cognitive measures ( Figure S4K [rid=SD3] ; Data S1 [this file] , page 5B [this file] ). We found that expression level of genes in repressive compartments was positively associated with AD pathology progression but negatively correlated with cognitive function ( Figure S4K [rid=SD3] ; Data S1 [this file] , page 5B [this file] ). Conversely, expression level of genes in active compartments was positively associated with cognitive function but negatively correlated with AD pathology, with the higher correlations observed in inhibitory neurons and astrocytes ( Figure S4K [rid=SD3] ; Data S1 [this file] , page 5B [this file] ). 
We found that, during the progression of AD pathologies, repressive genomic regions become more accessible, while active chromatin regions (i.e., promoters and enhancers) are repressed ( Figures S8C [rid=SD3] and S9A [rid=SD3] – S9C [rid=SD3] ; Data S1 [this file] , page 6A [this file] ). Conversely, repressive heterochromatin and quiescent regions are more repressed, while -regulatory regions are more active in individuals with higher cognitive function and resilience ( Figures S8D [rid=SD3] , S9A [rid=SD3] , and S9B [rid=SD3] ; Data S1 [this file] , page 6B [this file] ).

To systematically characterize the epigenomic and transcriptomic dynamics during AD, we collected 384 postmortem samples from 111 age-matched individuals with and without AD from the Religious Orders Study (ROS) and the Rush Memory and Aging Project (MAP), two longitudinal cohort studies of aging and dementia ( Figures 1A [rid=F1] and S1A [this file] ). Individuals exhibited varying degrees of AD pathology based on clinical diagnoses, clustering into normal individuals without AD pathologies (nonAD; = 57), early-stage AD (earlyAD, = 33), and late-stage AD (lateAD, = 21) ( Figures 1A [rid=F1] and S1A [this file] ; Table S1 [rid=SD2] ). We integrated all snATAC and snRNA data separately ( Figures S1B [this file] – S1D [this file] ). After quality control, we obtained 1,217,165 nuclei from snATAC and 2,263,395 nuclei from snRNA data ( Figures 1B [rid=F1] , 1C [rid=F1] , and S1B [this file] – S1D [this file] ). 
This multimodal atlas is hierarchically organized into three levels of cell-type annotations in both snATAC and snRNA datasets, including 7 major cell classes, 34 subclasses, and 67 high-resolution subtypes ( Figures 1B [rid=F1] , 1C [rid=F1] , and S1E [this file] – S1H [this file] ; Data S1 [rid=SD1] , pages 1 [rid=SD1] and 2 [rid=SD1] ). The seven cell classes include Exc, inhibitory neurons (Inh), oligodendrocytes (Oli), oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs), astrocytes (Ast), Mic/immune cells (Mic/Immune), and vascular cells (Vasc) ( Figures 1B [rid=F1] , 1C [rid=F1] , and S1E [this file] ). Among subclasses, we defined 17 excitatory neuron subclasses spanning neocortical layers and the entorhinal, hippocampal, and thalamic regions, along with 6 inhibitory neuron subclasses characterized by selective expression of individual marker genes: , , , , , or ( Figure S1G [this file] ). The high-resolution subtypes include 25 excitatory, 22 inhibitory, 4 astrocyte, 3 oligodendrocyte, 3 OPC, 4 microglia/immune (including 2 subtypes of microglia, CNS-associated macrophages [CAMs], and T cells), and 6 vascular subtypes ( Figures 1B [rid=F1] , 1C [rid=F1] , and S1H [this file] ). 
We analyzed the brain-regional diversity and cell-type composition of 7 major cell classes and 67 subtypes in 6 brain regions in both snATAC and snRNA datasets, observing clear brain-region specificity across different cell types ( Figures 1D [rid=F1] and S1F [this file] ; Data S1 [rid=SD1] , pages 1A [rid=SD1] and 1B [rid=SD1] ). Overall, neocortical brain regions (i.e., AG, MTC, and PFC) show greater cell fractions of excitatory neurons ( Figures 1D [rid=F1] and S1F [this file] ), and we identified 12 excitatory subtypes primarily found in various neocortical brain regions and 6 excitatory subtypes enriched in the entorhinal cortex, 6 in the hippocampus, and 1 thalamic-specific subtype (Exc NXPH1 RNF220) ( Figure 1D [rid=F1] ; Data S1 [rid=SD1] , pages 2A [rid=SD1] – 2F [rid=SD1] ). The thalamus, compared with other regions, exhibited a lower fraction of neuronal cell types and a higher fraction of various glial and vascular cell types ( Figures 1D [rid=F1] and S1F [this file] ). 
This analysis revealed distinct TF motif enrichment patterns across brain cell types ( Figures 1D [rid=F1] , S2A [this file] , and S2B [this file] ). Microglia-specific TFs (SPI1/PU.1, SPIB, SPIC) were associated with microglial identity and immune function ( Figures 1D [rid=F1] and S2B [this file] ), consistent with previous studies. 
Notably, among neuronal cell types, thalamic neuron subtypes displayed distinct TF enrichment patterns, compared with other brain regions ( Figures 1D [rid=F1] and S2C [this file] ). Further analysis revealed a strong enrichment of core circadian regulators (NR1D1/REV-ERBα, NR1D2/REV-ERBβ) and retinoic acid receptors (RORs: RORA, RORB, RORC) in both thalamic excitatory and inhibitory neurons, with inhibitory thalamic neurons additionally enriched for PITX and GSC family TFs ( Figures S2C [this file] and S2D [this file] ; Data S1 [rid=SD1] , pages 3A [rid=SD1] and 3B [rid=SD1] ). Functional enrichment analysis of NR1D1/2 and RORs-regulated genes revealed associations with neuronal projection development, synaptic signaling, and cell junction organization, as well as additional pathways involved in circadian entrainment, sleep regulation, memory, cognition, and lipid metabolism, aligning with thalamic functions of regulating sleep-wake cycles and cognitive functions ( Figure S2E [this file] ). Interestingly, our analysis revealed that the gene locus was highly enriched for TF binding sites of NR1D1/2 and RORs, along with their cCRE-gene regulatory interactions, suggesting a potential self-regulatory network that contributes to thalamic neuron-specific functions ( Figure S2F [this file] ). 
To elucidate the epigenomic regulatory elements that underlie the identity and function of various brain cell types, we computed cCREs in each of the 67 cell types, grouped them into regulatory modules, and examined their roles in transcriptional regulation and the interpretation of brain disease risk variants using GWAS data ( Figures 2A [rid=F2] – 2D [rid=F2] and S3A [this file] – S3E [this file] ). Across cell subtypes, we identified a union set of 1,010,153 cCREs ( Figure S3A [this file] ). These cCREs were highly enriched in active promoter and enhancer chromatin states, validating these regions as regulatory elements ( Figures S3B [this file] and S3C [this file] ). 
Functional enrichment reveals that the cell-type-specific modules are enriched for distinct functional pathways and Gene Ontology (GO) terms ( Figure S3D [this file] ). Modules specific to excitatory and inhibitory neurons are enriched for pathways related to synapse structure, neuronal signal transduction, and neuron migration ( Figure S3D [this file] ). Microglia/immune cell-associated modules are enriched for immune response and cell activation pathways, while vascular cell-associated modules are highly enriched for blood vessel morphogenesis and vasculogenesis ( Figure S3D [this file] ). 
We next leveraged our single-cell epigenomic landscape and regulatory modules to interpret non-coding genetic risk variants associated with complex traits and diseases ( Figures 2D [rid=F2] and S3E [this file] ). We found that bipolar disorder, intelligence, schizophrenia, and depression-related variants are enriched in the cCRE modules from excitatory and inhibitory neuron subtypes ( Figures 2D [rid=F2] and S3E [this file] ). Immune disorders (including inflammatory bowel disease and multiple sclerosis) and AD were enriched in microglia or immune cells, consistent with prior studies ( Figures 2D [rid=F2] and S3E [this file] ). Vascular cells were enriched for traits associated with blood pressure and hypertension ( Figures 2D [rid=F2] and S3E [this file] ). 
We validated the inferred epigenomic compartments using multiple genetic and epigenetic features, including CpG density, A/T content, enrichment in nuclear domains (active speckle-associated domains [SPADs] and repressive lamina-associated domains [LADs]), and EpiMap chromatin states ( Figures 3A [rid=F3] and S4A [this file] – S4D [this file] ; Data S1 [rid=SD1] , pages 4A [rid=SD1] – 4E [rid=SD1] ; STAR Methods [rid=S21] ). 
We then investigated large-scale epigenomic compartment alterations in AD ( Figures 3A [rid=F3] – 3D [rid=F3] and S4E [this file] – S4H [this file] ). LateAD samples exhibited more frequent transitions between repressive and active compartments ( Figures 3A [rid=F3] , S4E [this file] , and S4F [this file] ). Notably, oligodendrocytes, microglia/immune, and vascular cells in the lateAD entorhinal cortex showed the most pronounced compartment transitions, highlighting the entorhinal cortex as particularly vulnerable to epigenomic dynamics ( Figures 3A [rid=F3] and S4G [this file] ). 
To validate this globally compromised compartmentalization, we directly surveyed snATAC signals within previously defined compartment domains (i.e., SPADs and LADs) in the human brain ( Figures 3C [rid=F3] and S4H [this file] ). Consistent with the compartment transition analysis, a genome-wide overview of epigenomic alterations between lateAD and nonAD demonstrated that repressive chromatin marked by greater nuclear lamina interactions, higher A/T content, and weaker association with nuclear speckles was activated, while active chromatin characterized by lower nuclear lamina interactions, lower A/T content, and stronger association with nuclear speckles was repressed ( Figures 3B [rid=F3] – 3D [rid=F3] and S4H [this file] ). Notably, typically repressive chromosomes with more nuclear lamina interactions, such as chr18, chr4, and chr13, were widely activated in AD ( Figures 3B [rid=F3] , 3D [rid=F3] , and S4H [this file] ). Conversely, the active chromosomes, including chr19 and chr22, tended to be globally repressed in AD ( Figures 3B [rid=F3] , 3D [rid=F3] , and S4H [this file] ). 
Consistent with our snATAC analyses, active histone modifications (H3K27ac and H3K4me3) exhibited increased signals in repressive compartments and decreased signals in active compartments ( Figure S4I [this file] ). Conversely, the repressive histone modification H3K27me3 exhibited elevated signals in active compartments and reduced signals in repressive compartments, further validating the compromised compartmentalization in AD ( Figure S4I [this file] ). 
We observed that genes in repressive compartments showed overall increased expression in lateAD, while genes in active compartments exhibited decreased expression ( Figure S4J [this file] ; Data S1 [rid=SD1] , page 5A [rid=SD1] ). Motivated by the coordinated epigenomic and transcriptomic changes in AD, we then analyzed the relationship between gene expression in repressive and active compartments and various variables of AD pathology and cognitive measures ( Figure S4K [this file] ; Data S1 [rid=SD1] , page 5B [rid=SD1] ). We found that expression level of genes in repressive compartments was positively associated with AD pathology progression but negatively correlated with cognitive function ( Figure S4K [this file] ; Data S1 [rid=SD1] , page 5B [rid=SD1] ). Conversely, expression level of genes in active compartments was positively associated with cognitive function but negatively correlated with AD pathology, with the higher correlations observed in inhibitory neurons and astrocytes ( Figure S4K [this file] ; Data S1 [rid=SD1] , page 5B [rid=SD1] ). 
This single-cell resolution epigenomic information was further validated based on the independent external references, including Human Brain Atlas (HBA) snATAC cCREs and H3K27ac cCREs derived from sorted human brain cell types, as well as EpiMap chromatin states across multiple brain regions, revealing a high consistency of the epigenomic information derived from all alternative references with high statistically significant correlations ( < 2.2 × 10 and Spearman correlation > 0.97) ( Figure S5A [this file] ). 
Detailed analysis at cell class and subtype resolution across brain regions revealed region-specific and cell-type-specific patterns of epigenomic deterioration ( Figures 4A [rid=F4] and S5B [this file] ). Consistent with the compartment dynamic analysis, the entorhinal cortex and hippocampus showed a more pronounced decline of the epigenomic information in lateAD, compared with neocortical regions, aligning with the region-specific progression of AD pathology ( Figures 4A [rid=F4] and S5B [this file] ). 
To study the epigenomic changes across glial cell types and cell states, we examined the activation and inflammatory signatures in glial subtypes ( Figures 4B [rid=F4] and S5C [this file] – S5F [this file] ). Among the four annotated astrocyte subtypes, we observed distinct activation states, with Ast DCLK1 showing a relatively higher activation score ( Figures 4B [rid=F4] and S5C [this file] ). In oligodendrocytes, Oli OPALIN and Oli RAFGRF1 are more inflammatory with higher activity for inflammation or disease-associated oligodendrocyte genes ( Figures 4B [rid=F4] and S5D [this file] ). For microglia, we annotated classic homeostatic (Mic P2RY12) and activated (Mic TPT1) subtypes, the latter showing higher activity of canonical activation genes including , , , and ( Figures 4B [rid=F4] and S5E [this file] ). 
To further study epigenomic deterioration across microglial activation states, we inferred the microglial activation trajectory based on the activity of the canonical microglial activation genes ( Figure S5F [this file] ; STAR Methods [rid=S21] ). Integrating microglial activation trajectories with cell states from previously reported large-scale datasets, including ROSMAP and Seattle Alzheimer’s Disease Brain Cell Atlas (SEA-AD) datasets, revealed a progressive transition trajectory from early surveillance and homeostatic phases, through intermediate reactive states, to terminally activated microglia characterized by lipid metabolism, inflammatory, ribosome biogenesis, and disease-associated microglia (DAM) signatures ( Figure S5G [this file] ). Consistent trends were observed across all six brain regions, with the entorhinal cortex and hippocampus showing the most pronounced decline in epigenomic information in activated microglia ( Figure S5H [this file] ). 
Analysis across genotypes revealed that homozygotes exhibited the most severe epigenomic erosion, followed by heterozygotes, compared with non-carriers ( Figure S5I [this file] ). A similar pattern was observed in astrocytes, with early activation showing increased epigenomic information and AD-GWAS enrichment, followed by declines in terminally activated astrocytes ( Figure S5J [this file] ). 
We calculated continuous CR scores based on the discrepancy between observed cognitive function (from clinical diagnosis) and that expected from global AD pathology ( Figure S6A [this file] ; STAR Methods [rid=S21] ). Individual-level association analyses across various AD-related pathological, phenotypic, and cognitive variables showed that CR is positively associated with higher cognitive function and slower decline across multiple cognitive function domains while being negatively associated with AD pathology burden ( Figures S6B [this file] and S6C [this file] ). 
We further examined epigenomic information along microglial and astrocyte activation trajectories in the context of CR, and we found that unlike the loss observed in AD, cognitively resilient individuals preserved epigenomic information in activated glial states, compared with cognitively vulnerable individuals ( Figure S6D [this file] ). 
Consistent with the vulnerable subtypes identified in the analysis of epigenomic information dynamics during AD and CR ( Figures 4A [rid=F4] , 5A [rid=F5] , and 5B [rid=F5] ), vulnerable excitatory neuron subtypes in the entorhinal cortex (e.g., Exc RELN COL5A2, RELN GPC5), hippocampus (e.g., DG granule cells), and neocortical upper-layer (e.g., L2–3 CBLN2 LINC02306, L3–4 RORB CUX2) were more abundant in individuals with higher epigenomic information and CR but depleted in those with a higher global AD pathology burden ( Figures 5C [rid=F5] and S6E [this file] ). 
By investigating cell-type fraction changes across states along the microglial and astrocyte activation trajectories, we assessed their relationship with AD pathological variables, cognitive functions, cognitive decline slopes, and CR scores ( Figure S6F [this file] ). Our analysis revealed that the loss of epigenomic information was associated with a depletion of cell proportions in late-stage activated microglia and astrocytes, which correlated with an advanced AD pathology burden ( Figures 4D [rid=F4] , S5J [this file] , and S6F [this file] ). In contrast, individuals with preserved cognitive function, slower cognitive decline, and higher CR exhibited preserved epigenomic information and cell fractions in activated microglia and astrocytes ( Figures S6D [this file] and S6F [this file] ). 
Among the top DEGs with associations to epigenomic information dynamics across seven cell classes and six brain regions, several notable genes tied to higher epigenomic information include , , , and ( Figures S7A [this file] and S7B [this file] ). Interestingly, we identified several AD-GWAS risk genes among these genes, including and ( Figures S7A [this file] and S7B [this file] ). Conversely, genes associated with lower epigenomic information (i.e., higher expression levels in epigenomically eroded cells) include , , , , and ( Figures S7A [this file] and S7B [this file] ). has been implicated in cerebral amyloid angiopathy and AD.and are associated with cellular stress responses. Notably, we also found that , one major genetic risk factor of AD, is negatively associated with epigenomic information, particularly in astrocytes, across all brain regions ( Figures S7A [this file] and S7B [this file] ). 
Correlation analyses revealed that activation of PAGEs was positively correlated with AD pathology progression and negatively associated with cognitive function and resilience, indicating a protective role of Polycomb repression in preserving cognitive function and mitigating AD progression ( Figures S7C [this file] and S7D [this file] ). 
Given that several top-ranked DEGs associated with epigenomic information dynamics are linked to AD-GWAS risk variants ( Figures S7A [this file] and S7B [this file] ), we investigated how dysregulation of AD-GWAS risk genes correlates with epigenomic information dynamics ( Figure 6D [rid=F6] ). 
To achieve this, we performed sample-level embedding, based solely on epigenomic information, and examined the correlations with these pathological and cognitive variables ( Figures 6F [rid=F6] , S7E [this file] , and S7F [this file] ; STAR Methods [rid=S21] ). Notably, we found that sample-level epigenomic information is positively correlated with higher cognitive function, slower cognitive decline, and CR ( Figures 6F [rid=F6] and S7F [this file] ). Conversely, epigenomic information is negatively associated with a range of clinical and neuropathological features of AD, including Braak stage, global AD pathology, tangle density, NFT burden, amyloid level, and diffuse/neuritic plaque burden ( Figures 6F [rid=F6] and S7F [this file] ). 
To examine molecular associations between epigenomic stability, AD pathology, and cognition, we analyzed DEGs and DARs linked to epigenomic information dynamics, AD pathologies (e.g., global pathology, tangle density, plaque burden), cognitive functions, cognitive decline slopes, and CR across cell subtypes ( Figures 6G [rid=F6] , S8A [this file] , and S8B [this file] ). Consistent with sample-level trends ( Figure 6F [rid=F6] ), fold changes of DARs and DEGs linked to epigenomic information dynamics were positively correlated with cognitive function and resilience but negatively correlated with the progression of various AD pathologies ( Figures 6G [rid=F6] , S8A [this file] , and S8B [this file] ). Additionally, we generated genome-wide visualizations of epigenomic dynamics and performed chromatin-state enrichment analysis of the DARs ( Figures S8C [this file] , S8D [this file] , S9A [this file] – S9C [this file] , and S10A [this file] – S10D [this file] ). This compromised epigenomic identity emerges early in AD, predominantly affecting the most vulnerable entorhinal cortex and hippocampus ( Figures S10B [this file] and S10C [this file] ). With advanced AD progression, these epigenomic erosion signatures intensify in lateAD and extend into other cortical areas, highlighting the progressive and region-specific epigenomic deterioration in AD ( Figures S10B [this file] – S10D [this file] ). Conversely, repressive heterochromatin and quiescent regions are more repressed, while -regulatory regions are more active in individuals with higher cognitive function and resilience ( Figures S8D [this file] , S9A [this file] , and S9B [this file] ; Data S1 [rid=SD1] , page 6B [rid=SD1] ).

Following pre-processing that included the removal of macrophages and monocytes, we retained scRNAseq data from 441,088 live human microglia from 161 donors and 20 unique brain tissue types in downstream analyses ( Figure 1A [rid=F1] and Figure S1 [this file] ). These factors have variable levels of expression across cells ( Figure S1D [this file] ). We characterized the factors into seven broad categories based on their overlap of enriched biological processes, including T-cell activation, metabolism, antigen presentation, disease-associated spectrum, inflammation, cellular stress, and miscellaneous ( Figure S1E [this file] ). 
In our model, factors captured gene signatures of homeostatic microglial functions: the factor (scHPF_16) captured the classic ‘homeostatic’ signature that includes high expression of , and ( Figure S2 [this file] ). 
Among the four factors capturing metabolic processes, three factors showed GO enrichment for oxidative phosphorylation ( Figure S3 [this file] ). Of our 23 microglial factors, the three oxidative phosphorylation factors showed the largest proportion of genes annotated to the mitochondrion ( Figure S3B [this file] ). 
While most donors in the discovery cohort were female, there was some variation in the proportion of females across diagnostic categories ( Figure S4 [this file] ). Compared to female tissue, male tissue showed a significant depletion of microglia with a high co-expression of the motility (scHPF_9) and chemokine signaling (scHPF_5) factors, as well as enrichment of microglia with a high co-expression of the (scHPF_24) and motility (scHPF_9) factors ( Figure S4C [this file] - G [this file] ). In the same subset of AD donors, after covarying for sex, we found that among donors aged >85 years old, there was a strong depletion of microglia highly co-expressing the chemokine and motility factors (scHPF_5, scHPF_9) ( Figure S5 [this file] ); this effect became more prominent with increasing age with the co-expressed signature being almost entirely depleted in the oldest donors (>95 years, =19). 
In a similar targeted analysis in donors diagnosed with pathological AD, we compared deep frontal white matter (anterior watershed; AWS), temporal cortex (BA20/21), and the hippocampus to the frontal cortex (BA9/46) ( Figure S6 [this file] ). 
Given that postmortem processing may affect transcriptional profiles, we note that there were few consistent differences in factors associated with longer postmortem interval or time to tissue processing ( Figure S7 [this file] ). 
Nonetheless, the model is useful for describing within sample variation in repurposed datasets; for example, in glioma myeloid cells, we identified a strong downregulation of the stress factor (scHPF_14) ( Figure S8 [this file] ) and upregulation of the HLA /antigen presenting cell (APC) factor (scHPF_15) after topotecan treatment in slice culture ( Figure 2B [rid=F2] , C [rid=F2] and Figure S9 [this file] ). The model was also broadly applicable to an model system of iPSC-derived, murine-xenografted microglia (xMGs), recapitulating a previously reported upregulation of the factor (scHPF_26) in xMGs from 5xFAD-MITRG mice compared to WT ( Figure 2E [rid=F2] - H [rid=F2] and Figure S10 [this file] ). 
In iPSC-derived human microglia (iMGs), the model recapitulated cluster-derived signatures ( Figure S11A [this file] , B [this file] ). We also recapitulated the observation of upregulated IFN-I response (scHPF_20) in iMGs treated with apoptotic neuron material; further, we also noted, in this context, a subset of microglia which co-express the IFN-I response and the chemokine signaling factors (scHPF_20 and scHPF_5) ( Figure 2I [rid=F2] - L [rid=F2] and Figure S11 [this file] ). For example, HMC3 cells treated with Torin2, a second generation mTOR inhibitor, showed a strong upregulation of IFN-I response (scHPF_20), while cells treated with Camptothecin, a topoisomerase inhibitor, showed an upregulation of the factor (scHPF_3) ( Figure 2L [rid=F2] , M [rid=F2] and Figure S12 [this file] ). Notably, however, signatures identified in model systems before or after treatments aimed towards polarization towards specific subtypes do not fully capture the distribution of microglial factors observed in scRNA-seq or snRNA-seq data ( Figure S13 [this file] ). 
For example, strong polarization towards IFN-I response (scHPF_20) was observed across multiple model systems, such as in iMGs induced by expression of transcription factors regardless of gene targets for CRISPR perturbations ( Figure S14 [this file] ). In the case of CRISPR-edited HMC3 cells, different gene knock-outs resulted in similar dysregulation of oxidative phosphorylation factors ( Figure S15 [this file] ). 
Nonetheless, the 23 factors showed substantial alignment with previous annotations based on traditional cluster-based analyses with marker genes, with several factors showing cluster specificity (e.g., , , , IFN-I response) ( Figure S16A [this file] ). A number of microglial factors are significantly upregulated with worse AD outcomes at the donor level (FDR -value < 0.05), including the glycolytic (scHPF_2), NPY1R (scHPF_4), (scHPF_11) and (scHPF_26) factors ( Figure 3B [rid=F3] ), with the (scHPF_26) factor being robustly associated with amyloid levels across all tested brain regions ( Figure S16C [this file] ). For completeness, we deployed an alternative strategy examining the data at the cell level (using ); in this secondary analysis, there was significant enrichment of the factor (scHPF_26) ( Figure S17 [this file] , and Figure S18 [this file] ), which was supported by the upregulation of individual DEGs in tissues with intermediate to high NIA Reagan scores, including , and ( Figure S17I [this file] - J [this file] ). 
We sought to replicate the significant association of factors with AD-related traits using two independent sets of ROS-MAP participants with snRNAseq data: (1) a new sample set produced at Columbia University (CUIMC2) ( =212) and (2) a repurposed dataset produced at MIT from which we removed overlapping samples ( =130 independent samples) ( Figure S19 [this file] ). After rigorous FDR-correction for multiple testing (FDR < 0.05), we replicated the association of (scHPF_26) with pathological AD and amyloid levels in the ROS-MAP snRNA-seq data ( Figure 3C [rid=F3] ) and bulk RNA-seq data ( Figure S20 [this file] ). 
Several TFs were markers of factor identity themselves (present in the top 100 genes of one of our 23 factors); the chemokine (scHPF_5) factor had the largest number of TF genes in its signature ( = 20 TFs; see Figure S21 [this file] ). 
Concurrently, to identify regulons with robust signatures across the cytoplasmic and nuclear compartments, we built a second, independent ARACNe regulatory network in the ROSMAP CUIMC1 dataset ( Figure S22 [this file] ). 
Notably, , and showed significant overlap in predicted target genes between the cytoplasmic and nuclear compartment ( Figure S22B [this file] ). 
While there was an overlap across the targets of the four TFs ( Figure 4E [rid=F4] ), variance partition showed that the TFs accounted for 0.03-12% of the variance in factor (scHPF_26) expression individually; jointly, they explain an average 33% of variance ( Figure 4F [rid=F4] and Figure S23 [this file] ). 
The MERFISH-profiled microglia were projected onto the 23-factor scHPF model ( Figure S24 [this file] ). When considering microglia across grey and white matter, putative (scHPF_26) regulators and showed a significant association with ARACNe-predicted targets, while only showed an association in grey matter ( Figure 5E [rid=F5] and Figure S25 [this file] ). 
IFN-I response factor (scHPF_20) showed statistically significant spatial autocorrelation (i.e., non-random patterning of expression) ( Figure S27 [this file] ), as well as local ‘hotspots’ (i.e., aggregation of high scores) which were prominently observed in two donors and across adjacent sections ( Figure S28 [this file] ). IR neighborhoods showed greater expression of the IFN-I response (scHPF_20) marker genes, as well as our IFN regulator, ( Figure 5F [rid=F5] and Figure S24 [this file] ). 
Our hypothesis was that cells with high expression of the IFN-I response factor (scHPF_20) were likely to respond to a focal IFN signal and would therefore be more likely to form topologically restricted communities. , IR microglia tended to occur more frequently in neighborhoods containing other IR microglia across white and gray matter ( Figure S29 [this file] ). Notably, IR microglia were more likely to co-occur in spatial neighborhoods in gray matter (GM) than white matter (WM) ( Figure S29C [this file] ). In IR neighborhoods, most cell types, particularly astrocytes, showed significant upregulation of IFN-I response genes ( Figure S30 [this file] and Table S16 [rid=SD3] ), consistent with the concept that a source of IFN exists in the area and alters gene expression in its vicinity. 
The (scHPF_26) factor showed significant patterns of spatial expression in WM (6 of 12 tissues), GM layer I (8 of 8 tissues), and GM layers II-VI (9 of 12 tissues) ( Figure S31 [this file] ). We found a significant positive correlation between the (scHPF_26) factor expression and the Getis-Ord Gi* z-score, suggesting a higher expression is associated with the presence of spatial hotspots, or clustering of high expression microglia. ‘Hotspots’ were present in both AD and non-AD tissue, in WM and deep GM (layers II-VI) ( Figure S32 [this file] ). Across WM and GM layers, microglia were more likely to co-occur in a neighborhood with another microglia than microglia ( Figure S33 [this file] ). 
Interestingly, like the pattern of clustering seen among IR microglia and adjacent cell types ( Figure 5 [rid=F5] and Figure S26 [this file] ), microglia that express high levels of the factor (scHPF_26) appear to be spatially more proximal to each other than microglia in tissue, but do not appear to be in cellular neighborhoods that are eliciting a similar gene signature, suggesting that they may not be responding to a spatially limited focus of a given molecular signal in the tissue. 
To mitigate confounding of sex across diagnoses, we restricted the analysis to AD tissue only, focusing on four brain regions (AWS, BA9/46, BA20/21, hippocampus) ( Figure S4A [this file] , B [this file] ). Vertices were randomly sampled to a proportion of 5% to define neighborhoods and refined the “graph” scheme ( Figure S4C [this file] ). Subsequently, overlapping and concordantly differentially abundant neighborhoods were grouped into larger pseudo-cluster, ‘meta-neighborhoods’ using the Louvain clustering algorithm with a log fold-change greater than 1 required to retain edges between adjacent neighborhoods ( Figure S4D [this file] ). To identify overall enriched or depleted meta-neighborhoods, we compared the distribution of log-fold change across individual neighborhoods comparing a single meta-neighborhood versus all other neighborhoods (Student’s -test, FDR-corrected -value < 0.05) ( Figure S4E [this file] ). Therefore, to characterize factor expression, we compared the distribution of median factor scores within a single meta-neighborhood versus all others (Wilcoxon test, FDR-corrected p-value < 0.001) ( Figure S4F [this file] ). 
Given the confounding of age across diagnostic categories ( Figure S5A [this file] ), we restricted the analysis to AD tissue only, focusing on four brain regions (AWS, BA9/46, BA20/21, hippocampus). Moreover, these positively correlated modules exhibited the highest expression in female AD patients (Figure S2A [this file] ), and were involved in immunity, gliogenesis, protein folding, extracellular matrix organization, and myelination (Figure S2B–I [this file] and Table S3 [rid=bpa13318-supitem-0008] ). Sex‐associated DEGs derived from the control group showed considerable overlap with genes from ME6, an immune‐related gene module (Figures 2B [rid=bpa13318-fig-0002] and S2B [this file] ). The genes within this ME6 exhibited a strong positive correlation with AD, female, and age (Figures 2C–E [rid=bpa13318-fig-0002] and S2B [this file] ), and were highly expressed in MG (Figure S2J [this file] ), suggesting MG were involved in the different vulnerability to AD between sexes.

We annotated the 414k snRNA-seq cells from matched individuals with seven major cell type groups and identified high-resolution cellular subtypes, including 14 excitatory, 25 inhibitory subtypes, and 22 glial and vascular subtypes ( Figure 1B [rid=F1] , S1A [this file] , ). For snATAC-seq cells, we performed stringent QC based on transcription start site (TSS) enrichment and number of unique fragments ( Figure S1B [this file] , Methods [rid=S22] ). Chromatin accessibility information alone unambiguously distinguished the 7 major cell types in the brain and resulted in highly-compact clusters for each of the cell types ( Figure 1C [rid=F1] – D [rid=F1] , Figure S1C [this file] – D [this file] ). These included 22k excitatory neurons, 21k inhibitory neurons, 101k oligodendrocytes, 10k astrocytes, 7.2k oligodendrocyte progenitor cells (OPCs), 8.6k microglia, and 1.2k vascular cells ( Figure 1C [rid=F1] ), and showed negligible technical or batch effects ( Figure S1B [this file] ). 
We identified 367,242 unique ATAC peaks overall, with 80k to 200k in each cell type (except for vascular cells, likely due to their limited cell number) ( Figure 1E [rid=F1] ; Figure S1E [this file] ). We found 130,193 peaks that showed cell type specificity ( Figure S1F [this file] ), defined based on the fold change of peak intensity over other cell types ( Methods [rid=S22] ). Cell-type-specific peaks were consistent with cell type gene expression specificity ( Figure S1G [this file] ), and were enriched for cell-type-specific functional pathways, including synaptic signaling for neurons, axon ensheathment for oligodendrocytes, extracellular matrix organization and vasculature development in pericytes and endothelial cells, and chondroitin sulfate biosynthesis in OPCs ( Figure 1F [rid=F1] ). 
The cell-type-specificity of these regulators was further supported by the presence of TF footprints in the appropriate cell types ( Figure S1H [this file] ). 
The integrated and transferred RNA and ATAC subtypes show well-aligned marker gene expression and gene-score ( Figure 2D [rid=F2] – E [rid=F2] ), with much improved alignment between RNA and ATAC profiles of subtype marker genes in our integration over scGLUE and Seurat, two state-of-the-art single-cell modality integration methods based on deep learning and canonical correlation analysis, respectively ( Figure S2A [this file] ) . 
We computed a final set of peak-to-gene links for each cell type using the snATAC-snRNA integration, first building a set of z-scored peak-gene co-accessibility and accessibility-expression correlations and then training regression models on these features to classify high-confidence peak-to-gene links ( Figure S2B [this file] , Table S3 [rid=SD5] ). Resulting peak-to-gene links have on average 21 linked peaks per gene ( Figure S2C [this file] ) and decay in frequency as genomic distance increases ( Figure S2D [this file] ). These cell-type-specific peak-to-gene links showed superior recovery of Plac-seq interactions (Proximity ligation-assisted ChIP-seq) in four cell types compared to other existing approaches, especially in the cases of distal peak-gene interactions where a peak is not linked to the nearest gene ( Figure 2F [rid=F2] – G [rid=F2] , Figure S2E [this file] – F [this file] ). 
Many peak modules were significantly enriched for upstream TF regulators ( Figure S2G [this file] , Table S4 [rid=SD6] ), connecting upstream regulators with downstream targets and suggesting specific sub-programs in each cell type. Astrocyte modules showed highly stratified TF enrichments, including for SOX9/13 (M3), ETV6/7 (M6), RORA/B/C (M7), and STAT1/STAT3 for M2 ( Figure S2H [this file] ) . 
Analysis of peaks independently identified in AD and control samples showed a consistent microglia-specific enrichment signal that was modestly but not significantly higher in AD ( Figure S3A [this file] – B [this file] ). We extended this GWAS enrichment analysis into 24 other traits, and observed that other brain-related traits including schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, neuroticism were enriched for neuronal epigenomes and that the microglial epigenome was more relevant to immune-related disorders ( Figure S3C [this file] ; Table S5 [rid=SD7] ). LDSC analysis at the sub-cell-type level further revealed the cell types of action at a higher resolution ( Figure S3D [this file] ; Table S5 [rid=SD7] ). 
By contrast, the binding sites of interferon-regulatory factor family TFs IRF1/2/5/8, which had clear microglia epigenome-specific enrichments and TF footprinting, were relatively depleted for AD-GWAS loci ( Figure S3E [this file] ; Figure 3C [rid=F3] ). Microglia TFBS-containing peaks display preferences in their genomic distribution, which may correspond to different modes of regulation ( Figure S3F [this file] ). 
We then prioritized functional AD-GWAS variants for each overlapped locus based on peak-to-gene links supported by multiple lines of evidence, including genetic links (expression quantitative trait loci; eQTLs) and physical interactions from HiChIP and PLAC-seq ( Figure S3G [this file] ; Table S5 [rid=SD7] ). We discovered eight genes that were specifically prioritized in microglia, including , and several loci that were prioritized in multiple cell types ( Figure S3H [this file] ). 
Before calling aQTL, we first evaluated potential allelic bias from read mapping and found no difference in peak activity between minor and major alleles ( Figure S4A [this file] ). While the microglia epigenome is strongly enriched for AD-GWAS signal, including the AD status of individuals as a covariate when calling aQTLs had a negligible effect on microglia aQTL identification ( Figure S4B [this file] ). The aQTLs tended to be located near their associated gPeaks, at a median of distance of 23kb (aQTLs were called within 100kb of peaks), with 18.2% of within 10kb and 7.0% within 1kb of their gPeak ( Figure S4C [this file] ). For the aQTLs that are significant in a discovery cell type but do not pass the significance threshold in the replication cell type, aQTL effect directions are over 93% consistent once the nominal p-value in the replication cell type is below p=0.1, and 100% consistent when the nominal p-value reaches 1×10 ( Figure 4B [rid=F4] , Figure S4D [this file] ). We estimated the aQTL sharing for each pair of major cell types using this method and found that aQTL sharing is consistent with the cell type similarity ( Figure S4E [this file] , Methods [rid=S22] ). 
We found 631 variants that showed shared genetic effects at a sub-threshold level (5×10 <p-value<1×10 ) in microglia as both aQTLs and AD risk loci ( Figure S4F [this file] ). AD GWAS and aQTL loci were highly orthogonal, with the vast majority (>99%) being either aQTL or AD-GWAS only (considering both genome-wide significant and sub-threshold loci), even for microglia aQTLs ( Figure S4F [this file] ). Heritability enrichment analysis confirmed that AD-GWAS risk loci were not enriched for aQTL gPeaks in any cell type ( Figure S4G [this file] ). We discovered a total of 69 aQTL-GWAS colocalization events ( Figure S4H [this file] , Table S5 [rid=SD7] ). 
To identify the genes and regulatory regions that are potentially involved in AD etiology, we performed AD-differential gene and ATAC peak calling in each major cell type, and found that gene expression and ATAC peak changes were broadly consistent in each cell type ( Figure S5A [this file] ; Table S6 [rid=SD8] ). Peaks linked to differential genes in microglia were enriched for AD risk loci, driven by AD up-regulated microglial genes, which may play an important role in AD heritability ( Figure S5B [this file] ). To map altered regulatory programs in AD, we also asked which co-accessibility modules had differential ATAC accessibility across AD stages ( Figure S5C [this file] ; Table S6 [rid=SD8] ). Microglia showed increased accessibility in regulatory modules tied to ECM remodeling and interleukin-11 signaling ( Figure S5C [this file] , Figure 5A [rid=F5] ). 
We also asked whether specific subtypes of neurons and glia showed compositional changes during AD progression ( Figure 5D [rid=F5] , Figure S5D [this file] ). High-resolution subtypes within each major cell type showed consistent directionality of compositional change during AD progression between ATAC and RNA cells, including a significant decrease in an inhibitory subtype (Inh ) ( Figure 5D [rid=F5] , Figure S5D [this file] ). 
We first observed that the late-stage AD samples showed a significant decrease in TSS-enrichment compared to the non-AD and early-stage AD individuals ( Figure S6A [this file] ), which was not accounted for by either samples’ post-mortem interval (PMI) or individuals’ age of death ( Figure S6B [this file] ). Furthermore, the number of fragments per cell, another commonly-used quality metric, showed no noticeable difference between the AD groups ( Figure S6A [this file] ), suggesting that this TSS enrichment depletion was linked to AD pathology and not sample quality. 
We confirmed that the late-stage AD samples were significantly enriched for the reclaimed cells ( Figure S6C [this file] ). 
Despite the fact that these scores were calculated independently from cluster and marker-driven de-identified cell calls, cell-level erosion scores were highly predictive for de-identified status (p<2.2e-16, R=0.56) ( Figure 6A [rid=F6] ), and were unrelated to other quality metrics, such as the number of fragments per cell (R=0.1, Figure S6D [this file] – E [this file] ). We compared the stage-specific distributions of erosion scores and confirmed that late-AD samples had significantly higher epigenomic erosion than non-AD and early-AD samples while non-AD and early-AD samples had similar distributions of erosion scores ( Figure 6G [rid=F6] , Figure S6F [this file] ), consistent with late-stage cell identity loss ( Figure 6B [rid=F6] ). As additional evidence for the erosion of active chromatin states in AD, we compared AD up-regulated and down-regulated regions from a published AD ChIP-seq study profiling H3K27ac, a marker of active epigenomic regions ( Figure S6G [this file] ). 
Just as in the original snATAC-seq dataset, the multiome dataset contained multiple clusters of deidentified cells with eroded cellular identity ( Figure S6H [this file] ), which were highly enriched in the high erosion samples ( Figure S6I [this file] – J [this file] ). The eroded cells from MFC samples recapitulated the chromatin state changes observed in the PFC samples ( Figure S6K [this file] ), and matched the erosion score distributions from the PFC data ( Figure S6L [this file] ). 
We found that up-regulated regions in eroded cells were enriched for developmental processes and cell-cell adhesion pathways, whereas down-regulated regions were enriched for DNA damage and repair processes ( Figure S6M [this file] ; Table S7 [rid=SD9] ). Enrichments for erosion-associated DEGs (434 up, 387 down, Figure S6N [this file] ; Table S7 [rid=SD9] ) paralleled those of the epigenomic analysis, with up-regulated genes enriched for cell-cell adhesion and GTPase signaling and down-regulated genes enriched for neuronal components and synapse-associated terms ( Figure S6O [this file] ). Top up-regulated genes in eroded cells included MAML2, a NOTCH-related transcriptional coactivator, and neuronal development-implicated TF ZFHX3, suggesting a reset of the transcriptional landscape for neurons ( Figure S6N [this file] ) . Erosion DEGs significantly overlapped AD DEGs , and showed the strongest overlaps with up-regulated DEGs for global cognition and tangle density ( Figure S6P [this file] ). 
LD expansion for AD GWAS loci ( Figure S3G [this file] ) was based on the Phase 3 of European ancestry genome structure curated by 1000 Genomes . 
Lastly, the proportion of cell-type-sharing ( Figure S4C [this file] ) aQTLs was quantified as: where the represents the percentage of aQTLs of bin i, and the represents the aQTL directionality consistency of bin i. 
All of the composition analysis was done using propeller ( Figure 5B [rid=F5] – D [rid=F5] , Figure S5D [this file] and Figure 6B [rid=F6] ), a published method designed to test for compositional changes in single-cell data . 
For Figures 5B [rid=F5] – D [rid=F5] and S5D [this file] , we tested across all three AD groups (non-AD, early-AD, and late-AD).

We annotated 76 high-resolution cell types in 14 major cell type groups, including 32 excitatory neuron subtypes (436,014 nuclei, 32.2% of total) and 23 inhibitory subtypes (159,838 nuclei, 11.8% of total) (Extended Data Fig. 1b–d [rid=Fig6] , Supplementary Figs. 1 [this file] and 2 [this file] and Supplementary Table 2 [rid=MOESM3] ). We characterized these cell types in terms of their transcriptome size and proliferative status, compared our atlas with previously published data across species (Extended Data Fig. 1e,f [rid=Fig6] and Supplementary Figs. 3 [this file] – 5 [this file] ) and identified broad cell type identity programs using non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) and transcriptional regulons using SCENIC (Extended Data Figs. 2 [rid=Fig7] and 3 [rid=Fig8] and Supplementary Tables 3 [rid=MOESM3] and 4 [rid=MOESM3] ). 
The fraction of neurons increased significantly from the TH (14.4% neurons) to the three-layer allocortical HC (32.2%), the entorhinal periallocortex (36.6%) and the six-layered neocortical regions (AG, MT and PFC, 58.9%) (Fig. 1b–e [rid=Fig1] and Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] ). Glia, including astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs) and microglia/immune cells, tended to be less abundant in neocortical samples (Fig. 1b–e [rid=Fig1] ), in agreement with previous studies in humans and mice (Supplementary Fig. 7a–d [this file] ). Differences in the composition of major cell types between regions were reproducibly observed across study participants, irrespective of the individual’s disease status (Supplementary Fig. 7e–h [this file] ), suggesting that variability in the major cell type composition between regions is a fundamental characteristic of the human brain and is not affected by AD pathology. 
We first characterized the regional diversity of excitatory neuron subtypes, which were consistent across individuals and were either highly region-specific to the HC, EC and TH (7, 9 and 2 subtypes, respectively) or were predominantly shared across neocortical regions (12 subtypes) (Fig. 1f [rid=Fig1] and Supplementary Fig. 8 [this file] – 12 [this file] ). EC-specific subtypes that clustered separately from neocortical subtypes for the same layers were often marked by expression of , and , and contained subtypes from both the lateral (L2 ) and medial (L2 ) EC (Supplementary Fig. 10 [this file] ). Excitatory neurons in the TH were predominantly composed (74%) of a subtype ( ) that was not observed in the neocortex and is predicted to be regulated by , , and (Extended Data Fig. 2a,b [rid=Fig7] and Supplementary Figs. 9e–i [this file] and 11n,o [this file] ). We found that the thalamic–neocortex separation is conserved in mice and recapitulated both this divide and thalamic marker genes in independent single-cell, bulk and microarray data in both mice and humans (Supplementary Fig. 12 [this file] ). 
In contrast to excitatory neuron subtypes, the majority of inhibitory neuron subtypes (22 out of 23 subtypes) were observed in all five cortical regions (Fig. 1g [rid=Fig1] and Supplementary Figs. 13 [this file] – 17 [this file] ), although some inhibitory subtypes had regional biases, including and (enriched in neocortex), layer 6 (EC and HC) and (EC), suggesting that there are significant differences in inhibitory neuron composition between the neocortex and allocortex (Fig. 1g [rid=Fig1] and Supplementary Fig. 14 [this file] ). By contrast, the TH contained a single unique, thalamus-specific inhibitory subtype ( ) marked by genes that are involved in neurite outgrowth, such as the semaphorins and , and , and receptors for serotonin ( ), acetylcholine ( , ) and glutamate ( ) (Fig. 1g,h [rid=Fig1] and Supplementary Figs. 14 [this file] and 15 [this file] ). We recapitulated this thalamic difference and program genes in the mouse thalamus and human lateral geniculate nucleus (dLGN) using previously published single-cell data (Supplementary Figs. 16 [this file] and 17 [this file] ). 
As thalamic neurons expressed several typically glutamatergic neuron genes, we determined glutamatergic and GABAergic module scores for every neuronal cell to further examine the chimeric nature of this subtype (Supplementary Fig. 15g–k [this file] and Supplementary Table 5 [rid=MOESM3] ). These scores matched the cortical excitatory and inhibitory split and were negatively correlated both across and within broad neuronal classes (Fig. 1j [rid=Fig1] and Supplementary Fig. 15g,h [this file] ). Both thalamic inhibitory and excitatory neurons had intermediate scores, placing them between the cortical excitatory and inhibitory clusters, suggesting that they are less polarized with regard to the expression of cortical glutamatergic versus GABAergic programs (Fig. 1j [rid=Fig1] and Supplementary Fig. 15i–k [this file] ). Predicted cell–cell communication interactions were mostly shared across multiple regions, but the thalamus had multiple differential interactions (Supplementary Figs. 18 [this file] and 19 [this file] ). 
We identified multiple transcriptionally distinct subsets for each major glial cell type and determined their characteristic marker genes (Fig. 2a [rid=Fig2] and Supplementary Fig. 20 [this file] – 25 [this file] ). Among glial cell types, astrocytes had the highest regional heterogeneity, containing both highly neocortex-enriched ( ) and thalamus-enriched ( ) subtypes (Fig. 2a–c [rid=Fig2] and Supplementary Fig. 20 [this file] ). Region-specific astrocyte subtypes were experimentally validated using RNA in situ hybridization (Fig. 2d [rid=Fig2] ) and confirmed by analysing a separate snRNA-seq dataset (Supplementary Fig. 23m [this file] ). Cortical astrocytes were enriched for markers involved in glutamate processing and transport, whereas hippocampus- and anterior thalamus-enriched astrocytes had lower glutamate transporter activity and were enriched instead for focal-adhesion-related genes (Fig. 2c [rid=Fig2] and Supplementary Fig. 25a [this file] ). Notably, the thalamic interneurons shared multiple markers with neocortical astrocytes, including , and (Supplementary Fig. 23n [this file] ), suggesting that astrocytes in evolutionarily newer regions may share some functions with inhibitory neurons in older regions. 
We used our method to identify modules both across all cells in the atlas and for each major cell type independently, and recovered modules expressed to varying degrees, ranging from identity modules for each glial cell type to a cell cycle module found in just 0.7% of microglia (Fig. 2f [rid=Fig2] , Extended Data Fig. 5 [rid=Fig10] , Supplementary Figs. 26 [this file] – 36 [this file] and Supplementary Table 6 [rid=MOESM3] ). 
Using this approach, we identified 32 modules in astrocytes, including an astrocyte-wide program (M9, expressed in >99% of astrocytes) marked by and and enriched for cell junction assembly, and subtype- and region-specific identity programs such as thalamus-associated M19 ( , , ), which were enriched for sonic hedgehog signalling, M12 ( : forebrain neuron development) and M7 ( : synaptic membrane) (Fig. 2g,h [rid=Fig2] and Supplementary Fig. 31 [this file] ). 
In contrast to astrocytes, immune cells showed little regional specificity and oligodendrocyte-lineage cells had thalamus-enriched subtypes with minor transcriptomic differences to neocortex-enriched subtypes (Supplementary Figs. 21 [this file] – 25 [this file] ). Immune modules included identity programs, such as for T cells (M6), macrophages (M7) and cycling microglia ( , M5) as well as modules found across immune cells and enriched for genes involved in NF-κB signalling (M18), interferon (M20), p53 and DNA damage response (M22) and TGFβ signalling (M14) (Extended Data Fig. 6f [rid=Fig11] and Supplementary Fig. 32 [this file] ). Oligodendrocyte-lineage modules showed high regional specificity, and two OPC modules—thalamus-enriched M11 and EC-enriched M25—were marked by synapse-associated genes such as neural adhesion-related , and , and glutamate receptor , suggesting a role for OPC sensation and response to neuronal activity in specific brain regions (Extended Data Fig. 5c,e [rid=Fig10] and Supplementary Figs. 33 [this file] , 34 [this file] and 36 [this file] ). 
Among excitatory neurons, we identified one HC-specific (CA1 pyramidal neurons) and four EC-specific (L2 lateral EC, L3 , L5 and L2/3 neurons) subtypes that were significantly less abundant (OR = 0.38–0.66) in individuals with a pathologic diagnosis of AD (Fig. 3a [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Fig. 37a–c [this file] ). Notably, while the overall excitatory fraction was not associated with cognition, lower OPC fraction across regions and, in particular, in non-neocortex regions was significantly associated with impaired cognition (Supplementary Fig. 37d [this file] ). 
Notably, while expression, which is typically restricted to inhibitory neurons, was highly specific to two EC excitatory subtypes, its downstream partner was present across subtypes (Extended Data Fig. 7h,i [rid=Fig12] and Supplementary Fig. 37e,f [this file] ). 
To understand how vulnerable subtypes are altered in AD, we computed differentially expressed genes (DEGs) for each excitatory neuron subtype ( Methods [rid=Sec10] and Supplementary Fig. 38a–c [this file] ). DEGs linked to non-vulnerable subtypes were enriched for a diverse set of functions, including ubiquitin-ligase binding, heat-shock-family chaperones, ER protein processing and mediators of neuronal death, whereas vulnerability-associated DEGs were highly enriched only for mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation but included and , which are both associated with Reelin signalling (Extended Data Fig. 7l,m [rid=Fig12] and Supplementary Fig. 38d–f [this file] ). 
AD DEGs were consistent with published results both for region-specific DEGs and for DEGs computed jointly over all regions for multiple AD variables, and were further corroborated by comparisons with various independent studies (Supplementary Fig. 39 [this file] ). 
Such genes included and (broadly shared across regions) and , or , upregulated DEGs in excitatory neurons, microglia and astrocytes, respectively (Extended Data Fig. 8f [rid=Fig13] and Supplementary Fig. 40 [this file] ). In microglia, these included and , upregulated in the HC, each associated with microglia polarization, as well as upregulation of lipoprotein modifier and downregulation of transcription factor in the EC (Extended Data Fig. 8f [rid=Fig13] and Supplementary Fig. 40 [this file] ). 
To determine whether different pathologies induce distinct transcriptional responses, we computed DEGs for region-specific measurements of NFT and neuritic amyloid-β plaque burden (measured in each region except thalamus) (Fig. 4a [rid=Fig4] , Extended Data Fig. 11a,b [rid=Fig16] and Supplementary Fig. 41 [this file] ). 
Given the enrichment of NFT-associated or plaque-associated DEGs in expression modules, we next examined whether gene modules were enriched for AD DEGs (for AD pathology or for AD diagnosis) (Fig. 4k [rid=Fig4] , Extended Data Fig. 11g [rid=Fig16] and Supplementary Fig. 42 [this file] ). 
We independently identified modules for heat-shock chaperones, glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation in multiple cell types, which were correlated across cell types and were enriched for upregulated DEGs (Fig. 4k [rid=Fig4] , Extended Data Figs. 6a,b [rid=Fig11] and 11g [rid=Fig16] and Supplementary Fig. 42a,b [this file] ). 
The pathway peaked very early in the EC (ABC score of 1, low levels of AD pathology), later in the HC and midtemporal cortex (intermediate levels), and very late in the PFC (high levels) (Supplementary Fig. 42c [this file] ), suggesting that the glial metabolic response to AD may not be coordinated globally. 
Several CR-associated genes, including , , and (encoding a rate-limiting enzyme of polyamine biosynthesis), possess or promote antioxidant activities (Fig. 5c–f [rid=Fig5] and Supplementary Fig. 43a–d [this file] ). The expression of , , and in astrocytes was also positively associated with cognitive function (Fig. 5g [rid=Fig5] and Supplementary Fig. 43e [this file] ), and these genes exhibited the highest expression in astrocytes isolated from those individuals with the least cognitive decline over time (Fig. 5h [rid=Fig5] and Supplementary Fig. 43f [this file] ). Analysis of bulk RNA-seq data from the ROSMAP cohorts ( = 638) confirmed a significant positive association between the expression level of , and and multiple measures of cognitive function and CR to AD pathology (Supplementary Fig. 44a–d [this file] ). 
The expression of , which encodes glycerophosphocholine phosphodiesterase 1, an enzyme that is critical for cleaving glycerophosphocholine (GPC) to produce choline, was positively associated with measures of CR in astrocytes (Fig. 5c–f [rid=Fig5] and Supplementary Fig. 43a–d [this file] ). Conversely, , which encodes a phospholipase that catalyses the hydrolysis of intracellular phosphatidylcholine, a major membrane lipid, generating GPC, and , which encodes choline dehydrogenase, an enzyme that catalyses the conversion of choline to betaine aldehyde, were both negatively associated with multiple measures of CR in astrocytes (Fig. 5c–f [rid=Fig5] and Supplementary Fig. 43a–d [this file] ). Many of the CR-associated genes identified in PFC astrocytes were also associated with CR in astrocytes from other regions of the human brain (Fig. 5i [rid=Fig5] and Supplementary Fig. 45 [this file] ), corroborating a link between astrocytes and CR beyond the PFC.

We characterized these cell types in terms of their transcriptome size and proliferative status, compared our atlas with previously published data across species (Extended Data Fig. 1e,f [rid=Fig6] and Supplementary Figs. 3 [rid=MOESM1] – 5 [rid=MOESM1] ) and identified broad cell type identity programs using non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) and transcriptional regulons using SCENIC (Extended Data Figs. 2 [rid=Fig7] and 3 [rid=Fig8] and Supplementary Tables 3 [this file] and 4 [this file] ). 
As thalamic neurons expressed several typically glutamatergic neuron genes, we determined glutamatergic and GABAergic module scores for every neuronal cell to further examine the chimeric nature of this subtype (Supplementary Fig. 15g–k [rid=MOESM1] and Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ). 
We used our method to identify modules both across all cells in the atlas and for each major cell type independently, and recovered modules expressed to varying degrees, ranging from identity modules for each glial cell type to a cell cycle module found in just 0.7% of microglia (Fig. 2f [rid=Fig2] , Extended Data Fig. 5 [rid=Fig10] , Supplementary Figs. 26 [rid=MOESM1] – 36 [rid=MOESM1] and Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). Cells expressing these modules were enriched for diverse aspects of our dataset, including cellular subtype identity (205 modules), brain region (156, with 77 thalamus specific and 34 EC specific), AD status (73), genotype (78) and sex (24) (Fig. 2f [rid=Fig2] and Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ). 
We next investigate whether vulnerable subtypes share marker genes that might mediate their vulnerability, and identified 391 genes with significantly higher baseline (non-AD) expression in vulnerable subtypes (Fig. 3d [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ). 
Vulnerable and non-vulnerable inhibitory neuron subtypes differed in the expression of genes involved in neuron projection morphogenesis ( , and ), enzyme-linked receptor protein signalling pathways ( , and ) and heparan sulfate proteoglycan biosynthesis (Extended Data Fig. 7k [rid=Fig12] and Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ). 
To identify regional differences in cellular expression and function specific to individuals with pathologic AD, we computed DEGs for each major cell type in every region alone and across regions using a negative binomial linear mixed model framework, adjusting for both known covariates and potential unknown batch effects ( Methods [rid=Sec10] ) (Extended Data Fig. 8a [rid=Fig13] and Supplementary Table 9 [this file] ). 
We next identified genes with higher differential effects in either NFTs or neuritic plaques (Fig. 4c [rid=Fig4] , Extended Data Fig. 11c–f [rid=Fig16] and Supplementary Table 10 [this file] ). 
We also provide results for each of the excitatory subtypes either in its most prevalent region for EC, HC or TH subclasses, or across the neocortex for neocortical subtypes (Supplementary Table 9 [this file] ).

Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) adjustment was applied to control the false discovery rate (FDR), and genes were considered significantly differentially expressed at FDR <0.05 (Supplementary extended data Fig. 4 [this file] ). 
Importantly, qPCR independently confirmed the upregulation of ER stress markers (PERK), (BiP) and (IRE1a) [ 92 [rid=CR92] , 93 [rid=CR93] ] in KO iMG (Fig. S4 [this file] a). Immunoblotting of CRISPRi-targeted THP-1 cells showed increased IRE1a protein levels relative to non-targeting (NT) controls (Fig. S4 [this file] b,b’), supporting that ER stress induction reflects loss of SorLA function rather than artifacts from truncated protein. 
WT and KO iMG were stained with the ER marker calnexin (CANX) (see Fig. S4 [this file] c). 
SorLA-deficient iMG displayed pronounced structural ER stress (Fig. S4 [this file] c), including a 166.4% increase in ER fragment number per cell (WT: 2.98 ± 0.14; KO: 7.9 ± 0.97; = 0.01), a 44.2% reduction in perinuclear ER enrichment (WT: 70.58 ± 1.44%; KO: 39.37 ± 3.66%; = 0.008) (Fig. 4 [rid=Fig4] d,e), and a 59.9% increase in ER texture entropy ( = 0.01) (Fig. S4 [this file] d). 
As expected from a cohort consisting of aged individuals, the distribution of expression was strongly skewed (Fig. S4 [this file] e). Module scores for ER stress transcription factors , , , and were elevated in _low cells at the whole-population level (Fig. 4 [rid=Fig4] j), a pattern further supported by violin plots with individual nuclei displayed in the Supplementary Figure (Fig. S4 [this file] f′,f‴). A composite ER stress score showed the same shift (Figs. 4 [rid=Fig4] k and S4 [this file] g). Stress-responsive modules were similarly increased in _low cells, including interferon-stimulated gene (ISG) signatures, lipid-stress signatures, and the KO_ERstress signature derived from KO iMG (Figs. 4 [rid=Fig4] l and S4 [this file] h). 
These state-specific patterns were also corroborated by ER stress score comparisons across microglial subtypes (Fig. S4 [this file] i).

Cell suspensions were stained with antibodies, washed, filtered, and live microglia (CD11b /CD45 /7AAD−) were sorted using a BD Influx cell sorter (Fig. S5 [this file] c). 
For Supplementary Fig. S5 [this file] a,b, individual LDs were analyzed for projected area (pixels) and circularity (4πA/P ). 
In contrast, LD size distribution and circularity were largely unchanged (Fig. S5 [this file] a,b), indicating that SorLA loss increases LD abundance without major changes in droplet size distribution or morphology in these cells. 
To assess whether the lipid storage phenotype observed in vitro is also present in aged human microglia, we analyzed pMG purified from fresh autopsy DLPFC tissue [ 18 [rid=CR18] , 43 [rid=CR43] ]. pMG were identified by positive expression of CD11B and CD45, with dead cells excluded by 7-AAD (Fig. S5 [this file] c). 
Flow cytometry revealed significantly higher BODIPY staining in a CRISPR-mediated knockdown mixed-indel cell population (Fig. S5 [this file] d) and in confirmed KO clones (Fig. S5 [this file] e) compared to matched controls. This result was replicated using Nile Red, another fluorescent dye commonly used to assess LD accumulation (Fig. S5 [this file] f,g). PMA-treated KO cells exhibited a pronounced increase in BODIPY-positive LDs compared with WT controls, with an approximately sixfold elevation in BODIPY signal (Fig. S5 [this file] h,i). 
MAP2/NeuN-positive iNeurons generated by NGN2 induction from the same iPSC line used for iMG (Supplementary extended data Fig. 5 [this file] a,b) exhibited a marked increase in BODIPY staining in KO neurons compared with WT (difference ± SEM: 50.64 ± 5.06; = 0.0005; Supplementary extended data Fig. 5 [this file] c). To exclude an iPSC line-specific effect, we generated KO SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells, which similarly showed elevated BODIPY intensity relative to WT (difference ± SEM: 61.75 ± 16.07; = 0.01; Supplementary extended data Fig. 5 [this file] d). Consistent with this phenotype, KO SH-SY5Y cells also displayed increased PERK protein levels, indicative of ER stress activation (Supplementary extended data Fig. 5 [this file] e).

ApoE levels remained significantly higher in KO supernatants under serum-free conditions (Fig. S6 [this file] a), suggesting that elevated ApoE release is likely cell-intrinsic. Complementary biochemical analysis showed elevated EEA1 protein expression in KO THP-1 cells, consistent with early endosomal dysregulation accompanying the secretion-biased shift in ApoE trafficking (Fig. S6 [this file] b,b’). ICC further revealed that KO cells exhibit a visibly higher number of EEA1 early endosomes with increased perinuclear clustering, indicating an expanded early endosomal burden (Fig. S6 [this file] c,c’). 
Notably, BFA also reduced SorLA protein levels in WT cells (Fig. S6 [this file] d,d′), indicating that acute trafficking disruption suppresses expression. 
Consistent with increased LD burden, BFA robustly induced ER stress markers in WT cells and further exacerbated ER stress in SorLA-deficient THP-1 clones, as evidenced by increased BiP protein levels (Fig. S6 [this file] d,d′). At the transcriptional level, BFA strongly induced BiP/ , spliced , , and expression in WT cells, with a further enhanced induction observed in KO clones (Supplementary extended data Fig. 6 [this file] a), indicating heightened sensitivity of SorLA-deficient cells to trafficking-induced ER stress. 
This reduction in LD burden was accompanied by decreased BiP protein expression (Fig. 6 [rid=Fig6] l,l′) and a significant reduction in BiP mRNA levels, while other ER stress markers ( and ) showed trends toward reduction that did not reach statistical significance (Supplementary extended data Fig. 6 [this file] b). 
Instead, BFA treatment increased , and expression in KO THP-1 clones, whereas WT cells exhibited reduced ( , ) or increased ( , ) expression under the same conditions (Supplementary extended data Fig. 6 [this file] c). While in WT THP-1 cells, TUDCA treatment increased , , and expression, expression remained unchanged (Supplementary extended data Fig. 6 [this file] d).

The MS data demonstrated high similarity between technical replicates of IP-SorLA, Pearson = 0.97, Figs. 7 [rid=Fig7] b and Supplementary extended data Fig. 7 [this file] a,b), indicating robust reproducibility within the SorLA group. In contrast, replicates of IgG and IP-SorLA differed significantly ( = 0.3), highlighting clear distinctions in protein abundance between the two groups (Figs. 7 [rid=Fig7] c and S7 [this file] a,b). 
We observed reduced CANX protein levels in KO THP-1 cells compared to controls (Fig. 7 [rid=Fig7] f,g), despite a slight increase in its transcription (Fig. S7 [this file] c), indicating regulation at the protein level. 
In contrast, double labeling of SorLA with the early endosome marker EEA1 revealed only sparse co-localization, with most SorLA puncta positioned adjacent to rather than overlapping with EEA1-positive compartments (Supplementary Fig. S7 [this file] d,d’). 
GO cellular component (GO_CC) analysis identified statistically enriched terms including the transporter associated with antigen processing (TAP) complex, ER protein-containing complex, nuclear outer membrane-ER membrane network, ER-Golgi intermediate compartment, COPI vesicle coat, and MHC class I peptide loading complex (Figs. 7 [rid=Fig7] j and S7 [this file] e).

In both iNeurons (Fig. S8 [this file] b) and SH-SY5Y cells (Fig. S8 [this file] c), SUN2 was co-immunoprecipitated with SorLA, demonstrating that the SorLA–SUN2 association is not restricted to myeloid cells but is also present in neuronal contexts. 
Across five independent models, AlphaFold consistently predicted SorLA–SUN2 interfaces with favorable binding energies and extensive interfacial contacts (Fig. S8 [this file] d). Domain-level contact-site analysis revealed that predicted contacts were not uniformly distributed but were strongly enriched within VPS10-containing domains of SorLA, while SUN2 contact sites localized primarily to low-complexity regions (Fig. S8 [this file] e). Residue-level analyses further demonstrated clustering of high-intensity contact residues within these domains across multiple models (Supplementary extended data Fig. 8 [this file] a,b). 
Consistent with post-transcriptional regulation, overexpression using a CRISPR activation (CRISPRa) approach increased SUN2 protein levels (Fig. S8 [this file] f,f’). In contrast, bafilomycin-mediated lysosomal inhibition did not restore SUN2 protein levels in KO THP-1 cells and was accompanied by a reduction of both SorLA and SUN2 compared to untreated WT cells (Fig. S8 [this file] g,g′), arguing against lysosomal degradation as the primary mechanism underlying SUN2 loss. 
A positive correlation between SorLA and SUN2 protein abundance was also observed in an independent proteomic dataset derived from postmortem orbitofrontal cortex samples from an alcohol use disorder cohort (Fig. S8 [this file] h).

Among the three comparison groups, the predicted target genes with the highest numbers were (mitochondrial localization gene), (mitochondrial epistasis gene), and (mitochondrial epistasis gene; Figure S3D–L [rid=cns70634-supitem-0001] , Table S3 [this file] ). 
Furthermore, the Small Molecule Transport pathway‐specific PRS model displayed the most similar performance in both cohorts (ROSMAP:= 0.0035, = 0.061; ADNI:= 0.0035, = 0.05), while the mtRNA Granules pathway‐specific PRS model showed the most divergent performance (ROSMAP:= 0.00043, = 0.51; ADNI:= 0.0066, = 0.0092; Table S4 [this file] ). 
This suggests a potentially more nuanced role of this pathway in the context of AD (Table S8 [this file] ). 
The 74 MT pathway PRSs were constructed from curated mitochondria‐related pathways, as described above (Figure 2 [rid=cns70634-fig-0002] , Table S4 [this file] ). These were then combined with the top 20 MT pathway PRS metrics (Figure S6 [rid=cns70634-supitem-0001] , Table S5 [this file] ). Among the models, the neural network (nnet) exhibited the most substantial enhancement in predictive performance (Table S5 [this file] ). 
In ADNI, MT pathway PRSs and miRNA‐targeted genes (Table S6 [this file] ) most significantly predicted AD risk ( < 0.0001), with methylation and mRNA profiles also showing significant discriminatory power ( = 0.031 and 0.022; Figure S8 [rid=cns70634-supitem-0001] ). 
A competing endogenous RNA (ceRNA) network analysis was conducted to delineate the regulatory interactions among pivotal elements, integrating 15 miRNAs, 305 genes, 15 circRNAs, and 10 long non‐coding RNAs (lncRNAs) and 330 miRNA‐gene regulatory associations (comprising 305 genes; Figure 6A [rid=cns70634-fig-0006] , Table S7 [this file] ). 
Brain expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) analysis indicated these SNPs' influence on expression across brain tissues (Table S8 [this file] ). Comparative analysis of 68 mapped genes revealed significant expression trends for , , and , etc., across 54 GTEx tissues (Figure S11D [rid=cns70634-supitem-0001] , Tables S8 [this file] and S9 [this file] ). GWAS catalog annotation showed significant enrichment in AD/age‐related processes, such as AD or high‐density lipoprotein (HDL) levels (adj. = 6.69 × 10 ), body mass index age interaction (adj. = 3.75 × 10 ) and cerebrospinal fluid AD pathology levels (Aβ1‐42, p‐tau, t‐tau, etc.; adj. = 8.77 × 10 /8.70 × 10 /1.15 × 10 ; Figure S11E [rid=cns70634-supitem-0001] , Table S10 [this file] ). 
To identify the molecular landscape underlying this phenotype, we performed RNA‐seq on brain tissue, identifying 549 significantly differentially expressed genes (DEGs) (Figure 7J [rid=cns70634-fig-0007] and Table S11 [this file] ). 
This concentration was selected as it induces significant but recoverable cellular stress, making it ideal for mechanistic studies (Figure 8A [rid=cns70634-fig-0008] , Table S11 [this file] ). 
It demonstrates that the transcriptomic changes observed in the brains of cognitively impaired mice are directly responsive to the cellular pathways of mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress, thereby validating the relevance of this specific gene set to oxidative stress‐related pathways in AD pathogenesis (Figure 8E [rid=cns70634-fig-0008] , Table S11 [this file] ). 
Co‐expression analysis of GTEx tissues [ 55 [rid=cns70634-bib-0055] ] revealed novel, robust brain‐specific correlations ( vs. , vs. , and vs. ; Figure S12 [rid=cns70634-supitem-0001] , Table S12 [this file] ).
