FDR for carrier statistic was well-calibrated in all simulation settings with varying penetrance of causal variant, prevalence in causal variant noncarriers, and number of causal variants per causal gene ( Supplementary Figure 1 [this file] ). In this case, FDR showed substantial inflation for using gene expression from all noncarriers as null distribution, while using gene expression from noncarriers in the same group of carriers as null distribution consistently gave well-calibrated error rates ( Supplementary Figure 2 [this file] ). 
While all four methods controlled FDR at the nominal level ( Supplementary Figure 1 [this file] ), carrier statistic consistently achieved higher sensitivity than the three variants collapsing methods under various settings ( Figure 2 [rid=F2] ). 
Among the top 100 genes with largest carrier statistic, 67 genes have fold enrichment larger than 1, 32 genes have fold enrichment larger than 4/3, while only 6 genes have fold enrichment smaller than 3/4 ( Supplementary Figure 3 [this file] ).

The patients’ proteomic profiles clustered into five subtypes (Fig. 1a [rid=Fig1] and Supplementary Table 3 [this file] for the fit and stability statistics): subtypes 1, 2 and 5 recapitulated our previously detected subtypes with neuronal hyperplasticity (subtype 1), innate immune activation (subtype 2) and blood–brain barrier dysfunction (subtype 5); two additional subtypes emerged: one with RNA dysregulation (subtype 3) and one with choroid plexus dysfunction (subtype 4). We tested the robustness of the subtypes by clustering the weighted protein coexpression network again with the Louvain algorithm ( Methods [rid=Sec11] ), which also resulted in five protein clusters that were similar to the NMF protein clusters (93.5% overlap of cluster-specific proteins (Supplementary Table 4 [this file] , column X). Compared to controls, subtypes 1, 2 and 3 had increased CSF t-tau and p-tau levels, while subtypes 4 and 5 had mostly normal tau levels (see Table 1 [rid=Tab1] and Supplementary Table 5 [this file] for additional analyses stratified according to cognitive state and adjusted for sex and age). Compared to controls, subtypes differed in the rates of progression from MCI to dementia, with subtypes 2 and 5 having the highest risk, and subtype 4 the lowest (Fig. 2d [rid=Fig2] ), although differences between subtypes did not reach statistical significance (Supplementary Table 6a [this file] ). Subtype 3 individuals with dementia had the shortest average survival time of 5.6 years, which was shorter than subtype 1 with the longest average survival time of 8.9 years ( = 0.04; Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] and Supplementary Table 6b [this file] ), and steeper decline on Mini Mental State Examination (MMSE), language and memory tests (Extended Data Figs. 1 [rid=Fig4] and 2 [rid=Fig5] and Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ). Analysis of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans in individuals with dementia ( = 159) indicated that subtypes differed in the degree and anatomical location of cortical atrophy (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] and Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ). 
For each subtype, we compared the levels of 2,878 proteins against the control group (Fig. 1b [rid=Fig1] and Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ). Proteins with increased levels were associated with neuronal plasticity processes, including synapse assembly, axon guidance, neurogenesis and gliogenesis (Fig. 1e [rid=Fig1] ; see Supplementary Table 9 [this file] for all biological processes enriched). Comparing subtype 1 increased proteins with those studies, we found an overlap five of six from Lu et al. , 65 of 173 from Meyer et al. and 46 of 127 from Otero-Gracia (Supplementary Table 4 [this file] , columns AZ-BB). 
We found enrichment for and variants in and (Fig. 1f [rid=Fig1] and Supplementary Table 11a [this file] ). This subtype also included three of the four carriers and three of the four carriers (Supplementary Table 11b [this file] ). MRI analyses in our data indicated that this subtype had less atrophy compared to the other subtypes (Extended Data Fig. 3 [rid=Fig6] and Supplementary Table 9 [this file] ), and was restricted to the temporal and parietal lobes. 
Proteins with increased levels were associated with cytoskeleton organization, axonal transport, and proteasome and protein folding (Supplementary Tables 4 [this file] and 9 [this file] ). 
Moreover, a large subset of proteins with increased levels (45%) was associated with high expression in the lateral ventricle choroid plexus (Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ), including TTR, SPARC and extracellular matrix proteins such as DCN, LUM and COLA12. Furthermore, proteins increased in subtype 4 were enriched for fibroblasts (Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ), which produce extracellular matrix proteins and provide structural support to the choroid plexus. 
See Supplementary Tables 6a,b [this file] and 8 [this file] for the detailed statistical metrics. 
Furthermore, compared to our previous study, we found additional proteins altered in the blood–brain barrier subtype, which were associated with pericytes, cells that normally cover capillaries, and with particular vascular cell types, such as lower levels of PDGFRB, CDH2 (N-cadherin), MFGE8 (medin), HTRA1, LAMB1 (laminin), EDN1, LRP1 and JAM3, as well as increased levels of CDH5 (VE-cadherin), ANXA3, ICAM1, AMBP, VWF and PTPRB (Supplementary Table 4 [this file] , columns AV-AX). 
All five subtypes were observed in most replication cohorts with high subtype-specific probabilities and comparable frequencies as in the discovery cohort: on average 27.9% had subtype 1, 35.5% subtype 2, 5.8% subtype 3, 17.1% subtype 4 and 16.6% subtype 5 (Fig. 3a [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Table 12 [this file] ). All subtypes were compared to the control group, as well as to each other; results from all comparisons are reported in Supplementary Table 4 [this file] .

SUCRA rankings were generally robust to study exclusions ( Multimedia Appendix 10 [this file] ), and high certainty (low information entropy) in ranking probabilities was found for the CDR-SB, where donanemab produced the clinically most relevant effects ( Table 2 [rid=table2] ; Figure 2 [rid=figure2] ). 
In addition, we found no enhanced risks of nasopharyngitis; however, these events were not reported for donanemab and lecanemab, which were antibodies tested during the COVID-19 pandemic ( Multimedia Appendix 11 [this file] ). 
Safety SUCRA rankings ( Figure 2 [rid=figure2] ) remained moderately to highly stable to study exclusion, with 89% (17/19), 50% (8/16), and 82% (9/11) of studies not affecting any rank for tolerability, ARIA-E, and ARIA-H, respectively ( Multimedia Appendix 10 [this file] ). 
However, these estimates should be interpreted with caution due to the small number of studies and treatments included in the comparisons, leading to poor robustness of the SUCRA rankings ( Multimedia Appendix 10 [this file] ). 
After excluding influential studies ( Multimedia Appendix 12 [this file] ), we found greater risks and benefits of high-dose lecanemab and aducanumab (in the controversial EMERGE study [ 15 [rid=ref15] , 68 [rid=ref68] ]) for safety outcomes (ARIA-E, ARIA-H, and headaches), cognitive/functional outcomes (ADAS-Cog and CDR-SB), and biomarker outcomes (CSF and PET).

context_description:
For clinically relevant outcomes, summary of findings tables with rated certainty of evidence (vs placebo) according to the GRADE approach can be found in Figures S1-S8 in Multimedia Appendix 8 [this file] . 
Regarding the ADAS-Cog, 5 antiamyloid antibodies were significantly more effective than placebo in the frequentist NMA ( Table 2 [rid=table2] ; Figure S1 in Multimedia Appendix 8 [this file] ). 
In the MMSE, donanemab and solanezumab were the only treatments superior to placebo, with small effect sizes in the frequentist NMA ( Table 2 [rid=table2] ; Figure S2 in Multimedia Appendix 8 [this file] ). 
While aducanumab ( .04) and lecanemab ( .005) demonstrated relative benefits over placebo in the frequentist NMA with small effect sizes and CIs/PIs very close to zero ( Table 2 [rid=table2] ; Figure S3 in Multimedia Appendix 8 [this file] ), the Bayesian NMA results did not provide conclusive support for these effects. 
However, 4 interventions (gantenerumab > donanemab > lecanemab > aducanumab) were less tolerable than placebo since they increased treatment discontinuations due to AEs by large effect sizes ( Table 3 [rid=table3] ; Figure S4 in Multimedia Appendix 8 [this file] ). All other antibodies substantially increased the risk of total ARIA-E ( Table 3 [rid=table3] ; Figure S5 in Multimedia Appendix 8 [this file] ). 
The risk of ARIA-H was significant for 4 antibodies (aducanumab > donanemab > lecanemab > gantenerumab) ( Table 3 [rid=table3] ; Figure S6 in Multimedia Appendix 8 [this file] ), demonstrated conclusively by the frequentist and Bayesian NMAs. 
This revealed that the risk of headaches was higher with aducanumab, lecanemab, and donanemab in the frequentist NMA ( Figures 2 [rid=figure2] and 3 [rid=figure3] ; Figure S7 in Multimedia Appendix 8 [this file] ). 
When compared to placebo, 3 antibodies (bapineuzumab > donanemab > lecanemab) significantly increased the risk of infusion-related reactions ( Table 2 [rid=table2] ; Figure 3 [rid=figure3] ; Figure S8 in Multimedia Appendix 8 [this file] ), which showed mostly mild to moderate severity.

context_description:
Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic review and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA) guidelines were followed (S1 File [this file] ). We searched for published trials on Pubmed, Embase, and ClinicalTrials.gov on January 14th, 2024 with a combination of the following keywords: “Alzheimer”, “mild cognitive impairment”, “dementia”, “antibody”, “passive immunotherapy”, “randomized controlled trial, or “randomized clinical trial.” Detailed criteria for searching in each database are given inS1 File [this file] . 
Cases with multiple dosage groups in antibody arms were combined and referred to as the “antibody therapy group” (detailed in andS1 File [this file] ) [ 21 [rid=pmed.1004568.ref021] , 22 [rid=pmed.1004568.ref022] ]. The calculation methods for the SMD are described inS1 File [this file] [ 23 [rid=pmed.1004568.ref023] ]. The detailed methodology for the calculation of NNT is described inS1 File [this file] . 
Representative case studies are presented, and detailed comparisons are provided inS1 File [this file] . 
Trials involving patients with early-stage AD were associated with a significant negative impact on the effect size for both CDR-SB ( = 0.02) and ADAS-Cog ( = 0.01,S1 File [this file] ). 
The information available from each study is summarized inS1 File [this file] . The results of meta-analysis and meta-regression analysis on safety outcomes are reported in , ,S1 File [this file] . 
The definition of SAEs was similar across trials (S1 File [this file] ) and it was available in 11 trials except for Study 3000 and 3001 [ 32 [rid=pmed.1004568.ref032] ], in which it was not clearly defined. 
Although there was some variation in the definition of cerebral macrohemorrhage (S1 File [this file] ), we included 8 trials in the analysis. 
The NNT was 8 for CDR-SB and 4 for ADAS-Cog (S1 File [this file] ). 
The results of Aβ and tau PET are summarized inS1 File [this file] , respectively. 
CSF and plasma biomarker results are summarized inS1 File [this file] , respectively.

In 12 donors with neuropathologic AD and 12 age- and sex-matched controls (Fig. 1a [rid=Fig1] , Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] ) we obtained snRNAseq profiles from temporal cortex tissue (TCX) using 10x Genomics platform, which yielded 87,493 single nuclei transcriptomes (Fig. 1b [rid=Fig1] , Supplementary Data 1 [rid=MOESM4] ). We optimized a nuclei isolation method that enables detection of all known major brain cell types with high purity including rarer cell types (Supplementary Figs. 2 [this file] , 3 [this file] ). Quality control (QC) and filtration steps were applied based on number of genes, unique molecular identifiers (UMIs) per nuclei and predicted doublets (Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] ), resulting in 78,396 high quality nuclei in 35 clusters that were annotated for their types according to published cellular markers . We tested the associations of each cell cluster proportion with diagnosis, age, sex, ε4 and neuropathology measures (Supplementary Figs. 5 [this file] , 6 [this file] , Supplementary Data 4 [rid=MOESM4] – 6 [rid=MOESM4] ). 
Three vascular nuclei clusters were identified – cl.25, cl.26 and cl.30, containing 926 (AD:424, control:502), 739 (AD:313, control:426), and 488 (AD:237, control: 251) nuclei, respectively (Fig. 2a [rid=Fig2] , Supplementary Fig. 7 [this file] ). All three clusters express BBB-specific transcription factor (Fig. 2b [rid=Fig2] Supplementary Fig. 7B [this file] ), which is not expressed in any other clusters. Smooth muscle cell (SMC) markers of peripheral vasculature , have limited expression in the brain vascular clusters (Supplementary Fig. 7 [this file] ). 
Comparison of the astrocytic cluster DEGs in our study to a previously published study that focused on astrocytes revealed significant overlap, as well as unique genes (Supplementary Fig. 8 [this file] ). 
Using NicheNet and focusing on significant DEGs in astrocytic clusters, we identified a combined pool of 40 unique potential ligand genes that have corresponding targets in one or more of the vascular clusters (Supplementary Data 25 [rid=MOESM4] , Supplementary Fig. 9 [this file] ). There were 22, 4, and 2 predicted vascular targets in the pericyte cl.25, endothelial cl.26, and perivascular fibroblast cl.30, respectively, comprising 26 unique target genes (Supplementary Fig. 10 [this file] ). 
There were established AD genes amongst the top astrocytic ligands namely corresponding to predicted vascular target with high estimated regulation strength and with high regulation strength for . (Fig. 3a [rid=Fig3] , Supplementary Fig. 11 [this file] ). 
We selected genes representative of the biological functions associated with these 26 genes (Supplementary Fig. 11 [this file] , Supplementary Data 26 [rid=MOESM4] ). 
We found that all 6 genes had higher expression in the AD cases than in the controls, with all but 1 ( , = 0.066) reaching significance, thus validating our prior findings in the snRNAseq data (Supplementary Fig. 12A [this file] , Supplementary Data 27 [rid=MOESM4] ). For completeness, expression levels of the six prioritized vascular target genes were also tested for associations with AD-related neuropathologies (Supplementary Fig. 12B [this file] ), age, sex and ε4 (Supplementary Fig. 12C [this file] ). 
Of the 6 prioritized and qPCR-validated vascular genes, we focused on , a signaling molecule with known vascular functions , which shows upregulation in AD pericytes and has the strongest level of astrocyte ligand interactions (Supplementary Fig. 13 [this file] , Supplementary Data 25 [rid=MOESM4] , 26 [rid=MOESM4] ). The ligands of in astrocyte clusters include several known AD-related genes that are also DEGs in our study such as , and (Supplementary Fig. 13 [this file] ). 
Amongst the astrocytic ligands of , we prioritized , an angiogenic growth factor that is involved in multiple processes in the human brain that include synaptic plasticity, memory formation, cognition, and the progression of AD . is mainly expressed by astrocytes (Supplementary Fig. 14 [this file] ) and its expression is significantly downregulated in astrocytic cl.8 and OPC cluster (Fig. 3b [rid=Fig3] ). 
Using and as vascular and astrocytic markers, respectively (Supplementary Figs. 7b [this file] , 14 [this file] ), we performed co-staining with RNAscope. 
We also sought replication of our brain snRNAseq findings of upregulated pericytic and downregulated astrocytic in AD in external, independent snRNAseq datasets from multiple brain regions (Fig. 3f [rid=Fig3] , Supplementary Data 31 [rid=MOESM4] – 34 [rid=MOESM4] , Supplementary Figs. 15 [this file] , 16 [this file] ). In total, 4,730 pericytic nuclei were clustered into two subclusters (Supplementary Data 32 [rid=MOESM4] , Supplementary Fig. 15 [this file] ). Per.0 cluster demonstrates upregulation of solute transport genes, whereas Per.1 shows extracellular matrix organization gene upregulation (Supplementary Data 34 [rid=MOESM4] , Supplementary Fig. 15 [this file] ).

ALS/FTD donors were then grouped into terciles, referred to as TDPneg, TDPmed, and TDPhigh, based on pTDP-43 levels ( Fig. 1b [rid=F1] and Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). 
We obtained a total of 34,874 and 53,331 single-nucleus multiomes (snRNA-seq and snATAC-seq) from the Emory and Mayo cohorts, respectively, after quality control filtration using the ArchR multiome pipeline and Seurat snRNA-seq guidelines (see Methods [rid=S11] ; Fig. 1d [rid=F1] ; Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] – 2 [this file] ; Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). Uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) and unsupervised clustering with Seurat were applied to the combined snATAC-seq and snRNA-seq, resulting in a total of 31 distinct cell clusters for Emory samples and 20 distinct cell clusters for Mayo samples, excluding unassigned clusters ( Fig. 1d [rid=F1] and Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] ). Using SoupX , we found that there is minimal ambient RNA contamination ( Supplementary Fig. 4a [this file] ). Gene activity scores derived from snATAC-seq chromatin accessibility at proximal promoter regions were used to identify marker genes in each cell cluster ( Fig. 1d [rid=F1] - f [rid=F1] ; Supplementary Fig. 3b [this file] , d [this file] ; Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). A total of seven major cortical cell types were identified for both cohorts ( Fig. 1d [rid=F1] - f [rid=F1] ; Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] ). APA changes in 34 genes are associated with gene expression changes (Supplementary Fig. 1b [this file] ), likely impacting their corresponding protein levels (see below). 
To test whether TDP-43 directly regulates APA, we knocked down TDP-43 levels in cortical neurons differentiated from human stem cells (iNeurons) and performed RNA-seq for APA analysis (Fig. 1c [rid=Fig1] and Supplementary Fig. 1c,d [this file] ). TDP-43 KD caused widespread APA changes (Fig. 1d [rid=Fig1] and Supplementary Table 2 [rid=MOESM3] ; |∆PUI| > 0.1 and adjusted < 0.05 from APAlyzer), including 24 changes, that were also observed in FTD/ALS postmortem brain samples (Fig. 1b [rid=Fig1] and Supplementary Fig. 1a [this file] ). Applying the same analysis to published RNA-seq datasets, we also observed APA changes in human-induced pluripotent stem cell-derived motor neurons (iMNs) upon TDP-43 KD (Supplementary Fig. 1e [this file] ), in iNeurons carrying a pathogenic mutation (TDP-43-K263E), which disrupts RNA binding (Supplementary Fig. 1f [this file] ), and in patient-derived iMNs carrying a different pathogenic mutation (TDP-43-M337V), which disrupts TDP-43 intermolecular interactions (Supplementary Fig. 1g [this file] ). 
Both annotated and new polyA sites harbored known polyA signals located ~20 nts upstream (Supplementary Fig. 2a,b [this file] ). Consistent with previous findings , the majority of polyA sites we identified were in 3′ UTRs, though the new polyA sites had more diverse distributions within transcripts (Supplementary Fig. 2c [this file] ), consistent with the idea that they are normally repressed by TDP-43 under normal conditions. Furthermore, 3′ end-seq confirmed that loss of TDP-43 lengthened the 3′ UTR of (Fig. 2c [rid=Fig2] , left), which we also observed in our analysis of FTD/ALS postmortem brain samples (Fig. 1b [rid=Fig1] and Supplementary Fig. 1a [this file] ). 
Like recent findings in ALS samples and FTD samples (Fig. 1b [rid=Fig1] and Supplementary Fig. 1a [this file] ), as well as in our RNA-seq data from iNeurons (Fig. 1d [rid=Fig1] ), the majority of genes with APA changes (2,752 genes) detected by 3′ end-seq lengthened their RNA transcripts; 433 APA events were associated with at least a 1.5-fold change in RNA level (Fig. 2e [rid=Fig2] ), suggesting that APA changes could alter gene expression. 
TDP-43 KD activated 404 cryptic polyA sites in 372 genes (Supplementary Table 3 [rid=MOESM3] ); 65 cryptic polyA sites occurred downstream of a gene’s annotated 3′ end-seq, such as the FTD risk factor (Supplementary Fig. 2d [this file] ), (Supplementary Fig. 3e [this file] ) and , and (Supplementary Fig. 2e–g [this file] ; ref. ). In addition, 149 cryptic events induced premature polyadenylation in genes such as , and (Supplementary Fig. 2h–j [this file] ). Cryptic splicing of was recently reported , and we also confirmed this by qRT–PCR (Supplementary Fig. 2k [this file] ) and in RNA-seq data from FTD/ALS postmortem brain samples (Fig. 2f [rid=Fig2] ). 
Using GU content to estimate the strength of TDP-43 binding located downstream of APA sites, we found that TDP-43 KD caused a larger usage change in polyA sites with weak TDP-43 binding than sites with strong sites (Fig. 3c [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Fig. 2o [this file] ), suggesting that, when reduced, TDP-43 likely dissociates from weak sites first, then from stronger ones.

Notably, TDP-43 loss-induced APA changes are found in genes critical for neuronal function and disease-associated genes (Figs. 4 [rid=Fig4] – 6 [rid=Fig6] and Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] ), impacting their expression (for example, , , and ).

The updated pipeline consists of three steps: 1) indexing patients’ documents, 2) determining the presence of symptoms, and 3) identifying the onset of symptoms ( Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] and Supplementary Tables 1 [this file] – 3 [this file] ). Detailed in the Supplementary Methods [this file] , de-identified excerpts from patient records were used at each step to fine-tune a large language model, GPT-4o, with human labels as the gold standard. 
Compared with S1, subtypes S2–S6 were associated with significantly lower mortality risk (hazard ratios 0.55–0.37, all P < 0.01; Fig. 2b [rid=F2] and Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ). 
Similarly, age- and sex-adjusted survival curves, generated using a multivariable Cox proportional-hazards model, demonstrated lower mortality risks for all other subtypes compared to PSP-PF (hazard ratios 0.63–0.35, all P < 0.01; Fig. 2d [rid=F2] and Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ). 
The clinical presentation and progression of the early PSP subtypes are visualized in Figs. 3 [rid=F3] and 4 [rid=F4] (the raw data presented in Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). 
Respondek et al. reported that approximately two-thirds of patients with PSP-RS had frontal presentations three years post-onset.[ 14 [rid=R14] ] In the present cohort, the majority of PSP-PF patients who were evaluated for OM within three years of onset had it. (83.0%, 122/147, Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ) These patients would have been classified as PSP-RS under the MDS criteria and MAX rule due to the presence of both OM and PI. [ 10 [rid=R10] , 41 [rid=R41] , 42 [rid=R42] ] However, the MDS criteria and MAX rule have come under scrutiny for potentially underestimating the phenotypic diversity of PSP due to prioritizing PSP-RS over other phenotypes, including the PSP-F subtype.[ 11 [rid=R11] – 13 [rid=R13] ] The recognition of PSP-PF as an aggressive variant of PSP in this simple decision tree model may address these concerns and help clinicians differentiate subtypes and estimate prognoses at the bedside. 
Levodopa responsiveness in PSP-P could not be determined due to the small number of records containing this information (3/36 were assessed, shown in Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). 
Our study adopted one as the threshold for the number of the frontal presentations because early behavioral changes were often summarised in the records by the family or clinicians with a single description such as “personality change” or “apathy.” Additionally, when a higher threshold was tested, this generated many missing values, as indicated with “Frontal presentation (≥3)” ( Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). 
Among 79 patients who had cortical signs, 50 patients were assigned to PSP-PF, nine to PSP-RS, seven to PSP-PI, and six to PSP-SL (P = 0.10, supplementary Table 6 [this file] ), suggesting that most PSP patients with cortical signs at an early stage also exhibit other presentations, such as OM, PI, or SL.

In comparison, ~70% of DLB samples showed an increase in insoluble a-syn ( Fig. 2D [rid=F2] , Fig. S2C [this file] , D [this file] ), using the sensitive LB509 antibody (generated against purified Lewy bodies ). Analysis of insoluble FUS showed a 4-fold elevation in DLB brain, while only a subtle change was found with TDP-43 (~10 % increase) ( Fig. S2C [this file] , D [this file] ). 
Quantification of inclusion diameter showed that the nuclei of DLB brains contained a higher number of large inclusions (>2um diameter) and increased total puncta per cell with a stronger intensity ( Fig. 2E [rid=F2] , S2E [this file] ). 
We confirmed the interaction of a-syn with NONO/SFPQ by proximity ligation assays (PLA) ( Fig. 3A [rid=F3] ), and confocal microscopy showed that ~50% of cells contained nuclear a-syn colocalized with either NONO or SFPQ ( Fig. 3B [rid=F3] , Fig. S3A [this file] ). Nuclear accumulation was confirmed with three independent a-syn antibodies that react with both N and C-terminus including syn211 (residues 120–125), C20 (polyclonal c-term), and syn505 (residues 2–4) ( Fig. 3B [rid=F3] , Fig. S3B [this file] - D [this file] ). Syn505 preferentially detects pathological, soluble cross-linked oligomers and was generated against oxidized/nitrated a-syn epitopes . a-Syn and NONO/SFPQ colocalization was observed as a discrete diffuse pattern, as shown by 1um confocal slices taken throughout the nucleus of PD iPSn ( Fig. 3B [rid=F3] , Fig. S3A [this file] ). In focal planes beyond the nucleus, a-syn was also detected in a punctated pattern within neuronal extensions of both controls and PD iPSn, consistent with its expected synaptic localization ( Fig. S3B [this file] , D [this file] ). We also observed colocalization within discrete puncta in ~20% of PD iPSn but not controls ( Fig. S3C [this file] ). 
Analysis of post-mortem DLB brain showed that a-syn colocalized with NONO/SFPQ in the nucleus, while controls showed little colocalization ( Fig. S3E [this file] ). Importantly, NONO/SFPQ inclusions were not detected in Lewy bodies or neurites that histopathologically define synucleinopathies ( Fig. S3F [this file] ). 
This resulted in dramatic reduction of ADAR3 mRNA ( Fig. S4A [this file] , B [this file] ), which is consistent with previous findings in other non-neuronal cell types . This effect was specific to ADAR3, since the mRNA level of ADAR1 did not change, and the protein levels of ADARs 1 and 2 were mildly increased in PD iPSn ( Fig. S4D [this file] ). 
In many DLB cases, the edited transcript represented ≥50% of the total proportion of expressed transcripts ( Fig. S4E [this file] ). This is consistent with immunostaining data showing colocalization of diffuse, non-Lewy body a-syn with NONO/SFPQ ( Fig 3B [rid=F3] , Fig. S3 [this file] ), and soluble a-syn oligomers that trigger SFPQ conversion into aggregates ( Fig. 2 [rid=F2] ). 
Transcript networks with increased editing showed significant overlap with protein networks that are reduced in PD iPSn, including synapse, axon guidance and nervous system development ( Fig. S5A [this file] - C [this file] ; Supplemental Tables 9 [this file0] - 12 [this file3] ). Prioritizing functional categories of reduced proteins by p-value revealed that axon guidance/nervous system development categories were the most significantly affected proteomic categories ( Fig. S5D [this file] ). 
The inosine signal was abolished by treatment with RNAse, indicating that it was derived from RNA ( Fig 6B [rid=F6] ), and anti-inosine antibody specificity was confirmed by dot blot analysis ( Fig. S6A [this file] ). We next examined the mRNA localization of specific transcripts of the synaptic / axon / neuron projection categories with no or minimal change in total mRNA but with reduced protein levels in PD iPSn including CYFIP2, CADPS, DNM1, PRKAR2A, RTN4, and CTNNA2 ( Fig 4E [rid=F4] , Fig S5B [this file] , Fig. S6B [this file] , C [this file] ). 
Several of the axon/synaptic proteins were also decreased in DLB brain ( Fig. S6D [this file] - F [this file] ). 
Using HEK cells and a previously established A-to-I editing reporter , we found that editing was inhibited between 100 and 250nM of 8-aza ( Fig. S7A [this file] ), and concentrations above 1uM were toxic. Assessment of an endogenous ADAR target (CYFIP2 mRNA) showed 8-aza reduced editing by 40% in PD iPSn, which is similar to levels found in isogenic corrected lines ( Fig. S7B [this file] ). Both detection methods showed a ~50% reduction in inosine while the quantity of other nucleotides within the polyA mRNA were not changed ( Fig. 7A [rid=F7] ; Fig. S7C [this file] ). 
Quantification of total mRNA showed a slight increase in PRKAR2A and CTNNA2, while no changes were found in any other transcripts, indicating that the main effect of reduced A-to-I editing was to restore nuclear : cytosolic ratios of these particular transcripts ( Fig. S7D [this file] ). 
At day 120, synapses were quantified by immunofluorescence staining of fixed cultures by colocalization analysis of post-synaptic (PSD-95) and pre-synaptic (synaptophysin) markers ( Fig. 7K [rid=F7] , Fig. S7E [this file] ). We found a decline in the number of colocalized puncta in PD iPSn compared to isogenic controls ( Fig 7K [rid=F7] , Fig. S7E [this file] ). Both the staining intensity and colocalization of PSD-95 and synaptophysin were reduced in PD iPSn, while b-iii tubulin was not dramatically affected ( Fig. 7K [rid=F7] , Fig. S7E [this file] ). 8-aza treatment at 200nM for one month increased the levels of individual synaptic markers and improved their colocalization, suggesting improved synapse formation ( Fig. 7K [rid=F7] , Fig. S7E [this file] ). Confirmation by western blot showed that 8-aza rescued synaptophysin levels in PD iPSn ( Fig. S7G [this file] ). Importantly, no change was seen when isogenic corrected lines were treated with 8-aza, suggesting that the treatment is not toxic to control iPSn ( Fig. S7F [this file] ). Inhibiting A-to-I editing also reduced LDH release, further supporting that neuronal health was improved ( Fig S7G [this file] ).

Consistent with immunostaining in iPSn or DLB post-mortem brain, a-syn/NONO/SFPQ was observed as nuclear puncta, but was completely devoid in cytoplasmic Lewy inclusions that are comprised mainly of fibrillar a-syn ( Fig S3F [this file] ).

WB in the cortex lysate validated the depletion of CgA in CgA-KO/PS19 mice (Fig. 2C [rid=Fig2] ), where drastically reduced p-Tau (S202/T205, AT8) and p-Tau (S396/S404, PHF1) was found compared to PS19 mice (Fig. 2C [rid=Fig2] , S-Fig. 3D, E [this file] . Meanwhile, the levels of postsynaptic density protein 95 (PSD95) were significantly reduced in PS19 cortex lysates compared to WT, consistent with synaptic loss in PS19 mice, which was rescued in CgA-KO/PS19 (Fig. 2C [rid=Fig2] S-Fig. 3F [this file] ) . WB also revealed decreased pTau in hippocampus of CgA-KO/PS19 mice (S-Fig. 3G–I [this file] ). Like in cortex, WB in hippocampus also showed decreased PSD95 in PS19 mice, which was rescued in CgA-KO/PS19 mice (S-Fig. 3G, J [this file] ). Again, IHC analysis of hippocampus revealed decreased p-Tau in CgA-KO/PS19 compared of PS19 (S-Fig. 3K, L [this file] ) mice. 
Fibril-induced Tau pathology spread to the CA3 region of the contralateral hippocampus was evident in PS19 mice 6 weeks post-injection, but minimal in CgA-KO/PS19 mice, suggesting that CgA promotes Tau spread (Fig. 2J, K [rid=Fig2] , S-Fig. 3M, N [this file] ). Our control experiment with PBS injection showed no MC1+ aggregates at this age (S-Fig. 3O–P [this file] ). Furthermore, IHC staining with Myc and MC1 showed that K18 fibril induced Tau spreading pathology is from endogenous Tau aggregation rather than the injected K18 fibrils themselves (S-Fig. 3Q–R [this file] ). 
We performed ultrastructural analysis via transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and found amplified synapse numbers (marked by arrows) in the hippocampus of CgA-KO/PS19 mice compared to PS19 mice (S-Fig. 4A, B [this file] ), consistent with increased PSD95 levels in the cortical and hippocampal lysates (Fig. 2C [rid=Fig2] ; S-Fig. 3F, G, J [this file] ). Notably, PS19 mice had fewer synaptic vesicles (SVs) in their presynaptic neurons compared to WT and CgA-KO/PS19 mice (S-Fig. 4C, D [this file] ). 
In the Morris water maze (MWM) test, during the training phase, PS19 mice traveled prolonged distances and durations before reaching the platform and exhibited lack of improvement over the seven-day training period, compared to WT and CgA-KO mice (Fig. 3A–C [rid=Fig3] , S-Fig. 3A [this file] ), indicating impaired spatial learning in PS19 mice. In contrast, CgA-KO/PS19 mice exhibited a complete rescue of the learning deficit (Fig. 3A–C [rid=Fig3] ; S-Fig. 5A [this file] ). Notably, both body weight and swimming speed remained comparable between PS19 and CgA-KO/PS19 mice (Fig. 3F [rid=Fig3] S-Fig. 5B [this file] ), indicating that the reduced latency in CgA-KO/PS19 mice was not due to increased speed. 
Simultaneously, CgA-KO/PS19 mice exhibited reduced levels of proinflammatory cytokines including Interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β) (Fig. 4G [rid=Fig4] ), Interleukin-6 (IL-6) (Fig. 4H [rid=Fig4] ), Tumor Necrosis Factor-alpha (TNFα) (Fig. 4I [rid=Fig4] ), C-X-C Motif Chemokine Ligand 2 (CXCL2) (Fig. 4J [rid=Fig4] ), C-X-C Motif Chemokine Ligand 10 (CXCL10) (S-Fig. 6A [this file] ), C-X-C Motif Chemokine Ligand 1 (CXCL1) (S-Fig. 6B [this file] ), C-C Motif Chemokine Ligand 2 (CCL2) (S-Fig. 6C [this file] ), andC-C Motif Chemokine Ligand 3 (CCL3) (S-Fig. 6D [this file] ) in cortical extracts compared to PS19 mice. We further found that the plasma proinflammatory cytokine/chemokine levels such as TNFα (S-Fig. 6E [this file] ), IL-6 (S-Fig. 6F [this file] ), CXCL10 (S-Fig. 6G [this file] ), CXCL1 (S-Fig. 6H [this file] ), CXCL2 (S-Fig. 6I [this file] ), C-C Motif Chemokine Ligand 2 (CCL2) (S-Fig. 6J [this file] ), and CCL3 (S-Fig. 6K [this file] ) were higher in PS19 mice at both three and nine months of age compared to CgA-KO/PS19 mice. On the other hand, the anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10 level was higher in CgA-KO/PS19 than in PS19 mice (S-Fig. 6L [this file] ). On the other hand, Glial Fibrillary Acidic Protein (GFAP) levels showed a trend of reduction in CgA-KO/PS19 mice compared to PS19 mice (S-Fig. 6M, N [this file] ). 
Depletion of CgA in CgA-KO/PS19 genotype was again confirmed by absence of CgA mRNA (S-Fig. 7A [this file] ). Specifically, the Adra1 family genes (α , α , α ) were upregulated, while the Adra2 family genes (α , α , α ) were downregulated in PS19 compared to WT and CgA-KO/PS19 (Fig. 5A [rid=Fig5] ; S-Fig. 7B [this file] ), while no significant change was found in β-adrenergic receptors (Adrb) across all the groups. RT-qPCR further confirmed altered gene expression of and in PS19, which were restored upon CgA deletion (S-Fig. 7C–F [this file] ). Consistently, analysis of publicly available RNAseq data from control and AD patients showed altered expression ofS-Fig. 7G, H [this file] ) and (S-Fig. 7I, J [this file] ) in Braak stages V–VI compared to Braak stages 0–I in parahippocampal gyri, indicating a correlation with disease progression (RNAseq data obtained from the Mount Sinai Brain Bank [MSBB] study). Functional analysis highlighted the interconnected role of Adra signaling in various cellular functions (catecholamine transport, neuropeptide signaling, second messenger signaling, and potassium-ion transport), underscoring its significance in Tau pathology (S-Fig. 7J [this file] ). 
To investigate the spatial relationship between CgA, Adra1b and Tau, we performed IHC with CgA, Adra1b, and MC1 antibodies (S-Fig. 8 [this file] ). Adra1b was predominantly localized in axons, where it was associated MC1+ misfolded Tau species (S-Fig. 8B–D [this file] ). In contrast, CgA was observed as puncta in the soma of CA2 and CA3 regions of the hippocampus (S-Fig. 8C, D [this file] ), where it partially colocalized with MC1+ misfolded Tau species (S-Fig. 8C, D [this file] ). 
Along with the altered expression of Adra1, we also observed a downregulation of phosphodiesterases (PDEs), including PDE1, PDE3, and PDE9, in PS19 mice compared to WT and CgA-KO/PS19 mice (S-Fig. 9A [this file] . As anticipated, PS19 mice exhibited significantly higher cortical cAMP levels compared to WT and CgA-KO/PS19 mice (S-Fig. 9B [this file] ). Consistently, we observed elevated cortical cAMP levels in AD Braak stage VI compared to Braak stage 0–II samples (S-Fig. 9C [this file] ). 
Three weeks post-treatment, WB analysis revealed significantly lower levels of pTau (S202, S396, and S404) in PR-treated WT slices compared to DMSO-treated controls (Fig. 6B [rid=Fig6] , S-Fig. 10A, B [this file] ) and higher levels of pTau (S202, S396, and S404) in PE-treated slices compared to PBS-treated controls (Fig. 6B [rid=Fig6] ). At baseline, IHC analysis using the MC1 antibody also showed abundant misfolded Tau species in DMSO-treated WT slices (Fig. 6C [rid=Fig6] , S-Fig. 10C [this file] ) and fewer misfolded Tau species in PBS-treated CgA-KO slices (Fig. 6D [rid=Fig6] ). Dose-dependent decrease in Tau phosphorylation (S-Fig. 10D [this file] ) and Tau aggregation (S-Fig. 10E, F [this file] ) by PR in CgA-KO slices implicate that the inhibition of Tau pathology by CgA-KO is, at least partially, mediated by decreased Adra1 signaling. Likewise, PE caused dose-dependent increase in Tau phosphorylation (S-Fig. 10G [this file] ) and Tau aggregation (S-Fig. 10H, I [this file] ) in WT slices, reinforcing adrenergic signaling in Tau pathology. 
Remarkably, PR treatment significantly reduced levels of pTau (Fig. 6E–G [rid=Fig6] ) and misfolded Tau species (Fig. 6 [rid=Fig6] H, S-Fig. 10J [this file] ) in the hippocampus. 
Therefore, we assessed EPI and NE levels in the prefrontal cortex (Fig. 7A [rid=Fig7] S-Fig. 11A [this file] ), hippocampus (Fig. 7B [rid=Fig7] S-Fig. 11B [this file] ) and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) (Fig. 7C [rid=Fig7] S-Fig. 11C [this file] ) from AD patients. No significant change in NE level was detected in prefrontal cortex (S-Fig. 11A [this file] ) and hippocampus (S-Fig. 11B [this file] ), whereas CSF levels of NE was decreased S-Fig. 11C [this file] . NE levels did not differ between CBD patients and controls samples (S-Fig. 11D [this file] ). Strikingly, both EPI and NE levels were elevated in the cortices of PS19 mice compared to WT, CgA-KO, and CgA-KO/PS19 mice (Fig. 7E [rid=Fig7] S-Fig. 11E [this file] ). Plasma EPI levels were similarly changed in PS19 mice (S-Fig. 11F [this file] ), whereas NE levels were elevated in PS19 (S-Fig. 11G [this file] ) but unchanged in CgA-KO and CgA-KO/PS19 mice (S-Fig. 9F, G [this file] ). 
To further determine if EPI-induced Tau pathology is dependent on CgA, we treated CgA-KO OTSC with EPI and found that EPI failed to induce Tau phosphorylation (S-Fig. 11H–J [this file] ) or Tau aggregate formation (S-Fig. 11K, L [this file] ). 
To establish the CgA-EPI-Adra1 signaling axis in regulation of Tau pathogenesis, we previously treated CgA-KO OTSC with EPI (S-Fig. 11H–L [this file] ) and found no significant increase in Tau pathogenic burden. Remarkably, EPI + PR co-treatment significantly reduced EPI-induced increase in Tau aggregation (Fig. 7L, M [rid=Fig7] and Tau phosphorylation S-Fig. 11M–O [this file] ), indicating that EPI increases Tau pathology via activation of Adra1 signaling.

We collected a cohort of 60 tissue samples from 20 postmortem donors ranging in age from 34 to 74 years old, with equal representation of both sexes, and frozen tissue samples from three distinct regions of the CNS from each donor—primary motor cortex (Brodmann area 4 (BA4)), cerebellum (CB) and cervical spinal cord (CSC; Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). 
Although age-associated changes were most evident in the neuronal populations, especially in CXEX population (Extended Data Fig. 3a [rid=Fig10] and Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ), the number of nuclei per cell type, region and age group was too small to provide statistical power for additional comparisons and strong conclusions considering the age variable. Sex-based differences were primarily restricted to gonosomal genes (Extended Data Fig. 3b [rid=Fig10] and Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ). 
Promoters and enhancers exhibit open chromatin and H3K27ac enrichment, making our datasets well-suited to identify cCREs (Extended Data Fig. 6a,b [rid=Fig13] , Supplementary Table 2 [this file] and Methods [rid=Sec13] ). 
We checked the co-accessibility links within the OPCs and MOLs separately, and found interactions with the canonical enhancers, and the new enhancers in both populations, but the promoter–enhancer connection only in MOLs (Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ), suggesting that the chromatin looping concerning this enhancer is altered upon OLG lineage progression. 
Alongside expected TFs such as OLIG2 in MOLs and OPCs, IRF2 in MIGL and CUX2 and SATB1 in cortical neurons, we identified new regulators, including FOXN2 in MIGL and ZBTB20 and HMX1 in AST (Fig. 3b [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). 
However, each population also contained distinct high-strength regulators that may support lineage-specific functions, including ARX, MYC, SIX1 and FOXF2 in OPCs, and NFAT5, ARNT, ZNF566 and ZNF333 in MOLs (Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). 
The HOX TFs appeared only in the OLG lineage and not in other cell types, indicating a lineage-specific regulatory role (Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). 
Tissue was collected from 20 different donors ( = 10 male, = 10 female) within the ages of 34–74 years old (Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). 
Four guides per locus were cloned by annealing 1 µl of each complementary oligo (Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ) to a final volume of 25 µl annealing buffer (combine 500 µl 1 M Tris–HCl, pH 8.0, with 500 µl 5 M NaCl to final volume of 50 ml with ddH O) and incubated at 95 °C for 3 min, cooled to 22 °C at 0.1 °C s and diluted in 75 µl ddH O to yield 1 µM. 
See Supplementary Table 1 [this file] for detailed information on donor metadata.

context_description:
For peak-gene associations, similar spurious associations may arise as both peak and gene counts correlate with their respective sequencing depths, and the sequencing depths from these two data modalities tend to be correlated (Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] ). 
Hence, we evaluate their performance only on benchmark datasets and focus in this paper on methods that formally test peak-gene associations ( Supplementary Discussion [this file] ). 
Supported by recent evidence that Poisson modeling improves the downstream analysis of peak counts and the observation that peak counts display additional overdispersion compared to Poisson (Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] ), model ( 1 [rid=Equ1] ) is able to better leverage the quantitative information in peak counts, remove potential confounding due to sequencing depths, and improve power in detecting association. 
When sparsity levels of simulated peak counts vary, the power of scMultiMap remains the highest, with greater improvement on less sparse data (Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] ). 
Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] shows that scMultiMap also outperformed approaches in SCENIC+ with higher enrichment of reproduced pairs. 
These pairs show the largest numbers of overlaps, and the overlaps are statistically significant (Methods, see Supplementary Fig. 5 [this file] for percentages of overlaps). The enrichment by scMultiMap is also generally higher than approaches in SCENIC+ (Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] ). 
Similar analysis of Signac and SCENT’s results shows weaker enrichment among the identified trios (Supplementary Fig. 7 [this file] ). 
Using a bootstrap-based analysis ( Supplementary Methods [this file] ), we found significant variations in mean gene expression and mean peak accessibility across subjects (Supplementary Fig. 8 [this file] ). Interestingly, these variations tend to be correlated between peaks and genes (Supplementary Fig. 9 [this file] ), leading to spurious associations if left unaddressed. 
The enrichment is below 1 and statistically insignificant for approaches in SCENIC+ applied to the same cell types (Supplementary Fig. 10 [this file] ), suggesting relatively poor overlap with PLAC-seq pairs. The peaks from the significant peak-gene pairs from scMultiMap are also enriched for enhancer annotations on brain tissues from the same region and aged donors, as characterized by ChromHMM in the ENCODE consortium (Supplementary Fig. 11 [this file] , Supplementary Discussion [this file] ). 
The enrichment of reproduced pairs by SCENIC+ is also lower than scMultiMap across three cell types (Supplementary Fig. 12 [this file] ). 
We further applied scMultiMap to identify regulatory trios and studied the biological processes regulated by enriched TFs in five brain cell types (Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] f, g, Supplementary Fig. 13 [this file] ) (Methods). The trios also yielded enrichment for cell-type-specific functions in oligodendrocytes (e.g. axon ensheathment, lipoprotein metabolic process), inhibitory neurons (e.g. chemical synaptic transmission, migration of Purkinje cell) and microglia (e.g. regulation of gliogenesis, inflammatory response) (Supplementary Fig. 13 [this file] ). 
Similar analysis on astrocyte, another glial cell type critical to AD disease mechanisms , also revealed differentially associated peak-gene pairs and implicated pathways in lipid metabolism and neurofibrillary tangle assembly, both of which have been linked to AD in astrocytes (Supplementary Fig. 14 [this file] ). 
A detailed algorithm of IRLS is included in Supplementary Algorithm 2 [this file] . 
A detailed algorithm of WLS is included in Supplementary Algorithm 3 [this file] . 
Under the null hypothesis of independence between gene expression and peak accessibility, we show that and that asymptotically follows a standard normal distribution ( Supplementary Methods [this file] ). 
We propose to estimate ’s and ’s using a similar IRLS procedure and the estimation of variance and covariance follows analogously ( Supplementary Methods [this file] ). We note that when groups of subjects are present (e.g. control subjects and subjects with diseases), this will not remove the difference in covariance between groups and we model samples from each group separately ( Supplementary Discussion [this file] ). 
This re-implementation corrects a coding error in the -value calculation in its original implementation and speeds up computation ( Supplementary Methods [this file] ). We applied SCENT with fixed numbers of bootstrap samples in numerical analyses ( Supplementary Methods [this file] ). 
However, since SCENIC+ is not based on statistical tests, lacks -values and false positive control, it cannot be directly compared with methods that use statistical tests (see Supplementary Discussion [this file] ). Following the methods in SCENIC+ , we defined associated peak-gene pairs using three quantiles (85th, 90th, and 95th) of variable importance scores (see Supplementary Discussion [this file] ). 
More details can be found in Supplementary Methods [this file] . 
In specific, for promoter capture Hi-C data , we used interactions with a CHiCAGO score ≥5 ; for H3K27ac HiChIP data , we used the significant interactions based on FitHiChIP (FDR<0.1); for cell-type-specific eQTL, we used cis-SNPs significant in Naive CD14 Monocytes (FDR <0.05) ; for PLAC-seq , profiles chromatin loops between promoters and distal regulatory regions in NEUN neuronal, OLIG2 oligodendrocyte, PU.1 microglia nuclei isolated from human brain tissues, and we used the provided data on enhancers, promoters, and interactomes on these cell types to define enhancer-gene pairs ( Supplementary Methods [this file] ).

WGS data was processed with the in-house developed Nextflow pipeline NanoWGS ( Supplementary figure 1G [this file] , Supplementary Table 2 [rid=SD4] , Methods [rid=S10] ). We ascertained the ancestry of donors: 185 donors were of European ancestry, 2 of admixed American ancestry and 1 of East Asian ancestry ( Supplementary Figure 1H [this file] ), and we benchmarked the accuracy of SNP and indel calling of different ONT chemistries ( Supplementary Figure 1E [this file] – F [this file] , Methods [rid=S10] ). We observed peaks in variant numbers around 300 bps, 2–3 kbps and 6–7kbps, representing ALU, SVA and LINE-1 elements, respectively ( Supplementary Figure 1J [this file] – K [this file] ). 
We performed single-nucleus ATAC and RNA sequencing of the same donors, for the CC (115 controls, 75 PD patients) and SN (90 controls, 50 PD) ( Figure 1A [rid=F1] , Methods [rid=S10] ), using a combination of sn-multiome (snRNA+snATAC), snRNA-seq, and snATAC-seq (see Methods [rid=S10] , Supplementary Figure 2S [this file] & 2T [this file] ). For the SN, we obtained 376,394 RNA nuclei with a mean of 1,969 genes and 4,696 UMIs per nucleus ( Supplementary Figure 2D [this file] – F [this file] & Supplementary Figure 2J [this file] – L [this file] ) and identified the expected non-neuronal cell types ( Fig 2E [rid=F2] , Supplementary Figure 2W [this file] ). In the CC, we obtained 751,541 high quality nuclei with a mean of 2,541 genes and 7,150 UMIs per nucleus ( Supplementary Figure 2A [this file] – C [this file] & Supplementary Figure 2G [this file] – I [this file] ). Here we observe the expected cortical cell types including all the layered excitatory neurons and all inhibitory neuron types ( Supplementary Figure 2U [this file] , Supplementary Figure 3A [this file] ). 
We annotated nuclei using matched multiome RNA annotations and extrapolated annotations to the cluster level using a majority voting strategy (see Methods [rid=S10] , Figure 2B [rid=F2] , Figure 2D [rid=F2] , Supplementary Figure 2U [this file] – W [this file] ). For CC, this resulted in an atlas of 1,729,306 high-quality, annotated nuclei, with 1,707,448 high confidence chromatin accessibility peaks ( Supplementary Figure 2M [this file] – O [this file] , T [this file] , Supplementary Figure 3B [this file] ). For the SN, the atlas contains 1,370,425 high-quality, annotated nuclei and 1,292,285 chromatin accessibility peaks ( Figure 2F [rid=F2] , Supplementary Figure 2P [this file] – R [this file] , T [this file] ). 
The corresponding region is highly accessible in oligodendrocytes and lies upstream of the gene ( Supplementary Figure 4A [this file] ). 
caQTL and ASCA analyses gave highly concordant estimates of variant effects, even at relaxed FDR thresholds ( Supplementary Figure 4B [this file] – C [this file] ). Furthermore, variant effects were correlated across related cell types (e.g. L2/3-L6 neurons in CC) and between the same cell types across brain regions (e.g. microglia in CC and SN), even though all quantifications and testing were done independently for each cell type ( Figure 3E [rid=F3] , Supplementary figure 4D [this file] ). 
This resulted in identifying 41,686 variants with FDR<0.1 in broad neuronal classes, with caQTL slopes highly correlated with the underlying granular cell types ( Supplementary Figure 4E [this file] ). 
As an initial quality control of the methylation calls, we created CpG methylation pileups for samples with WGS data derived from CC, we compared the methylation levels at TSS of highly and lowly expressed genes and confirmed clear hypomethylation at highly expressed genes and high methylation at lowly expressed genes in all samples ( Supplementary Figure 5A [this file] ). Looking at the donor-specific pileups of all reads around TSS and CTCFs, we see clear hypomethylation which is more pronounced downstream of TSS at highly expressed genes ( Supplementary Figure 5B [this file] ) and decrease in accessibility with clear nucleosome patterning around CTCF motifs ( Supplementary Figure 5C [this file] ). We also observe clear haplotype-specific methylation at imprinted regions ( Supplementary Figure 5D [this file] ). 
The trained models showed good performance for predicting cell type-specific chromatin accessibility, with Spearman correlation of 0.76 in CC and 0.82 in SN between predictions and mean ATAC signal on the test set of highly variable regions across cell types ( Supplementary Figure 6A [this file] – F [this file] ).

Furthermore, high agreement (Spearman’s rho = 0.92 on 18,221 variants with matching cell types and absolute CREsted logFC above 0.05) was observed between DeepCC and the DeepBICCN2 model trained on mouse cortex data , suggesting conserved and sequence explainable features underlying the models’ predictions ( Supplementary Figure 6H [this file] ). 
Seqlets directly affected by caQTL-ASCA variants showed strong cell type-specific patterns ( Figure 4G [rid=F4] – J [rid=F4] , Supplementary Figure 7A [this file] ) and mapped to known cell type-specific regulators including SPI1 motifs (Ets family) for microglia and SOX family motifs for oligodendrocytes. 
SNP at chr1:213,602,214 falls into region specifically accessible in Microglia, and alternative allele (A) is predicted to reduce chromatin accessibility in that cell type in both CC and SN due to disruption of SPI1 binding motif ( Figure 4K [rid=F4] ), which agrees with the observed effects on chromatin accessibility by both caQTL and ASCA ( Supplementary Figure 7B [this file] ). Concordantly, this variant has significant effect observed in donors according to both caQTL and ASCA in L2/3 IT, L5 IT B, and L6 IT neurons ( Supplementary Figure 7C [this file] ). 
Furthermore, variants with higher ranks by CREsted ISM had higher absolute allelic imbalance ( Figure 5C [rid=F5] ) and caQTL slope ( Figure 5D [rid=F5] ) compared to the lower scoring variants, even when not statistically significant by either of these tests ( Supplementary Figure 8A [this file] – B [this file] ). Correlating predicted and observed log2-transformed gene expression values for each test set gene over all cell types, after mean subtraction across genes and cells, resulted in 0.67 mean Pearson correlation for the CC model, and 0.61 mean Pearson correlation for the SN ( Supplementary figure 9G [this file] – H [this file] ).

Some of the discrepancy may be explained by the difference in overall coverage in the two data sets ( Supplemental Fig. S1 [this file] ). 
Our comparison showed that the ONT bisulfite data set was highly correlated with the EpiQC data set (Pearson methylation frequency correlation = 0.969, root mean squared error [RMSE] = 9.367) ( Supplemental Fig. S2 [this file] ) and had significantly higher coverage than the EpiQC data set (26.03× and 92.95× mean coverage levels for the EpiQC and ONT bisulfite data sets, respectively) ( Supplemental Fig. S3 [this file] ). 
These sites are further subset into CpG sites with 0% methylation frequency and 100% methylation frequency ( Supplemental Tables S5, S6, S8–S11 [this file] ). 
Methylation proportions at both the low (0%–10% for R9) and high (90%–100% for R9) end of the spectrum saw a significant (Mann–Whitney test < 1.12 × 10 for 0.0–0.1 R9 > all R10, Mann–Whitney test < 1.12 × 10 for 0.9–1.0 R9 < all R10) shift in distributions between the two chemistries ( Fig. 1 [rid=GR279159GENF1] B–D; Supplemental Fig. S4 [this file] ). In contrast, the majority of R10 positions had 0.0 or 1.0 methylation proportions when R9 achieved 0.0 or 1.0 methylation proportion, respectively ( Fig. 1 [rid=GR279159GENF1] E; Supplemental Tables S5, S6 [this file] ). Relaxing the stringency and counting positions within 0.05 of 0 and 1 as the extremes had the predicted effect of bringing R9 and R10 much closer together by raw counts ( Supplemental Table S7 [this file] ). 
Supplemental Figure S5 [this file] shows more positions being identified as 0% or 100% methylated in R10 data relative to R9 data, concordant to what we had documented for the whole genome. 
We first examined the impact of strandedness on methylation calling differences and documented no influence ( Supplemental Fig. S6 [this file] ). S7–S11 [this file] ). We tested if variation in genome coverage between the R9 and R10 data sets contributed to methylation calling differences and found that this was not the case ( Supplemental Fig. S12 [this file] ). We did not notice any discrepancies in either a 100 or 1000 base window ( Supplemental Fig. S13 [this file] ). Finally, we examined the covariance of methylation call confidence in reads with at least 20 overlapping CpG sites and noted that R10 had a broader covariance distribution ( Supplemental Fig. S14 [this file] ). 
We also compared genome-wide CpG site methylation proportions for HG002 data sets generated using the ONT platform (R9 and R10), PacBio platform (HiFi data), and Illumina platform (bisulfite sequencing data; typically considered to be a “gold standard”) ( Fig. 3 [rid=GR279159GENF3] A; Supplemental Fig. S15 [this file] ).

Leveraging these advancements, we devised and refined an antibody-based proximity labeling approach to characterize the PAAS proteome in postmortem AD human brains and 5×FAD mice (Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] , Extended Data Figs. 1 [rid=Fig9] and 2 [rid=Fig10] , Supplementary Figs. 1 [this file] and 2 [this file] and Supplementary Movie [this file] ). 
Related to Supplementary Movie [this file] . , Immunofluorescence confocal deconvolved image demonstrating that PLD3 is highly enriched in axonal spheroids (red, PLD3) around amyloid plaques (blue, thioflavinS) in postmortem AD human brain. , Schematic of the pipeline for proximity labeling PAAS proteomics in postmortem brains. See also Extended Data Figs. 1 [rid=Fig9] and 2 [rid=Fig10] and Supplementary Figs. 1 [this file] and 2 [this file] . 
This protocol involved increased sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) concentration to 2% in basic Tris-HCl solution (pH 8.0), which enhanced protein extraction by effectively de-crosslinking proteins in fixed postmortem tissue (Supplementary Fig. 2a [this file] and Methods [rid=Sec12] ). The analysis revealed a diverse array of proteins, including the baits PLD3 and NeuN as well as axonal spheroid proteins RAGC and cathepsin B (Fig. 1i [rid=Fig1] and Supplementary Figs. 2b–d [this file] ). 
Human frontal cortex postmortem samples were obtained from 39 individuals from the Yale Alzheimer’s Research Center ( = 8 AD and = 2 control) and the Banner Sun Health Research Institute ( = 17 AD and = 12 control), with detailed clinical and neuropathological data (Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] ). For proteomics, we selected six individuals with AD (three females and three males) with the highest amyloid plaque burden (Supplementary Fig. 1c [this file] ) and eight unaffected controls (three females and five males). 
See also Extended Data Figs. 3 [rid=Fig11] – 7 [rid=Fig15] and Supplementary Figs. 3 [this file] – 6 [this file] . 
To ensure data stringency, we compared normalized total precursor intensity (NTPI) and normalized total spectra count (NTSC) methods (Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] ). As a result, 821 proteins remained, representing the PAAS proteome in AD, all exhibiting an FC enrichment > 1.95 (Fig. 2b,c [rid=Fig2] , Supplementary Figs. 4 [this file] – 6 [this file] and Supplementary Tables 1 [rid=MOESM3] and 2 [rid=MOESM4] ). 
Proteomic analyses in both humans and mice revealed hundreds of proteins previously unknown to be expressed in PAASs, alongside those already reported (Fig. 2d [rid=Fig2] , Extended Data Fig. 4a [rid=Fig12] , Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] and Supplementary Table 2 [rid=MOESM4] ). 
These findings reflect the axonal origin of PAASs and the accumulation of endolysosomal organelles, as shown by immunofluorescence and electron microscopy (Fig. 1b,c [rid=Fig1] and Supplementary Movie [this file] ) . Because PAAS structures lack pre-synaptic and post-synaptic features ( Supplementary Movie [this file] ), SNARE complex proteins and other synapse-related signatures likely indicate vesicle fusion processes within the endolysosomal pathway. 
Zoom-out images are shown in Supplementary Fig. 7 [this file] . See also Extended Data Fig. 4 [rid=Fig12] and Supplementary Fig. 7 [this file] . 
These included proteins linked to synaptogenesis, vesicle fusion and calcium signaling (for example, SYT11 and CAMK2A) and cytoskeleton dynamics (for example, SPTBN1) (Fig. 3e [rid=Fig3] , Supplementary Fig. 7 [this file] and Supplementary Table 2 [rid=MOESM4] ). A complete list of validated proteins is provided in Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] and Supplementary Table 2 [rid=MOESM4] . 
Top-ranked proteins associated with these processes included ATP8A1, C3, APOE, ATG9A, ATP8A2, TMEM30A, HEXB and HDLBP (Fig. 4c [rid=Fig4] ), all of which were identified in the PAAS proteome and increased in AD (Fig. 4d [rid=Fig4] , related to Fig. 2b [rid=Fig2] and Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] ). 
Among these, mTOR, RAGA (RRAGA), RAGC (RRAGC), LAMTOR1 and AKT1 were detected in the PAAS proteomes of humans and/or mice, whereas PIK3R4, RHEB and RAPTOR were not (Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] and Supplementary Tables 1 [rid=MOESM3] and 2 [rid=MOESM4] ). 
Our optimized model generated thioflavin S–positive amyloid deposits surrounded by abundant axonal spheroids (Fig. 6b [rid=Fig6] , Extended Data Figs. 9e,f [rid=Fig17] and 10a–c [rid=Fig18] and Supplementary Fig. 8a [this file] ). 
See also Extended Data Figs. 9 [rid=Fig17] and 10 [rid=Fig18] and Supplementary Fig. 8 [this file] . 
Consistent with findings in postmortem human brains (Fig. 5 [rid=Fig5] ), we detected expression of proteins associated with the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway localized within axonal spheroids (Fig. 6i [rid=Fig6] and Supplementary Fig. 8 [this file] ). 
A 7-day treatment with Torin1 significantly suppressed mTOR signaling, as evidenced by reduced phosphorylation of downstream effectors p-p70 S6K (Thr 389) and p-4E BP1 (Thr 37/46), without affecting total protein levels (Fig. 6j [rid=Fig6] and Supplementary Fig. 9 [this file] ). 
To investigate the role of mTOR signaling in axonal spheroid pathology in vivo, we employed a viral-mediated Cre/lox-based approach to induce knockout in 5×FAD mice (Fig. 7a–c [rid=Fig7] and Supplementary Fig. 1a–d [this file] ). 
See also Supplementary Figs. 10 [this file] – 12 [this file] . mo, months; NS, not significant. 
We infected floxed 5×FAD mice with AAV-PHP.eB-hSyn-Cre-GFP virus to achieve dense neuronal infection, inducing widespread heterozygous knockout in neurons (Fig. 7h [rid=Fig7] and Supplementary Fig. 10b,d,e [this file] ). This intervention significantly reduced the axonal spheroid halo size around plaques without affecting amyloid plaque size (Fig. 7i,j [rid=Fig7] and Supplementary Fig. 10e–h [this file] ). Notably, despite the role of mTOR in cell growth and maturation , heterozygous knockout did not change the size of neuronal cell bodies (Fig. 7k [rid=Fig7] and Supplementary Fig. 10f [this file] ). 
Using RNAscope in 5×FAD mice, we probed for mRNA species in axonal spheroids with a poly(A) tail probe and compared it to a scrambled control probe (Fig. 7p [rid=Fig7] and Supplementary Fig. 11a [this file] ). The poly(A) probe showed signal localization within axonal spheroids, whereas the control probe did not, confirming the presence of mRNA in these structures (Fig. 7q [rid=Fig7] and Supplementary Fig. 11b–d [this file] ). To examine local mRNA translation, we performed an in vivo puromycylation assay in 5×FAD mice (Fig. 7r [rid=Fig7] and Supplementary Fig. 12a [this file] ). Nascent proteins labeled by puromycin were detected in axonal spheroids, and treatment with the protein translation inhibitor anisomycin reduced the degree of labeling (Fig. 7s [rid=Fig7] and Supplementary Fig. 12a–c [this file] ), indicating that local mRNA translation occurs within spheroids. Neither the heterozygous nor homozygous mTOR deletion significantly affected the puromycin signal (Fig. 7a–c [rid=Fig7] and Supplementary Figs. 10a–d [this file] and 12d–f [this file] ). These results indicate that, under our experimental conditions (Supplementary Fig. 12d–f [this file] ), mTOR does not appear to control local protein translation within axonal spheroids. 
We developed a subcellular proximity labeling proteomics method for postmortem human and mouse brains , enabling detailed analysis of the protein composition and signaling pathways operating within PAASs (Fig. 8 [rid=Fig8] , Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] and Supplementary Table 2 [rid=MOESM4] ). 
Using this proteomic strategy, we identified numerous proteins enriched in PAASs, including previously unknown ones, alongside those already associated with these structures (Fig. 8 [rid=Fig8] , Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] and Supplementary Tables 1 [rid=MOESM3] and 2 [rid=MOESM4] ). Some of the identified proteins are also expressed in synapses, raising the possibility that PAASs may originate from pre-synaptic structures, although electron microscopy did not reveal pre-synaptic or post-synaptic features in PAASs ( Supplementary Movie [this file] ). (2) Cytoskeletal Dysregulation: Activated signaling pathways, such as actin cytoskeletal signaling, RAC signaling and actin nucleation by the ARP–WASP complex, were enriched within PAASs, whereas pathways such as RHOGDI signaling, which regulates Rho family GTPase, were inhibited (Fig. 3c [rid=Fig3] and Extended Data Fig. 4e [rid=Fig12] ) . 
However, although mTOR signaling is known to modulate local translation in neurons , our study did not detect changes in local translation levels after mTOR knockout or pharmacological inhibition (Supplementary Fig. 12d–f [this file] ). 
Proteins involved in calcium signaling, such as CAMK2 and calmodulin, were identified in PAASs (Fig. 3e [rid=Fig3] , Supplementary Fig. 7 [this file] and Supplementary Table 2 [rid=MOESM4] ), suggesting a role for local calcium signaling dysregulation in PAAS pathogenesis. 
However, the high enrichment of PLD3 in axonal spheroids likely increased biotinylation efficiency, resulting in our ability to capture most proteins previously described in PAASs, including endolysosomal-related proteins as well as cytoskeletal proteins (for example, SPTBN1) and cell surface receptors (for example, NTRK2) (Figs. 2d [rid=Fig2] and 8 [rid=Fig8] , Extended Data Fig. 4a [rid=Fig12] , Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] and Supplementary Table 2 [rid=MOESM4] ). 
Detailed demographic and clinical information can be found in Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] . For immunofluorescence proteomic validations, 25 severe AD and 14 unaffected control cases were used (Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] ). 
To stain phosphorylated Tau, anti-phospho-Tau S235 (1:1,000; Thermo Fisher Scientific), anti-phospho-Tau S396 (1:200) and anti-phospho-Tau S404 (1:200) were used (see RRIDs in Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). 
Thus, we optimized the protein extraction protocol and largely increased the protein extraction yield compared to previously published methods (Supplementary Fig. 2a [this file] ) .

The demographics, pathological notes, and other metadata for this study cohort are detailed in Table S1 [this file] . Extensive pathology information for PD samples is provided in Table S2 [this file] . 
Prior to differential analysis, as previously described, we estimated the impact of multiple technical variables as well as donor-level characteristics separately for the snRNA-seq experiments ( Table S1 [this file] ). 
Each diagnosis group comprised 6 females and 6 males ( Table S1 [this file] summarizes the demographic and neuropathological phenotypes). snRNA-seq was carried out on prepared gene expression libraries. After quality control (QC) filtering, expression data for nuclei from all four diagnosis groups were integrated, and data from 396,867 nuclei were retained across all four groups ( Table S2 [this file] ). 
DEGs (false discovery rate (FDR) adjusted -value < 0.05) were further categorized into positive (upregulated) and negative (downregulated) genes based on their average log fold change ( Fig. 2B [rid=F2] , Tables S3 [this file] - S6 [this file] ). 
In order to understand the potential functional significance of risk genes expressed in these disease-driver clusters, we performed marker gene analysis as above, comparing gene expression in disease-driver clusters of a particular cell type to all of the other clusters of that same cell type in NDD nuclei ( Tables S7 [this file] - S10 [this file] ). Notably, we also observed strongly inhibited expression of the major AD risk factor gene in this cell type ( Table S7 [this file] ). 
The Interneuron 2 inhibitory neuron subtype exhibited the highest number of shared downregulated DEGs (5,570; Fig. 5D [rid=F5] , Table S10 [this file] ). followed by the GABAergic neuron 1 subtype (3,898; Fig. 5E [rid=F5] , Table S11 [this file] ). Microglia 10 had the highest number of shared upregulated DEGs (248; Fig. 5F [rid=F5] , Table S12 [this file] ). 
In comparing AD and DLB, we found DEGs that were upregulated in DLB in only four out of the 29 cell subtype clusters, including excitatory neurons (clusters 5 and 9), and oligodendrocytes (clusters 1 and 2), which exhibited about 5,000 DEGs each (5347, 5030, 4630, and 4805, respectively), mainly upregulated in DLB ( Fig. 6B [rid=F6] , Ci [rid=F6] , Tables S13 [this file] - S16 [this file] ). 
Comparison of PD to DLB across all clusters also resulted mainly in DLB-upregulated DEGs ( Fig. 6B [rid=F6] , Di [rid=F6] , Tables S17 [this file] - S20 [this file] ). 
Comparing AD to PD yielded the most diverse pattern of transcriptional dysregulation as demonstrated by the variety of cell types with DEGs and the directionality of the differential expression ( Fig. 6B [rid=F6] , Ei [rid=F6] , Tables S21 [this file] - S25 [this file] ).

Using TensorQTL and applying a standard false discovery rate (FDR) threshold of q-value < 0.05, we identified 838 significant SV-eQTL (q-value <0.05) in the NABEC datasets affecting 779 distinct eGenes and 135 significant SV-eQTL in the HBCC affecting 134 distinct eGenes ( Table 1 [this file] ). 
In HBCC, we identified 1,165 eQTL affecting 1,142 distinct eGenes , 16 of which had an SV as the lead variant ( Table 1 [this file] ). 
In the NABEC cohort, SVs were identified as the most likely causal variant in 2.9% (59/2064) of eQTL, while in the HBCC cohort, SVs were the top probable causal variant in 1.4% (16/1142) of eQTL ( Table 1 [this file] ). 
Next, we examined promoter regions, identifying 652 SV-prom-mQTL in NABEC across 614 distinct promoters and 486 SV-prom-mQTL across 472 distinct promoters in HBCC ( Table 2 [this file] ). For gene bodies, we identified 1687 SV-gene-mQTL in NABEC for 1581 distinct genes and 658 SV-gene-mQTL in HBCC for 682 distinct genes ( Table 2 [this file] ), with 252 (NABEC: HBCC ; 16.0%, 37.0%) common between both cohorts, showing consistent SVs and effects (β). 
Next to further assess the relative contribution of SVs to methylation in the postmortem frontal cortex, we conducted a joint QTL analysis combining SVs and small variants( Table 2 [this file] ). 
In the HBCC cohort, SVs were the top probable causal variant in 3.7% (37/1012) of CGI-mQTL, 2.0% (44/2236) of prom-mQTL, and 3.9% (78/2023) of gene-mQTL ( Table 2 [this file] ).

caption: Supplementary file1 (TIF 20473 KB) Supplementary Fig. 1. The working hypothesis of single TBI-mediated AD-like pathology and memory loss. A single TBI results in a reduction in excitatory (EX) neuronal and oligodendrocyte (OLG) BAG3, leading to dysfunction of the autophagy-lysosomal pathway (ALP), as shown by decreased CTSD and LAMP1, and increased p62 puncta formation. Dysfunction of the ALP increases ptau accumulation in EX neurons and OLG, which further leads to synaptic dysfunction (decreased post-synaptic density 95 (PSD95)) and memory loss. Additionally, a single TBI results in gliosis, as shown by increased levels of GFAP in astrocytes and IBA-1 in microglia/macrophages. Notably, astrocytes upregulate BAG3, which may protect them from tau aggregates or facilitate astrocytic tau clearance. The reactive gliosis after TBI may also contribute to synaptic dysfunction and memory loss. Furthermore, intervention by BAG3 overexpression in neurons can attenuate deficiencies in the ALP, decrease ptau, and ameliorate post-synaptic density and memory deficits. The solid lines are based on the findings in this study, while the dotted line is hypothesized bidirectional relationship between gliosis and decreased BAG3 levels in EX neurons and OLG.

context_description:
We performed triple immunofluorescence (IF) staining with SATB2, OLIG2, and PHF1 (pSer396/pSer404) or CP13 (pSer202) and found that a single unilateral TBI increased ptau (PHF1-positive ( +) and CP13 +) in EX neurons (SATB2 +) and OLG (OLIG2 +) in the ipsilateral retrosplenial cortex (RSC) and hippocampus (HC) region of WT and hTKI mice compared with sham mice, respectively (Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] b–e and Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] a–d). Notably, there was no co-localization between ptau and inhibitory (IN) neurons (GAD1 +), astrocytes (GFAP +), microglia/macrophages (IBA-1 +), or oligodendrocyte precursor cells (PDGFR-α+) (Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] f–i). 
Thus, astrocytes may upregulate BAG3 as a compensatory mechanism, to protect themselves from tau accumulation (Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] g) or to facilitate the clearance of tau aggregates. 
Notably, we found that overexpression of neuronal BAG3 can reduce the number of cells with ptau accumulation in the CA2–CA3 region of the hippocampus compared to AAV-CT (Fig. 6 [rid=Fig6] d and Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] e). 
In this study, we found that a single unilateral TBI altered the cell-type-specific expression of BAG3 (Fig. 4 [rid=Fig4] and Supplementary Fig. 6 [rid=MOESM6] ), which is associated with decreased ALP-associated genes and increased p62 puncta formation (Fig. 8 [rid=Fig8] a–g), ptau in EX neurons and OLG (Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] b–e and Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] a–d), gliosis (Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] f–k and Supplementary Fig. 3 [rid=MOESM3] ), synaptic dysfunction (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] a–d), and cognitive deficits (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] e–h) in WT and hTKI mouse models. 
Decreased BAG3 correlates well with the reductions in CTSD and LAMP1, and the increases in p62 puncta formation (Fig. 8 [rid=Fig8] a–g) and ptau accumulation (Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] b–e and Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] a–d, f–i) in EX neurons and OLG in both WT and hTKI mouse models. 
The observed PHF1 + cells in WT sham animals are few in numbers and mostly localized to OLIG2 + cells (Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] and [ 32 [rid=CR32] ]), rather than neurons. In this study, we show that TBI can promote ptau in OLG, indicating TBI not only increases the neuronal vulnerability to ptau but also enhances the vulnerability of OLG Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] b–e and Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] ). 
Although we have not validated if the overexpression of BAG3 specifically in astrocytes can prevent AD-like pathology and cognitive deficits induced by TBI in this study, increased BAG3 in astrocytes is probably a protective and compensatory response of astrocytes to degrade tau in pathological conditions because there is no ptau found in astrocytes (Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] g) in animal models with TBI.

We sought to investigate changes of astro- and microgliosis in the RSC (cortical region proximal to the injury site), the corpus callosum (CC; white matter region proximal to injury site), and the lateral posterior nucleus of the thalamus (LP; a thalamic nucleus distal to the injury site) (Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] i) in WT and hTKI mice with TBI compared to sham controls. Furthermore, we found that the immunoreactivity and the percentage of area occupied by GFAP increased in the ipsilateral RSC region of WT and hTKI mice with TBI (Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] a, b, d, e). Microgliosis was also evident in the ipsilateral RSC region of WT and hTKI mice, as shown by the increase of IBA-1 immunoreactivity and percentage of area occupied by IBA-1 staining in WT mice with TBI (Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] a, c) while the surface area of IBA-1 + microglia was reduced in hTKI mice subjected to TBI (Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] d, f), compared to the sham controls. Additionally, we found that the immunoreactivity of GFAP and IBA-1 was increased in the ipsilateral LP of WT TBI and hTKI TBI mice compared to sham controls, indicating that deep brain structures distal from the site of injury are also affected by micro- and astrogliosis after TBI (Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] g, h). Overall, these results indicate that a single CCI TBI is sufficient to induce sustained glial activation in regions proximal and distal to the injury site Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] f–k and Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] a–h). 
In this study, we found that a single unilateral TBI altered the cell-type-specific expression of BAG3 (Fig. 4 [rid=Fig4] and Supplementary Fig. 6 [rid=MOESM6] ), which is associated with decreased ALP-associated genes and increased p62 puncta formation (Fig. 8 [rid=Fig8] a–g), ptau in EX neurons and OLG (Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] b–e and Supplementary Fig. 2 [rid=MOESM2] a–d), gliosis (Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] f–k and Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] ), synaptic dysfunction (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] a–d), and cognitive deficits (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] e–h) in WT and hTKI mouse models. 
We indeed found increased dyshomeostatic astrocytes and microglia, which are evidenced by the upregulation of GFAP and IBA-1 immunoreactivity and the decrease in microglia branches (i.e., less area of IBA-1 immunoreactivity per microglia) in both WT and hTKI mouse models with TBI in several regions, both proximal and distal to the injury site (Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] f–k and Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] ).

We found a consistent trend, showing an inverse relationship between BAG3 and PHF1 levels at single cell levels, i.e., cells with accumulation of ptau have significantly reduced BAG3 compared to cells without ptau accumulation (Fig. 4 [rid=Fig4] e–h, Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] , Fig. 5 [rid=Fig5] d–g, and Supplementary Fig. 7 [rid=MOESM7] ) although global BAG3 increased in animal models and human post-mortem brain tissues with TBI and AD (Supplementary Fig. 8 [rid=MOESM8] ).
