To study how the LRRK2 G2019S mutation impacts astrocytes in the prefrontal cortex, a cortical region linked to PD, we stained sections from the frontal cortices of age and sex-matched control and LRRK2 G2019S mutation-carrying PD patients ( Supplemental Table 1 [this file] ) with glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP, a marker for astrocyte branches) and phosphorylated ERM (Phospho-ERM, which are enriched in PAPs) ( Figure 1A [rid=F1] ). 
Affinity-purified proteins from cortices were analyzed using quantitative liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS) ( Figure 6B [rid=F6] ), identifying 30,815 unique peptides corresponding to 4,081 unique proteins ( Supplemental Tables 2 [this file] - 4 [this file] ). Comparative analysis revealed 344 proteins with significantly altered proximity to Ezrin in LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes (fold-change >1.5 or < −1.5, < 0.05); 190 gained, and 154 lost Ezrin proximity ( Figure 6C [rid=F6] ; Figure S14C [rid=SD2] - D [rid=SD2] ; Supplemental Table 5 [this file] ). Gene Ontology (GO) analysis of these proteins showed enrichment in phospholipid binding, microtubule binding, and membrane transporter and cell-adhesion mediator activity were over-represented in differentially enriched proteins ( Figure 6D [rid=F6] ; Supplemental Table 6 [this file] ). Unexpectedly, GO-term analyses of biological processes highlighted enrichment in catabolic processes, macroautophagy, negative regulation of developmental growth, and intracellular transport ( Figure 6E [rid=F6] ; Supplemental Table 7 [this file] ). 
To assess global cytosolic changes, we analyzed the Astro-Cyto-BioID dataset across genotypes, identifying 195 differentially enriched proteins (78 gained, 117 lost in LRRK2 G2019S ; Figure S14E [rid=SD2] ; Supplemental Table 8 [this file] ). GO-term analysis revealed an enrichment of proteins associated with phospholipid binding and vesicle trafficking ( Figure S14F [rid=SD2] - G [rid=SD2] ; Supplemental Tables 9 [this file] - 10 [this file] ). 
To identify potential direct Ezrin interactors affected by LRRK2 G2019S, we compared protein abundance in Astro-Ezrin-BioID to Astro-Cyto-BioID within each genotype (Ezrin/Cyto fold -change > 1.5, < 0.05, 346 proteins in WT and 335 proteins in LRRK2 G2019S ; Supplemental Tables 11 [this file] - 12 [this file] ). Using these filters, we narrowed down our list to 28 as “gained proximity to Ezrin in LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes” and 30 as “lost proximity to Ezrin in LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes” ( Figure 6F [rid=F6] - H [rid=F6] ; Supplemental Table 13 [this file] ). 
None of the control subjects had a history of dementia or neurological or psychiatric disorders at the time of death (See Supplemental Table 1 [this file] ). 
To assess technical reproducibility, we calculated the % coefficient of variation (%CV) for each protein across 3 injections of an SPQC pool that were interspersed throughout the study ( Table S4 [this file] ). 
Those fold changes and p-values are presented for all proteins in Tables S5 [this file] , S7 [this file] , S9 [this file] , and S10 [this file] . False Discovery Rate (FDR) correction was performed using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure, and these values are reported (“p.adjusted”) in Tables S5 [this file] , S7 [this file] , S9 [this file] , and S10 [this file] . Within supplemental tables [this file] , we have labeled proteins significantly more abundant (“Up”, fold change >1.5 and unadjusted p-value <0.05), or less abundant (“Down”, fold change >−1.5 and unadjusted p-value <0.05) in a particular genotype or BioID sample group.

We found a significant increase in phospho-ERM signal colocalized with both S100β and MAP2 ( Figure S1A [this file] - C [this file] ). 
This phospho-ERM increase was localized to layers (L)1 and L2–3 of the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) and the primary motor cortex (MOp) ( Figure 1E [rid=F1] - L [rid=F1] ; Figure S2A [this file] - C [this file] ) but was absent in both the primary sensory cortex (SSp) and the dorsal medial striatum (DMS) ( Figure S2D [this file] - I [this file] ). In the ACC and MOp L1 and L2/3 of LRRK2 G2019S mice, phospho-ERM was significantly increased and colocalized with S100β and MAP2 but not Iba1 (microglia marker), with a predominant localization to astrocytes in the ACC and MOp of LRRK2 G2019S mice ( Figure S3A [this file] - C [this file] ). In both cases, the phospho-ERM signal was eliminated after λ-PPase treatment, confirming the phospho-ERM antibody specificity ( Figure S4A [this file] - F [this file] ). 
We did not detect any increase in the levels of GFAP ( Figure S5A [this file] - C [this file] ). 
In the ACC of the LRRK2 G2019S mice, there was a significant decrease in intracortical excitatory synapse density in both layers and ages we analyzed (~30%) when compared to the WT controls ( Figure 2C [rid=F2] - D [rid=F2] and Figure S6A [this file] - B [this file] ). However, no differences in excitatory synapse density were observed between genotypes in the MOp ( Figure 2E [rid=F2] - F [rid=F2] and Figure S6C [this file] - D [this file] ). 
We chose Ezrin because Ezrin is highly abundant and specifically enriched in astrocytes compared to its family members, Radixin and Moesin[ 21 [rid=R21] ] ( Figure S7A [this file] - B [this file] ). Switching the amino acid threonine (T) at location 567 with alanine (A) results in a version of the protein that cannot be phosphorylated (Phospho-dead Ezrin, Figure S7C [this file] )[ 28 [rid=R28] , 29 [rid=R29] ]. 
To determine if phospho-dead Ezrin can reduce ERM phosphorylation in astrocytes of LRRK2 G2019S mice, we retro-orbitally injected 9-week-old WT and LRRK2 G2019S mice with AAVs to express Hemagglutinin (HA)-tagged WT Ezrin or phospho-dead Ezrin under the control of the astrocyte-specific GfaABC1D promoter ( Figure S7D [this file] ). However, neither WT nor phospho-dead Ezrin overexpression impacted Rab10 phosphorylation ( Figure S8 [this file] ), showing that phospho-dead Ezrin selectively reduces ERM hyperphosphorylation in astrocytes. 
We found that, in WT ACC, WT Ezrin overexpression in astrocytes had no effect on excitatory synapse density ( Figure S9 [this file] ). We also found that, in the MOp L1 and L2–3 of LRRK2 G2019S mice, neither the WT nor the phospho-dead Ezrin overexpression in adult astrocytes restored inhibitory synapse density back to the levels in the WT MOp overexpressed with WT Ezrin ( Figure S10 [this file] ). 
To image and reconstruct the morphology of individual whole astrocytes, we collected 100-μm thick mouse brain sections ( Figure S11A [this file] ). However, this alteration of astrocyte morphology did not change the number of ALDH1L1+/SOX9+ cells (number of astrocytes) in the LRRK2 G2019S ACC and MOp ( Figure S11B [this file] - D [this file] ). 
Similar to LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes, astrocytes transfected with shLrrk2 (~90% reduction, Figure S12A [this file] - B [this file] ) exhibited significantly smaller territory volumes (~36% reduction) and reduced complexity ( Figure 5E [rid=F5] - G [rid=F5] ). 
An Ezrin mutant in which the T567 residue is switched to aspartate (D) prefers Ezrin’s open conformation, thereby mimicking the phosphorylated state (Phospho-mimetic Ezrin, Figure S4C [this file] )[ 55 [rid=R55] , 56 [rid=R56] ]. 
Biotinylated proteins were detected in astrocytes using immunohistochemistry and immunoblotting for HA and Streptavidin ( Figure S13 [this file] ). 
Principle component analyses (PCA) of BioID results showed that distinct clustering between Cyto-BioID (control) and Ezrin-BioID (bait) samples, with further separation between WT or LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes ( Figure S14A [this file] ). Radixin and Moesin, known as Ezrin family proteins, were significantly enriched in the Ezrin-BioID sample compared to Cyto-BioID ( Figure S14B [this file] )[ 57 [rid=R57] ]. Comparative analysis revealed 344 proteins with significantly altered proximity to Ezrin in LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes (fold-change >1.5 or < −1.5, < 0.05); 190 gained, and 154 lost Ezrin proximity ( Figure 6C [rid=F6] ; Figure S14C [this file] - D [this file] ; Supplemental Table 5 [rid=SD1] ). 
To assess global cytosolic changes, we analyzed the Astro-Cyto-BioID dataset across genotypes, identifying 195 differentially enriched proteins (78 gained, 117 lost in LRRK2 G2019S ; Figure S14E [this file] ; Supplemental Table 8 [rid=SD1] ). GO-term analysis revealed an enrichment of proteins associated with phospholipid binding and vesicle trafficking ( Figure S14F [this file] - G [this file] ; Supplemental Tables 9 [rid=SD1] - 10 [rid=SD1] ). 
To test if Atg7 is required for astrocyte morphology, we developed a short hairpin RNA (shRNA) that targets both rat and mouse which effectively reduced mRNA in mouse cells ( Figure S15A [this file] ). Knockdown of Atg7 in rat astrocytes significantly reduced neuron-induced astrocyte morphogenesis in a neuron-astrocyte co-culture assay ( Figure S15B [this file] - C [this file] ). , Atg7 knockdown in WT astrocytes reduced astrocyte territory volume and morphological complexity, resembling the LRRK2 G2019S astrocytes transfected with shControl ( Figure 7I [rid=F7] - K [rid=F7] ).

Each dataset was sequenced using a single PromethION R9 flow cell, yielding on average 116 Gb of base-called reads (~37X coverage assuming 3.1Gb genome) with an estimated average across bases read quality above Q10 ( Figure 1 [rid=F1] ; Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). 
Analysis of a single ONT human sample at 30–40x coverage took 22–25 wall-clock hours if run on the Terra environment (2200–2500 CPU hours; estimated Google Cloud computing cost about 100$; Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). 
We benchmarked the performance of small variant (substitutions and indels shorter than 50 bp) calls produced by the updated PEPPER-Margin-DeepVariant and compared them to Illumina-based small variant calls produced by DeepVariant ( Figure 2 [rid=F2] ; Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). 
The results were consistent with the GIAB benchmark analysis, confirming the reduced SNP error rate of ONT-based methods, compared to Illumina within the Tier1 benchmark regions ( Figure 2 [rid=F2] ; Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). 
In exons (defined by the GIAB benchmark and representing <0.1% of all indels) F1-scores were 0.9230 for ONT and 0.9923 for Illumina ( Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). 
Using the Shasta + Hapdup combination, we generated assemblies for 14 brain samples and three cell lines ( Extended Data Figure 2 [rid=F8] ; Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ). Mean NG50 of the phase blocks was ~2 Mb; switch error rate of cell line assemblies was 0.07–0.19% ( Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ). 
Compared to the trio-binned ONT HG002 assemblies produced from a recent long-read benchmarking study , our assemblies had slightly reduced contiguity (due to lower read depth and length), but better QV and phasing accuracy ( Extended Data Figure 3 [rid=F9] ; Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ). 
HPRC-based assembly concordance was only slightly higher (0.970), compared to Hapdup ( Figure 3 [rid=F3] ; Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). 
To investigate the quality of our SV calls further, we used the assemblies generated by the HPRC as a benchmark on three cell lines and evaluated the concordance of SV calls inside various regions of the human genome ( Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ).

Out of a total of 2428 genes mapped to PD-GWAS regions, defined as ± 500 Kb of GWAS-SNVs, 628 were DEGs in at least one cell subtype (hereafter designated as PD GWAS-DEGs), including (Exc5 and Micro3), (Inh2), and (OPC1) (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] C, Fig. S4B [this file] , Table S3 [rid=MOESM2] ). and are not only PD GWAS loci in non-mendelian PD cases, but are also established fPD genes [ 4 [rid=CR4] ]. We also described the most highly enriched up- and downregulated PD GWAS-DEG pathways for individual cell subtype clusters (Fig. S5A [this file] and B, respectively). 
Moreover, Exc5 was the only neuronal cluster showing a significant and robust overexpression of (Figs. 2 [rid=Fig2] C, S4B [this file] ), further supporting a role for this neuronal subtype in later PD stages along the neuropathological progression of the disease [ 45 [rid=CR45] , 46 [rid=CR46] ]. To this end, we first examined the expression of 10 canonical markers in all Exc and Inh neuronal clusters to annotate neuronal subtypes (Fig. S6 [this file] ). The vesicular glutamate transporter was expressed in all Exc subtypes (Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] B, Fig. S6 [this file] ), indicating the predominance of glutamatergic neurons within our TC samples, and markers for GABA transmission ( , ) were expressed among Inh neuron clusters, as expected. Nuclei were isolated from frozen post-mortem human TC tissues of 12 PD and 12 normal control individuals, 6 females and 6 males from each diagnosis group (Table 1 [rid=Tab1] and Table S1 [this file] summarize the demographic and neuropathological phenotypes). 
After quality control (QC) filtering, a total of 208,081 nuclei from all 24 TC samples were retained for snRNA-seq (Table S1 [this file] ). Following dimensional reduction by principal component analysis (PCA) and uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP), Louvain community detection was used to delineate 36 nuclei clusters with distinct gene expression profiles (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] A, Table S2 [this file] ) and representing subtypes of the six major cell types. Cell subtypes were each given a unique label according to their most common cell type (e.g., the 12 clusters of excitatory neurons were labeled Exc1-Exc12; Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] A, Table S2 [this file] ). 
We did not identify any significant changes in either major cell type or cell subtype cluster proportions between the PD and the control groups (Fig. S3A [rid=MOESM1] ), as expected according the low McKeith scores in the TC tissues of the PD group (Table 1 [rid=Tab1] and S1 [this file] ). 
First, we analyzed the contributions of 41 metadata variables (listed in Table S1 [this file] ) to sample variance and found that the number of nuclei after QC filtering, median number of genes per cell, and average library size contribute significantly to the variability in gene expression. In contrast, microglia separated into only 3 clusters, with the bulk of nuclei belonging to the Micro1 cluster (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] A, Table S2 [this file] ). 
A granulated analysis at the cell subtype level revealed a total of 11,612 unique DEGs, with the highest numbers of DEGs in Exc5, Micro1, and OPC1 clusters (n = 3899, 5640, and 5382, respectively; Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] B, Table S3 [this file] ). We then integrated the cell subtype DEGs dataset with 90 PD-GWAS loci [ 5 [rid=CR5] ] (Table S3 [this file] ). Out of a total of 2428 genes mapped to PD-GWAS regions, defined as ± 500 Kb of GWAS-SNVs, 628 were DEGs in at least one cell subtype (hereafter designated as PD GWAS-DEGs), including (Exc5 and Micro3), (Inh2), and (OPC1) (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] C, Fig. S4B [rid=MOESM1] , Table S3 [this file] ). and are not only PD GWAS loci in non-mendelian PD cases, but are also established fPD genes [ 4 [rid=CR4] ]. 
Next, we further characterized the transcriptional profile of Exc5 cells compared to all other excitatory neuron clusters using FindMarkers in Seurat (Methods) and identified 432 upregulated and 498 downregulated marker genes (|log FC| threshold of ≥ 0.25 and a gene-level FDR-adjusted value threshold of < 0.01; Table S4 [this file] ). 
In the snATAC-seq dataset, 167,445 nuclei were retained after QC filtering (Table S5 [this file] ) and Louvain community detection distinguished 32 cell subtype clusters representing the same six major cell types as in the snRNA-seq data (Fig. 4 [rid=Fig4] A). 
We applied a threshold coaccessibility score of ≥ 0.2 [ 56 [rid=CR56] , 57 [rid=CR57] ] between each peak and at least one other peak in the network and revealed a total of 29,968 CCANs across all 22 clusters (Table S6 [this file] ). The analysis identified 115 unidirectional CCANs (Table S6 [this file] ), including 2 CCANs overlapping PD GWAS-DEGs (Fig. 4 [rid=Fig4] E). 
Thus, we first identified a total of 142 cCREs linked to 104 unique PD GWAS-DEGs (out of 628 total PD GWAS-DEGs examined) across 18 clusters (Fig. 5 [rid=Fig5] ; Table S7 [this file] ). The analysis revealed enrichment of TF binding sites (TFBS) within 125 cCREs linked to a total of 90 unique PD GWAS-DEGs across 17 out of the 18 analyzed cell subtypes (fold-enrichment cutoff ≥ 1.2 and FDR < 0.05; Fig. 5 [rid=Fig5] , Table S8 [this file] ). Notably, Exc5 showed the highest number of cCRE-linked upregulated PD GWAS-DEGs, and the strongest enrichment for TF-DEGs (Fig. 5 [rid=Fig5] A, Table S8 [this file] ). For downregulated PD GWAS-DEGs, the strongest enrichment for TF-DEGs was found in Micro1 and OPC1 (Fig. 5 [rid=Fig5] Biv-vi, Table S8 [this file] ). Enrichment for binding sites of TF-DEGs in cCREs linked to upregulated and downregulated PD GWAS-DEGs was also identified in other cell subtype clusters (Fig. 5 [rid=Fig5] Bi-iii, Table S8 [this file] ). 
Among the targeted DEGs, postsynaptic scaffold protein-encoding [ 62 [rid=CR62] ] was predicted to be regulated by the highest number of TF-DEGs (n = 27; Fig. 6 [rid=Fig6] A, Table S8 [this file] ). 
We identified a total of 1175 unique variants predicted to impact binding of a total of 599 TFs, including 1035 SNVs, 27 insertions, and 113 deletions (Table S9 [this file] ). TFs showing changes in the affinity of their binding sites also included TF-DEGs, with the highest number (n = 24) identified in the Exc5 cluster (Table S10 [this file] ). 
Out of the 1175 candidate regulatory variants, 19 were in LD with a PD GWAS-SNV (r and D′ ≥ 0.5; Table S11 [this file] ). A prominent example involved the PD GWAS-DEGs , , , and (Fig. 7 [rid=Fig7] A, Table S11 [this file] ). The major allele of another deletion variant in this region (rs5820529) was in high LD with the same PD GWAS-SNV (r = 0.554, D′ = 0.87; Fig. 7 [rid=Fig7] A, Table S11 [this file] ). 
A second example of PD risk variants potentially impacting regulation of multiple Exc5 PD GWAS-DEGs was discovered on chromosome 17. cCREs of 5 PD GWAS-DEGs ( , , , , and ) had predicted differential binding at 3 variant loci with high LD to PD GWAS-SNV rs12600861 (Fig. 7 [rid=Fig7] B, Table S11 [this file] ). 
On chromosome 16, two SNVs (rs12445650, rs58726213) showed strong LD with PD GWAS-SNV rs12600861 (r = 0.801, D′ = 0.901) within cCRE peaks linked to the PD GWAS-DEG in Exc5 nuclei (Fig. 7 [rid=Fig7] C, Table S11 [this file] ). 
Sequence variants in high LD with PD risk alleles were also identified in other cell subtype clusters, including in cCREs of upregulated PD GWAS-DEGs in neuronal cluster Exc3 (Fig. 7 [rid=Fig7] D, Table S11 [this file] ), and downregulated PD GWAS-DEGs in microglial cluster Micro1 (Fig. 7 [rid=Fig7] E, Table S11 [this file] ), as well as numerous other subtype clusters (Table S11 [this file] ). 
The demographics and other metadata for this cohort are detailed in Tables 1 [rid=Tab1] and S1 [this file] . Complete pathology analysis results of PD samples are provided in Table S12 [this file] . 
Age and post-mortem interval (PMI) of female PD was compared to female Normal, and age and PMI of male PD was compared to male Normal (Table S13 [this file] ). 
Counts of predicted major cell types based on the label transfer were examined for each of the 36 clusters (Table S2 [this file] ), and clusters were manually annotated based on the majority cell type for each cluster (e.g., ‘Exc1’, ‘Exc2’, etc.). Most frequent cell types comprised over 90% of cells in each cluster with the exceptions of Astro4, Micro2, Micro3 and OPC2 (Table S2 [this file] ). 
Prior to differential analysis, as previously [ 57 [rid=CR57] ] we estimated the impact of multiple technical variables as well as donor-level characteristics separately for the snRNA-seq (Table S1 [this file] ) and snATAC-seq (Table S5 [this file] ) experiments. 
In order to focus on the most significant marker genes, we used a log FC threshold of > 0.25 and a gene-level FDR-adjusted -value threshold of < 0.01, and identified 432 positive (upregulated) marker genes, and 498 negative (downregulated) marker genes for the Exc5 cluster (Table S4 [this file] ). 
For analyses of shared pathways among clusters, Micro3 was excluded, as the majority cell type in this cluster represented below 50 percent of total nuclei in the cluster (Table S2 [this file] ).

Single-cell multiomic technologies enable joint analysis of chromatin conformation and gene expression (Supplementary Table 1 [this file] and Supplementary Note 1 [this file] ). 
The MUSIC workflow contains two major steps (Supplementary Note 2 [this file] ). 
These read pairs resolved 533,233,368 uniquely mapped, non-duplicate and barcode-complete (containing cell barcode, 10X barcode, I7 barcode and either DNA or RNA linker) (UMNDBC) read pairs (Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). This mixed-species dataset showed low species-mixing rates at both the cellular and chromatin complex level, supporting the ability of MUSIC to generate data at both single-cell and single-complex resolution (Extended Data Fig. 3a,b [rid=Fig7] and Supplementary Note 3 [this file] ). 
Analysis involving downsampling of reads suggested that this difference was not due to variation in read numbers between pairwise and multiplex interactions (Supplementary Note 4 [this file] and Extended Data Fig. 5b [rid=Fig9] ). In addition, compared with pairwise contacts, multiplex interactions showed higher contact frequencies at submegabase to several megabase genomic distances, indicating enrichment of long-range chromatin interactions in the multiplex complexes (Fig. 2e [rid=Fig2] and Supplementary Note 5 [this file] ). 
In addition, MUSIC recapitulated the known chromatin association patterns of premessenger RNAs (pre-mRNAs) and nuclear speckle-associated RNAs (nsaRNA) (Fig. 2l,m [rid=Fig2] and Supplementary Note 6 [this file] ). 
We generated a MUSIC dataset on 14 postmortem samples of human frontal cortex from tissue donors aged 59 years and above (Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ). MUSIC FC resolved comparable numbers of single-nucleus RNA (snRNA) reads and DNA–DNA contacts versus other methods (Supplementary Note 7 [this file] and Extended Data Fig. 6b–d [rid=Fig10] ). 
Clustering analysis based on MUSIC snRNA reads identified seven cell types: excitatory neurons, inhibitory neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, oligodendrocyte precursors, microglia and vascular cells (Fig. 3a [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Note 8 [this file] ). In addition, a joint analysis of MUSIC FC with a snRNA-seq dataset of human frontal cortex showed highly consistent clustering structures and clustering-based cell type assignments between the two datasets (Supplementary Note 9 [this file] ). 
In addition, regression analysis showed that those factors with the greatest correlations to LCS-erosion score included transcriptomic age, cell type, Alzheimer’s disease pathology and sex (Supplementary Note 10 [this file] ). 
We compared cell type variation in chromatin contacts (Fig. 3b [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Fig. 3a [this file] ) with eQTL–target pairings in an association test. This test identified significant enrichment of supporting DNA–DNA contacts from the same cell type as the eQTL–target pair ( < 2.2 × 10 , chi-square test, degrees of freedom = 25; Supplementary Fig. 3b [this file] ). 
Recognizing the potential false negatives, we exercised caution in data analysis and interpretation (Supplementary Note 11 [this file] and Extended Data Fig. 9a [rid=Fig13] ). Furthermore, the loss of XIST–chromosome X association in single female cells correlates with greater sex difference in gene expression in the human frontal cortex (Supplementary Note 12 [this file] ). 
Consistently, sequential fluorescence in situ hybridization analysis showed a larger conformational difference between Xa and Xi in excitatory neurons compared with inhibitory neurons or astrocytes in female mice (Supplementary Note 13 [this file] ). 
Every set of cell barcodes contains 96 unique barcodes, each being unique in this 14 bp dsDNA (Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). 
The index adaptors contain three segments, namely the 24 nt Illumina P7 sequence, an 8 nt unique identifier sequence called I7 and the 34 nt Illumina Read2 sequence (Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). 
We designed a total of three sets of index adaptors to allow for the construction of three libraries from three input samples and sequencing them together (Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). 
The universal adaptor contains an Illumina P5 sequence and an Illumina read1 sequence (Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). 
The supernatant was removed following centrifugation at 500 for 5 min at 4 °C, which left a purified pellet of isolated nuclei (Supplementary Fig. 1a,b [this file] ). 
Each barcode takes the form of 7 nt_overhang-dsDNA-7 nt_overhang (Extended Data Fig. 2d,i [rid=Fig6] and Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). 
The second set of barcodes is composed of eight barcodes (index barcodes), each being 8 nt (I7 in Extended Data Fig. 1h [rid=Fig5] and Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ).

Additionally, we confirmed these findings using tau protein fragments and mutants in an ELISA assay, which localized the epitope to tau residues 13-HAGTYGLGD-21 ( Supplementary Fig. 5 [this file] ), consistent with the minimal epitope of residues 16-TYGL-20.

Across the five regions, we identified 203,714 putative myeloid cells, which were filtered down to 93,679 bona fide microglia by excluding vessel-associated macrophages and monocytes ( Figure 2C [rid=F2] , S2A [this file] , B [this file] ). Within the HIP, microglia were enriched in CA2 and CA4, while in the cerebellum they were more abundant in white matter ( Figure S2B [this file] ). 
FlowSOM clustering of morphology alone yielded four meta-clusters: (1) small, rounded cells lacking nuclei (likely fragments), (2) branched cells with some concavity, (3) rounded cells with nuclei, and (4) large, branched cells ( Figure 2I [rid=F2] , S2D [this file] , E [this file] ). 
When we clustered microglia based on protein expression (FlowSOM), the clusters formed a near-continuous gradient rather than discrete populations ( Figure S3A [this file] – E [this file] ). The MSC reflected the observed cluster gradient, with one extreme having overall low expression of immune proteins and the other high ( Figure 3B [rid=F3] , C [rid=F3] , S3J [this file] ). 
Calculating region-specific spectrums and comparing them to the combined dataset showed robust consistency ( Figure S3F [this file] – H [this file] ). We also attempted a morphology-based continuum (MSC-morph), which did not correlate well with proteomic changes ( Figure 3D [rid=F3] , S3I [this file] – K [this file] ), reinforcing that morphology alone is insufficient to define microglial states. 
To quantify protein differences among regions at different continuum intervals (low, mid, high), we developed a binned permutation test (PCTBP) ( Figure S3L [this file] – M [this file] ). This analysis revealed that VDAC1, ApoE, CD44, Iba1, and P2RY12 contributed most to regional variation ( Figure 3F [rid=F3] , S3N [this file] ). 
We assigned each microglial cell a local environment by tallying the nearest pixel clusters within a 20 μm radius ( Figure 4F [rid=F4] , S4A [this file] – C [this file] ). 
We recalculated an MSC using overlapping microglial markers (Iba1, CD45, P2RY12, Tmem119, HLA-DR, TREM2, ApoE, CD68, C1q, CD44, K48-linked polyubiquitin), obtaining similar low-to-high immune gradients ( Figure S5A [this file] – C [this file] ). 
Despite this shared continuum, inter-individual variation was high ( Figure S5D [this file] ). For example, CA1 microglia showed significantly higher P2RY12, HLA-DR, and CD44 across all continuum bins, while caudate microglia consistently expressed more ApoE ( Figure 5B [rid=F5] , 5C [rid=F5] , Figure S5C [this file] ). 
Genes in the high cluster were linked to proteins involved in antigen presentation and immune regulation ( Figure 5E [rid=F5] , F [rid=F5] , S5E [this file] ). 
We segmented plaques (Aβ) and tangles (PHF-tau) ( Figure S6A [this file] – C [this file] ). Although microglia around plaques or tangles expressed elevated HLA-DR, ApoE, CD68, and CD74 ( Figure S6D [this file] - G [this file] )—consistent with “disease-associated microglia” (DAM) —these cells were relatively rare (<1% of the total microglial population). 
Collectively, the proteomic spectrum of AD microglia displayed a distinctive shift at the high-activation end ( Figure S7A [this file] ). Compared to cognitively normal brain aging, AD high MSC microglia showed significantly higher CD44 and CD33 and significantly lower immune engulfment and presentations proteins HLA-DR, P2RY12, ApoE, and engulfed post-synaptic protein PSD95 ( Figure 7B [rid=F7] , C [rid=F7] , S7A [this file] ). This effect was restricted to CA1 relative to Caudate tissue except for ApoE ( Figure S7B [this file] ). Like the heterogeneity seen between cognitively normal patients, AD microglia density distributions varied among patients and brain region ( Figure S7C [this file] ). 
Subsequent immunohistochemical staining for Iba1 and HLA-DR in the SN, MFG, HIP, and caudate of the same cohort confirmed that the CA1 region alone showed a significant decrease in HLA-DR–expressing microglia in AD relative to cognitively normal aging ( Figure S7D [this file] ), consistent with its known susceptibility in AD. 
High continuum, CA1 AD microglia had significantly more Aβ40 and PHF-tau ( Figure 7E [rid=F7] , S7A [this file] ). Spatially, these cells were also significantly enriched near parvalbumin (inhibitory synapses) rather than PSD95 (excitatory synapses) ( Figure 7D [rid=F7] , S7E [this file] , F [this file] ), suggesting a possible link to hippocampal hyperexcitability in AD due to a potential microglial-mediated loss of inhibitory synaptic connections. Neighborhood analyses further showed glutamine synthetase (a sign of healthier astrocytic metabolism) was significantly higher near cognitively normal high continuum microglia, whereas GFAP (reactive astrogliosis) was significantly higher near AD high continuum microglia ( Figure 7E [rid=F7] , F [rid=F7] , S7F [this file] , G [this file] ). 
The parabolic expression of P2RY12 ( Figures 3B [rid=F3] , S3J [this file] ) underscores that certain markers do not simply rise or fall monotonically but may peak at intermediate activation levels. 
Notably, CA1 vs. caudate differences in microglial proteins persisted across low, mid, and high continuum bins ( Figures 5B [rid=F5] – C [rid=F5] , S5C [this file] ). Furthermore, integrating single-cell ATAC-seq data ( Figure 5D [rid=F5] – F [rid=F5] , S5E [this file] ) demonstrated that a wide spectrum (epi-MSC) of microglial signatures from synaptic maintenance to antigen presentation and immune regulation exists in cognitively normal human brains. 
We imaged a large collection of AD CA1 and Caudate brain area, identifying some microglia associated with typical proteopathy (i.e., DAMs), and many that were not ( Figures 6 [rid=F6] , S6 [this file] ). Conventional, two-color immunohistochemistry across multiple regions confirms a selective decrease in HLA-DR–expressing microglia in AD hippocampus ( Figure S7D [this file] ). While a small fraction of MSC very high microglia near plaques or tangles (i.e., DAMs) do upregulate antigen presentation and broad reactivity ( Figure S6 [this file] ) the majority of microglia at the higher end of our continuum ( Figure 7D [rid=F7] , E [rid=F7] ), display a more diffuse, possibly “exhausted” or “dysfunctional” immune proteomic phenotype, with significantly lower immune regulatory proteomic features . 
Our neighborhood analyses ( Figure 7E [rid=F7] - G [rid=F7] , S7F [this file] ) reveal that AD high continuum microglia are associated with parvalbumin-rich inhibitory interneurons and reactive astrocytes (GFAP-high, glutamine synthetase–low). 
Our approach also emphasizes the importance of retaining spatial context, as local tissue architecture ( Figures 4 [rid=F4] , S4 [this file] ) and disease hallmarks ( Figures 6 [rid=F6] – 7 [rid=F7] ) shape microglial states in ways that dissociated single-cell data alone cannot fully capture .

Among the significant genes ( < 0.01) (Supplementary Table S10 [this file] ), verification was achieved for ( -TSMR = 7.30E - 05, OR: 3.45, 95% CI: 1.87 – 6.36) (Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] ), underscoring its essential contributions to the development of PPD. 
Based on Bonferroni-corrected -values ( = 0.05/783 = 6.39 × 10 ), we detected that upregulation was a significant risk factor for depression ( = 1.10 × 10 ; OR: 3.98, 95% CI: 2.15–7.37) and mood disorders ( = 1.98 × 10 ; OR: 3.72, 95% CI: 2.03–6.80) but not significantly associated with other diseases (Fig. 4b [rid=Fig4] and Supplementary Table S11 [this file] ). 
To further investigate the role of in PPD, we conducted an integrative analysis combining gene methylation and expression data across specific tissue types, including key brain regions and peripheral blood samples (Supplementary Table S12 [this file] and S13 [this file] ).

Using mass spectrometry, we profiled brain proteomes from the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex of 1,362 multiancestry donors that included AA, Hispanic and NHW (Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). After clumping (at LD < 0.1), we identified 7,852 independent candidate pQTLs in the AA population, 7,499 in the Hispanic population and 40,087 in the NHW population (Supplementary Table 2a [this file] ), consistent with the corresponding sample size and statistical power. The genomic inflation factors for these pQTL mappings were similar to those of published plasma pQTL mapping studies (Supplementary Table 2b [this file] ). 
MESuSiE identified 5,133 95% credible sets that likely contained causal pQTLs in at least one population for 3,336 unique genes (Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). 
To examine putative causal pQTLs that were shared or specific to a population, we used a threshold of category.PIP > 50% and found 1,367 putative causal pQTLs assigned to one of these categories (Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ). Specifically, at category.PIP > 50%, 75.9% of the causal pQTLs were shared across all three populations (Table 1 [rid=Tab1] and Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ). The 858 putative multiancestry causal pQTLs corresponded to 797 unique genes (pGenes; Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ). 
Full results are provided in Supplementary Table 4 [this file] . 
Full lists of these causal pQTLs are provided in Supplementary Tables 3 [this file] and 4 [this file] . 
Consistently, we found that most of the causal pQTLs were shared across all three populations with the smaller NHW proteomic dataset (82.8% and 98.9% were multiancestry causal pQTLs at category.PIP > 0.5 and category.PIP > 0.9, respectively; Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). 
We found that these multiancestry causal pQTLs were significantly more enriched than the candidate pQTLs for promoter regions (8% versus 5%), untranslated regions (UTRs; 13% versus 8%), synonymous sites (2% versus 1%) and nonsynonymous sites (13% versus 5%) (Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ). 
To evaluate the accuracy of cross-ancestry prediction of genetically regulated protein abundance for the pGenes corresponding to the 858 multiancestry causal pQTLs, we performed cross-ancestry prediction for these pGenes in the AA population using NHW data ( Methods [rid=Sec10] and Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ). The single-ancestry prediction (using AA proteomic and genetic data to predict genetically regulated protein levels in the AA population) had a median cross-validation of 0.19 (s.d.: 0.14; maximum: 0.69) for these pGenes (Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ). 
To understand how genetic variation contributes to neurologic and psychiatric disorders through brain protein expression, we integrated population-matched pQTLs with GWAS results for 21 neurologic and psychiatric disorders (21 GWASs in participants of European ancestry, 10 in those of African ancestry and 4 in Hispanic participants; Supplementary Table 9 [this file] ). 
We identified one candidate causal protein for Parkinson’s disease (GBA1) and two for alcohol use disorder (METAP1 and ADH5) in participants of African ancestry (Table 2 [rid=Tab2] and Supplementary Table 10 [this file] ). In the NHW population, for psychiatric conditions, we identified 216 candidate causal proteins for major depression, 170 for bipolar disorder, 257 for schizophrenia, 31 for post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), 10 for anxiety, 44 for attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), 2 for opioid addiction, 30 for insomnia, 2 for cannabis use disorder, 125 for neuroticism, 76 for tobacco use, 10 for anorexia and 55 for alcohol use disorder (Table 2 [rid=Tab2] and Supplementary Table 11 [this file] ). For neurologic conditions, among NHW participants, we found 64 candidate causal proteins for Alzheimer’s disease, 1 for Lewy body dementia, 10 for stroke, 18 for Parkinson’s disease and 16 for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (Table 2 [rid=Tab2] and Supplementary Table 11 [this file] ). 
Full results are provided in Supplementary Tables 10 [this file] and 11 [this file] . 
We found that although the PWAS/SMR approach was more conservative, it was less prone to false positive findings (Supplementary Note B [rid=MOESM1] and Supplementary Tables 12 [this file] – 16 [this file] ). 
Through SMR , we identified 119 multiancestry causal pQTL–protein–trait triads in the NHW population (Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Table 17 [this file] ) but none in either African or Hispanic participants, likely owing to the lower GWAS sample sizes for these ancestries. For neurologic disorders, we found eight multiancestry causal pQTL–protein pairs for Alzheimer’s disease, five for Parkinson’s disease and two for stroke (Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Table 17 [this file] ). For psychiatric disorders, we found 2 multiancestry causal pQTL–protein pairs for alcohol use disorder, 2 for anxiety, 4 for ADHD, 14 for bipolar disorder, 3 for cannabis use disorder, 2 for insomnia, 21 for major depressive disorder, 16 for neuroticism, 1 for PTSD, 32 for schizophrenia and 14 for tobacco use (Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Table 17 [this file] ). 
Detailed results are provided in Supplementary Table 17 [this file] . 
Notably, approximately one-third (40 of 119) of the multiancestry causal pQTL in these triads were in coding regions (24% nonsynonymous and 7.6% in the 3′ UTR or 5′ UTR; Table 3 [rid=Tab3] and Supplementary Table 17 [this file] ). 
Full results are provided in Supplementary Table 17 [this file] . 
We examined physical protein–protein interactions (PPIs) among the candidate causal proteins for each condition and found that many interacted with each other (Supplementary Table 18 [this file] ). As another example, 7 of 10 anxiety candidate causal proteins interacted with each other, with a range of 1–3 PPIs per protein (Fig. 4b [rid=Fig4] and Supplementary Table 18 [this file] ). Through gene set enrichment analysis, we found that candidate causal proteins in Alzheimer’s disease were enriched for genes involved in endosomal processes (Fig. 4a [rid=Fig4] and Supplementary Table 19 [this file] ), those in schizophrenia for cellular components of the glutamatergic synapse, and those in anxiety for cellular components of the dendritic tree, somatodendritic compartment and the synapse, and for neuron projection and glutamatergic neurotransmission (Fig. 4b [rid=Fig4] and Supplementary Table 19 [this file] ). 
Full results are provided in Supplementary Tables 18 [this file] and 19 [this file] . 
Of the 1,140 protein–trait pairs identified in the NHW population (Table 2 [rid=Tab2] ), approximately 25% were targeted by drug compounds that had been tested in clinical trials, and many of these drug compounds had been approved for treatment of a medical condition (Supplementary Tables 20 [this file] and 21 [this file] ). In addition, approximately one-third of the 119 multiancestry causal pQTL–protein–trait triads were targeted by at least a drug compound that had been tested in clinical trials (Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Tables 20 [this file] and 22 [this file] ). 
Moreover, only 471 of the 858 pQTLs were identified as causal pQTLs in SuSiE (Supplementary Table 23 [this file] ). 
We performed quality control of proteomic data in the AMP-AD-Rush ( = 619), AMP-AD-Banner ( = 198) and AMP-AD-Diversity ( = 1,105; Rush, Mayo, Mount Sinai, Emory; Supplementary Table 25 [this file] ) datasets separately following our prior approach . 
They comprised 181 AA (9,304 proteins), 168 Hispanic (9,036 proteins) and 1,013 NHW (9,725 proteins) individuals (Supplementary Table 24 [this file] ). 
We examined the overlap between brain and plasma pGenes (‘shared’ pGenes) and the pGenes found only in brain analysis or plasma analysis (‘unique’ pGenes) for each plasma pQTL dataset (Supplementary Tables 25 [this file] – 27 [this file] ). Of our brain pGenes, we found that 91% shared pGenes with plasma pGenes from the Icelanders dataset, 84% shared pGenes with ARIC plasma pGenes and 98% shared pGenes with UKB plasma pGenes (Supplementary Table 28 [this file] ).

Data from 11 cohorts of older adults that collected structural brain MRI (T1w) were used together with clinical information or neuropsychological scores of interests (Table 1 [rid=hbm70089-tbl-0001] , see Appendix A [this file] and Table S1 [this file] , for details). 
See Appendix A [this file] for more details. 
Thus, we only used the UKB in our analyses of parental history (Appendix A [this file] , Table 1 [rid=hbm70089-tbl-0001] , Table S1 [this file] ). 
We have summarised the MRI acquisition parameters used in the different studies in Appendix A [this file] . 
Mean and variances of the ROI based measurements were comparable between samples, that were acquired on different machines (Figure S1 [this file] ). 
As a check of compatibility of the different datasets, we contrasted the mean and variance of the vertex‐wise measurements calculated on the healthy individuals from the different samples (Figures S2–S5 [this file] ). Of note, average cortical thickness was larger in the UKB (Figure S3 [this file] ) than in the other samples, which is a known consequence of the combined use of the T1w and T2‐FLAIR images in the FreeSurfer processing (Lindroth et al. 2019 [rid=hbm70089-bib-0110] ). We observed some variability of the vertices' variance between samples, although concordance remained high (Figures S2–S5 [this file] ). This led us to flag ‘noisy’ vertices that exhibited outlying variance in at least one sample (> 6SD from the regression lines shown in Figures S2–S5 [this file] ), which could suggest they are prone to measurement error in some of the samples. About 1% of the vertices were flagged, equally distributed across each type of measurement (Figures S6 [this file] and S7 [this file] , Table S2 [rid=hbm70089-supitem-0002] ), although some brain regions contained a large proportion of flagged vertices (37% of anterior cingulate [thickness] consisted in flagged vertices, 35% of entorhinal gyrus [thickness], 18% of temporal pole [thickness], and 35% of the accumbens [surface area], Table S2 [rid=hbm70089-supitem-0002] ). 
The two vertex‐wise models (i.e., fitting all measurements as a single random effect, or fitting them as 4 modality‐specific random effects) yielded comparable morphometricity estimates (Figure S8 [this file] ). 
The vertex‐wise morphometricity we presented in Figure 1 [rid=hbm70089-fig-0001] was meta‐analysed across all the discovery samples, and we note that the estimates appeared consistent across the different cohorts, as shown in the forest plots, and estimates of between‐sample heterogeneity (Figures S9 [this file] and S10 [this file] ). The exception was for the MMSE and CDR scores, that showed a heterogeneous morphometricity across samples, even when controlling for disease and MCI status (Figure S10 [this file] ,= 74%, ‐test, ‐value < 0.05/24). However, the heterogeneity was greatly reduced (= 51% and= 23%, ‐value > 0.05) when estimating the morphometricity with modality‐specific random effects (Figure S11 [this file] ), even if the meta‐analysed result remained the same. Finally, we observed that controlling for disease status, when studying neuropsychological scores reduced the between‐cohort heterogeneity of results, as the morphometricity was inflated in the cohorts that contained Alzheimer's cases (Figure S12 [this file] ). 
An increase of one SD in hippocampal volume was associated with a 0.79‐point score increase (SE = 0.17, ‐value = 3.3e‐6, see Figure S13 [this file] for forest plot). 
Left hippocampus volume was still associated with RAVL delayed recall score ( = 0.79‐point increase per volume SD, SE = 0.11, ‐value = 9.6e‐14, Figure S13 [this file] ), but so were right hippocampus ( = 0.62) and right or left amygdala volumes ( = 0.49 and = 0.52). 
Alzheimer's disease conversion was associated with thicker lateral occipital gyrus, as well as thinner hippocampus, middle temporal, and fusiform gyri (Figure S14 [this file] , Table S6 [rid=hbm70089-supitem-0002] ). However, immediate recall was further associated with pars triangularis, while delayed recall was associated with the amygdala and the parahippocampal gyrus (Figure S15 [this file] ). The RAVLT memory scores, that evaluate how many words of a list can be remembered, only implicated the hippocampus, amygdala, and the entorhinal cortex (for immediate recall) (Figure S15 [this file] ). 
Lastly, the CDR, FAQ and MMSE were significantly associated with ROIs, mostly found to be associated with Alzheimer's disease, even if we controlled for disease status in the analyses (Figure S16 [this file] ). 
In comparison, the LMM with a single random effect, identified significant vertices for only 3 traits (AD versus HC, conversion at 2 and 3 years; 34 significant clusters in total) while the LMM with four random effects only found associations with AD versus HC (1 cluster; Figure S17 [this file] , Table S8 [rid=hbm70089-supitem-0002] ). In addition, we observed thinner cortex in the temporal lobe (entorhinal, fusiform, parahippocampal, superior and middle temporal gyri, temporal pole) as well as associations in the insula, posterior cingulate, paracentral and precuneus (Table S9 [rid=hbm70089-supitem-0002] , Figure 4a [rid=hbm70089-fig-0004] , also see Figure S18 [this file] for unthresholded map). 
The concordance presented in Figure 5 [rid=hbm70089-fig-0005] does not take show whether the association was found with volume, thickness, or surface area, see detailed Sankey plots for all details (Figure S 19 [this file] ). Furthermore, several clusters identified using GLM and LMM did not overlap, despite being located in the same grey‐matter regions (e.g., hippocampus, Figure S19 [this file] ). 
The analyses of Alzheimer's conversion consistently implicated the hippocampus (Figure S20 [this file] ), and the GLM and LMM identified clusters in the amygdala that were not detected in the ROI based analysis. Only one of the three LMM‐identified cluster (in right amygdala thickness) partially overlapped with a GLM cluster (Figure S20 [this file] ). 
Similarly, we observed mixed concordance for the ROI and GLM findings for the neuropsychological scales (Figures 21–25 [this file] ). 
Some brain regions in the hippocampus and amygdala, were significantly associated with up to 6 distinct traits (Figure S26 [this file] , Table S11 [rid=hbm70089-supitem-0002] ), and may be of particular interest as they could point out to key brain regions associated with Alzheimer's, functioning and cognition. 
We found consistent vertex‐based morphometricity estimates in the PISA and MEMENTO replication samples, compared to those from the meta‐analysis (correlation between discovery and replication estimates 0.76 in PISA, 0.74 in MEMENTO, Figure S27 [this file] ). Concordance was also observed for ROI based morphometricity (correlation between discovery and estimates: 0.80 in PISA, 0.84 in MEMENTO, Figure S28 [this file] ). 
Previous publications (Frisoni et al. 2008 [rid=hbm70089-bib-0020] ; Schuff et al. 2009 [rid=hbm70089-bib-0053] ; Vijayakumar and Vijayakumar 2012 [rid=hbm70089-bib-0063] ) have reported somewhat larger hippocampal reductions in AD (equivalent to cohen's in −0.26 −0.36, Appendix B [this file] ), although we can expect their results to be inflated by winner's curse due to small sample sizes (Marek et al. 2022 [rid=hbm70089-bib-0041] ), the inclusions of more severe cases, or unaccounted sex and age differences between cases and controls (Appendix B [this file] ). Importantly, the entorhinal cortex, often reported to be an early site of atrophy (Johnson et al. 2012 [rid=hbm70089-bib-0029] ), was not significant in the ROI analysis, but several atrophied clusters were found at the vertex‐wise level (Figures 5 [rid=hbm70089-fig-0005] and S19 [this file] , Tables S9 [rid=hbm70089-supitem-0002] and S10 [rid=hbm70089-supitem-0002] ), which highlights the added value of high‐resolution analyses. Furthermore, reduced thickness and surface area in parts of the hippocampus and amygdala was observed several years prior to the diagnosis (see Table S11 [rid=hbm70089-supitem-0002] for the list of vertex‐wise markers of AD versus HC also associated with AD conversion, Figures S14 [this file] and S20 [this file] ), which confirms that the atrophy appears in early stages of the disease process (Johnson et al. 2012 [rid=hbm70089-bib-0029] ). 
While AD status was always based on a clinical assessment (NINCDS/ADRDA, DSM‐IV or ICD10 criteria, Appendix A [this file] ), some cohorts used additional inclusion criteria (e.g., MMSE score threshold for dementia severity). Of note, the modalities of recruitment and the screening of the healthy controls also varied depending on the cohort (Appendix A [this file] ), which can further induce variability in the results. Lastly, MCI were typically defined using the Petersen/Winblad criteria, but the definition of impairments varied across the samples (Appendix A [this file] ).

We also found that RFT to be more conservative that Bonferroni's correction for multiple testing (Table S8 [this file] ). Overall, RFT halved the number of significant clusters (120 versus 307 using GLM, 12 versus 34 using LMM, Table S8 [this file] ).

We sought to replicate the 94 ROI associations that were significant in the meta‐analysis of clinical cohorts (Table S7 [this file] ). In addition, we also replicated the positive associations between bilateral hippocampal volume and RAVLT delayed memory score (Table S7 [this file] ). In addition, logical memory scores (immediate and delayed) were associated with hippocampal, and amygdala volumes, as well as with entorhinal thickness (Table S7 [this file] ). 
The replicated associations were with logical memory delayed recall score (entorhinal, hippocampus and amygdala) as well as with Alzheimer's conversion (bilateral hippocampus, amygdala, and right entorhinal gyrus) (Table S9 [this file] ). 
Prediction accuracy was comparable across the three predictors as indicated by overlapping confidence intervals: = 0.12 (95% CI 0.05–0.19, ‐value = 3.5e‐12), = 0.07, (95% CI 0.01–0.15, ‐value = 4.6e‐7) and = 0.13, (95% CI 0.05–0.22, ‐value = 6.2e‐13, which corresponds to OR = 4.1 or AUC = 0.71) (Table S12 [this file] ). We also found that the ROI or vertices associated (via GLM) with RAVLT scores had significant predictive power in PISA, although prediction accuracy was limited (< 0.035, Table S12 [this file] ). 
Overall, the ROI and vertex‐wise approaches led to comparable prediction (Table S12 [this file] ). 
Furthermore, the brain risk scores could predict some of the cognition scores (Graded Naming Test, and RAVLT scores), as well as the individuals' genetic risk (Figure 7 [rid=hbm70089-fig-0007] , Table S13 [this file] ). In MEMENTO, the AD versus HC predictors could significantly predict multi‐domain amnestic MCI status, AD conversion (at all time frames), a series of neuropsychological scores (MMSE, CDR, naming test, visual memory), as well as status and total Tau protein level, measured from lumbar punction (Figure 7 [rid=hbm70089-fig-0007] , Table S13 [this file] ). The AD brain scores achieved comparable prediction accuracy (< 0.06) as the specific predictors of AD conversion or neuropsychological scores (MMSE, CDR) (Table S12 [this file] ). 
Our results suggest some overlap between the grey‐matter regions associated with early (pre‐diagnostic) AD risk, disease progression and memory domains (Figure 6 [rid=hbm70089-fig-0006] , Table S11 [this file] ), which progresses our understanding of the clinical correlates of grey‐matter atrophy and allows cross‐trait prediction. Our results are robust and generalisable to other cohorts or studies, as shown by the high replication rate (Tables S7 [this file] and S9 [this file] ) and out‐of‐sample prediction accuracy (Table S12 [this file] ). 
Our ROI‐level results confirmed the known atrophy of hippocampus volume (cohen's = −0.17), amygdala volume ( = −0.15) and of the medial temporal lobe (e.g., reduced thickness in fusiform [ = −0.08] and parahippocampal gyrus [ = −0.05]) (Table S7 [this file] ), which are known to play an important role in memory processing (Raslau et al. 2015 [rid=hbm70089-bib-0047] ). All the ROI level associations (in subcortical and medial temporal cortex) were matched by one or several significant clusters in the vertex‐wise analysis (Tables S9 [this file] and S10 [this file] , Figures 5 [rid=hbm70089-fig-0005] and S19 [this file] ) which offers a more fined grained localisation of the grey‐matter associations. We confirmed these brain regions (ROIs) to be implicated in memory processes, as indicated by their association with episodic memory (RAVLT and logical memory scores, Table S7 [this file] , even after controlling for disease status). Importantly, the entorhinal cortex, often reported to be an early site of atrophy (Johnson et al. 2012 [rid=hbm70089-bib-0029] ), was not significant in the ROI analysis, but several atrophied clusters were found at the vertex‐wise level (Figures 5 [rid=hbm70089-fig-0005] and S19 [rid=hbm70089-supitem-0001] , Tables S9 [this file] and S10 [this file] ), which highlights the added value of high‐resolution analyses. The vertex‐wise analysis further pinpointed localised regions in the amygdala and hippocampus that were simultaneously associated with AD status and episodic memory scores (Table S11 [this file] ). Furthermore, reduced thickness and surface area in parts of the hippocampus and amygdala was observed several years prior to the diagnosis (see Table S11 [this file] for the list of vertex‐wise markers of AD versus HC also associated with AD conversion, Figures S14 [rid=hbm70089-supitem-0001] and S20 [rid=hbm70089-supitem-0001] ), which confirms that the atrophy appears in early stages of the disease process (Johnson et al. 2012 [rid=hbm70089-bib-0029] ). 
Coherent with this hypothesis, we found locally reduced right and left putamen thickness, associated with AD status as well as with impaired functioning (Functional Assessment Questionnaire, Table S11 [this file] ). 
In the cortex, we identified additional regions (ROIs only) associated with Alzheimer's disease (Figure 3 [rid=hbm70089-fig-0003] , Table S7 [this file] ), including several (with inferior parietal, postcentral [parietal], middle temporal, transverse temporal, inferior temporal [temporal], paracentral, superior frontal [frontal]) that replicated in an independent cohort (PISA), which gives confidence in the findings. Our findings in the frontal and temporal lobes might reflect disease progression and general decay in cognition and functioning, that these regions encode (Johnson et al. 2012 [rid=hbm70089-bib-0029] ), which was corroborated by associations of the same ROI with MMSE and CDR scores (Table S7 [this file] ). 
They included thicker lateral occipital cortex and larger cortical area of the middle temporal gyrus (Table S7 [this file] ), which replicated in the MEMENTO cohort. Together, the identified markers of AD conversion, could significantly predict an individuals' risk of receiving a diagnosis within 5 years of the brain MRI, in an independent sample (MEMENTO, Table S12 [this file] ). 
Currently, the identified brain regions largely overlapped with those found to be associated with AD (Figure 6 [rid=hbm70089-fig-0006] ), although larger imaging samples should reveal many more relevant (and specific) grey‐matter regions, as indicated by the gap between morphometricity (Figure 1 [rid=hbm70089-fig-0001] ) and the variance currently explained by the identified regions (see prediction, Table S12 [this file] ). 
The overlapping patterns of association we observed between AD and neuropsychological scores (Figure 5 [rid=hbm70089-fig-0005] ) led to performant cross‐trait prediction, in non‐diseased individuals (Figure 7 [rid=hbm70089-fig-0007] , Table S13 [this file] ). Thus, we found that AD brain scores were associated with MCI status (memory and language impairments), AD conversion, AD genetic risk (incl., APOE e4), total Tau level from cerebral spinal fluid (associations with phosphorylated Tau or Amyloid‐beta did not reach significance), and a wide range of cognitive scores (Figure 7 [rid=hbm70089-fig-0007] , Table S13 [this file] ), which can shed light on the nature of the AD‐related grey‐matter markers reported above. For example, our AD brain score could (partly) differentiate MCI from HC in PISA (Figure 7 [rid=hbm70089-fig-0007] , Table S13 [this file] ), while the direct analysis of MCI versus HC did not yield significant prediction accuracy (Table S12 [this file] ). 
For example, the significant ROI associated with AD could explain 12% (SE = 3.6%) of the variance in case control status in PISA (Table S12 [this file] ), while we estimated a ROI based morphometricity of 21% (SE = 3.6%, Figure 1 [rid=hbm70089-fig-0001] , Table S4 [this file] ) across the discovery samples (= 27%, SE = 7.7% in PISA). Even more strikingly, the significant vertex‐wise measurements accounted for 13% (SE = 4.4%, Table S12 [this file] ) of AD variance, well short of the vertex‐wise morphometricity of 100% (SE = 6.4%, Figure 1 [rid=hbm70089-fig-0001] , Table S5 [this file] ). 
However, we found 94 significant ROI associations (Table S7 [this file] ) but 307 clusters of significant vertices (Figure 4 [rid=hbm70089-fig-0004] , Table S9 [this file] ), which indicates that vertex‐wise analysis are also well powered using our current sample size. The different number of findings can be explained by the fact that vertex‐wise analyses allow the detection of several, independent clusters of significant vertices within a ROI (e.g., Figure S19 [this file] ). In addition, each atlas used to define the ROIs (here we used Desikan‐Killiany) removes signal of interest in specific part(s) of the brain (Fürtjes et al. 2023 [rid=hbm70089-bib-0022] ), which likely explains why we have detected significant vertices in ROIs that did not reach significance (Figure 5 [rid=hbm70089-fig-0005] , Figure S19 [this file] ). 
Compared the current state of the art (GLM), LMM lead to parsimonious brain maps of associations (30 clusters versus 103 for AD versus HC, Tables S9 [this file] and S10 [this file] ), as it controls for all brain measurements (fitted as a random effect) which prevents redundant associations from reaching significance (Couvy‐Duchesne et al. 2022 [rid=hbm70089-bib-0010] ). For proof, the 30 ‘LMM’ clusters account for the same amount of information as the 103 identified using GLM (Figure 7 [rid=hbm70089-fig-0007] , Tables S12 [this file] and S13 [this file] ).

In primary care (Sweden), the accuracy was 85% (95% CI = 82–88%) (Fig. 1a–c [rid=Fig1] ), which was significantly lower than in secondary care (Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). 
A numerically lower accuracy in older participants was observed across all cohorts, except for the Brescia cohort (Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). The significant effect of age on accuracy persisted even after excluding participants with CKD, which is known to be more common in older individuals (Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). 
Plasma p-tau217:Aβ42 (Lumipulse) was available for 502 primary care participants and 911 secondary care participants (Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). 
MS-based p-tau217 and %p-tau217 data were available in a subset of patients from the Malmö ( = 337), Gothenburg ( = 164) and Brescia ( = 118) secondary care cohorts, as well as the primary care cohort ( = 513) (Supplementary Table 4 [this file] and Extended Data Fig. 6 [rid=Fig11] ). 
A cost-effectiveness analysis was performed comparing the Lumipulse p-tau217 assay with CSF analysis and amyloid PET imaging (Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ) and is available at https://bbrc-lab.shinyapps.io/Cost-effectiveness_analysis_plasma_p-Tau217 (https://bbrc-lab.shinyapps.io/Cost-effectiveness_analysis_plasma_p-Tau217) . This calculation assumes that 14.7% of patients fall into the intermediate group (the total proportion in the present study) and require further testing (Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ). A screenshot of the app is shown in Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] . 
First, the CSF Aβ42:40 ratio was used as a reference standard, instead of CSF Aβ42:p-tau181, with the FDA-approved cutoff of ≤0.072 pg ml for positivity (Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] ) . Second, analyses were performed in the Swedish primary care cohort using only the CSF Aβ42:p-tau181 outcome, excluding those for whom Aβ pathology was defined by amyloid PET = 87; Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] ). Third, a single cutoff established using the highest Youden index for AD pathology was used, instead of defining it at 90% specificity (Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] ). 
This decline was not attributable to any specific cohort (Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ), including the primary care cohort (Extended Data Fig. 3 [rid=Fig8] ), which had older participants and showed lower accuracy for Lumipulse p-tau217. 
Given the considerable variation in costs for these tests across countries and centers, we created an online application to calculate the cost savings of using plasma p-tau217 (Lumipulse) compared with the local costs of CSF AD core biomarkers or amyloid PET (Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] ). For example, using the approximate costs of CSF AD core biomarkers or amyloid PET in the United States of America, we estimated savings of up to 60% compared with solely using CSF tests and up to 81% compared with amyloid PET, using a two-cutoff approach and assuming that 14.7% of patients fall into the intermediate zone, which was the pooled proportion of intermediate results in the present study (Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ).

More SVs were detected in MSBB compared to Mayo, due to ancestry differences as the Mayo data is composed of European ancestry individuals only, while MSBB has more diverse populations, including individuals of African and Admixed American ancestry ( Supplementary Figure S3 [this file] ). 
Duplications and inversions were less reproducible ( Supplementary Figure S4 [this file] ). Further, allele frequency comparisons of SVs in common with the 1000 Genomes Project and gnomAD-SV showed high overall reproducibility with R equal to 0.75 and 0.71, respectively ( Supplementary Figure S5 [this file] ). We also observed that about 75% of SVs were in Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium depending on the study ( Supplementary Figure S6 [this file] ). We performed confirmation of 3,581 SVs identified with short-reads and accessed a confirmation of 84.3% of them ( Figure 2d [rid=F2] , Supplementary Figure S7 [this file] ). 
Comparison between different brain regions showed 98% of shared SV-eQTL with the same direction of effect (β) ( Supplementary Figure S8 [this file] ). 
A total of 210 SV-eQTL could be mapped significantly associated in both datasets. ( Supplementary Figure S9 [this file] ). 
These molecular phenotypes were measured for a partially overlapping set of samples ( Supplementary Figure S10 [this file] ) and included gene expression for 15,582 genes (n=456), 110,092 splicing junctions proportions measured by “percent spliced in” values (PSI) (n=505), histone acetylation (H3K9ac) peaks (n=571), and proteomic data for 7,960 proteins (n=272). 
For instance, more than 87% of SVs associated with H3K9ac peaks (haSVs) had at least one breakpoint within 500 kb of the closest gene, while more than 93% of splicing associated SVs (sSV) were found within 50 kb of the respective gene bodies ( Supplementary Figure S11 [this file] ). 
The correlation of effect sizes between eQTLs and pQTLs was 0.71 (Pearson correlation) and between pQTLs and haQTLs 0.77, while eQTLs and haQTLs showed slightly weaker correlation (Pearson correlation = 0.59) ( Figure 4d [rid=F4] , Supplementary Figure S12 [this file] ). By contrast, 50% and 47% of splicing and histone associated SVs were also SV-eQTLs, respectively ( Supplementary Figure S13 [this file] ). 
Additionally, only 43 (5%) gene-sample pairs were replicated between both phenotypes, reflecting the modest correlation (Spearman’s ⍴ = 0.38) observed between average RNA expression and protein levels ( Supplementary Figure S14 [this file] ). 
In AD (539 cases, and 368 controls) no SVs were associated with the disease, however, some suggestive hits were observed ( Supplementary Figure S15 [this file] ). 
Additionally, effects of rare SVs seem to be attenuated at protein levels, given a lower proportion of outliers explained by nearby SVs and an even lower proportion of effects shared between RNA and proteins, reflecting low correlation observed in the expression levels ( Supplementary Figure S14 [this file] ).

All biochemical measures were transformed by either the natural log or square root to achieve an approximately normal distribution including the Aβ40/42 ratio (Fig. S 1 [this file] ). 
These assays were also used to collect genotypes from an additional 1564 Mayo Clinic Brain Bank (MCBB) samples with available DNA to enable assessment with AD-related neuropathology measures of Braak stage, Thal phase, neuropathological diagnosis of AD, and age at death (combined = 2005, Table S 7 [this file] ). Taqman genotyping assays were performed using 10 ng of dried-down DNA and the QuantStudio 7 Flex system (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA) for 7 variants (Table S 14 [this file] ). 
PCA plots were generated using the ploty_ly() package in R (v3.6) (Fig. S 5 [this file] ). 
Genomic inflation values (λ) were calculated in R (v3.6.2) for each biochemical measure with and without adjustment of ε2 and -ε4 alleles (Fig. S 6 [this file] ); there was no evidence for genomic inflation (0.97 < λ < 1.02). QQ plots were generated in R (v3.6) with the ggplot package (Fig. S 6 [this file] ). 
A graphical description of the datasets integrated in each analysis is outlined in Fig. S 7 [this file] . 
Demographics including neuropathology scores are outlined in Table S 1 [this file] . Quantitative brain biochemical measures were previously collected and transformed to approximate a normal distribution (Table S 2 [this file] , Fig. S 1 [this file] ) [ 32 [rid=CR32] ]. Altogether, we identified genome-wide significant (GWS, < 2.98 × 10 ) SNP-endophenotype associations at 8 unique loci: 6 unique loci for Aβ40, 3 for APOE, and 1 for the ratio of Aβ40/Aβ42 (Table 1 [rid=Tab1] , Figs. 2 [rid=Fig2] , 3 [rid=Fig3] and 4 [rid=Fig4] , Table S 3 [this file] ). 
The estimated proportion of biochemical measure variance explained by the index SNPs based on the of linear regression models ranged from 7 to 27%, with 4 (rs429358) alone explaining between 6.6 to 14% (Table S 4 [this file] ). 
More broadly, we detected 1813 variants with a < 1 × 10 ranging from 26 variants for total tau to 341 for APOE (Table S 3 [this file] ). While not reaching GWS, the most significant SNPs for the remaining traits include, Aβ42: TBS-rs147370282, TX-rs10219590, FA-rs461939; Aβ40/42: TBS-rs9890231, TX-rs483082; total tau: TBS-rs34678552, TX-rs76878089, FA-rs1634993; and p-Tau: TBS-rs2294557, TX-rs10987782, and FA-rs11651012 (Fig. S 2 [this file] , Table S 3 [this file] ). Interestingly we found associations that approach GWS for total tau ( = 8.03E-07) and total tau ( = 9.48E-06) with rs117691004 which is located in the gene known to play a role in Parkinson’s Disease [ 77 [rid=CR77] ] (Table S 3 [this file] ). 
We found a total of 30 unique GWS variants at or proximal to the gene with at least one associated with six of the biochemical measures (Table S 3 [this file] ). These two SNPs are in linkage disequilibrium (LD) with 4 in our dataset (rs283815: = 0.73, D′ = 0.87; rs483082: = 0.92, D′ = 0.99) which is likewise associated with the same biochemical traits (Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] , Table S 3 [this file] ). We further examined the rs283815-APOE association after adjusting for ε2 and ε4 dose, for diplotypes, and in the -33 only sample subset ( = 141, β = − 3.79, 2.16E-03) finding that this association remained nominally significant (Table S 5 [this file] ). These variants at the region (rs429358, rs283815, and rs483082) represent the most significant associations across all fractions of Aβ40, Aβ40/42, and APOE, but no fractions of Aβ42, total tau, or p-Tau ( > 0.031) (Table S 6 [this file] ); indicating that they likely impact disease risk through effects on APOE and Aβ40, but not tau. 
We expanded the cohort size and validated the GWAS genotypes by genotyping these variants or their proxies in the GWAS study samples ( = 441) and additional Mayo Clinic Brain Bank (MCBB) participants ( = 1564) using TaqMan assays or Sanger sequencing (Table S 7 [this file] ). A high level of concordance, > 98%, was observed between the array-based genotyped or imputed alleles and those collected by TaqMan and sequencing (Table S 8 [this file] ). Association results using the TaqMan genotypes in place of the array-based genotypes showed only minor variations in effect size and significance, demonstrating consistency of the results (Table S 5 [this file] ). Genotypes for the index GWS variants were also extracted from three independent whole genome sequence (WGS) datasets available from the Accelerating Medicines Partnership AD (AMP-AD) study through the AD knowledge portal ( www.synapse.org (http://www.synapse.org) ) which includes the Mayo Clinic RNAseq (Mayo, = 344) [ 42 [rid=CR42] ], Mount Sinai Brain Bank (MSBB, = 267) [ 43 [rid=CR43] ], and Rush Religious Orders Study and Memory and Aging Project (ROS-MAP, = 1091) [ 44 [rid=CR44] ] studies (Table S 7 [this file] ). Meta-analyses for available genotypes and common AD-related phenotypes were conducted across these 4 independent datasets for each SNP using fixed and random effects models (Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] , Fig. S 3 [this file] , Table S 9 [this file] ). 
Rs283815 was also associated with age at death and plasma amyloid, although the rs283815 associations were no longer significant after adjustment for ε2 or ε4 (Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] , Tables S 9 [this file] and S 10 [this file] ). The intronic variant rs34805055 (increased Aβ40 ) associated with increased CSF p-Tau ( = 0.03) and plasma tau levels ( = 0.04) (Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] , Tables S 9 [this file] and S 10 [this file] ). 
We found that while all loci harbored DE genes in at least 1 brain region, 3 index genes and 1 gene implicated through the above QTL analysis were consistently DE in 2 or more brain regions. was downregulated in AD for 3 datasets while and were upregulated in AD for 2 (Table S 11 [this file] ). We found 67 genes at the implicated loci that were DE in at least one cell type between samples with AD pathology and those with no AD pathology, 90% of which were dysregulated in neurons (Table S 12 [this file] ). Collectively these results implicate dysregulation of and at the novel loci identified by this study and , and at the established Chr19q13 AD locus (Fig. S 4 [this file] ). 
All but one of these were in noncoding regions, the exception being rs157581 in LD with rs283815, a synonymous missense variant in (Table S 9 [this file] ). 
Five of the seven novel index genes have variants that associate ( < 1E-05) with AD-related phenotypes (Table S 9 [this file] ). 
Of the 26 variants present in our dataset, only associations with the ε4 tagging variant survived Bonferroni correction for 26 tests ( < 1.93E-03), however; 9 others were nominally significant ( < 0.05) for at least one biochemical fraction with six having directions of effect consistent with AD risk, based on prior knowledge, and the direction of effect for the ε4 tagging variant (Table S 13 [this file] ). The protective allele of rs1080826 (A) at the locus associated with lower levels of Aβ42 , Aβ42 and total tau (Table S 13 [this file] ). 
In our current study, while we cannot rule out the possibility there may be associations at the locus that affect Aβ42 or tau brain biochemical levels, based on the 95% confidence intervals of these associations (Table S 6 [this file] ), these effects would likely be small.

We provide the list of microglial signature genes that are also expressed at high levels in bulk brain tissue data (Table S5 [this file] ), which can serve as a validated resource for microglial signature gene markers in bulk RNAseq datasets. 
Significant overlap was observed across all datasets, with 350 genes common to all datasets (Figure 1c‐d [rid=acel13606-fig-0001] , Tables S3 [this file] –S4, S8 [this file] ). 
We identified 7 modules with significant associations (Figure 2 [rid=acel13606-fig-0002] ; Figure S5 [rid=acel13606-sup-0001] ; Table S9 [this file] ). 
Our microglial signature (Tables S1–S3 [this file] ) had significant overrepresentation of the age‐associated ME14 genes (Table S9 [this file] ; OR = 1.55 [95% CI = 1.23‐INF], = 0.001), highlighting age‐related increases in microglial signature genes. 
Analysis of the scRNAseq data from these samples revealed 13 distinct cell clusters, which were annotated using established neuronal and glial marker genes from the literature (Darmanis et al., 2015 [rid=acel13606-bib-0018] ; Keren‐Shaul et al., 2017 [rid=acel13606-bib-0039] ; Masuda et al., 2019 [rid=acel13606-bib-0051] ; Mathys et al., 2019 [rid=acel13606-bib-0053] ; Olah et al., 2020 [rid=acel13606-bib-0065] ; Rangaraju et al., 2018a [rid=acel13606-bib-0069] ; Sankowski et al., 2019 [rid=acel13606-bib-0070] ; Zhou et al., 2020 [rid=acel13606-bib-0091] ; Figure 3a [rid=acel13606-fig-0003] , Tables S10 [this file] ‐S16). Each myeloid cluster had cellular contributions from all samples, albeit with some variability in their proportions, likely due to intrinsic differences between individuals (Figure 3b [rid=acel13606-fig-0003] , Table S11 [this file] ). 
Expression levels of the top marker genes per cluster are shown (Figure 3c [rid=acel13606-fig-0003] ; Figure S8 [rid=acel13606-sup-0001] ; Table S12 [this file] ). Our microglial signature was significantly enriched in more clusters expressing more activated markers (Table S13 [this file] ), implicating this as the dominant expression profile within our samples. 
To determine whether the bulk microglial co‐expression networks (Figure 2a,c [rid=acel13606-fig-0002] ‐e, Figure S5 [rid=acel13606-sup-0001] ) were representative of microglial subtypes, we performed enrichment analyses of the module genes within the myeloid clusters with sufficient cell numbers (Figure 3e [rid=acel13606-fig-0003] ; full enrichment statistics provided in Table S15 [this file] ). 
The forest plot in Figure 4a [rid=acel13606-fig-0004] highlights the individual and combined associations for networks of interest across the datasets where age, sex, or information was available (Table S17 [this file] ). 
Hypergeometric tests of enrichment showed significant overlap between several of the original and integrated clusters, showcasing the high congruence between our data and Olah et al (Tables S18–S20 [this file] ). To further identify where our individual cells clustered when combined with the Olah dataset, we overlaid the cell IDs from the original clusters to the integrated dataset and calculated the percentage overlap (Table S20 [this file] ). Additionally, enrichment of our microglial signature in the integrated single‐cell dataset was observed in several clusters, many of which highly expressed markers of activated microglia (Table S18 [this file] ). This is similar to what we observed in our single‐cell data (Table S13 [this file] ), supporting the notion that our microglial signature is enriched for activated cells. 
A small cluster highly enriched for mature oligodendrocyte and some neuronal marker genes were observed (Table S11 [this file] ). 
To check whether these correlations hold for external datasets, we downloaded raw reads in FASTQ format for three external bulk microglia datasets listed in Table S17 [this file] .

For any set of covarying transcripts, some individuals will be expected to have low values of expression for multiple transcripts in the set, and these will be enriched in the low-expression transcripts of that individual. We thus reasoned that clustering of the variance components of low-expression genes should independently identify the major axes of covariance. For each individual in the Morocco study, up to 100 transcripts that are outliers for low expression (that is, more than two standard deviations below the mean standardized expression values of all transcripts in the individual sample) were identified. PC1 was computed for these transcripts, two-way hierarchical clustering of the 189 scores (rows) across the 189 individuals (columns) is shown in the upper plot (A). Nine distinct clusters are observed, seven of which uniquely cluster with the BIT score for one of the first seven Axes (indicated by arrowheads). The rows marked Axis 2b appear to be a subset of Axis 2, and the small unmarked cluster of rows between Axes 3 and 5 may define a new Axis, but further analysis indicates that the scores are driven by very low expression in just the indicated individuals. The lower panel (B) shows the heat map generated by only including the two individuals whose low-expression PC1 most strongly correlates with the respective BIT. Only one individual is close to BIT 7 (which was not uniquely represented by one of the Chaussabel modules), and no individuals are close to BIT 8 or BIT 9. These results are consistent with the first 7 Axes being the major axes of variation, though not necessarily the only ones.
