EV morphology was characterized using transmission electron microscopy (TEM, Figure S1 [this file] ). The average size of hNSC EVs was 115.0 ± 0.4 nm in diameter with a mean stock concentration of 7.90 × 10 ± 6.58 × 10 per mL (Figure S1A,B [this file] ). iMGL‐EVs were 118.6 ± 1.1 nm in diameter at a concentration of 1.01 × 10 ± 2.67 × 10 per mL (Figure S1C,D [this file] ). 
One month after the last RO injection, all cohorts of animals were administered cognitive function tests, including Object Recognition Memory (ORM), Elevated Plus Maze (EPM), and Fear Extinction Memory Consolidation (FE) as described in the Supporting Information [this file] . 
There was no statistically significant difference in time spent in the central zone, defined as the inner 60% of the ORM arena field (Figure S2A [this file] ). Statistical analysis showed no significant difference in the percentage of exploration time spent in the open arms across any of the experimental groups (Figure S2B [this file] ). 
We also investigated the effects of EV treatment on learning and memory in the amygdala‐cortical‐hippocampal circuit via a 5‐day contextual‐based fear memory and consolidation task (Figure S2C,D [this file] ). All four experimental groups exhibited a significant and comparable increase in time spent freezing during the tone‐shock conditioning phase on Day 1 (Figure S2C [this file] ; T –T ; 45%–55% on T ), with neither vehicle‐treated nor EV‐treated AD mice affected in their acquisition of the conditioned fear response. There was no significant difference between groups in the time spent freezing during the extinction test on Day 5 (Figure S2D [this file] ). 
To assess the impact of EV treatment on post‐synaptic density, we performed PSD‐95 staining in the mPFC at 10 weeks post‐EV injection (Figure S3 [this file] ). 
We did not find any significant difference in CD9 expression levels between the three AD groups in the PRh regions at 10 weeks, nor in either brain region at 16 weeks post‐treatment (Figure S4A–C [this file] ). At 10 weeks post EV‐treatment, GFAP expression levels were significantly decreased in the mPFC region of both hNSC‐ and iMGL‐EV‐treated AD mice compared to the vehicle‐treated AD group (Figure 4B [rid=acel70341-fig-0004] ; < 0.01), but not for the PRh region (Figure S4D [this file] ). There were also no significant differences in GFAP immunoreactivity in either brain region at the later time point (Figure S4E,F [this file] ). Concurrently, dual immunofluorescence and colocalization analysis of a complement anaphylatoxin component C3d with astrocytes (GFAP , Figure S5A–C [this file] ) showed a significant reduction in C3d‐GFAP colocalization in the AD brain treated with hNSC‐ and iMGL‐EV (mPFCs) compared to the vehicle‐treated AD group at 10 weeks post‐EV injections, indicating reduced astrocytic activation. 
Box plot representation of NF‐κB, apoptosis, oligodendrocytes, and inflammatory signaling‐related genes showed downregulation of these genes in the AD brains treated with iMGL‐EVs compared to those treated with hNSC‐EVs brains (Figure S6 [this file] ). 
The analysis used both weighted and non‐weighted gene expression levels to generate Pathway Scores and Directed Global Significance Scores, respectively, both of which were normalized to vehicle‐treated AD expression (see Figure S7A,B [this file] ). 
To investigate the effects of EV treatment on inflammatory response chemokines in the Alzheimer's brain, a multiplex ELISA was performed to analyze cytokine levels in the brains of WT, AD + Vehicle, AD + hNSC‐EV, and AD + iMGL‐EV mice 10 weeks post‐EV treatment (Figure S8 [this file] ).

context_description:
Reanalysis of our previously generated scRNA-seq dataset of xMG isolated from xenotransplanted MITRG versus amyloid-accumulating 5x-MITRG mice containing 10,817 MITRG and 8,577 5x-MITRG xMG, identified a greater than 3-fold expansion of an amyloid-responsive population commonly referred to ‘disease-associated microglia (DAM)’ ( Figure 1A [rid=F1] - C [rid=F1] , Table S1 [this file] ). When compared to all other populations of microglia in the brain, these amyloid-responsive cells were significantly enriched in several genes associated with the DAM signature ( Figure 1D [rid=F1] , Table S1 [this file] ). Of these significantly altered genes, expression was highly enriched in the DAM cluster and displayed a log fold change (LFC) of 5.51 and expression in 55.4% of the DAM cluster, compared to 3.4% of all other cells ( Figure 1E [rid=F1] , Table S1 [this file] ). 
Reanalysis of single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) from xMG isolated from these BCBM mice, containing 5,883 control and 12,214 BCBM xMG, identified the expansion of a tumor-responsive population of microglia that exhibited a greater than 4-fold increase in the brains of BCBM mice ( Figure 7B [rid=F7] - C [rid=F7] , Table S1 [this file] ). When compared to all other populations of microglia in the brain, these tumor-associated microglia (TAM) expressed several significant differentially expressed genes (DEGs), with many of the most highly upregulated genes being associated with a microglial interferon response ( Figure 7D [rid=F7] , Table S1 [this file] ). Of these, expression was highly enriched in the TAM cluster and displayed an LFC of 4.86 and expression in 85% of the TAM cluster, compared to 8.5% of all other cells ( Figure 7E [rid=F7] , Table S1 [this file] ). 
At 5 months of age, mice were fed either a control or 0.2% cuprizone diet for 4 weeks ( Figure 7G [rid=F7] ). xMG were isolated, and scRNA-seq analysis resulted in 6,647 control and 5,946 cuprizone-treated xMG identifying a 9-fold increase in the proportion of cells within the interferon (IFN) responsive microglial cluster of cuprizone-treated mice ( Figure 7H [rid=F7] - I [rid=F7] , Table S1 [this file] ). As with the TAM, this population of demyelination-responsive microglia was significantly enriched in DEGs associated with the microglia interferon response ( Figure 7J [rid=F7] , Table S1 [this file] ) with the gene exhibiting a LFC of 2.99 and expression in 90.2% of the IFN cluster and 32.8% of all other cells ( Figure 7K [rid=F7] , Table S1 [this file] ).

In 7-month-old App mice miR-223 levels were markedly decreased by 44% in the cortex and 24% in the hippocampus relative to WT controls at 7 months ( Figure 1B [rid=F1] ), with a 63% decrease in the cortex and 51% decrease in the hippocampus at 12 months of age ( Figure S1A [this file] – B [this file] ). 
At 5 days post injection, miR-223 levels were increased by 3-fold in the cortex, demonstrating its successful overexpression ( Figure S1C [this file] ). Additionally, we found a trend towards increased miR-223 levels at the end of behavioral testing at post-injection day 17, demonstrating a relatively long half-life of the injected oligonucleotide ( Figure S1C [this file] ). In the open field test, we found no differences in average velocity due to oligonucleotide injection relative to a no-surgery sham control, demonstrating that mice recovered from the injection with no overt issues ( Figure S1D [this file] ). Moreover, we found that App mice treated with a miR-223 inhibitor demonstrated a trend towards less exploratory behavior compared to scrambled treated App mice, suggesting increased anxiety in the former ( Figure S1D [this file] ). All mice successfully learned the location of the escape hole, with App mice not yet showing impairment in latency to hole presumably due to the relatively early stage of hippocampal pathology at 7 months of age ( Figure 1D [rid=F1] , S1E [this file] – H [this file] ). Likewise, treatment with miR-223 inhibitor did not change the number of errors made by App mice ( Figure S1F [this file] ). Unexpectedly, we found that miR-223 inhibitor treatment also partially improved latency and time in target zone on the probe test ( Figure S1I [this file] – K [this file] ). 
All mice were able to associate the tone with the shock, with miR-223 mimic-treated App mice showing a trend towards faster learning ( Figure S1L [this file] ). Inhibitor treatment did not influence the tone response ( Figure S1M [this file] ). On the context test, miR-223 mimic or inhibitor treatment did not influence freezing response ( Figure S1N [this file] ). 
In the cortex, miR-223 reduced the number of plaques per unit area ( Figure S2A [this file] – C [this file] ). Treatment with miR-223 inhibitor did not alter amyloid pathology in either region when measured by AmyloGlo or ThioS ( Figure S2A [this file] – E [this file] ). 
In the cortex, there was a trend towards decreased expression of miR-223 targets, however this was not statistically significant ( Figure S3A [this file] ). In the hippocampus, we found a substantial downregulation of miR-223 target expression, confirming direct target engagement following mimic treatment ( Figure S3A [this file] ). At day 17, we found that miR-223 validated target genes were significantly downregulated in the cortex ( Figure S3B [this file] ). However, we found a strong induction of miR-223 targets in the hippocampus ( Figure S3B [this file] ), possibly due to rebound effects that have been reported when using RNA interference (RNAi) . 
At day 5 in the cortex, we found 143 DEGs when comparing miR-223 to scrambled control ( Figure 1K [rid=F1] , Figure S3C [this file] ). At day 17 in the cortex, there were no genes meeting our FDR cutoff (FDR < 0.1), possibly due to the overall small effect size on individual gene expression elicited by miR-223 as well as the relatively long period post-treatment ( Figure S3C [this file] , E [this file] ). However, miR-223 treatment reduced the expression of genes in pathways related to cytokine production and the adaptive immune response ( Figure S3F [this file] ). Using this method, we found that miR-223 treatment has an overall dampening effect on genotype-related DEGs (WT:Scr and App :Scr DEGs = 682, WT:Scr and App :miR223 = 125, Figure S3D [this file] ), which we annotate as “miR-223-protected DEGs”. Downregulated genes that were restored by miR-223 treatment included inhibitor of inflammatory signaling , as well as the Adiponectin receptor ( Figure S3G [this file] ). 
At day 17 in the hippocampus, we surprisingly found the largest number of DEGs with 150 genes changed between miR-223 and scrambled control App mice ( Figure S3C [this file] – D [this file] , H [this file] ). Notably, upregulated genes were strongly associated with neuron projection development, while we observed a downregulation in aerobic respiration ( Figure S3I [this file] ). As in the cortex, miR-223 had an overall dampening effect on genotype-related DEGs (WT:Scr and App :Scr DEGs = 2812, WT:Scr and App :miR223 = 1140, Figure S3C [this file] , D [this file] ). Notable genes related to neuronal function upregulated by miR-223 include encoding the APOER2 receptor for Reelin, and ( Figure S3J [this file] ). 
In both the cortex and hippocampus, we found that changes in gene expression due to miR-223 were negatively correlated with those due to genotype ( Figure S3K [this file] ), demonstrating an overall reversal of the disease-associated transcriptome by miR-223. 
As miR-223 ameliorated behavioral deficits, reduced amyloid pathology and induced the expression of multiple neuronal genes, we next assessed whether this was associated with normalized expression of synaptic marker proteins by performing 6-plex IHC with antibodies against Aβ42, dystrophic neurite marker LAMP1, pre- and postsynaptic markers SYP and SAP102, cholinergic marker ChAT, and neuronal marker MAP2 ( Figure S4A [this file] ).

Treatment with mimic repressed several targets, including , which was previously proposed as a therapeutic target for inhibition in AD ( Figure S7I [this file] ) . RNAseq gene expression profiling identified 2851 differentially expressed genes in the hippocampus of children with ASD, including genes implicated in genetic analysis studies [ 53 [rid=CR53] – 56 [rid=CR56] ] and genes involved in synaptic regulation, blood vessel and blood-brain barrier regulation, immune signaling, ECM organization, and calcium channel activity (Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] , Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] , and Supplementary Table 1 [rid=MOESM2] ). 
Pathway analysis identified upregulation of pathways involved in immune and inflammatory response (ex:R-HSA-877300; GO0006959), vasculature regulation (ex:hsa04610) and ECM organization (ex: R-HSA-1474244) (Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] , Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] , and Supplementary Table 1 [rid=MOESM2] ). We identified downregulation of several pathways involved in synaptic signaling and synaptic transmission (ex:GO0099504; R-HSA-112314) (Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] , Supplementary Figs. 1 [this file] , 2 [this file] , and Supplementary Table 1 [rid=MOESM2] ). 
Tryptase alpha/beta1 (TPSAB1) labeling was used to confirm the presence of mast cells in the human hippocampus of subjects with ASD and control subjects (Supplementary Fig. 3A–C [this file] ). Immunofluorescence confirmed that MMP9 expression colocalized with mast cells (Supplementary Fig. 3D [this file] ) and microglial cells labeled with IBA1 (Supplementary Fig. 3E [this file] ). Densities of MMP9 labeled mast cells were not altered in the DG or CA4 of subjects with ASD compared to control subjects (Supplementary Fig. 3F–H [this file] ). 
Brevican (BCAN) expression was observed in cells with astrocytic morphology, and 20–30% of these GFAP cells displayed co-expression of BCAN (Supplementary Fig. 4A, B [this file] ). Quantification of BCAN+ and GFAP+ cells in the CA4 area of the hippocampus revealed increase density of GFAP cells co-expressing BCAN (Supplementary Fig. 4C [this file] ). Statistical comparison of the percentages of GFAP cells expressing BCAN between groups provides additional support for increased expression of BCAN in GFAP cells in children with ASD (Supplementary Fig. 4F [this file] ). 
Glial cells were traced using the Sholl analysis probe in Neurolucida 360 (Supplementary Fig. 5A, B [this file] ) and branches were quantified for measures of branch intersections, length, surface area, volume, diameter, nodes and endings (Supplementary Fig. 5C [this file] ). In control subjects, GFAP astrocytes co-expressing BCAN had significantly fewer branch intersections along with decreased branch length, surface area, volume and diameter (Supplementary Fig. 5D–J [this file] ). In comparison, GFAP astrocytes co-expressing BCAN from subjects with ASD had fewer branch intersections, nodes, and endings, along with decreased branch length (Supplementary Fig. 5K–P [this file] ). 
MMP9 is also produced by mast cells [ 68 [rid=CR68] , 69 [rid=CR69] ], and our data shows MMP9 expression predominantly in microglia and to a lesser extent in neurons and mast cells in the hippocampus of children with ASD (Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] ). 
Our observed increase of BCAN positive astrocytes in children with ASD together with impaired astrocyte morphology suggests that increased expression of CSPGs may be associated with immature glial cells in the hippocampus of children with ASD (Fig. 5 [rid=Fig5] , Supplementary Figs. 4 [this file] and 5 [this file] ). 
Our observed decreased gene expression in several pathways involved in synaptic regulation (Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] and Supplementary Figs. 1 [this file] and 2 [this file] ), as well as decreased mRNA and protein expression of synaptic markers together indicate decreased synaptic signaling in the developing hippocampus of children with ASD. 
All other data are available in the main text or supplementary materials [this file] .

In our cohort, the only three donors that died for causes different from euthanasia (donors 7, 8 and 10—Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ) exhibited three out of the four lowest myelin damage scores among the control group. 
The drugs administered during euthanasia (thiopental or propofol followed by a neuromuscular blocking agent such as rocuronium; Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ) primarily act centrally or at the neuromuscular junction and are not known to induce structural damage to peripheral myelin . Additionally, the donors were elderly adults, negating the relevance of the developmental neurotoxicity described for some anesthetic agents (Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ). 
However, we did not find a significant correlation between levodopa daily equivalent dose and myelin damage in our cohort (Supplementary Fig. 7 [this file] ), suggesting that the observed pathology is independent of levodopa treatment. 
We further acknowledge that the sex distribution between groups may represent a limitation of this study, even though we did not find sex differences in myelin damage in any of the groups (Supplementary Fig. 6b [this file] ).

Control sn multiome datasets were generated from 11 non-diseased pituitaries acquired at autopsy, including both sexes and spanning the age range of the NFPA patients ( Fig. 1A [rid=F1] , Tables S1 [this file] and S2 [this file] ). The four NFPA specimens were macroadenomas, based on their size, having maximal diameters between 23.6 and 67 mm ( Table S1B [this file] ). Pre- and post-operative hormone measurements in the NFPA patients, as well as pathology assessments of the NFPA samples are provided in Table S2 [this file] . As formerly demonstrated with the protocol used for frozen pituitary samples, the resulting adenoma and control sn multiome datasets met stringent quality control (QC) criteria, indicating their high quality (see Tables S3 [this file] – S5 [this file] and Methods). Only cells that exceeded QC benchmarks for both RNA-seq and ATAC-seq data were used for further analyses, amounting to a total of 34,819 NFPA cells and 51,535 control pituitary cells (including 5,451 gonadotropes) ( Tables S3 [this file] – S5 [this file] ). 
We identified three main cell clusters in all NFPA samples, which consisted of adenoma cells, immune cells, and vascular cells ( Fig. 1B [rid=F1] and Fig. S1A [this file] ). This allowed annotation of clusters for the five secretory cell types (gonadotrope, somatotrope, lactotrope, corticotrope, and thyrotrope), six non-endocrine cell types (including stem cells, immune cells, vasculature-related cells, and pituicytes), and adenoma cells ( Fig. S1B [this file] ). The female NFPA sample had an additional cluster of stem cells ( Fig. S1C [this file] ). In addition, the expression levels of several characteristic gonadotrope markers, and , showed high inter-tumor variation ( Fig. S2 [this file] ). Inter-tumor heterogeneity was further supported by differences observed in the bulk methylation profiles of the four NFPA samples ( Fig. S3A [this file] ), in particular, in the methylation status of , , and ( Fig. S3B [this file] ). The extent of methylation in was in line with its RNA expression level, which was negligible in PA_004_M, while being relatively high in the remaining NFPAs (see Fig. 1F [rid=F1] and Fig. S2A [this file] ). 
To investigate the microenvironment of NFPAs, we re-clustered the non-endocrine cells from all adenoma and control samples based on their gene expression profiles ( Fig. 2A [rid=F2] and Fig. S4 [this file] ). Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) plots were used to visualize major CNS cell populations ( S1A-B Fig [this file] ), including astrocytes, microglia, neurons, oligodendrocytes and OPCs. Cluster identities were validated using canonical marker genes for microglia (FYB1, C3, S1C-D Fig [this file] ), astrocytes (AQP4, GJA1, S1E-F Fig [this file] ), oligodendrocytes (MOBP, MBP, S1G-H Fig [this file] ), neurons (GRIN1, GAD2, SLC17A7, S1I-K Fig [this file] ), and endothelial cells (CLDN5, S1L Fig [this file] ). Lineage progression from OPCs to NFOLs was confirmed by the expression of stage-specific markers (SOX6, BMP4, TNS3, TCF7L2, CASR, FYN, ITPR2, S1O-V Fig [this file] ). The analysis revealed that GPR17 expression was largely restricted to the oligodendrocyte lineage, with no detectable transcripts in other major CNS cell types, including astrocytes, microglia, neurons, or endothelial cells ( S1 Fig [this file] ). Other COP-associated markers (e.g., SOX6, TNS3, FYN) showed enrichment but were not exclusively restricted to this population ( S1 [this file] O, R, U Fig [this file] ). As illustrated in the UMAP projection ( Fig 1B [rid=pone.0354525.g001] ), GPR17 expression appeared to peak within the COP population and decline as cells transitioned toward myelin-forming and mature oligodendrocytes ( S1Q Fig [this file] ). 
The exclusive expression of GPR17 in OPCs is further shown in our bioinformatic analysis of human scRNAseq data, where transcripts were absent in neurons and other glial populations ( S1 Fig [this file] ).

Large inclusions (observed up to ~20 μm diameter) showing diffuse αSyn immuno-fluorescence and distinctly surrounded by neuromelanin granules correlated to an ultrastructure of loosely packed and randomly arranged fibrillar material intermixed with dispersed vesicles and clustered mitochondria ( = 13; Fig. 2b [rid=Fig2] , Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] ). 
Also shown in Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] . 
A clear ring of neurofilament immunostaining could be seen surrounding some halo LBs (Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] ), consistent with previous reports . 
Additionally, DAPI staining was seen in the center of the halo LBs, most prominently in the three-layered LB (Fig. 3c [rid=Fig3] , Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] ). 
In contrast, our samples have excellent tissue ultrastructural preservation, and we observed examples of each type of halo LB within the same patient (Supplementary Fig. 3a [this file] ), supporting our hypothesis that these “layered” ultrastructures are different stages of halo LB maturation. 
Here, the staining pattern matched more precisely with the ultrastructural fibrillar distribution, but still also showed a pronounced peripheral density for αSyn (Supplementary Fig. 3b [this file] ). 
We also observed examples of dopaminergic neurons containing multiple halo LBs ( = 17; Fig. 5 [rid=Fig5] , Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] ). 
The CLEM localization for these inclusions is shown in Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] . 
Finally, we additionally observed αSyn inclusions ( = 2) in neurons exhibiting clear morphological signs of degeneration or pathological stress (Supplementary Fig. 5 [this file] ). 
This composition significantly differed from the mitochondria-rich pale-bodies, which only showed sparse vesicles and membrane fragments (Fig. 2B [rid=Fig2] , Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] ). 
While these large membranous-only inclusions were observed only twice, additional small (<5 µm) membranous-only aggregates were observed with higher frequency ( = 6; Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] ). In other examples, the membranous material was uniformly distributed and intermixed with fibrils ( = 10; Fig. 6b [rid=Fig6] ) or showed dense fibril accumulations surrounded by a distinct halo of densely packed membranous material of varying thickness ( = 19; Fig. 6c [rid=Fig6] , Supplementary Fig. 7 [this file] ). Finally, some inclusions were predominantly fibrillar, with no specific ultrastructural arrangement of the fibrils, and a halo of sparsely distributed membranous material located towards the periphery ( = 23; Supplementary Fig. 8 [this file] ). 
The segmentation of an electron tomogram taken from within the central aggregate ( ) did not reveal the presence of any fibrillar material (also see Supplementary Fig. 9 [this file] ). 
A defining feature of these neuritic inclusions was the presence of a membrane surrounding the αSyn immunopositive regions (Fig. 6 [rid=Fig6] , Supplementary Figs. 6 [this file] – 8 [this file] ; black arrows), ruling out the possibility of them being extracellular LBs . However, in our observations, a ring of organized cytoskeleton filaments (likely corresponding to the ring of neurofilament staining observed by immuno-fluorescence (Fig. 1f [rid=Fig1] )) could often be observed between the boundary membrane and the αSyn immunopositive region (Fig. 6c [rid=Fig6] , Supplementary Figs. 7 [this file] c, 8b [this file] ), ruling out the possibility that they are enlarged lysosomes. Additionally, the membrane could sometimes be observed extending along a projection leading away from the αSyn immunopositive area (Supplementary Figs. 7 [this file] b, 8c [this file] ). 
In the section shown, this fourth aggregate shares no direct intermixing of boundaries with the main inclusion body, but the two structures are connected by a continuous tract of mitochondria and large vesicles in the surrounding space (Fig. 7 [rid=Fig7] , black arrows) and show a closer spatial arrangement when observed in adjacent sections (Supplementary Fig. 9 [this file] ). 
For the main aggregate body, tomography and segmentation additionally did not identify any fibrillar material mixed amongst the densely accumulated membranes (Fig. 7a [rid=Fig7] ), and neither could any fibrillar material be identified in any of the adjacent sections by EM (Supplementary Fig. 9 [this file] ). Finally, in the Morris water maze test for spatial learning and memory, cKO AL mice demonstrated slower escape latencies (Fig. S2A [this file] ) and lower path efficiency (Fig. S2B [this file] ) during the acquisition phase, indicating impaired spatial learning. During the probe trial on day 5, cKO AL mice spent less time in the target quadrant compared to WT AL controls (Fig. S2C [this file] ), confirming spatial memory deficits. 
Similarly, CR reduced anxiety-like behavior, as measured by decreased time spent in corner regions of the open field (Fig. 1F-G [rid=Fig1] ) and increased center exploration (Fig. S3A-B [this file] ), across both genotypes. In the novel object recognition test for memory (Fig. 1H-I [rid=Fig1] ), cKO CR mice showed increased novel object exploration, measured by both zone entries (Fig. 1J-K [rid=Fig1] ) and target zone dwell times (Fig. S3C [this file] ). Novel object preference indices (calculated from head entries and zone occupancy time) demonstrated enhanced object discrimination in cKO CR mice compared to cKO AL mice over 40 weeks (Fig. 1J-K [rid=Fig1] ; S3C [this file] -D). 
We conducted water maze testing monthly from week 8 to 48 in WT and cKO mice under AL and CR conditions, respectively (Figs. 2 [rid=Fig2] ; S4 [this file] ). The visible platform test was performed after escape latency and memory tests on day 5 of week 48, and the consistency across genotypes in locating the visible platform shows a lack of confounding visual deficits (Fig. S4C [this file] ). However, cKO CR mice displayed faster swim speeds than cKO AL and WT CR animals during week 48 (Fig. S4D [this file] ). Thus, to control for swim speed differences, we used both latency and path efficiency to assess spatial learning abilities (Fig. 2A-C [rid=Fig2] ; S4 [this file] A-B). Baseline performance was comparable across all groups at week 8, indicating similar spatial learning skills across genotypes prior to CR intervention (Fig. 2B [rid=Fig2] ; S4B [this file] ). These genotype-dependent effects on memory retention were further supported by analyses of latency to first entry into the target zone (Fig. S4E [this file] ) and the time to cross the previous location of submerged platform (Fig. S4F [this file] ). 
In addition, cKO CR mice traveled longer distances (Fig. 1E [rid=Fig1] ) and spent more time exploring the center region (Fig. S3B [this file] ) than cKO AL mice at 8 weeks.

To define sRNAs dysregulated in AD, we profiled gray matter of the temporal cortex from Braak VI AD patients and age-matched neurologically normal controls using an sRNA array platform ( Table S1a [this file] , b [this file] ). Robust detection fl-tRNAs and tRFs showed separation of expression profiles of the two RNA classes across samples on the principal component analysis (PCA) ( Fig. S1a [this file] ). 329 probes detected sRNAs dysregulated in AD (p-value < 0.05, fold change ≥1.5) ( ), including 161 upregulated species, of which 132 (82%) were tRFs ( Fig. 1b [rid=F1] ; ). tRFs were the most prominently upregulated class, with several already abundant tRFs further increased in AD ( Fig. S1b [this file] , c [this file] ). Mapping of tRF boundaries revealed enrichment around the anticodon stem–loop, consistent with ANG-mediated cleavage ( Fig. S1d [this file] ) . 
In contrast, most downregulated tRFs were mitochondrial-derived (mt-tRFs): 80.2% of downregulated probes corresponded to mt-tRFs, with 77.9% being 5′mt-tRFs ( Fig. S1d [this file] – f [this file] ; ). 
As expected, miR-132, an miRNA linked to both amyloid and Tau pathology , was downregulated ( Fig. S1g [this file] ). Reanalysis of an independent sRNA-seq dataset from AD prefrontal cortex (GSE48552) confirmed widespread tRF accumulation, with 5’Glu and 5’Gly being the most abundant and further elevated in AD ( Fig. 1h [rid=F1] ; Fig. S1h [this file] ; ). 
To assess the specificity of 5’Glu and 5’Gly accumulation in AD, we reanalyzed published sRNA datasets from Frontotemporal Lobar Dementia with Tau pathology (FTLD-MAPT; E-MTAB-12731, batch 1) and sporadic Parkinson’s Disease (PD; GSE72962, GSE 64977) ( ). 5’Glu and 5’Gly , together with another highly abundant 5’Gly , were upregulated in the prefrontal cortex of FTLD-MAPT, mirroring the pattern observed in AD ( Fig. S2a [this file] – d [this file] ). In contrast, these 5’tRFs were not elevated in the PD prefrontal cortex ( Fig. S2e [this file] – h [this file] ), indicating their association with tau pathology rather than a general neurodegenerative stress response. 
Neurotoxicity was dose-dependent ( Fig. S3a [this file] , b [this file] ), and at selected concentrations (glutamate: 3 μM rat, 0.5 μM human; H O: 0.5 μM rat, 5 nM human; 1/2t Aβ: 0.25 μM rat, 0.5 nM human), viability loss did not exceed 10% at 24h ( Fig. S3a [this file] , b [this file] ). No morphological abnormalities or increased apoptosis were detected by imaging or 7-AAD/ Annexin V assays ( Fig. 2a [rid=F2] ; Fig. S3c [this file] ). 
The signals were abolished by pre-transfections of the corresponding antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs), confirming specificity of 5’tRF detection ( Fig. S4a [this file] ). In contrast, probes for other fragments from the same parental tRNAs (3’Glu , 3’Gly , iGlu , iGly ) exhibited distinct patterns and no stress responsiveness ( Fig. S4b [this file] ). In stressed neurons, both 5’Glu and 5’Gly showed minimal colocalization with the stress granule marker G3BP1 ( Fig. S4c [this file] ). 
Because glutamatergic, oxidative, and Aβ stresses promote Tau hyperphosphorylation , we assessed Tau pS396 (associated with early disease stage) and Tau oligomerization using Tau 22 and TOMA1 antibodies that recognize misfolded oligomeric Tau ( Fig. S5a [this file] ). Western blot (WB) showed induction of phosphorylated and oligomeric, but not total, Tau in stressed rat and human neurons ( Fig. S5b [this file] , c [this file] ). Consistent with these results, increased cytoplasmic oligomeric Tau puncta was observed by immunofluorescence ( Fig. S5d [this file] ). 
To test this, we performed 5′tRF pull-down assays in neurons transfected with synthetic biotinylated 5′tRF mimics, including 5’Glu and 5’Gly , designed with similar end-modifications to control for sequence-independent effects ( Table S2 [this file] ). Following cross-linking and stringent streptavidin-based purification ( Fig. 4a [rid=F4] ), WB analysis revealed selective co-precipitation of phosphorylated (pS396) and oligomeric (Tau22) Tau with 5’Glu and 5’Gly , but not with other 5′tRFs ( Fig. 4b [rid=F4] , Fig. S6a [this file] ), indicating specific 5’tRF interactions with pathological Tau species. 
CLIP–qRT-PCR confirmed significant enrichment of 5’Glu in Tau pS396 and PHF1 complexes ( Fig. 4f [rid=F4] , Fig. S6b [this file] , c [this file] ). It was significant relative to total Tau complexes and the enrichment persisted after normalization to elevated tRF levels in PS19 tissue ( Fig. 4g [rid=F4] ; Fig. S6b [this file] , c [this file] ). Although a modest enrichment was observed in PHF1 complexes relative to total Tau ( Fig. S6b [this file] ), this effect was lost after RNA normalization ( Fig. S6c [this file] ). CLIP-qRT-PCR in naive and glutamate- or 1/2t Aβ-stressed primary neurons similarly showed selective enrichment of 5’Glu in Tau pS396 and PHF-1 complexes compared to total Tau complexes, which remained significant after normalization to RNA input ( Fig. 4f [rid=F4] , g [rid=F4] ; Fig. S6b [this file] , c [this file] ). Apparent 5’Gly enrichment in Tau pS396 complexes in stressed neurons was abolished by RNA normalization ( Fig. 4f [rid=F4] , g [rid=F4] ), and no 5’Gly enrichment in stressed or naïve neurons was observed in PHF-1 complexes ( Fig. S6b [this file] , c [this file] ). 
Imaging of stressed rat and human neurons, as well as Tau P301S human iNs, revealed overlap between 5’Glu (green) and oligomeric Tau (TOMA1, red) intensity peaks ( Fig. S6d [this file] ). The overlap between 5’Gly and TOMA1 was limited ( Fig. S6e [this file] ). Quantification confirmed increased co-localization of 5’Glu with TOMA1 puncta across all models, whereas 5’Gly showed minimal co-localization ( Fig. S6f [this file] , g [this file] ). 
Notably, 5’Glu , 5’Gly and 5’Gly induced Tau phosphorylation at several residues associated with intraneuronal NFT (S396, Thr181, and S262) and promoted Tau misfolding and oligomerization (Tau22 and TOMA1), without altering total Tau, in both rat primary and human neurons 24 hours after transfection ( Fig. 5a [rid=F5] , Fig. S7a [this file] ). In contrast, these 5’tRFs had no effects on phosphorylation at Thr231, an early pre-NFT epitope ( Fig. 5a [rid=F5] ). 5’Cys also increased pS396 and Tau22 signals, whereas other tested 5’tRFs had no effects ( Fig. 5a [rid=F5] , Fig. S7a [this file] ). Consistently, immunofluorescence revealed a 3–4-folds increase in cytoplasmic TOMA1-positive Tau puncta in neurons overexpressing 5’Glu , 5’Gly , and 5’Gly ( Fig. 5b [rid=F5] , c [rid=F5] ; Fig. S7b [this file] , c [this file] ). 
To assess the effects of 5’tRFs on neuronal morphology and health, we imaged transfected neurons over 6 days and monitored neurite lengths and branching. 5’Glu , 5’Gly , and 5’Gly impaired neuronal growth, reducing neurite length and branching in both rat and human neurons, compared to untreated cultures and neurons transfected with other tRFs ( Fig. 5e [rid=F5] , f [rid=F5] , Fig. S7d [this file] , e [this file] ). Moreover, they reduced neuronal viability by 17–20% ( Fig. 5g [rid=F5] , Fig. S7f [this file] ). 
We utilized specific ASOs ( Table S3 [this file] ), optimized for high affinity, potency, specificity, and low-toxicity . Neurons were transfected with tRF-targeting or non-targeting control oligonucleotides ( Table S3 [this file] ). The anti-tRFs ASOs robustly reduced the cognate 5’Glu and 5’Gly without affecting the corresponding fl-tRNAs ( Fig. S8a [this file] , b [this file] ). In Tau-biosensor reporter cells, 5’Glu -ASO reversed 5’Glu -induced Tau aggregation, as measured by FRET ( Fig. 7g [rid=F7] ), with no effect in the absence of 5’Glu overexpression ( Fig. S8c [this file] ). 
However, 5’Glu -ASO modestly but significantly increased neurite length and branch points (by 2.5–10%) in stressed WT rat and human neurons, with faster responses observed in rat cultures ( Fig. S8d [this file] – g [this file] ), and similarly enhanced neurite length in Tau P301S human iNs ( Fig. 7h [rid=F7] ). The ASO had no effect on non-stressed neurons ( Fig. S8h [this file] – j [this file] ). Together, reduced Tau oligomerization ( Fig. 7a [rid=F7] – d [rid=F7] , f [rid=F7] , g [rid=F7] ) and improved neuronal viability above basal levels in both normal and mutant cultures ( Fig. 7i [rid=F7] , Fig. S8k [this file] ), support the potential of 5’Glu -targeting strategies for tauopathies.

Following methylome quality control (QC) checks ( Figures S1 [this file] A–S1E), we recovered data from 66,174 nuclei (median 1,347 per donor). We observed anticipated global methylation levels ( Figures S1 [this file] C–S1E) and recovered high-quality RNA libraries from 27,515 nuclei following QC filtering ( Figures S1 [this file] F–S1H; see “ nuclei-level quality control [rid=sec8.4.2] ”). The yield of nuclei per donor did not significantly differ between groups ( Figure S1 [this file] I, = 0.82, Welch’s test). Donors were well represented in every cluster ( Figure S2 [this file] A), and clusters were readily annotated by projection into reference datasets ( Figure S2 [this file] B). Annotations were generally concordant across RNA and methylation modalities ( Figures S2 [this file] C and S2D), aligned with our NeuN staining and the known accumulation of mCH in neurons ( Figures S2 [this file] E and S2F), and reflected anticipated cortical cell types and canonical marker gene transcript levels and gene body hypomethylation ( Figure S3 [this file] ). 
Four clusters were aggregated into the L4/5 IT subclass, reflecting a gradient of laminar-specific transcript levels ( Figure S3 [this file] ). 
Between groups, donors did not differ in sample quality metrics ( Figure S4 [this file] ) or cell-type abundance ( Figure S5 [this file] ). 
We next assessed differential gene expression (DGE) between neurotypical control (NT-CTL) and ASD samples in pseudobulk (generated by summing gene counts from the same cell type and donor) using DESeq2 ( Figure S6 [this file] ; Table S3 [rid=mmc4] ). Of note, two clusters ( Figure S6 [this file] A) comprised the L2/3 IT subclass and differed in RNA levels of genes known to distinguish L2 and L3 neurons, including and (L2) and (L3 [xref] [rid=bib51] ; Figure S6 [this file] B). When we performed DGE analysis at the cluster level, DEGs were concentrated specifically in the putative L2 cluster ( Figures S6 [this file] C and S6D). The increased number of DEGs in putative L2 neurons compared with L3 neurons was robust to downsampling analysis ( Figure S6 [this file] E). We observed a significant correlation between transcriptomic ASD effects in our data and those published in a previous single-cell study of transcriptional changes in ASD [xref] [rid=bib44] ( Figures S6 [this file] F and S6G), supporting the robustness of our data. Many of the top pathways suggested that upregulated transcripts converged on the cellular response to stress, including the unfolded protein response pathway ( Figure S6 [this file] H), as has been observed previously. [xref] [rid=bib39] 
In addition, methylation strongly varies by +1 sequence context ( Figures S1 [this file] C–S1E). 
While the former provides single cytosine resolution, the latter offers higher coverage due to the region binning ( Figures S7 [this file] A and S7B), more flexible covariate adjustment structures, and testing of non-CG methylation levels. 
As expected, cell type explained 80%–99% of the global variance across combined pseudobulk methylomes ( Figures S7 [this file] C and S7D). Within each cell type, age explained more variance than any other known donor feature ( Figure 1 [rid=fig1] G; Figure S7 [this file] E), consistent with past reports. [xref] [rid=bib4] We then examined differential methylation by diagnosis and age, in addition to an exploratory analysis of age-dependent ASD effects. 
DMRs ranged in size (median ±SD = 132 ± 185 bp, examples in Figures S8 [this file] and S9 [this file] ) and were very cell-type specific (<2% of DMRs overlap across cell types). In excitatory neurons, DMRs further segregate by age, consistent with methylation patterns associated with cell-type and age effects being much larger than those that vary with diagnosis ( Figure S9 [this file] ). 
We further validated this TF motif analysis by assessing ASD-DMRs that overlap with chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing (ChIP-seq) peaks [xref] [rid=bib58] [xref] [rid=bib59] and observed concordant enrichment patterns ( Figure S10 [this file] A). 
We tested for between-diagnosis differences in regulon levels, as measured by the transcript levels of the putative downstream gene targets of TF (see “ SCENIC TF-RNA (regulon) analyses [rid=sec8.4.14] ”; Figure S10 [this file] B). For example, both studies show ASD-associated increases in and regulons in neurons and decreases in the regulon in oligodendrocytes ( Figures S10 [this file] B and S10C). Beyond the TFs implicated by ASD-DMRs in motif analyses, we reproduced the directionality of previously reported ASD regulons (e.g., decreased regulon levels in Exc L2/3 neurons; Figures S10 [this file] D and S10E). 
This promoter enrichment was evident relative to a background of all candidate DMRs and in a smaller background set matching the GC content of our ASD-DMRs ( Figure 2 [rid=fig2] D) and is supported by chromHMM genomic annotation analysis [xref] [rid=bib61] [xref] [rid=bib62] and a previous report [xref] [rid=bib47] ( Figure S11 [this file] A). Promoter enrichment was broadly observed in age (but not cell type) DMR sets, but it was most pronounced in the ASD control comparison set ( Figure S11 [this file] B). 
We observed significant enrichment of ASD-DMRs with H3K27Ac-bound regions in the prenatal brain (Bonferroni-corrected < 0.02, excluding OLIGO_HYPO; Figure 2 [rid=fig2] E) and in fetal brain enhancers ( Figure S11 [this file] A). DMRs that distinguish cell types were also strongly enriched in prenatal enhancers and open chromatin ( Figure S11 [this file] C), consistent with methylation patterns generally reflecting activity in the developing brain. Our cell-type DMRs significantly overlapped those previously identified [xref] [rid=bib65] ( Figure S11 [this file] D) using different donors and methods, reinforcing the validity of our data and approach. 
We observed significant, and largely cell-type-specific, overlap between neuronal ASD-DMRs (particularly those in excitatory neurons) with trajectory DMRs that are variable between the second and the third trimesters and in post-natal development ( Figure S12 [this file] A). The overlap of ASD-DMRs with fetal brain enhancers ( Figure 2 [rid=fig2] E) and regions dynamically methylated during prenatal development ( Figure S12 [this file] A) is consistent with recent reports of prenatal regulatory regions that are associated with ASD risk genes. [xref] [rid=bib4] In sum, ASD-DMRs implicate regulatory regions active during prenatal and post-natal development and exhibit significant cell-type specificity. 
After stratifying mGenes to cell types, we found that, in every cell type, transcript levels of mGenes were significantly more likely to vary with age relative to non-mGenes in the BrainSpan background ( Figure S12 [this file] B). For the majority of cell types, mGenes exhibited the highest RNA levels in prenatal as opposed to post-natal tissue ( Figure S12 [this file] C). We then investigated common trajectories of mGene transcript levels ( Figures S12 [this file] C and S12D) across development periods, which included seven prenatal stages and eight post-natal stages. [xref] [rid=bib67] The three most common trajectories observed were marked by higher RNA levels during prenatal periods, but we did not observe a peak of mGene transcript levels in any particular stage of development ( Figures S12 [this file] E and S12F). 
First, we assessed whether ASD-DMRs overlap putative enhancers that are dysregulated in ASD [xref] [rid=bib41] and observed strong overlap between DMRs hypermethylated in microglia, which are associated with genes involved in morphological and immune signaling ( Figure S13 [this file] A), and overlapped downregulated regions identified in H3K27Ac profiling of ASD cortex ( Figure S13 [this file] B). 
We observed a small, but significant, negative correlation between ASD effect sizes in transcript levels and gene body mCA in Exc L2/3 IT neurons (Pearson’s correlation r = −0.08, = 4.1E−7; Figure S13 [this file] C). 
Next, we assessed whether our cell-type-resolved ASD-DMRs overlapped differentially methylated sites and regions identified in previous (bulk) analysis from ASD cortical tissue. [xref] [rid=bib42] [xref] [rid=bib47] We found limited overlap between different bulk ASD methylome analyses ( Figure S13 [this file] D). While the absolute overlap between published ASD-DMRs and those identified in this study was small (<3% of previously reported ASD-DMRs were detected in our dataset), it was more than expected by chance ( Figure S13 [this file] E). For example, DMRs hypermethylated in bulk dup15q cortex [xref] [rid=bib42] overlapped hypermethylated ASD-DMRs identified in this study ( Figure S13 [this file] E) as well as cell-type DMRs ( Figure S13 [this file] F). When considering genes implicated by each set of ASD-DMRs, we similarly found limited overlap between studies ( Figures S13 [this file] D and S13H; cross-study Jaccard index 0.00056 to 0.058). 
We represent transcript levels measured in our study and those from a larger study [xref] [rid=bib39] with highly overlapping donors ( Figure S14 [this file] ). 
Age explained the largest proportion of methylome variation within almost all cell types, in genic and intergenic features, and in CpG- and CpA-cytosine contexts ( Figure 1 [rid=fig1] G; Figure S7 [this file] E). There was no significant difference in either CpG or CpA global methylation levels nor the rate of global methylation accumulation in ASD cases after multiple test correction (diagnosis and age-by-diagnosis interaction term; lowest unadjusted = 0.03 in Inh MGE; Figures S15 [this file] A and S15B). Cell-type composition also varied with age ( Figure S15 [this file] C). The abundance of OPCs decreased, while the relative abundance of oligodendrocytes increased with age, as has been observed in mouse [xref] [rid=bib69] and human. [xref] [rid=bib70] The abundance of inhibitory neurons decreased with age, as has been reported previously, [xref] [rid=bib71] with a significant decrease in the abundance of CGE-derived neurons specifically in autistic donors relative to controls ( Figure S15 [this file] C; significant age ∗ diagnosis interaction term). 
We went on to identify just over 1.4 million CpG DMRs associated with age (age-DMRs; Table S10 [this file1] ) in a series of pairwise comparisons between young donors (2–16 years), young adults (17–30 years), and adult donors (40–60 years; see “ de novo DMR calling with DSS [rid=sec8.4.11.1] ”). Age effects were most pronounced in variance-explained ( Figure 1 [rid=fig1] G; Figure S7 [this file] E) and sheer number of DMRs ( Figure 3 [rid=fig3] B) in excitatory neurons, followed by non-neuronal cells and then inhibitory neurons ( Figure 3 [rid=fig3] B). The number of age-associated features detected per cell type was uncorrelated to cluster size (Spearman’s ρ ≤ 0.18), mirrored in number of age-DEGs in our paired transcriptome data, and was consistent with previous reports [xref] [rid=bib71] ( Figure S16 [this file] ; Tables S11 [this file2] and S12 [this file3] ). 
We observed significant overlap of age-DMRs with external reference ChIP-seq datasets, including the broad pan-cell-type enrichment in motifs, oligodendrocyte-specific , and neuronal enrichments in and neurogenins ( Figure S17 [this file] A). We also noted significant changes in TFs previously associated with aging ( Figure S17 [this file] D), such as increased regulon levels of well-known aging genes and , which are associated with senescence and cell stress. [xref] [rid=bib76] 
We considered the canonical “Horvath” clock, [xref] [rid=bib6] trained on pan-tissue data, and a “cortical clock” trained specifically on the human prefrontal cortex. [xref] [rid=bib77] Clock performance was highly cell-type dependent, with high performance of Exc L2/3 in both clocks and poor performance of MGE-derived inhibitory neurons and microglia in both clocks ( Figure 3 [rid=fig3] E; Figure S18 [this file] ). Additional analyses ( Figure S19 [this file] ) suggested that this differential performance by cell type may be attributable to true biological differences in epigenetic aging between cell types rather than technical factors like sequencing depth. There were large differences in the degree of overlap between clock probes and age-DMRs (range of 0%–35% of probes overlapped by cell type; Figure 3 [rid=fig3] F) as well as between clock probes and cell-type DMRs (0.51%–49.4% of probes overlapped; Figure S19 [this file] ). For example, Inh MGE had among the lowest-percentage overlaps and remained one of the least age-predictive cell types even when subsampling all pseudobulk data to the same depth, whereas higher-performance cell types, such as Exc L2/3, approached the performance of a high-coverage “pseudotissue,” constructed by summing counts across all cell types for a given donor ( Figure S19 [this file] ). Last, we found no evidence of differences in predicted epigenetic age between ASD cases and neurotypical controls in any cell type ( Figure S18 [this file] ), consistent with a previous bulk array study. [xref] [rid=bib42] 
We found that the trajectory of global mCA accumulation did not vary by diagnosis ( Figure S15 [this file] B) but did vary significantly by cell type; mCA increased with age in excitatory neurons, astrocytes, and MGE-derived interneurons ( Figure 4 [rid=fig4] A). In excitatory neurons, specifically L4/5 neurons, mCA accumulation plateaued by 25 years of age ( Figure 4 [rid=fig4] A; Figure S16 [this file] ). We examined common methylation patterns over age in bins and found that ≥75% of CA-DMBs in Exc L2/3 neurons plateaued to mCA/CA >0.60 by age 25 ( Figure S20 [this file] ). 
We then examined enrichments between genomic annotations and age-DMBs, first assessing transposable elements, which are theorized both to be a destabilizing element in aging [xref] [rid=bib78] and to be regulated by CH methylation. [xref] [rid=bib79] In excitatory neurons, mCA accumulated with age in transposable elements, including long terminal repeats (LTRs) and short interspersed nuclear elements (SINEs/Alu), while mCG accumulated in long interspersed nuclear elements (LINEs) with age ( Figure S20 [this file] ). 
We next leveraged the broad age range of donors in this dataset to identify diagnosis effects that vary with age, in contrast to pan-age ASD effects (examples in Figure 5 [rid=fig5] A; Figures S21 [this file] A and S21B). We first turned to modeling predefined features (promoters, genes, and 500-bp bins) to be able to formally model and test for age-by-diagnosis interaction effects ( Table S16 [this file7] ). 
We detected similar numbers of age-dependent ASD effects in each cell type ( Figure S21 [this file] C), but the timing of effects varied between cell types: the largest mean differences observed in neuronal cell types and astrocytes were concentrated in young donors ( Figure 5 [rid=fig5] B; Figure S21 [this file] D). Age-dependent ASD-DMBs were enriched in intergenic regions and quiescent or chromatin-repressed regions ( Figures S21 [this file] E and S21F). We considered whether age-dependent diagnosis effects were reflected at the transcriptional level but did not detect any significant age-dependent diagnosis effects in this dataset or in RNA data from a larger single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) study [xref] [rid=bib39] ( Figure S22 [this file] ). 
Given the extensive effects of age on the DNA methylome and the detection of age-by-diagnosis interactions in predefined features, we also repeated the ASD-DMR discovery procedure (including rigorous permutation of case-control labels; Figure 2 [rid=fig2] A) within three age-stratified subsamples of the cohort ( Figure 1 [rid=fig1] B; age strata: young 2–16, middle 17–30, and older 40–60 years of age) to control for age and potentially detect age-dependent diagnosis effects ( Figures S23 [this file] A and S23B; Table S17 [this file8] ). We confirmed that age-stratified diagnosis DMRs are not more likely to be caused by genetic variation than all-donor DMRs ( Figure S23 [this file] C). In each age stratum, we again observed enrichment in promoters ( Figure S11 [this file] B) and enrichment of the AP-1/Fos TF family motifs in hypomethylated DMRs in MGE-derived interneurons ( Figure 5 [rid=fig5] C; Figure S23 [this file] D). However, we also detected additional stratum-specific motifs, for example, ETS-like TF motifs that were specifically enriched in hypermethylated DMRs in microglia of older adult donors ( Figure 5 [rid=fig5] C; Table S18 [this file9] ).

Single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) data from isolated nuclei revealed that 96.4% of TDP-43+/NeuN+ and 95.4% of TDP-43−/NeuN+ nuclei were indeed neuronal ( Figures 1C [rid=F1] and S1A [this file] ). Transcripts containing known cryptic exons in the , , and genes were detected in TDP-43− neurons but were absent or very rare in TDP-43+ neurons ( Figures 1D [rid=F1] , 1E [rid=F1] , S1B [this file] and S1C [this file] ), confirming the presence of TDP-43 disease pathology in isolated TDP-43− neurons. 
Both TDP-43+ and TDP-43− neurons encompassed all major clusters of excitatory and inhibitory neurons ( Figure 1C [rid=F1] ), though inhibitory neurons were notably depleted in the TDP-43− population ( Figures 1C [rid=F1] and S1D [this file] ), confirmed by the reduced expression of inhibitory neuron markers in TDP-43− neurons compared to TDP-43+ neurons in previously generated bulk RNA-seq data from FTD brains ( Figure S1E [this file] ) . 
Cells that did not pass quality control (QC) criteria, such as amplification uniformity , were excluded from downstream analyses ( Figures S2 [this file] , S3 [this file] and Table S2 [rid=SD4] , see STAR Methods [rid=S14] ). SCAN2 recovered approximately 35% of sSNVs and 24% of sIndels, producing a somatic mutation catalog with >67,000 sSNVs and >12,000 sIndels with an aggregate estimated error rate of <10% ( Figure S2 [this file] and Table S4 [rid=SD6] ). 
To investigate potential mutagenic mechanisms, we performed mutational signature extraction, a technique that can identify underlying processes based on the types and frequencies of mutations . mutational signature extraction was performed on neuronal mutations from the three neurodegenerative conditions, along with (1) 81 neurons from AD, as well as 190 neurons and 40 glial cells from neurotypical controls previously amplified using multiple displacement amplification (MDA), an earlier whole-genome amplification method , and (2) an additional 66 oligodendrocytes from neurotypical controls amplified using PTA This analysis resulted in six SNV signatures (SBS-A to SBS-F, Figure S4A [this file] ) of which only SBS-B showed an increase in PTA neurons from all three neurodegenerative conditions compared to control PTA neurons, although the increase in ALS neurons did not reach statistical significance ( Figures S4B [this file] and S4C [this file] ). 
mutational signature extraction of sIndels identified three distinct signatures, IDA, ID-B, and ID-C ( Figure 3C [rid=F3] and S5A [this file] ). ID-A burdens were significantly increased in PTA neurons from the three neurodegenerative conditions compared to control PTA neurons, while burdens of ID-B showed no difference across PTA neurons from all conditions ( Figures 3D [rid=F3] and S5B [this file] – C [this file] ). ID-C was elevated only in MDA-amplified AD neurons, but not in PTA-amplified AD neurons ( = 3.9 × 10 , Wilcoxon rank sum test), suggesting that this signature may represent overfitting to MDA-specific artifacts ( Figure S5C [this file] ). 
Consistent with the overall burdens of sSNVs and sIndels, the levels of these mutational signatures did not differ between TDP-43+ and TDP-43− neurons ( Figure S6 [this file] ), further indicating that nuclear TDP-43 depletion does not enhance mutagenesis in individuals with expansions. 
In parallel, we analyzed neuronal nuclei that were positive for both TOP1cc and NeuN antibody staining from the prefrontal cortex of FTD, AD, and control brains using flow cytometry and found higher fractions of neurons with increased TOP1cc immunoreactivity in disease brains (2.8-11.6%) compared to controls (0.2-0.5%) ( Figure S7A [this file] ). 
This association with transcriptional activity was confirmed by comparing each sIndel category against several other signals that correlate with transcriptional activity: local levels of open chromatin (measured by single-nucleus ATAC-seq ), active and inactive histone marks , chromatin states , and promoters and enhancers active in neurons ( Figures S7B [this file] and S7C [this file] ). 
Consistent with this, diseased neurons show upregulated TOP1 expression but reduced expression of pathways responsible for clearing TOP1ccs ( Figure S8 [this file] ). 
We performed PTA-based scWGA and scWGS on three cerebellar granule cell neurons from each of the diseased brains for which cortical neurons were collected ( Figures 6A [rid=F6] and S9 [this file] ) . 
We found that genes encoding RNRs and RNase H2 subunits were downregulated across various neuronal subtypes in our snRNA-seq data from FTD brains compared to controls ( Figure S10A [this file] ). A similar trend of reduced expression was also observed in previously published snRNA-seq data from AD neurons ( Figure S10A [this file] ), although most of these changes were not statistically significant, likely due to the low abundance of these transcripts in neurons and differences in tissue lysis and nuclear isolation protocols. However, qPCR on cDNA from neurons of FTD and AD brains with high levels of ID-A sIndels and control brains confirmed significantly reduced expression of and in FTD and AD neurons compared to control neurons ( Figures 7B [rid=F7] and S10B [this file] ). 
Finally, we observed a strong correlation between ID-A and SBS-B—which resembles COSMIC SBS30, a signature associated with oxidative DNA damage—in cortical neurons from all three disease conditions after removing three outlier ALS neurons that exhibited elevated sSNV burdens, possibly driven by another mechanism not involving TOP1 ( Figures 7C [rid=F7] , S10C [this file] , and S11 [this file] ). 
Given the increased oxidative damage observed in neurons from the three neurodegenerative conditions manifested as increased oxidative sSNV signature exposure ( Figures S4A [this file] and S4B [this file] , SBS-B), the increased level of single-strand breaks in FTD and AD brains is likely a result of TOP1cc trapping by local oxidative DNA damage ( Figures 5A [rid=F5] – 5D [rid=F5] ). Our snRNA-seq analyses showed that genes involved in TOP1cc resolution are downregulated ( Supplementary Fig. S8 [this file] ). 
TDP-43 pathology has been observed in a subset of AD and CTE cases , raising the possibility that nuclear TDP-43 depletion is the underlying shared cause of ID-A deletions; however, this appears unlikely since we did not observe an association between ID-A deletions and TDP-43 depletion status in ALS and FTD brains ( Figures 2D [rid=F2] and S6 [this file] ), and TDP-43 knockdown in iPSC-derived neurons did not induce TOP1cc formation ( Figure S12 [this file] ). Brain samples were obtained from multiple independent sources ( Table S1 [rid=SD3] ) , and levels of somatic mutations, particularly ID-A deletions, did not correlate with postmortem interval across samples ( Figure S13 [this file] ).

We obtained expression data for 16,651 genes and 3,237 proteins, which generally showed poor correlation (Supplementary Fig. 1a–c [this file] ). Notably, structural axonal proteins, whose gene transcripts primarily reside in neuronal somas, did not correlate well with protein levels, while proteins expressed by oligodendrocytes and microglia showed stronger correlation with their gene transcripts (Supplementary Fig. 1d–g [this file] ). The primary drivers of variance in the transcriptomics and proteomics datasets were lesion presence/absence and the foamy phenotype (Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] ), similar to the lipidomics data. Most differentially expressed genes and proteins were consistent across all lesion types (Fig. 3a,c [rid=Fig3] ), reflecting general lesion features such as demyelination (Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] ), oligodendrocyte loss and astrogliosis. We observed increased expression of genes and proteins involved in cholesterol recycling, lipid droplet formation, oxylipin production and ferroptosis (Supplementary Figs. 4 [this file] and 5 [this file] ), aligning well with the lipidomics dataset. 
In addition, we observed significantly higher expression of immunoglobulin receptors and complement components and their receptors in lesions with foamy microglia (Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] ), indicating increased immunoglobulin-mediated phagocytosis . 
To this end, we examined snRNA-seq-derived transcriptional microglial states reported in ref. (Fig. 4a [rid=Fig4] ), determined gene signatures for each state and analyzed their expression in the bulk transcriptome, adjusted for total microglia abundance (Fig. 4b [rid=Fig4] and Supplementary Fig. 7 [this file] ). The Micro_D profile was characterized by marker genes such as , , , and (Fig. 4f,g [rid=Fig4] and Supplementary Fig. 8 [this file] ). Micro_D marker genes were also significantly enriched in lesions with foamy microglia at the protein level (Supplementary Fig. 9 [this file] ). , a marker for lysosomal stress and previously characterized to be highly expressed in ALs , emerged as the strongest Micro_D marker gene (Fig. 4f [rid=Fig4] ). 
Next, to obtain an integrated molecular profile that we could link to disease progression, we performed multi-omics factor analysis (MOFA) (Fig. 5a–h [rid=Fig5] and Supplementary Fig. 10 [this file] ). Factor 3 contained increased CE, BMP and oxylipin levels along with their oxylipin-generating enzymes ALOX15B and TBXAS1, as well as IgG1, C1QC and , while axonal and synaptic proteins were downregulated (Fig. 5h [rid=Fig5] and Supplementary Figs. 11 [this file] and 12 [this file] ). 
MAGL activity also significantly associated with MOFA factor 3 (Fig. 6b [rid=Fig6] ), and its mRNA levels were highest in the Micro_D cluster (Supplementary Fig. 8f [this file] ), suggesting expression of MAGL directly by foamy microglia. MAGL catalyzes the conversion of the endocannabinoid (eCB) 2-arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG) into arachidonic acid (AA) in the brain, which is a precursor for oxylipins (Fig. 6f [rid=Fig6] and Supplementary Fig. 13 [this file] ). 
For example, AA-derived oxylipins 12-HHTrE, PGD2 and 15-HETE, which are strongly associated with MOFA factor 3 (Fig. 5h [rid=Fig5] and Supplementary Fig. 14 [this file] ), significantly correlated with the proportion of lesions with foamy microglia. 
Detailed filtering criteria and analysis choices are specified in Supplementary Methods [this file] . Methods for weighted gene-coexpression network analysis (WGCNA) , single-cell deconvolution and gene set enrichment can be found in Supplementary Methods [this file] . 
A total of 11 samples had data for two data modalities and 7 samples had data from only one data modality (Supplementary Fig. 10a [this file] ).

Principal components analysis (PCA) of the proportions of different 30-bp variants separated individuals into two distinct clusters along PC1 ( Fig. 1B [rid=F1] ; Fig. S1B [this file] ). 
Visualization of TRACT alleles by coloring the ten most common variants ( Fig. 1D [rid=F1] ; Fig. S1C [this file] ) confirmed that TRACT alleles contain two distinct sequence compositions that correspond to differences in TRACT length. 96.96% of TRACT alleles ( = 574) have a sequence composition that is characterized by a high proportion of variant 2 (yellow in Fig. 1D [rid=F1] ; 18.69% ± 2.42%) and a low proportion of variant 3 (blue in Fig. 1D [rid=F1] ; 10.76% ± 1.07%). 
TRACT alleles cleanly clustered together based on flanking sequence variants, suggesting that TRACT arose on only one haplotype ( Fig. S2 [this file] ). Consistent with our estimate that 4–5 individuals would be homozygous for TRACT under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, both alleles from five individuals with high variant 3 proportion clustered with TRACT alleles (red arrowheads in Fig. S2 [this file] ). 
TRACT is found in all super populations: Africans, Ad-Mixed Americans, East Asians, Europeans, and South Asians ( Fig. S3 [this file] ).

Similarly, variants that are 1 bp from variant 2 are enriched in TRACT individuals ( Fig. 3C [rid=F3] , Fig. S4 [this file] ). 
To examine whether extant TRACT alleles exhibit germline instability, we examined the Platinum Pedigree (PP), a 4-generation pedigree of 23 individuals with long-read assembled genomes ( Porubsky et al., 2025 [rid=R38] ) ( Fig. S5 [this file] ). [xref] [rid=bib35] Here, by adding a large fragment size selection step, we increase on-target read proportion for a single locus compared to the other main known published Nanopore Cas9 capture method applied for sample multiplexing [xref] [rid=bib35] ( Table S4 [this file] ). We add a fragment size selection step to increase the on-target read mapping proportion ( Table S4 [this file] ), therefore allowing for (1) increased sampling to facilitate STR genotyping accuracy and (2) the re-distribution of read availability to allow for multiplexing multiple samples.

Surprisingly, just 3 hours post-injection, FITC+ cells were observed in the blood, spleen, and even peripheral bone marrow, indicating the FITC isomer had leaked from the initial s.c. injection and spread globally likely via the vasculature ( Fig 4K [rid=F4] , Fig S3E [this file] ). Blood or Bone Marrow (BM) samples and nuclei suspensions from frozen brain tissue sampled from the frontal cortex to the spinal cord, and FACS sorted into PU.1 myeloid nuclei, NeuN neuronal nuclei , and PU.1 NeuN (DN) stromal/immune cell nuclei ( Figure 1A [rid=F1] and Figure S1A [rid=SD1] ), were subjected to targeted deep sequencing ( , see Methods [rid=S27] , Table S2 [rid=SD3] , S3 [this file] ) at an average depth of ~1100X ( Figure S1B [rid=SD1] ), and to droplet digital PCR (ddPCR) ( Table S3 [this file] ). BRAFc.1799T>A (corresponding to BRAF ) was the variant most frequently detected, present in multiple PU.1 brain samples, from all histiocytosis patients ( Figure 1B [rid=F1] and Table S3 [this file] ). BRAF detection was confirmed by ddPCR ( Table S3 [this file] ). In contrast, BRAF was not detected in NeuN and DN samples from histiocytosis patients and in NeuN , PU.1 and DN samples from controls ( Figure 1C [rid=F1] , Figure S1C [rid=SD1] and Table S3 [this file] ). 
Single nuclei genotyping (Tapestri) of brain PU.1+ nuclei from patient #6, which presented with clonal hematopoiesis (TET2 and DNMTA3 variants at AF~50%) with a JAK2 variant subclone at 40% AF, as well as a brain specific BRAF clones ( Figure 1B [rid=F1] , Figure 4C [rid=F4] , Table S3 [this file] ), showed that the BRAF nuclei present in the patient’s brain (at AF 3.5%) also carried the TET2 and DNMT3A variants ( Figure 4D [rid=F4] ). It is of note that the PU.1 TET2/ DNMT3A/JAK2 variant was absent from the cerebellum by bulk targeted sequencing ( Table S3 [this file] ). Therefore, it is possible to conclude that a bone-marrow derived brain PU.1 TET2/DNMT3A/BRAF subclone was associated to patient #6 brain lesions ( Figure 4D [rid=F4] and Table S3 [this file] ). 
Interestingly, single nuclei genotyping (Tapestri) of brain PU.1+ nuclei from patients #8 and #3, who also presented with TET2 and BRAF clones detectable in the brain and blood or bone marrow ( Figure 1B [rid=F1] , Figure 4C [rid=F4] and Table S3 [this file] ), showed that the TET2 and BRAF variants were mutually exclusive at the single nuclei level ( Figure 4E [rid=F4] ), indicating that the patients carried independent hematopoietic clones, both able to colonize the brain. Of note, the TET2 clone was also detected in the unaffected frontal cortex of patient 8 ( Table S3 [this file] ), indicating that the BRAF clone was a better match with the brain lesions than the TET2 clone. 
In contrast to the above, the 2 pediatric-onset LCH patients (patients #1 and #2), did not present with detectable CH, and the BRAF variant was not detected in their white blood cells, even after separation into myeloid and lymphoid cells by flow-sorting ( Figure S6A [rid=SD1] ) and analysis by ddPCR at a depth >8000x ( Figure 4C [rid=F4]F [rid=F4] , figure S6B [rid=SD1] , Table S3 [this file] ). 
Similarly, neither CH clones nor the BRAF variant were detected in the bone marrow of patient #5, at a sequencing depth of ~5000x ( Figure 4C [rid=F4] , G [rid=F4] , Figure S6B [rid=SD1] and Table S3 [this file] ). 
Patient #7 presented with multiple cancers, and clonal hematopoiesis (TET2 mutation at AF 35%), however, the TET2 variant was undetectable in the brain, while the BRAF variant was undetectable in the bone marrow at a depth of ~5000x ( Figure 4C [rid=F4] and Table S3 [this file] ). A similar pattern was observed in patient #4 ( Figure 4C [rid=F4] and Table S3 [this file] ). 
DNA sequencing data processed for selection of somatic variants are available for all patients and samples in Supplementary table 3 [this file] . 
To quantify mutational load we took into consideration the panel used for sequencing each sample: HemePACT (2.88 Mb) or the extended panel HemeBrain-PACT (3.44 Mb) (see Supplementary Table 1 [rid=SD2] - 3 [this file] ).

Double labeling with PCP-2 and calbindin, another marker for PCs , confirmed that the observed changes were due to PC degeneration rather than selective downregulation of PCP-2 in severe P10 SMA mice ( Fig. S1A [this file] ). 
None of these models exhibited PC loss or cerebellar alterations at disease end-stage ( Fig. S1B [this file] – G [this file] ), indicating that PC degeneration and cerebellar hypoplasia are specific features of severe SMA that are not present in other motor neuron diseases. 
At P5, we found no significant differences in input resistance (R ), time constant (τ) and capacitance of SMA PCs ( Fig. S2A [this file] - D [this file] ), suggesting neither changes in their passive membrane properties nor in their morphology occur at the onset of degeneration. Moreover, while these SMA PCs exhibited no alteration in rheobase, they had lower resting potential (RMP) and lower voltage firing threshold (V ) ( Fig. S2E [this file] - G [this file] ). The action potentials (APs) of SMA PCs were narrower with a mildly increased amplitude compared to controls ( Fig. S2H [this file] - J [this file] ). In agreement, SMA PCs showed significantly higher evoked firing frequencies ( Fig. S2K [this file] , L [this file] ) and a tendency toward increased spontaneous firing ( Fig. S2M [this file] ), suggesting that an increased output of the cerebellar cortex may take place before substantial loss of PCs. 
At a later disease stage (P10), SMA PCs were hyperexcitable as indicated by an increased R and decreased rheobase ( Fig. 2B [rid=F2] - D [rid=F2] ), while RMP, V and AP amplitude were unaltered ( Fig. S2N [this file] - P [this file] ). A significantly decreased capacitance and unchanged τ are indicative of smaller soma size and proximal dendritic trees in vulnerable SMA PCs from lobules VI/VII ( Fig. 2E [rid=F2] and Fig. S2Q [this file] ), which agrees with the morphological analysis ( Fig. 2F [rid=F2] - H [rid=F2] ). In contrast, PCs located in lobule III, which are resistant to death, showed no morphological signs of impairment ( Fig. S2R [this file] ). 
To do so, we used antibodies against vesicular GABA transporter (VGAT) as a marker for inhibitory synapses originating from basket, stellate, and Golgi neurons as well as neighbouring PC cells ( Fig. S3A [this file] ). Consistent with this, we observed small parallel fiber synapses exclusively expressing VGLUT1 on the soma and proximal dendrites of PCs, whereas larger VGLUT2 climbing fiber synapses were found contacting the soma and primary dendritic shafts in P10 mice ( Fig. S3B [this file] ). VGLUT1 parallel fiber synapses were reduced by ~30% on the soma and ~50% on both proximal (0–50 μm from the soma) and distal (50–100 μm) dendrites of PCs in the vulnerable lobules VI and VII of mice at P10 ( Fig. 3A [rid=F3] , B [rid=F3] ), whereas resistant PCs in lobule III showed no reduction ( Fig. S4A [this file] , B [this file] ). Inhibitory VGAT synapses were also selectively reduced albeit to a lesser extent (~30% decrease onto the soma and proximal dendrites but unchanged onto distal dendrites) in vulnerable PCs of lobules VI/VII ( Fig. 3C [rid=F3] , D [rid=F3] and Fig. S4C [this file] - D [this file] ). In contrast, VGLUT2 synapses from climbing fibers were spared or only mildly affected in PCs of vulnerable and resistant lobules of mice ( Fig. 3E [rid=F3] , F [rid=F3] and Fig. S4E [this file] - F [this file] ). To test whether synaptic loss is limited to the severe form of SMA, we investigated synaptic density onto PCs in the milder mouse model and found that all three types of synapses were unaltered at disease end-stage ( Fig. S4G [this file] , H [this file] ). 
In contrast, SMA PCs in the resistant lobule III did not show differences in facilitation or EPSC amplitudes compared to control PCs ( Fig. S4I [this file] - K [this file] ). 
Although SMA GCs in vulnerable lobules had slightly smaller and wider AP ( Fig. S5A [this file] - D [this file] ), all other passive and active functional properties were unaltered compared to control GCs ( Fig. S5E [this file] - N [this file] ). Moreover, repetitive 100-Hz-stimulation of mossy fibers resulted in similar short time depression in control and SMA GCs ( Fig. S5O [this file] - R [this file] ), indicating that the mossy fiber to GC synapses, which mediate the main sensory input to the cerebellar cortex, is unaltered in SMA. 
We leveraged the fact that developing PCs in lobules VI/VII do not express parvalbumin until the second postnatal week, in contrast to the early expression of both PCP-2 and calbindin ( Fig. S6 [this file] ) confirming previously reports in wild-type mice. 
Moreover, the majority (~80%) of PCs from the intermediate mouse model of SMA was p53 but did not express p-p53 at disease end-stage ( Fig. S7A [this file] - D [this file] ), in agreement with the lack of PC death in this model ( Fig. S1F [this file] , G [this file] ). 
While we found no p-p53 immunoreactivity in control tissue, nuclear p-p53 accumulation was detected in small degenerating PCs of the SMA cerebellum ( Fig. 6F [rid=F6] and Fig. S7E [this file] ). 
AAV9-p53 exclusively transduced PCs in the cerebellum with ~70% efficacy measured by GFP expression ( Fig. S7F [this file] , H [this file] ). 
Interestingly, robust expression of mCherry-Bcl-xL in ~90% of SMA PCs did neither alter p53 expression nor rescue these neurons from degeneration ( Fig. 6G [rid=F6] - I [rid=F6] and Fig. S7G [this file] , H [this file] ), suggesting that p53 may be acting through a non-apoptotic downstream pathway. 
SMA mice injected ICV at P0 with AAV9-L7–6-GFP exhibited highly selective expression of GFP in ~90% of PCs as early as 24 hours after injection, while no GFP was detectable in the cerebrum, dorsal root ganglions (DRGs), spinal cord, and muscles up to 10 days after injection ( Fig. S8A [this file] - E [this file] ). Gems were observed in ~90% of PCs from SMA mice injected with AAV9-L7–6-SMN, whereas less than 1% of PCs contained gems in SMA mice treated with AAV9-L7–6-GFP ( Fig. S8F [this file] , G [this file] ). In contrast, AAV9-L7–6-SMN did not elevate SMN expression in vulnerable lumbar L1 motor neurons of SMA mice. ( Fig. S8H [this file] , I [this file] ). 
Furthermore, AAV9-L7–6-SMN improved the number of inhibitory VGAT synapses likely originating from neighboring rescued PCs ( Fig. 7F [rid=F7] , G [rid=F7] and Fig. S3A [this file] ). In contrast, the loss of excitatory VGLUT1 synapses from parallel fibers onto PCs was not reversed by AAV9-L7–6-SMN ( Fig. S9A [this file] - C [this file] ), highlighting the non-cell-autonomous origin of this defect. These improvements were cerebellum-specific as AAV9-L7–6-SMN treatment did not ameliorate spinal cord pathology, including p53-mediated motor neuron death, NMJ denervation, and loss of proprioceptive synapses ( Fig. S9D [this file] - K [this file] ). 
We found that selective SMN restoration in PCs moderately improved gross motor performance as assessed by righting reflex and body posture assays until P4, while it had essentially no effects on weight gain and survival in SMA mice ( Fig. 7H [rid=F7] - J [rid=F7] and Fig. S9L [this file] ), indicating a cerebellar involvement in the early postnatal motor phenotype of SMA. In contrast, other acoustic features such as call duration, frequency jumps, and peak frequency were not improved by AAV9-L7–6-SMN gene delivery in SMA mice ( Fig. S9M [this file] - O [this file] ).
