To directly detect somatic variants in sALS and sFTD brains, we obtained postmortem frozen tissues of several brain regions and SCs from individuals diagnosed with sALS or sFTD, as well as from age-matched controls through the Massachusetts Alzheimer’s Disease Research Center, Oxford Brain Bank and Target ALS Foundation (Fig. 1a [rid=Fig1] and Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). We performed molecular inversion probe (MIP)-panel sequencing of 88 neurodegeneration-associated genes at ~1,800× deduplicated depth across 1,787 samples from 291 ALS, 117 FTD and 144 neurotypical control individuals (Fig. 1a,b [rid=Fig1] , Supplementary Fig. 1 [rid=MOESM1] , Supplementary Table 2 [this file] and Supplementary Note [rid=MOESM1] ). 
Overall, 20.6% (60 of 291) ALS, 25.6% (30 of 117) FTD and 0.7% (1 of 144) control cases carried repeat expansions or pathogenic germline mutations in ALS and FTD genes (Fig. 2a [rid=Fig2] and Supplementary Tables 3 [this file] and 4 [this file] ). 
In addition, predicted deleterious germline variants in dominant ALS/FTD genes were found in an additional 14.1% of ALS, 18.8% of FTD and 4.9% of control cases with significant enrichment observed in both ALS (odds ratio (OR) = 3.20, 95% confidence interval (CI) = 1.37–8.69, = 3.2 × 10 ) and FTD (OR = 4.51, 95% CI = 1.77–13.01, = 5.5 × 10 ) cases (Fig. 2a [rid=Fig2] and Supplementary Tables 3 [this file] and 4 [this file] ). While most predicted deleterious variants were nonsynonymous SNVs requiring functional validation, two new frameshift variants (p.L46Rfs*18 and p.D250Tfs*6) identified in FTD cases were probably pathogenic (Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ), as loss-of-function mutations are known to cause FTD in a dominant manner . This includes 1 case carrying both expansion and a pathogenic variant in , as well as 12 additional cases carrying combinations of pathogenic and predicted deleterious variants (Fig. 2d [rid=Fig2] and Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ) . 
The remaining call set contained 98 unique somatic SNV and indel candidates (a total of 149 candidates, including shared ones observed in multiple regions of the same individuals; Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ). After excluding these, 64 of 85 candidates (75.2%) were validated as somatic (Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). 
No protein-altering variants in ALS/FTD genes were observed in controls or in ALS/FTD cases carrying pathogenic germline variants (Supplementary Tables 6 [this file] and 7 [this file] ). 
Pathogenicity prediction identified six predicted deleterious somatic SNVs in known ALS and FTD genes (Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ), which account for 2.3% and 1.3% germline-free ALS and FTD cases, respectively (2.1% for overall). 
Amplicon sequencing across multiple CNS regions showed that (p.K594I) and (p.L248F) were restricted to the PMC (Fig. 4d [rid=Fig4] and Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ), whereas (p.H54R) and (p.T787R) showed their highest VAFs in the SC (2.16% and 0.97%, respectively), where they were originally identified, and were detected at much lower levels in other brain regions (Fig. 4d [rid=Fig4] and Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ). 
We profiled predicted deleterious somatic variants across all expressed genes in bulk RNA-seq data from 789 postmortem brain and SC tissue samples of 143 sALS cases and 23 age-matched controls generated by the New York Genome Center (NYGC) ALS Consortium (Supplementary Table 9 [this file] ; 81 sALS and 11 control cases overlapped with our MIP cohort) using RNA-MosaicHunter , which detects clonal somatic variants from bulk RNA-seq data using a Bayesian probabilistic model. 
Although we did not observe a significant increase in the burden of total or predicted deleterious somatic variants in germline-free sALS cases (Supplementary Fig. 3 [rid=MOESM1] ), we identified predicted deleterious somatic SNVs in and in multiple CNS regions of two sALS cases lacking other pathogenic or predicted deleterious germline/somatic variants (Fig. 5a [rid=Fig5] and Supplementary Table 10 [this file] ); both cases overlapped with our MIP cohort. Amplicon sequencing revealed broad CNS distribution of the (p.H566Y) variant (VAF = 5.3–12.3%) and the (p.R1962C) variant (VAF = 0.1–5.2%), with the variant extremely low in the cerebellum (0.1%), thoracic SC (0.8%) and lumbar SC (0.8%; Fig. 5d [rid=Fig5] and Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ). Notably, the (p.R1962C) variant was undetectable in cultured fibroblasts from the patient (Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ), indicating a late developmental, CNS-restricted origin. 
Fresh-frozen postmortem human brain and SC tissues were collected by the Massachusetts Alzheimer’s Disease Research Center, Oxford Brain Bank, Target ALS Foundation and NIH NeuroBioBank (Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ) according to their respective institutional protocols, written authorization and informed consent; the tissues were subsequently obtained for this study with the approval of the Boston Children’s Hospital Institutional Review Board. 
Primer sets targeting each identified somatic SNV were designed using BatchPrimer3 (Supplementary Table 11 [this file] ). 
Germline and somatic variants identified and validated in this study are listed in the Supplementary Tables [this file] .

Our primary analysis excluded the UK Biobank cohort from the AD and PD GWAS datasets (‘Materials and methods’ section). -MR results for all genetically predicted plasma protein levels assessed across the three tested neurodegenerative diseases are provided in Supplementary Table 3 [this file] . All had the same minor allele with similar frequencies (MAF difference ≤ 0.20) ( Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] ). 
We identified a significant (FDR < 0.05) potential causal effect of TNFSF13 levels on sex-combined ALS [IVW odds ratio (OR) = 0.89; FDR = 0.03], supported by genetic colocalization (PP H4 = 0.85) ( Fig. 2 [rid=awaf474-F2] and Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ). We also identified potential causal effects of four protein levels (FCGR2A, OMG and CTSB and NFKBIE) on PD in at least one of the sex-specific analyses ( Fig. 3 [rid=awaf474-F3] and Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ). Of these, OMG, FCGR2A and NFKBIE were significant in the male, but not female-specific analysis (IVW OR = 0.41; IVW OR = 1.18; IVW OR = 0.73, respectively), although only FCGR2A showed SDE ( Fig. 3 [rid=awaf474-F3] and Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ). For each of these four proteins, colocalization analyses also supported a shared causal signal (PP H4 > 0.70) with PD ( Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ). 
Five of which (BLNK, GRN, ORM1, SERPINF2, TREM2) have similar effect sizes in males and females (SDE FDR ≥ 0.05), whereas four (CSF3, MAMDC2, PCDH17, CD2AP) showed significant differences in effect sizes (SDE FDR < 0.05) ( Fig. 4 [rid=awaf474-F4] and Supplementary Tables 4–5 [this file] ). 
MR results with the MR Egger method were nominally significant ( -value < 0.05) for 10 out of 16 exposure-outcome pairs that were also FDR-significant with the IVW or Wald ratio method, further reinforcing the putative causal effects ( Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ). 
To further support the identified -MR and colocalized signals based on the primary -pQTL dataset (UK Biobank), we used two independent sets of plasma cis-pQTLs for validation ( Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). To explore how possible technology differences may influence results, we extracted from Pietzner et al. the normalized Spearman correlation values of protein levels obtained between the two technologies (Supplementary data in Pietzner . ) of the significant proteins that we used for validation ( Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ). By applying a Bonferroni-corrected -value threshold of 0.0045, to account for the number of -MR validation tests performed, followed by sensitivity analyses and genetic colocalization, we successfully validated the potential causal associations of OMG on male-specific PD, and of GRN, SERPINF2 and TREM2 on sex-combined AD ( Table 1 [rid=awaf474-T1] and Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). 
Supplementary Table 6 [this file] contains full validation results. 
Through cis-MR secondary analyses including UK Biobank in the AD or PD GWAS, we identified some proteins that were not significant when including UK Biobank (e.g. TREM2 and PCDH17 for AD) and others that were significant only when including UK Biobank (e.g. FCGR2B for PD and OMG for AD) ( Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] and Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). Scatter plots of the main MR analysis for Tier 1 exposure-outcome pair traits with more than one instrumental variable are available in Supplementary Figs 4 [this file] and 5 [this file] . 
MR results for all CSF proteins assessed across ALS, AD and PD are provided in Supplementary Table 8 [this file] . Colocalization analyses suggested a shared causal signal (PP H4 > 0.7), without evidence of SDE (FDR ≥ 0.05) ( Fig. 6 [rid=awaf474-F6] , Supplementary Table 9 [this file] and Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] ).

We trained machine learning classification models on publicly available datasets of small molecules for various ADMET properties [xref] [rid=bib22] ( Table S1 [this file] ) to predict classes of microbiome metabolites in terms of these properties ( Figure 3 [rid=fig3] A and Data S4 [rid=mmc5] ). 
For the ADMET properties of interest, the XGBoost Tree (XGBT) model consistently outperformed all other tested models, followed by either RF or support vector machine (SVM), when evaluating the model’s predictive ability using the Cohen’s κ metric ( Figure S1 [this file] ). 
To better understand which molecular characteristics drive model performance, we analyzed the feature importance of the XGBT models for each ADMET endpoint ( Figures S1 [this file] B–S1G). 
We found that most metabolites predicted to be absorbed by the intestine were also predicted to cross the BBB and to not cause liver damage, indicating potentially coordinated physicochemical properties of metabolites that enable both absorption across various barriers and reduced risk of liver damage induced by these absorbable metabolites ( Figure S2 [this file] A). 
Consistent with the microbiome metabolite results, 97.1% of metabolites were predicted to be non-mutagenic ( Figure S2 [this file] D), further supporting the idea that even pathogenic bacteria are unlikely to produce large numbers of mutagenic compounds. 
To further contextualize these global ADMET trends, we next examined genus-level patterns among major gut microbiome taxa ( Figures S2 [this file] B–S2D and Table S4 [this file] ). Analysis of shared metabolites across these genera revealed extensive overlap, with the majority of metabolites (600 compounds) shared among all seven genera ( Figure S2 [this file] B). 
The predicted distributions across all five ADMET endpoints (HIA, BBB penetration, liver safety, mutagenicity, and cardiotoxicity) were largely consistent with those observed for the larger microbiome metabolite dataset, with only minor genus-specific variations ( Table S4 [this file] ). As a representative example, HIA prediction results are shown in Figure S2 [this file] C, where all genera exhibited similar proportions of predicted intestinally absorbable metabolites (HIA = 1). 
The external validation sensitivity on this dataset (86.0%; Figure S3 [this file] A) further supports the model’s ability to recognize absorbable microbiome metabolites. 
Among these, 77.33% were predicted to be BBB penetrant ( Figure S3 [this file] B), compared with 59.9% across all microbiome metabolites, corresponding to an odds ratio of 2.3 (Fisher’s exact test, = 5 × 10 ; Figure 4 [rid=fig4] A). 
It is also important to note the apparent similarity between the achieved recall values (86% for intestinal absorption and 77% for BBB penetration) and the proportion of positive samples in the respective training datasets ( Table S1 [this file] and Figure S1 [this file] A). 
We curated a list of 12 candidate metabolites ( Figures S3 [this file] C and S3D; Table S2 [this file] ) based on our machine learning model prediction for prospective experimental evaluation using high predictive confidence, while ensuring commercial availability, and sufficient aqueous solubility of the metabolites to enable experimental testing. 
Remarkably, all six metabolites predicted to be toxic demonstrated dose-dependent liver cell toxicity ( Figures 4 [rid=fig4] C and S3 [this file] C; Table S2 [this file] ), exhibiting a dose-dependent pattern similar to the well-known liver-toxic drug isavuconazole, which was used as a positive control in our experiments ( Figure 4 [rid=fig4] B). Conversely, none of the metabolites predicted to be safe showed any statistically significant cytotoxicity at any of the tested concentrations ( Figures 4 [rid=fig4] D and S3 [this file] D; Table S2 [this file] ). 
We further examined the interpretability of the IL-8 secretion model to identify molecular features that most strongly influenced predictions ( Figure S1 [this file] G). 
To validate these predictions, we selected three positively predicted metabolites as well as four negatively predicted metabolites for further experiments ( Figures 4 [rid=fig4] H and 4I; Table S3 [this file] ). Both true positive metabolites are well known for their anti-inflammatory properties, [xref] [rid=bib40] [xref] [rid=bib41] but the model correctly predicted that they could stimulate IL-8 secretion with high confidence (probability for spermidine = 0.76, probability for spermine = 0.64; Figure 4 [rid=fig4] G and Table S3 [this file] ). 
To further contextualize the IL-8 secretion stimulation by spermine and spermidine, we tested these metabolites for their potential to stimulate the secretion of other cytokines, including IL-1α, IL-6, IL-12p70, and TNF-α ( Figure S3 [this file] E).

The majority of variants unique to LASI-DAD are extremely rare ( Figure S4 [this file] ) and fall below the detection thresholds of the other two panels (∼0.1% in the 1000G SAS panel and ∼0.2% in the TOP-LD SAS panel, based on their respective sample sizes). However, specific estimates differed considerably between LASI-DAD and the other two panels, as evidenced by the wide band around the red diagonal lines on the scatterplots ( Figure S5 [this file] ). 
Specifically, the LASI-DAD panel imputed a total of 14,985,203 variants of moderate quality suitable for downstream analyses, which is substantially higher than that imputed by the TOPMed (12,249,623 variants) and GAsP (8,614,897 variants) panels ( Figure S6 [this file] A). Importantly, the LASI-DAD panel also achieved higher imputation accuracy for these variants, as measured by both the Pearson correlation and NRD rate, than the TOPMed or GAsP panels ( Figures S6 [this file] B and S6C). 
Finally, we found that the imputation accuracy varied for samples from different states or territories of India, with the LASI-DAD panel exhibiting the smallest variation ( Figure S7 [this file] ). For example, the TOPMed panel, which consists of nearly 50% EUR samples, exhibits a strong correlation between the imputation accuracy and the average %ANI for each state ( = 0.77; Figure S8 [this file] ). 
This heterogeneity is further highlighted by global genetic PCs, showing that LASI-DAD significantly broadens the genetic boundaries typically seen in the 1000G SAS panel ( Figure S9 [this file] ).

Variance component analysis indicated that 28.9% (95% credible interval (CrI) 20.4–36.5) of the phenotypic variance was captured marginally by DNAm compared with 56.3% (95% CrI 45.8–66.8) by SNPs (Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] A and Additional file 2 [this file] : Table S1). 
We found variance estimates to be largely concordant between the two methods (Additional file 1 [rid=MOESM1] : Fig. S2 and Additional file 2 [this file] : Table S1). We find that models with and without these adjustments yield comparable estimates (Additional file 2 [this file] : Table S1). This also yielded comparable estimates with 34.8% (95% CI 26.8–42.9) of the phenotypic variance was captured by DNAm marginally (Additional file 2 [this file] : Table S1). 
Incorporating the GIANT PGS as a fixed effect in the BayesR + variance component analyses attenuated the marginal variance estimates for both DNAm and SNPs (from 28.9% (95% CrI 20.4–36.5) to 22.1% (95% CrI 13.7–31.7) for DNAm and 56.3% (95% CrI 45.8–66.8) to 26.0% (95% CrI 0.41–48.1) for SNPs; Additional file 1 [rid=MOESM1] : Fig. S3 and Additional file 2 [this file] : Table S1). Given GS accounts for 18,000 of the 4 million EUR individuals in the GIANT height GWAS [ 4 [rid=CR4] ], we performed sensitivity analysis using an earlier iteration of the GWAS [ 18 [rid=CR18] ] and found comparable results (estimate of variance captured jointly by DNAm of 18.6% (95% CrI 10.3–28.5); Additional file 2 [this file] : Table S1). 
The BayesR + analyses identified two height-associated DNAm loci (cg07386640, cg09612304) with a posterior inclusion probability (PIP) greater than 95%, with no other DNAm loci having a PIP greater than 80% (Additional file 2 [this file] : Table S2). 
DNAm levels at cg09612304 was previously reported to be nominally associated with CRP levels [ 23 [rid=CR23] ] and CCL14 protein levels [ 25 [rid=CR25] ] (Additional file 2 [this file] : Table S2). 
We assessed the predictive ability of the MPS, obtaining an incremental R of 1.0% ( value of MPS = 9.2 × 10 ) in LBC1936 and 0.1% ( = 0.2) in LBC1921 (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] and Additional file 2 [this file] : Table S3). 
Health and lifestyle factors are listed in Additional file 2 [this file] : Table S7. 
The MPS explained a smaller percentage of the variation at later time points (0.1%, 1.0% and 0.2% at the 15-17 and 24 year time points and in parents, respectively; Additional file 2 [this file] : Table S4). 
While these factors were associated with height, they were not associated with the MPS, despite displaying directionally consistent, but weaker associations (except for FER; Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] and Additional file 2 [this file] : Table S5). We examined the association between DNAm predicted blood cell proportions (Bcell, CD4T, CD8T, Eos, Mono, Neu, NK) and the MPS in the LBC36 and LBC1921 and find no association between the MPS and cell type proportions (Additional file 2 [this file] : Table S6). 
We conducted a PheWAS of the MPS in the LBC1936 to identify associated covariates including 20 phenotypes, encompassing three subgroups: those broadly associated with health and lifestyle factors, lung function and proxies of measured height (Additional file 2 [this file] : Table S7). In age- and sex- adjusted linear regression analyses (after Bonferroni correction, < 0.05/20 = 0.0025) the MPS was associated with years of education, father’s job class, deprivation index and smoking status (current smokers) (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] and Additional file 2 [this file] : Table S5). When jointly adjusting for all health and lifestyle factors (see health and lifestyle factors in Additional file 2 [this file] : Table S7), the MPS remained a small but significant predictor of height ( = 3.5 × 10 ; incremental R of 0.05%; Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] , Additional file 2 [this file] : Table S3 and Table S8).

The strength of these associations ( Table S10 [this file] ), plus their mutual exclusivity ( Fig. S2 [this file] ), suggested that these host haplotypes are in linkage disequilibrium with the integrated virus. 
We confirmed this location using targeted locus amplification (TLA) and optical genome mapping (OGM), a technique that has been used previously to identify iciHHV-6 integration sites ( 52 [rid=B52] ) ( Fig. 3b [rid=F3] , Fig. S4 [this file] ). This sequence read enabled the design of a primer (9q_TJ1, Table S3 [this file] ) that, when paired with a DR primer, amplified a 1.6 kb fragment containing the virus-host junction in the 2B-9q34.3 cell line ( Fig. 3c [rid=F3] , Table S3 [this file] ) and in samples from 206 participants with B6_9q_hap1. Sequence analysis of both samples identified a rearranged HHV-6B viral genome with two tandem DRs at the telomeric end of the viral genome and integration into host DNA at DR -T1 rather than DR -T2 ( Fig. S5 [this file] ). The virus-host junction was subsequently PCR amplified in a 4.6 kb fragment in 45/50 samples from individuals with B6_9q_hap2 using a U100 primer paired with 9q_TJ1 ( Fig. S5 [this file] ). 
Overall, 282 (46.5%) of the 606 iciHHV-6B genomes in GS:SFHS had viral genomes assigned to the B6_9q ancestral lineage: 226 (37.3%) to B6_9q_T2 and 56 (9.2%) to B6_9q_T1 ( Fig. 3 and 4 [rid=F3 F4] , and Fig. S3 [this file] ). 
A clade B6-associated haplotype was also identified at the end of chromosome 21q in 10 individuals with iciHHV-6B ( Fig. S2 and Table S10 [this file] ). OGM confirmed viral integrations into the short arm of chromosome 7 and the long arm of chromosome 21 ( Fig. 3b [rid=F3] and Fig. S4 [this file] ). 
Testing of available DNA from 569 iciHHV-6-positive individuals, using a previously described 17p integration site PCR assay and Sanger sequencing, identified a 1.5 kb junction fragment in 122 (22%) iciHHV-6B-positive samples ( Fig. S3 [this file] ). Three individuals who lacked satisfactory 17p integration site analysis had genomes classified in B8_17p based on haplotype analysis ( Fig. S3 [this file] ) or clade assignment based on either the presence of the clade B8-specific SNP or the clade B8-specific sequence of the proximal variable region of T1 ( 9 [rid=B9] ). Overall, 125 (0.53%) GS:SFHS participants had iciHHV-6B genomes classified in B8_17p ( Fig. 4 [rid=F4] and Fig. S3 [this file] ). 
Sanger sequencing showed that the pattern of telomere and telomere-like repeats was the same as that in the 1-ciHHV-6B cell line ( Fig. 3C [rid=F3] ) ( 9 [rid=B9] , 34 [rid=B34] ), which has a 17p integration demonstrated by FISH ( 3 [rid=B3] ) and TLA ( Fig. S4 [this file] ). 
Clade B5-specific SNP genotyping or possession of an iciHHV-6B-associated chromosome 19q haplotype ( Fig. 4 [rid=F4] ; Fig. S3 and Table S10 [this file] ) identified 62 iciHHV-6B genomes (10.2%) that we have classified in the B5_19q ancestral viral lineage. 
Clade B4-specific SNP genotyping or possession of an iciHHV-6B-associated chromosome 11p haplotype ( Fig. S3 and Table S10 [this file] ) identified 41 iciHHV-6B (6.8%) genomes that we have classified in the B4_11p ancestral lineage ( Fig. 4 [rid=F4] ; Fig. S3 [this file] ). 
Using the 17p integration site assay ( Table S3 [this file] ), amplicons with an estimated size of 1.5 kb were detected in samples from 23/40 iciHHV-6A-positive individuals from 10/22 GS:SFHS families. HHV-6 WGS of the viral genome from one of the GS:SFHS participants showed that the viral genome was deleted from the 5′-end to position 146,988 relative to U1102 (GenBank accession: X83413.2 (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/nuccore/X83413.2) ) with no evidence of telomere repeats in the reference viral sequence at the point of the deletion (U DR ; Fig. S5 [this file] ). 
Genomes with unusual compositions were stably inherited within pedigrees ( Fig. S1 [this file] ). 
The prevalence of iciHHV-6A was much lower and did not show statistically significant differences within the UK, although the proportion of iciHHV-6A-positive individuals was higher in participants self-identifying as English or living in England ( Table S5 [this file] ). iciHHV-6A prevalence was similar to that reported from the CARTaGENE study in Quebec, Canada ( 30 [rid=B30] ), but iciHHV-6B prevalence was higher in both Scotland and England than in Quebec. 
We confirm that iciHHV-6 is inherited in a normal fashion, with no evidence for selection for or against iciHHV-6-positive individuals within this study ( Table S8 [this file] ). We also show that children with iciHHV-6 are equally likely to inherit the virus from their mother or their father ( Table S8 [this file] ). Although the numbers are relatively small, we found no evidence that iciHHV-6A or iciHHV-6B-positive mothers had fewer children than controls ( Table S9 [this file] ). 
GS:SFHS is a family-based cohort study that included 23,930 individuals aged 18–98 years at recruitment ( https://genscot.ed.ac.uk/ (https://genscot.ed.ac.uk/) , Fig. S1 [this file] ). 
The BGS is a UK-wide cohort study of women aged >16 years in the UK, focused on risk factors for breast cancer ( 46 [rid=B46] ) ( https://www.breakthroughgenerations.org.uk/home (https://www.breakthroughgenerations.org.uk/home) , now called the Generations study and funded by Breast Cancer Now, Table S2 [this file] ). 
Screening of the GS:SFHS cohort ( = 23,930; Table 1 [rid=T1] and Table S1 [this file] ) and 8,030 individuals from BGS was performed using an HHV-6 DR1 TaqMan qPCR assay duplexed with a human β-globin gene assay ( 48 [rid=B48] ) ( Table S3 [this file] ). qPCRs were performed in a final volume of 12.5 µL and included 100 ng of template DNA, 1× TaqMan Universal MasterMix (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Paisley, UK), DR1 primers and probes at 300 nM and 200 nM, respectively, and β-globin primers and probe at 50 nM and 200 nM, respectively. 
The selected samples were assayed using an HHV-6 U7 ( 63 [rid=B63] ), an HHV-6A-specific DR6A, and an HHV-6B-specific DR6B ddPCR assay ( Table S3 [this file] ). 
GS:SFHS samples were also analyzed with qPCR assays detecting the HHV-6A and HHV-6B POL genes, as described previously ( 64 [rid=B64] ) ( Table S3 [this file] ). Samples that were positive for HHV-6 DR1 and either DR6A or DR6B but negative for U7 and POL were analyzed using ddPCR assays for U100A or U100B as appropriate ( Table S3 [this file] ). 
Custom clade-specific viral SNP genotyping assays (Thermo Fisher Scientific) were designed to detect the B4-specific SNP at position 67,748, B5-specific SNP at position 47,851, B6-specific SNP at position 100,966, B8-specific SNP at position 60,158, and a C > T variant at position 42,889 in some clade B6 genomes ( Table S3 [this file] ). 
In samples with DR -only iciHHV-6B genomes, this sequence was amplified without nested PCR using DR421R paired with TJ1F (94°C, 2 min; 35 cycles 94°C 15 s, 64°C 30 s, 68°C 1.5 min; 68°C 2 min; Table S3 [this file] ). 
All iciHHV-6-positive samples were assayed using a chromosome 17p integration site assay, which amplifies A2_17p, B8_17p, and B9_17p junction fragments ( 2 [rid=B2] , 10 [rid=B10] , 34 [rid=B34] , 44 [rid=B44] , 71 [rid=B71] ) ( Table S3 [this file] ). iciHHV-6B-positive samples with clade B6 genomes were also assayed using two novel 9q integration site assays, which amplify two related B6_9q junction fragments, B6_9q_T2 and B6_9q_T1. 
Sequencing reactions utilized primers St17p or 9q_TJ1 and either HHV-6A_ins_seq (A2_17p), HHV-6B_ins_seq3 (B8_17p), or DR8FT2 (B6_9q_T2 and B9_17p; Table S3 [this file] ). 
Data were available for 19,967 GS:SFHS participants with known iciHHV-6 status ( Table S1 [this file] ).

In the sex-stratified analyses, two CpGs were significantly associated with self-report antidepressant exposure in females, cg26277237 (β = 0.030, = 1.77 × 10 ) and cg02183564 (β = 0.023, = 4.29 × 10 ) (Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ) and there were no significant associations with antidepressant exposure in males (Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] ). Of the eight CpG sites significantly associated with antidepressant exposure in the overall analysis, all demonstrated a larger effect size in females (Supplementary Figs. 7 [this file] - 8 [this file] ).

Prescription-derived antidepressant exposure was measured using antidepressant prescriptions from Public Health Scotland (Supplementary Methods), according to the British National Formulary (BNF) paragraph code ‘040303’, which largely corresponds to Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical (ATC) subclass ‘N06A’ (Supplementary Table 9 [this file] ) ( = 174,454, = 7544) (Supplementary Table 10 [this file] , Supplementary Figs. 36 [this file] - 43 [this file] ). Using the V1 samples from the reliability dataset (see Appendix S1 [this file] ), different ICC thresholds for the EpiScores were benchmarked to optimise the ICC for the final InflammAge biomarker (Figure S5 [this file] ).

Associations were significant despite the extremely healthy nature of UKB neuroimaging participants: raw LBA estimates suggested UKB participants were similarly healthy to those in the MRi-Share and HCP cohorts who were chronologically four decades younger, on average ( SFig.1 [this file] - 2 [this file] ). 
Results remained stable but yielded fewer significant age correlations when this analysis was repeated for males and females separately ( SFig.13 [this file] ). 
Note that the raw HCP data unexpectedly showed strong age correlations for ICV (i.e., smaller skulls at older ages contradicting our pre-registered expectations; = −0.20, = 4.2×10 ; SFig.13 [this file] ) which seems to have been driven by 303 participants >31-years with small skulls that were excluded in the HCP data we analysed (e.g., in Fig. 3B [rid=F3] ; SMethods [rid=SD3] ). Additional analyses in the age-homogeneous and repeatedly MRI-scanned LBC1936 cohort showed that LBA increased with advancing chronological age, even when MRI measures at each visit were processed independently of each other (i.e., in this analysis MRI data was processed with the FreeSurfer cross-sectional rather than the longitudinal processing stream; SFig.12 [this file] & description in SMaterials [rid=SD2] ).

Genome-wide association analysis (Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] and ESM Table 6 [this file] ) identified one non-synonymous SNP in the gene (encoding cubilin) (rs1801222, XP_011518010.1 (XP_011518010.1) :p.S253F, NM_001081.4 (NM_001081.4) : c.758T>C), which passed the genome-wide significance threshold (additive model; adjusted =1.86×10 ; unadjusted =5.99×10 ; OR 1.56 [95% CI 1.36, 1.79] for AG vs GG; OR 2.43 [95% CI 1.85, 3.20] for AA vs GG). The top ten associated loci are summarised in ESM Table 6 [this file] and were analysed using both the GWAS catalogue [ 25 [rid=CR25] ] and Gene Atlas [ 26 [rid=CR26] ] for previously reported associations with vitamin B deficiency, or related traits or phenotypes. 
To determine whether the association with rs1801222 was applicable to individuals of South Asian ancestry, the largest minority ethnic group in the UK, we identified a total of 577 individuals (135 metformin-induced vitamin B -deficient cases and 442 metformin-tolerant controls) (ESM Table 7 [this file] ). 
A logistic regression model was fitted comparing vitamin B -deficient cases ( =3386, of which 555 were metformin-induced) vs non-vitamin-B -deficient controls (373,387, of which 7323 were metformin tolerant), including a binary metformin covariate and an rs1801222 × metformin interaction term (ESM Table 8 [this file] ). 
We next sought to replicate the association between the rs1801222 A allele and metformin-induced vitamin B deficiency risk observed in our UKB cohort in three independent clinical cohorts (ESM Table 9 [this file] ). 
In line with the UKB cohort data (ESM Table 9 [this file] ), vitamin B deficiency was more prevalent in the AA genotype group treated with metformin vs GG (OR 2.17 [95% CI 1.80, 2.60]; <0.0001). A significant increase in the risk of vitamin B deficiency for the AA genotype was found in non-metformin treated individuals vs GG genotype (OR 1.28 [95% CI 1.05, 1.56]; =0.017), but not for AG vs GG (OR 1.01 [95% CI 0.87, 1.18]; =0.849) (ESM Table 9 [this file] ). 
In the DPPOS year 1 cohort (5 years of follow-up), rates of vitamin B deficiency were 1.6%, 3.1% and 6.1% for the GG, GA and AA genotype groups, respectively, in the placebo arm vs 3.1%, 5.2% and 10.2% in the metformin arm (ESM Table 9 [this file] ). 
In DPPOS year 9, vitamin B deficiency rates were 4.4%, 5.9%, and 4.9% for GG, AG and AA genotype groups in the placebo arm, vs 5.7%, 6.6%, and 18.7% in those respective genotype groups in the metformin arm (ESM Table 9 [this file] ).

Our data show a significant association between metformin-induced vitamin B deficiency risk and a non-synonymous SNP (rs1801222) in the gene, which encodes the cubilin receptor (ESM Table 6 [this file] , Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] ). This association was replicated in two independent cohorts of individuals with type 2 diabetes (Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] and ESM Table 9 [this file] ).

Among the 13,678 genes, 4,405 (32.2%) were deleted and 8,601 (62.9%) duplicated at least once ( Fig. S1a [this file] , Table ST4 [this file] ). Given that deletion/duplication may occur multiple times, we observed a total of 28,108 and 77,695 deleted and duplicated genes, respectively ( Fig. S1 [this file] , Table ST4 [this file] ). 
Most cortical regions showed (Bonferroni) significant negative associations ( Table ST3 [this file] ) with cognitive ability for deletions (n=128) and duplications (n=112, Fig. 2 [rid=F2] ). For deletions and duplications, the largest effect sizes were observed in sensorimotor (Cohen’s d = −0.12) and association (Cohen’s d = −0.06) regions, respectively ( Tables ST5 [this file] , ST8 [this file] ). These patterns of effect sizes across the cerebral cortex were robust and highly correlated between discovery, replication, and full datasets, as well as between the UK Biobank and the other unselected populations ( Fig. S2 [this file] , Table ST9 [this file] ). 
Sensitivity analysis showed that these negative correlations ( Table ST6 [this file] ) could also be observed using two independent gene expression resources (Human Protein Atlas (HPA) and BrainSpan , Fig. S3 [this file] ), alternative methods for defining cortical gene sets ( Fig. S4 [this file] ) or across discovery and replication data subsets ( Fig. S2 [this file] ). 
Specifically, they showed positive and negative correlations, respectively, with multiple hierarchies of the cerebral cortex, including anatomical, cytoarchitecture, gene expression, functional connectivity, and electrophysiology gradients ( Fig. 3a [rid=F3] , b [rid=F3] , Table ST7 [this file] ). 
Overall, the mirror effects between deletion and duplication effect size were strengthened (correlation increasing from −0.25 to −0.41, spin permutation p-value <0.05, Table ST6 [this file] ) with increasing regional specificity of gene expression. Deletions demonstrated a 1.4-fold increase (Welch test FDR p-value=2e-2) in effect size for genes with the higher sensorimotor specificity ( Table ST10 [this file] ). A related analysis also demonstrated that genes with elevated brain expression were those driving the spatial distribution of effect sizes along the cortical gradient, compared to non-brain-elevated and ubiquitously expressed genes ( Fig. S8 [this file] ). Multiple sensitivity analyses showed these spatial patterns were stable ( Tables ST9 [this file] ) across i) data subsets ( Fig. S2 [this file] ), ii) demographic parameters (sex, age, ancestry, Fig. S6 [this file] ), iii) different levels of tissue specificity ( Fig. S8a [this file] ), and iv) quality metric of gene expression data (stability score, Table ST9 [this file] ). 
We first show that genetic constraint does not correlate with the cortical gradient ( Fig. S7 [this file] ). As expected, increasing intolerance to loss of function was associated with increasing effect sizes on cognitive ability ( Fig. 5-d [rid=F5] , Table ST5 [this file] ). However, the spatial patterns of effect sizes remained similar and significantly anticorrelated between deletions and duplications for the three groups (−0.38 < r < −0.73, spin permutation p-value<1.3E-3, Fig. 5-d [rid=F5] , Table ST6 [this file] ). These findings were unchanged using alternative dosage sensitivity scores (probability of haploinsufficiency (pHS), probability of triplosensitivity (pTS)) and constraint metrics (Missense Z-score , Fig. S9 [this file] , Table ST6 [this file] ). 
Overall, results show that the spatial patterns of effect sizes on cognitive ability remained similar and anticorrelated between deletions and duplications across all stratifications ( Fig. S8 [this file] , Tables ST6 [this file] , ST9 [this file] ). Sensitivity analysis showed that molecular and sub-cellular biological functions (as detailed by GO-terms ) did not explain the pattern of CNV effects across the cerebral cortex ( Methods [rid=S8] , Fig. S10 [this file] , Tables S11 [this file] , S12 [this file] ). 
Previous studies have shown that both deletions and duplications are associated with a decrease in cognitive ability (inverted U-shape effects, Table ST2 [this file] ). 
Briefly, after phenotypic and genotypic quality control, we included 238176 participants from UK Biobank with fluid intelligence scores (February 2022 release), and 20116 participants from five general population cohorts (CARTaGENE (CaG) , Generation Scotland (G-Scot) , IMAGEN , Lothian Birth Cohort (LBC) , and Saguenay Youth Study (SYS) ) previously pooled and studied ( Table ST1 [this file] ).

In order to elucidate the interplay between the biological effects of T21 versus the co-occurring conditions of DS, we analyzed multidimensional datasets from a subset of 502 total research participants, 356 with DS (T21) and 146 euploid controls (D21), enrolled in the Human Trisome Project cohort study (HTP, NCT02864108 (NCT02864108) ) with available demographics, clinical, and multi-omic data (Fig. 1a [rid=Fig1] , Supplementary Fig. 1a, b [this file] and Supplementary Data 1 [rid=MOESM3] ) . As expected for the population with DS, HTP participants display variable rates of many co-occurring conditions and other clinical phenotypes, including (in decreasing order of prevalence) CHDs, thyroid disease, sleep apnea, visual impairments, various skin diseases, hypotonia, hearing loss, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), recurrent otitis media, vitamin D deficiency, and obesity, among others (Supplementary Fig. 1c, d [this file] and Supplementary Data 1 [rid=MOESM3] ). Notably, these clinical phenotypes are observed in a highly variegated and combinatorial fashion across the cohort (Fig. 1b [rid=Fig1] and Supplementary Fig. 1e [this file] ). Furthermore, medical complexity is not significantly different between males and females (Supplementary Fig. 1f [this file] ). This is illustrated by the differential pattern of co-occurring conditions associated with obesity versus hypotonia (Fig. 1e, f [rid=Fig1] and Supplementary Fig. 1e [this file] ). 
Notably, these datasets were generated from largely overlapping set of samples, with various subsets of participants contributing to each omic data type (Supplementary Fig. 1g [this file] ). Overall, we compared the levels of ~ 22,000 features between cases and controls across 100 clinical phenotypes to identify molecular and cellular biosignatures differentially associated with co-occurring conditions in DS at various statistical cut-offs after multiple hypothesis corrections (e.g., < 0.1, < 0.05, < 0.01, see Methods, Supplementary Fig. 1h [this file] , and Data Resource ). 
When comparing cases versus controls across 100 clinical phenotypes throughout the various -omic datasets, obesity emerged as the condition annotated in the medical records with the greatest number of significant differences ( < 0.1) in both the plasma proteome and metabolome (Fig. 2a, b [rid=Fig2] , Supplementary Fig. 2a [this file] , Data Resource ). Given that research participants could have experienced weight changes over time and to account for potential differences in how obesity was annotated in their medical records, we repeated the analysis by defining obesity as BMI > 30 for adults ( > 19 years old) and BMI percentile > 95 (for 19 and younger) at the time of the research blood draw used to generate the omic datasets, which produced nearly identical results (Supplementary Fig. 2b [this file] ). In addition, by using BMI as a continuous variable, we were able to compare the biosignatures tracking with BMI in DS versus BMI in euploid controls (Supplementary Fig. 2c–f [this file] ). This exercise revealed a similar general pattern of BMI-associated changes in the two karyotype groups, with an overall attenuation of changes observed per unit of BMI among participants with DS, more obviously in the metabolome dataset, as well as notable quantitative differences at the feature- and pathway-levels (Fig. 2c–f [rid=Fig2] and Supplementary Fig. 2c–e [this file] ). 
Leptin (LEP), an adipocyte-derived hormone and master regulator of energy balance, is among the most significantly elevated proteins in the plasma of individuals with T21 and obesity, increasingly steadily with BMI (Fig. 2c, d [rid=Fig2] and Supplementary Fig. 2e [this file] ). Indeed, we observed elevated plasma insulin (INS) levels in cases of obesity (Fig. 2c, d [rid=Fig2] ), along with multiple other changes associated with insulin resistance and consequent metabolic dysregulation, such as elevated levels of fatty acid binding proteins (FABP3, FABP4) and glucokinase (GCK), alongside decreased sex-hormone binding globulin (SHBG), adiponectin (ADIPOQ), and insulin receptor (INSR) (Fig. 2c [rid=Fig2] and Supplementary Fig. 2g [this file] ). In addition, key modulators of insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF1) signaling, such as IGBFP1 and IGFBP2, were among the most significantly depleted proteins in obesity cases (Fig. 2c [rid=Fig2] , Supplementary Fig. 2g [this file] ), consistent with their known suppression by insulin . 
Several acute phase reactants induced downstream of interleukin 6 (IL6) signaling are upregulated with obesity in DS, including C-reactive protein (CRP), serum amyloid A proteins (SAA1/2), IL1 receptor antagonist (IL1RN), and haptoglobin (HP), as well as IL6 itself (Fig. 2c, d [rid=Fig2] and Supplementary Fig. 2e [this file] ). 
Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) revealed key biosignatures significantly associated with obesity and high BMI, with some quantitative differences between euploid controls versus DS (Supplementary Fig. 2d [this file] ). 
Most prominent among the many metabolic changes associated with obesity in DS is dysregulation of the glutamate-glutamine cycle, as demonstrated by high levels of glutamate along with lower levels of glutamine, resulting in a reduced glutamine-to-glutamate ratio in those with obesity (Fig. 2e, f [rid=Fig2] and Supplementary Fig. 2h, i [this file] ). Notably, we also observed lower levels of (5-L-glutamyl)-L-glutamine, a glutamate-glutamine conjugate dipeptide, likely reflective of the overall lower levels of glutamine (Supplementary Fig. 2i [this file] ). 
Analysis of the impact of clinical phenotypes on the whole blood transcriptome of people with DS revealed that history of atrioventricular canal (AVC, also known as atrioventricular septal defect - AVSD), a severe form of CHD, associates with the greatest number of significant differences in the whole blood transcriptome, with > 1600 mRNAs being either upregulated or downregulated in those with this diagnosis at < 0.1 (Fig. 3a, b [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Fig. 3a–c [this file] , Data Resource ). Importantly, this outsized transcriptome signature associated with AVC is not explained by a larger number of cases nor by potential confounding effects of CHD surgical repair (Fig. 3b [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Fig. 3a [this file] ). 
Comparative analysis of gene signature changes associated with AVC versus those associated with T21 status revealed significant concordance, with AVC history exacerbating several biosignatures commonly observed in DS (Fig. 3c [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Fig. 3d [this file] ). 
Having a history of AVC or other forms of CHD also influences the plasma proteome, with PFO and AVC having the greatest number of significant associations at < 0.1 (Supplementary Fig. 3e [this file] ). Consistent with whole blood transcriptome results, proteomic alterations associated with AVC are enriched for proteins involved in inflammatory signaling (IFNγ response, TNFα signaling), as well as apoptosis and bile acid metabolism (Supplementary Fig. 3f [this file] ). 
Importantly, these changes in gene expression, protein levels, and immune cell types associated with AVC are observed well beyond early childhood, indicating persistent, lifelong molecular biosignatures in those with a history of this severe form of CHD (Supplementary Fig. 3g–i [this file] ). 
Interestingly, each co-occurring neurological condition displays a unique proteomic profile, both in terms of individual dysregulated proteins and the pathways involved (Fig. 4d [rid=Fig4] and Supplementary Fig. 4a, b [this file] ). 
Importantly, this phenomenon is clearly exacerbated in individuals with history of seizure disorders (Fig. 4e [rid=Fig4] and Supplementary Fig. 4b [this file] ). Other examples include proteins involved in general organization of the extracellular matrix, such as Matrilin 3 (MATN3), Fibromodulin (FMOD), and Follistatin Like 1 (FSTL1) (Fig. 4e [rid=Fig4] and Supplementary Fig. 4c [this file] ). In fact, we also observed increased plasma levels of CASP3 (Caspase 3) in those with a history of seizures (Supplementary Fig. 4c [this file] ). 
Lastly, we also observed upregulated plasma levels of proteins involved in axon growth, neuronal migration, and mRNA dendritic transport in those with autism, such as filamin A (FLNA), Dihydropyrimidinase Like 3 (DYPSLE3), and Fragile X Messenger Ribonucleoprotein 1 (FMR1) (Supplementary Fig. 4d [this file] ). 
For example, whereas celiac disease associates with the largest number of significant changes in the plasma proteome and immune cell subsets, GERD has the strongest biosignatures in the transcriptome and metabolome (Fig. 5a–c [rid=Fig5] and Supplementary Fig. 5a, b [this file] ). 
In the plasma proteome, celiac disease associated with elevation of many immune factors involved in regulation of T and B cell function (Fig. 5d, e [rid=Fig5] and Supplementary Fig. 5c [this file] ). Among immune cells, celiac disease is associated with decreased frequency of naive regulatory CD4 + T cells, an additional sign of strong T cell activation, along with increased frequency of plasmablasts and IgM memory B cells, indicative of terminal B cell differentiation into antibody-producing cells (Fig. 5f [rid=Fig5] and Supplementary Fig. 5d [this file] ). In fact, at the transcriptome level, celiac disease associated with not only the elevation of multiple inflammatory signatures (e.g., IFNγ Response, IFNα Response, Inflammatory Response), but also with the clear overexpression of many immunoglobulin sequences (Supplementary Fig. 5e, f [this file] ). 
Participants with history of GERD show the strongest changes in the whole blood transcriptome relative to other GI conditions, with strong over-induction of genes involved in heme metabolism and hypoxia, which are generally elevated in DS , such as (Fig. 5g, h [rid=Fig5] and Supplementary Fig. 5e [this file] ). Conversely, GERD also associates with decreased expression of genes involved in oxidative phosphorylation, indicative of a differential metabolic and energetic profile relative to the overall population with DS, which shows elevation of these genes (Supplementary Fig. 5g [this file] ). Indeed, GERD showed the strongest metabolic changes among GI conditions, marked by strong amino acid depletion (Fig. 5i, j [rid=Fig5] and Supplementary Fig. 5i [this file] ). 
For example, when investigating clinical variables associated with plasma levels of leptin, we not only confirmed the significant positive association with obesity, but also with hidradenitis suppurativa, an inflammatory skin condition that is more common in those with obesity (Supplementary Fig. 6a [this file] ). Likewise, when testing for clinical phenotypes associated with varying levels of plasma levels of glutamate, we observed that this amino acid correlates positively not only with obesity, but also with high cholesterol and hidradenitis suppurativa, both of which track with obesity (Supplementary Fig. 6b [this file] ). 
Pathways analysis revealed that mRNAs with multiple clinical associations are highly enriched for immunoglobulin sequences (i.e., adaptive immune response signature), IFN-stimulated genes (i.e., IFNγ response, antiviral mechanisms by IFN), and other immune processes (i.e., neutrophil degranulation, response to bacterium, inflammatory response) (Supplementary Fig. 6c [this file] ). For example, beyond the association of specific immunoglobulin sequences with celiac disease described earlier (Supplementary Fig. 5f [this file] ), we found many other examples suggestive of autoantibody production in those with specific clinical phenotypes, such as in the case of duodenal atresia (Fig. 6b [rid=Fig6] ). 
Among metabolites, beyond dysregulation of the glutamate-glutamine cycle in obesity and accompanying conditions, depletion of N-acetylornithine stands out as a phenomenon associated with diverse clinical phenotypes in DS, including many with an inflammatory component, such as recurrent otitis media, asthma, frequent/recurrent pneumonia, and pharyngitis (Supplementary Fig. 6d [this file] ). Other associations indicative of immunometabolic dysregulation include elevation of sphingolipids (i.e., sphingosine-1-phosphate, sphinganine-1-phosphate) in those with history of recurrent otitis media, PDA, and adenoidectomy (a corrective procedure for OSA) (Supplementary Fig. 6d [this file] ). Among immune cell subsets, dysregulation of T cell lineages stands out as the immune phenomenon with the most clinical correlates, as illustrated by depletion of CD8+ naïve T cell subsets and elevation of effector subsets in those with severe forms of CHD and Grave’s hyperthyroidism (Supplementary Fig. 6e [this file] ). 
An analogous exercise can be done with the plasma proteome (Supplementary Fig. 7a [this file] ). For example, decreased plasma levels of proteins in the EMT signature, a hallmark of the proteome of people with DS, is maximal in those with general seizures, but clearly not associated with hyperopia (see above, Fig. 4 [rid=Fig4] and Supplementary Fig. 7a, b [this file] ). 
Per sample FCS files were then uploaded to CellEngine (CellCarta, version accessed 2021) and gated on live singlets (i.e., PARP negative, excluding CD3 + CD19 + doublets) (Supplementary Fig. 8 [this file] ).

Briefly, NA-TWAS first normalized the single-cell count data before aggregating it based on the suggestion of a recent benchmarking paper , while AN-TWAS aggregated the single-cell count data first and applied normalization on the pseudo-bulk count (Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] , see Section “Other TWAS methods under comparison”). 
For the rare NK cell type, however, all methods exhibited low power when the gene expression sample size is 500, reflecting the limited predictive performance of the Stage 1 models (Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] ). 
All methods, including scTWAS, successfully controlled the type-I error rates across all cell types (Supplementary Table 1 [this file] , Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] ). Under a null Stage 1, all methods yielded out-of-sample close to 0 as expected (Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] ). 
First, we varied per-gene trait heritability (Supplementary Fig. 5 [this file] ). Second, we considered a sparser genetic architecture with three causal -SNPs (Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] ), which reduced Stage 1 predictability and, in turn, Stage 2 power. Third, we introduced LD reference mismatch at Stage 2 by using an out-of-sample LD matrix (Supplementary Section 1.3.1 [this file] ), where results were similar to the matched-LD setting (Supplementary Fig. 7 [this file] ). Finally, when we introduced horizontal pleiotropy (Supplementary Section 1.3.2 [this file] ), all three methods exhibited inflation (Supplementary Figs. 8 [this file] and 9 [this file] ), consistent with the well-known sensitivity of standard TWAS to pleiotropic effects. 
Figure 2 [rid=Fig2] b shows that scTWAS generated a median of 16% and 32% more significantly predicted genes compared to AN-TWAS and NA-TWAS, respectively (nominal -values < 0.05 for Pearson correlation, Supplementary Fig. 10 [this file] ). 
Furthermore, at the subtype level (Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] c and Supplementary Fig. 18 [this file] ), scTWAS identified markedly more predictable genes than the other methods across the 75 subtypes, with the largest gains observed in microglia subtypes. 
However, cell-type-specific TWAS improved prediction accuracy for a subset of genes and uncovered regulatory patterns that were obscured in the bulk analysis (Supplementary Figs. 13 [this file] and 14 [this file] a), with scTWAS yielding the largest number of unique findings and underscoring the value of cell-type-specific analyses. 
Figure 4 [rid=Fig4] a compares the total number of significant gene-trait associations identified by three methods across cell types (also see Supplementary Fig. 11 [this file] for a breakdown by individual GWAS). 
We also compared with the bulk-like TWAS constructed from the same OneK1K dataset (Section “Prediction model training and evaluation”), which confirmed the complementary role of cell-type-specific TWAS relative to bulk TWAS by identifying associations that may be missed in bulk analyses, with scTWAS yielding the largest number of new findings (Supplementary Fig. 15 [this file] ). 
We highlight a few examples here, while a complete list of significant genes is provided in Supplementary Tables 3 [this file] – 5 [this file] . scTWAS uniquely identified an association between and RA and SLE in Mono and NK cells, uncovering its cell-type-specific roles in disease mechanisms. is a well-documented transcription factor critical in the regulation of immune responses, particularly in the production of type I interferons, and has been proposed as a therapeutic target for autoimmune diseases . Furthermore, a comparison with the bulk-like TWAS showed that scTWAS identified dozens of associations that were not observed in the bulk-like analysis (Section “Prediction model training and evaluation”, Supplementary Fig. 15 [this file] ). 
Next, we investigated the similarity and specificity of scTWAS findings across immune cell types. 21 out of 64 RA genes identified by scTWAS were specific to a single-cell type, while the majority were shared across two or more cell types (also see Supplementary Fig. 16 [this file] for a detailed UpSet plot). A similar trend of cell-type similarity and specificity was also observed in SLE and asthma (Supplementary Fig. 16 [this file] ), where among the genes identified by scTWAS, 20 of 41 were cell-type-specific for SLE, and 57 of 111 were cell-type-specific for asthma. 
In contrast, many scTWAS signals were cell-type-specific (Supplementary Fig. 17 [this file] ). We further compared with the bulk-like TWAS evaluated on the same ROSMAP dataset (Section “Prediction model training and evaluation”), which shows that scTWAS identified dozens of associations that were not observed in the bulk-like analysis (Section “Prediction model training and evaluation”, Supplementary Fig. 14 [this file] b). 
See Supplementary Methods [this file] for more details on the algorithm. 
To be compatible with the above traditional TWAS framework, NA-TWAS and AN-TWAS propose to apply various normalization strategies prior to applying the framework (Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] ). 
Full details are provided in the Supplementary Section 1.3 [this file] . 
For ROSMAP models, we adjusted for covariates including the first three genotype PCs, age at death, sex, post-mortem interval, study (ROS or MAP), and a hidden batch effect covariate inferred by principal component analysis ( Supplementary Methods [this file] , Supplementary Figs. 19 [this file] and 20 [this file] ). 
We then applied the same normalization procedure used in AN-TWAS (see Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] ).

Using established marker proteins for neurons, astrocytes, microglia, oligodendrocytes, and endothelial cells reported by Johnson et al. , we observed that AsymAD brains exhibited higher neuronal abundance, but lower levels of microglia, oligodendrocytes, and endothelial cells compared to AD ( Supplementary Fig. 1a [this file] , b [this file] ). 
We observe that the initial enrichment of neuronal, microglial, and endothelial proteins in uncorrected data was removed post-correction, confirming that the final set of DEPs reflects protein levels independent of cell-type composition ( Supplementary Fig. 1ci [this file] - iii [this file] ). 
For the pathways associated with upregulated DEPs in AsymAD vs AD, we observed enrichment for metabolism, translation, the TCA cycle, and ETC, suggesting that AsymAD individuals retain metabolic, mitochondrial and translational activity better than AD ( Supplementary Fig. 1d [this file] ). In contrast, pathways associated with downregulated DEPs in AsymAD vs AD showed enrichment for AUF1-mediated RNA destabilization, translational inhibition, and components of the innate immune system, indicating a potential shift toward enhanced protein synthesis and reduced inflammatory response in AsymAD ( Supplementary Fig. 1e [this file] ). 258/1757 DEPs mapped to the MitoCarta 3.0 database, indicating significant alterations in mitochondrial protein expression in AD compared to AsymAD. For AD vs Control, we identified 198 overlapping DEPs, confirming that our strategy yielded a reliable and conservative set of mitochondrial proteins ( Supplementary Fig. 1f [this file] - h [this file] ). 
KNN imputation did not introduce major shifts in mean or variance and preserved the overall distribution of protein expression ( Supplementary Fig. 2a [this file] , b [this file] ). Among the classifiers, RFE selected 43 features ( Supplementary Fig. 2c [this file] , d [this file] ) and achieved the best performance (train AUC = 0.92, validation AUC = 0.88, accuracy = 0.81) ( Fig. 3c [rid=F3] ). Notably, several proteins involved in BCAA and fatty acid metabolism were enriched among predictors of AsymAD ( Supplementary Fig. 2e [this file] ). 
We also observed upregulation of DAP3 ( )) and FIS1 ( ), essential for mitochondrial maintenance ( Supplementary Fig. 2f [this file] - g [this file] ). 
snRNA-seq data from the BA9 brain region were analyzed, with individuals classified as Control, AD, or AsymAD, based on previously established criteria published in Johnson et al. ( Supplementary Fig. 3a [this file] ). Specifically, excitatory neurons were grouped into superficial, mid-layer, and deep-layer excitatory neurons, while inhibitory neurons were grouped into PVALB, VIP, SST, and LAMP5 subtypes ( Supplementary Fig. 3b [this file] ). 
Similar result was observed for oligodendrocytes from the cell type resolved proteomics data analysis performed earlier ( Supplementary Fig 1b [this file] ). Remaining cell types showed trends that did not reach significance ( Supplementary Fig. 3c [this file] ). 
To investigate why oligodendrocytes uniquely exhibited downregulation in AsymAD, we compared this cell type across all three conditions: AD vs Control, AsymAD vs AD, and AsymAD vs Control ( Supplementary Fig. 3d [this file] ). 
NADH exhibited the highest number of interacting protein partners (144) ( Supplementary Fig. 4a [this file] ), primarily enriched in pathways related to the electron transport chain (ETC), Complex I biogenesis, and mitochondrial protein degradation ( Supplementary Fig. 4b [this file] ). L-glutamic acid followed with 69 interacting partners ( Supplementary Fig. 4a [this file] ), involved in neurotransmission and synaptic signaling. Across all identified compounds, ‘metabolism of amino acids and derivatives’ emerged as the most significantly targeted pathway, highlighting the importance of metabolic regulation in the context of AsymAD ( Supplementary Fig. 4b [this file] ).

To investigate the cell-type-specific impacts of LoF variants in AD, we selected 12 carriers of rare PTC variants, including splice (c.4416+2T>G and c.5570+5G>C), frameshift (p.Leu1403fs, p.Glu709fs) and nonsense (p.Trp1245*, p.Trp1085*) variants, from the ROSMAP cohort (Fig. 1a,b [rid=Fig1] and Supplementary Tables 1 [this file] and 2 [this file] ). PTC variants are presumed to cause haploinsufficiency, and were associated with lower ABCA7 protein levels in the PFC compared with in matched non-carriers, in a previously available dataset in which a subset overlapped with our sequencing patients (Extended Data Fig. 1a [rid=Fig5] and Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). Twenty-four matched controls without PTC variants were selected on the basis of AD pathology, age, sex, genotype and cognitive status (Fig. 1c [rid=Fig1] , Extended Data Fig. 1b,c [rid=Fig5] , Supplementary Table 4 [rid=MOESM3] and Supplementary Note 1 [this file] ). 
After extensive quality control—including genotype–transcriptome matching to confirm sample identities and rule out potential sample swaps and correcting for batch effects (Extended Data Fig. 1e [rid=Fig5] , Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] and Supplementary Table 5 [rid=MOESM4] )—our final dataset consisted of 102,710 high-quality cells from an initial total of 150,456 cells, representing inhibitory neurons, excitatory neurons, astrocytes, microglia, oligodendrocytes and oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs; Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] ). 
We validated these expression patterns using an independent dataset (Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ), confirming significantly higher expression in neuronal versus glial populations from the human temporal cortex. 
To minimize redundancy and clearly identify biological themes, we grouped these genes into non-overlapping clusters through graph partitioning (Fig. 2a,b [rid=Fig2] , Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] and Supplementary Note 2 [this file] ). 
To assess whether transcriptional patterns associated with LoF extend to more common variants, we analysed carriers of the prevalent missense variant p.Ala1527Gly (rs3752246; minor allele frequency ≈ 0.18) within the ROSMAP cohort (Fig. 2c [rid=Fig2] and Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). 
These results are further supported by analyses of / dihedral angle distributions and secondary structure persistence, as described in Supplementary Note 3 [this file] and Extended Data Fig. 7 [rid=Fig11] . 
To experimentally validate the effects of LoF predicted by our single-cell dataset, we generated two isogenic iPS cell lines homozygous for distinct LoF variants using CRISPR–Cas9 editing (Fig. 3a [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] ). We differentiated these iPS cells into induced neurons (iNs) through doxycycline-inducible expression (Supplementary Fig. 5a [this file] ). Wild-type (WT) and LoF neurons both expressed neuronal markers, formed robust neuronal processes within 2–4 weeks (Supplementary Fig. 5b,c [this file] ), and exhibited electrophysiological activity (Extended Data Fig. 8a–e [rid=Fig12] ). 
To investigate mitochondrial alterations in LoF iNs in more depth, we analysed the expression of 1,136 genes encoding mitochondrial proteins from the MitoCarta database (Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). Upregulated genes in p.Tyr622* neurons included mitochondrial apoptosis pathway genes (such as and ) and OXPHOS subunits, previously identified in clusters PM.1 and T.10 (Fig. 3f [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Table 11 [this file] ). Conversely, downregulated genes were enriched for β-oxidation ( and ), mitochondrial metabolite transport ( ) and oxidative stress detoxification ( ) (Fig. 3f [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Table 11 [this file] ). 
Analysis of MitoCarta genes confirmed a significant reversal in the expression of genes encoding mitochondrial proteins (Extended Data Fig. 12h [rid=Fig16] ), including reduced apoptosis-related genes ( and ; Fig. 3f [rid=Fig3] ), restored mitochondrial metabolic signatures (Supplementary Table 14 [this file] ) and elevated mitochondrial fusion regulators ( and ), which support mitochondrial biogenesis and function . 
We next considered cells in marker-gene expression space defined by known major cell-type markers for human PFC: astrocytes (159 markers), excitatory neurons (113), inhibitory neurons (83), microglia (97), oligodendrocytes (179), OPCs (143) and vascular cells (124) (Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). 
Additional covariates (defined in Supplementary Note 1 [this file] ) included sex, NFT, amyloid burden, age at death, PMI, sequencing batch and status. 
Clusters were annotated by hypergeometric enrichment (Python gseapy) for Gene Ontology Biological Process pathways (Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ), using all genes in the embedding as background. 
Fast GSEA (fGSEA; R implementation ) with 10,000 permutations tested enrichment of WikiPathways gene sets (Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ) among differentially expressed genes. 
We treated gene–pathway grouping as a graph partitioning problem (Supplementary Note 2 [this file] ). Among three graph-partitioning algorithms tested (Supplementary Note 2 [this file] ), the METIS and the Kernighan–Lin algorithms showed the lowest loss and highly comparable performance (within 1.8% loss; Rand index = 0.98 after 5.0 × 10 ). 
Excitatory neurons were annotated by cortical layer using published marker gene sets (Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ) according to the procedures described in the ‘Cell type annotations’ section. Annotations were validated using independent marker genes (Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). 
Participants carrying the p.Ala1527Gly variant with available PFC snRNA-seq data from a previous study (Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ) were identified using methods described in the ‘Variant calling and ROSMAP participant selection’ section. 
Colonies were expanded, screened by genomic DNA extraction (DNeasy Blood & Tissue Kit, Qiagen, 69504) and Sanger sequencing to confirm the Y622* mutation (Supplementary Table 16 [this file] ). 
For mitochondrial health staining, live cells were incubated with MitoHealth dye (Thermo Fisher Scientific, H10295 (H10295) ) according to the manufacturer’s protocols for 30 min at 37 °C, fixed (4% paraformaldehyde/4% sucrose, 15 min, room temperature), permeabilized (0.1% Triton-X, 5 min), blocked (2% BSA, Fisher Bioreagents, BP9703) and incubated overnight at 4 °C with NeuN antibody (1:500), followed by incubation with secondary antibodies (1:1,000) for 2 h and Hoechst (1:2,000, Invitrogen, H3570) for 10 min (Supplementary Table 17 [this file] ). 
For visualization, confocal images were pseudocoloured to enhance the signal contrast; representative unprocessed images are provided in Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] . 
Differential expression analysis (edgeR, limma-voom) retained protein-coding genes expressed at ≥1 CPM in ≥1 sample, normalized counts and used linear modelling with empirical Bayes moderation with contrasts based on experimental conditions (treatment/genotype). fGSEA (10,000 permutations) of WikiPathways gene sets (Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ) was performed using ranked differentially expressed genes (score: sign(log[FC]) × −log [ ]), as described above (see the ‘Gene-set enrichment and Kernighan–Lin pathway clustering’ section).

context_description:
To complement this in situ analysis, PFC samples were subfractionated into a plaque-enriched insoluble fraction and a soluble fraction devoid of amyloid plaques (Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] ). 
Selective removal of Li from the mouse diet (a 92% reduction) led to an 89% reduction in mean serum Li and a 47–52% reduction in mean cortical Li in the non-plaque fraction (Extended Data Fig. 2a–c [rid=Fig7] and Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] ). 
We analysed 64,772 and 54,374 high-quality nuclei from Li-deficient and control mice, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] ). Based on the expression of previously validated cell-type-specific markers (Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] ), the relative abundance of the resolved cell types was unchanged after 5 weeks of Li deficiency (Fig. 3a [rid=Fig3] ). 
In astrocytes, pathways of neurodegeneration, electron transport chain and monovalent cation transport were upregulated (Supplementary Fig. 5 [this file] and Supplementary Tables 5 [rid=MOESM7] and 6 [rid=MOESM8] ). Proteomic analysis of the hippocampus in Li-deficient 3xTg mice showed significantly reduced abundance of synaptic and myelin protein components and increased abundance of proteins involved in neuroinflammation, lipid metabolism and mitochondrial membrane organization (Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] and Supplementary Table 7 [rid=MOESM9] ). 
Reduced abundance of synaptic proteins was confirmed by proteomic analysis of the Li-deficient 3xTg hippocampus (Supplementary Fig. 6a,b [this file] and Supplementary Table 7 [rid=MOESM9] ). 
Li deficiency downregulated the expression of myelin-related genes in oligodendrocytes and reduced the abundance of myelin-associated proteins (Fig. 3c,d [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Fig. 6b [this file] ). 
The snRNA-seq analysis of Li deficiency showed a reduction in the number of microglia expressing the gene , which encodes a homeostatic marker, and an increase in microglia expressing (Supplementary Fig. 7a [this file] ), similar to the reactive microglial state observed in AD . Isolated microglia showed a high degree of purity and did not exhibit stress-related markers (Supplementary Fig. 7b,c [this file] ). RNA sequencing showed major transcriptome changes in microglia associated with Li deficiency in both 3xTg and wild-type mice with highly significant overlap (Supplementary Tables 9 [this file1] – 12 [this file4] ). Genes downregulated by Li deficiency were enriched in the GO terms DNA damage response, cellular response to stress, import into cell and protein catabolic process (Fig. 4a,b [rid=Fig4] and Supplementary Table 12 [this file4] ). 
Li deficiency also increased the density of CD68 reactive microglia in a second transgenic AD mouse model, J20 (Supplementary Fig. 7d [this file] ). 
To further explore the Li–Aβ interaction in vivo, LiO and LiC were administered to J20 and 3xTg mice at a low dose in the drinking water (4.3 μEq l Li), resulting in a serum Li level in the physiological concentration range observed in ageing humans and mice (Supplementary Fig. 8a,c,d [this file] , Extended Data Fig. 1c [rid=Fig6] and Methods [rid=Sec11] ). Serum and hippocampal Li levels were not significantly different after administration of low-dose LiO or LiC (Supplementary Fig. 8a,b [this file] ). 
LiO did not significantly affect swimming speed, visual platform localization or locomotor performance in the open-field test (Extended Data Fig. 10d–h [rid=Fig15] and Supplementary Fig. 9a–f [this file] ). 
This resulted in a modest elevation of mean serum and cortical Li levels that overlap with the range of endogenous Li in untreated mice (Supplementary Fig. 10a [this file] ). 
Administration of LiO to wild-type mice prevented age-related loss of dendritic spines in CA1 and CA3 hippocampal neurons, whereas the control salt NaO had no significant effect (Supplementary Fig. 10b [this file] ). Notably, long-term administration of LiO to ageing wild-type, 3xTg or J20 mice did not alter serum levels of blood urea nitrogen, creatinine or thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) (Supplementary Fig. 11 [this file] ). 
To image subfractionated Aβ and phospho-tau (Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] ), 10 μl of the freshly collected plaque-enriched and non-plaque fractions was layered onto albumin-coated glass slides and allowed to dry overnight. 
Examples of cell-type markers include (excitatory neurons), (granule cells), and (inhibitory neurons), (oligodendrocytes), , (astrocytes), (OPCs), (pericytes), and (microglia), and (endothelial cells), and (choroid plexus cells; Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] ). 
To validate the purity of the isolated microglia, we determined that microglial markers ( , and ) were strongly enriched, whereas neuronal ( and ), astrocytic ( and ) and oligodendrocyte ( and ) marker genes were negligibly expressed (Supplementary Fig. 7b,c [this file] ). We also verified that markers of ex vivo microglia activation ( , , and ) were minimally expressed in our samples (Supplementary Fig. 7b,c [this file] ). Differential gene expression analysis was done using DESeq2 (ref. ) to identify DEGs between Li-deficient and control microglia, with an adjusted value cut-off of 0.05 (Supplementary Tables 10 [this file2] and 11 [this file3] ). Results are summarized in Fig. 4a [rid=Fig4] and provided in Supplementary Table 12 [this file4] .

Relative to AL, the CR group had significantly less mean fat mass in all biosample cohorts at both 12M and 24M ( value range 0.028 to <1e-02) ( Figures S1 [this file] A–S1C). There were no significant differences in fat free mass between treatment groups, with the exception of the muscle cohort at 24M, for which CR participants had significantly less fat free mass compared with AL ( = 0.02) ( Figures S1 [this file] D–S1F). 
Network analysis of miR-4659a-3p identified CR-linked pathways involved in cellular senescence, PI3K/AKT activation, adaptive immune system, Ca2+ pathway, signaling by ErbB and Wnt, metabolism of nitric oxide, eNOS activation and regulation, and oxidative stress-induce senescence ( Tables S1 [this file] , S2 [rid=mmc2] A, S2 [rid=mmc3] B, and S3 [rid=mmc4] A–S3D). Network and enrichment analyses based on miR-143-5p identified numerous mRNA targets and CR-linked pathways including ERK/MAPK/RAF target signaling, innate immune system, glucagon signaling in metabolic regulation, glycosaminoglycan metabolism, regulation of cytoskeletal remodeling, signaling by TGF-beta receptor complex, and post-translational protein modification ( Tables S1 [this file] , S2 [rid=mmc2] A, S2 [rid=mmc3] B, and S3 [rid=mmc4] A–S3E). 
Of these, we noted several with established associations in longevity, aging, and CR-related research: circadian/BMAL1 clock, IGF1R and IRS-mediated signaling, aging, regulation of cell cycle and growth, insulin signaling, MAPK/ERK, PI3K/AKT/p53, and ErbB signaling, oxidative stress-induced senescence, learning and memory, androgen receptor signaling, carbohydrate-related processes, gluconeogenesis, regulation of actin cytoskeleton, and neurotrophin signaling ( Tables S1 [this file] , S2 [rid=mmc2] A, and S3 [rid=mmc4] A–S3E). 
While these findings reinforce the tissue-specific nature of the response to caloric restriction (CR), they do not exclude the possibility that larger sample sizes or other methodological considerations could reveal limited overlap ( Table S4 [this file] ). 
With respect to metabolic-signaling (key CR-related pathways), we observed several perturbed pathways in plasma: gluconeogenesis, ceramide, and fatty acid/lipid metabolism; in muscle: glucagon, glyoxylate, dicarboxylate, and propanoate metabolism; and in both, plasma and muscle: biotin metabolism ( Tables S1 [this file] and S3 [rid=mmc4] A–S3E). 
The higher concordance of 24M human data with prolonged CR in rhesus monkeys suggests that 24M data more effectively captures chronic changes, aligning more closely with the physiological responses observed during extended periods of dietary intervention ( Table S5 [this file] ). 
Given that the biosample cohorts for plasma, muscle, and adipose did not fully overlap at either timepoint interval (BL:12 and BL:24—with 25 individuals contributing all three tissue types at BL:12M and 12 individuals at BL:24M—we conducted a sensitivity analysis restricted to the 25 fully sampled individuals at 12M to assess the consistency of tissue-specific responses ( Table S4 [this file] ). 
The curated list of CR-linked pathways was developed from a thorough literature search using the terms ‘caloric/dietary restriction’ and ‘aging’ / ‘longevity’, and was further filtered to only include ‘animal’ or ‘human’ studies ( Table S1 [this file] ).
