The resulting recombinant proteins, 2xMBD2-Tn5, NTD-MeCP2-IDR-Tn5 (NTD-N-terminal domain, IDR-intrinsically disordered region), 2xMeCP2-Tn5, and 4xMeCP2-Tn5, were expressed in and subsequently purified using a chitin resin to ensure high purity (Supplementary Fig. 1a, b [this file] ). 
All constructs show similar enrichment patterns ( = 2 per construct, see Supplementary Fig. 2a [this file] for correlation analysis). 
Initial characterization in human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) (Supplementary Fig. 1c–f [this file] ) revealed strong enrichment in CpG-rich regions across all variants (Fig. 1b [rid=Fig1] ). The individual domain combinations show remarkably similar enrichment profiles, with Pearson correlations >0.8 between biological replicates and different constructs, and a comparable fraction of reads in peaks (FRiP scores >0.35) (Fig. 1b, c [rid=Fig1] , and Supplementary Fig. 2a–e [this file] ), and outperformed CUT&Tag using an antibody against 5-Methyl-Cytosine (Supplementary Fig. 2a, b [this file] ). Across all constructs, about 2000 peaks were shared, and roughly 7000 peaks overlapped specifically between 2xMBD2 and 2xMeCP2 (Supplementary Fig. 2d [this file] ). By contrast, using an antibody against 5-Methyl-Cytosine yielded only 32 detectable peaks, indicating that this approach does not work on nuclei (Supplementary Fig. 2b, d [this file] ). 
Visual inspection confirmed clear enrichments in highly methylated regions as compared to public whole-genome bisulfite sequencing data on human embryonic stem cells (Fig. 1c [rid=Fig1] ), omitting CpGs with high accessibility as measured by ATAC-Seq and lacking DNA methylation (Supplementary Fig. 2b [this file] ). 
We used ChIP-Seeker to further characterize genomic regions showing high enrichment of C CUT&Tag signal and confirmed the enrichment in gene bodies and promoters (Supplementary Fig. 2e [this file] ). We further validated our ChromHMM annotation with CUT&Tag measurements of histone modifications from iPSCs, ATAC-Seq and a Tn5 coupled to the CXXC-domain of MLL1 that recognizes unmethylated CpG island (unC CUT&Tag, Fig. 1d [rid=Fig1] and Supplementary Fig. 2f–i [this file] ). 
Quantitative analysis revealed that MBD-fusion proteins recognize regions with CpG methylation between 40–100% (Fig. 1e [rid=Fig1] ), contrasting sharply with histone modification peaks, which showed no CpG methylation enrichment except for H3K9me3 (Fig. 1e [rid=Fig1] and Supplementary Fig. 2j [this file] ). 
Based on superior binding affinity, correlation with bisulfite sequencing, higher dynamic range, and peak detection, we selected 2×MBD2-Tn5 for detailed characterization (Fig. 1f [rid=Fig1] , Supplementary Fig. 2c, d [this file] , Supplementary Data 1 [rid=MOESM3] contains all metadata) . We determined 600 ng of Tn5 on 50–200 k nuclei as the optimal starting amount (Supplementary Fig. 3a, b [this file] ). 
C CUT&Tag performed efficiently on isolated DNA (Supplementary Fig. 3c–k [this file] ), and we determined 600 ng of Tn5 on 5 to 50 ng of DNA as the optimal range (Supplementary Fig. 3f, g [this file] ). The methylation enrichment signals showed high overlap with those from intact nuclei (Supplementary Fig. 3h–k [this file] ). Of these, 2800 peaks are unique to nuclei, whereas 17,800 are unique to isolated DNA (Supplementary Fig. 3h [this file] ). The binding profile of DNA methylation from isolated DNA is also comparable to previously established technologies (MeDIP, MBD-Seq) relying on pulldowns and classical library preparation involving end repair and adapter ligation (Supplementary Fig. 4a–e [this file] ). 
See Supplementary Fig. 5f [this file] and Source Data for gene ontology terms on the differential regions. 
Overall, treatment with GSK3484862 reduced global DNA methylation from 80% to 20% (Supplementary Fig. 5a, b [this file] ). Residual peaks also exhibit high CpG content, indicating that the observed binding likely occurs at genuinely methylated regions rather than reflecting nonspecific transposition (Supplementary Fig. 5c, d [this file] ). 
We found an increase in H3K27me3 at loci depleted in DNA methylation (Fig. 2b [rid=Fig2] ) , often coinciding with CpG islands (Fig. 2c [rid=Fig2] and Supplementary Fig. 5e [this file] ). When we analyzed the genome-wide distribution of H3K27me3, we found that H3K27me3 increased at Polycomb-responsive regions upon DNA methylation depletion, as well as many enhancers and promoters (Fig. 2d [rid=Fig2] ) associated with morphogenesis and regulation of membrane potential (Supplementary Fig. 5f [this file] , Source Data). 
Bisulfite and enzymatic conversion of libraries from both nuclei and genomic DNA yielded signal distributions nearly identical to unconverted libraries (Fig. 3b, c [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Fig. 6a, b [this file] ), indicating no substantial bias introduction. 
We differentiated iPSCs into multi-region brain organoids, collecting samples at day 16 (primarily neuroepithelium) and day 210 (mixed neuronal populations with emerging astrocytes) (Fig. 4a [rid=Fig4] and Supplementary Fig. 7a [this file] ). Differential peak analysis revealed systematic methylation changes during neural development (Fig. 4b [rid=Fig4] and Supplementary Fig. 7b [this file] ). 
We benchmarked the DNA-methylation dynamics against published WGBS data (Supplementary Fig. 7c [this file] ). 
Using 22 h post-fertilization (hpf) zebrafish embryos, we successfully profiled genome-wide DNA methylation patterns using C CUT&Tag (Supplementary Fig. 8a–c [this file] ). We benchmarked these data against previously published MethylCap and whole-genome methylation datasets from zebrafish embryos (Supplementary Fig. 8b–d [this file] ). Moreover, peaks identified by both methods showed elevated DNA methylation levels and CG content compared to shuffled control regions and displayed highly similar genomic distributions, as assessed using ChIPseeker (Supplementary Fig. 8e [this file] ).

A total of 1556 participants received study medication (SAF) for a mean (SD) duration of 7.0 (4.4) months (exposure with umibecestat of 6.9 [4.4] months and with placebo of 7.1 [4.3] months; Table S2 [this file] ) and were included in this pooled analysis (umibecestat pooled, = 937; umibecestat 50 mg, = 704; umibecestat 15 mg, = 233; placebo, = 619; Figure 1 [rid=alz14237-fig-0001] ).

Study clinicians screened participants for psychological readiness to receive results; participants were eligible if they had (1) a Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS) score of 6 or lower (participants with scores 7–10 could be included based on investigator judgement) and (2) a Modified State-Trait Anxiety Inventory for adults (STAI-AD) score of 17 or lower (participants with scores of 18 or 19 could be included based on investigator judgement; appendix [this file] pp 2, 10). 
These experienced health-care providers received training at investigator meetings on how to conduct the disclosure sessions, including guidance regarding the lifetime risk estimates provided by the study, calculated for each genotype, and talking points to guide the disclosure session ( appendix [this file] pp 11–13). 
Scores and disclosure related adverse events were reviewed by the independent Disclosure Monitoring Advisory Group (DMAG; appendix [this file] p 14). Other measures collected to characterise the impact of disclosure included knowledge of genetic disease, perceived risk (rated on a scale of 0–100% believed chance of developing Alzheimer’s disease), perceived threat of Alzheimer’s disease, and test-related distress using the Impact of Genetic Testing in Alzheimer’s Disease (IGT-AD) scale ( appendix [this file] pp 15–17). 
Due to the early termination, missing data structurally increased at later timepoints ( appendix [this file] p 18). 
Multivariable longitudinal associations of baseline variables with missing data (with non-missing data as the reference) by group are described in the appendix [this file] (p 19). 
Following disclosure, there were differences on several assessments by group ( table 3 [rid=T3] ; appendix [this file] pp 20). 2–7 days after disclosure, there was an increase in scores for knowledge of genetic disease, and this increase varied by group. homozygotes had the greatest observed increase in mean knowledge scores (adjusted mean change score difference [β]=0·59, 95% CI 0·28–0·91, compared with non-carriers; table 3 [rid=T3] and appendix [this file] pp 21–22). 
There was an increase in DSD scores 2–7 days after disclosure in all groups, with homozygotes having significantly greater change from baseline than heterozygotes (β=1·76, 95% CI 1·28–2·24) and non-carriers (β =1·55, 1·06–2·05), although unstandardised effect sizes were less than 0·5 baseline standard deviations ( table 3 [rid=T3] ; appendix [this file] pp 21–22). 
At 2–7 days after disclosure, homozygotes reported greater levels of test-related distress (IGT-AD) compared with heterozygotes (β=6·45, 95% CI 5·65–7·24) and non-carriers (β=12·14, 11·34–12·94; appendix [this file] pp 21–22). 
At 2–7 days after disclosure, homozygotes perceived their risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease as increased, on average, compared with baseline; heterozygotes and non-carriers perceived their risk as decreased ( appendix [this file] pp 21–22). 
We observed an dose-dependent change in perceived threat (ie, worry about developing Alzheimer’s disease) at 2–7 days after disclosure, with non-carriers having greater score decrease than homozygotes (β=−1·22, 95% CI −0·92 to −1·52) and heterozygotes (β=−0·69, −0·86 to −0·52), and heterozygotes having a greater decrease than homozygotes (β=−0·53, −0·81 to −0·24; appendix [this file] pp 21–22). 
Few participants (<0·50% or n<36 at each period) had GDS scores indicating moderate severity of depressive symptoms (scores 9–11), and even fewer had scores suggestive of severe symptoms (scores 12–15, n<11 at each period; table 4 [rid=T4] ; appendix [this file] pp 38–40). Severe depressive symptoms were observed in all three genotype groups ( table 4 [rid=T4] ; appendix [this file] pp 38–40). 
It is noteworthy that, after disclosure, heterozygotes and non-carriers believed their chances of developing Alzheimer’s disease were far greater than the provided risk estimates ( appendix [this file] p 12), even after adjusting for key variables.

The outline of the work is shown in Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] c, and the specific estimation approaches tested are described in Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S1. 
The demographic information of the individuals, as well as RNA quality metrics and tissue sample characteristics, are provided in Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S2 and Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] c. 
For 42/49 subjects, two different tissue samples were sent for sequencing, while the same tissue extract was sequenced twice for seven of the individuals (Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] c, Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S2). 
For the purpose of this analysis, we leveraged two RNA-seq datasets from PFC tissue samples of 49 individuals, comprising Parkinson’s disease patients and controls (Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] c, Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S2). These methods were selected because they have substantial differences in multiple parameters that can impact the performance of estimation approaches such as cell type markers, estimation algorithm and the type of outcome (Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S1), as well as publication date (2015–2020) and general popularity. 
However, upon closer examination, the correlation values varied between cell types (Additional file 1 [this file] : Fig. S1a). The median estimated proportion of neurons, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes produced by the three applicable methods was of similar magnitude and comparable to the proportions expected based on IHC data (Additional file 1 [this file] : Fig. S1b). 
For this purpose, we leveraged the data available from 42 individuals for which RNA-seq was carried out twice in two different (but neighbouring) tissue samples from the same Brodmann area, and seven individuals for which the same tissue sample RNA extract was sequenced twice (Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] c, Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S2). 
In contrast, when we compared transcriptomics-based and WGBS-based estimates derived from the same tissue extracts (Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] c, Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S2), we observed minimal to no correlation between the methods (IQR − 0.11–0.09), with the single exception of oligodendrocytes, for which moderate correlation was observed ( = 0.69, = 0.67, Figs. 2 [rid=Fig2] d and 3 [rid=Fig3] ). 
In the AD dataset, 52, 50, 38, 38 and 29%, out of the differentially acetylated regions identified based on NoCellAdjustment, CETS_Shuffled, CETS, MSPneuron and MSPall models, respectively, overlapped with a unique cell type-specific promoter/enhancer region (Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S3).

We observed no correlation between the number of Numts detected in each sample and its genomic sequence coverage (r = 0.003, S1 Table [this file] ), indicating that our results are robust across a range of sequence depths [ 59 [rid=pbio.3002723.ref059] ]. The detected Numts ranged from 22 bp to 8,172 bp in length, with a median of 73 bp, a mean of 1,169 bp, and s.d. 1,882 bp ( S1 Table [this file] ), consistent with previous results from population-scale data in blood DNA [ 4 [rid=pbio.3002723.ref004] , 6 [rid=pbio.3002723.ref006] , 7 [rid=pbio.3002723.ref007] ]. 
Given the existence of mitochondrial DNA defects alterations in the human brain with cognitive decline [ 60 [rid=pbio.3002723.ref060] ], we next stratified individuals with tissue-specific Numts by their cognitive status into no cognitive impairment (NCI), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and Alzheimer’s dementia (AD, COGDX score, Methods, S1 [this file] and S2 [rid=pbio.3002723.s002] Tables). 
We obtained these 1,187 samples from 1,170 individuals, where only 17 participants in the data set contributed 2 tissue different samples to the sequencing data ( S1 [this file] and S3 [rid=pbio.3002723.s003] Tables). All the alignment statistics are presented in S1 Table [this file] , along with the clinical characteristics of the study participants.

To determine the pathways and molecular processes downstream of genetic risk for late‐onset AD (LOAD) in human neurons, we performed unbiased proteomic profiling by TMT‐MS of iNs from 53 ROSMAP participants (Figure 1A [rid=alz13680-fig-0001] , Supplemental Tables S1, S2 [this file] ). IPSC models capture genetic risk and resilience factors from the person from whom they were derived, and in this cohort a range of PRS for LOAD is represented (Figure 1B [rid=alz13680-fig-0001] , Supplemental Table S1 [this file] ). Strikingly, the only KEGG (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes) gene set negatively associated with LOAD PRS was “proteasome” (FDR = 0.017) (Figure 1C [rid=alz13680-fig-0001] , Supplemental Table S3 [this file] ). Differential protein analysis comparing iNs from non‐cognitively impaired (NCI) individuals ( = 35) and those from AD individuals ( = 18) revealed 760 differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) defined by an adjusted ‐value < 0.05 and a logFC of > 0.25 or < −0.25 (Supplemental Table S4 [this file] ). 
Of note, chymotrypsin‐like activity is the rate‐limiting catalytic site in proteasomal proteolysis.[rid=alz13680-bib-0045] Across ROSMAP iNs, a spectrum of basal proteasome activity was observed (Figure 2B [rid=alz13680-fig-0002] , Supplemental Table S5 [this file] ). Rather, analyses of the correlation between TMT‐MS profiles and proteasome activity revealed that the top three associated pathways were “oxidative phosphorylation,” “Parkinson's disease,” and “Alzheimer's disease,” each of which was elevated with lower proteasome activity (Figure 2E [rid=alz13680-fig-0002] , Supplemental Tables S6, S7 [this file] ). 
Thus, we next performed a deeper analysis of tau to look at both the major forms of 50‐60 kDa (MAJ) tau, as well as the high molecular weight (HMW) form of aggregated tau previously reported by us[rid=alz13680-bib-0028] and others.[rid=alz13680-bib-0046] In these Western blot analyses, we also examined different phospho‐epitopes to determine whether distinct proteoforms of tau are differentially associated with particular proteasome components (Figures 3F–J [rid=alz13680-fig-0003] , see Supplemental Figure 3 [rid=alz13680-supitem-0003] for representative Western blots for each epitope, Supplemental Table S8 [this file] for all quantifications). 
Interestingly, TMT‐MS analyses revealed reduced levels of additional proteasome subunits (Figure 4G [rid=alz13680-fig-0004] , Supplemental Tables S9 [this file] , S10), supporting prior findings that mutations lead to tau accumulation and proteasome disruption. Interestingly, gene sets involved in neuronal activity (KEGG long‐term potentiation, KEGG long‐term depression) are positively associated with mutation (Supplemental Table S11 [this file] ), supporting the prior finding that proteasome inhibition prevents the turnover of synaptic proteins that mediate synaptic activity.[rid=alz13680-bib-0051] 
To explore all protein‐level changes in human neurons with mild proteasome inhibition, we first examined the proteomic profile of iNs treated with 5 nM bortezomib for 72 h (Supplemental Table S12 [this file] ). 5 nM was chosen based on findings that bortezomib inhibits proteasome‐mediated intracellular proteolysis of long‐lived proteins with a concentration of ∼0.1 μM that inhibits 50% of the proteolysis and has been shown to kill cells at 24 and 48 h with IC50s of 100 and 20 nM, respectively.[rid=alz13680-bib-0052] At 72 h, neuronal morphology remained grossly intact (Supplemental Figure 4A [rid=alz13680-supitem-0004] ), and the level of apoptosis regulators Bax and p53 were unaltered (Supplemental Figure 4B [rid=alz13680-supitem-0004] ), while proteasome activity was reduced by 75% with an accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins (Figure 5B,C [rid=alz13680-fig-0005] , Supplemental Figure 4C [rid=alz13680-supitem-0004] ). It’s important to note that astrocytes are quite heterogeneous, displaying multiple morphologies within the same well ( Figure S1D [this file] ). While the majority of astrocytes in maturation media exhibited morphologies similar to those shown in Figure 1D [rid=F1] , a smaller subset displayed more extensive branching ( Figure S1D [this file] ), and this population was reduced in all other media conditions tested. 
By the end of the co-culture period (day 27), the cultures consisted of an approximate ratio of 6:2:3 (iNs:iAs:iMGs) ( Figures 1G [rid=F1] and S1E [this file] ), likely reflecting differences in cell adhesion and proliferation across cell types (see STAR Methods [rid=S13] for more details). To determine the optimal media for TC, we compared TCM1, TCM4, and TCM5 across paired MCs and TCs ( Figures S1F [this file] and S1G [this file] ). In TCM1, we observed a reduced expression of microglia markers and a more amoeboid morphology ( Figures S1F [this file] and S1G [this file] ). Based on this observation, we established TCM6, which consists of a 1:1 ratio of BrainPhys to DMEM/F12/NBM and includes all iA supplements and growth factors except dbcAMP ( Figure S1H [this file] ; Table S2 [rid=SD3] ). However, both media conditions yielded similar results, with robust expression of cell-specific markers and characteristic star-like morphology of astrocytes ( Figures S1I [this file] and S1J [this file] ). 
Cells in each culture condition showed minimal expression of pluripotency markers and an enrichment of excitatory neuron markers for iNs, astrocyte markers for iAs, and microglial markers for iMGs ( Figures S2A [this file] – S2G [this file] ). Marker genes from clusters identified in our previous analysis also labeled distinct clusters of iAs in this dataset ( Figure S2F [this file] ). 
Next, we performed differential expression analysis between MCs and TCs ( Figure S2H [this file] ; Table S3 [rid=SD4] ) to identify cell-type-specific responses to co-culture. Building on this observation, we used multielectrode array (MEA) recordings to compare mean firing rate and network dynamics in MCs and TCs ( Figures 2J [rid=F2] – 2M [rid=F2] and S3A [this file] – S3C [this file] ). Neuronal firing (mean firing rate) was consistently higher in TCs compared to MCs across two glial genetic backgrounds ( Figures 2J [rid=F2] and S3A [this file] ), with this difference emerging only after glial introduction and persisting thereafter. To assess network connectivity, we employed the MATLAB-based MEA Network Analysis Pipeline (MEA-NAP), revealing that mean edge weight—a measure of electrode-to-electrode connection strength—was also elevated in TCs ( Figures 2L [rid=F2] – 2M [rid=F2] , S3B [this file] , and S3C [this file] ). 
To validate this observation, we measured levels of interleukin-1β (IL-1β) and tumor necrosis factor (TNF) in the media from paired glial MCs and TCs and found that the secreted levels of these cytokines were reduced in TCs ( Figures 3B [rid=F3] , S3D [this file] , and S3E [this file] ). 
Since microglial morphology is highly dynamic in response to environmental stimuli and reflects their functional state (outlined in Paolicelli et al. ), these transcriptomic changes align with alterations in inflammatory signaling and correspond to the pronounced morphological differences observed between paired iMG MCs and TCs ( Figures 4A [rid=F4] and S3F [this file] ). 
We then performed differential gene expression analysis to compare MC and TC within microglial cell clusters ( Figures 4B [rid=F4] and 4C [rid=F4] ; Table S3 [rid=SD4] ), within neuron clusters ( Figures S3G [this file] and S3I [this file] ; Table S3 [rid=SD4] ), and within astrocyte clusters ( Figures S3H [this file] and S3J [this file] ; Table S3 [rid=SD4] ). Interestingly, within astrocytes, a disease-associated-like cluster was also identified (cluster 3, expressing , , , , , , and ) as well as a synapse-associated state (cluster 1, expressing , , , and ) ( Figure S3J [this file] ; Table S3 [rid=SD4] ). 
Six of the top 20 DAM markers defining cluster 3 at the RNA level ( Table S3 [rid=SD4] ) were detected in the secretome dataset, and among these, SPP1, APOE, LIPA, ASAH1, and PSAP were all upregulated at the protein level in TCs ( Figures 4E [rid=F4] and S4A [this file] ). However, since APOE is more highly expressed in astrocytes and both SPP1 and APOE were also upregulated in iAs in TCs ( Figures S2I [this file] , S4B [this file] , and S4C [this file] ), it is difficult to conclusively determine the proportion of microglial cell- versus astrocyte-secreted levels in the TC. Therefore, we measured the levels of TREM2 and GPNMB, two DAM markers more restricted to microglial expression ( Figures S2I [this file] , S4D [this file] , and S4E [this file] ). 
In accord, we found that APOE protein levels also decreased following treatment of TCs with TNF + IL-1α + C1q ( Figure 5N [rid=F5] ), while SPP1 and GPNMB levels were not significantly changed ( Figures S4F [this file] and S4G [this file] ). 
Next, we evaluated the capacity of our TC model to elicit both known and yet-to-be discovered transcriptional responses in microglia upon exposure to high levels of Aβ by establishing TCs with iNs carrying fAD mutations ( Figures 6A [rid=F6] – 6C [rid=F6] and S5A [this file] – S5F [this file] ). Compared with isogenic WT iNs, TCs containing fAD iNs exhibited elevated Aβ42 and Aβ40 levels in the media, along with an increased Aβ42:40 ratio ( Figures 6D [rid=F6] , 6E [rid=F6] , and S5G [this file] ). Additionally, microglia clustered around X34-labeled Aβ in fAD cultures ( Figure S5H [this file] ). 
We performed scRNA-seq to compare WT and fAD TCs and observed notable shifts in cellular cluster compositions within each major cell type ( Figures 6H [rid=F6] , 7A [rid=F7] – 7C [rid=F7] , and S6A [this file] – S6H [this file] ; Table S6 [rid=SD7] ). At the protein level, TREM2, APOE, SPP1, and GPNMB also were downregulated ( Figures 7E [rid=F7] – 7G [rid=F7] and S7A [this file] – S7C [this file] ), and these changes required the presence of astrocytes ( Figures 7H [rid=F7] , 7I [rid=F7] , S7D [this file] , and S7E [this file] ). After clustering (Supplementary Fig. 1a–e [this file] ), a total of 37,943 cells were annotated into 23 clusters using a predefined set of marker genes (Supplementary Fig. 1c [this file] ). 
To reveal heterogeneity within oligodendrocytes, we grouped the aforementioned oligodendrocytes into six classes described in a published database , as follows (Fig. 1a [rid=Fig1] and Supplementary Fig. 2a [this file] –d and 3a [this file] ): (1) Differentiation-committed oligodendrocyte precursors (COPs) and newly formed oligodendrocytes (NFOL) that express Sox6, Pdgfra, and Cspg4. (2) Myelin-forming oligodendrocytes (MFOL) that express Ctps, Ablims, and Thbs3. (3) Mature oligodendrocytes 1, 2 (MOL 1, 2) that express Il33, Ptgds, and Opalin. (4) Mature oligodendrocytes 3, 4 (MOL 3, 4) that express Klk6, S100b, Anxa5, Cd59a and Mgst3. Moreover, we discovered an additional oligodendrocyte cluster, which gradually increased in the 3-, 6-month-old App KI mice (Fig. 1b–d [rid=Fig1] and Supplementary Fig. 2e [this file] ). This cluster was present in the UMAP plot even with down-sampled data (400, 1,200, and 2,400 cells) (Supplementary Fig. 2f [this file] ). Remarkably, we found that this cluster shared some signatures with MOL2, while Alzheimer’s disease risk factors such as C4b, Apoe and Cd74 are strongly expressed (Supplementary Fig. 2c [this file] , 3a [this file] , 3b [this file] , and Source data file). 
We further confirmed the lineage transitions of DAOs and homeostatic MOLs from COP and NFOL in control and AD brains (Fig. 1e–g [rid=Fig1] and Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] ), but density from the DAO cluster exclusively appeared in 3 and 6-month-old AD brains (Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] g). 
We reanalyzed previously published single-cell transcriptome datasets from postmortem AD brains (Supplementary Fig. 5a–c [this file] ) . 
Notably, consistent with scRNA-seq results, we observed a significant increase in Mbp + , Cd74+ oligodendrocytes in 3- and 6-month-old App KI and 6-month-old 5xFAD mice, whereas the number of NeuroD1+ post-mitotic neurons significantly decreased (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] a, b [rid=Fig2] , Supplementary Fig. 6a–c [this file] , and Supplementary Fig. 7a [this file] , b [this file] ). We further confirmed an increase in Cd74+ and Oligo2+ AD-associated oligodendrocytes in App KI mice using flow cytometry (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] c, d [rid=Fig2] , and Supplementary Fig. 6d [this file] ). 
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analysis revealed that 6-month-old App KI mice exhibited a thinner myelin layer relative to the axon diameter (Fig. 2e [rid=Fig2] and supplementary fig. 8 [this file] ). 
Consistently, we found a significant increase in Mbp+ and Cd74+ DAOs in the hippocampus of premature progeria (6-month-old) and 13-month-old mice (Supplementary Fig. 9a–d [this file] ), whereas the number of NeuroD1-positive post-mitotic neurons decreased in the hippocampus of 13-month-old mice (Supplementary Fig. 9e and f [this file] ). We further confirmed that the genes enriched in DAOs were highly correlated with gene signatures shown in the aged human brain (Supplementary Fig. 10a, b [this file] ), indicating that Cd74-positive DAOs increased in the aged brains and had transcriptional profiles more similar to the aged human brain. 
In particular, we found significant alternations in the transcriptional profiles between DAOs and MOL 3/4 clusters and GO-term of up-regulated genes in DAO versus MOL3/4 showed the interleukin & chemokine production and ERK signaling (Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] a and c [rid=Fig3] ), which was also confirmed during the disease progression in AD mice brain (Supplementary Fig. 11a, b [this file] ). 
Additionally, we determined the transcriptional correlation between DAOs and DAMs. We first identified microglia with a high DAM module score based on previously published DAM signatures (Supplementary Fig. 1e [this file] , 12a, b [this file] ), that gradually increased during AD progression (Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] e, f [rid=Fig3] , and Supplementary Fig. 12c [this file] ). 
Supplementary Fig. 13a–c [this file] shows efficient inhibition of phosphor 44/42 MAPK signaling in primary oligodendrocytes upon treatment with 200 ng/ml SCH772984, a specific Erk1 and Erk2 inhibitor. Remarkably, oligodendrocytes treated with SCH772984 exhibited a significant increase in Mbp+ branching compared with the controls, whereas the number of Cd74+ cells significantly decreased (Supplementary Fig. 13d [this file] , 13e [this file] , and Fig. 4a–c [rid=Fig4] ). 
First, in order to examine the potential interactions between DAOs and other neuronal cell types, AD DAOs were co-cultured with AD neurons, astrocytes, and microglia treated with SCH772984 (Supplementary Fig. 14a [this file] ). We found that AD DAOs with other neuronal cell types did not increase the number of Mbp+ branches in the presence and absence of SCH772984 treatment (Supplementary Fig. 14b–f [this file] ), suggesting that inhibition of ERK/MAPK signaling in other neuronal cell types did not contribute to the phenotypic changes in DAOs (Fig. 4d–f [rid=Fig4] ). Moreover, to investigate whether other neural cell types can contribute to the AD-associated phenotypes via ERK signaling, each of the neurons, microglia, astrocytes and oligodendrocytes isolated from AD mice were subjected to SCH772984 treatment, and AD pathology was determined after co-culture with the remaining untreated AD neuronal cell types (Supplementary Fig. 15a [this file] ). Remarkably, we found that ERK1/2-inhibited oligodendrocytes significantly diminished the Aβ42/40 ratio in the AD primary neuronal cultures (Supplementary Fig. 15b [this file] ). Also, we observed a decrease in the amyloidogenic processing marker C99 in the AD neuronal cultures with SCH772984 treatment (Supplementary Fig. 15c–e [this file] ), indicating that AD oligodendrocytes predominantly contribute to the pathophysiology of AD via ERK signaling. 
Consistent with previous results, systemic administration of SCH772984 significantly reduced the occurrence of DAOs in the hippocampus of App KI mice (Fig. 5b, c [rid=Fig5] , and Supplementary Fig. 16a–d [this file] ) but not Cd74 + Iba1+ microglia (Supplementary Fig. 16c, d [this file] ). 
Moreover, we confirmed a decrease in the number of Aβ plaques (Fig. 5m, n [rid=Fig5] ), coupled with an increase in the number of NeuroD1+ cells in the SCH772984-treated AD mouse hippocampus (Supplementary Fig. 16e, f [this file] ).

Memory (54 studies) and executive function (39 studies) were most frequently assessed when defining SCA, typically using the Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test (AVLT, 25 studies) and the Trail-Making Test Part B (TMT-B, 31 ­studies) ( Table S4 [this file] ). 
Among 20 included studies examining genetic/epigenetic biomarkers ( Table 2 [rid=gnaf277-T2] and Table S5 [this file] ), 14 investigated the 4 carrier rate. 
(+) Superagers had greater cortical thickness in multiple regions than same-age controls and even had similar cortical thickness with young controls, especially in the cingulate cortex, prefrontal cortex, etc. (Please refer to Table S10 [this file] for detailed regions.) 
(+) Superagers had greater GMV than controls in multiple regions, including the medial temporal area, cingulate cortex, middle frontal cortex, etc. (Please refer to Table S10 [this file] for detailed regions.) 
(+) Superagers had higher FA and lower MD, RD, and AD than controls in multiple fibers, including the cingulum bundle, the corpus callosum, etc. (Please refer to Table S11 [this file] for detailed fibers.) 
Core AD biomarkers, including amyloid β (Aβ ), total tau protein (t-tau), and phosphorylated tau protein (p-tau) found in CSF or peripheral plasma, were examined in three studies to assess neuropathological resistance in SCA ( Table 2 [rid=gnaf277-T2] and Table S6 [this file] ). 
Six histological studies examined whether SCA reflects resistance to AD-related neuropathology or distinct neurophysiological mechanisms ( Table 2 [rid=gnaf277-T2] and Table S7 [this file] ), and these biomarkers are derived from postmortem brain tissue analysis, revealing microscopic changes linked to cognitive aging. 
In addition to the findings for AD-related pathology, histological studies have identified several distinctive neurobiological features associated with SCA ( Table 2 [rid=gnaf277-T2] and Table S7 [this file] ). 
Fourteen PET studies examined various pathophysiological markers in SCA, including Aβ, tau, glucose metabolism, and -acetyl aspartate ( Table 2 [rid=gnaf277-T2] and Table S8 [this file] ). 
Structural MRI findings from 22 studies measured physical brain characteristics, including cerebral thickness (CT), GM volume, white matter hyperintensity (WMH), etc., and revealed consistent brain preservation patterns in SCA ( Table 2 [rid=gnaf277-T2] and Table S9 [this file] ). A representative result regarding GM substrates of SCA was defined by Sun et al. (2016) [rid=gnaf277-B77] as a “superaging signature.” Based on prior work, we summarize an updated GM preserved signature of SCA as shown in Figure 3A [rid=gnaf277-F3] and Table S10 [this file] . 
White matter investigations, though fewer in number, revealed important microstructural findings ( Table 2 [rid=gnaf277-T2] and Table S9 [this file] ). WM fibers that showed significantly greater integrity in SCA are summarized in Figure 3B [rid=gnaf277-F3] and Table S11 [this file] . 
Using functional MRI (fMRI) and related techniques, SCA individuals were found with unique advantages in dynamic brain functional activity that are strongly associated with their superior cognition ( Table 2 [rid=gnaf277-T2] and Table S12 [this file] ). Benchmarking the “superaging signature” proposed by brain structural studies, a “supernormal map” was defined as significantly differentiating SCA individuals and normal controls longitudinally ( Wang et al., 2019 [rid=gnaf277-B82] ), and regions in this map are similar to the structurally preserved regions summarized by this review ( Figure 3A [rid=gnaf277-F3] and Table S10 [this file] ). 
Among the 62 included studies, 19 (30.6%) studies employed multidomain approaches ( Table S13 [this file] ), yet only two ( Gardener et al., 2021 [rid=gnaf277-B28] ; Pudas et al., 2013 [rid=gnaf277-B68] ) of them explored cross-domain interactions.

To understand the microglia cell intrinsic contributions of a mutation in the gene that causes autosomal dominant FTLD-tau, we leveraged human iPSCs from mutation carriers . iPSCs from two independent donors who are heterozygous carriers of the IVS10+16 mutation ( IVS10+16/WT; FTD1 and FTD2) were compared with CRISPR-corrected isogenic controls in which the mutant allele was corrected to WT ( WT/WT; ; Supplemental Figure 1 [this file] ; Figure 1D [rid=F1] ). iPSCs were differentiated into iMGLs using a growth factor-based approach through hematopoietic progenitor cells (HPCs) as previously described ( Figure 1D [rid=F1] ; see Materials and Methods). 
To begin to understand the extent to which the IVS10+16 mutation impacts microglial transcriptional states, we analyzed mutant and isogenic control iMGLs by RNA sequencing ( Figure 1I [rid=F1] ; Supplemental Figure 1 [this file] ; ). Principal component analyses (PCA) revealed that the presence of the IVS10+16 mutation was sufficient to drive global transcriptional signatures ( Supplemental Figure 1E [this file] ). 
In WT iMGLs, -tubulin exhibits a radial array pattern originating from the microtubule organizing center (MTOC) ( Figure 2B [rid=F2] – C [rid=F2] ; Supplemental Figure 2 [this file] ). However, in the presence of the mutant allele, -tubulin distribution is shifted to the periphery ( Figure 2B [rid=F2] – C [rid=F2] ; Supplemental Figure 2 [this file] ). 
IVS10+16 iMGLs phagocytosed significantly less myelin than isogenic controls ( Figure 3C [rid=F3] – E [rid=F3] ); however, there was no difference in zymosan A uptake ( Supplemental Figure 3 [this file] ). 
In addition to altering genes in TREM2-related pathways that contribute to transcriptional regulation of proinflammatory cytokines, transcriptional regulation of DAM genes, actin cytoskeleton rearrangement, and phagocytosis ( Figure 4F [rid=F4] ), we also observed a significant reduction in and other endolysosomal genes ( Figure 4F [rid=F4] ; Supplemental Figure 4A [this file] ). Consistent with these findings, we identified a broad number of genes enriched in glycolysis that were altered in IVS10+16 iMGLs ( Supplemental Figure 4B [this file] – C [this file] ). IVS10+16 iMGLs exhibited a significant increase in genes involved in mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, the mechanism by which cells translate nutrients into energy ( Supplemental Figure 4B [this file] – C [this file] ). 
We identified genes and pathways associated with the adaptive immune response, the innate immune function, metabolism, and lysosomal functions that are dysregulated in mutant microglia ( Supplemental Figure 4D [this file] ).

The study sample included 1,072 individuals ( Supplementary Figure 2 [this file] ) at low risk to develop dementia late in life, where 64.3% ( 689) were women. They also displayed higher TIV ( 0.001) and global WMHV ( 0.001), which increased with higher Fazekas scores ( Supplementary Figure 3 [this file] ). Nonetheless, when comparing between individuals with different cardiovascular risk profiles, we observed that genetic predisposition to WMH was higher in obese, hypercholesterolemic and hypertensive individuals compared to the non-risk counterparts within each group ( Supplementary Figure 4 [this file] ). Global WMHV increased across all age ranges and was higher in hypertensive individuals and women when compared to their counterparts ( Supplementary Figure 5 [this file] ). Detailed results are provided in Supplementary Results [this file] . 
Results from the logistic regression model did not show a significant association between higher genetic predisposition to WMH and pathological WMH levels ( = 0.471; Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ). The odds of displaying pathological WMH levels were higher with age (OR = 2.028, 0.001) and positive history of hypertension (OR = 1.863, 0.02; Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ). 
Non-hypertensive individuals were mainly younger ( 1.26×10 ), with a higher proportion of non-obese ( 8.60×10 ) and non-hypercholesterolemic ( 1.69×10 ) participants and higher percentage of women ( 5.14×10 ) when compared to their counterparts ( Supplementary Figure 6 [this file] ). Non-obese individuals were physically more active ( 4.66×10 ) than their counterparts, characterized by a higher percentage of low educated ( 0.02) and non-hypertensive ( 8.60×10 ) individuals, when compared to obese group ( Supplementary Figure 7 [this file] ). Women were characterized by a higher percentage of low educated ( 3.74×10 ) and non-hypertensive ( 5.14×10 ) individuals than men ( Supplementary Figure 8 [this file] ). In the hypercholesterolemic group we observed a higher proportion of old ( 3.42×10 ) and hypertensive participants ( 1.69×10 ) when compared to their counterparts ( Supplementary Figure 9 [this file] ). In the group with lower educational attainment (5–10 years) we found a higher proportion of non-obese individuals ( 0.02), and women ( 3.74×10 ; Supplementary Figure 10 [this file] ). Moreover, older participants were characterized by a higher percentage of hypertensive ( 3.42×10 ) and hypercholesterolemic ( 1.26×10 ) individuals when compared to their counterparts ( Supplementary Figure 11 [this file] ). The inactive group was mainly characterized by a higher proportion of young ( 3.81×10 ), obese ( 4.66×10 ) and low-educated ( 0.05) individuals when compared to the active group ( Supplementary Figure 12 [this file] ). 
Among them, around 25% ( 6) had a regulatory role and were found to be associated with gene expression levels (i.e., eQTLS; Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ). These SNPs have been related to several GWAS-catalog specific traits, such as AD, C-reactive protein, HDL, parental longevity, serum alanine aminotransferase, WM microstructure, cerebral amyloid deposition, hypertension and amyloid- 42 levels ( Supplementary Results [this file] ). Enrichment analysis of the genes identified significantly enriched biological pathways ( < 0.05) mainly involved in neuronal structure and synaptic organization and vascular-related processes, mainly related to brain–blood barrier and transport ( Figure 3 [rid=fig3] ; Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ). From a general overview, the enrichment analysis results of the non-cohort specific SNPs related to WMHV, suggest an overall contribution of these genes into lipoprotein metabolic processes ( Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). 
At a regional level, SBP was significantly associated with WMHV in frontal and parietal areas (FDR < 0.05), as well as with periventricular WMH in basal ganglia ( = 0.092 [0.019, 0.164], FDR = 0.03; Figure 4B [rid=fig4] ; Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ). DBP positively correlated with juxtacortical and deep WMHV in frontal and parietal regions, as well as with periventricular WMH in the basal ganglia and frontal, occipital and temporal regions (FDR < 0.05; Figure 4B [rid=fig4] ; Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ). Non-significant correlations were found between regional WMHV and neither HR nor PP ( Figure 4B [rid=fig4] ; Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ). The PRS of WMH was uniquely significantly associated with higher RPP ( = 0.074 [0.004, 0.145], 0.038; Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ). Nonetheless, a positive trend was also observed for the association between the PRS and DBP ( = 0.070 [−0.001, 0.140], 0.051) and MAP ( = 0.067 [−0.002, 0.136], 0.058), although results did not reach statistical significance ( Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ). Further description of the results and the sample characteristics can be found in Supplementary Results [this file] . 
Same partially mediated paths were observed for the subset of non-hypertensive individuals ( Figure 5 [rid=fig5] ), regardless of the fact that they displayed lower median values for DBP and MAP when compared to hypertensive individuals ( Supplementary Results [this file] ). At a regional level, both DBP and MAP partially mediated the association between the PRS and periventricular frontal (DBP: Prop.mediated = 0.07, 0.04; MAP: Prop.mediated = 0.095, 0.001), periventricular occipital (DBP: Prop.mediated = 0.074, 0.04; MAP: Prop.mediated = 0.058, 0.001) and juxtacortical frontal (DBP: Prop.mediated = 0.010, 0.04; MAP: Prop.mediated = 0.105, 0.04) WMHV ( Figure 6 [rid=fig6] ; Supplementary Table 9 [this file] ). Additionally, RPP partially mediated the association between the PRS of WMH and deep parietal WMHV (Prop.mediated = 0.113, 0.001; Figure 6 [rid=fig6] ; Supplementary Table 9 [this file] ). In non-hypertensive individuals, the three metrics mediated the association between the PRS of WMH and deep parietal WMHV (DBP: Prop.mediated = 0.087, 0.04; MAP: Prop.mediated = 0.092, 0.001; RPP: Prop.mediated = 0.076, 0.001; Supplementary Figure 13 [this file] ; Supplementary Table 10 [this file] ). RPP partially mediated the association between the PRS of WMH and periventricular frontal WMHV (Prop.mediated = 0.082, 0.001; Supplementary Figure 13 [this file] ; Supplementary Table 10 [this file] ). Finally, DBP was additionally partially mediating the association between genetic risk of WMH and periventricular temporal WMHV (Prop.mediated = 0.061, 0.04) in non-hypertensive individuals ( Supplementary Figure 13 [this file] ; Supplementary Table 10 [this file] ).

The lead clone displayed a normal karyotype ( Figure S1A [this file] ), demonstrating that there were no major chromosomal abnormalities introduced during the gene editing or subsequent clonal expansion. A western blot against TDP-43 shows a shift of approximately 35 kDa in the two TDP-43 positive bands, corresponding to the molecular weight of Halo (33 kDa) ( Figure 1C [rid=F1] , S1B [this file] ). 
We sorted for cells highly expressing the GFP sgRNA marker and then sorted the cells containing the lowest 25% of Halo signal into one tube and the cells containing the highest 25% of Halo signal into another ( Figure 2A [rid=F2] ). sgRNAs targeting the TARDBP transcription start site decreased Halo-TDP-43 levels in both the iPSC and iNeuron screens ( Figure 2B [rid=F2] and S2A [this file] , Tables S2 [rid=SD2] and S4 [rid=SD4] ), indicating that our screen successfully identified genes that decrease TDP-43 levels. Non-targeting guides are clustered in the middle of the rank plot for each screen, showing that gene knockdown is needed to alter Halo-TDP-43 levels ( Figure 2B [rid=F2] and S2A [this file] ). Among genes whose knockdown decreases Halo-TDP-43 levels, we identified all eight components of the BORC complex, which regulates anterograde lysosome transport in axons as hits in the iNeuron, but not the iPSC screen ( Figure 2B [rid=F2] – C [rid=F2] and S2A [this file] , Tables S2 [rid=SD2] and S4 [rid=SD4] ). Knockdown of genes related to mitochondrial function also decrease Halo-TDP-43 levels ( Figure 2C [rid=F2] and S2B [this file] ). Further, we identified genes whose knockdown increases Halo-TDP-43 levels, including genes involved in RNA processing ( Figure 2D [rid=F2] and S2C [this file] , Tables S1 [rid=SD2] and S3 [rid=SD3] ). In comparing the top GO terms associated with genes that increase or decrease Halo-TDP-43 levels, we found only one hypergeometric test (HGT) term associated with both the neuron and iPSC screens, nonsense mediated decay (NMD) independent of the exon junction complex (EJC), although it is associated with increased Halo-TDP-43 levels in iNeurons and decreased Halo-TDP-43 levels in iPSCs ( Figure S2D [this file] – G [this file] ). 
We performed GO analysis on common hits from the meta-analysis across screens and found enrichment in many interesting categories, including ubiquitination, neddylation, autophagy, protein targeting, cell division/differentiation, and cytoskeletal related terms ( Figure S3A [this file] – F [this file] ). 
We used automated microscopy and analysis to visualize and quantify the Halo-TDP-43 signal in cells after each gene knockdown ( Figure 4A [rid=F4] ). 34 of 59 (58%) tested genes altered Halo-TDP-43 levels in the microscopy validation ( Figure 4B [rid=F4] – G [rid=F4] , S4A [this file] – D [this file] , Table S5 [rid=SD6] ). To determine if results from Halo-TDP-43 expression assays also applied to endogenous, untagged TDP-43 levels, we selected 22 genes from different groups in our list that passed Halo validation and performed immunofluorescence microscopy for endogenous (untagged) TDP-43 ( Figure 4D [rid=F4] – G [rid=F4] , 5A [rid=F5] – B [rid=F5] , S4E [this file] – F [this file] , Table S5 [rid=SD6] ). Of these, 18 (82%) gene knockdowns showed changes in endogenous TDP-43 levels ( Figure 4D [rid=F4] – G [rid=F4] , S4E [this file] – F [this file] , Table S5 [rid=SD6] ). 
Chloroquine (decreases lysosomal acidity), CTSBI (inhibits cathepsin B protease), ammonium chloride (NH Cl, inhibits lysosome-phagosome fusion), and GPN (ruptures lysosomal membranes) all consistently decreased Halo-TDP-43 levels, while Bafilomycin A1 (BafA1, prevents lysosomal acidification and fusion with autophagosomes), LLOME (causes lysosomal membrane rupture), and apilimod (PIKfyve inhibitor) did not cause changes in Halo-TDP-43 levels ( Figure 6A [rid=F6] – B [rid=F6] , S5A [this file] – C [this file] ). Further, two protein translation inhibitors, anisomycin and cycloheximide (CHX) also decreased Halo-TDP-43 levels ( Figure 6A [rid=F6] , S5B [this file] ). 
Intriguingly, upon restricting lysosomes to the soma by knocking down a BORC subunit, we find that the fraction of motile Halo-TDP-43 in the periphery is reduced ( Figure 6E [rid=F6] , S5D [this file] ). 
Using qPCR, we found TDP-43 mRNA levels were unchanged or slightly increased upon BORCS6 KD ( Figure 7A [rid=F7] , S6A [this file] ). As expected, we observed statistically significant reduction of TDP-43 mRNA upon TDP-43 KD via CRISPRi ( Figure 7A [rid=F7] , S6A [this file] ). 
We found that NT and BORCS6 KD samples were substantially separated on a PCA plot, with over 90% of the variability between the samples being explained by a single principal component ( Figure S6B [this file] ). We found many sites changed upon BORCS6 KD ( Figure S6C [this file] ), with these genes relating to GO Biological Process terms like splicing, catabolism, and transport/localization ( Figure S6D [this file] – E [this file] ). However, we did not observe any changes in TDP-43 polyA site usage upon BORCS6 KD ( Figure S6C [this file] ), so alternative polyA cannot explain the changes in TDP-43 protein levels. 
Surprisingly, we did not observe a change in TDP-43 translation ( Figure S7A [this file] ). Longer half-lives were also observed in d15 neurons although the changes in both abundance and half-life were reduced ( Figure S7B [this file] – E [this file] ), suggesting the neurons may be better able to compensate for the loss of BORC at later time points. In comparing the KEGG and REACTOME terms shown as enriched in our proteins with longer turnover times in BORCS6 KD neurons ( Figure 8F [rid=F8] , S7F [this file] ) to the mRNAs whose localization is altered in BORC KO neurons , we observe many of the same categories are enriched, including ribosome and biosynthetic pathways. We were able to detect 10 proteins with significantly changed phosphosites upon BORCS6 KD: KRI1 and RALY have phosphosites increased upon BORCS6 KD while OXSR1, ELAVL4, MAP4, ADD2, CSNK2B, FIP1L1, and RSF1 have phosphosites decreased upon BORCS6 KD at d7 ( Figure S7G [this file] ). At d15, only BASP1 showed a significantly decreased phosphosite ( Figure S7H [this file] ). interestingly, ADD2, CSNK2B, MAP4, OXSR1, and RALY are detected to have differential phosphorylation and increased half-life, suggesting these phosphosites may contribute to regulation of the turnover of these proteins. 
Treatments were as follows: 50 μM Chloroquine (Selleck Chemicals, S6999) for 24 hours; 50 μM CA-074me (Selleck Chemicals, S7420), a Cathepsin B Inhibitor (CTSBI), for 6 hours; 30 mM Ammonium Chloride (NH Cl) (Sigma-Aldrich, A9434) for 5 hours; 500 nM Bafilomycin A1 (BafA1) (LKT Labs, B0025) for 4 hours; 1x Lysosome Protease Inhibitor Cocktail (20 μM E64 (Selleck Chemicals, S7379), 10 μM pepstatin A (Selleck Chemicals, S7381) and 50 μM leupeptin (Sigma-Aldrich, L2884); referred to in Figure S5B [this file] – C [this file] as Protease Inhibitor) for 4 hours; 1 mM L-Leucyl-L-Leucine methyl ester (hydrochloride) (LLOME) (Cayman Chemical Company, 16008) for 4 hours; 400 μM Gly-Phe-β-naphthylamide (GPN) (Cayman Chemical Company, 14634) for 1 hour; 500 μM Sodium (meta) arsenite (NaAsO2) (Sigma-Aldrich, S7400), 1 hours; 40 μM Anisomycin (Sigma-Aldrich, A5862) for 1 hour; and 0.1 mg/mL Cycloheximide solution (CHX) (Sigma-Aldrich, C4859) for 45 minutes.

In the discovery cohort (stage 1), 4,464 proteins were significantly associated with age (false discovery rate (FDR)<0.05; Figure 2 [rid=F2] ), with 64% (2,842 proteins) increasing and 36.3% (1,622 proteins) decreasing with age ( Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). For sex, 1,347 proteins were significantly associated, with nearly equal proportions showing higher levels in males (49.5%, 667) and females (50.5%, 680) ( Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). Fewer number of proteins were affected by APOE4 status (344 proteins), with 53% (181) had higher levels in APOE4 carriers ( Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). With amyloid status, 3,212 proteins were significantly associated ( Supplementary Table 4 [this file] ): 1,133 proteins (35.3%) had higher levels in individuals with abnormal amyloid; 2,079 proteins (64.7%) had higher levels in individuals with normal amyloid. 
In the replication cohort (stage 2), the same 6,175 CSF proteins were tested ( Supplementary Tables 1 [this file] – 4 [this file] ). 
To examine proteomic changes using a different platform (stage 3 orthogonal validation), we analyzed CSF mass-spectrometry proteomic data from 101 individuals in Emory Diversity cohort ( Supplementary Tables 1 [this file] – 4 [this file] ). 
The analysis constructed 16 modules for 4,917 proteins ( Figure 3a [rid=F3] ; Extended Data Figure 5 [rid=F12] ; Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ). 
Thirteen modules were significantly associated with age (at FDR<0.05; Figure 3a [rid=F3] ; Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). 
For the 1,145 diseases that were examined with each of 16 modules, 106 diseases were significantly enriched with eight modules (M2, M3, M5, M6, M7, M9, M13, and M15) at FDR<0.05 ( Figure 4a [rid=F4] ; Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ). Subsequent gene ontology (GO) enrichment revealed that six modules (M2, M3, M5, M6, M7, and M13; out of eight) showed enrichments for GO biological processes (BP) at FDR < 0.05 ( Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ). To examine cellular context of these modules and individual proteins, we also performed enrichment analysis using human brain cell-type expression data ( Supplementary Table 9 [this file] ). In addition, to explore whether any of these proteins were related with AD outcome later in life, we performed survival analysis using the Cox proportional hazards model ( Supplementary Tables 10 [this file] – 11 [this file] ). 
The biological functions of the other four modules were shown in Supplementary Tables 7 [this file] – 8 [this file] . 
Many of these plasma proteins were significantly affected by four factors: 2,462 proteins associated with age, 3,247 with sex, 148 with APOE4 status, and 1,081 with amyloid status (FDR<0.05; Figure 6 [rid=F6] ; Supplementary Table 12 [this file] ). 
The male-specific CSF proteomic aging model based on 48 proteins provided a decent performance in testing data in terms of correlation between biological age and chronological age (training ρ=0.91; testing ρ=0.75; Figure 7 [rid=F7] ; Supplementary Table 13 [this file] ). 
To obtain cellular context of these modules and individual proteins, we also performed enrichment analysis using cell type expression data from human brain cells ( Supplementary Table 9 [this file] ). 
Detailed participant demographics and characteristics are provided in Supplementary Table 10 [this file] .

We analyzed CSF from 140 control and 160 AD participants by TMT-MS and SomaScan proteomic approaches ( Table S1 [this file] , S2 [this file] ). S2D [rid=SD5] , Table S3 [this file] ). Median correlation between measurements common to the two platforms was 0.59, with a broad distribution of correlation values ( Fig. 2B [rid=F2] , Table S4 [this file] , Data file S2 [rid=SD3] ). Differential abundance analysis on both proteomic datasets demonstrated a similar number of increased proteins in AD, with an overlap of approximately 21 percent between the platforms ( Fig. 2, F [rid=F2] and G [rid=F2] ; Tables S5 [this file] and 6 [this file] ) due to differences in coverage and statistical significance. 
We integrated the proteomic measurements from TMT-MS and SomaScan to construct a protein co-expression network of AD CSF from a total of 5,242 protein assays between the two platforms, which included proteins measured by either platform and proteins measured by multiple aptamers in SomaScan, with no missing values ( Fig. 3A [rid=F3] , Tables S7 [this file] and 8 [this file] , Data file S3 [rid=SD1] ). 
To do so, we used a serum network generated from greater than 4,100 proteins measured by SomaScan in over 5,400 Icelandic individuals ( 27 [rid=R27] ), and performed overrepresentation analysis across the networks ( Fig. 5 [rid=F5] , Table S9 [this file] ).

A redundant set of well-known cell-type markers was selected from the literature [ 31 [rid=CR31] , 55 [rid=CR55] , 56 [rid=CR56] ] (Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S3). Principal component analysis (PCA) was performed on the reference panel using R function (version 3.3.3) to verify that the expressions of these gene were clustering samples by their cell types (Additional file 1 [this file] : Figure S1b Additional file 1 [this file] : Figure S2a). 
Only samples predicted with a composition > 80% were kept for the reference panel (Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S2; Additional file 1 [this file] : Figure S2b). 
To emulate heterogeneous tissue with known and controlled cellular composition, we generated chimeric libraries pooling reads (to a total of 400,000) contributed from the human reference samples (see Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S2). The proportion of reads that the libraries of neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and microglia provided to the chimeric libraries varied in predefined ranges (Additional file 1 [this file] : Figure S3). Refer to Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S4 for detailed description of the 32 different distributions. 
In addition, we generated RNA-seq from parietal lobe for participants of the Knight-ADRC (84 late-onset cases, carriers of genetic risk factors and 16 controls; Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S1) and The Dominantly Inherited Alzheimer Network (DIAN; 19 carriers of mutations in , , ) (Table 1 [rid=Tab1] ; Fig. 1 [rid=Fig1] ) We employed the same pipeline to process all of the samples in order to avoid any bias. 
However, the species heterogeneity of the reference samples we compiled ruled out this attempt, as the PCA showed that differences between the human and mice donor samples dominated the transcriptome-wide profiles (Additional file 1 [this file] : Figure S1a). For this reason, we curated a list of marker genes that have been described to tag these distinct cell types [ 31 [rid=CR31] , 55 [rid=CR55] , 56 [rid=CR56] ] (Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S3). A visual inspection of the expression of these marker genes in the samples we compiled suggested a divergent transcriptomic profile among the cell types (Additional file 1 [this file] : Figure S2a). The PCA showed that their expression was sufficient to cluster samples of neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and microglia with their respective cell types, regardless of the species of the reference samples (Additional file 1 [this file] : Figure S1b; Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S2). However, we found that all of these outliers correspond to samples not correctly purified or that were sequenced in early stages of differentiation (Additional file 1 [this file] : Supplementary Results). Our final reference panel (Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S2; Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S3) had a very high confidence to predict cell types with a mean predicted accuracy = 95.2%, s.d. = 4.3 (Additional file 1 [this file] : Figure S2b), and a RMSE = 0.06 (Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S5). 
We observed an accurate prediction in these independent cell lines (mean neuronal proportion = 94.8%, s.d. = 1.1%; Additional file 1 [this file] : Figure S4a). We observed an average of neuronal proportion = 96.7% and s.d. = 1.2% (Additional file 1 [this file] : Figure S4b). Similarly, we assessed the RNA-seq data generated for iPSC-derived microglia (n = 10) deposited in the AMP-AD portal (synapse ID: syn7203233) and inferred their cellular population structure and observed a mean microglia proportion = 86.6% and s.d. = 7.1% (Additional file 1 [this file] : Figure S4c). 
We combined randomly sampled reads from neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and microglia to create chimeric libraries that mimic bulk RNA-seq from brain, but with a range of pre-defined cell-type distributions (Additional file 1 [this file] : Figure S3). This process was repeated 23,040 times, choosing distinct human samples to represent each cell type and varying the proportions in 32 alternative distributions (see “ Methods [rid=Sec2] ” and Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S4). 
In the TC, we observed a significant higher astrocyte relative proportion (β = 0.23; = 5.01 × 10 ; Table 2 [rid=Tab2] ; Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] ; Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S6) in AD brains compared to control brains. We also found a significant lower relative proportion of neurons (β = − 0.17; = 1.58 × 10 ; Table 2 [rid=Tab2] ; Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] ; Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S6) and oligodendrocytes (β = − 0.07; = 1.8 × 10 ; Table 2 [rid=Tab2] ; Additional file 1 [this file] : Figure S5; Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S6). 
The distribution of microglia was similar in the TC and CB from AD and control brains (Table 2 [rid=Tab2] ; Additional file 1 [this file] : Figure S5). We observed a significant lower relative proportion of microglia in PA brains compared to AD in both TC and CB (Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S7; Additional file 1 [this file] : Figure S6). 
Replicating our findings from the Mayo dataset, we observed a significant lower relative proportion in neurons and increase in astrocytes in all four areas (Table 2 [rid=Tab2] ; Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] ; and Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S6). The strongest effect size was detected in the PHG and STG ( < 3.49 × 10 ) (Table 2 [rid=Tab2] ; Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S8). We also observed a significant and strong correlation between neuronal and astrocyte relative proportions and the last ascertained clinical status (CDR), the number of amyloid plaques and Braak staging (Table 2 [rid=Tab2] ; Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] ; Additional file 1 [this file] : Figure S7). 
We generated RNA-seq data from the parietal lobe of participants enrolled in Knight-ADRC (84 LOAD, 3 ADAD, and 16 neuropath-free controls) and DIAN (19 ADAD) studies (Table 1 [rid=Tab1] ; Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S1). We selected the LOAD and ADAD participants to match for CDR at death, brain weight, and sex distributions (see Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S1). 
We observed a significant lower relative proportion of neurons (β = − 0.02, = 2.66 × 10 ) and significant higher relative proportion of astrocyte in AD (β = 0.03, = 5.48 × 10 ) for the combined LOAD and ADAD brains compared to controls (Table 3 [rid=Tab3] ; Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] ; Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S9), consistent with our findings in the Mayo and MSBB datasets. We did not observe a significant difference in the compositions of microglia or oligodendrocytes (Table 3 [rid=Tab3] ; Additional file 1 [this file] : Figure S8). 
We also observed significant lower relative neuronal proportion (β = − 0.09; = 4.71 × 10 ; Table 3 [rid=Tab3] ; Fig. 3a [rid=Fig3] ; Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S9) and increased relative astrocyte proportion (β = 0.11; = 5.24 × 10 ; Table 3 [rid=Tab3] ; Fig. 3a [rid=Fig3] ; Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S9) in ADAD brains compared to LOAD. 
We observed a significant lower relative proportion of neurons (β = − 0.06 for each of the ε4 alleles; = 9.91 × 10 ) and increase of relative proportion of astrocytes (β = 0.10; = 4.15 × 10 ) from the TC included in the Mayo Clinic dataset (Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S10; Fig. 4a [rid=Fig4] ; Additional file 1 [this file] : Figure S9a). This finding was replicated when we performed a multi-area analysis of the MSBB dataset (β = − 0.04; = 2.60 × 10 and β = 0.05; = 1.31 × 10 for neurons and astrocytes, respectively; Table 4 [rid=Tab4] ; Fig. 4a [rid=Fig4] ; Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S10; Additional file 1 [this file] : Figure S9a). We observed a significant association in the multi-area analysis of the MSBB dataset (β = − 0.03 = 4.01 × 10 ; Table 4 [rid=Tab4] ; Fig. 4b [rid=Fig4] ; Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S11; Additional file 1 [this file] : Figure S9b) and also a significant increase in relative proportion of astrocytes (β = 0.03; = 1.23 × 10 ; Table 4 [rid=Tab4] ; Fig. 4b [rid=Fig4] ; Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S11; Additional file 1 [this file] : Figure S9b). 
This platform produced reliable cell proportion estimates, as was shown by the evaluation of independent datasets of iPSC-derived neurons and microglia, mice cortical neurons (Additional file 1 [this file] : Figure S4), and simulated chimeric libraries. 
However, we found significantly decreased microglia in brains exhibiting PA (Additional file 1 [this file] : Table S7; Additional file 1 [this file] : Figure S6), proving that these studies are sufficiently powered to identify significant differences.

We obtained blood and tissues including lung, jejunum (intestines), and lymphoid organs (spleen, lung-associated lymph nodes (LLN), mesenteric lymph nodes (MLN)) from 138 human organ donors, aged 2 – 93 years old (with the majority (124/138) being adults (18 yrs or older)) ( Figures 1A [rid=F1] and S1A [this file] ; Table S1 [rid=SD2] ), through established research protocols with organ procurement organizations (see STAR methods [rid=S18] ). We analyzed these samples using histology, high-dimensional flow cytometry, retrospective radiocarbon ( C) birth dating, turnover, and whole genome bisulfite sequencing (WGBS) along with RNA-sequencing (RNAseq) to determine the role of tissue and subset on T cell maintenance with age ( Figure S1A [this file] ). 
In the spleen and MLN, there were also changes in tissue morphology and collagen content as an indicator of fibrosis (Sirius red staining), vasculature, and cellularity with age that were not observed in mucosal sites ( Figure 1E [rid=F1] and S1B [this file] ). Overall, there was increased fibrosis with age in the spleen but not in the other LN and mucosal sites ( Figure 1F [rid=F1] and S1C [this file] ). 
In the spleen, there was punctate distribution of CD3 T cells around vessels across all ages, while in LNs CD3 T cells were concentrated near follicles in younger donors and exhibited more diffuse distribution in older individuals ( Figure 1E [rid=F1] and S1B [this file] ). Macroscopic changes in LLN structure were mostly due to accumulation of particulates ( Figure S1B [this file] ) as previously reported . 
We assessed T cell proportions, lineages, subset composition, and functional attributes across a broad age range using high-dimensional flow cytometry across blood, spleen, lung, jejunum, LLN, and MLN from 91 human donors aged 11 – 93 years ( Figure 1A [rid=F1] ; Table S1 [rid=SD2] ; see Figure S2A [this file] for gating strategy). 
The large number of donors enabled a detailed assessment of age-associated changes for the major CD4 and CD8 T cell subsets delineating naïve, central memory (T ), effector memory (CD69 CD103 T ), tissue-resident memory (T ) cells comprising CD69 CD103 and CD69 CD103 subsets, and T cells ( Figure S2A [this file] ), controlling for co-variates. By contrast, CD4 T cell subsets exhibited fewer changes in composition over this age range; memory T cell subsets frequencies were stable with age in most sites except for increased frequency of T cells in the lungs and T cells in lymphoid organs ( Figure S3A [this file] ; see Table S3 [rid=SD4] and S4 [rid=SD5] ). 
Between sites, CD103 and CD101 was predominantly expressed by T cells in the lung and jejunum; CD49a was expressed by T cells in the lung and LLN, CXCR6 was most highly expressed by T cells in LN, and PD-1 was expressed by T cells in all sites except jejunum ( Figure 4A [rid=F4] , S4A [this file] , and S4B [this file] ). CD69 CD103 T cells had higher expression of CD49a, CD101, and CXCR6 and lower expression of PD-1 compared to CD69 CD103 T cells ( Figure S4D [this file] ). Expression of these core markers did not change with age in any site with the exception of decreased CD103 expression by T cells in the LN ( Figure 4B [rid=F4] and S4C [this file] ), which was independent of sex and CMV serostatus ( Table S2 [rid=SD3] ). CD69 CD103 T cells also exhibited minimal changes in expression of other core markers with age ( Figure 4C [rid=F4] and S4E [this file] ). 
CD8 T cells in the blood, spleen, and lungs (i.e., blood-rich tissues) had higher frequencies of CD57 and KLRG1 expression compared to jejunum and LNs ( Figure 5A [rid=F5] and S5A [this file] ). A majority of CD57 cells in the blood, spleen, and lung co-expressed KLRG1, while jejunum T cells did not express KLRG1 ( Figure 5B [rid=F5] and S5A [this file] ). CD57, KLRG1, and CD244 expression increased with age on CD8 T cells in blood and lymphoid tissues (spleen, LLN, and MLN) but not in mucosal sites (lung and jejunum) ( Figure 5C [rid=F5] and S5B [this file] ). 
Moreover, expression of CD57 and KLG1 was highest in circulating populations (T and T cells), lowest in CD69 CD103 T cells, and intermediate in CD69 CD103 T cells ( Figure 5D [rid=F5] ); this hierarchy was also observed by combinatorial analysis of all 3 markers ( Figure S5D [this file] ). Expression of individual markers did not vary with age, except for increased CD57 expression by T cells in the blood and MLN and CD69 T in the lung ( Figure 5E [rid=F5] ) and increased KLRG1 expression by T cells in the spleen ( Figure S5C [this file] ). 
To distinguish patterns between circulating and resident subsets that differ largely based on residence phenotypes, we performed WGBS of sorted CD8 CD69 CD103 T and CD69 CD103 T cells isolated from four tissues containing substantial numbers of these subsets (lung, spleen, MLN, and jejunum) of donors aged 7 – 92 years old (n = 10) (see Figure S2B [this file] for sorting gating strategy; see Table S1 [rid=SD2] and S6 [rid=SD7] for sample information).

By comparing the relationship between lysosomal damage and autophagy in BV2 cells, C8D1A cells, and HT22 cells, it was discovered that only in BV2 cells, lysosomal damage and deterioration of the lysosomal internal environment emerged, particularly characterized by decreased ATP levels and increased pH within the lysosomes and a decline in autophagy occurred in a time- and concentration-dependent manner following the phagocytosis of Aβ oligomers ( Fig. 4 [rid=F4-ad-16-6-3601] , 5 [rid=F5-ad-16-6-3601] , Supplemental Fig. 1 [this file] ).

The final round of clustering identified expected and novel subpopulations within each major class, with the optimal number of subclusters determined by two clustering robustness metrics ( Methods [rid=S12] , Fig. 1D [rid=F1] , S1 [this file] , S2 [this file] ). The final set of nuclei had a median of 2,156 genes and 5,149 unique molecular identifiers (transcripts) detected, with some variation across major cell classes ( Fig. S1 [this file] ). 
Overall, we identified 61 clusters across all major classes ( Fig. S2 [this file] ), not including non-microglial immune cells, whose numbers were too low for robust clustering and were thus subject to label transfer using the Azimuth reference resource[ 30 [rid=R30] ] ( Methods [rid=S12] ). 
To ensure robustness across all three population groups, we used a stratified approach whereby we assessed cluster proportion associations in each group and then performed a meta-analysis across the three groups, keeping only results that had an FDR-adjusted p-value <0.05, consistent sign of association in all three groups, and I < 50% ( Methods [rid=S12] , Supplemental Table 1 [this file] ). It is important to note that this stratified approach identifies conserved signatures associated with AD phenotypes despite our three population groups not being matched across demographic variables, most notably the age at death ( Fig. S1 [this file] ). 
Higher proportions of this microglial subgroup were also associated with higher PHFtau tangle density in both cortical regions, and with higher neuritic plaque counts in the DLPFC; this latter finding is consistent with prior single-nucleus studies on DLPFC[ 11 [rid=R11] ]. + microglia show high expression of genes associated with lipid processing, cell migration, and vascular reorganization ( Figure S3 [this file] ). In individuals with a clinical diagnosis of MCI, these include an over-representation of -high microglia (with enrichment of mitochondrial process-associated genes) in STG and an under-representation of + cytokine-expressing microglia in DLPFC ( Fig. 1F [rid=F1] , S3 [this file] ). 
After microglia, astrocyte clusters showed the largest number of conserved signatures associated with AD phenotypes, particularly in the caudate ( Fig 1F [rid=F1] ). + astrocyte proportions were higher in the AC in individuals with higher neuritic plaque counts; this cluster is enriched in genes associated with lipid processing ( Fig. S3 [this file] ). Additionally, + + astrocytes were less abundant in the AC in individuals with a clinical diagnosis of AD dementia; whereas cortical astrocytes expressing have been classified as fibrous (as opposed to protoplasmic)[ 31 [rid=R31] ], + astrocytes in the caudate are less well studied, and their gene expression profile shows enrichment for processes associated with immune response signaling ( Fig. S3 [this file] ). 
As an illustrative case, we identified 10 factors in astrocytes ( Fig. 2A [rid=F2] ); some of these factors recapitulate the separation of nuclei into discrete clusters (e.g. Factor 8 is restricted to the + cluster), while others capture coordinated gene expression spanning multiple clusters ( Fig. 2B [rid=F2] , C [rid=F2] , S4 [this file] ). This was particularly the case for oligodendrocytes: oligodendrocyte factor 4 (with high expression of and enriched in genes associated with immune signaling and lipid processing, Fig. S5 [this file] ) is more prevalent in individuals with higher neuritic plaque counts, higher PHFtau tangle density, and a clinical diagnosis of Alzheimer’s dementia, in both the STG and the AC. By contrast, oligodendrocyte factors 3 (high expression of and enriched for genes associated with synaptic vesicle recycling) and 5 (high expression of and enriched for cytoskeleton-associated genes) were lower in both cortical regions in individuals with a clinical diagnosis of Alzheimer’s dementia ( Fig. 2D [rid=F2] , E [rid=F2] , S5 [this file] ). 
By contrast, we did identify tens to hundreds of peaks that differed significantly across our transcriptomically-defined subclusters ( Fig. 3A [rid=F3] , B [rid=F3] , S6 [this file] ), consistent with previous studies[ 22 [rid=R22] ]. 
Thus, whereas this study is powered to ask about conserved signatures across all the population groups, it is less well-powered to ask about group-specific signatures, especially given confounders such as age of death ( Fig. S1 [this file] ). Thus, findings like putatively differential chromatin accessibility at the AD-associated locus containing ( Fig. 3c [rid=F3] ), or the lack of cross-population group reproducibility of vulnerable neuronal signatures identified from prior studies (e.g. + + GABAergic neurons, Fig. 4b [rid=F4] , Supplemental Table 1 [this file] ) does not necessarily indicate race- or ethnicity-specific differences, but could rather be due to lack of power in the overall study design. 
P-values and effect sizes plotted in Figures 1 [rid=F1] and 2 [rid=F2] are all from ANCOM-BC, with the corresponding values for the quasibinomial model reported in Supplemental Table 1 [this file] , For the quasibinomial model, we took advantage of the fact that relative cell type proportions are naturally distributed in the closed interval [0 - 1].
