To test generalisability of MIND genetic associations, we computed the genetic correlation using LD Score Regression (LDSC) between each edge in the discovery and validation cohorts (Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] ). 
MIND edge-associated genome loci exhibited both highly distributed effects on similarity across the network (e.g., shown in Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] B) and highly specific effects on edges connected to a single cortical area (e.g., , shown in Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] A). However, on average, genetic variants that were more significantly associated with MIND at any edge were also associated with a higher number of edges (Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] B), suggesting a general tendency for distributed rather than localised effects of genetic variation on MIND network phenotypes. 
Both MIND gradients were more heritable than MIND edges (on average): ; (Supplementary Figs. 3 [this file] C and 4 [this file] A). G1 was significantly associated with 31 loci at the genome-wide threshold of < 5 × 10 ; G2 was associated with a single locus at this threshold (see Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] A). This discrepancy between the number of associated loci for G1 and G2 was consistent with our finding that G1 was roughly ten times polygenic than G2 ( = 0.33%, = 3.7% using SBayesS; Supplementary Figs. 3 [this file] C) . In addition, we observed that G1 was under significantly stronger negative selection ( ) compared to G2 ( = − 0.58, = − 0.08 using SBayesS; Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] C). 
As shown in Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] B, genetic correlations between G1/G2 and whole-brain CT, MD, ICVF, MC, and surface area (SA) were generally weak-moderate (0.04 < ∣ ∣ < 0.36 for all comparisons), although four of these comparisons were statistically significant (G1-SA = − 0.12; ICVF-G1 = − 0.36; G2-SA = − 0.19; G2-MD = 0.19, all < 0.05). 
To test this, we calculated the phenotypic covariance matrix , representing the between-subject co-variation in MIND similarity for each possible pair of cortical areas, and found that this was strongly coupled with the genetic correlation matrix ( = 0.85), as predicted by Cheverud’s conjecture and previous work on structural MRI genetics (Supplementary Fig. 5 [this file] ). 
Neither gradient was colocated with cortical maps of evolutionary expansion or areal allometric scaling, suggesting that the observed dual origin trends did not simply reflect changes in cortical size across species or individuals (Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] D). 
Areal G1 and G2 scores showed varying degrees of spatial alignment with the genetic PCs of individual MRI features (0.06 < ∣ ∣ < 0.77; Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] C). Interestingly, strong spatial alignments (e.g., areal G1-CT PC1, ∣ ∣ = 0.77) did not reflect strong underlying genetic correlations (G1-global CT, = − 0.04; Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] B), suggesting that similar spatial patterning did not necessarily imply genetic concordance. Paleocortical distance was more strongly associated with areal G1 than with the first genetic principal component of any individual structural feature (Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] D). In addition, areal G2 showed stronger correlations with brain maps indexing laminar complexity of cortical myeloarchitecture (i.e., the first microstructural profile covariance gradient; ∣ ∣ = 0.89) and cytoarchitecture (i.e., externopyramidization; ∣ ∣ = 0.72) than did individual feature PCs (Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] D). 
In comparison to MIND, which showed substantial differences in both polygenicity ( ) and negative selection ( ) between G1 and G2, there were no significant differences between FC1 and FC2 on these parameters ( = 0.007 [0.004, 0.011], = 0.01 [0.005, 0.017]; = − 0.52 [−0.96,−0.8], = −1.09 [−1.30,−0.86]; Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] A). 
FC1 was not significantly genetically correlated with global measures of brain structure (CT, MC, ICVF, MD, or SA; Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] B), suggesting that the genetic overlap between MIND G1 and FC1 reflected a shared network organisation rather than associations with simpler univariate structural metrics. 
The causal relationship of MIND G1 on FC1 was significantly replicated when using MIND summary statistics from the (non-overlapping) replication cohort in a strict two-sample setting (IVW = 0.19, = 1.3 − 05; Weighted Median = 0.14, = 1.7 − 03; Supplementary Fig. 7 [this file] B), and was robust across a range of commonly-used two-sample MR methods and sensitivity analyses (Supplementary Figs. 6C–D [this file] , 7 [this file] ). 
Follow up analysis provided tentative evidence for a forward (but not reverse) causal effect of G1 on schizophrenia (G1 → SCZ, MR-APSS = 0.037, = 0.04 uncorrected; SCZ → G1, MR-APSS = − 0.004, = 0.90 uncorrected; Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ), consistent with the possibility that paleocortical architecture may contribute to schizophrenia risk. Subsequent MR analysis demonstrated no forward causal effect of G2 on any disorders or traits (Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). 
The bottom row reports the size of all comparison GWAS, with estimated effective sample size reported for case-control traits and total sample size for quantitative traits (see Supplementary Table 2 [this file] ). 
Colocalisation analysis between G1 and FC1 suggested a high probability (0.928) of a shared causal variant, with the 95% credible set containing multiple eQTLs of and such as , the SNP most strongly associated with G1, as highlighted in the gradient-level Manhattan plot in Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] A. 
The of the final four selected features are reported in Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] A. 
Nevertheless, we additionally performed several replication and sensitivity analyses of our main MIND-FC MR analysis including a) replicating the effect of G1 on FC1 using four standard two-sample MR methods (Inverse-Variance Weighted MR, Simple Median, Weighted Median, and MR-Egger) using MIND G1 (exposure) summary statistics derived from both the discovery and (fully non-overlapping) validation cohorts (Supplementary Fig. 7 [this file] ), b) testing robustness to MR-APSS model assumptions (Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] C) and c) replicating the original MR-APSS results using a threshold of < 5 − 05 (see Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] D). 
The same method of spatial association was used to compare regional G1 and G2 scores with the genetic principal components and other brain maps analysed in Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] .

We developed a framework that extends unsupervised deep representation modeling to WM tracts (UDR-WM, Fig. 1a [rid=Fig1] , Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] ). We found that these UDIP-FA dimensions were largely independent, with an average absolute pairwise Pearson correlation of 0.082 ± 0.065 (Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] ). 
We projected the 128-dimensional UDIP-FAs into a two-dimensional space using Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) for unsupervised dimensionality reduction (Fig. 2a [rid=Fig2] , Supplementary Fig. 3 [this file] ). Across all tracts, the UDIP-FAs significantly accounted for population-level variation (Bonferroni-corrected < 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁶, F-test), with coefficients of determination ( ) ranging from 0.298 to 0.768 and a mean of 0.470 (Supplementary Data 1 [this file] ). As expected, UDIP-FA explained the substantial variance in WM microstructural metrics (tract-averaged FA and RD), significantly outperforming its predictive power for cortical morphology (e.g., surface area, volume) and anthropometric traits (e.g., BMI) (Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] ). 
We found that UDIPs were significantly more enriched in WM compared to GM and CSF (Fig. 2b [rid=Fig2] , Supplementary Fig. 5 [this file] ), and exhibited distinct enrichment patterns across different WM tracts ( https://udip-fa.github.io/Dim_visualization/ (https://udip-fa.github.io/Dim_visualization/) ). For example, UDIP-FA dimension 1 was notably enriched in the right uncinate fasciculus (UNC-R, effect size statistic = 22.44, Bonferroni-corrected = 4.99 , permutation test, Methods, Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] ) and the genu of the corpus callosum (GCC, effect size statistic = 23.40, Bonferroni-corrected = 4.99 , Permutation test). Conversely, UDIP-FA dimension 2 showed significant enrichment in the right medial lemniscus (ML-R, effect size statistic = 28.34, Bonferroni-corrected = 4.99 , Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] ) and the middle cerebellar peduncle (MCP, effect size statistic = 27.22, Bonferroni-corrected = 4.99 ). 
UDIP-FA demonstrated strong sensitivity to age (mean absolute error (MAE) = 3.93 ± 0.04, Pearson’s = 0.77 ± 0.01; Fig. 2c [rid=Fig2] ), outperforming that used the traditional FA value from different WM regions (Supplementary Fig. 7 [this file] ) . 
To rigorously benchmark performance, we compared UDIP-FA against a baseline model derived from standard WM tract measures (Supplementary Fig. 8 [this file] ). Given the substantial differences in case numbers, primary tract-level interpretation in the main text focused on DEP, EPI, and MS, whereas results for AD, PD, and SCZ were treated as exploratory (Supplementary Fig. 9 [this file] ). 
A total of 115 UDIP-FAs (89.8%) were significantly heritable (FDR-corrected < 0.05), with heritability estimates ranging from 6.9% to 85.2% (mean = 52.0%; Fig. 3A [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Data 2 [this file] ). 39 (30.5%) UDIP-FAs showed high heritability ( ). The heritability of our UDIP-FAs was significantly higher than that of a previous study (mean = 34.9%, = 3.94 × 10⁻¹³, Mann–Whitney U test, Fig. 3b [rid=Fig3] ), and was higher than that of the top principal components (PCs) derived from WM tracts and voxel-wise FA maps (explaining >90% variance; Supplementary Fig. 10 [this file] ). 
Regional association plot at 7q31.31 showing overlap between the UDIP-FA index variant rs379381 and previously reported bone mineral density (BMD) association signals, including total body BMD (index variant rs380138; Supplementary Fig. 13 [this file] ). 
To leverage the full sample to accurately identify variants associated with WM tracts, we employed a multi-stage GWAS analysis to ensure robust, replicable results (Methods, Supplementary Fig. 11 [this file] ). First, for the single variants, we found 128 UDIP-FA measures that showed consistent GWAS results across discovery and replication cohorts, with a high paired genetic correlation (GC = 0.969 ± 0.152; Supplementary Data 3 [this file] ) that was evaluated by LD score regression (LDSC) . 
At a genome-wide significance threshold of = 5 × 10⁻⁸, we identified 420 lead SNPs (LD < 0.1) across 300 genomic loci in the discovery cohort (Supplementary Fig. 12a [this file] , Supplementary Data 4 [this file] ). Among these, 182 lead SNPs (43.13%) were successfully replicated in the replication cohort ( < 0.05/420, Supplementary Data 5 [this file] , Supplementary Fig. 12b [this file] ). In this way, at a genome-wide significance threshold of = 5 ×10⁻⁸, we identified 939 lead SNPs (LD < 0.1) in 586 genomic locus regions (Supplementary Fig. 12c [this file] , Supplementary Data 6 [this file] ). 
The results showed that 52.29% of lead SNPs associated with UDIP-FA did not have matching variant–trait records in our NHGRI-EBI GWAS Catalog lookup (Fig. 3c [rid=Fig3] , Supplementary Data 7 [this file] ). Interestingly, 42 of the identified lead SNPs were also associated with bone density traits (e.g., femoral neck and heel bone mineral density), particularly we observed shared colocalizations with femoral neck bone density and total body bone mineral density in the 7q31.31 region (Fig. 3e [rid=Fig3] , Supplementary Fig. 13 [this file] ).

More detailed information on the diagnostic criteria and medication status for healthy participants and patients can be found in Text A in S1 Appendix [this file] . Details on imaging parameters and preprocessing pipeline can be found in Text B in S1 Appendix [this file] and Table A in S2 Appendix [rid=pmed.1004860.s003] . In addition, details on the impact of 1.5T scanner acquisitions on predictive performance and PAD difference can be found in Text C in S1 Appendix [this file] and Tables B and C in S2 Appendix [rid=pmed.1004860.s003] . 
Specifically, we processed the regional microarray expression data from the Allen Human Brain Atlas (AHBA) [ 38 [rid=pmed.1004860.ref038] ] using the abagen toolbox ( https://github.com/netneurolab/abagen (https://github.com/netneurolab/abagen) ) to map the transcriptomic data onto 1,016 parcellated brain regions from the augmented Schaefer-1016 (details on transcription data processing can be found in Text D in S1 Appendix [this file] ) to generate regional gene expression matrix (1,016 ROIs × 15,632 genes) as the predictive variable. 
Results showed excellent predictive performance of the model (without age correction: = 0.68–0.88, mean absolute error-MAE = 1.65–4.97, coefficient of determination- = 0.45–0.76; after age correction: = 0.89–0.93, MAE = 1.15–3.75, = 0.76–0.84, Fig C in S3 Appendix [rid=pmed.1004860.s004] ), with consistently high performance and low coefficient of variation across folds (without age correction:0.9%–12.1%, after age correction:0.5%–10.5%, Tables E and F in S2 Appendix [rid=pmed.1004860.s003] , details can be found in Text E in S1 Appendix [this file] ), indicating the effectiveness of the brain age prediction model and highlighting the necessity of age-bias correction. 
In addition, fraction am litude of low-frequency fluctuation (fALFF) from functional MRI (fMRI) was also used to predict brain age under the same prediction framework (Details on fMRI preprocessing pipeline can be found in Text B in S1 Appendix [this file] ). 
We further examined age × group interaction effects on PAD (details can be found in Text F in S1 Appendix [this file] ) and identified significant interactions for AD and MCI (Table J in S2 Appendix [rid=pmed.1004860.s003] ), with estimated divergence ages of approximately 57 years for AD and 68 and 80 years for MCI (Fig G in S3 Appendix [rid=pmed.1004860.s004] ). 
Details on the implementation of all these datasets, atlases, and predictive models can be found in Text G in S1 Appendix [this file] . The Spearman rank correlation coefficient was used to evaluate the consistency of the PAD difference sequence pattern among diagnostic categories across datasets, brain atlas resolutions, and prediction models (details can be found in Text H in S1 Appendix [this file] ). 
Moreover, the bootstrapping analysis showed that the identified brain features consistently exhibited high selection frequency across 1,000 resampling conditions, indicating their robustness and stability (details on bootstrapping analysis can be found in Text I in S1 Appendix [this file] and Fig J in S3 Appendix [rid=pmed.1004860.s004] ). 
However, the deconfounding approach, leave-one-site-out (LOSO) validation and site difference analysis of PAD demonstrate that site is not a major confounding factor for brain age prediction in this study, and that the observed PAD differences are unlikely to be driven by site-related acquisition effects (details on deconfounding, LOSO validation, and site difference analysis can be found in Text J in S1 Appendix [this file] , Figs M–O in S3 Appendix [rid=pmed.1004860.s004] , and Tables Q–U in S2 Appendix [rid=pmed.1004860.s003] ).

Details on imaging parameters and preprocessing pipeline can be found in Text B in S1 Appendix [rid=pmed.1004860.s002] and Table A in S2 Appendix [this file] . In addition, details on the impact of 1.5T scanner acquisitions on predictive performance and PAD difference can be found in Text C in S1 Appendix [rid=pmed.1004860.s002] and Tables B and C in S2 Appendix [this file] . 
The sample overlap between the corresponding training sets of different diagnostic groups can be found in Table D in S2 Appendix [this file] . 
Results showed excellent predictive performance of the model (without age correction: = 0.68–0.88, mean absolute error-MAE = 1.65–4.97, coefficient of determination- = 0.45–0.76; after age correction: = 0.89–0.93, MAE = 1.15–3.75, = 0.76–0.84, Fig C in S3 Appendix [rid=pmed.1004860.s004] ), with consistently high performance and low coefficient of variation across folds (without age correction:0.9%–12.1%, after age correction:0.5%–10.5%, Tables E and F in S2 Appendix [this file] , details can be found in Text E in S1 Appendix [rid=pmed.1004860.s002] ), indicating the effectiveness of the brain age prediction model and highlighting the necessity of age-bias correction. 
The PAD difference between patient and HC in different age range was also investigated by dividing into “young,” “adult,” and “old” subgroups (Fig F in S3 Appendix [rid=pmed.1004860.s004] and Tables G–I in S2 Appendix [this file] ). We further examined age × group interaction effects on PAD (details can be found in Text F in S1 Appendix [rid=pmed.1004860.s002] ) and identified significant interactions for AD and MCI (Table J in S2 Appendix [this file] ), with estimated divergence ages of approximately 57 years for AD and 68 and 80 years for MCI (Fig G in S3 Appendix [rid=pmed.1004860.s004] ). 
Results showed that the identified PAD difference sequence pattern among diagnostic group were highly consistent across training sets ( = 0.90, = 8.80e − 04, Fig 4a [rid=pmed.1004860.g004] and Table K in S2 Appendix [this file] ), brain atlas resolutions ( = 1.00/0.98/0.99 and all < 1.00e − 16 for AS-216/516/816, Fig 4b [rid=pmed.1004860.g004] and Table K in S2 Appendix [this file] ) and prediction models ( = 0.83/0.91/0.88 and = 3.18e − 03/3.07e − 04/1.98e − 03 for SVR/BPNN/RF, Fig 4c [rid=pmed.1004860.g004] and Table K in S2 Appendix [this file] ). 
The identified brain regions are summarized in Tables L–N in S2 Appendix [this file] . 
The top 8 significant GO terms (Tables O and P in S2 Appendix [this file] ) were labeled for each diagnostic group (only 3 significant GO terms were identified in PLS − gene set for MCI). 
However, the deconfounding approach, leave-one-site-out (LOSO) validation and site difference analysis of PAD demonstrate that site is not a major confounding factor for brain age prediction in this study, and that the observed PAD differences are unlikely to be driven by site-related acquisition effects (details on deconfounding, LOSO validation, and site difference analysis can be found in Text J in S1 Appendix [rid=pmed.1004860.s002] , Figs M–O in S3 Appendix [rid=pmed.1004860.s004] , and Tables Q–U in S2 Appendix [this file] ). However, our site-wise performance analyses indicated excellent cross-site generalizability (Table S in S2 Appendix [this file] ), and diagnostic group differences were evaluated using standardized effect sizes (Cohen’s ) rather than direct comparisons of PAD values. 
The overlap rates between training sets for each pair of diagnostic groups are provided in Table D in S2 Appendix [this file] .

Details on samples construction for training and testing can be found in Fig B in S3 Appendix [this file] . 
Results showed excellent predictive performance of the model (without age correction: = 0.68–0.88, mean absolute error-MAE = 1.65–4.97, coefficient of determination- = 0.45–0.76; after age correction: = 0.89–0.93, MAE = 1.15–3.75, = 0.76–0.84, Fig C in S3 Appendix [this file] ), with consistently high performance and low coefficient of variation across folds (without age correction:0.9%–12.1%, after age correction:0.5%–10.5%, Tables E and F in S2 Appendix [rid=pmed.1004860.s003] , details can be found in Text E in S1 Appendix [rid=pmed.1004860.s002] ), indicating the effectiveness of the brain age prediction model and highlighting the necessity of age-bias correction. We also investigated the impact of sample size on the performance of brain age prediction and observed that the larger training sample size the better performance and the smaller variability (Fig D in S3 Appendix [this file] ). 
Results showed that no PAD difference was observed in almost all the diagnostic groups (Fig E in S3 Appendix [this file] ). 
The PAD difference between patient and HC in different age range was also investigated by dividing into “young,” “adult,” and “old” subgroups (Fig F in S3 Appendix [this file] and Tables G–I in S2 Appendix [rid=pmed.1004860.s003] ). We further examined age × group interaction effects on PAD (details can be found in Text F in S1 Appendix [rid=pmed.1004860.s002] ) and identified significant interactions for AD and MCI (Table J in S2 Appendix [rid=pmed.1004860.s003] ), with estimated divergence ages of approximately 57 years for AD and 68 and 80 years for MCI (Fig G in S3 Appendix [this file] ). 
Ten-fold cross-validation confirmed the predictive performance of all models (Fig H in S3 Appendix [this file] ), which were used to predict the brain age in the diagnostic groups, followed by calculating the PAD difference between patient and HC. 
PAD difference T-maps for each diagnostic group were displayed in Fig 5a [rid=pmed.1004860.g005] with false discovery rate (FDR) corrected in Fig 5b [rid=pmed.1004860.g005] , whose reproducibility across different scales of brain atlas was validated (Fig I in S3 Appendix [this file] ). Moreover, the bootstrapping analysis showed that the identified brain features consistently exhibited high selection frequency across 1,000 resampling conditions, indicating their robustness and stability (details on bootstrapping analysis can be found in Text I in S1 Appendix [rid=pmed.1004860.s002] and Fig J in S3 Appendix [this file] ). 
The first (the third for MDD) partial least squares (PLS) component explained 8.1%, 5.4%, 5.1%, 7.2%, 7.0%, 6.3%, and 5.3% variance in SZ, BP, MDD, AUD, TUD, AD, and MCI, which were not observed by chance (permutation test, = 0.006 for SZ, = 0.014 for BP, = 0.048 for MDD, = 0.019 for AUD, = 0.046 for TUD, = 0.047 for AD, and = 0.048 for MCI, Fig K in S3 Appendix [this file] ). PLS1 (PLS3 for MDD) scores were positively correlated with the PAD difference T-map in SZ (spatial permutation tests, = 0.24, = 0.002), BP ( = 0.21, < 0.001), MDD ( = 0.22, < 0.001), AUD ( = 0.21, = 0.002), TUD ( = 0.22, = 0.001), AD ( = 0.23, < 0.001), and MCI ( = 0.22, < 0.001), respectively (Fig L in S3 Appendix [this file] ). 
However, the deconfounding approach, leave-one-site-out (LOSO) validation and site difference analysis of PAD demonstrate that site is not a major confounding factor for brain age prediction in this study, and that the observed PAD differences are unlikely to be driven by site-related acquisition effects (details on deconfounding, LOSO validation, and site difference analysis can be found in Text J in S1 Appendix [rid=pmed.1004860.s002] , Figs M–O in S3 Appendix [this file] , and Tables Q–U in S2 Appendix [rid=pmed.1004860.s003] ).

This study included 50 DXA-derived bone structural measures and 488 MRI-derived brain structural measures to investigate bone-brain associations (Supplementary Data 1 [this file] ). 
In our discovery dataset, which included 35,089 white British individuals of European ancestry, we identified 8519 bone–brain associations (34.9% of examined pairs; Fig. 2A [rid=Fig2] , Supplementary Figs. 1 [this file] – 10 [this file] , and Supplementary Data 2 [this file] ) at the Bonferroni-corrected significance level ( < 2.05 × 10 , across 50 × 488 tests), suggesting widespread structural connections between bone and brain. A total of 5609 associations (Supplementary Data 2 [this file] ) were successfully replicated with nominal significance ( < 0.05) and concordant effect directions. 
Given the versatile role of the hypothalamus and its established association with bone homeostasis in animal studies , we additionally parcellated the hypothalamus into 10 subregions and found that the posterior hypothalamus exhibited the strongest associations with bone measures (Supplementary Fig. 11 [this file] , Supplementary Data 3 [this file] , and supplementary text). 
To explore potential sex differences in bone-brain associations, we conducted sex-specific analyses and identified 5647 significant bone-brain pairwise correlations ( < 2.05 × 10 ) in females ( = 18,193) and 3600 significant correlations in males ( = 16,896; Supplementary Figs. 12 [this file] – 33 [this file] and Supplementary Data 4 [this file] ). Overall, females exhibited stronger (two-sample -test < 0.001; Supplementary Fig. 34 [this file] ) and more widespread bone–brain correlations compared to males. No significant heterogeneity was observed among females and only one heterogeneous pair (FDR < 0.05) was detected among males (Supplementary Data 5 [this file] ), indicating that the observed sex differences in bone–brain associations are unlikely to be substantially confounded by age-related effects. 
The strength of bone-brain correlations varies substantially across cortical regions (Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] and Supplementary Data 2 [this file] ). 
To investigate the biological factors contributing to the variation in bone-brain correlation strength across cortical regions (Fig. 2B [rid=Fig2] ), we examined 30 spatial distribution maps (Supplementary Fig. 35 [this file] and Supplementary Data 6 [this file] ) that capture different aspects of cortical microarchitecture. After accounting for spatial autocorrelation using surrogate maps , we found significant correlations between the spatial distribution of GABA ( = 0.611, = 2 × 10 ) and 5HT-1b ( = 0.449, = 1.5 × 10 ) neurotransmitter receptors and the cross-regional variability in the strength of correlations between cortical surface area and bone measures, after applying a 5% false discovery rate (FDR) correction (Fig. 2E [rid=Fig2] and Supplementary Data 7 [this file] ). 
Considering the unique evolutionary specializations in humans and the rapid growth of both the brain and bone during development , we also explored how brain evolution and developmental expansion may shape the regional variability of bone-brain connection strength (Supplementary Fig. 35 [this file] and Supplementary Data 6 [this file] ). Our results (Fig. 2F [rid=Fig2] and Supplementary Data 7 [this file] ) demonstrated that the regional variability of cortical surface area and thickness was positively associated with their functional evolutionary hierarchy ( = 0.553, = 7 × 10 ) and developmental expansion ( = 0.498, = 1 × 10 ), suggesting that evolutionary and developmental processes may also influence regional differences in bone–brain communication. 
This analysis identified 1767 independent [linkage disequilibrium (LD) < 0.1] genome-wide significant bone-single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) associations (Supplementary Figs. 36 [this file] – 85 [this file] and Supplementary Data 8 [this file] ) across 393 unique genetic loci (Fig. 3A [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Data 9 [this file] ) at a Bonferroni-corrected threshold of < 1 × 10 (5 × 10 /50). These included 7 novel loci that did not overlap with previously reported suggestive associations ( < 5 × 10 ; 1 for BMD, 6 for BMC; Supplementary Data 10 [this file] ), as well as 18 loci that did not overlap with genome-wide significant signals ( < 5 × 10 ) reported in prior GWAS of bone mineral traits (10 for BMD and 11 for BMC, with 3 overlapping between BMD and BMC; Supplementary Data 11 [this file] ) . 
SNP-based heritability for 50 bone measures, grouped into anatomical categories and color-coded accordingly (see Supplementary Data 1 [this file] and the underlying GWAS summary statistics for details of the bone measures). 
The linkage disequilibrium score regression (LDSC) intercepts for all 50 bone measures were close to 1 (mean intercept = 1.021, range = 0.993–1.043; Supplementary Data 12 [this file] ), suggesting that genomic inflation can be largely attributed to polygenicity rather than confounding factors. Additionally, we conducted sex-specific GWAS for male and female participants (Supplementary Data 13 [this file] ), which revealed highly consistent genetic effects at genome-wide significant loci across sexes (Pearson’s = 0.965; Supplementary Fig. 86 [this file] ). 
Of the 1767 independent significant bone–SNP associations, 830 (46.97%, spanning 199 loci) reached nominal significance ( < 0.05) with consistent effect directions in the non-white British European cohort (Supplementary Data 14 [this file] ). 
At the Bonferroni-corrected significance level ( < 1 × 10 , across 50 tests), significant heritability was observed for all bone measures, with an average of 29.17% (range = 20.67–43.55%; Fig. 3B [rid=Fig3] and Supplementary Data 15 [this file] ). Notably, while there was a moderate correlation (Pearson’s =0.541, = 5.07 × 10 ), for bone measures was significantly higher in males compared to females (mean = 31.28% in males vs. 24.86% in females; = 2.25 × 10 , two-sample -test; Supplementary Figs. 87 [this file] – 89 [this file] and Supplementary Data 15 [this file] ). Heritability estimates obtained using GCTA-GREML were on average slightly higher but highly correlated with LDSC estimates (Pearson’s =0.894, < 0.001; Supplementary Data 15 [this file] and Supplementary text). Additionally, we calculated pairwise genetic correlations among 46 local bone measures (excluding the four whole-body measures) and found strong positive correlations across measures (mean = 0.733, range = 0.325–0.993; Supplementary Fig. 90 [this file] and Supplementary Data 16 [this file] ). 
Rather than using the five anatomical categories, the best-fitting model was a bifactor model with one general factor and five specific genomic factors (F1–F5) (Fig. 3C [rid=Fig3] , Supplementary Fig. 91 [this file] , and Supplementary Data 17 [this file] ), as evidenced by its excellent fit [ (df = 943) = 931,651, AIC = 931,927, CFI = 0.991, SRMR = 0.042]. 
GWAS on the six genomic factors identified 21 loci that were not detected among the 50 bone measures (Supplementary Fig. 92 [this file] and Supplementary Data 18 [this file] ), indicating that these latent factors capture shared genetic components across bone measures and substantially enhance discovery power. Gene-level association analysis using MAGMA revealed 230 unique genes ( < 5.23 × 10 , 50 × 19,110 tests; Supplementary Data 19 [this file] ) associated with bone measures, corresponding to 1726 significant bone–gene pairs. For the latent genomic factors, 112 unique genes ( < 4.41 × 10 , across 6 × 18,909 tests; Supplementary Data 20 [this file] ) were identified, corresponding to 123 significant factor-gene pairs. In parallel, using FUMA positional mapping, expression quantitative trait locus (eQTL) mapping, and chromatin interaction mapping, we identified 510 unique genes associated with bone measures (Supplementary Data 21 [this file] ), 324 of which were not captured by MAGMA, indicating additional regulatory mechanisms beyond proximity-based assignment. 
In the MAGMA gene-set enrichment analyses, 225 unique Gene Ontology (GO) gene sets exhibited significant enrichment for at least one bone measure at the 5% FDR level (Supplementary Data 22 [this file] ). Similar gene sets and enrichment patterns were observed when using a ±10 kb annotation window size (Supplementary Data 23 [this file] and S24 [this file] ). Partitioned LDSC analysis of tissue and cell types revealed significant enrichments for bone measures in active gene regulatory regions across multiple tissues, including bone, muscle, cardiovascular system, and nervous system at the 5% FDR level (Supplementary Data 25 [this file] ). Additional enrichment analysis of the latent genomic factors can be found in supplementary text (Supplementary Data 26 [this file] and S27 [this file] ). 
To investigate the genetic underpinnings of these associations, we used cross-trait LDSC to estimate genome-wide genetic correlations between 50 bone measures and 70 complex traits and disorders (Supplementary Data 28 [this file] ). After applying a 5% FDR correction, we identified significant genetic correlations spanning physiological conditions, personality traits, cognitive functions, food preferences, musculoskeletal disorders, neurodegenerative disorders, and psychiatric disorders (Fig. 4A [rid=Fig4] , Supplementary Fig. 93 [this file] , and Supplementary Data 29 [this file] ). 
As a sanity check, PRS derived from the discovery GWAS of the 50 bone measures significantly predicted their respective phenotypes in an independent cohort of non-white British Europeans, explaining a mean incremental phenotypic variance ( ) of 4.13% (range = 0.59–14.23%; Supplementary Fig. 94 [this file] and Supplementary Data 30 [this file] ), with 14 bone measures having an greater than 5%. We then evaluated the association between the 50 bone PRS and 204 complex traits across multiple categories (Supplementary Data 31 [this file] ). Full details, including the strength and direction of associations, are provided in Supplementary Fig. 95 [this file] , and Supplementary Data 32 [this file] . 
Several brain disorders with significant genome-wide genetic correlations with bone measures also exhibited significant local genetic associations at one or more genomic loci ( < 9.78 × 10 , see “Methods” section for details on multiple testing correction; Supplementary Figs. 96 [this file] – 101 [this file] and Supplementary Data 33 [this file] ). 
In addition, we uncovered significant local genetic correlations for bone–brain pairs that did not exhibit genome-wide genetic correlations (Supplementary Figs. 102 [this file] – 105 [this file] and Supplementary Data 33 [this file] ). 
While no significant genome-wide genetic correlations were identified, we uncovered 519 significant region-specific genetic correlations across multiple genomic loci ( < 1.17 × 10 , see “Methods” section for details on multiple testing correction; Fig. 5A [rid=Fig5] , Supplementary Fig. 106 [this file] – 115 [this file] , Supplementary Data 34 [this file] and 35 [this file] ), suggesting that shared genetic components are concentrated within specific genomic regions rather than broadly distributed across the genome. Moreover, the corticospinal tract showed the greatest number of significant associations with bone measures at both phenotypic (501 pairs, Supplementary Data 2 [this file] ) and genetic levels (170 pairs, Supplementary Data 34 [this file] ), suggesting that the observed phenotypic associations may, in part, reflect shared genetic influences. 
This analysis identified variants associated with both bone measures and a wide range of complex traits and disorders, including cognitive performance, education, brain structure and function, psychological traits, personality, smoking behavior, neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric disorders, sleep disorders, anthropometric traits, musculoskeletal disorders, and various conditions related to the immune, endocrine, and cardiovascular systems (Supplementary Data 36 [this file] ). 
We then performed enrichment analyses on the genes (Supplementary Data 37 [this file] ) harboring overlapping genetic signals between bone measures and brain-related traits or disorders to elucidate the biological mechanisms underlying bone-brain associations. At the 5% FDR level, our analysis revealed significant enrichments (Supplementary Fig. 116 [this file] and Supplementary Data 38 [this file] ) in several Gene Ontology (GO) terms related to the canonical Wnt signaling pathway, chondrocyte differentiation, and embryonic morphogenesis. Additionally, we identified several significant Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) terms, with the Wnt signaling pathway again emerging as the most prominent (Supplementary Data 38 [this file] ). 
The results were highly consistent with the primary analysis, and the canonical Wnt signaling pathway remained the most significantly enriched term (Supplementary Data 39 [this file] and S40 [this file] ). In total, we identified nine genes involved in the canonical Wnt signaling pathway ( , , , , , , , , ), along with eight additional genes ( , , , , , , , ) that either regulate signaling modules within this pathway or act as downstream effectors (Supplementary Fig. 117 [this file] and supplementary text). 
We further explored the translational potential of the 17 bone-brain overlapping genes involved in the canonical Wnt signaling pathway (Supplementary Fig. 117 [this file] ). Among these genes, 13 were classified as druggable (Supplementary Data 41 [this file] and 42 [this file] ) according to the Drug-Gene Interaction Database (DGIdb) and the Druggable Genome database , indicating known or predicted molecular features that are compatible with pharmacological targeting. This analysis prioritized 32 compounds spanning multiple drug classes at Bonferroni-corrected significance ( < 2.24 × 10 ), including antimalarials, antiarrhythmics, antihypertensive agents, antipsychotic agents, antidepressants, antiepileptics, and anti-Parkinson agents (Supplementary Data 43 [this file] ). 
Our analysis revealed multiple regions with high colocalization probabilities between bone and brain measures (Supplementary Data 44 [this file] ). For example, both global brain volume (PPH4 = 0.973; Fig. 5B [rid=Fig5] ) and total cortical surface area (PPH4 = 0.865; Supplementary Fig. 118 [this file] ) showed strong evidence of shared association signals with bone measures in the 11p14.1 region. Additional colocalized signals were observed in the 6q22.32 region for the middle frontal gyrus, lateral orbitofrontal cortex, and caudal anterior cingulate cortex (PPH4 > 0.977; Supplementary Figs. 119 [this file] – 121 [this file] ).

iPSCs from 14 AD and 8 healthy aged donors representing different APOE haplotypes (APOE23 n= 5, APOE33 n= 6, APOE34 n= 7, APOE44 n= 4; Table S1) were differentiated into iMG following established methods . iMG were validated by a 6-marker microglial panel and FACS sorted ( Figures 1A [rid=F1] , S1A [this file] ). This protocol includes first converting iPSCs into induced hematopoietic progenitor cells (iHPCs) and then into iMG ( Figure S1B [this file] ). We captured high-quality whole cell transcriptomes from 40,723 iMG, with comparable numbers of cells from each line (Table S1, Figure S1C [this file] ). Nearly all microglia express the microglial canonical markers AIF1, CST3, and CSF1R ( Figure S1D [this file] ). The resulting clusters were Activated Response (ARM), Ribosomal Response (RR), MHC Class II response (HLA(1) and HLA(2)), Homeostatic (HM), Female-enriched disease-associated microglia (FDAMic), G2 cell cycle, G1 cell cycle and Cytokine Response (CRM) ( Figure 1B [rid=F1] , Table S2). iMG derived from each iPSC line were well represented in each of the nine clusters ( Figure S1E [this file] ), and each cluster expressed canonical microglia markers ( Figure S1F [this file] ). This cluster expressed APOE, TREM2, FUCA1, C1QA, CD68 ( Figure 1D [rid=F1] , Table S2), lysosomal hydrolases ( Figure S1G [this file] ), and lysosomal V-ATPases ATP6V0C, ATP6V1F, ATP6V0E1 (Table S2), highlighting the cluster’s role in clearance . Notably, this cluster had low expression of proinflammatory cytokines (CCL4, IL1B) and high expression of the homeostatic microglia marker MERTK ( Figure S1H [this file] / I [this file] ). Importantly, the ARM population had reduced expression of BHLHE40/41, whose KO in previous studies identified these transcription factors’ role in shifting microglia into an ARM state ( Figure S1J [this file] ) . When analyzing each cluster by sex, one cluster was overrepresented by the female lines and overlapped with the signature of FDAMics (RPL13, RPLP1, SPP1, RPS19, ACTB, RASGEF1B, PSAP, CSF1R) ( Figure S1K [this file] / L [this file] ) . Comparison of female and male microglia revealed higher expression of TLR7 and TLR8 in females ( Figure S1M [this file] ). 
Interestingly, we saw a significant increase of APOE4 iMG represented in the FDAMic cluster, largely driven by the female APOE4 iMG ( Figures S2A [this file] – B [this file] ), and an increasing trend in the ribosomal response cluster and the G2 cell cycle cluster ( Figures 2B [rid=F2] – C [rid=F2] ). We saw a significant decrease in APOE4 iMG represented in the ARM cluster ( Figures 2B [rid=F2] – C [rid=F2] , S2A [this file] ). We compared APOE44 to APOE33 iMG and observed negative Cohen’s D for the majority of predicted reactions in APOE44 relative to APOE33, indicating systemic differences in metabolic utilization between the two, including FAO, cholesterol metabolism and citric acid cycle ( Figures 2E [rid=F2] , S2C [this file] ). 
Group 1 includes genes (N=186) that are highly expressed in APOE23 iMG and low in APOE44 iMG, creating a linear downward trend ( Figure S2D [this file] ). Pathway analysis revealed terms associated with reduced expression in endosomal and lysosomal activity (i.e., GM2A, SCARB2) ( Figures 2F [rid=F2] , S2E [this file] , Table S3). Group 4 is enriched for translation-related genes (N=80) that are upregulated in APOE44 ( Figures 2G [rid=F2] , S2D [this file] – E [this file] , Table S3). Females exhibited a substantially greater number of differentially expressed genes (n=1,513) compared to males (n=140), with only 44 genes overlapping between sexes ( Figure S2F [this file] ). Gene enrichment analysis further indicated that females drive the majority of pathway-level changes observed in the combined analysis ( Figures S2G [this file] – H [this file] ). 
Similar to our findings in the iMG model, the dysregulated genes in postmortem brain tissue of APOE44 samples revealed alterations in ribosomal, lysosomal and mitochondrial pathways in microglia ( Figures S2I [this file] – K [this file] , Table S4). We compared the directionality of genes identified in Groups 1 and 4 between our scRNA-seq dataset and ROSMAP microglia and observed a modest correlation (R = 0.144) ( Figures S2L [this file] – N [this file] ). 
To visualize neutral lipids, we used the BODIPY dye and found that APOE44 iMG have significantly more puncta per cell, indicative of increased neutral lipid accumulation ( Figure S3A [this file] – B [this file] ). 
These data were in agreement with our scRNAseq results, also indicating that lysosomal and endosomal pathways were being downregulated (i.e., LAMP1, LAMP2, HEXA, HEXB) ( Figures 3I [rid=F3] – K [rid=F3] , S3C [this file] , Table S6). Of the 84 identified lysosomal hydrolases and V-ATPases, 53 were significantly downregulated in APOE44 iMG, supporting lysosomal impairment ( Figure S3D [this file] ). Further, p62 (SQSTM1) and LC3B (MAP1LC3B2) were both upregulated, supporting a buildup of autophagosomes ( Figure S3E [this file] ). Proteins related to protein synthesis and trafficking were also dysregulated, suggesting ER stress (RPS24, RPS17, SEC24D) ( Figure S3F [this file] ) . We observed that proteins important in MAM function, such as VDAC2 and HSPA9 (GRP75) were downregulated in APOE44 iMG implying a dysregulation of exchange between the ER and the mitochondria ( Figure S3F [this file] ) . 
We did not observe differences in proton leak, spare capacity, or non-mitochondrial oxygen consumption, although there was a downward trend ( Figure S4A [this file] ). Because we also observed an increase in LDHA (lactate dehydrogenase) gene expression levels in APOE44 donor iMG ( Figure S4B [this file] ), we were interested in whether APOE44 microglia shifted their bioenergetics from OXPHOS to glycolysis. We quantified the relative abundance of lactate in iMG and found that APOE44 microglia had significantly larger intracellular pools ( Figures 4C [rid=F4] , Figure S4C [this file] ). We found that there was no difference in the incorporation of glucose into citrate and other TCA metabolites after 24 hrs ( Figure 4E [rid=F4] , S4D [this file] ). 
To further assess the health of the mitochondria, we measured mitochondria membrane potential (MMP) and observed a significant reduction in APOE44 iMG, typically a sign of dysfunctional mitochondria ( Figures 4G [rid=F4] , S4E [this file] ) . APOE44 iMG exhibited a decreased GSH/GSSG ratio, but no change in total glutathione, indicative of reduced ROS scavenging ( Figure 4I [rid=F4] , S4F [this file] ). This finding is supported by our proteomics data revealing a reduction of proteins important in detoxification like SOD2, NQO1 and SQOR ( Figure S4G [this file] ). 
Our scRNAseq showed that ALOX5AP (arachidonate 5-lipoxygenase activating protein), a microglia-specific dioxygenase that catalyzes the peroxidation of polyunsaturated fatty acids and promotes inflammation, was significantly upregulated in APOE44 donor iMG ( Figure S4H [this file] ) . These results agree with our RNAseq data and with the postmortem data (ROSMAP), where AD individuals had an increase in the percentage of microglia expressing ALOX5AP compared to control individuals ( Figure S4I [this file] ). 
This cluster expresses known senescent markers CDKN2A (p16) and CDKN1A (p21) ( Figure 5B [rid=F5] ), and G2 cell cycle markers like KI67, TOP2A, and CENPF, and DNA damage/replication genes like RRM1, BUB1B, and H2AFX ( Figure S5A [this file] , S5B [this file] , S5C [this file] ) . Using the Vybrant DyeCycle dye with verapamil to avoid dye efflux, we isolated cells with 4N DNA content from APOE44 microglia using FACS ( Figures 5F [rid=F5] , S5D [this file] ). To analyze these results based on cell cycle phase, we looked at p16+ microglia separated by predefined ROSMAP clusters and found that the MKI67+ cluster, or the G2 cluster, contained a larger percentage of the p16+ microglia compared to the other two clusters, supporting our finding that G2 senescent-like microglia can occur ( Figure S5E [this file] ). 
Interestingly, APOE44 iMG treated with GW3965 and APOE33 iMG moved closer together on the secondary axis of variation, defined by G1 phase genes and immune response genes ( Figure S6A [this file] , Table S7). Unbiased hierarchical clustering analysis demonstrated that APOE44 iMG treated with GW3965 were relatively equidistant from APOE33 iMG and APOE44 iMG treated with DMSO, supporting a shift of APOE44 back towards APOE33 ( Figure S6B [this file] ), although significant differences remain between the two, indicating that GW3965 partially rescues the transcriptomic phenotype ( Figure S6C [this file] – D [this file] ). We observed that NFKB1 and NFKB2, both elevated in APOE44 iMGs, are suppressed by GW3965 ( Figure S6E [this file] ). Module scores of differentially upregulated genes overlapped the most with the ARM cluster whereas downregulated genes overlapped the most with the CRM cluster ( Figure S6F [this file] ). However, this increase was accompanied by induction of lipogenic and lipid storage programs, including SREBF1 and PLIN2 ( Figure S6G [this file] ; Table S7). 
Strikingly, the opposite pattern was observed in APOE44 iMGs, where coculture resulted in a reduction of multiple lipid species, including a significant decrease in triglycerides ( Figures 7B [rid=F7] , S7A [this file] ). Abundance of ceramide C18:1/18:0 was increased in both the APOE33 and 44 iMG after coculturing with iNs, indicating this ceramide might be taken up by the iMG from the iNs ( Figures 7B [rid=F7] , S7A [this file] , Table S5). iNs cocultured with APOE33 iMG had a significant increase in numerous lipids, including sphingomyelins (SMs) and free cholesterol, when compared to iNs cultured with APOE44 iMG ( Figures 7D [rid=F7] , 7E [rid=F7] , Table S5). 
To evaluate the functional consequences of reduced lipid support, we co-cultured iNs with APOE33 or APOE44 iMG and stained for PSD95, Synapsin, and Tuj1 ( Figure S7B [this file] ). iNs co-cultured with APOE44 iMG displayed reduced Synapsin puncta density and decreased PSD95/Synapsin colocalization (normalized to Tuj1 area), indicating impaired synaptic formation ( Figure 7F [rid=F7] , 7G [rid=F7] ). We found that APOE44 iMG produced and secreted significantly less APOE in comparison to APOE33 iMG, which we were able to rescue with the LXR agonist GW3965; this rescue could be due to the increase in APOE mRNA with GW3965 ( Figures 7H [rid=F7] , S7C [this file] – D [this file] ). 
Interestingly, this line accumulated higher levels of intracellular APOE protein, consistent with impaired secretion rather than reduced synthesis ( Figure S7E [this file] ). 
Upregulated proteins were related to MHC Class II response and inflammation, whereas downregulated proteins were related to DNA replication ( Figure S7F [this file] – G [this file] ). Notably, we observed minimal concordance in the directionality of transcripts and proteins across the two pairs, as reflected by a low coefficient of determination ( Figure S7H [this file] – I [this file] ). Nevertheless, both lines at the proteomic level show an increase in MHC Class II response and inflammatory response and a decrease in lysosomal proteins ( Figure S7I [this file] ). Additionally, directionality of transcripts and proteins between APOE44 and APOE33 iMGs within each pair showed limited overlap ( Figures S7J [this file] – K [this file] ), highlighting the importance of functional assays to contextualize molecular changes.

In each of these analyses, we observed neuronal enrichment in NeuN+ samples, microglial enrichment in Pu.1+ samples, and oligodendrocyte enrichment in NeuN-/Pu.1- samples ( Figure 1C [rid=F1] and Supplementary Figure 9C [this file] ). Since enhancers are known to have long range effects and may not necessarily regulate their nearest genes, we also restricted the analysis to peaks proximal to gene transcription start sites (TSS) (<5 kilobases) and observed the same results ( Figure 1C [rid=F1] and Supplementary Figure 9A [this file] ).

Quantification of the lipidome data revealed that all individual lipid classes detected were within a normal physiological or pathological range to guarantee deep profiling (Fig. S1 [this file] B). 
The comparative analysis displayed the PE species of ⍺, β, γ, and δ (Fig. S2 [this file] A & S2 [this file] B), which were exclusively identified with significant changes in both SQA and VA groups (Fig. S2 [this file] C & S2 [this file] D) and were the same top four PE identified in Fig. 2 [rid=Fig2] A–B.

Organ-specific biodistribution confirmed these patterns (Fig. S3 [this file] B).

As expected, the performance of fSuSiE also tended to improve as the density of the molecular trait measurements increased (i.e., more CpGs), and as the SNPs produced larger changes in methylation ( Supplementary Figures 3 [this file] – 8 [this file] ). 
To confirm this striking result, we performed additional simulations to specifically confirm that, given sufficiently strong signals, fSuSiE can indeed accurately produce a single-variant CS even in the presence of very strong LD (see Online Methods [rid=S8] , “ Additional simulations to assess single-variant CSs [rid=S28] ” and Supplementary Fig. 15 [this file] ). 
The results ( Fig. 3C [rid=F3] , Supplementary Fig. 9 [this file] ) showed a consistent gain in power for fSuSiE, with the gains being greatest in the more challenging WGBS decay simulations. (We did not use the wavelet simulations here because in these simulations the causal SNPs produced changes, mostly small, to all CpGs.) This illustrates the ability of fSuSiE to combine borderline association signals across spatially-proximal affected CpGs to more accurately identify these signals. 
The tradeoff is that the SPS prior also increases running time ( Fig. 3D [rid=F3] , Supplementary Fig. 10 [this file] ). 
To illustrate the inferences produced by fSuSiE, Fig. 4 [rid=F4] presents a detailed example of H3K9ac fine-mapping in a 3.7-Mb TAD on chromosome 1. (See also Supplementary Fig. 11 [this file] for a detailed methylation example.) We used fSuSiE to analyze the genotypes at 16,642 SNPs and H3K9ac measurements at 269 peaks within this TAD, for individuals. fSuSiE produced 4 CSs ( Fig. 4A [rid=F4] ) corresponding to 4 independent signals of genetic effects on histone acetylation levels at one or more peaks ( Fig. 4B [rid=F4] ). 
Consistent with the increases in power shown in the simulations, fSuSiE identified many more putative causal SNPs than SuSiE-topPC, and at a much higher resolution; for example, fSuSiE identified 1,372 single-variant CSs for H3K9ac and 6,355 single-variant CSs for DNA methylation, compared to just 56 and 328, respectively, from SuSiE-topPC ( Fig. 5A [rid=F5] ; see also Supplementary Fig. 12A [this file] , B [this file] ). These observations suggest potential coordinated cis-regulatory effects ( Supplementary Fig. 13 [this file] ). fSuSiE also produced a much higher proportion of single-variant CSs compared to SuSiE fine-mapping analysis of RNA and protein expression ( Fig. 5A [rid=F5] ), again highlighting the benefits of joint analysis of multiple traits [ 59 [rid=R59] ]. (Although the increase in single-variant CSs outputted by fSuSiE in the real data is consistent with results in the simulations, and consistent with the expectation that joint analysis will improve fine-mapping resolution, it is also prudent to point out a limitation of fSuSiE: fSuSiE assumes that, once genetic effects are accounted for, the molecular trait data at different locations are independent. 
More generally, enrichments of haSNPs and mSNPs in predefined functional annotations [ 64 [rid=R64] , 65 [rid=R65] ] were largely consistent between fSuSiE and SuSiE-topPC, suggesting that the additional discoveries of fSuSiE maintain similar functional characteristics ( Supplementary Fig. 14 [this file] ). 
The fSuSiE methylation fine-mapping suggests another potential causal variant: rs1884913 (PIP > 0.99, MAF = 23.2%), an mSNP that lies within the CS for AD, and affects methylation levels at 6 CpGs near the TSS ( Fig. 6A [rid=F6] , Supplementary Fig. 11 [this file] ). 
Our SuSiE and fSuSiE analyses suggest that the top association for AD, rs679515 ( , MAF = 20.0%) is a solid candidate causal variant: first, rs679515 is the only SNP that overlaps CSs for both expression and expression; second, this SNP is one of the top SNPs in a CS for H3K9ac, with PIP = 0.14 ( Fig. 6B [rid=F6] , Supplementary Fig. 11 [this file] ).

However, total intracellular p-tau (Thr181) did not show significant differences between trisomic and disomic neurons (Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] ), which prompted us to focus on the aggregated fraction. Furthermore, the accumulation of p62-interacting p-tau (Thr181) was abnormally increased in trisomic neurons compared to isogenic control neurons (Fig. 2b [rid=Fig2] and Supplementary Fig. 5 [this file] ). Notably, 4-PBA, a chemical chaperone compound capable of inhibiting aneuploidy-associated stress , efficiently prevented protein aggregation in all trisomic neurons (Supplementary Fig. 6 [this file] ) and suppressed p-tau (Thr181) elevation in the medium (Fig. 2d [rid=Fig2] ). 
Furthermore, nearly all differentiated cells were positive for CD44 or vimentin, astrocyte-restricted precursor cell markers, but negative for SOX1, an early marker for neural stem cells, indicating that these differentiated cells have the properties of astrocyte precursor cells (Supplementary Fig. 7 [this file] ) . 
Quantification of protein aggregation and aCasp3 intensity revealed no significant increase in either measure compared with the respective corrected disomic controls, indicating that the additive effect is specific to Tri21 astrocytes (Supplementary Fig. 8 [this file] ). 
However, overexpression was not observed in any trisomic neurons, including Tri21 (Supplementary Fig. 9a [this file] ). 
Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) priming induced the production of the pro-inflammatory cytokine precursor pro-IL-1β (Supplementary Figs. 9b, c [this file] , and 10a–d [this file] ), and the subsequent activation by amyloid β (Aβ) treatment led to the synthesis of mature IL-1β in both cDi21 and Tri21 astrocytes (Fig. 5c, d [rid=Fig5] , Supplementary Figs. 9d, e [this file] , and 11a–d [this file] ). The production of pro-IL-1β was higher even in DMSO-treated Tri21 astrocytes than in DMSO-treated cDi21 astrocytes (Supplementary Fig. 9c [this file] ). Moreover, Aβ stimulus alone, in the absence of prior LPS priming, was sufficient to induce the interaction between NLRP3 and the apoptosis-associated speck-like protein containing a C-terminal caspase recruitment domain (ASC) (Supplementary Fig. 9f, g [this file] ), and the maturation of IL-1β (Fig. 5c, d [rid=Fig5] , and Supplementary Fig. 9d, e [this file] ), suggesting that the priming step is intrinsically activated in Tri21 astrocytes. However, caspase-1 activity was not significantly altered by combined LPS priming and Aβ stimulation in either Tri21 or cDi21 astrocytes (Supplementary Fig. 9h, i [this file] ). Of note, IL-1β overproduction in Tri21 astrocytes was suppressed by NLRP3 inhibitors (Supplementary Figs. 12a–c [this file] and 13a–c [this file] ). However, treatment with multiple TLR4 inhibitors, including TAK-242, IAXO-102, and TLR4-IN-C34, did not suppress IL-1β production or NLRP3 activation in Tri21 astrocytes (Supplementary Figs. 14 [this file] and 15 [this file] ). 
Abnormal accumulation of protein aggregates and apoptotic cell death in Tri21 neurons were abolished by co-culture with NLRP3 inhibitor-treated Tri21 astrocytes (Fig. 6a, b [rid=Fig6] ), but not by the direct administration of the NLRP3 inhibitors to the neurons (Supplementary Fig. 16a, b [this file] ).

To explore the underlying mechanism, we treated ABCA1-GFP overexpressing HeLa cells with recombinant ApoE3 (rE3) or ApoE4 (rE4). rE4 treatment resulted in lower total ABCA1 protein levels than rE3 treatment, indicating greater ABCA1 degradation (Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] A). ABCA1-binding complexes were enriched for proteomic analysis (Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] A and Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] B). Proteomic analysis revealed 768 shared proteins between rE3 and rE4 treatments, with 314 proteins unique to rE4 (Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] C). Nine of these proteins (Supplementary Table 4) showed higher expression in the rE4 treatment group than in the rE3 group (Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] D). Reducing caveolin-1, but not, AP2B1 expression by siRNA increased plasma membrane ABCA1 levels in mouse primary astrocytes (Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] F, Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] E), supporting that caveolae-mediated endocytosis regulated ABCA1 degradation. Surprisingly, reducing caveolin-1 expression significantly decreased ABCA1-mediated cholesterol efflux (Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] G) despite an increase in total ABCA1 protein levels (Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] F). Furthermore, overexpression of caveolin-1 in astrocytes enhanced cholesterol efflux (Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] G). 
Cholesterol loading, by adding LDL, led to increased caveolin-1 expression (Fig. 3 [rid=Fig3] H and I) and showed a dose-dependent increase in baby hamster kidney (BHK) cells (Supplementary Fig. 4 [this file] H).

We identified 12 heterozygous carriers of ABCA7 LoF variants, including splice region variants (c.4416+2T>G and c.5570+5G>C), frameshift variants (p.Leu1403fs and p.Glu709fs), and nonsense ‘stop gained’ variants (p.Trp1245* and p.Trp1085*) ( Figure 1A [rid=F1] - C [rid=F1] ; Data S1 [this file] ). These variants have previously been associated with increased AD risk in genetic association studies ( Table S1 [this file] ) [ 11 [rid=R11] , 14 [rid=R14] ] and are presumed to induce risk via ABCA7 haploinsufficiency [ 48 [rid=R48] ]. Analysis of published proteomic data for a subset of the 12 ABCA7 PTC-variant carriers and controls [ 49 [rid=R49] ] ( Table S6 [this file] ) confirmed that ABCA7 PTC-variant carriers indeed had lower ABCA7 protein levels in the human PFC compared to non-carriers (p=0.018; Figure 1D [rid=F1] ; Figure S1A [this file] ). 
We next selected 24 ABCA7 PTC non-carrier controls from the ROSMAP cohort that were matched to the ABCA7 LoF variant-carriers based on several potentially confounding variables, including Alzheimer’s disease (AD) pathology, age at death, intervals, sex, APOE genotype, and cognitive status ( Figure 1C [rid=F1] ; Figure S1B [this file] , C [this file] ; Data S2 [this file] ; Supplementary Text [this file] ). We confirmed that none of the 36 selected subjects carried damaging variants in other known AD risk genes ( , , , , and ) [ 14 [rid=R14] ] and verified genotypes in a subset of ABCA7 LoF carriers and matched controls using Sanger sequencing ( Figure S1D [this file] ). 
Accurate genotype assignments were confirmed by matching each single-cell library to its corresponding whole genome sequencing data ( Figure S1E [this file] ). Following extensive quality control measures—including detailed analysis and correction of batch effects ( Figure S2 [this file] ; Data S3 [this file] ; Methods [this file] )—our final dataset consisted of 102,710 high-quality cells ( Figure 1E [rid=F1] ), out of an initial total of 150,456 cells. This dataset encompassed diverse populations of inhibitory neurons (In, & +), excitatory neurons (Ex, & +), astrocytes (Ast, +), microglia (Mic, +), oligodendrocytes (Oli, & +), and oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs, +) ( Figure 1E [rid=F1] ; Figure S3A [this file] - E [this file] ). Post-quality control, cell types were robustly represented across subjects ( Figure S3F [this file] , G [this file] ), and gene expression profiles showed high consistency within cell types (mean correlation 0.95) ( Figure S3H [this file] , I [this file] ). 
We controlled for known and unknown covariates and considered only genes detected in >10% of cells within each specific cell type ( Methods [this file] ; Data S4 [this file] ). 
The two-dimensional visualization effectively captured the transcriptional landscape of ABCA7 LoF gene changes across all major cell types ( Figure 1F [rid=F1] ; Figure S4A [this file] ). To summarize this landscape in terms of biological pathways, we grouped genes into clusters based on their positions in the projection and analyzed each cluster for enrichment in biological pathways using the Gene Ontology Biological Process database ( Figure 1G [rid=F1] ; Methods [this file] ). This analysis identified several biological pathways correlated with ABCA7 LoF in the human PFC, including pathways related to cellular stress and apoptosis, synaptic function, DNA repair, and metabolism ( Figure 1G [rid=F1] ; Data S5 [this file] ). 
Overlapping differentially expressed genes across cell types are summarized in Figure S5A [this file] , B [this file] . 
Our snRNAseq data suggest that excitatory neurons expressed the highest levels of ABCA7, compared to other major cell types in the brain ( Figure S6A [this file] ). ABCA7 transcripts were detected (count>0) in 30% of excitatory neurons and 15% of inhibitory neurons, while the detection rate was considerably lower (<10%) for microglia and astrocytes and an order of magnitude lower (<3%) for oligodendrocytes and OPCs ( Figure S6A [this file] , B [this file] ). We validated this expression pattern in an independent published dataset [ 51 [rid=R51] ] ( Table S6 [this file] ), where bulk RNA sequencing of NeuN- (glial) and NeuN+ (neuronal) cell populations derived from six human temporal cortex samples showed significantly higher ABCA7 levels in the neuronal population versus the glial cell population (p=0.021; Figure S6C [this file] ). Several control genes, whose expression patterns in glial versus neuronal cells are well established ( , , and ), had expected expression patterns that matched those in the snRNAseq data ( Figure S6B [this file] , C [this file] ). 
To this end, we first estimated statistical overrepresentation of biological gene sets (WikiPathways, N pathways = 472) among up and down-regulated genes in ABCA7 LoF excitatory neurons vs controls (by GSEA; Methods [this file] ). We observed a total of 34 pathways with evidence for transcriptional perturbation at p<0.05 in excitatory neurons ( Data S6 [this file] ). Enrichments of these pathways were driven by 268 unique genes (“leading edge” genes [ 52 [rid=R52] ]; Data S6 [this file] ). 
To extract unique information from leading-edge genes and limit pathway redundancy, we next separated these genes and their associated pathway annotations into non-overlapping groups, formalized as a graph partitioning problem ( Figure 2A [rid=F2] ; Figure S7 [this file] ; Methods [this file] ; Supplementary Text [this file] ). Establishing gene-pathway groupings of approximately equal size revealed eight biologically interpretable “clusters” associated with ABCA7 LoF in excitatory neurons ( Figure 2A [rid=F2] , B [rid=F2] ; Data S7 [this file] ). Cortical layer-specific analysis indicated that these perturbation patterns remained largely consistent across cortical layers, from deeper to superficial regions ( Figure S8 [this file] ). 
Cluster PM.0, characterized by transcriptional regulators of lipid homeostasis ( , , ), exhibited evidence for down-regulation in ABCA7 LoF and featured pathways related to "SREBP Proteins" and "Adipogenesis" ( Figure 2B [rid=F2] ; Data S7 [this file] ). Cluster PM.1 comprised multiple mitochondrial complex genes ( , ) responsible for ATP generation from carbohydrate and lipid catabolism and showed up-regulation in ABCA7 LoF ( Figure 2B [rid=F2] ; Data S7 [this file] ). Clusters PM.2, PM.3, and PM.6 were up-regulated in ABCA7 LoF excitatory neurons and characterized by pathway terms such as "DNA Damage Response" (PM.2 & PM.3) and "DNA Replication" (PM.6) ( Figure 2B [rid=F2] ; Data S7 [this file] ). Genes in clusters PM.4, linked to “Proteasome Degradation” and "ciliogenesis"; PM.5, associated with “Apoptosis” and “TNFalpha Signaling Pathway”; and PM.7, linked to “GABA receptor Signaling,” “Gastric Cancer Network 1,” and “Prader-Willi and Angelman Syndrome”, included both up- and down-regulated genes ( Figure 2B [rid=F2] ; Data S7 [this file] ). 
Remarkably, all clusters displayed directional trends in p.Ala1527Gly neurons consistent with the directionality observed in ABCA7 LoF neurons ( Figure 2B [rid=F2] , E [rid=F2] , F [rid=F2] ), while controlling for pathology, age, sex, and other covariates ( Methods [this file] ). 
To directly investigate local structural consequences of the p.Ala1527Gly variant, we performed molecular dynamics simulations using newly available cryo-EM structures of ABCA7 in both the ATP-bound closed ( Figure 2G [rid=F2] , H [rid=F2] ) and ATP-unbound open ( Figure S9A [this file] , B [this file] ) conformations [ 54 [rid=R54] , 55 [rid=R55] ]. Specifically, simulations were conducted on a 239-residue region of ABCA7 embedded within a lipid bilayer, comparing the Ala1527 and Gly1527 variants over a 300-ns timescale ( Figure 2I [rid=F2] ; Figure S9C [this file] ; Figure S10 [this file] ; Methods [this file] ; Supplementary Text [this file] ). 
Both variants demonstrated stable conformational behavior in the ATP-unbound open state ( Figure S9C [this file] - E [this file] ). These results are further supported by analyses of / dihedral angle distributions and secondary structure persistence, as detailed in the Supplementary Text [this file] ( Figure S10 [this file] ). 
The first LoF variant, ABCA7 p.Glu50fs*3, was generated by a single base-pair insertion in ABCA7 exon 3, resulting in a PTC early in the ABCA7 gene ( Figure 3A [rid=F3] ; Figure S11A [this file] - C [this file] ). The second LoF variant, ABCA7 p.Tyr622*, was generated by a single base-pair mutation in ABCA7 exon 15 ( Figure 3A [rid=F3] ; Figure S11A [this file] - C [this file] ). 
We differentiated isogenic iPSCs into neurons (iNs) via lentiviral delivery of a doxycycline-inducible NGN2 expression cassette as previously described [ 57 [rid=R57] ] ( Figure S12A [this file] ). At 2 and 4 weeks post-NGN2 induction, cells expressed neuronal markers TUJ1 and MAP2 and exhibited robust neuronal processes as demonstrated by pan-axonal staining ( Figure S12B [this file] , C [this file] ). Both WT and ABCA7 LoF lines were capable of firing action potentials upon current injections ( Figure S13A [this file] , B [this file] ). Although the ABCA7 genotype did not alter resting membrane potential ( Figure S13E [this file] ), ABCA7 LoF iNs fired action potentials more readily and at lower current injection thresholds compared to WT iNs ( Figure S13F [this file] , G [this file] ), indicating a hyperexcitability phenotype. 
To investigate whether transcriptional changes associated with ABCA7 LoF observed in human neurons are recapitulated in iNs, we performed bulk mRNA sequencing on ABCA7 WT, p.Glu50fs*3, and p.Tyr622* iNs (N=2, N=5, and N=5, respectively) after four weeks in culture ( Data S8 [this file] ). 
K/L partitioning of these leading edge genes identified 9 clusters for p.Tyr622* ( Figure 3C [rid=F3] ) and 10 clusters for p.Glu50fs*3 ( Figure S14A [this file] ). Eight of nine p.Tyr622* T clusters and eight of ten p.Glu50fs*3 G clusters showed significant overlap (FDR-adjusted p < 0.05) ( Figure S14B [this file] ), indicating substantial concordance between the two ABCA7 variant lines. 
Specifically, we found significant overlap in 5 out of 9 p.Tyr622*-associated clusters ( Figure 3D [rid=F3] ) and in 7 out of 10 p.Glu50fs*3-associated clusters ( Figure S14C [this file] ) with the clusters identified in excitatory neurons, with the majority (4 out of 5 and 6 out of 7, respectively) showing concordant directional changes. 
Due to the transcriptional similarity between the two LoF lines, our primary analysis focuses on the patient variant p.Tyr622*, with results for the p.Glu50fs*3 variant provided in supplementary materials [this file] ( Figure S14 [this file] ). Notably, a mitochondrial cluster (T.10) demonstrated the most robust overlap with data (PM.1) and was consistently upregulated in both the p.Tyr622* and p.Glu50fs*3 lines, mirroring the findings in neurons ( Figure 3D [rid=F3] ; Figure S14C [this file] ). 
Among the most significantly upregulated genes in p.Tyr622* versus WT iNs were genes encoding components of mitochondrial apoptosis pathways (e.g., , ) and OXPHOS subunits (previously captured in clusters PM.1 and T.10) ( Figure 3F [rid=F3] ; Table S4 [this file] ). Conversely, downregulated genes were significantly enriched (padj < 0.05) for key metabolic processes, including -oxidation ( and genes), mitochondrial metabolite transport ( genes), and oxidative stress detoxification ( ) ( Figure 3F [rid=F3] ; Table S4 [this file] ). These MitoCarta mitochondrial gene expression profiles were highly correlated between p.Tyr622* and p.Glu50fs*3 relative to WT iNs ( Figure S14E [this file] ). 
To directly assess mitochondrial function in ABCA7 LoF neurons, we measured the oxygen consumption rate (OCR) of WT and ABCA7 LoF iNs over time using the Seahorse metabolic flux assay ( Figure S15A [this file] , B [this file] ). The OCR-driven movement of protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane during OXPHOS builds and maintains the mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm)( Figure S15C [this file] ), and measuring OCR in the presence of mitochondrial inhibitors provides several functional readouts. To assess the spare respiratory capacity, we normalized the OCR measured following pharmacological collapse of the proton gradient to the basal OCR, with higher values indicating more spare respiratory capacity [ 60 [rid=R60] ] ( Figure S15D [this file] ). We then quantified the proportion of basal oxygen consumption that can be attributed to rebuilding the membrane potential lost due to proton leakage through the membrane (i.e., uncoupled mitochondrial OCR) rather than due to ATP synthesis [ 60 [rid=R60] ] ( Figure S15E [this file] ). 
While spare respiratory capacity was comparable between WT and ABCA7 LoF iNs ( Figure S15F [this file] ), ABCA7 LoF iNs showed significantly reduced uncoupled mitochondrial respiration ( Figure 3G [rid=F3] ). Consistent with this observation, expression levels of UCP2 - a member of the mitochondrial uncoupling protein family expressed in the brain [ 64 [rid=R64] ] - were reduced in ABCA7 LoF iNs ( Figure S15G [this file] ). 
TMRM accumulation was higher in p.Tyr622* iNs relative to WT ( Figure 3I [rid=F3] ), and the specificity of this TMRM signal was validated by showing drastically reduced TMRM signal intensity after depolarization of the ΔΨm with the uncoupler FCCP ( Figure S15H [this file] ). 
Since ABCA7 functions as a lipid transporter, we examined the lipidome of WT and ABCA7 LoF iNs using LC-MS ( Data S9 [this file] ). Comparing lipidomic profiles between WT and p.Glu50fs*3 iNs revealed significant alterations across multiple lipid classes, including neutral lipids, phospholipids, sphingolipids, and steroids ( Figure S16A [this file] , B [this file] ). Among these, triglycerides (TGs)—particularly species enriched in long-chain, predominantly polyunsaturated fatty acids—were frequently altered, showing significant upregulation in p.Glu50fs*3 iNs ( Figure S16B [this file] , C [this file] ). 
In line with ABCA7’s established preference for phospholipids [ 26 [rid=R26] , 68 [rid=R68] , 69 [rid=R69] ], several phospholipid species also exhibited notable differences ( Figure S16B [this file] ). Phosphatidylcholines (PCs), which are essential structural components of biological membranes and potential ABCA7 substrates [ 26 [rid=R26] , 54 [rid=R54] ], were most prominently affected; the majority (≈64% of perturbed PC species) showed increased abundance in p.Glu50fs3 iNs ( Figure S16B [this file] ). Further analysis based on fatty acid saturation—an important factor influencing membrane fluidity—revealed significant enrichment of saturated PCs among the upregulated species (hypergeometric p=0.026) ( Figure S16D [this file] ). In contrast, polyunsaturated fatty acid-containing (PUFA) PCs showed mixed directionality, with several highly unsaturated species showing decreased abundance ( , PC(44:7) and PC(38:7)) ( Figure S16E [this file] , F [this file] ). 
Consistent with p.Glu50fs*3 iNs, upregulated lipids in p.Tyr622* iNs were significantly enriched for saturated PCs (hypergeometric p=0.044) ( Figure 3K [rid=F3] ; Figure S16G [this file] , H [this file] ). However, PUFA PCs and long-chain triglycerides were not reliably detected in this LC-MS run ( Figure S16I [this file] , J [this file] ), leaving it unclear whether p.Tyr622* iNs exhibit the same changes in PUFA PC or long-chain triglycerides as p.Glu50fs*3 iNs. 
LPCAT3 expression was reduced in p.Tyr622* and p.Glu50fs*3 iNs compared to WT ( Figure S16K [this file] , L [this file] ), aligning with increased levels of saturated PCs in these cells. 
Targeted LC-MS analysis confirmed that CDP-choline treatment increased its concentration in the media from undetectable to detectable levels ( Figure S17A [this file] ). Additionally, both CDP and choline specifically accumulated in media conditioned by p.Tyr622* cells after treatment ( Figure S17A [this file] ), indicating extracellular hydrolysis of CDP-choline. While intracellular CDP and CDP-choline could not reliably be detected in this experiment, intracellular choline levels significantly increased after treatment ( Figure S17B [this file] ) and expression levels of choline transporters were significantly upregulated ( Figure S17C [this file] ). 
Consistent with these changes, we observed increased expression of , the enzyme responsible for the rate-limiting step in PC synthesis through the Kennedy pathway ( Figure S17C [this file] ). Additionally, expression of several LPCAT genes, including LPCAT3, was elevated after treatment ( Figure S17D [this file] ), coinciding with observed increases in both saturated and unsaturated PC species ( Figure 4A [rid=F4] ; Figure S17E [this file] ). 
While most of the metabolites increasing or decreasing after treatment could not be annotated, a principal component analysis of the overall metabolite changes indicated that CDP-choline treatment reversed the separation of WT and pTyr622* iN along the axis of the first principal component (PC1; Figure S17F [this file] ). Transcriptionally, CDP-choline treatment also induced significant changes, clearly distinguishing treated from untreated samples ( Figure S17G [this file] ). 
Further analysis using the MitoCarta database confirmed a significant reversal in expression of genes encoding mitochondrial proteins, including reduced expression of apoptosis-related genes ( , ; Figure 4F [rid=F4] ), restoration (upregulation) of the mitochondrial metabolic signature ( Table S5 [this file] ), and increased expression of regulators of mitochondrial fusion ( , ), a process which enables high metabolic capacity, dissipation of mitochondrial membrane potential, and mitochondrial biogenesis [ 75 [rid=R75] ]. Overall, ABCA7 LoF-related changes to expression of MitoCarta genes were significantly reversed following CDP-choline treatment ( Figure S17H [this file] ). 
To determine whether CDP-choline treatment could restore mitochondrial uncoupling to WT levels, we repeated the Seahorse assay on p.Tyr622* iNs with and without CDP-choline treatment ( Figure S17I [this file] , J [this file] ). CDP-choline treatment significantly increased uncoupled respiration in p.Tyr622* iNs, restoring it to WT levels ( Figure 4G [rid=F4] ), with no significant change in spare respiratory capacity ( Figure S17K [this file] ). Consistent with this finding, both TMRM staining ( Figure 4H [rid=F4] ) and MitoHealth fluorescence per NeuN-positive surface ( Figure S17L [this file] ) confirmed a decrease in the mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) in treated cells. 
Indeed, p.Tyr622* iNs secreted significantly higher levels of A 40 and showed a trending increase in A 42 secretion into the media, as measured by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), although absolute levels remained relatively low ( Figure S18A [this file] ). To study CDP-choline’s effects in a model with stronger pathology, we differentiated p.Tyr622* and WT lines into cortical organoids matured for ≈ 6 months ( Figure S18B [this file] ), a stage at which we observed robust A secretion (approximately two- to four-fold higher levels of A 40 and A 42 compared to iNs)( Figure S18C [this file] ). This effect was not observed at lower concentrations or shorter treatment durations ( Figure S18C [this file] ). 
Additionally, relevant processed datasets are available in the supplementary files [this file] of this manuscript.
