During the training phase of MBA Net, 5353 T2-FLAIR images from healthy individuals were employed, sourced from two publicly accessible datasets and one community cohort: the Open Access Series of Imaging Studies (OASIS), the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), and the PolyvasculaR Evaluation of Cognitive Impairment and Stroke (PRECISE) (Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ) . Comparative evaluation against existing models showed the superior performance of MBA Net, as detailed in Supplementary Table 2 [this file] . In contrast, analysis of covariance adjusting for age and sex indicated significant differences in BAG values (F = 81.2, < 0.0001) and chronological age (F = 390.7, < 0.0001), but not in sex distribution (F = 3.4, = 0.07) (Supplementary Table 3 [this file] ). 
In the inference process, the model estimated the CBA of 10,890 patients with AICVD from the Third China National Stroke Registry (CNSR-III) study (Supplementary Fig. 1 [this file] , Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ) . Baseline characteristics of both included and excluded patients from the CNSR-III study are detailed in Supplementary Table 4 [this file] . The mean CBA was 62.4 ± 12.4 years, while the mean BAG was 0.2 ± 5.3 years (Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ). 
The analysis of BAG across various clinical phenotypes revealed significantly higher BAG levels in male patients, as well as in those with a history of ischemic stroke, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, hypercholesterolemia, smoking, or pre-stroke dependency (defined as a pre-stroke modified Rankin Scale [mRS] score of 2-5) (Supplementary Fig. 2 [this file] ). 
Of the 10,890 patients included, 52.0% (5658) had a positive BAG and 48.1% (5242) had a negative BAG (Supplementary Table 5 [this file] ). Similarly, positive BAG was independently associated with increased risk of composite vascular events (3 months: adjusted HR = 2.03, 95% CI = 1.73–2.38; 5 years: adjusted HR = 1.53, 95% CI = 1.39–1.68) and ischemic stroke (3 months: adjusted HR = 2.34, 95% CI = 1.96–2.79; 5 years: adjusted HR = 1.60, 95% CI = 1.44–1.78) (Supplementary Table 6 [this file] ). These findings were further supported by consistent trends observed in the cumulative incidence curves (Fig. 3a [rid=Fig3] , b [rid=Fig3] , Supplementary Figs. 3a [this file] , b [this file] and 4a [this file] , b [this file] ). 
Among 10,890 patients, 7142 (65.6%) were classified as normal aging, 1961 (18.0%) as accelerated aging, and 1787 (16.4%) as decelerated aging (Supplementary Table 7 [this file] ). In contrast, the decelerated aging group showed substantially reduced risks of stroke recurrence (3 months: adjusted HR = 0.41, 95% CI = 0.30–0.55; 5 years: adjusted HR = 0.54, 95% CI = 0.45–0.64), composite vascular events (3 months: adjusted HR = 0.51, 95% CI = 0.39–0.66; 5 years: adjusted HR = 0.64, 95% CI = 0.55–0.75), and ischemic stroke (3 months: adjusted HR = 0.42, 95% CI = 0.31–0.57; 5 years: adjusted HR = 0.54, 95% CI = 0.46–0.65) (Supplementary Table 8 [this file] ). Cumulative incidence curves were consistent with these associations (Fig. 3c [rid=Fig3] , d [rid=Fig3] , Supplementary Figs. 3c [this file] , d [this file] and 4c [this file] , d [this file] ). 
However, the negative BAG group had a significantly higher risk of hemorrhagic stroke compared to the positive BAG group at 5 years (2.1% vs. 1.0%, < 0.001) (Supplementary Table 9 [this file] ). When stratified by three-level BAG classification, the risk of hemorrhagic stroke at both 3 months and 5 years was highest in the accelerated aging group and lowest in the decelerated aging group, with the normal aging group serving as reference (3 months: 0.8% vs. 0.5% vs. 0.1%, = 0.01; 5 years: 2.5% vs. 1.5% vs. 0.7%, < 0.001) (Supplementary Table 10 [this file] ). 
A significant interaction between BAG and smoking status was observed for the 3-month recurrent stroke risk (Supplementary Table 11 [this file] ). Interactions were significant between BAG and chronological age, history of diabetes mellitus, and pre-stroke mRS score in relation to 5-year stroke recurrence risk (Supplementary Table 12 [this file] ). 
Furthermore, comparative analyses revealed that masked BAG outperformed unmasked BAG in predicting stroke recurrence, thereby underscoring the enhanced clinical utility of the masking strategy in improving model robustness and predictive accuracy (Supplementary Tables 13 [this file] , 14 [this file] and 15 [this file] ). 
This study employed two publicly accessible datasets, along with a community cohort, to develop the brain age prediction model: OASIS, ADNI, and PRECISE (Supplementary Table 1 [this file] ) . 
The detailed definitions of clinical outcomes are presented in Supplementary Table 16 [this file] . 
When BAG was analyzed as a categorical variable in relation to clinical outcomes, multivariable models were adjusted for baseline characteristics that significantly differed between groups (Supplementary Tables 5 [this file] and 7 [this file] ), as well as clinical features of the index event, including admission diagnosis, NIHSS score, TOAST classification.

Additionally, tau pathology (Braak stages) and neuritic plaque density (CERAD scores) were comparable across genotypes ( Figure S1B [this file] – C [this file] ), which minimizes potential confounding when investigating genotype effects. The tissue quality, assessed by RNA integrity number (RIN), was comparable between control and AD samples and across the three genotype groups ( Figure S1D [this file] ). 
Quality assessments showed that the number of unique RNA molecules (nCount RNA), or detected genes (nFeature RNA), and the percentages of mitochondrial (percent.mt) and ribosomal (percent.rb) genes were comparable to previous studies ( Figure S1E [this file] – J [this file] ). By contrast, percent.mt and total nuclei recovery were comparable across AD pathology status or genotype groups ( Figure S1K [this file] – N [this file] and Table S2 [rid=SD3] ). 
The cell annotations were further validated by top cluster-enriched genes ( Figure S2A [this file] and Table S3 [rid=SD4] ) and comparison with snRNA-seq data ( Figure S2B [this file] ). Despite variations, the seven major cell populations were consistently recovered in all samples ( Figure S2C [this file] ), and cell clustering patterns were similar across control/AD and groups ( Figure S2D [this file] and E [this file] ). When comparing cell compositions across groups, we observed a higher proportion of oligodendrocytes in AD compared to controls ( Figure S2F [this file] ). Additionally, carriers showed a higher percentage of microglia compared to individuals, regardless of AD pathology status ( Figure S2G [this file] ). Among carriers, AD brains had lower percentage of OPCs than controls ( Figure S2H [this file] ). 
We employed mixed-effects models incorporating covariates, including RIN and sequencing saturation, to control for potential confounding effects ( Figure S3A [this file] – U [this file] ). Sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of our DEG findings despite sample-quality variations ( Figure S4A [this file] – C [this file] ). 
We then examined their association with Braak stage and CERAD score ( Figure S5A [this file] ). Our analysis revealed that correlations between AD-associated transcriptomic signatures and pathological staging were genotype-dependent ( Figure S5B [this file] ). For instance, in excitatory neurons, the NADH dehydrogenase complex assembly pathway was negatively associated with Braak stage and CERAD score in carriers but showed no such association in or individuals ( Figure S5B [this file] ). In oligodendrocytes, axon ensheathment and myelination pathways correlated significantly with CERAD score but not with Braak stage in cases ( Figure S5B [this file] ). 
The anti-dMBP antibody showed filamentous immunoreactivity consistent with myelin-localized MBP ( Figure S6A [this file] ). It also recognizes mislocalized and aggregated MBP, which is considered degraded MBP ( Figure S6A [this file] ). In two testing cases, intracellular dMBP immunoreactivity was markedly higher in the older (71-year-old) AD brain than in the younger (23-year-old) control ( Figure S6A [this file] ). We confirmed that dMBP was mislocalized, appearing intracellularly and along vessel-like structures ( Figure S6B [this file] – F [this file] ). 
Given the similar transcriptomic profiles between excitatory and inhibitory neurons ( Figure S2B [this file] ), it is not surprising that transcriptomic changes in inhibitory neurons correlated closely with those in excitatory neurons across genotype groups when comparing AD and control ( Figure S7A [this file] – C [this file] ). Consistently, inhibitory and excitatory neurons shared many pathway changes ( Figure S7D [this file] – F [this file] ), including upregulation of Fc receptor signaling (GO:0038093) in carriers and upregulation of viral gene expression (GO:0019080) and protein targeting to ER (GO:0045047) in carriers. We also observed the highest number of DEGs in carriers, including 312 upregulated and 174 downregulated genes in inhibitory neurons ( Figure S7G [this file] ). Interestingly, both upregulated and downregulated DEGs were enriched in synaptic transmission pathways ( Figure S7H [this file] and I [this file] ). We also noticed substantial overlaps in DEGs between inhibitory and excitatory neurons, especially in carriers ( Figure S7J [this file] – L [this file] ). However, the overlap in synaptic function-related DEGs was primarily among upregulated genes in excitatory neurons ( Figure S7M [this file] ). 
Reclustering analysis identified 15 subpopulations with distinct marker gene expressions ( Figure S7N [this file] and O [this file] ). Among these, In4 PYR3 TSHZ2 and In5 LAMP5 NRG1 (Rosehip) exhibited the most prominent upregulation of synaptic transmission-related gene sets ( Figure S7P [this file] and Tables S8 [rid=SD9] – S9 [this file0] ). 
For instance, OPCs upregulated response to interferon-gamma (GO:0034341) in carriers and response to interleukin-1 (GO:0070555) in homozygotes ( Figure S8A [this file] and B [this file] ). Among OPC subclusters, OPC1 and OPC2 showed the most prominent upregulation of immune response pathways, including cellular response to cytokine stimulus (GO:0071345) ( Figure S8C [this file] – E [this file] and Tables S8 [rid=SD9] – S9 [this file0] ). 
In astrocytes, homozygotes showed significant upregulation of the cytokine production (GO:0001816) pathway, driven by genes including , , , and ( Figure S9A [this file] ). The upregulation was consistently observed in Ast1 and Ast2 subpopulations ( Figure S9B [this file] – D [this file] and Tables S8 [rid=SD9] – S9 [this file0] ). 
Vascular cells also showed altered immune responses in AD, notably in carriers ( Figure S10A [this file] ). These included response to cytokine (GO:0034097), driven by genes including , , , and ( Figure S10B [this file] ). 
We found that IL-6 levels were significantly elevated in AD brains compared to controls among homozygotes, with a trend toward upregulation in carriers with AD ( = 0.077) ( Figure S11A [this file] ). In contrast, IL-1β showed a trend of upregulation in carriers ( = 0.067) but downregulation in carriers ( = 0.072) ( Figure S11B [this file] ). No significant differences in IL-8 levels were observed in any genotype ( Figure S11C [this file] ). 
Next, we correlated cytokine levels with Braak stage and CERAD score and found that IL-6 correlated significantly with CERAD scores in carriers and homozygotes, but not in cases ( Figure S11D [this file] and E [this file] ). A similar correlation, though not statistically significant, was observed between IL-6 levels and Braak stage ( Figure S11D [this file] and E [this file] ). IL-1β levels correlated positively with both Braak stage and CERAD scores only in carriers ( Figure S11F [this file] and G [this file] ). Whereas IL-8 levels did not correlate with AD pathological markers in any genotype ( Figure S11H [this file] and I [this file] ). We observed that IL-6 and IL-8 positively correlated with cytokine production gene sets in astrocytes and microglia, while IL-1β correlated with interferon-gamma response gene sets in OPCs, in an genotype-dependent manner ( Figure S11J [this file] ). 
We found no significant differences in the proportions of cell types between sexes ( Figure S12A [this file] ). Further comparisons of AD-associated gene expression changes between sexes showed positive correlations between males and females in excitatory neurons, oligodendrocytes, and astrocytes ( Figure S12B [this file] and Table S10 [this file1] ). Notably, a weak negative correlation was observed in inhibitory neurons ( Figure S12B [this file] ). Pathway analyses revealed shared and sex-specific changes ( Table S11 [this file2] and Figure S12C [this file] – H [this file] ). In excitatory neurons, common changes included protein and RNA metabolism and neuroinflammation pathways ( Figure S12C [this file] ). For example, RNA processing pathways were altered in oligodendrocytes ( Figure S12E [this file] ), while immune response pathways were altered in OPCs, astrocytes, and microglia ( Figure S12F [this file] – H [this file] ).
